title: fix(lockfile): let a packslip signer replace leftover cosign or minisign provenance
body:
Fixes #15988.

A global \`mise.lock\` entry written by \`mise backends switch\` on 2026.11.0 or earlier can have \`backend = "packslip:…"\` together with the old backend's \`provenance = "cosign"\`. \`mise install\` then adds the Packslip \`signer\`, but every later \`mise upgrade\`, \`mise lock --bump\` and \`tool_update\` auto-update failed with:

\`\`\`
lockfile generation would downgrade recorded provenance; previous files were preserved: recorded cosign but the new entry has no provenance.
\`\`\`

The only fix was editing the lockfile by hand. A verified Packslip signer already replaced leftover GitHub-attestations provenance; it now also replaces leftover \`cosign\` and \`minisign\`, so these entries upgrade normally. SLSA stays ratcheted, as before. Without a signer the ordinary provenance check still applies.

Tested with a unit test (cosign/minisign replaced with a signer, refused without one) and a new e2e test, \`lockfile/test_lockfile_packslip_legacy_provenance\`, that re-locks an hk entry carrying \`provenance = "cosign"\`. I did not confirm the e2e test fails without the fix. The stale \`provenance\` line is not removed from an entry that is otherwise unchanged.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: unavailable.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes trust/downgrade rules in lockfile generation; wrong logic could weaken provenance ratcheting, though SLSA is explicitly excluded and behavior is test-backed.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Packslip lock bumping** no longer fails when an entry still has legacy `provenance = "cosign"` or `minisign` from an older `mise` backend switch but a verified Packslip `signer` is present.
> 
> `provenance_is_downgrade` now treats a Packslip signer as replacing **any non-SLSA** recorded provenance (not only GitHub attestations), so `mise lock --bump`, upgrades, and similar flows can clear stale cosign/minisign without a manual lockfile edit. **SLSA provenance remains ratcheted**; without a signer, the usual downgrade rules still apply.
> 
> Coverage adds unit cases for cosign/minisign with and without a signer, plus e2e `test_lockfile_packslip_legacy_provenance` simulating an edited lock entry and a successful `--bump`.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 5fde648d18c8121b04c827e0aefbcc62f166747e. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>

title: fix(upgrade): speed up the tracked config scan, summarize its warnings and expire unused configs
body:
`mise upgrade` (`mise up`) scans every config file mise has ever loaded so that it does not remove a version another project still uses. With many tracked configs that scan was slow, and every broken or offline project it touched printed its own warning, often several times:

```
mise WARN  error loading tracked config file ~/scratch/a/mise.toml: Invalid TOML …
mise WARN  error loading tracked config file ~/scratch/a/mise.toml: Invalid TOML …
mise WARN  error loading tracked config file ~/scratch/a/mise.toml: Invalid TOML …
mise WARN  Failed to resolve tool version list for dummy: …
mise WARN  Remote versions cannot be fetched for my-bare-tool …
```

Now `mise upgrade` and the deferred prune that runs after it print one line instead:

```
mise WARN  upgrade ignored 7 problem(s) with tracked configs; run `mise prune --dry-run` to see them
```

`mise prune` itself still reports each problem.

### Faster scan

On a machine with 1,422 tracked configs, `mise prune --dry-run --tools` (offline) dropped from about 15.7s to 6.1–6.4s. The scan compared every tracked config with every other one to find a project's parent configs, task includes and aliases. It now builds an index of tracked configs by directory once. It also reads each installed tool's catalog once instead of once per lockfile entry, and parses each tracked config only once per command.

`mise upgrade` now works out what other projects use offline, against installed versions only. That is also more accurate: a project with `node = "20"` keeps the 20.x it has installed, instead of mise resolving 20 to a newer remote release and leaving the installed one unprotected.

### Tracked configs expire

The tracked list only grew, so old scratch projects kept versions alive and slowed every scan. mise now records when each tracked config was last loaded (or tool stub last run). The new `prune.forget_unused_after` setting forgets configs unused for that long:

```toml
[settings]
prune.forget_unused_after = "90d" # default; "0s" keeps entries until the file is deleted
```

mise records a use to within a day, so a value under a day counts as a day. Running a tool stub counts as a use, including when mise runs its cached binary directly.

A tracked file that no longer exists stops protecting its versions straight away. Its entry is kept for a week in case the project comes back (an unmounted volume, a re-clone), then forgotten. `mise prune` still forgets missing files immediately. A forgotten project is tracked again the next time you run mise in it; `mise install` there reinstalls any of its tools that were pruned.

Entries written by earlier mise versions carry their creation time, not when they were last used, so their age counts from the first time this version reads the list.

### Validation

- New unit tests cover expiry, the week-long grace for missing files, migration of old entries, and the directory index.
- I ran the prune, upgrade and tracked-config e2e tests.
- I timed the scan against a copy

title: fix(packslip): stop zsh completion cleanup erroring in snapshot-restored shells
body:
## Problem

In a zsh shell restored from a snapshot (Claude Code does this), every `mise hook-env -s zsh` printed errors like:

```text
__mise_clear_completions:unfunction:11: no such hash table element: _git-wt
__mise_clear_completions:unfunction:24: no such hash table element: _wt
```

The snapshot brings back `__mise_clear_completions` and the `__mise_completion_*` variables, but not the `_<cmd>` completion functions it removes, and the cleanup called `unfunction` without checking.

## Fix

The generated cleanup now only runs `unfunction _<cmd>` when that function exists, and returns a clean status when it doesn't. A unit test covers the generated zsh cleanup.

Fixes #15989

---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Small change to generated zsh shell strings plus tests; no runtime Rust logic or security-sensitive paths.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes noisy errors when **zsh completion teardown** runs in shells restored from a snapshot (e.g. after `mise hook-env -s zsh`), where `__mise_clear_completions` and saved completion state may still exist but the per-command `_<cmd>` stubs do not.
> 
> The generated zsh cleanup no longer always calls `unfunction _<cmd>` when there is no saved prior function. It only removes the stub if `${+functions[_<cmd>]}` is set, matching the snapshot case without changing restore behavior when a saved function was captured.
> 
> Adds a unit assertion on the emitted cleanup script and an optional **integration test** that runs the generated script under real `zsh` and expects success with empty stderr.

title: registry: add reylo
body:
Adds a `reylo` shorthand so `mise use reylo` installs [Reylo](https://reylo.dev), a CLI that infers types for SQL queries from the database itself. Requested in discussion #15820.

```sh
mise use reylo
reylo --version   # reylo 0.8.1
```

The entry uses `aqua:reylosql/reylo` (recipe merged upstream in aquaproj/aqua-registry#64719 and already in the vendored registry) with `github:reylosql/reylo` as the fallback. Releases from v0.7.0 on attach per-platform tarballs for macOS, Linux (glibc and musl) and Windows.

## Popularity

- GitHub: 1,617 stars, MIT, not a fork; repo created 2026-10-21; latest release v0.8.1 (2026-11-21)
- npm: the `reylo` package has about 34k downloads a week (2026-11-14 to 2026-11-20)
- Note: this is below the usual bar of thousands of stars and the project is a month old; the discussion author maintains it.

## Validation

- `mise ls-remote aqua:reylosql/reylo` and `github:reylosql/reylo` both list versions (0.7.0 visible; 0.8.x hidden by `minimum_release_age`).
- Not run: `mise test-tool reylo`.

Co-authored-by: colinhacks <3084745+colinhacks@users.noreply.github.com>

> 
> The entry wires **aqua:reylosql/reylo** as the primary backend with **github:reylosql/reylo** as fallback, semver ordering, and a smoke test that checks `reylo --version` output.

title: fix(task): stop a backgrounded mise run from hanging on SIGINT
body:
A `mise run` started in the background by a script could hang forever when it was sent SIGINT. This fixes that, and gives every e2e test a time limit, because the hang held a CI job for 60 minutes with no output.

## The hang

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
mise run server &
mise_pid=$!
# ...
kill -INT "$mise_pid"
wait "$mise_pid" # sometimes never returned
```

A shell without job control leaves SIGINT ignored for a command it starts with `&`. The SIGINT handler in mise is installed the first time its exit signal is polled, and the command and the exit signal were polled in random order. When the command went first, it could start the task while SIGINT was still ignored. The task inherited that, and a shell cannot trap a signal that was ignored when it started. So when mise later passed the SIGINT on, the task never saw it, and mise waited for a task that had no reason to end.

The exit signal is now polled first, so the handler is in place before any task starts.

Measured with 3000 `mise run quick &` from a non-interactive bash, 48 at a time, on a 32-CPU machine kept busy by 96 spinning processes, where the task records whether it started with SIGINT ignored:

| | tasks started with SIGINT ignored |
| --- | --- |
| before | 13 of 3000 |
| after | 0 of 3000 |

Without the extra load it was 0 of 200 before the fix, which is why this shows up on a loaded CI runner and not on a desk.

This is the step `e2e/tasks/test_task_history` hung on in [this run](https://github.com/jdx/mise/actions/runs/44948173542/job/136980629965): it backgrounds `mise run trapped`, whose task loops until it gets SIGINT, sends mise a SIGINT and waits. The test itself did not hang in my local runs; the race above is what I could measure. A new unit test fails without the fix.

## A time limit for e2e tests

A test that has not finished after 300 seconds (900 for a `*_slow` test) is now killed and fails with what it had printed and a list of its processes, instead of holding the step until GitHub's limit:

```
>>> E2E tasks/test_scratch_hang
SUCCESS: [mise --version | grep -c .] output is equal to '1'
starting a background task and a background child
now waiting forever
tasks/test_scratch_hang is still running after 10s; its processes:
    PID    PPID    PGID STAT     ELAPSED COMMAND
4166442 4166412 4166442 S          00:10 bash …/e2e/run_test tasks/test_scratch_hang
4166445 4166442 4166442 S          00:10 bash --noprofile --norc -euo pipefail -c source …
4166540 4166445 4166442 Sl         00:09 mise run sleeper
4166541 4166445 4166442 S          00:09 sleep 601
4166610 4166540 4166610 S          00:09 sleep 600
ERROR: E2E test tasks/test_scratch_hang timed out: killed after exceeding its 10s time limit (E2E_TEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS)

E2E: ran 1 tests (0 passed, 1 failed), skipped 0 tests

Failed e2e tests (1):
  - tasks/test_scratch_hang (timed out)
```

That is a scratch test (not committed) run with `E2E_TEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=10 E2E_MAX_ATTEMPTS=2 mise run test:e2e test_scratch_

title: fix(set): edit configs that use [[env]] instead of panicking
body:
`mise set KEY=value` and `mise unset KEY` crashed when the target `mise.toml` writes its environment as `[[env]]` groups instead of one `[env]` table:

```toml
[[env]]
STAGE = "one"

[[env]]
STAGE = "two"
```

```console
$ mise set NEW=1
The application panicked (crashed).
Message:  called `Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value
```

`mise unset STAGE` panicked the same way, and so did both commands on an inline `env = { STAGE = "one" }`. 2026.11.6 is affected. Both commands now edit these files.

## What the commands do with `[[env]]`

mise reads `[[env]]` groups in file order, and a later group overrides an earlier one (`mise env` exports `STAGE=two` above). The edits follow that order, so the result is what it would be with a single `[env]`:

- **`mise set KEY=value`** rewrites the last group that sets `KEY`. When no group sets it, `KEY` is added to the last group. Either way the new value is the one that reading the groups in order ends with.
- **`mise unset KEY`** (and `mise set --rm KEY`) removes `KEY` from every group. Removing it from the last group only would bring an earlier group's value back.
- **`mise set KEY`** prints the value from the last group that sets `KEY`. It printed the first group's value (`one` above), which is not what mise exports.

With the file above:

```console
$ mise set NEW=1 STAGE=three
$ cat mise.toml
[[env]]
STAGE = "one"

[[env]]
STAGE = "three"
NEW = "1"
$ mise unset STAGE
$ cat mise.toml
[[env]]

[[env]]
NEW = "1"
```

This is my reading of what the commands should do; the alternatives I considered were always appending to the last group (leaves a stale duplicate behind) and removing from the last group only (the key would still be set). Say so if you want different rules.

Other details:

- Comments and formatting are kept, including a comment after a value that gets replaced.
- A group left empty by `mise unset` stays in the file as an empty `[[env]]`, the same way an emptied `[env]` does.
- The inline spellings, `env = { .. }` and `env = [{ .. }, { .. }]`, are edited in place by the same rules.
- `mise set` on `env = []` fails with an error that names the file, since there is no table to add the key to. `mise unset` leaves that file as it is.
- `mise set --age-encrypt` goes through the same code and follows the same rules.

## Keys with a dot

`mise set _.path=./bin` has always written `path` into a nested `env._` table. The rules for a `KEY` that contains a dot are now the same for both commands:

1. **An entry named exactly `KEY` is that variable.** With `"my.var" = "x"` in the file, `mise set my.var=y` updates it and `mise unset my.var` removes it, and nothing else is touched. `mise set my.var=y` used to leave `"my.var"` alone and add an `[env.my]` table.
2. **Otherwise the dots descend into nested tables.** `mise unset _.path` now removes what `mise set _.path=./bin` wrote, from every group, and drops a nested table it empties. It used to look only for an entry named `_.path` and leave the nested one in

--- e2e/cli/test_set_env_groups (+123/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,123 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+# `mise set` and `mise unset` edit a config that writes its environment as
+# [[env]] groups. mise reads the groups in file order, so a later group
+# overrides an earlier one.
+cat <<EOF >mise.toml
+# base values
+[[env]]
+STAGE = "one"
+ONLY_FIRST = "a"
+
+# overrides
+[[env]]
+STAGE = "two" # the value mise uses
+EOF
+assert "mise set STAGE" "two"
+
+# A key no group sets goes into the last group.
+assert "mise set NEW=1" ""
+assert "cat mise.toml" '# base values
+[[env]]
+STAGE = "one"
+ONLY_FIRST = "a"
+
+# overrides
+[[env]]
+STAGE = "two" # the value mise uses
+NEW = "1"'
+assert "mise set NEW" "1"
+
+# A key two groups set is updated in the last one, so the new value wins.
+assert "mise set STAGE=three" ""
+assert "cat mise.toml" '# base values
+[[env]]
+STAGE = "one"
+ONLY_FIRST = "a"
+
+# overrides
+[[env]]
+STAGE = "three" # the value mise uses
+NEW = "1"'
+assert "mise set STAGE" "three"
+
+# A key only an earlier group sets is updated where it is.
+assert "mise set ONLY_FIRST=z" ""
+assert "cat mise.toml" '# base values
+[[env]]
+STAGE = "one"
+ONLY_FIRST = "z"
+
+# overrides
+[[env]]
+STAGE = "three" # the value mise uses
+NEW = "1"'
+assert "mise set ONLY_FIRST" "z"
+
+# unset removes the key from every group, or the earlier value would take over.
+assert "mise unset STAGE" ""
+assert "cat mise.toml" '# base values
+[[env]]
+ONLY_FIRST = "z"
+
+# overrides
+[[env]]
+NEW = "1"'
+assert_fail "mise set STAGE" "Environment variable STAGE not found"
+
+# `mise set --rm` goes through the same code.
+assert "mise set --rm NEW" ""
+assert_fail "mise set NEW" "Environment variable NEW not found"
+assert "mise set ONLY_FIRST" "z"
+
+# unset removes a dotted key from the nested table that set wrote it to.
+assert "mise set _.path=./bin" ""
+assert "cat mise.toml" '# base values
+[[env]]
+ONLY_FIRST = "z"
+
+# overrides
+[[env]]
+
+[env._]
+path = "./bin"'
+assert "mise unset _.path" ""
+assert "cat mise.toml" '# base values
+[[env]]
+ONLY_FIRST = "z"
+
+# overrides
+[[env]]'
+
+# A variable named with a dot is that variable: the table the dots would descend into is
+# left alone.
+cat <<EOF >mise.toml
+[env]
+"FOO.value" = "literal"
+FOO = { value = "keep", redact = true }
+EOF
+assert "mise set FOO.value=changed" ""
+assert "cat mise.toml" '[env]
+"FOO.value" = "changed"
+FOO = { value = "keep", redact = true }'
+assert "mise unset FOO.value" ""
+assert "cat mise.toml" '[env]
+FOO = { value = "keep", redact = true }'
+
+# An edit that would leave an env mise cannot load is refused, and the file stays as it was.
+assert_fail "mise unset FOO.value" "cannot unset FOO.value"
+assert_fail "mise set NEW.name=1" "cannot set NEW.name"
+assert "cat mise.toml" '[env]
+FOO = { value = "keep", redact = true }'
+assert "mise unset FOO.redact" ""
+assert "cat mise.toml" '[env]
+FOO = { value = "keep" }'
+
+# An inline table is edited too.
+cat <<EOF >mise.toml
+env = { STAGE = "one" }
+EOF
+assert "mise set NEW=1" ""
+assert "cat mise.toml" 'env = { STAGE = "one", NEW = "1" }'
+assert "mise unset STAGE" ""
+assert "cat mise.toml" 'env = { NEW = "1" }'
--- src/cli/set.rs (+3/-1)

title: feat(backend): warn about tool options core tools and dotnet do not read
body:
A tool in `mise.toml` can carry options. Most backends already refuse an option they do not read, but core tools (node, python, go, ruby, java, rust, bun, deno, elixir, erlang, swift, zig, dotnet) and the `dotnet:` backend accepted anything and said nothing. A typo such as `lazy_bin` for `lazy_bins`, or an option copied from a `github:` tool, had no effect and no message.

Those tools now print a warning when they are installed, and the install still succeeds:

```toml
[tools]
node = { version = "22.11.0", lazy_bin = "node" }
```

Before: `mise install` printed nothing about `lazy_bin`.

After:

```text
mise WARN  node@22.11.0: option `lazy_bin` is not used by the core backend, so it has no effect (did you mean `lazy_bins`?)
```

Backends that already rejected unread options keep doing so, and the error now names the closest option:

```text
github:BurntSushi/ripgrep: option `asset_patern` is not used by the github backend
hint: Did you mean `asset_pattern`?
```

The warning appears at install only, the same point where the other backends fail, and once per tool and option. `mise ls` and shell activation are unaffected. `aqua:`, `asdf:` and `vfox:` tools are still not checked: aqua reads extra options as recipe variables, and plugins define their own.

The behavior per backend is documented in [Options a backend does not read](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/#unread-options).

## Validation

Unit tests cover the suggestion at the top level and inside a platform override, the once-only warning, and that every option the schema documents for python, java, rust and dotnet is accepted. The e2e test `test_ignored_tool_options` covers the hint, the warning on a core tool, and that `mise ls` and `mise hook-env` stay quiet. A real install of `bun` with an unread option printed one warning and installed. Clippy with `-D warnings` and `mise run lint` pass.

## Questions for review

- Warning or error for core tools and `dotnet:`? These options are ignored today and configs that carry them install fine, so this warns. Rejecting them like the other backends is `OptionSpec::new` in place of `warn_only` per tool, and breaks any config with a stray option.
- aqua stays unchecked. Checking it means comparing against the variables the resolved package declares, which needs the registry package at install.
- A tool that is already installed with a mistyped option is never reported, for the warning and the existing errors alike.
- This overlaps jdx/mise#15974, which adds a tool options page with a per-backend table. Whichever merges second should fold the new section into that page, and `AGENTS.md` still says these definitions are read "to reject unknown options".

title: test(docs): check that the error reference quotes messages mise still prints
body:
The [error messages](https://mise.jdx.dev/errors.html) page is written by hand, so it drifts: a
message gets reworded in the source and the page keeps the old text, and new messages never get
added. Someone who pastes a message into the page's search then finds nothing.

This is a first step. A unit test now reads every message the page quotes and fails when its
fixed text is no longer in mise's Rust source, naming the line:

```text
docs/errors.md:332: `<command> is not a mise binary` is not in the source
```

Placeholders such as `<tool>` and numbers are treated as variable. A message that cannot be
checked this way, because mise builds it from several strings or a dependency words it, is marked
on the page with a reason:

```md
<!-- errors: unchecked `HTTP status client error (404 Not Found)`: worded by the reqwest crate -->
```

Two page fixes come with it:

- A syntax error in a config file reached through a symlink: the page said mise prints the
  parser's message. It prints `details hidden because the file is reached through a link out of
  the project` after the position.
- New entry for the warning `task <name> has sources defined but no matching files found`, with
  its cause (the `sources` patterns match no file) and what still works.

What this does not do: it only catches a quoted message that disappears from the source. It does
not find messages that are missing from the page. Stable warning IDs and a reference generated
from the source would close that gap and are not part of this change.

Validation: the new test and its unit tests pass; altering a quoted message on the page makes it
fail; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check`
and `mise run lint` pass. The docs site build was not run.

title: test(schema): fail when declaration types drift from the dotfiles and daemons parsers
body:
mise's JSON schema for `[dotfiles]`, `[dotfile_groups]`, `[daemons]` and `[daemon_providers]` is generated from declaration types that nothing parses into, so a key or value added to a parser can be missing from the schema. An editor that reads the schema then flags a config mise accepts.

This adds tests that compare those declarations with what mise reads, and fixes what they found. A schema-aware editor no longer reports these as invalid:

- `mise` and `port` on a task daemon (`[daemons.<name>]` with `task = ...`)
- `tool` on a preset daemon, which `docs/daemons.md` already documents
- `mode = "fnox"` on a `[dotfile_groups]` entry
- `format = "ini"` on a `[dotfile_groups]` entry that merges

No runtime behavior changes: only `schema/mise.json`, the declaration types and tests. The new tests are enum-value checks for the dotfiles declarations in `mise-system` and `mise-config`, and a new module in `mise-daemons` that checks each daemon key and enumerated value mise reads against the declaration.

All but the preset `tool` key are also fixed by hand in jdx/mise#15974, with identical text.

## Validation

`cargo test -p mise-config`, `cargo test -p mise-daemons -p mise-util` and the declaration and schema tests of `mise-system` and `mise` pass, including `schema_matches_parser`; so do clippy with `-D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check` and `mise run lint`. With the declaration fixes reverted, the new tests fail in all three crates and name the missing key or value. The full unit and e2e suites were not run.

## Questions for review

- A preset daemon reads `mise = false`, but neither the docs nor the declaration list it. The test carries it as an explicit exemption; it could be declared and documented instead.
- The systemd `type` enum is not tested: mise writes the value through as given, so there is no parser-side list to compare with.
- `strum` becomes a dev-dependency of `mise-daemons`.

title: fix(schema): label experimental config from the checks that gate it
body:
## Problem

The `[experimental]` markers that editors show from `schema/mise.json` were typed by hand into doc comments, and had drifted from what mise does:

- `[bootstrap.users]` and `[bootstrap.groups]` were marked experimental, but mise applies them without `experimental = true`.
- Tools of the `spinel:` backend need `experimental = true`, and the schema did not say so.
- Daemons, task caching and a few `[task_config]` keys were marked in three different spellings (`[experimental] …`, `experimental …`, `Experimental …`).

## Outcome

The schema's label now comes from the same constant that the runtime check names, so the two cannot disagree without a test failing.

Before, hovering `[bootstrap.users]` in an editor:

> [experimental] Linux users that bootstrap creates or removes, keyed by user name

After:

> Linux users that bootstrap creates or removes, keyed by user name

And for a `spinel:` tool, before:

> a tool installed with the spinel backend

After:

> [experimental] a tool installed with the spinel backend

Every gated key now uses the one `[experimental] ` prefix, for example `[experimental] Project daemons: custom pitchfork commands or managed presets.`

mise's behavior is unchanged: no check was added or removed, and the error messages are the same.

## How it works

`crates/mise-config/src/experimental.rs` lists the config that needs `experimental = true`. A schema key is labelled with `#[schemars(transform = crate::experimental::NAME.labels())]`, and the code that gates it calls `Settings::ensure_experimental(mise_config::experimental::NAME.what)`. Tests in that file fail on a label with no check, a constant with no label, a hand-typed label, and an `ensure_experimental` call that names neither a constant nor an entry of the list of gates the schema has no key for.

## Validation

- `cargo test -p mise-config` (43 passed, including `schema_files_are_up_to_date` and the three new tests)
- `cargo test -p mise -p mise-daemons -p mise-settings -p mise-config -- daemons experimental schema ensure_experimental` (59 passed, including `schema_matches_parser`)
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `mise run test:e2e test_spinel_experimental`
- `mise run lint`

## Questions for review

- Should `[bootstrap.users]` and `[bootstrap.groups]` need `experimental = true` after all? This only corrects the label to match what mise does today.
- `Settings::experimental_enabled(&…)` ignores its argument at runtime; it exists so the three daemon checks that read the setting as a bool name the config they gate.
- Two checks gate one form of a value and not a key (a task `file` with a `git::` source, and `[task_config].includes` with remote sources), so they stay unlabelled.
- This overlaps jdx/mise#15974, which removes the same two labels by hand. Whichever merges second regenerates the schema with `mise run render:schema`.

title: fix(deps): make each workspace crate compile on its own
body:
mise's library crates are published separately, but several of them only compiled as part of the whole workspace. Building `mise-daemons`, `mise-ui`, `mise-system-packages`, `mise-oci` or `mise-system` by itself, or depending on one from crates.io, failed to compile. This does not affect the `mise` binary or anyone installing mise.

Before:

```
$ cargo check -p mise-daemons
error[E0432]: unresolved imports `sigstore_verify::trust_root::TufBootstrap`, `sigstore_verify::trust_root::TufConfig`
  --> crates/mise-sigstore/src/lib.rs:14:66
```

The same error appears for a new crate whose only dependency is `mise-daemons = "2026.11.12"`.

After: `cargo check -p <crate>` passes for every workspace member.

Three things were only switched on by other members of the workspace:

- `mise-sigstore` always needs sigstore-verify's `tuf` feature, but only enabled it together with a TLS backend. It is now always on.
- `mise-util` always needs gix's network client for `git clone`, but only enabled it together with a TLS backend. It is now always on; the TLS features still choose the HTTP transport.
- `mise-system` and `mise-oci` link Lua through vfox and had no way to ask for the bundled copy. Both gain a `vendored-lua` feature (off by default, so builds against a system Lua are unchanged).

To keep it fixed, `mise run test:crates-standalone` runs `cargo check` on each member crate by itself, and the lint job runs it as one extra step in its existing cached target directory. On a warm cache it takes 10–20 seconds locally.

Validation: the new task passes on this branch and fails for `mise-daemons` with the manifests from main; `mise run lint` and `cargo fmt --check` pass; `Cargo.lock` is unchanged.


**Questions for review**

- `mise-system` uses vfox only for the `SystemDependency` type. Moving that type out of vfox would remove the Lua link instead of adding a feature for it.
- The crates already published as 2026.11.12 stay broken until the next release.
- The first CI run after merge builds from a cold cache. If that costs too much on PRs that change `Cargo.lock`, dropping the `--all-targets` pass is the cheap cut.

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+#MISE description="Check that each workspace crate compiles on its own"
+set -euo pipefail
+
+# Every member crate is published by itself, so it has to compile with only the
+# features its own manifest turns on. A workspace build cannot show that: Cargo
+# gives a dependency the features of every member that uses it, so a feature one
+# crate forgot is supplied by another.
+#
+# Each crate is checked twice: as a dependency (the library alone) and with its
+# tests, whose dev-dependencies add features of their own.
+#
+# Pass crate names to check only those. The default is every member except
+# `mise`, which a plain `cargo clippy` already builds by itself in CI.
+
+if [[ ${1:-} == --help ]]; then
+	cat >&2 <<EOF
+Usage: mise run test:crates-standalone [CRATE...]
+
+Runs cargo check on each workspace crate by itself, so a crate that only
+compiles when the rest of the workspace turns on a feature for it fails.
+EOF
+	exit 0
+fi
+
+metadata=$(cargo metadata --no-deps --format-version 1)
+if [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; then
+	crates=("$@")
+else
+	# A read loop, because the Bash 3.2 that macOS ships has no mapfile.
+	crates=()
+	while IFS= read -r crate; do
+		crates+=("$crate")
+	done < <(jq -r '.packages[].name | select(. != "mise")' <<<"$metadata")
+fi
+
+failed=()
+for crate in "${crates[@]}"; do
+	args=(--package "$crate" --ignore-rust-version)
+	# Without the feature, vfox links the system's Lua 5.1, which CI runners
+	# and most development machines do not have.
+	if jq -e --arg crate "$crate" \
+		'.packages[] | select(.name == $crate) | .features | has("vendored-lua")' \
+		<<<"$metadata" >/dev/null; then
+		args+=(--features vendored-lua)
+	fi
+	echo "::group::$crate"
+	if ! cargo check "${args[@]}" || ! cargo check "${args[@]}" --all-targets; then
+		failed+=("$crate")
+	fi
+	echo "::endgroup::"
+done
+
+if [[ ${#failed[@]} -gt 0 ]]; then
+	echo "These crates do not compile on their own: ${failed[*]}" >&2
+	echo "Reproduce one with: cargo check -p <crate> --all-targets" >&2
+	exit 1
+fi
+echo "All ${#crates[@]} crates compile on their own."

title: fix(task): follow blob redirects and honor Retry-After in the remote cache client
body:
The [remote cache protocol](https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/remote-cache-protocol.html) lets a cache server answer a blob download with a `307` redirect to a presigned object-store URL, and send `Retry-After` when it is busy. mise did neither.

**Redirects.** With a server that delegates downloads, every blob read failed and the task ran without the cache:

```
mise WARN  remote task cache lookup failed for <key>; using local cache only: remote cache blob failed digest verification
```

mise now follows the `307` and restores the entry. The redirected request is a plain `GET`: the cache's bearer token and `mbx-cache-*` headers are never sent to the delegated host, the URL must be HTTPS (or loopback HTTP), only one redirect is followed, and the content is still verified against its digest. Errors from the delegated host leave its signed URL out of the message.

A redirect on any other request, such as a blob upload, used to count as success although nothing was stored. It is now a failed request with a warning.

**Retry-After.** On `429` or `503` mise retried on its own schedule (about 200ms, 1s, 4s). It now waits as long as `Retry-After` asks (seconds or an HTTP date) when that is longer, up to 30 seconds in total per request. A server asking for more ends the retries right away, so the task runs without the cache instead of waiting.

The protocol document now states these rules. The protocol version is unchanged.

**Validation**

- `cargo test -p mise-cache-core`: 30 passed, with new tests against local mock servers for the redirect (headers withheld, digest checked, one hop, unsafe targets rejected, signed URL kept out of errors), redirected `PUT`, and `Retry-After` on 429 and 503.
- `cargo test -p mise --lib task_cache`: 41 passed.
- `mise run test:e2e test_task_artifact_cache_remote_modes test_task_artifact_cache_remote_secrets`: 2 passed.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `mise run lint`: clean.

**Questions for review**

- A `Retry-After` longer than the 30-second limit ends the retries at once. The alternative is to wait 30 seconds and retry anyway.
- The 30-second limit is a constant, not a setting.
- The redirected request carries no credentials even when it points back at the cache's own origin, so a server redirecting to itself has to put the grant in the URL.
- Redirected uploads to a presigned URL stay unsupported; the protocol document now says so.
- `httpdate` becomes a direct dependency of `mise-cache-core`. It was already in `Cargo.lock`.

title: fix(config): deprecate MISE_USE_TOML=0
body:
`MISE_USE_TOML=0` is a switch from the time mise wrote `.tool-versions` by default. It was not documented anywhere, and it still changes three things:

- `~/.tool-versions` becomes a global config file.
- `mise use --global` writes to `~/.tool-versions` when the global config directory has no TOML file.
- The deprecated `mise local` creates `.tool-versions` instead of `mise.toml`, and `mise local --parent` finds one.

It is now deprecated, with removal in mise 2027.11.0. When the variable changes what a command does, mise prints once per run:

```text
mise WARN  deprecated [env.MISE_USE_TOML]: MISE_USE_TOML=0 is deprecated. mise still reads .tool-versions files. To write one, use `mise use --path .tool-versions`; to keep ~/.tool-versions as the global config, set MISE_GLOBAL_CONFIG_FILE=~/.tool-versions. This will be removed in mise 2027.11.0.
```

Nothing else changes: the variable keeps working until removal, and mise keeps reading `.tool-versions` files with or without it.

## When the warning prints

- Not when the variable is unset, or set but without effect (for example `MISE_GLOBAL_CONFIG_FILE` is set, or there is no `~/.tool-versions`).
- Not from shims or `mise hook-env`, which run on every command and every prompt.
- With the variable set and `~/.tool-versions` present, on every other command, since that file is being loaded as global config because of the variable. Warning only on writes would be quieter, but people who rely on the global read would get no notice before removal.

## Also fixed

With a `.tool-versions` file as the global config, every command printed `Error loading settings file ~/.tool-versions: TOML parse error`, because the settings loader tried to parse it as TOML. That includes the `MISE_GLOBAL_CONFIG_FILE=~/.tool-versions` setup the warning recommends, so the loader now skips `.tool-versions` files, which hold no settings.

## Docs

`MISE_USE_TOML` gets an entry with a deprecation banner in the environment variables page, and the `mise local` help calls it deprecated.

## Validation

New e2e test `config/test_use_toml_deprecated` covers the warning with the variable set, its absence without it, and both recommended replacements. The existing e2e tests that set the variable, the config unit tests, Clippy with `-D warnings` and `mise run lint` pass. The full unit suite was not run. The unit-test harness still sets `MISE_USE_TOML=0`; it can go with the variable.

title: chore: run clippy in mise run lint
body:
`mise run lint` did not run Clippy, while CI denies Clippy warnings. A contributor could pass lint locally and fail CI. On `main`, a `v.len() == 0` added to `src/lib.rs` passes `mise run lint`; with this change it fails with `len_zero`.

`mise run lint` now includes a new `lint:clippy` task that runs the commands of the CI lint job:

```sh
cargo clippy --ignore-rust-version -- -D warnings
cargo clippy --all-features --all-targets --ignore-rust-version -- -D warnings
```

On Windows it runs the `windows-lint` command instead. `mise run lint:clippy` runs Clippy alone.

## What stays the same

- The git pre-commit hook runs only the hk steps, so it does not run Clippy and is no slower. A commit that passes the hook can still fail Clippy; `mise run lint` is the check to run before pushing.
- CI is unchanged in what it checks: the lint step sets `MISE_TASK_SKIP: lint:clippy`, because the dedicated Clippy steps right after it already run these commands in their own target directories.

## Cost

Measured locally for `mise run lint`:

| State | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Warm, nothing changed | 6s | 9s |
| After `touch src/lib.rs` | 15s | 35s |

The first Clippy run in a checkout that had only been built took 255s.

## For review

- No reason is recorded for why the hk Clippy step was commented out (it happened in #5629, an unrelated PR). This PR assumes it was the cost in the pre-commit hook, which runs every hk step, and keeps Clippy out of hk for that reason.
- AGENTS.md and `docs/contributing.md` named `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` as the CI command. CI on Linux runs the two commands above, without `--workspace`; the docs now say so.
- The Windows command is copied from CI and was not run.
- The `pre-commit` mise task (not the git hook) runs `mise run lint`, so it now includes Clippy.

title: chore(docs): keep docs/cli intact when render:usage fails
body:
`mise run render:usage` deleted `docs/cli` and then regenerated it. When a later step failed (a broken guide link caught by `cli-reference.ts`, a markdownlint error, a `usage generate` failure), the contributor was left with about 250 modified or missing pages and had to know to run `git restore docs/cli`. A panic in `mise usage` did similar damage one step earlier: the shell redirect had already truncated `mise.usage.kdl` to 0 bytes.

The task now writes everything to a scratch directory in the repository and moves it into place only after the step that produces it has passed:

- `mise.usage.kdl` and `tasks.md` are replaced once their command succeeds.
- The pages are generated, fixed up and linted in the scratch directory, then swapped over `docs/cli` at the end.
- The scratch directory is removed on success, failure and interrupt.

A failed run now exits non-zero with `docs/cli` exactly as it was. The output of a successful run is unchanged: `mise run render:usage` and `mise run render` on a clean tree produce no diff.

## For review

- `docs/.vitepress/cli-reference.ts` takes an optional target directory so it can work on the scratch copy; the default is still `docs/cli`.
- markdownlint runs inside the scratch directory with the pages at `docs/cli` relative to it, because `.markdownlintignore` (which lists `docs/cli/watch.md`) is matched against paths relative to the working directory.
- The final swap is two renames, since a rename cannot replace a non-empty directory. An interrupt between them is handled by the exit trap; only a SIGKILL in that window can leave `docs/cli` missing.
- `render:mangen` and `render:completions` still redirect straight onto tracked files and are not changed here.

## Validation

Run by hand, each ending with `docs/cli` hash-identical to before and no scratch directory left: a failing `mise usage` (broken KDL), a failing `usage generate`, a failing `cli-reference.ts`, and SIGINT during generation. `mise run lint` passes. There is no automated test for the task.

title: test(cli): check that "Source code" links in the CLI reference point at real files
body:
Every page of the CLI reference ends with a "Source code" link to the file that implements the command. Those links come from one hand-written template in `src/assets/mise-extra.usage.kdl` that maps command paths to files, and nothing checked the result. The five `mise daemons providers` pages linked to `src/daemons/providers.rs`, which does not exist, so the link was a 404.

A unit test now reads the link on every committed page under `docs/cli` and fails when the file is missing, naming the page and the path:

```text
source code links to files that do not exist; fix the paths in src/assets/mise-extra.usage.kdl and run `mise run render:usage`:
docs/cli/daemons/providers.md: src/daemons/providers.rs
docs/cli/daemons/providers/ls.md: src/daemons/providers.rs
…
```

The providers pages now link to `src/daemons/provider_commands.rs`. That path fix is also in #15974 with identical lines; whichever merges second keeps only the rest.

The test checks that the file exists, not that it is the right file for the command. It reads the committed pages because rendering all of them in the test took longer than the unit suite allows one test; the render check in CI keeps those pages equal to what the template produces.

## Validation

The new test fails on `main` with the five providers commands and passes with the fix. Clippy with `-D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check` and `mise run lint` pass. The seven changed generated lines were edited to match the template change; `mise run render:usage` was not re-run.

title: test(e2e): fail when there is no built mise binary to test
body:
`mise run test:e2e` could pass without testing your change. When `target/debug/mise` was missing (for example after the target directory was garbage-collected, or when the runner was started without the build step), the harness ran every test against whatever `mise` was next on `PATH`, usually an installed release, and reported the result as if it were your build.

The harness now tests exactly one binary and says so when it cannot find it.

Before, with no `target/debug/mise`:

```text
PASS: cli/test_version (0s, 1 assertion)
E2E: ran 1 tests (1 passed, 0 failed), skipped 0 tests
```

After:

```text
ERROR: No mise build at '/…/target/debug/mise'. Run 'mise run build' first, or set MISE_E2E_BIN=/path/to/mise to test another mise binary on purpose.
```

A `target` symlink whose destination is gone is treated the same way, and the run stops once, before any test starts.

To run the suite against another binary on purpose, such as a release build, set `MISE_E2E_BIN=/path/to/mise`. That variable already selected the binary for `MISE_E2E_DOCKER=1` runs; it now works for local runs too (the file must be named `mise`).

## For review

- The release workflow's `e2e-linux` job tests the release tarball in `$HOME/mise/bin` and has no debug build, so it relied on the fallback. It now sets `MISE_E2E_BIN="$HOME/mise/bin/mise"`. title: fix(task): do not export output in the silent style as OpenTelemetry logs
body:
With `otel.logs` on, a task run in the `silent` output style could still have every line of its output exported to the OpenTelemetry collector. The [docs](https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/opentelemetry.html#what-is-exported) say output in the silent style is not exported, and someone who silences a task because its output should not leave the machine would not expect it in their log backend.

## When it happened

mise decided whether to export a task's output from the task's own `silent = true` key only. The other ways to select the silent style were not checked:

- `mise run --silent` and `mise run --output silent`
- `MISE_TASK_OUTPUT=silent` or the `task.output` setting
- `output = "silent"` on the task

In those cases the lines were exported whenever mise read the task's streams for another reason: the `task.logs` setting, or a task whose output is captured for the task cache. With neither, the streams go to `/dev/null` and nothing was exported.

```toml
[tasks.deploy]
run = "echo token=abc123"
```

```sh
export MISE_OTEL_ENABLED=1 MISE_OTEL_LOGS=1 MISE_TASK_LOGS=1
mise run --output silent deploy
```

Before, the collector received a log record with the body `token=abc123` for the `deploy` span. Now it receives the spans and no log record. A task with `silent = "stdout"` or `silent = "stderr"` is unchanged: the stream that is not silenced is still exported.

## Validation

The `test_task_otel_export` e2e test now runs a task in the silent style four ways (`--output silent`, `--silent`, `MISE_TASK_OUTPUT=silent`, and `output = "silent"`) with task logs on and checks that the local collector receives none of its lines, then that the same task in the default style is still exported. Before the fix it failed with all four runs exported. The task cache path goes through the same check and was not exercised separately.

> **Low Risk**
> Scoped change to OTLP log forwarding when output style is silent; e2e coverage added. No auth or core execution path changes beyond telemetry export behavior.
> 
> **Overview**
> When **OpenTelemetry task logs** are enabled, mise no longer forwards stdout/stderr to OTLP for tasks running in the **silent output style**. The gate now uses the resolved `TaskOutput::Silent` (covering `--silent`, `--output silent`, `MISE_TASK_OUTPUT`, `output = "silent"`, and related settings) instead of only the task's `silent = true` flag—so streams piped for task logs or the artifact cache are **not** exported while still silent to the user.
> 
> The **e2e** `test_task_otel_export` case exercises those silent variants with task logging on and confirms normal output is still exported afterward. Comments in `task_output_forwarder` and `task_executor` document when hooks run vs when export is skipped.

title: docs: review every page against the code and correct CLI help
body:
The docs site was restructured in October, and since then feature PRs have added to pages one at a time. This is a second pass over the README, every page of the site and the other Markdown files in the repository, checking each against the current code, plus two additions to the landing page.

## What readers get

- **Corrected facts.** Each page was read against `src/`, `crates/`, `settings.toml` and the generated CLI reference. Wrong or stale flags, defaults, key names and command output are fixed; options and caveats the code has and the page lacked are added; text repeated across pages is now one sentence and a link.
- **A [Tool options](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/tool-options.html) page.** The options every tool accepts (`os`, `depends`, `postinstall`, `install_env`, templates, the table form, options on the command line) move out of the dev tools overview into their own page. Its "Unknown options" section has a table of what each backend does with an option it does not read (fail the install, warn, or pass it to a plugin) and shows the messages mise prints, including the "did you mean" suggestion.
- **A [Language server](https://mise.jdx.dev/lsp.html) page.** `mise lsp` moves out of the editors page: what it serves, each feature, the `initializationOptions` that switch features off, and editor setup.
- **Dotfiles history is shorter.** The page keeps the tasks (save, roll back, undo, track); its reference tables move to the dotfiles reference.
- **Glossary and error reference.** 14 terms the site used without defining, and the paranoid plugin error.
- **`[[env]]` and systemd service types.** The environments page now explains `[[env]]`, which splits a file's environment into groups so one file can set a variable twice or use `_.source` at two points, and says how `mise set` and `mise unset` edit such a file. The systemd page lists the values `type` accepts.

```toml
[[env]]
_.source = "scripts/base.sh" # exports APP_HOST

[[env]]
APP_URL = "https://{{ env.APP_HOST }}"
_.source = "scripts/urls.sh" # reads $APP_URL
```

Every moved heading has a redirect, so links in released mise binaries and from other sites still land on the right section.

## Landing page

- A "Lock and verify what you install" section shows a `mise.lock` and links to checksums and attestations, minimum release age, and config trust. Each claim says where it stops: the lockfile covers the platforms you lock, the release-age filter needs a backend that reports release dates, and trust is asked for outside CI.
- A "Fit mise into your setup" grid links to the guides for existing projects, CI, editors, coding agents, secrets and monorepos.
- The bootstrap section moves above the walkthrough, and the hero no longer overflows at phone widths.
- On docs pages, a TOML block with a file title shows its playground and copy buttons in the title bar instead of over the code.

title: fix(system-packages): warn about unsupported brew requirements only when pouring
body:
A tap formula that names a custom Homebrew `Requirement` class made every `mise bootstrap packages` run warn that the requirement "is not enforced", even when the formula was already installed and up to date:

```text
$ mise bootstrap packages upgrade --dry-run brew:incoai/tap/splash
mise WARN  ignoring unsupported Homebrew requirement SplashMacOSRequirement in incoai/tap/splash; it is not enforced
mise brew: all formulae already poured
```

The warning is only useful when mise is about to pour or build a formula without enforcing its requirement. mise now holds it until it knows the formula needs work, so the no-op run above only prints `brew: all formulae already poured`. A real install, an upgrade, or a dry run that lists the formula to pour or build still warns, with the same message.

Support for custom requirements is unchanged: they are still skipped, not enforced.

Fixes #15963

## Implementation

The metadata shim already reports skipped requirements. `evaluate_formula` used to `warn!` right away, before the keg check. They are now kept on `Formula::unsupported_requirements`, and `install_via_pour` warns for the formulae in `to_pour` (selected by `formulae_to_pour`, worded by `unsupported_requirement_warnings`), after the "already poured" early return.

## Testing

- Unit tests for reading the field from tap metadata, and for when the warning appears: nothing warns when every formula is already poured, a missing formula warns, and in a mixed batch only the missing one warns.
- `tolerates_custom_requirement_classes` now asserts the requirement is recorded. It needs a real Ruby and returned early on my machine (none installed), so CI is its first real run.
- `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean on the touched crates.

> UI/timing change for existing warning text only; requirement handling and install logic are otherwise unchanged.
> 
> **Overview**
> Stops noisy warnings on no-op `mise bootstrap packages` runs when tap formulae already have a poured keg but declare custom Homebrew `Requirement` classes that mise skips.
> 
> **`Formula::unsupported_requirements`** is added in brew metadata and populated from tap shim output instead of warning during `evaluate_formula`. **`install_via_pour`** now derives the pour set via **`formulae_to_pour`**, returns early when everything is already poured, then emits one warning per skipped requirement only for formulae in **`to_pour`** (real install, upgrade, or dry-run that would pour/build).
>

title: feat(task): add --no-global and --global to the mise run task picker
body:
`mise run` opens a task picker, and it lists global tasks (from `~/.config/mise/config.toml`) next to the project's own. With many global tasks the project's tasks get lost, and `mise tasks ls --no-global` had no counterpart for the picker.

`mise run` now takes `--no-global` and `--global`:

```
$ mise run --no-global
Tasks
Select a task to run
❯ build  build the project
  test   test the project

$ mise run --global
❯ dotfiles-sync  global: sync my dotfiles
  notes          global: open notes
```

- Either flag opens the picker even when a `default` task exists, like `--all`.
- They combine with `--all` and `--multi`.
- They conflict with a named task, `--affected`, and each other.

From discussion jdx/mise#15971.

Tested with a new e2e test that drives the picker through a pty (`test_task_run_no_global_picker`), the existing `--multi` and `--all` picker tests, and clippy with `-D warnings`.

title: fix(task): read a task tool's pin from its own lockfile when a parent lists the tool
body:
With `--locked` (or `MISE_LOCKED=1`), a task whose `tools` pins a tool was run without that tool on its `PATH` whenever a parent or global config listed the same tool at another version. The task still exited 0, so the pin decided nothing.

```toml
# mise.toml
[tools]
jq = "1.6"

# child/mise.toml
[tasks.where]
tools = { jq = "1.7.1" }
run = "jq --version"
```

After `mise lock` in both directories, `MISE_LOCKED=1 mise run where` from `child/` warned `jq@1.7.1 is not in the lockfile` and ran a different `jq` (or none). Now it prints `jq-1.7.1`, the same as without `--locked`.

## Cause

`load_runtime_args` gives a runtime argument the lockfile of the config that already lists the tool. For a task's `tools` that was the parent's `mise.lock`, which records `1.6` and not `1.7.1`; the pin in `child/mise.lock` was never read. #15958 fixed the case where no config lists the tool; this is the case where one does.

## Fix

A task declares its own tools, so task tool arguments (`with_task_tool_args`) now always use the default lockfile lookup. `mise x tool@1` is unchanged and keeps the owner scope.

## Testing

- New e2e `tasks/test_task_tools_locked_parent` fails without the fix (`jq@1.7.1 is not in the lockfile`) and passes with it.
- Extended the `runtime_args_without_config_do_not_borrow_stale_pins` unit test.
- `cargo clippy -p mise --all-targets -- -D warnings` fails only on an existing lint in `crates/mise-ui`, which also fails on `origin/main`.

Fixes #15965

title: docs(exec): explain PATH entries before shims in child lookup
body:
With the default settings, `PATH` directories that come before mise's shims stay ahead of mise's tool directories in the environment `mise exec` gives its child. Direct lookup in `mise exec -- <command>` gives mise's tools priority, so the two can disagree:

```sh
PATH="$OTHER_NODE_BIN:$SHIMS:/usr/bin:/bin"
mise exec node@24.18.0 -- node --version              # v24.18.0
mise exec node@24.18.0 -- /usr/bin/env node --version # the other Node
MISE_ACTIVATE_AGGRESSIVE=1 \
  mise exec node@24.18.0 -- /usr/bin/env node --version # v24.18.0
```

This documents that ordering in the `mise exec` help and the `activate_aggressive` setting, including the `MISE_ACTIVATE_AGGRESSIVE=1 mise exec -- <command>` workaround. The ordering is unchanged; it mirrors `mise activate`, where entries before the shims win.

Generated docs (`docs/cli/exec.md`, man page, usage spec) were re-rendered with `mise run render`. Docs only; nothing was built or tested.

Fixes #15964

title: fix(ci): satisfy clippy on Windows and the latest beta
body:
`windows-lint` fails on `main` with a clippy error in `src/task/task_cache.rs`: when the `#[cfg(unix)]` ctime block is compiled out, `source_changed_since` is left with `if … { return true; } false`. This moves the ctime check into a `#[cfg(unix)]` helper (with a `#[cfg(not(unix))]` stub returning `false`), so behavior on Unix is unchanged.

It also fixes the lints the latest beta clippy adds, so lint stays green on newer toolchains:

- `then(|| …)` → `then_some(…)` in `mise-ui`
- test modules moved to the end of `src/backend/spm.rs` and `mise-system`'s `history/sync/network.rs` (`items_after_test_module`)
- `current = String::new()` after a push → `std::mem::take` in `tool_version_options.rs`

No user-facing change. Test modules were moved verbatim.

Validation: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes on beta, and `cargo +stable clippy -p mise --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes on stable (the stable run was before the beta-lint edits), both on Linux. The Windows target was not run locally, so `windows-lint` in CI is the confirmation.

title: fix(task): put a locked task tool's install dir on the task's PATH
body:
A tool pinned in a task's `tools` and locked with `mise lock` was installed but missing from the task's `PATH` on a machine that had never run the task before the lockfile existed.

```toml
[tasks.where]
tools = { "npm:prettier" = "3.6.2" }
run = "command -v prettier || echo 'prettier: not found'"
```

After `mise lock` and with an empty data directory, `mise run where` installed `prettier` under `installs/npm-prettier/3.6.2~aube~<digest>` but printed `prettier: not found`. If another copy of the command was on `PATH`, the task ran that copy and reported no error, so the pin decided nothing. The same pin under `[tools]` worked.

Now `mise run where` prints `…/3.6.2~aube~<digest>/node_modules/.bin/prettier`, the same as the `[tools]` form.

## Cause

Installing a task's tools read the lockfile, so the tool resolved with its dependency graph and installed under the `~aube~<digest>` directory. Running the task built its toolset through `load_runtime_args`, which gives an argument no config lists a "no owner" lockfile scope, so no lock entry was read. The tool resolved to the plain `3.6.2` directory, which doesn't exist on a fresh machine, and its bin path was never added. A tool listed in `[tools]` has an owning config, which is why that case worked.

The "no owner" scope is meant to stop `mise x tool@1` from borrowing a stale pin from an unrelated config. A task's own `tools` are declared by the task, so `ToolsetBuilder::with_task_tool_args` keeps the default lockfile scope for them, matching what the install step uses. `mise x` is unchanged.

## Testing

- New e2e `tasks/test_task_tools_locked_npm` follows the report: lock, wipe the installs, run the task. It fails (status 127) without the fix and passes with it.
- Extended the `runtime_args_without_config_do_not_borrow_stale_pins` unit test.
- `cargo clippy -p mise --all-targets` gives no warnings in the changed files. `-D warnings` fails on an existing lint in `crates/mise-ui`, which also fails on `origin/main`.

Fixes #15957

title: feat(daemons): export a project reference's port and URL under its own name
body:
A daemon in one project can now reach a daemon it references from another project by the name the reference was given, in the environment and in pitchfork templates.

```toml
# shop/mise.toml
[daemons.search]
project = "../search"

[daemons.app]
run = "node server.js"
depends = ["search"]
```

Before, `shop` had no `SEARCH_PORT` or `SEARCH_URL`, and `{{ daemons.search.url }}` did not resolve. Now:

- `SEARCH_PORT` and `SEARCH_URL` are exported into the referencing project, named after the reference (`[daemons.search]`), taking the port and URL from the referenced project's daemon. Only those two variables cross over.
- `depends` entries that name a reference are written as `{ id = "search/app", as = "search" }`, so `{{ daemons.search.url }}` resolves. This needs pitchfork 2.36.0 or later (the `as` form, pitchfork#1144). mise probes `pitchfork schema` for it and caches the answer by executable identity; an older pitchfork still gets plain IDs, so nothing breaks.
- Collisions follow the existing rules: names that fold onto one variable export neither, and a variable a local daemon already exports wins over the reference's.

Docs: `docs/daemons/sharing.md` and the minimum-version table in `docs/daemons.md`.

Closes discussion jdx/mise#15944.

## Test plan

- `cargo test -p mise-daemons -p mise --lib -- tests::` passes.
- `e2e/cli/test_daemons` passes, including a new block covering `SEARCH_PORT=4100`, plain IDs with an old pitchfork, and `as = "search"` with a new one.
- `test_daemons_pitchfork` and clippy (`mise-ui`) fail identically on origin/main.

title: feat(dotfiles): let a dotfile group entry deploy outside the group's target
body:
Every entry of a dotfile group had to lie inside the group's target. A package whose files land in two places therefore needed two groups, or a second root that existed only to hold the stray directory. On Windows, for example, VS Code reads its settings from `~/AppData/Roaming/Code` while one of its extensions reads `~/.crossnote`.

An entry can now deploy outside the group's target, so that package is one group:

```toml
[dotfile_groups.vscode]
root = "vscode/.config"
target = "~/AppData/Roaming"

[dotfile_groups.vscode.entries]
"~/.crossnote" = { source = "crossnote", mode = "symlink" }
```

`vscode/.config/Code` is walked into `~/AppData/Roaming/Code`, and `~/.crossnote` links to `vscode/.config/crossnote`, which the walk skips.

- An entry outside the target has no path in the tree, so it needs a `source` (a `merge` edit too), unless its mode takes none, such as `absent`. Without one, mise ignores the group and says the entry needs a source.
- The same applies to a `variants` target and to the file a block, line, or merge edit changes.
- The entry belongs to the group like any other: it applies only while the group is selected, and `mise dot unapply --group` and `mise dot apply --prune` remove it with the rest of the group.
- An entry still cannot be the group's target itself or a directory that contains it.

The docs also show how to deploy only a group's entries and nothing else from its root, with `exclude = ["/*"]`. That already worked; it is now documented and tested.

Configs that were valid before behave the same.

Stacked on https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15953. Requested in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15921.

title: feat(dotfiles): default a dotfile group's root to its name
body:
A `[dotfile_groups.<name>]` table had to set `root`, even when the group's directory has the same name as the group. Adding a table only to set one option, such as `exclude`, therefore stopped the group from deploying, and mise explained it with a warning that was wrong: it said no table declares the group.

`root` now defaults to the group name, so a table that leaves it out deploys the directory named after the group, the same directory a selected name with no table deploys:

```toml
[dotfile_groups.kitty]
exclude = ["README.md"]
```

This deploys `~/.dotfiles/kitty` into `~` and skips `README.md`. Before, mise ignored the group with `root: is required`.

When a group's table is invalid for another reason (an unknown key, a bad `mode`), mise still ignores the group and says why, but no longer also prints `[bootstrap] dotfile_groups names "kitty", but no [dotfile_groups] table declares it`.

Existing configs are unaffected: a table that sets `root` behaves as before.

Reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15921.

Co-authored-by: lhs-12 <45565870+lhs-12@users.noreply.github.com>

> **Dotfile groups** no longer require an explicit `root`: when `[dotfile_groups.<name>]` omits it, mise deploys the directory named after the group (same as an implicit selected group with no table). title: fix(lock): record platforms a tool has no build for in mise.lock
body:
When a tool has no build for one of the platforms you lock, `mise lock` now records that in `mise.lock`. `mise lock --check` then knows the gap is expected and passes, instead of failing on a platform the tool can never support. Before, mise.lock kept no trace of the gap, so `--check` could not tell "no build exists" from "the download failed".

```toml
# mise.toml
[tools]
diffoci = "0.1.8"   # ships Linux and macOS builds only
```

```bash
mise lock --platform linux-x64,windows-x64
MISE_OFFLINE=1 mise lock --check   # mise.lock is up to date
```

mise.lock now holds:

```toml
[[tools.diffoci]]
version = "0.1.8"
backend = "aqua:reproducible-containers/diffoci"
specifiers = ["0.1.8"]
unsupported_platforms = ["windows-x64"]

[tools.diffoci."platforms.linux-x64"]
checksum = "sha256:01e6…"
```

## Behavior

- **`mise lock`** writes `unsupported_platforms` (in both generate and merge mode) when the backend reports it has no build for a platform. A platform is never in both `unsupported_platforms` and `platforms`. The next `mise lock` asks the backend again, so a platform that gains a build gets a normal entry and leaves the list.
- **Node and PyPy** now report a missing build this way. Before, they returned empty lock data, so `mise lock` recorded nothing and `--check` failed. Node does this when `node.compile` is off and nodejs.org has no archive for the platform (for example linux-riscv64). PyPy does it for a platform it publishes no build for (for example pypy3.7 on macos-arm64).
- **`mise lock --check`** skips listed platforms unless you name them with `--platform`. A named platform fails with:
  ```
  diffoci@0.1.8 has no build for platform windows-x64, as mise.lock records; set the tool's `os` option to skip that platform (--locked mode)
  ```
  Set `os = ["linux", "macos"]` on the tool, and the check passes. Re-locking then drops the entry.
  A platform missing for any other reason, such as a failed download, still fails the check.
- **`mise install --locked`** on a listed platform fails with the same "no build" message instead of "No lockfile URL found".
- **Auto-lock during install** (`lockfile_platforms` including a platform the tool lacks) treats a listed platform as done. Before, every `mise install` resolved that platform again and printed the same warning.

This replaces the heuristic from #15941, which skipped a platform in `--check` when no other tool in the lockfile had an entry for it. That rule guessed from the other tools and could hide a real failure. #15941 has not been released, so no released mise has that behavior.

## Compatibility

The lockfile format version does not change. An older mise ignores `unsupported_platforms`, but it drops the field if it rewrites `mise.lock`. If an existing `mise.lock` already lacks a platform for a tool with no build there, the first `mise install` that auto-locks or the next `mise lock` adds the list once. In this repository's own `mise.lock`, CI added it for cargo-insta, which has no linux-ar

title: feat(prune): add --system and prune replaced system installs after upgrade
body:
Old versions of tools installed with `mise install --system` piled up in `/usr/local/share/mise/installs` with no way to clean them. In #15932, npm-installed CLIs updated through `mise upgrade` left about 40 GB of old versions behind: `mise ls --prunable` was empty and `mise prune` removed nothing.

Two things caused this:

- `mise upgrade` scheduled the replaced system version for removal, but the next command dropped that receipt with `WARN ignoring tool purgatory entry outside the user installs directory`, so the old version stayed forever.
- `mise prune` only considers the user's own installs directory, on purpose, because it only knows the config files that user has loaded.

## What changes

**Upgrades clean up after themselves.** When `mise upgrade` replaces a system install, the old version is removed after the [`upgrade.prune_after`](https://mise.jdx.dev/configuration/settings.html#upgrade.prune_after) grace period, the same as a user install. That cleanup runs during a later, unrelated command, which must never prompt for a sudo password, so when removing the old version (or rebuilding the system shims afterwards) needs `sudo` mise keeps it and says so:

```text
kept <tool>@<old version> in the system installs directory; remove it with `mise prune --system` or upgrade with `--prune`
```

`mise upgrade --prune` removes it during the upgrade, using `sudo` when needed.

**New `mise prune --system`** prunes the system installs directory instead of your own:

```sh
mise prune --system --dry-run   # list unused system versions
mise prune --system             # remove them, with sudo if the directory is root-owned
```

A version is kept when a config file your user has loaded (including `/etc/mise/config.toml`) still selects it, or when a process you can inspect runs from it, including one started through a runtime link such as `installs/<tool>/latest`. mise cannot see other users' configs, so it warns that another user who still uses a removed version has to reinstall it. A system copy of a version you also have in your own installs directory is pruned on its own; your copy, its downloads and its cache stay. Afterwards the system version links and shims are rebuilt, so shims for tools with no system version left are removed.

`mise reshim --system` also keeps the shim of a system version you have in your own installs directory too. It used to drop that shim, because the installed-version listing named only your copy. `--system` implies `--tools` and cannot be combined with `--configs`. Plain `mise prune` and `mise ls --prunable` still leave the system directory alone.

`mise uninstall` of a system version in a root-owned directory now uses `sudo` too, instead of failing with a permission error. If `sudo` is unavailable, the version stays listed as installed.

## Implementation notes

- Removal goes through the existing privileged helper (`mise __publish-system-install`) with a new `remove` request. As root it accepts only a plain version direc

title: feat(upgrade): add a per-tool bump option to exclude a tool from --bump
body:
`mise upgrade --bump` rewrites every tool's request past its configured range. For some tools that is never wanted: `node = "lts"` bumps to a non-LTS Current, Java vendor selectors bump to an unrelated version, and deliberately pinned tools get rewritten. Until now the only control was `-x` on every invocation, which tools that run `mise upgrade` for you (such as topgrade) cannot pass.

A tool can now opt out with a `bump` option:

```toml
[tools]
node = { version = "lts", bump = false }
```

`mise upgrade --bump` and `mise outdated --bump` then treat that tool like plain `mise upgrade`: it is upgraded within its request and mise.toml is not rewritten. Plain `upgrade` is unaffected. Naming the tool (`mise upgrade node --bump`, `mise outdated --bump node`) still bumps it, so an explicit request wins over the config.

`bump` is not available in `.tool-versions`, which has no table to hold it.

`mise outdated` now passes the tools it was asked about as a filter rather than only narrowing the toolset, so it can tell a named tool from a sweep. Output for existing configs is unchanged.

Discussion: https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15946

Verified with a new e2e test (`test_upgrade_bump_option`) and the existing bump tests. `cargo clippy` reports one unrelated error in `crates/mise-ui` that also fails on `origin/main`.

> 
> **Overview**
> Adds a per-tool **`bump`** option in `mise.toml` (default true). When set to **`false`**, broad **`mise upgrade --bump`** and **`mise outdated --bump`** behave like a normal in-range upgrade: the tool updates within its version request and **`mise.toml` is not rewritten**; **`--pin`** on a sweep also skips rewriting those entries.

> **Explicit tool names on the CLI still bump** even when `bump = false`. Outdated/upgrade paths use new **`OutdatedSelection`** fields (`named_tools`, `honor_bump_option`) and **`bump_applies` / `bump_enabled()`** to decide when backend-wide “past the range” resolution applies. User-facing hints and vulnerability warnings call out opt-out tools and how to bump them by name.

title: feat(audit): add `mise audit` and `mise upgrade --vulnerable`
body:
Closes https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15936, which asked for a vulnerability checker like `brew vulns` and `brew upgrade --vulnerable`.

## `mise audit`

`mise audit` looks up each tool version the current config uses in the [OSV.dev](https://osv.dev) database and lists the advisories that affect it. It exits 1 when it finds any, so it can gate CI.

```toml
[tools]
"npm:lodash" = "4.17.15"
go = "1.22.0"
zig = "0.13.0"
```

```
$ mise audit
Tool        Version  ID                   Severity  Fixed    Summary
npm:lodash  4.17.15  GHSA-35jh-r3h4-6jhm  high      4.17.21  Command Injection in lodash
npm:lodash  4.17.15  GHSA-p6mc-m468-83gw  high      4.17.19  Prototype Pollution in lodash
go          1.22.0   GO-2024-2887         -         1.21.11, 1.22.4  Unexpected behavior from Is methods for IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses in net/netip
...
mise not checked, no known advisory source: zig@0.13.0
mise 88 known vulnerabilities in 2 tools. Run `mise upgrade --vulnerable` to upgrade them.
```

(Output trimmed.) `mise audit node python` checks only those tools, and `--json` prints `{"vulnerabilities": [...], "unchecked": [...]}` with an `osv.dev` link for each advisory.

Which tools are covered:

- Package registry tools (`npm:`, `pipx:`, `cargo:`, `gem:`, `go:`, `dotnet:`) are looked up by package name. npm git and tarball sources are not registry packages, so they are listed as not checked.
- Tools released from GitHub (`github:`, `aqua:`, `packslip:`, `gitlab:`) are looked up by repository and version, which OSV matches against the release tags (`1.7` finds jq's `jq-1.7`). aqua tools use the repository their version resolves to, and packslip subprojects their repository. Go programs are also looked up as Go modules, which carry fixed versions. A `github:` or `gitlab:` tool with its own `api_url` (GitHub Enterprise, a self-hosted GitLab) is listed as not checked.
- Of the core tools, go (as the Go standard library), node, python, deno, bun and erlang are covered.
- Anything else (zig, `conda:`, `path:` and `ref:` versions…) is listed as **not checked**, never reported as clean.
- A configured version that does not resolve (a registry outage, a missing package) fails the audit rather than dropping out of it, and so does naming a tool that has no configured version (`mise audit node` asks for `node@VERSION`).

Severity is the advisory's own rating, or computed from its CVSS v3 vector; it is `-` when the record has neither. Duplicate advisories (a GHSA and its CVE alias) are shown once. mise doesn't order versions here: "Fixed" lists the fixed versions as the advisory gives them.

`mise audit` needs network access to `api.osv.dev` and fails in offline mode. It sends only tool names and versions, with URLs and credentials left out.

## `mise upgrade --vulnerable`

`--vulnerable` filters a normal `mise upgrade` down to the installed tools that have a known vulnerability. It composes with the existing flags:

With `"aqua:jqlang/jq" = "1"` in the config a

title: fix(lock): skip platforms a tool has no build for in --check
body:
`mise lock --check` failed on a lockfile that `mise lock` had just written whenever one tool had no build for a platform that another tool in the same lockfile had. Running `mise lock` again changed nothing, so the hint could not fix it.

```toml
[tools]
diffoci = "0.1.8" # no Windows build
gh = "2.103.3"
```

```sh
mise lock
mise lock --check   # before: "No lockfile URL found for diffoci@0.1.8 on platform windows-x64", exit 1
```

Without `--platform`, `--check` takes every platform any entry in the lockfile has and checks each tool against all of them. `mise lock` records nothing for a platform a tool has no build for, so `--check` could not tell that apart from an entry that went missing.

Now, when no platform is named (`--platform` or `lockfile_platforms`), `--check` skips a platform where a tool has entries on other platforms but none on that one. This is the rule `mise lock` already uses to decide when to warn about an unavailable platform. A tool with no entries at all still fails, and a named platform is always checked:

```sh
mise lock --check                        # passes
mise lock --check --platform windows-x64 # still reports the missing entry
```

Limits: the check is offline, so it cannot prove a tool has no build for a platform. An unnamed `--check` therefore also accepts an entry that is missing for another reason (for example one deleted by hand, or a failed cross-platform fetch) when the tool has entries elsewhere; naming the platform catches it. The current platform is always checked, and a platform whose lock options differ from the host's (per-platform `asset_pattern`, Swift distro) is still checked strictly. Recording skipped platforms in the lockfile would avoid this but changes the format, so this PR doesn't do it.

Extended `e2e/lockfile/test_lockfile_check`, which passes. Clippy and lint were not run.

Fixes https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15930

title: fix(deps): watch aube-workspace.yaml and workspace members' manifests
body:
`mise deps` with the `aube` provider now notices changes to `aube-workspace.yaml` and to workspace packages' `package.json`. Before, the provider only watched the root `package.json` and `aube-lock.yaml`, so editing a catalog, an override, or a member's dependencies could leave it "fresh" until the lockfile changed:

```
mise deps aube --explain   # Status: fresh
```

The provider now also lists the workspace file (`aube-workspace.yaml`, and `pnpm-workspace.yaml` when present, since aube falls back to it) and each member's `package.json` as sources. An explicit `sources = [...]` still replaces the defaults, and a missing or unreadable workspace keeps the previous behavior.

This mirrors the pnpm change in #15926. Member discovery now accepts either workspace file (`pnpm_member_manifests` became `workspace_member_manifests`).

Fixes discussion #15935.

## Test plan

- Unit test for member discovery from `aube-workspace.yaml`
- `mise run test:e2e test_deps` checks `mise deps --list` shows `aube-workspace.yaml` and a member manifest
