title: fix(lock): refuse version upgrades that drop a platform in generate mode
body:
`mise lock` now refuses a version upgrade that would drop a platform the old version supported, in the default `generate` mode as well as in `merge` mode.

Previously, if a tool's new release had no build for one platform (for example Renovate bumping Temurin to a release Adoptium had only published for some platforms), `mise lock` exited 0, pruned the old version and wrote a lockfile without that platform:

```text
✓ Pruned 1 stale version entry from mise.lock: java@temurin-21.0.0+35.0.LTS
exit 0
```

It now fails and leaves the lockfile untouched:

```text
mise ERROR failed to resolve java@temurin-21.0.1+12.0.LTS for windows-x64; refusing to replace locked version(s) temurin-21.0.0+35.0.LTS that support this platform
```

The check from #11664 only ran in `merge` mode. In `generate` mode (the default since #14893) no per-platform results exist and the stale versions are already gone from the rebuilt lockfile, so it could never fire. The new check compares the rebuilt lockfile against the previous one, and keeps the same rules as before: tools with several current versions, platforms excluded by `os`, and platforms the old version never locked are not refused.

Covered by unit tests only; an e2e needs a tool whose new release lacks a platform, which can't be reproduced offline.

Fixes discussion #15929.

title: docs(watch): say that ::: tasks share one watcher
body:
`mise watch --restart a ::: b` starts one watchexec over the union of both tasks' sources, so a change to `a`'s sources also restarts `b`. That is how it works today, but the help never said so, and the wording "rerun them whenever one of their `sources` changes" reads as per-task.

The `mise watch` help and CLI reference now state that tasks separated by `:::` share one watcher, and point to the ways to restart them independently: a separate `mise watch` per task (for example from a wrapper task), or `mise daemons`.

```
mise watch --restart a ::: b    # a change to a's sources restarts a and b
mise watch --restart a          # restarts only a
```

Docs only; no behavior change. Reported in discussion #15934.

title: fix(secrets): let tasks, including global ones, list keys from your own fnox config
body:
A key you keep in your own fnox config (fnox's global config, or a `fnox.toml` in or above your home directory) can now be listed by a task, and tasks in your global mise config can list secrets.

Since jdx/mise#15133 and jdx/mise#13974, neither worked. A project task that named one of your own keys failed with `X comes from your own fnox config, so the project cannot grant it`, and a task in `~/.config/mise/config.toml` that listed any secret failed with `which is not project config`. The only way to use such a key was to type `mise run --secrets KEY <task>` on every run.

Both refusals are removed:

```toml
# ~/.config/mise/config.toml
[tasks.gh-release]
secrets = ["GH_TOKEN"]          # now allowed in a global task
run = 'gh release create "$@"'
```

```toml
# a project's mise.toml
[secrets.fnox]

[tasks.eval]
secrets = ["OPENAI_API_KEY"]    # each developer's own key, from ~/.config/fnox/config.toml
run = './run-evals.sh'
```

`mise run eval` now starts the task with `OPENAI_API_KEY` set. The same applies to a `{{ secrets.NAME }}` reference in a task's `env`, and to tasks defined in system config or in a config file in or above your home directory.

## Why

The refusals did not protect a key from a project you do not trust. A task is the project's code and runs as you, so it can run `fnox get KEY` itself, or call `mise run --secrets KEY other-task`; only the declarative `secrets = [...]` form was blocked. They did block ordinary use: a team task that expects each developer's own API key, and personal tasks in the global config. The docs now describe the handling of your own keys as scoping, not protection.

## What stays the same

- `--secrets-all` still leaves your own keys out, so a run that asks for everything gets the project's keys only and a signed-out provider behind one of your keys cannot fail it. A task that names one of your own keys itself still receives it under `--secrets-all`; other tasks in the same run do not.
- Remote tasks (`git::`, `oci::`, URL includes) still cannot list secrets, and tasks started by hooks, `watch_files`, daemons or `mise bootstrap` are still refused.
- A task that lists secrets still needs a project that declares `[secrets.fnox]`, so a global task that lists secrets works only when run inside such a project.
- mise secrets is still experimental.

## Compatibility

`mise secrets ls --json` and `mise tasks validate` no longer report problems of kind `personal` or `not_project_config`.

## Tests

The secrets unit tests and the 20 e2e tests under `e2e/secrets` pass locally. `test_mise_secrets_personal_keys` and `test_mise_secrets_cli_grants` now expect these grants to work, and a new unit test covers a task that lists one of your own keys under `--secrets-all`. The full unit and e2e suites were not run locally.

title: fix(java): resolve sdkman temurin hotfixes by their canonical version
body:
`.sdkmanrc` entries for recent Temurin hotfix releases fail to install. With `idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools = ["java"]` and

```
java=25.0.5.1+2-tem
```

`mise install` reports `no metadata found for version temurin-25.0.5+102`. The #15877 fix for #15872 computed the catalog version as `hotfix * 100 + build`, but Adoptium changed how it encodes those builds, so the formula no longer matches (reported in discussion #14872).

The catalog (mise-java#647) now lists a Temurin hotfix under its canonical Java version, the same name SDKMAN uses: `temurin-25.0.5.1+2` and `temurin-25.0.4.1+1`, where it used to list `+100000002` and `+101`. mise therefore no longer translates a hotfix: `java=25.0.5.1+2-tem` resolves to `temurin-25.0.5.1`, which selects that release. Regular releases written with a `.0` fourth component, such as `21.0.13.0+9`, still map to `temurin-21.0.13+9`.

This needs the regenerated catalog, which is live now. Anyone pinning an old hotfix string, such as `temurin-25.0.4+101`, has to switch to `temurin-25.0.4.1+1`.

## Testing

Unit tests cover the hotfix and padded-version cases and the `.sdkmanrc` parse. `cargo clippy -p mise --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes on stable. I did not run an end-to-end install against the live catalog.

title: fix(config): name the config file in Tera deprecation warnings
body:
## Problem

`mise install` and `mise reshim` read every tracked config, including ones from other folders. A deprecated Tera helper in such a file warned with no hint of where it came from, and `mise config` and `mise doctor` don't list the file, so the user couldn't find what to fix:

```
mise WARN  deprecated [tera-v1-slice]: Tera v1 template helper `slice` is deprecated in mise templates. Use Tera 2 slice syntax like `array[start:end]` instead. This will be removed in mise 2027.4.0.
```

## Fix

Deprecation warnings raised while rendering a config's templates now name the file:

```
mise WARN  deprecated [tera-v1-slice]: Tera v1 template helper `slice` is deprecated in mise templates (in ~/src/adjacent/.mise.toml). Use ...
```

The warning is kept, since it is actionable. Rendering records the config path in a thread-local for the duration of the render (`mise_util::tera::template_source`).

Fixes discussion #15924.

title: fix(deps): watch pnpm-workspace.yaml and workspace members' manifests
body:
`mise deps` with the `pnpm` provider now notices changes to `pnpm-workspace.yaml` and to workspace packages' `package.json`. Before, the provider only watched the root `package.json` and `pnpm-lock.yaml`, so editing a catalog, an override, or a member's dependencies could leave it "fresh" until the lockfile changed:

```
mise deps pnpm --explain   # Status: fresh
```

The provider now also lists `pnpm-workspace.yaml` and each member's `package.json` (from the `packages` globs, including `!` exclusions) as sources. An explicit `sources = [...]` still replaces the defaults, and a missing or unreadable workspace falls back to the previous behavior. Members are found through the same discovery the Node workspace tasks use, so `node_modules` is never walked.

This mirrors the uv change in #15918. The issue's second request, pointing one uv provider at several independent projects, is not part of this PR.

Fixes #15922.

## Test plan

- Unit test for member manifest discovery (members, `!` excludes, non-workspace roots)
- `mise run test:e2e test_deps` checks `mise deps --list` shows `pnpm-workspace.yaml` and a member manifest

title: fix(ci): build linux release tarballs with the stable Rust toolchain
body:
The release PR for 2026.11.11 (#15873) fails: all six `build-tarball-linux-*` jobs die compiling `parking_lot_core v0.10.0` with `use of unstable library feature 'cfg_select'`.

The linux jobs never install a toolchain. `cross` builds with the runner image's default, which is Rust 1.94.0, while the workspace needs `rust-version = "1.95"`. The rattler bump (#15806) pulled in `parking_lot 0.13`, which is what exposed it.

This adds a `rustup update stable --no-self-update && rustup default stable` step to the linux job, the same one the test workflows use, before llvm-tools and the build.

Once merged, #15873 needs to pick this up (rebase or merge main) before its builds can pass.

> CI-only change that bumps the host Rust toolchain before existing cross builds; no application code or release artifact logic changes.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Adds a `Setup Rust toolchain` step** to the `build-tarball-linux` job in the release workflow, running `rustup update stable --no-self-update && rustup default stable` immediately after installing `cross` and before PGO/llvm and the tarball build.
> 
> **Cross** uses the runner’s default Rust toolchain, which was behind the workspace **`rust-version`**, so linux release builds were failing on dependencies that need a newer compiler (e.g. unstable `cfg_select` via **`parking_lot_core`**). title: fix(backend): resolve one compatible gem dependency graph when vendoring
body:
Stacked on #15907. When mise copies a gem tool's dependencies out of the Ruby's own gem directory so they survive a Ruby patch upgrade, it now picks one compatible set of dependency versions across the whole graph instead of settling each dependency in turn.

Before, each unresolved dependency took its newest candidate that did not conflict with what was already activated. A choice made early could still rule out a later dependency. For example, with a tool needing `a` and `b`, where `a-2` needs `c-2`, `a-1` needs `c-1`, and every `b` needs `c-1`, taking `a-2` first left `b` with no valid `c`. Now the script searches the graph with backtracking, newest candidate first, and copies exactly the set it settles on (`a-1`, `b-2`, `c-1`). If no compatible set exists, the install still succeeds: the script warns (saying whether it found a real conflict or gave up) and copies the newest candidate of each dependency instead. The search is capped so a pathological graph cannot hang an install.

The search checks requirements on already-chosen gems first and branches on the most constrained dependency, so a pinned gem is not buried behind unrelated choices.

Tests run the script against a hand-built `GEM_HOME` and Ruby gem directory with an installed Ruby (they print `skipping` and pass when none is found):
- the conflicting-candidate case (root needs `a >= 1` and `c = 1`; `a-2` needs `c = 2`)
- backtracking across the graph (the example above)
- the warn-and-copy-newest fallback when nothing is compatible, and a pinned gem queued behind unrelated choices
- extensions land in the copied spec's `extension_dir`, with `gem.build_complete`, when `Gem.default_ext_dir_for` is stubbed to point outside the gem directory; no compiling involved

`cargo test --lib vendor_` passes. Clippy is clean for `src/backend/gem.rs`; the local toolchain flags an unrelated lint in `crates/mise-ui`, so the full `-D warnings` run did not finish here.

title: fix(config): stay quiet about ignored settings in tracked configs of other folders
body:
## Problem

When a config tracked from another folder sets a global-only setting (for example `github.credential_command` in a git worktree copy of the global config), unrelated commands warn about it:

```
mise WARN  github.credential_command in non-global config /path/copy/mise/config.toml is ignored for security reasons
```

`mise install` and `mise bootstrap` hit this through the reshim step, which loads tracked configs, and the warning repeats for every mise process a hook or task starts. The file's settings never apply to the current folder, so the user can't act on it.

## Fix

Resolving settings for the root of a tracked config now runs with the "ignored setting" warnings suppressed. The warning is unchanged where the file really applies, e.g. `mise ls` inside the folder that owns it.

Fixes discussion #15914.

title: feat(task): add if_pool to take a lock only where a pool is declared
body:
A task that names a shared lock, such as `lock = "xcode"`, takes that lock on every machine. Where `task.lock_pools` doesn't declare the name, it is one exclusive lock shared by every task on the machine that uses it. A task author who wants to join a pool only where one exists had no way to say so. The result on other machines was either needless serialization or turns taken with an unrelated task.

`lock` tables now accept `if_pool`. With `if_pool = true` the task takes the lock only on a machine whose `task.lock_pools` declares that name, and runs without it everywhere else:

```toml
[tasks.benchmarks]
run = "..."
lock = { name = "xcode", if_pool = true }
```

With `xcode = "2"` in the global config, two concurrent `mise run benchmarks` start together. On a machine with no `xcode` pool, the task takes no lock. It combines with `count`, and the default (`false`) keeps today's behavior.

The task author decides this because they know whether the lock protects something unique. A machine-level default for undeclared names would also change locks that rely on a single holder, so it is left out of this change.

Discussion: https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15910

## Testing

- `reads_if_pool` unit test for parsing and serializing.
- `e2e/tasks/test_task_lock_pools` covers a task with and without a declared pool, and with `count`.
- `workspace clippy` fails in `crates/mise-ui` (`unnecessary_lazy_evaluations`, a file this PR doesn't touch), so clippy was not verified for the changed crates.

title: fix(task): don't fail command inputs when a loaded machine delays the pipe drain
body:
A task whose `cache.command_inputs` runs a short script could fail before starting with `command output pipes did not close within 10s`, even though the script had exited and closed its pipes. It happened on heavily loaded machines (many tasks computing cache keys at once while every core was busy), and rerunning the same `mise run` passed.

After the command exits, mise waits up to 10 seconds of wall-clock time for its output readers to reach EOF. That deadline was checked before the output channel was polled, so if the process was descheduled past it, mise failed even when the pipes were already closed or had output waiting.

Now the channel is always polled first, and once the deadline passes the readers get one extra 1-second grace window before mise reports the pipes as held. A grandchild that really holds the pipes open still fails and is still killed, about 1 second later than before.

Only `execute_hashes_async` is affected. The other two drain loops just abandon the readers at the deadline and never raise this error.

I could not reproduce the load-dependent failure itself. The new test (`..._ignores_late_deadline_when_pipes_closed`) forces a zero-length deadline on a finished command and failed before this change. It passes now, along with the existing drain tests.

Closes the problem reported in discussion #15867.

Co-authored-by: brodienguyen <32996052+brodienguyen@users.noreply.github.com>

> Narrows false positives in command-input hashing drain logic; genuine stuck-pipe behavior is unchanged aside from ~1s later failure.

>

After the main deadline, it grants a new **`PIPE_DRAIN_GRACE`** (1s) window so reader tasks can deliver already-buffered output before mise treats the pipes as stuck and kills the process group. title: registry: add rtk-proxy
body:
`rtk` looks for its `rtk-proxy` daemon next to itself or on `PATH`, but the daemon ships as separate `rtk-proxy-<target>` archives in the same `rtk-ai/rtk` release, so installing `rtk` with mise never provides it. This adds an `rtk-proxy` shorthand:

mise use -g rtk-proxy

The entry uses the `github:rtk-ai/rtk` backend with a per-platform `asset_pattern` (macOS, Linux musl, Windows x64; the release has no Windows arm64 proxy). aqua has no recipe for the proxy. Verified by installing 1.2.0 on linux-x64 and running the binary; `mise ls-remote github:rtk-ai/rtk` lists versions.

Note: the proxy is licensed separately (BUSL-1.1, converting to Apache-2.0 on 2030-09-09; production use is allowed alongside `rtk`, but not as a paid or hosted service).

title: fix(bootstrap): report an unresolvable cask per entry instead of aborting
body:
Fixes #15900

One cask that cannot be resolved, such as one from a tap whose repository is returning 404, no longer hides every other package.

Before, with this config:

```toml
[bootstrap.packages]
"brew:jq" = "latest"
"brew-cask:nonexistent-owner/tap/example" = "latest"
```

`mise bootstrap packages status` printed only the fetch error and exited 1, `apply` stopped after the brew part, and `mise bootstrap` never reached repos, dotfiles, tools or hooks.

Now the bad entry gets its own line and the rest are reported as usual:

```
brew      jq                                        missing
brew-cask nonexistent-owner/tap/example             error (failed to fetch Homebrew cask ...)
```

- `status` shows `error` with the message (`"state": "error"` in `--json`), and `status --missing` exits non-zero.
- `apply` records the unresolved entry as a failure, still applies the other packages, and exits non-zero at the end.
- The docs sentence about failing managers now mentions this case.

The cask manager's status query turns a resolve failure into a new per-package `PackageState::Unresolved`, which the status, bootstrap, driver and resource code handle.

Added `e2e/cli/test_bootstrap_packages_unresolved_cask` (one good cask, one that 404s); it passes. `cargo test -p mise-system --lib` could not build here (missing `lua51`), and clippy only reports an existing `mise-ui` lint that also fails on main.

title: fix(http): verify downloads against checksum_url at install
body:
Fixes the gap reported in discussion jdx/mise#15901.

## Problem

For an `http:` tool, `checksum_url` / `checksum_expr` were read only by `mise lock`. `mise install` without a `checksum` or a `mise.lock` entry never compared the download to the published checksum. With a lockfile enabled it recorded the download's own blake3 digest instead, so a wrong or tampered artifact installed with exit 0.

## Change

When nothing else pins the download (no `checksum`, no lockfile entry) and `checksum_url` is set, install now resolves the published checksum for the current platform, verifies the download against it, and records it in `mise.lock`.

```toml
[tools."http:my-tool"]
version = "1.0.0"
url = "https://example.com/my-tool-1.0.0.tar.gz"
checksum_url = "https://example.com/SHA256SUMS"
```

A mismatch now fails the install with a checksum error. If the published checksum cannot be resolved (unreachable, no matching entry), install fails instead of silently skipping verification. A `checksum` or lockfile entry still takes precedence. The docs for `checksum_url` say so.

## Testing

`e2e/backend/test_http_checksum_url_install` covers mismatch, unresolvable, and matching checksums. `test_http_lock_install_verify` and `test_http_lock_skips_unresolved` still pass.

title: fix(backend): copy gem tool dependencies out of Ruby's gem directory
body:
`gem:` tools no longer break after a Ruby patch upgrade when one of their dependencies was installed only in the old Ruby's own gem directory.

Before, with `parser` installed by hand into Ruby 4.0.9 and `mise use gem:rubocop`, upgrading to Ruby 4.0.10 made `rubocop` fail with `Gem::MissingSpecError: Could not find 'parser'`. `GEM_HOME` points at the tool's `libexec`, but RubyGems counts gems in the active Ruby's gem directory as installed, so `parser` was never copied into `libexec`. The wrapper's minor version link then pointed at a Ruby that lacks it.

After `gem install`, mise now walks the tool's runtime dependencies and copies any that resolved outside `libexec` (other than default gems, which ship with every Ruby) into `libexec`, including native extension builds. Reusing bundled gems instead of rebuilding them, from #15644, is kept.

Fixes #15904

I checked this by hand with the debug binary on Ruby 4.0.10 with `parser` 3.3.10.0 installed by hand: `libexec/gems` now contains `parser-3.3.10.0`. The new `test_gem_ruby_deps_slow` e2e test mirrors that, but I could not run it to completion here because compiling Ruby fails in my sandbox.

> **Medium Risk**
> Touches gem install post-processing and copies files from Ruby's gem paths into tool installs; failures are best-effort but incorrect vendoring could still leave subtle runtime gem errors.
> 
> **Overview**
> **gem:** installs now **vendor runtime dependencies** that RubyGems satisfied only from the active Ruby's gem tree into the tool's `libexec` (`GEM_HOME`), so gems like `rubocop` keep working after a Ruby patch bump when a dependency (e.g. `parser`) was installed globally on the old patch.

It resolves a compatible dependency set (backtracking, with a best-effort fallback and warning), copies gems/specs/cache (and native **extensions** when they live outside the gem dir) into `libexec`, and skips default gems. Failures are **non-fatal** (warning only).

title: fix(java): map sdkman temurin releases with a .0 fourth segment
body:
`.sdkmanrc` files with a recent regular Temurin release failed to install, because SDKMAN now writes a `.0` fourth segment for those too:

```
java=21.0.13.0+9-tem   # before: no metadata found for version temurin-21.0.13.0
java=8.0.512.0+9-tem   # before: no metadata found for version temurin-8.0.512.0
```

The earlier hotfix mapping only handled a non-zero fourth segment (`26.0.2.1+1` → `temurin-26.0.2+101`) and returned nothing for `.0`, so those versions fell through unmapped. A `.0` fourth segment now maps to the three-part version plus its build number (`temurin-21.0.13+9`), which matches the catalog entry `temurin-21.0.13+9.0.LTS` without also matching a hotfix build such as `21.0.13+101`.

Fixes the follow-up reported in [#15872](https://github.com/jdx/mise/issues/15872#issuecomment-7004114311).

title: fix(upgrade): see a new commit of an npm git source tracking HEAD
body:
Fixes #15903

## Problem

A tool installed from a git source that tracks the default branch (`npm:git+ssh://…` with `version = "latest"`) is sometimes not upgraded, and `mise upgrade --prune` then leaves the old commit behind:

```
$ mise upgrade --prune
mise All tools are up to date      # the remote has a newer commit
```

`mise upgrade` compared the installed commit and the new one as version strings. A commit SHA is not a version, so a new commit that happened to sort below the installed one was reported as up to date. Whether an upgrade ran, and so whether `--prune` had anything to remove, depended on how the two hashes sorted.

## Fix

A git source tracking HEAD now declares its versions unordered, as tarball sources already do: a different commit is a newer one.

## Testing

- `git_head_and_tarball_versions_are_unordered` asserts the new classification; it fails against the old predicate.
- `test_npm_git` advances the remote six times and checks that each `mise upgrade --prune` installs the new commit and removes the old one. It depends on the random SHAs, so the unit test is the deterministic guard.
- I reproduced the "All tools are up to date" output on the unfixed build with a local `git+file://` remote.

> **Fixes npm git sources pinned to `latest` so `mise upgrade` treats any new commit as an upgrade**, instead of comparing commit SHAs as ordered version strings (which could mark a newer remote as "up to date" when its hash sorts below the installed one).

title: feat(system-packages): fetch private release assets for tap download strategies
body:
Fixes #15889.

A tap formula that ships its own download strategy, typically to fetch assets from a private GitHub release, could not be installed: the strategy class could not be loaded, and a source whose URL named a strategy was rejected outright.

```ruby
require_relative "../custom_download_strategy" # requires "download_strategy"

class Widget < Formula
  url "https://github.com/acme/private/releases/download/widget-1.0/widget-1.0.tar.gz",
      using: PrivateReleaseDownloadStrategy
```

Now:

- The metadata shim loads such a tap: `require "download_strategy"` and the Homebrew strategy base classes are stubbed, and the `using:` class on the source URL and on a `bottle do` `root_url` is recorded.
- mise does not run the Ruby strategy. When the URL is a GitHub release asset (`github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/download/<tag>/<file>`), it resolves the asset through the GitHub API and downloads it with the credentials mise is configured with (`github.credential_command`, `MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN`, ...), then checks the sha256 as before. This covers both source builds and bottles.
- Any other URL with a custom strategy, and the symbol strategies (`:git`, ...), are still rejected with the existing message. Symbol options such as `:nounzip` are ignored as before.

Stacked on #15893 (it adds the bottle metadata this extends).

Verified: the shim output for a private repro tap, `jdx/homebrew-mise-repro-private` (source and bottle both record the strategy), and that the asset API route returns the pinned sha256. The Ruby-driven unit tests cannot run in my sandbox (nested sandbox is denied, as on main), so `records_custom_download_strategies` has not run locally; I did not run an end-to-end install.

title: feat(bootstrap): update mise before tools with --self-update and tool_update.self_update_first
body:
Automatic tool updates and mise's own updates run independently, so tools can update with an older mise. This adds two opt-in ways to update mise first. Defaults are unchanged.

## `mise bootstrap --self-update`

Updates mise, then runs the same bootstrap again in a new process so every phase uses the new version. If the update fails, nothing is applied. It is skipped by `--dry-run` and for subcommands.

```sh
mise bootstrap --self-update --upgrade   # mise, then every package and tool
```

## `tool_update.self_update_first`

When on, each automatic tool update pass (from a shell prompt or the `tool-update` service) first checks for a newer mise the way `self_update.auto` does, using its `check_duration`, and installs it. The tools then update with the new mise. If the mise update fails, the tools are skipped until the next interval and `mise doctor` shows the error.

```toml
[settings]
self_update.auto = true
tool_update.self_update_first = true
```

It needs `self_update.auto` on, and is skipped in CI, offline and prefer-offline modes, and for packager-installed mise. The update runs in the detached update process, never in the prompt hook itself.

From jdx/mise discussion 15895.

## Validation

`cargo check -p mise` and `mise run build` pass; docs, schema and man page are regenerated. The self-update path itself was not exercised end to end (it needs a downloadable release), and no tests were added.

title: feat(system-packages): support virtualenv_install_with_resources in source builds
body:
Formulae that use Homebrew's `Language::Python::Virtualenv` can now be built from source. Before, a formula such as `qmk/qmk/qmk` stopped with:

```
formula uses `virtualenv_install_with_resources (install-time helper)`, which mise's source-build shim does not support
```

The shim now implements `virtualenv_create` and `virtualenv_install_with_resources`, following Homebrew's `Library/Homebrew/language/python.rb`:

- A venv is created in the keg's `libexec` from the formula's `python@3.x` dependency (falling back to `python3` on `PATH`), with `--system-site-packages --without-pip`.
- Each `resource` is downloaded, verified against its declared sha256, staged, and installed one at a time in declaration order using `pip install --no-deps --no-binary=:all:`, so every runtime package is a verified resource. As in Homebrew, pip builds in an isolated environment by default (fetching a backend such as setuptools itself; those build requirements are not covered by the formula sha256 checks, as in Homebrew); `build_isolation: false` switches to `--no-build-isolation --no-index`. `without:`, `start_with:` and `end_with:` are honored, in the order given.
- The formula's own source is installed last, and the console scripts it creates are symlinked into the keg's `bin`. Scripts keep the venv's python in their shebang, which is already the final keg path.

The empty `Language` stub shared with the metadata shim is unchanged (a test keeps the two identical); the implementation reopens it afterwards.

Part of #15887.

## Testing

A new test builds a fake formula whose resource is a local sdist with an in-tree PEP 517 backend. It checks the console script is linked into `bin` and runs, importing the resource. Breaking the linking step makes it fail. It runs the real shim under Ruby and the system Python, with the resource pre-seeded in the download cache. It does not exercise a real external build backend.

Not verified: a real `qmk` build, which needs network access and a full toolchain. Several `brew::tap` tests fail in this sandbox with "Permission denied" both before and after the change.

+        private

+      end

+      def virtualenv_create(venv_root, python = "python", formula = self, system_site_packages: true, without_pip: true)

+      def virtualenv_install_with_resources(system_site_packages: true, without: nil, start_with: nil, end_with: nil, using: nil)

+        excluded = Array(without).map(&:to_s)

+        tail = last.filter_map { |n| by_name[n] }

title: feat(system-packages): pour bottles declared by third-party taps
body:
Formulae from third-party taps were always built from source, even when the tap publishes bottles. The tap shim now reads the formula's `bottle do` block (`root_url`, `rebuild`, per-tag `sha256`) and builds bottle URLs with Homebrew's rules: `ghcr.io` roots by blob digest, other roots as `name-version.tag.bottle.tar.gz`, defaulting to the tap's GitHub release. The ghcr bearer token is now sent only to `ghcr.io`.

Stacked on the dotless-version PR (same file). Fixes #15887. Part of #15889. Private release assets still need GitHub token auth and are not handled.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: unavailable.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes bottle selection, download auth, and tap install paths where wrong tag/cellar choice could install incompatible bottles or fall back to source unexpectedly; logic is heavily tested but affects real package installs.
> 
> **Overview**
> Third-party tap formulae can now **pour prebuilt bottles** when the tap’s Ruby metadata shim successfully parses a `bottle do` block, instead of always building from source.
> 
> The tap metadata shim learns **`BottleSpec`** (root URL, rebuild, per-tag checksums/cellar) and emits bottle file URLs using Homebrew rules (**ghcr.io** blob paths vs `name-version.tag.bottle.tar.gz`). Formulas with **`post_install`**, **`pour_bottle?` restrictions**, missing roots, or unsupported root options still export **no bottles** and stay on the source path. Metadata from tap source is flagged with **`from_tap_source`** because it lacks per-tag `variations`.
> 
> Bottle picking moved to **`select_bottle`**: core/published tap JSON still prefers the newest compatible host tag (with **cellar path** checks for taps); tap-source metadata only accepts the **exact host tag** or **`all`** (and on Linux from tap source, native arch bottles are skipped except **`all`**). Downloads send the anonymous **ghcr.io bearer token** only for **ghcr.io** URLs.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit dede142e6b1b1c4f3f6f6d5fc523c4bd8b8ad029. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>

title: fix(system-packages): infer a dotless version from a tap formula URL
body:
A tap formula whose archive is named like `LUFA-210130.tar.gz` failed with "could not infer formula version". A plain number that ends the filename is now read as the version (`210130`), as Homebrew does; dotted versions still take priority.

Part of #15887. `qmk` itself still cannot be installed: it needs `virtualenv_install_with_resources`, which the source-build shim reports as unsupported.

title: feat(pypi): allow exclude-newer = false on an index
body:
`mise lock` fails for a `pypi` tool whose package comes from an index that serves no upload times, such as a PEP 503 HTML index like GitLab's. With `minimum_release_age` set (it defaults to `24h`), uv treats every release from such an index as newer than the cutoff and filters it out. The only workaround was `minimum_release_age = "0s"`, which switches the cutoff off for the whole dependency graph.

An entry in `indexes` now accepts `exclude-newer = false`, which mise passes through to the generated `[[tool.uv.index]]` table. uv then skips the cutoff for packages from that index only:

```toml
[tools."pypi:zensical"]
version = "0.1.2"
with = ["my-zensical-theme==1.2.3"]
indexes = [{ name = "private", url = "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/1/packages/pypi/simple", explicit = true, exclude-newer = false }]
sources = { my-zensical-theme = { index = "private" } }
```

Only `false` is accepted. Any other value, including a time-based cutoff, is rejected with an error that points to `minimum_release_age`, so there is a single place to set a cutoff. The schema and the `indexes` docs are updated.

Requested in discussion jdx/mise#15883.

Co-authored-by: sisp <sisp@users.noreply.github.com>

title: fix(unuse): remove tools from the global file that declares them
body:
`mise unuse -g` always edited `~/.config/mise/config.toml`, even when `mise use -g` had put the tool elsewhere. With a split global config this silently did nothing:

```toml
# ~/.config/mise/config.toml
[settings.write_targets]
tools = "{{ config_source | dirname }}/conf.d/tools.toml"
```

```sh
mise use -g jq     # writes conf.d/tools.toml
mise unuse -g jq   # before: exit 0, nothing removed
```

Now `unuse -g` (and `unuse` run from `$HOME`) removes the tool from every global config file that declares it, the same files `use -g --remove` considers. System and override configs are skipped. If no global file declares the tool, it falls back to `config.toml` as before.

`unuse` also now warns `none of the given tools are declared in <files>; nothing was removed` when nothing matched, instead of exiting 0 silently. This applies to all `unuse` modes.

Fixes discussion jdx/mise#15881.

Validation: new e2e `test_unuse_global_write_targets` (single target file, a tool declared in two global files, and the warning) and the existing `test_unuse` pass. Clippy was not clean locally because of an existing `mise-ui` lint that also fails on origin/main.

title: ci: stop using pull_request_target in workflows
body:
Public-repo `pull_request_target` workflows are blocked by default from December 2, 2026. This removes every use of the trigger in mise.

- Remove `conventional-commits` and `draft-limit`; neither is a required check. PR titles should still follow Conventional Commits because they feed the release notes, and `AGENTS.md` and `docs/contributing.md` now say CI no longer checks them.
- Run `release-window` and `auto-merge-release` on `pull_request`. They only act on the same-repo `release` PR, which gets a write token and secrets under `pull_request`. `release-window` skips fork PRs, which cannot set statuses; mise does not accept them. The `release-window` status keeps the same name and head-commit key, so the required check is unchanged.

title: fix(config): accept legacy tool names in enable_tools and disable_tools
body:
`MISE_ENABLE_TOOLS=nodejs` used to leave node off `PATH`, even though `[tools]` accepts `nodejs` as a spelling of `node`:

```sh
# mise.toml: [tools] node = "24.19.0"
MISE_ENABLE_TOOLS=node   mise x -- sh -c 'command -v node'   # works
MISE_ENABLE_TOOLS=nodejs mise x -- sh -c 'command -v node'   # node not on PATH
```

`enable_tools` and `disable_tools` entries were only trimmed, then compared as written against the canonical tool name, so `nodejs`, `golang`, `dotnet-core` and a `core:` prefix matched nothing. The same mismatch meant `disable_tools = ["nodejs"]` did not disable node.

The filters now resolve those spellings the same way `[tools]` does. `unalias_backend` moves into `mise-config` so `mise-settings` can call it; `crate::backend::unalias_backend` re-exports it, so existing callers are unchanged.

Fixes #15875

Tests: a unit test for the normalization and `e2e/config/test_config_enable_tools_legacy_names`; the existing `test_config_enable_tool*` e2e tests still pass.

title: fix(oci): relocate uv long-path launchers in pipx layers
body:
`mise oci push` could produce an image where a `pypi:` tool (for example `pypi:sqlfluff`) failed with `exec: <host path>/.mise-uv/.venv/bin/python: not found`. This showed up in CI, where the checkout path is long.

When the venv's python path is too long for a shebang, uv writes a two-line launcher instead:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
'''exec' '/builds/.../.mise/installs/pypi-sqlfluff/4.4.0/.mise-uv/.venv/bin/python' "$0" "$@"
' '''
```

The layer builder only rewrote the first line, so the second kept the host path. It now rewrites the `'''exec'` line too. Local installs have short paths and get a normal shebang, which is why they worked.

`TOOL_LAYER_RELOCATION_VERSION` goes from 2 to 3, so layers pushed earlier with the broken launcher are not reused from `--cache-from`.

Fixes #15869

## Testing

- Added `relocates_uv_long_path_launcher`. The `mise-oci` and `mise` lib relocation tests pass (15).
- Clippy was not run on the touched crates: it stops on an unrelated `mise-ui` lint on this toolchain.

title: fix(task): run each tool's rustup check once per mise run
body:
With `rust` in the config, every `mise run` started `rustup show profile` and `rustup component list --installed` twice each, even for a task that never uses rust (reported in discussion 15870). `mise run` installs missing tools in two passes (the config toolset, then the tasks' tools), and each pass asked rustup about every configured rust toolchain.

The rust backend now remembers, for the current process, that a toolchain's rustup state check passed, so `mise run noop` starts rustup once instead of twice. The cache is keyed by the resolved `CARGO_HOME`/`RUSTUP_HOME` runtime, the install path and the request options, so a different project's rust homes or components are checked separately. The cheap checks (install marker, symlink target) still run on every pass, and a failed check is retried. Other backends are unchanged.

`mise exec` already checked once and is unchanged. Skipping the check for tools a run doesn't need is a larger design question left open in the discussion.

Validation: unit tests cover a passed check running once, a failed check being retried, and separate keys not sharing a result; the existing rust backend tests pass. I did not measure rustup process counts end to end.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: 2.1.326.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Process-local cache only affects rust install satisfaction; failed states still re-query rustup, and keys separate homes/options.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Fixes duplicate rustup subprocess calls during `mise run`** when rust is in the config. Each run used to hit the toolchain twice (config toolset pass + task tools pass), spawning `rustup show profile` and component/target list queries repeatedly.
> 
> The expensive rustup state verification is extracted into **`rustup_state_satisfied`** and wrapped with a **per-process memo** (`check_once` + `VERIFIED_RUSTUP_STATE`). Keys combine the resolved runtime homes, install path, and tool options so different projects or option sets stay isolated. **Failed checks are retried**; **passed checks are skipped** on later passes in the same process. Cheaper checks (install marker, symlink target) still run every time.
> 
> New **unit tests** cover one-time reuse on success, retry on failure, and separate cache keys.
>

title: fix(java): map sdkman temurin hotfix versions to the catalog build
body:
`.sdkmanrc` entries for Temurin hotfix releases now install. With `idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools = ["java"]` and

```
java=26.0.2.1+1-tem
```

`mise install` failed with `no metadata found for version temurin-26.0.2.1`. mise dropped the `+1` build and looked up `temurin-26.0.2.1`, but the Java catalog lists that release as `temurin-26.0.2+101` (the hotfix number followed by the two-digit build; the same shape appears as `21.0.12+101` and `25.0.4+101`). It now resolves to `temurin-26.0.2+101`.

Only Temurin is mapped, since it's the only vendor whose catalog shape I checked. Other vendors and three-component versions parse as before.

Fixes #15872

title: ci: update the Rust toolchain before building mise
body:
CI builds of `main` and of every open PR are failing. `trusted / build-ubuntu`, the release-plz run on main, and the registry and vfox builds stop with:

```
error[E0658]: use of unstable library feature `cfg_select`
  --> parking_lot_core-0.10.0/src/thread_parker/mod.rs:78:1
```

#15806 updated rattler, which pulled in `parking_lot_core` 0.10.0. That version needs Rust 1.95 (the same version as this repo's `rust-version`), but the runners ship 1.94. The jobs build with `--ignore-rust-version`, which skips the version check, so the failure shows up as a compiler error.

This adds `rustup update stable --no-self-update` before the `cargo build --all-features --ignore-rust-version` step in `test-impl.yml`, `test-vfox-impl.yml`, `registry-impl.yml` and `release-plz.yml`.

I did not run the workflows locally; the checks on this PR are the test. If `rustup update` does not get the runner to 1.95, the next step is pinning or reverting the rattler update.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: claude-code_2-1-326_agent.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

> **Overview**

> 
> This targets failures from dependencies (e.g. **`parking_lot_core` 0.10**) that need **Rust ≥ 1.95** while runners still ship an older stable toolchain—even when builds use **`--ignore-rust-version`**.
>

title: feat(github): hint in mise token github when gh keeps its token in the keyring
body:
When `gh auth login` stores its token in the system keyring (macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager), `hosts.yml` keeps only the user. mise never runs `gh auth token` on its own, so `mise token github` printed `github.com: (none)` even though `gh auth status` succeeded, with no hint why.

Now, when `hosts.yml` has a logged-in user for the host but no token, `mise token github` still prints `(none)` on stdout and adds a hint on stderr:

```
$ mise token github
github.com: (none)
hint: gh is logged in to github.com but keeps its token in the system keyring, which mise does not read.
Set `credential_command = 'gh auth token --hostname "$MISE_CREDENTIAL_HOST"'` under [settings.github].
See https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/github-tokens.html#gh-keyring
```

The hint is shown only when no token source supplied one, `github.gh_cli_tokens` is enabled, and `hosts.yml` has a user but no token for that host. It goes to stderr so scripts reading stdout are unaffected, and `--raw` behaves as before. mise still does not run `gh` by default.

Tested with `mise run test:e2e test_token_github` (new cases for the hint, a different host, `gh_cli_tokens=false` and an env token). `cargo clippy` reports one error in `crates/mise-ui`, which also fails on `origin/main`; nothing from this change.

Suggested by FalkWoldmann in discussion jdx/mise#15816.

title: fix(shim): create shims for path: tool versions
body:
`mise reshim` now creates shims for tools configured with a `path:` version.

Previously, a config such as:

```toml
[tools]
"github:owner/ccmux" = "path:~/src/ccmux/bin"
```

left the shims directory empty. `mise which ccmux` and `mise env` found the executable, but a shim-based shell reported `command not found: ccmux`, because shim generation only listed installs found in the install directory, and a `path:` version has none. `get_desired_shims` now also lists the bins of configured `path:` versions.

Fixes #15798

## Test plan

- New e2e test `e2e/cli/test_reshim_path_version`: configures a `path:` tool, runs `mise reshim`, and checks the shim exists and runs.
- Ran it with `test_reshim_stale_install` and `test_shims`; they pass.

title: fix(bootstrap): let the host choose its config environments when no remote env is set
body:
`mise bootstrap remote` ran the host's `mise bootstrap` with an empty `MISE_ENV=` whenever neither `--remote-env` nor `mise_env` was set. An empty `MISE_ENV` selects no environment, so the host's own miserc `env` (global or project) was never read. A plain `mise bootstrap` on the host loaded those environments; through `bootstrap remote` it loaded none.

Now, with no `mise_env` or `--remote-env`, mise runs the host command as `env -u MISE_ENV ...`. An inherited `MISE_ENV` on the host is still cleared, and the host's miserc picks its environments. With either set, the command is unchanged (`MISE_ENV=server,linux`).

```
# before
env 'MISE_TRUSTED_CONFIG_PATHS=...' 'MISE_ENV=' mise --cd ... bootstrap
# after
env -u MISE_ENV 'MISE_TRUSTED_CONFIG_PATHS=...' mise --cd ... bootstrap
```

The remote docs now say the host chooses when neither is set. Follow-up to #12182, reported in [discussion 12179](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12179#discussioncomment-19695572) by @Guria.

Co-authored-by: Guria <36270+Guria@users.noreply.github.com>

> **Medium Risk**

>

title: feat(dotfiles): approve harmless values in the history secret scan
body:
Tracked dotfile history refuses to publish saved versions that look like they hold a secret. When the match is a harmless placeholder, such as `"CONTEXT7_API_KEY" = "ctx7_api_key"` in `~/.codex/config.toml`, every later save of the file creates a new blob with the same placeholder and automatic sync fails again. The only ways out were `--allow-plaintext-history` for one sync, or the global `history.allow_plaintext_history`, which also turns off the check for real secrets and for plaintext copies of files now marked for encryption.

This adds a global-only setting that approves specific values:

```toml
[settings.history]
allow_secret_values = ["ctx7_api_key"]
```

The scan blanks each listed value before it looks at a line, so:

- the placeholder no longer blocks the sync, in any file or saved version;
- the same key with a different value, or a real token on the same line, is still refused;
- the encryption check and the rest of the history scan stay on.

Entries are literal strings and have to be the value, not the key name. Like `history.allow_plaintext_history`, mise ignores the setting in project config. It can also be set with `MISE_HISTORY_ALLOW_SECRET_VALUES` (comma-separated). The refusal message now mentions the setting.

I chose a global list over a per-entry option because per-entry approvals live in the history manifest that machines merge, which is a much larger change. A per-entry option could follow if wanted.

Discussion: https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15788

Tested with unit tests in `secrets.rs` and `e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_secret_scan`, which now covers a listed value passing and a real token next to it still blocking.

title: fix(activate): detect Git Bash when mise runs behind the Scoop shim
body:
Fixes #15799.

## Problem

With mise installed through Scoop, `eval "$(mise activate bash)"` in Git Bash fills `PATH` with broken entries such as `D:/c/Scoop/apps/mise/current/bin`. Bash splits these on `:` into `D` and `/c/Scoop/...`. Activating with the real binary (`D:\Scoop\apps\mise\current\bin\mise.exe`) works.

## Cause

mise only converts `PATH` to POSIX form when it recognizes the shell it runs under, and it checked only its immediate parent process. Scoop's `shims\mise.exe` starts the real mise as a child, so the parent was the shim, no shell was detected, and native Windows paths reached bash unconverted.

## Fix

When looking for the launching shell, skip any `mise.exe` ancestors (up to four) and use the first other process. The MSYS/Cygwin runtime-DLL check is unchanged, so PowerShell, WSL and BusyBox are still not treated as emulators.

## Testing

- Unit test for the launcher check; `windows_posix` tests pass on Linux and on Windows.
- `cargo clippy -p mise-util --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean on Windows, which compiles the Windows-only `parent_executable`.
- Not run: an end-to-end repro through a real Scoop shim. The Windows box has no Scoop or mise installed.

> Fixes broken `PATH` entries when mise is invoked via Scoop’s shim in Git Bash by **walking the Windows parent-process chain** instead of trusting only the immediate parent.
>

It uses **`GetProcessTimes`** so a reused pid that started after the child is treated as a dead end, not the real launcher. The first non-shim executable is returned—typically the shell—so MSYS/Git Bash detection and POSIX `PATH` mapping work again.

title: feat(bootstrap): install and remove MacPorts ports with the macports package manager
body:
Macs that use [MacPorts](https://www.macports.org/) instead of Homebrew can now declare their ports in `[bootstrap.packages]` and have `mise bootstrap` install them like any other manager. Requested in discussion #15818.

```toml
[bootstrap.packages]
"macports:git" = "latest"
"macports:ripgrep" = "latest"
"macports:bc" = { state = "absent" }
```

```sh
mise bootstrap packages apply --manager macports --dry-run
mise bootstrap packages apply --manager macports
```

## Behavior

- **Availability:** macOS with `port` on `PATH` or at `/opt/local/bin/port` (the installer only adds it to `PATH` in shell profiles). Elsewhere, entries are skipped.
- **Installed state:** `port -q installed <ports>`, read without sudo. Only the active version counts, so an installed-but-inactive port shows as missing and `port install` reactivates it.
- **Changes:** `port -N install`, `port -N uninstall`, and `port -N sync` then `port -N upgrade`. `apply --update` runs `port -N sync` first. All go through the existing sudo handling. mise never runs `port selfupdate`.
- **Names:** `port` has no `--` separator, so mise rejects names it would read as options, variants, version selectors, globs, `field:value` selectors, or pseudo-ports like `outdated`.
- **Version pins** are checked against the active installation (version, `version_revision`, or the full spec) but cannot be installed, since a ports tree only holds the current Portfile; they are skipped with the usual warning.
- **Defaults:** `macports` is not added to the default order for unprefixed keys; opt in with `system_packages.prefer`. mise does not install MacPorts itself.

Docs are in `docs/bootstrap/packages/macports.md`.

## Validation

- Unit tests for the `port installed` parser, pin matching, and name validation pass (`cargo test --workspace --lib macports`).
- `test_system_status` and `test_system_use` pass on Linux, including the "macports is not available" path.
- `e2e/cli/test_system_macports` drives the manager against a fake `port` and `sudo`, but it only runs on macOS and **has not been run**: I developed this on Linux and never ran a real `port`. In particular, whether `port -q installed` exits 0 when none of the names are installed is unverified.

title: fix(bootstrap): preview dotfiles declared by a template-rendered config in --dry-run
body:
`mise bootstrap --dry-run` now previews the dotfiles declared by a conf.d config that a `mode = "template"` dotfile renders. Before, the preview listed only the render step, so it reported nothing pending when a real `mise bootstrap` would apply more.

```toml
# ~/.config/mise/config.toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.config/mise/conf.d/extra.toml" = { source = "~/src/extra.toml.tera", mode = "template" }

# ~/src/extra.toml.tera (rendered to conf.d/extra.toml)
[dotfiles]
"~/marker.txt" = { content = "hello\n" }
```

With `extra.toml` already rendered and `~/marker.txt` missing:

```
# before
$ mise bootstrap --only dotfiles --dry-run
render ~/src/extra.toml.tera -> ~/.config/mise/conf.d/extra.toml (if changed)

# after
$ mise bootstrap --only dotfiles --dry-run
render ~/src/extra.toml.tera -> ~/.config/mise/conf.d/extra.toml (if changed)
mise bootstrap: dotfiles
write inline content to ~/marker.txt
```

A dry run never runs commands, so the simulation that predicts the config after the dotfiles phase used to drop every template-rendered target, and the entries it declares were never planned. It now renders the template with a command-free renderer: no `exec()`, environment, file reads or secrets. When that succeeds, the preview plans against the rendered text. A template that needs any of those is not rendered and its target leaves the simulation as before, so a stale file on disk is never previewed.

Follows #15387, which did this for copied configs.

Fixes #15824.

Validation: `test_bootstrap_dotfiles_config_first` gains a case for this and fails without the change, and `test_bootstrap` (stale rendered configs are not retained) still passes.

title: feat(github): add version_order = published_at
body:
`version_order = "published_at"` makes `latest` follow whichever GitHub release was published most recently, even when its version number is lower than an earlier one.

With `prerelease = true`, a repository that ships stable and alpha builds can make `latest` pick a stale release. GitHub does not always list releases in publication order: for `openai/codex`, `0.170.0` (published 03:40 UTC) is listed ahead of `0.171.0-alpha.13` (published 05:47 UTC), so the default `source` order resolves `latest` to `0.170.0` while `semver` picks the alpha.

```toml
[tools]
"github:openai/codex" = { version = "latest", prerelease = true, version_prefix = "rust-v", version_order = "published_at" }
```

Releases are sorted oldest to newest by publication date, so `mise latest`, `mise upgrade`, and `auto_update` all agree. A release without a date sorts first and never beats a dated one. It is accepted on github, gitlab, and forgejo tools; aqua and http still reject it. The registry's `version_order` is unchanged.

Fixes #15844

## Test plan

- Unit tests for the date sort and for which backends accept the value.
- `cargo test -p mise-config` (schema regenerated).

title: fix(dotfiles): name the missing /<id> when a merge key has none
body:
A `[dotfiles]` merge entry whose key has no `/<id>` suffix was read as `<parent dir>/<id>`, and the errors that followed pointed the wrong way:

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.config/app/settings.toml" = { source = "src/settings.toml", merge = true }
```

mise split the key at its last `/`, so the target became the directory `~/.config/app` and the id `settings.toml`. The warning then said to fix the extension or add a `format`. Following that advice with `format = "toml"` led to `failed read_to_string: ~/.config/app` in `mise dot status`. Neither message said the key was missing its id.

Now mise says the key is missing its `/<id>` and suggests the fixed key when the target has no format:

```
"~/.config/app".settings.toml: the key is missing its /<id> segment, so "settings.toml" was read as the id and "~/.config/app" as the target; did you mean "~/.config/app/settings.toml/<id>" (for example "~/.config/app/settings.toml/shared"), ignoring entry
```

The check only fires when the id looks like a file name with a supported extension and the target has no format. It looks at the key alone, never the filesystem, so a key like `~/settings.toml/defaults.toml` stays valid even while `~/settings.toml` is a directory that a whole-file entry replaces. The `format = "toml"` variant from the issue still reaches the read error; that case depends on filesystem state and is not covered.

Fixes #15828

## Test plan

- Unit tests cover the missing-id hint and that a file-like id under an existing directory is not refused.
- `cargo test --workspace --lib -- edits::` passes (17 tests).

title: fix(install): leave a read-only shared dir's global links alone for tools installed only there
body:
Fixes #15814.

A non-root `mise install` no longer fails with `failed to rebuild runtime symlinks` when a tool it needs is installed only in another user's read-only shared installs dir (`system_installs_dir` or `MISE_SHARED_INSTALL_DIRS`).

Before, user B's `mise install` of unrelated tools tried to rewrite the `global` links in the administrator's dir to follow B's global config, then exited 1 because the dir is read-only:

```text
mise ERROR 23 runtime symlink repair(s) failed:
failed to rebuild runtime symlinks for aqua:BurntSushi/ripgrep in /macbox.noindex/tools/mise/installs/aqua-burnt-sushi-ripgrep: sudo requires a password but no TTY is available.
```

Now the install exits 0 and the shared dir is left unchanged.

## Cause

A dir counted as shared when `installs_dir != backend.ba().installs_path()`. For a tool installed only in a shared dir, install state points `installs_path` at that shared dir, so the check saw it as the user's own. The read-only guard from #15526 was skipped and `global` links followed the user's config.

## Change

`is_own_installs_dir` compares with the tool's dir under the user's own installs root. It replaces the comparison in the rebuild loop, `list_symlinks_for_dir`, and the `heal_links` gate. The identity-layout pin check is left as is.

## Test

New e2e `test_install_shared_only_global_link_read_only` covers both `MISE_SYSTEM_INSTALLS_DIR` and `MISE_SHARED_INSTALL_DIRS`. It passes alongside `test_install_system_global_link_read_only`, `test_shared_install_dirs`, `test_install_system`, `test_install_system_readonly` and `test_prune_shared_installs`. I did not confirm it fails without the fix; the issue reports that it does.

Thanks to @any-victor for the diagnosis and patch.

title: fix(install): accept absolute archive symlinks that point into the archive
body:
Installing a tool whose archive links into its own `/opt` tree failed since the archive symlink check landed in 2026.10.19:

```
$ mise install github:osquery/osquery@5.23.1
failed: symlink …/5.23.1/usr/bin/osqueryctl points outside of …/5.23.1: /opt/osquery/bin/osqueryctl
```

osquery's tarballs ship absolute links such as `usr/bin/osqueryi -> /opt/osquery/bin/osqueryd`, and the target is in the same archive. #15015 handled this for smolvm only.

Before the containment check, mise now rewrites an absolute link to a relative one when its target, read as a path below the install directory, exists in the extracted tree. `usr/bin/osqueryi` becomes `../../opt/osquery/bin/osqueryd`. The rewritten link goes through the normal check, so it is refused if it still leaves the tree.

Links to paths that are not in the archive (`/run`, `/etc/passwd`), targets containing `..`, and links that reach a link leaving the tree are left alone and still fail as before. This applies on Unix to every backend that runs the check. The smolvm guest-rootfs handling is unchanged.

One behavior change: such a link now points at the install's own copy instead of the host's `/opt/...` path.

Tested with unit tests for a rewritten link, a link to a host path, and a chain through an escaping link, plus the existing aqua backend tests. I did not install osquery.

Refs #15013.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: claude-code_2-1-326_agent.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes post-extraction symlink handling used to block path escape during installs; logic is constrained and tested, but mistakes could weaken containment or rewrite links incorrectly.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Unix archive installs** were failing when tarballs ship **absolute symlinks** whose targets live inside the extracted tree (e.g. `usr/bin/tool` → `/opt/pkg/bin/tool` in osquery-style layouts). Before the existing `ensure_symlinks_stay_within` walk, mise now runs **`rebase_absolute_symlinks_into_tree`**, which rewrites such links to **relative** paths when `root.join(target)` exists and the replacement still stays under the install root; chained absolute links are fixed in repeated passes.
> 
> Links to paths **not present in the tree**, unsafe targets, or chains that still escape are **unchanged** and still fail the containment check. **smolvm guest-rootfs rebasing is untouched.** After rebasing, rebased links resolve to the **install’s own files**, not the host’s absolute paths.

title: docs(task): say that dependencies with different arguments run separately
body:
The docs say a shared dependency "runs once", but mise dedups tasks on name, arguments and `env` together. With `depends = ["update:base"]` on `update:personal`, running `mise run 'update:*' --dry-run` runs `update:base --dry-run` and then a second, argument-less `update:base`.

title: fix(bootstrap): run a monorepo root bootstrap task
body:
`mise bootstrap` no longer skips the root `bootstrap` task of a monorepo.

With this config, `mise run bootstrap` ran the task but `mise bootstrap` logged "no `bootstrap` task defined" and skipped it:

```toml
monorepo_root = true

[monorepo]
config_roots = ["pkg"]

[tasks.bootstrap]
run = "echo BOOT"
```

A monorepo names the root task `//:bootstrap`. The check added in #14858 rejected every name containing `:`, so it rejected this one too. The only workaround was `alias = "bootstrap"`. The phase now also accepts exactly `//:bootstrap`; `system:bootstrap` and a sub-project's `//pkg:bootstrap` are still not the special task.

title: fix(windows): start mise.exe on Server Core by linking the C runtime statically
body:
Fixes #15813.

On Windows Server Core images such as `mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0-windowsservercore-ltsc2022`, the documented install succeeds but `mise.exe` then exits silently with `0xC0000135` (`STATUS_DLL_NOT_FOUND`). The release binaries imported `VCRUNTIME140.dll`, and Server Core doesn't include the VC++ redistributable.

The Windows MSVC builds (x64 and arm64) now link the C runtime statically (`-C target-feature=+crt-static`), so `mise.exe` and `mise-shim.exe` start without installing `vcredist` first. The release build also fails if either exe still imports `vcruntime140.dll`, so this can't regress unnoticed. The x64 Windows CI jobs get the same flag so they test what ships.

Not verified locally (no Windows toolchain here): the Windows release build on this PR is the check that vendored Lua and the other C dependencies link cleanly with the static CRT. The binary should grow by a small amount (my estimate: a few hundred KB); the release job will show the real number.

title: fix(task): fall back to global tasks for bare depends in monorepo tasks
body:
## Problem

In a project with `monorepo_root = true`, a task could not `depends` on a task from the global config:

```toml
# ~/.config/mise/config.toml
[tasks.greet]
run = "echo ran-greet"

# mise.toml
monorepo_root = true

[tasks.t]
depends = ["greet"]
run = "echo ran-t"
```

`mise run //:t` failed with `task not found: greet`. A bare dependency name was rewritten to the parent's project (`//:greet`), and nothing fell back to the global `greet`.

## Fix

- A bare `depends` name now falls back to the unscoped task name when the parent's project has no task with that name. A project task still shadows a global one.
- `depends = ["::greet"]` no longer fails with the internal message `':task' pattern should be expanded before matching`. It now gives an error that says what to write instead.

Explicit forms such as `:task` and `//path:task` behave as before.

Fixes #15811

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**

> **Overview**
> Fixes monorepo tasks that use a **bare** `depends` name (e.g. `depends = ["hello"]`) when the dependency lives in global config, not in the parent project.

> After resolving the name in the parent project (as before), **`match_tasks_with_context`** retries against **unscoped** tasks only if nothing matched—so globals are found without pulling in another project's `//…` or grouped tasks like `tools:install`. Local project tasks still **shadow** globals with the same name. Explicit syntax (`:hello`, `//path:task`, `./…`) is unchanged; invalid `::…` patterns now get a clearer error instead of an internal “should be expanded” message.
>

title: fix(doctor): stop crashing on a plugin repo with no commits
body:
`mise doctor` panicked with ``called `Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value`` when an installed asdf or vfox plugin's git repo had a remote but no commits yet. Doctor already shows `(unknown)` when it can't read a plugin's commit, but the short-SHA lookup panicked before it could. Now it returns an error and doctor prints the plugin as `<url>#(unknown)`. The same lookup is used when installing or updating plugins, which now report an error in this case instead of crashing.

The full-length SHA lookup already returned an error here; this applies the same handling to the short one, as suggested by the reporter in #15808.

A new unit test runs the HEAD helpers against an empty repo; it panicked before this change and passes now.

Fixes #15808

title: feat(bootstrap): accept permissions as another name for mode in files and directories
body:
`[dotfiles]` and `[bootstrap.files]` both manage files, but they name the same things differently, which [discussion 15784](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15784) points out. The most confusing case is permissions: `[dotfiles]` uses `permissions = "0600"`, while `[bootstrap.files]` uses `mode = "0600"`, and `mode` in `[dotfiles]` means something else (how a file is deployed).

`[bootstrap.files]` and `[bootstrap.directories]` now accept `permissions` as another name for `mode`, so the same key works in both places:

```toml
[bootstrap.directories."/opt/example"]
permissions = "0750"

[bootstrap.files."/opt/example/app.conf"]
content = "port = 8080"
permissions = "0640"
```

`mode` keeps working and nothing is deprecated. An entry that sets both `mode` and `permissions` fails to load.

## Docs

- `[bootstrap.files]` has a table comparing its keys with `[dotfiles]` (permissions, templates, removal, owner and group, links).
- The "which section runs something in the background" table in `[bootstrap.services]` now lists `[daemons]`, and the daemons page says when a user service is the better fit.

## Not in this PR

The sections stay separate, since they cover different scopes (a home directory you edit versus machine state that may need root; a project's daemons versus a machine's services). `template = true` versus `mode = "template"` and `state = "absent"` versus `mode = "absent"` are unchanged: in `[dotfiles]` those are deployment modes, and many parts of mise read that key.

## Validation

Unit tests for the alias and the both-keys error, an e2e case in `test_bootstrap_system_files_no_sudo` applying a file and a directory with `permissions`, and the `schema_matches_parser` test against the regenerated `schema/mise.json`.

title: fix(lock): skip the not-in-lockfile warning for tools excluded by os
body:
With `tool_config.locked = true`, a tool limited to another OS with `os = [...]` printed `Failed to resolve tool version list ... is not in the lockfile` on every command, even though mise never uses that tool on this machine.

```toml
[tool_config]
locked = true

[tools]
swift = { version = "6.4.0", os = ["linux"] }
```

On macOS, `mise ls` and `mise env` warned about swift. swift's lock entry carries a Linux-only `swift_platform` option, so the macOS lookup never matched it. The `os` filter was only applied after resolution.

When every request for a tool is excluded by `os` on this host, the lockfile-miss is now logged at debug level instead of warned. Other resolution errors still warn, and `mise lock` resolution is unchanged.

Fixes #15786

## Test plan

- New e2e `test_lockfile_os_excluded_locked` fails without the change and passes with it.
- `test_lockfile_tool_config_locked` still passes.

title: fix(core): bound the rust beta/nightly release-age cutoff search by fetch_remote_versions_timeout
body:
`mise install rust@beta` (or `nightly`) with an explicit past `minimum_release_age` looks up the build the channel pointed at on the cutoff day by probing one dated manifest per day, up to 90 days back for beta and 30 for nightly. Nothing bounded that search in time. Against a slow or misbehaving dist server (a mirror, a captive portal, a server under load) the install could spend minutes probing, ignoring `fetch_remote_versions_timeout` entirely. The reporter measured 93 s and 92 requests with `MISE_FETCH_REMOTE_VERSIONS_TIMEOUT=20s`.

The whole search now shares one `fetch_remote_versions_timeout` deadline, like the other remote version lookups. When the budget runs out the install stops probing and fails with a message that says the cutoff could not be verified, instead of the misleading "no build found within 90 days":

```console
$ MISE_FETCH_REMOTE_VERSIONS_TIMEOUT=20s mise install rust@beta
mise ERROR Failed to install core:rust@beta: could not verify the rust beta build the release-age cutoff allows within 20s; raise fetch_remote_versions_timeout or check the rustup dist server
```

Healthy servers are unaffected: a 404 for a missing date is fast, so the search still finds the newest build well inside the budget. `prefer_offline` still skips the lookup entirely, and the "no build found" error is kept for a search that really covered the whole window.

Fixes #15797

## Validation

- New unit tests cover the deadline cutting a slow search short, and the search still returning the newest existing date or "not found" within budget (`cargo test -p mise --lib plugins::core::rust`, 75 passed).
- Not tested against a real slow mirror.

title: docs(bootstrap): move the settings plugin author guide into Writing plugins
body:
The guide to writing a bootstrap settings plugin (the `SettingsRead` and `SettingsWrite` hooks, `[bootstrap-settings]` in `mise.plugin.toml`, and the rules a plugin must follow) was buried at the bottom of [Bootstrap settings plugins](https://mise.jdx.dev/bootstrap/settings-plugins.html), under Bootstrap → Platform-specific. Plugin authors looking under Plugins → Writing plugins found every other plugin type there but not this one.

It now has its own page, **Plugins → Writing plugins → Settings plugins** (`/settings-plugin-development.html`), laid out like the package manager plugin guide. The bootstrap page keeps everything a user needs to declare and apply settings, and links to the new guide. Its URL is unchanged, so existing links and the `mise bootstrap settings --help` link still work, and links to the moved `#settingsread`, `#settingswrite` and `#rules` sections redirect to the new page.

The guide's quick start now declares a sample section and runs a real `apply` followed by `status --missing`, since `status` and `--dry-run` never call `SettingsWrite`. It also states how mise recognizes a settings plugin: by `metadata.lua` plus both settings hooks, with `backend_install.lua` taking precedence. The `mise.plugin.toml` table is optional.

Settings plugins are also listed alongside the other types in the plugin type table on [Plugins](https://mise.jdx.dev/plugins.html), the hook-file table in the Lua reference, and the testing table in Publishing plugins, whose settings row now exercises a real write.

Requested in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15785.

## Validation

- `mise run docs:build` passes, including its link, redirect and social-metadata checks.
- `hk run check` (oxfmt, markdownlint, render-llms) passes on the changed files.

title: chore: set up entire graph and brain for agents
body:
Agents working in this repo can now query a local code graph and a repository brain instead of grepping and re-deriving context. This wires up the two official Entire plugins, `entire-graph` and `entire-brain`, for the repo.

- `.entire/agent-guide.md` is the shared operating guide (when to use `entire graph query`, `impact`, `neighbors`, `entire brain brief`, and so on). `AGENTS.md` (and so the `CLAUDE.md` symlink) points to it through a small managed block.
- `.claude/settings.json` gains one PreToolUse hook on Edit, Write, MultiEdit and NotebookEdit that runs `entire brain hook pre-edit`. It does nothing when the `entire` CLI is not installed.

Everything else stays local: the brain and graph stores are per machine, and the graph's Claude SubagentStart hook lives in the untracked `.claude/settings.local.json`.

Contributors who want it install the plugins and build the brain once:

```sh
entire plugin install brain --yes   # also installs graph
entire brain setup
```

Not validated beyond building the brain locally (5,480 files and 66,117 symbols indexed) and running `entire plugin doctor`. This changes agent configuration only, no mise behavior.

@@ -0,0 +1,99 @@
+# Entire repository agent guide — Graph and Brain
+
+Use Graph EVERY time you need to find code or a code relationship, not only at the
+start. Both tools run, in this order, and neither replaces the other:
+
+    1. entire brain brief "<task>" --json
+    2. entire graph query --repo . --profile full --head --format agent --max-context-bytes 4096 --query "<task>"
+
+The brief answers why, and what was decided; the query answers where, and what
+depends on it. Step 2 holds for small edits, follow-up work, and tasks that already
+name the file: a named file answers where code is, not what else depends on it. Do
+not skip either step on the grounds that the available context feels sufficient, and
+do not treat having done one as having done the other.
+Each later locate or relationship question MUST also go through Graph:
+
+    entire graph query --repo . --profile full --head --format agent --max-context-bytes 4096 --query "<task>"
+    entire graph def --repo . --head --max-context-bytes 4096 <Name>
+    entire graph neighbors --repo . --head --format agent --max-context-bytes 4096 --symbol <Name> --direction in
+    entire graph impact --repo . --head --max-context-bytes 4096 --symbol <Name>
+
+query finds the code for a description. def shows what a named symbol is.
+neighbors lists callers (--direction in) or callees (--direction out). impact gives
+the blast radius before you change a symbol. Use these, not grep, for definitions,
+callers, references and dependents. Use grep/rg only for literal strings, config
+keys, environment-variable names and file names.
+
+--head reads the committed tree from a cache. Drop --head only when the answer
+depends on uncommitted edits. The first call in a large repository can take tens of
+seconds while that cache loads; later calls take about a second. Run the command
+directly: it needs no timeout wrapper, and macOS has no timeout command.
+A Coverage or Completeness line lists files Graph could not parse, often minified or
+generated ones. It does not mean the results are partial; only a failure in the
+language you asked about can hide a fact, and then you check that one relation in
+source. Static relations can be incomplete: an empty result is not proof of no callers.
+
+Questions about why something is the way it is, what was decided, or what was
+tried before are answered by durable memories. Retrieve them directly; the brief's
+memories section is a sample, not the search:
+
+    entire brain recall "<question>" --json
+
+recall ranks decisions, rejected approaches, invariants and gotchas first. query
+mixes memories with history and documentation and can rank documentation above the
+recorded decision.
+
+Reuse useful code locations from the brief. Use Brain retrieval for previous
+decisions, attempts, documentation, and durable memories - Brain's episodic record
+of what was decided, what went wrong before, and what must stay true. Record one
+when you learn something durable that the code does not already state:
+

title: fix(bootstrap): pull the source before loading its config on --from --update
body:
`mise bootstrap --from <url> --update` now fast-forwards the source checkout even when the commit it already has holds a config that does not parse. Before, a source with a TOML typo could not pick up its own fix: the command failed on the broken file before it ran `git pull`, and only pulling by hand unblocked it.

```
$ mise bootstrap --from <url> --from-dir ~/source --update --yes
mise::config::parse_error
  × Invalid TOML in config file
   ╭─[~/.config/mise/conf.d/demo/mise.toml:1:5]
 1 │ [env
```

#15731 fixed this for plain `--update`; the `--from` path opens its history scope separately, so it was left out. That scope reads the config the existing checkout holds. Now, when reusing a checkout whose config fails to load, `--from … --update` pulls without the history record but under the same operation lock (reason logged with `MISE_DEBUG=1`), then bootstraps from the fixed commit. When the config loads, behavior is unchanged, and any other error opening the scope, such as a lock timeout, still stops the run. Dry runs are unchanged.

Fixes #15727.

## Test plan

- `e2e/cli/test_bootstrap_update_config_checkout` gains a `--from … --update` case: the source checkout is on a commit that does not parse (`mise env` fails), the origin has the fix, and the update pulls it and runs the fixed task. It passes; I did not run it without the fix.
