title: fix(backend): kill a hung asdf list-all at fetch_remote_versions_timeout
body:
`fetch_remote_versions_timeout` did not stop an asdf plugin's `bin/list-all` that hangs. mise logged nothing and waited until the script exited on its own, holding the tool-version lock the whole time (a CI `mise install` waited behind one for hours).

```sh
mkdir -p /tmp/sleepy/bin
printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\nsleep 600\necho 1.0.0\n' > /tmp/sleepy/bin/list-all
chmod +x /tmp/sleepy/bin/list-all
mise plugins link sleepy /tmp/sleepy
MISE_FETCH_REMOTE_VERSIONS_TIMEOUT=5s mise ls-remote sleepy
```

Before, this printed nothing until the script finished. Now it fails after about 5s with `timed out after 5s` and a hint to change `fetch_remote_versions_timeout`, and the script's process group is killed.

The cause was `run_with_timeout`: it ran the work in `thread::scope`, which joins the thread before returning, so the timeout error only surfaced after the script exited, and the child was never killed. `list-all` and `ruby-install --update` now run through `CmdLineRunner::with_timeout`, which kills the process group at the deadline.

Behavior change: `bin/list-all` now runs with stdin closed, including under `--raw`, where it used to inherit stdin. mise runs `list-all` in many non-interactive places (background version fetches, `ls-remote`, completions, CI), where a prompt could never be answered, so a plugin that relies on prompting here is unlikely to work today. A script that does read stdin now gets EOF.

Not changed: the python-build `git.update` call still uses `run_with_timeout`. Git runs several subcommands there, so it needs its own change.

Fixes #15421

> **Medium Risk**
> Changes how remote version listing and ruby-install updates run subprocesses and enforce timeouts, affecting lock duration and failure modes on slow or stuck network/plugin scripts.
> 
> **Overview**
> **`fetch_remote_versions_timeout` now actually stops hung plugin work** instead of waiting for `bin/list-all` (or child processes like `curl`) to exit on their own, which could hold version-listing locks for hours.
> 
> ASDF **`bin/list-all`** is run via **`CmdLineRunner::with_timeout`** and **`output_isolated`** (64 MiB cap), which **kills the script’s process group** at the deadline and surfaces a **`timed out after …`** error with a hint to adjust **`fetch_remote_versions_timeout`** / **`MISE_FETCH_REMOTE_VERSIONS_TIMEOUT`**. The backend path is updated to **`await`** the now-async **`fetch_remote_versions`**.

title: fix(github): skip Python wheels and gems when autodetecting assets
body:
The `github:` backend could install a Python wheel instead of the native binary when a release publishes both. `manylinux_2_17_x86_64.whl` scores as an OS, arch and glibc match, so on Linux x86_64 it beat the musl tarball:

| Asset | Score |
|---|---:|
| `rshellcheck-1.0.0-py3-none-manylinux_2_17_x86_64.whl` | 175 |
| `rshellcheck-rshellcheck-linux-x64-1.0.0.tgz` | 160 |
| `rshellcheck-1.0.0-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz` | 150 |

Wheels and gems are now left out of automatic selection, like `.deb` and `.rpm`. An explicit `asset_pattern` can still pick one.

When `asset_pattern` looks like a regular expression (`^…$`, `\.`, `(?:`, `.*`, `|`), the "No matching asset found" error now says it is a glob and points to `matching_regex`, which keeps platform autodetection. This applies to GitHub, GitLab and Forgejo.

Not covered: npm `.tgz` packages such as `rshellcheck-rshellcheck-linux-x64-1.0.0.tgz` are ordinary tarballs and still outscore the musl archive (160 vs 150) in that release. Telling them apart needs a fuzzier heuristic, so I left it out. Related to #15418, which I did not mark as fixed.

## Testing

- `cargo test --lib backend::asset_matcher` (89 passed, including new tests for wheels/gems and the regex hint)
- `cargo clippy --lib -- -D warnings`

title: chore(ci): ignore the astral-tokio-tar and pin-utils advisories by their published IDs
body:
`cargo deny check` fails on main, and so on every open PR's `trusted / lint` job. title: fix(aqua): keep .exe on raw Windows downloads when completion is off
body:
On Windows, `mise use aqua:SonarSource/sonarqube-cli` installed the executable as `sonar` instead of `sonar.exe`.

The aqua recipe sets `complete_windows_ext: false` and relies on the Windows override URL ending in `.exe`. mise only added `.exe` when `complete_windows_ext` was on, so the raw binary lost its extension. Direct aqua installs of the same package produce `sonar.exe`.

Now, when a raw-format package's Windows asset URL ends in `.exe`, an extensionless install name gets `.exe` appended even if `complete_windows_ext` is off. Other OSes, names that already have an extension, and non-`.exe` URLs (such as `.bin`) are unchanged.

Fixes #15411

## Validation

- New unit test in `aqua-registry` covering the cases above.
- `cargo test --lib backend::aqua` (145 passed) and `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` pass.
- Not run on a real Windows install.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: unavailable.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Scoped to Windows raw installs and filename derivation; guarded by format, OS, and URL suffix checks with new unit tests.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes Windows installs where raw Aqua packages with `complete_windows_ext: false` and an `.exe` download URL were written as extensionless binaries (e.g. `sonar` instead of `sonar.exe`).
> 
> Adds **`raw_windows_exe_name`** on registry package metadata: on Windows, for raw/empty format, when completion is disabled and the install name has no extension, it inspects the resolved URL or asset (ignoring query/fragment) and appends **`.exe`** only if that path ends in `.exe`. Non-Windows, zip/non-raw formats, names that already have an extension, and non-`.exe` downloads are unchanged.
> 
> The Aqua backend applies this via **`complete_raw_windows_exe`** after existing Windows extension completion on install binary paths and on **`srcs_for_platform`** link **src**/**dst** paths (with and without explicit `files` entries), aligning mise with direct Aqua behavior for recipes like SonarSource CLI.

title: feat(task): run tasks at another revision with mise run --at
body:
"Does this test fail on main too?" and "what did this task print before the change?" today mean stashing, checking out, running and switching back, or setting up a worktree by hand. `mise run --at REV TASK` checks REV out into a temporary worktree, runs the task there with that revision's own config and tasks, and removes the worktree:

```console
$ mise run hello
[hello] $ cat greeting.txt
new
$ mise run --at HEAD~1 hello
mise running at HEAD~1 (99aa37f674f7) in /tmp/mise/run-at/99aa37f674f7-R2cVx1/ex
[hello] $ cat greeting.txt
old
```

Your own checkout is never touched.

## Behavior

- **Flags:** `--at REV`, plus `--at-setup CMD` to prepare the worktree, such as installing dependencies, since a fresh checkout has no `node_modules` or `target/`.
- **Where it runs:** a detached `git worktree` at `$MISE_TMP_DIR/run-at/<sha12>-XXXX/<repo-name>`, in the same subdirectory you ran mise from.
- **How:** a child `mise` runs your arguments without `--at`, `--at-setup` and `-C`, and its exit code is returned.
- **Environment:** setup and tasks get `MISE_RUN_AT_SOURCE` (your checkout) and `MISE_RUN_AT_REV` (the commit).
- **Trust:** nothing is weakened.
  - The worktree is a linked worktree of your repository, so mise's existing rule gives its config your main checkout's trust.
  - The child requires explicit trust, so a config at REV is never trusted by prompt, `--yes` or implicit trust.
  - Before anything runs, the configs from the worktree root down to the task directory are checked. An untrusted one is refused, naming the checkout to `mise trust`.
  - In paranoid mode a config at REV is always refused, because content-bound trust is tied to a path and the worktree's path is new each time.
- **Submodules:** each is initialized with `--reference` to your local clone of it when you have one, then nested ones with `git submodule update --init --recursive`.
- **Cleanup:** the worktree is removed on success, failure, `--timeout` and Ctrl-C. I checked Ctrl-C by sending SIGINT to the process group: nothing was left.

## Open questions

1. Trust maps to the main checkout, not to the linked worktree you may be running from. Should it map to your current checkout?
2. In paranoid mode `--at` can't run a project config at all. Should a config whose content matches a trusted one be accepted?
3. `git worktree add` runs your `post-checkout` hook. Should mise turn hooks off for it?
4. `--timeout` doesn't cover `--at-setup`.
5. A `mise.toml` above your checkout doesn't apply in the worktree. This is documented.

## Validation

- **e2e:** the new `e2e/tasks/test_task_run_at` (28 assertions) covers:
  - old against new output, and the exit code;
  - a submodule at REV, `-C`, setup, and a bad revision;
  - your tree left untouched and no worktree left behind;
  - refusal after `mise trust --ignore`, including with `--yes`, and paranoid mode.
- **Unit tests:** `cargo test -p mise --lib task::` (575 passed), plus a new test for the argument stripping.
- **Lint:** `cargo cl

 ```
 
+## Run tasks at another revision
+
+`--at REV` runs tasks as they are at another git commit, without touching your
+checkout. It answers questions like "does this test fail on `main` too?":
+
+```sh
+mise run --at main test
+mise run --at HEAD~1 bench > before.txt
+```
+
+mise checks REV out into a detached
+[`git worktree`](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree) under its temporary
+directory, runs the tasks there with that revision's own config, tasks and
+tools, and removes the worktree afterwards, also when a task fails, the tasks
+time out (`--timeout`) or you press Ctrl-C. The run exits with the tasks'
+status. Uncommitted changes in your checkout play no part: REV is a commit.
+
+- The tasks run in the same directory, relative to the repository root, as
+  the one you ran mise from. The worktree directory has your checkout's name.
+- Submodules are initialized at REV, using your clones of them as a reference,
+  so only objects they lack are fetched. Git hooks do not run, neither your
+  checkout's nor any that REV keeps in the repository.
+- Ignored files are not there: a fresh worktree has no `target/`,
+  `node_modules/` or `.env`. Pass `--at-setup CMD` to prepare them. It runs in
+  the worktree's copy of the directory you ran mise from (not a task's `dir`)
+  before the tasks start, as a plain shell command outside
+  mise's environment, with `MISE_RUN_AT_SOURCE` set to your checkout and
+  `MISE_RUN_AT_REV` to the commit. The tasks get both variables too:
+
+  ```sh
+  mise run --at main --at-setup 'cp -R "$MISE_RUN_AT_SOURCE/node_modules" .' test
+  ```
+
+  With `--dry-run`, mise prints the setup command instead of running it.
+  `--timeout` limits only the tasks, not the setup command.
+
+- A `mise run --at` inside a `--at` run (where `MISE_RUN_AT_REV` is set) is
+  refused.
+
+- Config is looked up from the worktree, so a `mise.toml` in a directory above
+  your checkout (other than the global config) does not apply.
+
+- [Daemons](/daemons.html) that the tasks require keep running after the run,
+  as they do after any `mise run`, but their project is gone with the worktree.
+  `mise daemons prune` stops them and removes their state.
+
+The config at REV is the config of the same project, at another commit, so it
+shares the [trust](/cli/trust.html) of the repository's main checkout, as any
+linked worktree does. If the main checkout is not trusted, `--at` refuses to
+run before anything starts. It never trusts the config at REV on its own: not
+by a prompt, not with `--yes`, and not the way `mise run` trusts the config of
+the directory you run it in. In [paranoid mode](/paranoid.html), which ties
+trust to a file's path and contents, a config at REV is never trusted, because
+the worktree is a new path on every run.
+
 ## Task environment {#task-environment}
 
 Tasks run with the project's [environment variables](/environments/) and tools,
--- e2e/tasks/test_task_run_at (+134/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,134 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+# `mise run --at REV` runs tasks in a temporary git worktree of REV, with that
+# revision's config, and removes the worktree afterwards.
+
+export MISE_TRUSTED_CONFIG_PATHS=""
+unset CI GITHUB_ACTIONS GITHUB_ACTION 2>/dev/null || true
+export MISE_TMP_DIR="$PWD/tmp"
+git config --global user.email e2e@example.com
+git config --global user.name e2e
+# The submodule below is cloned from a local path.
+git config --global protocol.file.allow always
+
+mkdir sub
+git -C sub init -q
+echo sub-v1 >sub/version.txt
+git -C sub add version.txt
+git -C sub commit -qm v1
+
+mkdir repo
+cd repo || exit 1
+git init -q
+git submodule add -q ../sub sub
+mkdir -p pkg
+touch pkg/.keep
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[tasks.hi]
+run = "echo version-one"
+
+[tasks.where]
+run = "basename $PWD; echo source=$MISE_RUN_AT_SOURCE"
+
+[tasks.sub]
+run = "cat sub/version.txt; cat \"$(git -C sub rev-parse --git-path objects/info/alternates)\""
+
+[tasks.fail]
+run = "exit 7"
+
+[tasks.setup-check]
+run = "cat setup.txt"
+EOF
+# A hook kept in the repository, and a directory that is a symlink out of it.
+mkdir -p .githooks ../outside
+printf '#!/bin/sh\ntouch "%s/../hook-ran"\n' "$PWD" >.githooks/post-checkout
+chmod +x .githooks/post-checkout
+ln -s ../outside escape
+git add mise.toml .gitmodules sub pkg/.keep .githooks/post-checkout escape
+git commit -qm one
+
+echo sub-v2 >../sub/version.txt
+git -C ../sub commit -qam v2
+git -C sub pull -q
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[tasks.hi]
+run = "echo version-two"
+EOF
+git rm -q escape
+mkdir escape
+touch escape/.keep
+git add mise.toml sub escape/.keep
+git commit -qm two
+git config core.hooksPath .githooks
+
+# Normal mode: the first `mise run` trusts the checkout, and the worktree
+# shares that trust.
+assert "mise run hi" "version-two"
+assert "mise run --at HEAD~1 hi" "version-one"
+assert "mise run --at HEAD hi" "version-two"
+assert_contains "mise run --at HEAD~1 where" "repo"
+assert_contains "mise run --at HEAD~1 where" "source=$PWD"
+
+# Submodules are initialized from the local clone, at REV's commit.
+assert_contains "mise run --at HEAD~1 sub" "sub-v1"
+assert_contains "mise run --at HEAD~1 sub" "modules/sub"
+
+# Flags after the task belong to it; `-C` and `--at` before it are mise's.
+assert "mise -C pkg run --at=HEAD~1 hi" "version-one"
+
+# A setup command runs first, in the worktree; its failure stops the run.
+assert "mise run --at HEAD~1 --at-setup 'echo setup-ran >setup.txt' setup-check" "setup-ran"
+
+# No hook runs: not one that REV keeps in the repository.

title: feat(task): keep each task's last output behind the task.logs setting and print it with mise tasks log
body:
Output styles that hide or shorten a task's output (`replacing`, `timed`, `silent`, the 64 KiB `summary` tail) lose detail. Rerunning the task to see it is slow, and sometimes it doesn't fail the same way twice. With the new opt-in `task.logs` setting, mise keeps each task's full output from its last run, and `mise tasks log NAME` prints it.

Task logs are off by default. Turn them on in `mise.toml`:

```toml
[settings]
task.logs = true
```

or for one shell with `export MISE_TASK_LOGS=1`:

```console
$ export MISE_TASK_LOGS=1
$ mise run --output prefix hello
[hello] $ cat greeting.txt
[hello] new
[hello] Finished in 35.5ms
$ mise tasks log hello
$ cat greeting.txt
new
$ mise tasks log --path hello
~/.local/state/mise/task-logs/402c3a60….log
```

With the setting off, `mise tasks log` says that task logs are off and how to turn them on.

## Behavior

- **Off by default:** with `task.logs` off, mise writes and removes no log, and its output plumbing is what it was before this PR: nothing is piped only for a log, and `silent` tasks discard their output.
- **Where logs live:** `$MISE_STATE_DIR/task-logs/<hash of project and task>.log`, one per task per project (a global task gets one per project it runs in, and one for its runs outside any project). The directory is `0700` and each log `0600`. Each run replaces the task's log with one atomic write when the task ends, pass or fail. A run whose command never starts (cancelled first, or a missing program) keeps the previous log.
- **Contents:** the `$ command` line of each run entry, then the task's output, redacted like the terminal output, plus the URL credential redaction mise's logger applies (`https://user:pw@host` is logged as `https://[redacted]@host`).
- **Size:** the newest 4 MiB is kept, and a first line says how much older output was dropped.
- **Pointer on failure:** under `replacing` or `timed`, or `summary` when it held only the end, a failing task adds one line, `full output: <path>`.
- **What isn't logged:** output mise doesn't pipe: `raw` and `interactive` tasks, and an `interleave` task with nothing to redact (the default for a single task). Piping them anyway would change what the task sees: colors, progress bars and `isatty`.

## Also in this PR (for every piped output style, setting on or off)

- **Bounded line reads:** mise used to hold a whole line in memory however long it was. Lines over 1 MiB now arrive in pieces. A piece is cut only where redaction allows, using the redactor's own matches (new `Redactor::match_spans`): redacting each piece hides exactly the bytes redacting the whole line hides, and a URL's credentials are never split.
- **`CmdLineRunner::with_on_spawn`:** a hook that runs once the process has started.

## Open questions

1. Should a default `interleave` run pipe its output when stdout isn't a terminal and logs are on, so it's logged too? That changes how partial lines and their order come out.
2. The log is written when a task ends, so `tail -f` shows nothing

title: feat(task): record task run durations and add mise tasks history
body:
People deciding what to run before a push, and tools that plan around slow checks, need to know how long a project's tasks usually take. Today each tool times them itself. mise now records each task run's start, duration and result, and `mise tasks history` shows them:

```console
$ mise tasks history hello
hello  2026-11-04 23:25:26  89.0ms  ok
hello  2026-11-04 23:25:26  92.0ms  ok
hello  2026-11-04 23:25:26  88.0ms  ok
$ mise tasks history --summary
hello      3  0  89.0ms  88.0ms  ok
test:unit  3  0  -       1.0ms   skipped
```

The summary columns are runs, failures, median duration, last duration and last status. The median counts only runs that executed and passed, so `test:unit`, skipped as up to date, has none.

## Behavior

- **Store:** `$MISE_STATE_DIR/task-history/<project hash>/<task hash>.json`, with `{version, root, runs}`. The project is the monorepo root, else the project root, else the current directory.
- **Each run:** `task`, `args` (redacted like terminal output), `started_at`, `duration_ms`, `status` (`ok`, `failed`, `cached`, `skipped` or `cancelled`) and `exit_code`.
- **Bound:** the last `task.history_limit` runs per task, 20 by default. `task.history = false` or a limit of 0 turns recording off. It's on by default, since a record is about 1 KB, stays on the machine, and history only helps if it was being collected before someone asks.
- **Concurrency:** a writer takes a file lock beside the task's file, then reads, appends, trims and replaces it atomically, off the async runtime. Readers take no lock.
- **Failures:** recording never fails a run; errors are logged at debug level.
- **Not recorded:** dry runs, and tasks with nothing to run (only `depends`).
- **Command:** `mise tasks history [TASK] [--summary] [--json]`.

## Open questions

1. A duration is the task job's wall time, including environment setup and lock waits: a `sleep 0.2` task records about 350 ms. Should mise also record command-only time?
2. Failures before a task starts, such as a tool that won't install, aren't recorded.
3. The output has no header row, like `mise tasks ls`. Should `--summary` get one, or p90 and max, or `--since`?

## Validation

- **e2e:** the new `e2e/tasks/test_task_history` (16 assertions) covers ok, failed (exit 3), skipped and cached runs, arguments, the JSON shape, the summary, the bound, and both ways to turn it off.
- **Unit tests:** `cargo test -p mise --lib task::` (580 passed). The new ones cover trimming, 8 threads writing at once, a corrupt file and the median. The `command_effects` test passes too.
- **Lint:** `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean, and `mise run render` regenerated the CLI docs and schema.

title: feat(task): select tasks by their sources with --affected outside a monorepo
body:
`mise run --affected` used to work only at a monorepo root, choosing *projects*. Anywhere else it failed with "requires a monorepo root configuration". Now, outside a monorepo, it runs only the matching tasks whose `sources` match a changed file, so a single project can run "what my change touches" from its task declarations:

```toml
[tasks."test:unit"]
run = "echo unit"
sources = ["src/**"]

[tasks."test:docs"]
run = "echo docs"
sources = ["docs/**"]
```

```console
$ mise run --affected --affected-uncommitted --affected-explain --dry-run "test:*"   # after editing src/a.rs
Affected tasks (HEAD~1...HEAD):
  test:unit
    changed source: src/a.rs
Unaffected tasks:
  test:docs
[test:unit] $ echo unit
```

## Behavior

- **What selects a task:** a changed file matches its `sources`, or the config file that defines it changed, which the up-to-date check also counts as a source.
  - Matching uses the up-to-date check's matcher, relative to the task's directory, with `!` exclusions.
  - Changes are read from the whole repository, so `../shared/*.txt` still matches.
- **Change detection** is unchanged: `--affected-base`, `--affected-head`, `--affected-committed`, `--affected-uncommitted`, `--affected-untracked` and their environment variables.
- **Tasks without `sources`** run whenever anything changed, since the up-to-date check already treats them as always stale. Skipping them could silently drop tests in CI. When nothing changed, nothing runs.
- **Tasks whose sources use `{{usage.*}}`** also run, since their sources aren't known before their arguments are parsed.
- **Not included:** global tasks are left out, as in monorepo mode.
- **Dependencies** of a selected task still run, subject to the up-to-date check.

title: feat(task): add task tags and select tasks with --tag
body:
Tasks can now say what they are with `tags`, and `mise run --tag` runs every task with a tag. A project's lint, test and build tasks were only recognizable by naming convention. Now `mise run --tag lint` runs all of them, and tools that run a project's checks, such as CI scripts and agent toolkits, can read a task's purpose from `mise tasks ls --json` rather than guess it from the name.

```toml
[tasks."lint:rust"]
run = "cargo clippy"
tags = "lint"

[tasks."lint:docs"]
run = "markdownlint docs"
tags = ["lint", "docs"]

[tasks."test:e2e"]
run = "./e2e/run"
tags = ["test", "slow"]
```

```console
$ mise run --tag lint
[lint:docs] $ markdownlint docs
[lint:rust] $ cargo clippy
...
$ mise tasks ls --tag slow
test:e2e
```

## Details

- **Config:** `tags` takes a string or a list, as `alias` does. A file task sets them with `#MISE tags=[...]`.
- **Merging:** a template adds its tags to those of every task that extends it, and a `[tasks.x]` overlay adds to a file task's tags.
- **Meaning:** mise gives no tag a meaning of its own. The docs list conventional ones: `build`, `test`, `lint`, `format`, `slow`.
- **`mise run --tag NAME`:** can be repeated, and selects tasks with any of the tags.
  - With no task name it picks from every task. With a pattern (`mise run --tag slow 'test:*'`) it keeps the matches that have the tag, and fails if none does.
  - It combines with `--affected`, where finding nothing is not an error. In a monorepo, `mise run --tag lint '//...:**'` reaches every project.
  - Dependencies run whatever their tags.
- **Listing:** `mise tasks ls --tag` (and `mise tasks --tag`) filters the list. `tasks ls --json`, `tasks info` and the MCP task list show `tags`:

  ```json
  [{"name": "lint:docs", "tags": ["lint", "docs"]}, {"name": "lint:rust", "tags": ["lint"]}, {"name": "test:e2e", "tags": ["test", "slow"]}]
  ```
- **Why `tags` rather than a single `kind`:** a task is often more than one thing (`["test", "slow"]`), and a fixed list of kinds would turn away `bench`, `docs` or `deploy`. "Task group" already means a parallel `run = [{tasks = [...]}]` entry, so that name was taken.
- **Why a flag rather than a `tag:lint` pattern:** task names can contain `:`, so a pattern would collide with real task names.

## Open questions

1. Should repeated `--tag` match all of the tags (`--tag test --tag slow` meaning slow tests) instead of any?
2. Should `mise tasks ls -x` get a Tags column? It's left out, since it changes existing output.
3. Should `depends` be able to select by tag?

## Validation

- **`e2e/tasks/test_task_tags`** (12 assertions) covers the JSON listing, `--tag` filters on `tasks ls` and `run`, combining with a pattern, and leaving untagged tasks out.
- **Unit tests:** `cargo test -p mise-config` (26 passed) and `-p mise --lib -- task:: schema_matches_parser` (576 passed). `test_parses_all_fields` covers `tags`.
- **Lint:** `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean. `mise run render` regenerate

title: feat(task): write a JSON report of a run with --report-file
body:
Tools that run a project's tasks, such as CI dashboards and agent toolkits, today have to parse `mise run`'s output to learn what ran and how each task ended. `mise run --report-file <PATH>`, or `MISE_TASK_REPORT_FILE`, writes a JSON report instead when the run ends. That happens whether the run passes, fails, is interrupted or stops at `--timeout`.

```console
$ mise run --report-file report.json ci   # ci depends on lint and deploy; deploy depends on test, which exits 3
$ jq -c '.status, [.tasks[] | {name, status, exit_code}]' report.json
"failed"
[{"name":"lint","status":"passed","exit_code":0},{"name":"test","status":"failed","exit_code":3},{"name":"ci","status":"not_run","exit_code":null},{"name":"deploy","status":"not_run","exit_code":null}]
```

## The report

- **Top level:** `version`, the run's `status` (`passed`, `failed`, `cancelled` or `timed_out`), timestamps and `duration_ms`.
- **`tasks`:** every task the run scheduled, dependencies included, in the order they started, then the ones that never started. Each has `name`, `args`, `status`, `exit_code`, `duration_ms` and timestamps.
- **Task status:**
  - `passed` or `failed`;
  - `cancelled`, stopped by Ctrl-C, `--timeout` or another task failing;
  - `skipped`: outputs up to date, `skip_if` met, or listed in `task.skip`;
  - `cached`: restored from the artifact cache;
  - `not_run`.
- **Redaction:** arguments are redacted like terminal output.
- **Stability:** a `version` bump means a field changed meaning; new fields can appear without one.

## Details

- **Writing:** the report is written atomically. A relative path resolves against the directory mise started in, and the flag conflicts with `--dry-run`.
- **Timeouts:** the report state lives outside the run, so it's still written when `--timeout` drops the run. Tasks still running then are marked `cancelled`.
- **Nested runs:** tasks don't inherit `MISE_TASK_REPORT_FILE`, so a `mise run` inside a task can't overwrite the outer report.
- **Cache hits:** a new `restored` flag on the executor's run outcome tells a cache restore (`cached`) apart from an up-to-date skip (`skipped`).

## Open questions

1. **No task started:** if mise fails before any task starts (a task not found, a tool that won't install), the report says `failed` with no tasks and no message. An `error` field could say why, but error text can contain secrets.
2. **What `duration_ms` measures:** it's the task job's wall time, including environment setup, not only its commands.
3. **Skip reasons:** all of them are `skipped`. A `reason` field could be added later without a version bump.

## Validation

- **`e2e/tasks/test_task_run_report`** (15 assertions) covers:
  - passed, failed (exit code kept, report still written) and skipped tasks, and one not run;
  - the environment variable, and its removal for nested runs;
  - `--timeout`, giving `timed_out` with the task `cancelled`.

  `cached` has unit coverage only, since the artifact cache is experimental.

title: fix(lock): bind the bumped request when a version argument rewrites the config
body:
`mise lock tiny@3.0.1` with `tiny = "2"` in `mise.toml` rewrites the config to `tiny = "3"`, but the lockfile bound the version argument instead:

```toml
# mise.toml
tiny = "3"

# mise.lock (before)
[[tools.tiny]]
version = "3.0.1"
specifiers = ["3.0.1"]
```

Lockfile lookups need an exact request binding, so a later lookup for `"3"` missed that entry. The config bump was planned only after the targets were bound and written. The lockfile now binds the request the config will hold (`specifiers = ["3"]`), by computing the bumps before binding. The config edit itself is still applied (or deferred for atomic runs) at the same point as before.

Found while reviewing #15386, which fixes the replacement request that this change binds; the two are independent.

The e2e test in `test_lock_version` asserts `specifiers = ["3"]` and failed before this change.

title: feat(task): add a summary output style that prints only what failed
body:
A passing test suite can print thousands of lines: passing tests, install progress, build output. Nobody reading a CI log, and no coding agent, needs those, while a failing task's output is all that matters. This adds a `summary` output style. It holds each task's output until the task ends, then prints one line for a task that passed and everything a task printed if it failed. It's opt-in, through `--output summary`, `MISE_TASK_OUTPUT=summary`, `task.output` or a task's `output`, and no default changes.

```console
$ mise run --output summary test
[lint] $ cargo clippy -- -D warnings
[lint] error: unused variable: `x`
[lint]  --> src/main.rs:12:9
[unit] passed in 4.2s
[lint] ERROR task failed
```

For an agent, set `MISE_TASK_OUTPUT=summary` in its environment. jouet, an agent toolkit, plans to do that for the sessions it sets up.

## Behavior

- **A task that passed** prints `[name] passed in 4.2s`.
  - With `--no-timings` or `task.timings = false`, it prints `[name] passed`.
  - From the artifact cache, it prints `[name] passed (cached)`.
  - If it ran nothing, it prints what mise said about it: `[name] sources up-to-date, skipping`, or in a dry run the commands it would run.
  - A task that only has dependencies prints nothing.
- **A task that failed** prints everything it wrote, labelled with its name as in `prefix`, including mise's `$ command` line.
- **A task mise stopped** because another one failed, or because the run was interrupted, prints `[name] cancelled`.
- **The run's closing messages** still print: `ERROR task failed`, and the `--continue-on-error` failure summary.
- **What's held for tasks that never finished**, after an interrupt, is printed at the end.
- `raw` and `interactive` tasks still get the terminal, and `--quiet` drops the passed lines too.

A task that keeps running, such as a dev server, prints nothing until it exits or the run is interrupted. The docs say to give such tasks `output = "interleave"`.

## Validation

- **`e2e/tasks/test_task_output_summary`** (16 assertions) covers:
  - a passing task's output hidden behind its line;
  - a failing task's stdout, stderr and closing error shown;
  - no line for a task with only dependencies;
  - the up-to-date line;
  - dry-run commands shown;
  - `--no-timings`;
  - selection through `MISE_TASK_OUTPUT`;
  - no change in default output, also under an agent (`CLAUDECODE=1`).

  It passes along with the existing output-style e2e tests.
- **Unit tests:** `cargo test -p mise --lib task::` (575 passed), `-p mise-config`, `-p mise-settings`, and `schema_matches_parser`.
- **Lint:** `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean. `mise run render` regenerated the schema, CLI docs and man page.

title: test(e2e): print one line for each passing test by default
body:
`mise run test:e2e NAME` used to stream every test's full output, even when it passed: each `DEBUG: $` command, each `SUCCESS:` assertion, and mise's own install and lock output. A passing run of one test could be pages of text. People and agents then scrolled or grepped the log to find out whether it passed and which tests ran.

Now a passing test prints one line, with its time and how many assertions passed. A failing test still prints everything it wrote:

```console
$ mise run test:e2e '^test_zz_fail$' '^test_version$'
>>> E2E cli/test_zz_fail
DEBUG: $ echo a
SUCCESS: [echo a] output is equal to 'a'
DEBUG: $ echo a
ERROR: E2E assertion failed: [echo a] expected 'b' but got 'a'
cli/test_zz_fail: 0s
ERROR: E2E test cli/test_zz_fail failed: exited with status code 1
Test environment can be examined in /tmp/test_zz_fail.OkmdwS

PASS: cli/test_version (1s, 1 assertion)
E2E: ran 2 tests (1 passed, 1 failed), skipped 0 tests

Failed e2e tests (1):
  - cli/test_zz_fail
```

## What changed

- **Named tests go through the same runner as `--all`.** `mise run test:e2e NAME...` now uses `e2e/run_all_tests`, one test at a time by default, unless `E2E_JOBS` sets a higher number. Before, named tests went through a separate loop that streamed their output.
- **Quiet locally, as on CI.** Passing tests' output is hidden locally as it already was on CI. Set `E2E_SHOW_PASSING_LOGS=1` to see it.
- **The pass line names any warning.** A passing test's "took Ns but is not marked as slow" warning is still printed. On CI that also brings back the annotation, which was lost along with the hidden passing logs.
- **The summary counts failures:** `E2E: ran N tests (P passed, F failed)`.

One trade-off: output now appears when each test finishes, not as it runs. `docs/contributing.md` says so and describes the new output.

Tested by running a passing selection and a selection with a deliberately failing test (deleted afterwards). `hk check` is clean on the changed files.

title: fix(lock): keep a registry-only aube graph when a lockfile is not trusted
body:
`MISE_SAFE=1 MISE_LOCKED=1 mise install npm:prettier` failed with "no embedded-aube dependency graph in the revision 2 lockfile; run `mise lock` to repair it", and `mise lock` could not repair it. The lockfile already had the graph. Since 2026.11.0, safe mode treats every project lockfile as untrusted (#15235), and an untrusted lockfile dropped the aube graph along with its URLs.

```toml
# mise.toml
[tools]
"npm:prettier" = "3.3.3"
```

After `mise lock`, `MISE_SAFE=1 MISE_LOCKED=1 mise install` now installs it. The graph pins integrity hashes and aube fetches from the user's registry, so it is kept when it names no place to download from. It is still dropped, as before, when a package has a tarball URL, git or directory source, or the importers have a `link:` or `file:` dependency, since only a trusted lockfile may choose those.

This also applies to untrusted projects outside safe mode. Related to #15363; the checksum-only core backends are in #15392.

Not covered: `mise ls --missing` can still report an npm tool as missing after a safe-mode install, which needs its own fix.

> Changes lockfile trust/safe-mode sanitization and npm install validation; incorrect allowlist logic could retain malicious download hints or reject valid registry locks.
> 
> **Overview**
> Untrusted lockfiles (including under **`MISE_SAFE`**) no longer always strip **`aube`** npm dependency graphs. **Registry-only** graphs that pin packages via **`integrity`** and fetch through the normal registry are **retained**; graphs that embed tarball URLs, git/path/link sources, aliases, bad snapshots, or other non-registry shapes are still dropped, validated by new **`aube_graph_names_only_registry`**.

title: registry: fix odin shim on windows
body:
Fixes #15398.

On Windows, `mise use odin@latest` installed Odin but created no `odin` shim. Only `lld-link`, `radlink` and `wasm-ld` were shimmed, and `mise which odin` failed with "No executable found for configured tool: odin".

The Windows zip puts `odin.exe` at the install root and also ships a `bin/` directory with those bundled linker tools. The github backend uses `bin/` whenever it exists, so it never looked at the root. This sets `bin_path = "."` in the registry entry so mise uses the install root.

I reproduced the missing shim with mise 2026.11.1 on Windows. I have not verified the fix on Windows, and I did not check the Linux or macOS archive layouts.

title: fix(dotfiles): do not follow user directory links in a symlink-each target
body:
A `symlink-each` entry followed a directory link the user had made inside its target, and wrote its links into wherever that link pointed. `mise dot unapply` then treated the user's link as an empty directory and removed it (on Linux the removal failed with `Not a directory` and stopped partway).

```text
test-target/
└─ sub -> ~/old-dotfiles        (the user's own link)
```

```sh
mise dot apply --yes   # wrote old-dotfiles/a.txt through the link
```

Now:
- apply reports a directory link beneath the target as a conflict that needs `--force`; with `--force` the link is replaced by a real directory. The target itself and links above it are still followed (a target that is a link to the real directory keeps working), so `~/.config/app` under a symlinked `~/.config` keeps working, and Stow-style folded links into the source keep being unfolded.
- the empty-directory cleanup that `unapply` runs for `symlink-each` and `copy` entries never removes a link to a directory.

An unapply of a record an older mise wrote through such a link is not changed here.

Part of #15356 (problem 1).

## Test plan
- `mise run test:e2e test_dotfiles_files`: a link beneath the target blocks apply and nothing is written through it; `--force` replaces it with a real directory.
- unit test: `remove_empty_dirs_upward` leaves a directory link alone.

title: ci(docs): run the showreel job on the large Namespace profile
body:
## Summary

The docs deploy for the v2026.11.1 release failed ([run 41894886608](https://github.com/jdx/mise/actions/runs/41894886608)): the showreel job's Docker build ran out of memory on the Namespace runner, so no render was left and the `docs` job refused to build the site.

```
ERROR: failed to build: failed to solve: ResourceExhausted: process "/bin/sh -c apt-get update && ... apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends dbus dbus-user-session libpam-systemd systemd systemd-sysv ..." did not complete successfully: cannot allocate memory
```

This moves the trusted showreel job from `namespace-profile-endev-linux-amd64` to `namespace-profile-endev-linux-amd64-large`, which other workflows already use. The cache tag stays `mise-docs-showreel`, so the first run on the new profile starts with a cold bundled cache.

Untrusted runs still use `ubuntu-latest`.

title: fix(exec): complete files after the command in mise exec
body:
`mise x -- <cmd> <Tab>` offered nothing in zsh, bash and fish: not the wrapped command's arguments, and not even file names.

```console
$ mise x -- ls some-prefix<Tab>      # before: no candidates
$ mise x -- ls some-prefix<Tab>      # after: files, as in a bare shell
```

The first word after `--` still completes from the commands on `PATH`. Every word after it now completes file names.

## Cause

Completers are keyed by argument name. `exec`'s `-c --command <COMMAND>` flag carries `type=command` and shares the name `COMMAND` with the `-- COMMAND` positional, so that closed command-name set answered for every word of the command line. After the first word it matched nothing, and the shell got no file fallback.

## Fix

The forwarded `COMMAND` arguments declare `type=command_args` on the argument itself, so the flag's completer can no longer shadow it. This also applies to `mise dot capture --` and `mise bootstrap repos exec --`, which had the same trailing-command shape. `mise.usage.kdl` is regenerated.

This does not delegate to the wrapped command's own completion (for example `git <Tab>` offering subcommands). That needs a usage feature; I'm looking at it separately.

Reported in discussion jdx/mise#15364.

## Validation

New unit test in `src/cli/completion.rs` covers `mise x -- `, `mise x node@22 -- `, `mise exec -- ` (commands) and later words (files). `cargo clippy -p mise --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean.

> 
> **Overview**
> **Fixes empty tab completion** for `mise x -- <cmd> …` (and similar “run a command after `--`” flows) in bash, zsh, and fish. The **first word after `--` still completes executable names from `PATH`**; **every later word now falls back to file/directory completion**, matching a normal shell.
> 
> The regression came from **`exec`’s `-c/--command` flag and the `-- COMMAND` positional both using the name `COMMAND`**, so the flag’s closed `type=command` completer answered for the whole forwarded line and offered nothing after the command word.
>

title: fix(dotfiles): keep links to dangling symlink-each sources
body:
A `symlink-each` source that contains a dangling symlink reported success but left no link in the target: the first `mise dot apply` printed `created 1 symlink(s)`, wrote the state, then `mise dot status` showed the entry as `missing`.

```text
src/
├─ a.txt
└─ dangling -> /nowhere
```

```sh
mise dot apply --yes   # created 2 symlink(s), but tgt/dangling does not exist
mise dot status        # differs (1 file(s) linked, 1 missing)
```

Cause: with no state yet, apply prunes links whose source is gone (`legacy_stale_links`) and tested that with `exists()`, which follows links. A dangling source link counted as gone, so the link apply had just made was removed again. The walk, the state and the relative-link code already treat dangling sources as deployable, so the check now uses `symlink_metadata` and a source entry that exists as a link is kept.

Part of #15356 (problem 2).

## Test plan

title: fix(dotfiles): adopt the origin's history when the local checkpoints hold no files
body:
Fixes the `mise dot origin set` failure on a second machine reported in discussion #15379.

## Problem

A machine whose only checkpoint holds no files (for example it tracks a path that does not exist yet, so the baseline checkpoint is empty) could not connect to a history another machine had already published:

```
$ mise dot origin set <origin> --sync manual
Error: local and origin histories are unrelated. Neither history was replaced.
```

The error came after `[history.origin]` was already written, so `mise dot sync` and `mise dot pull` failed the same way afterwards. Only `mise bootstrap --adopt` worked.

## Fix

- A local history that shares no ancestry with the origin's and has never held a tracked file is dropped, so the machine adopts the origin's history like any machine with no checkpoints. Nothing is lost: such a history holds only mise's own metadata.
- Any other unrelated history is still refused, and now before `[history.origin]` is written, so a refused `origin set` leaves nothing behind.

Verified with a new e2e (`test_dotfiles_origin_set_second_machine`): the empty-baseline machine connects and pulls the origin's file; a machine with its own tracked file is refused and has no `[history.origin]`.

Notes: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes. I could not reproduce the exact empty checkpoint from the report with a bare machine (that case already skipped the empty root), only the tracked-but-missing-file variant, so the report may involve another route to an empty checkpoint.

## Popularity

Not applicable (no registry change).

title: fix(bootstrap): stop spawning git for each encrypted file in history snapshots
body:
Fixes #15361.

Every history snapshot started a `git cat-file blob` process for each encrypted tracked file, only to check the `mise-encrypted-file-v1` header. With 17 encrypted files, a no-op `mise bootstrap services apply -y` (two snapshots) started 34 of these processes, about 410 ms by the reporter's measurement.

The header check now reads full object ids in-process with gix, as `cat_object` already does, so a snapshot no longer spawns git per encrypted file. A blob shorter than the header is never read, and an id that isn't a blob is still an error. Anything that isn't a full hex object id still goes through git as before. The other callers of `HistoryRepo::blob_starts_with` (replay, checkpoint, and sync) get the same speedup.

To check the effect on a setup with encrypted tracked files:

```bash
t=$(mktemp); GIT_TRACE2_EVENT=$t mise bootstrap services apply -y
grep -c '"cat-file","blob"' "$t"   # was 34 for 17 files; should now be 0
```

I did not run this repro or measure timings; the 410 ms figure is from the issue. The new unit test `blob_starts_with_matches_git` checks the gix path against the git-backed one for a match, a mismatch, a short blob, a tree id and a missing object. The `history` unit tests and `cargo clippy -p mise -p mise-system --all-targets -- -D warnings` pass.

One tradeoff: the gix path loads the whole blob once its header says it is long enough, where the git-backed check read only the first bytes. gix 0.89 has no cheap streaming reader here. Callers check encrypted content that is already bounded.

> **Low Risk**
> Localized read-path optimization with parity testing; behavior for full object ids should match Git aside from reading whole blobs for prefix checks on bounded encrypted content.
> 
> **Overview**
> History snapshots were spawning **`git cat-file blob`** once per encrypted tracked file just to see if a blob starts with **`mise-encrypted-file-v1\n`**. **`HistoryRepo::blob_starts_with`** now handles full hex object ids the same way **`cat_object`** already does: **gix** reads the object header in-process, returns **`false`** without loading the blob when it is shorter than the prefix, errors on non-blobs, and only falls back to Git for non-id specs.
> 
> A new unit test **`blob_starts_with_matches_git`** asserts the in-process path matches the Git-backed implementation for matching and non-matching blobs, short blobs, trees, and missing objects.
> 
> **Tradeoff:** when the header says the blob is long enough, the gix path loads the full blob to compare the prefix (Git could read only the first bytes).

title: fix(lock): resolve core tool downloads from checksum in safe mode
body:
`MISE_SAFE=1 MISE_LOCKED=1 mise install` failed for `node`, `python` and `go` with "No lockfile URL found", even when the project's `mise.lock` had a URL and checksum for them. This worked in 2026.10.25.

Safe mode ignores the URLs in a project lockfile (#15235) and keeps the checksums. Locked mode then only accepted such a checksum-only entry for aqua and github tools, so every other backend failed, and the hint to run `mise lock` could not help.

```toml
# mise.toml
[settings]
locked = true

[tools]
node = "22.12.0"
go = "1.23.4"
```

`MISE_SAFE=1 MISE_LOCKED=1 mise install` now installs both. node, python and go work out their own download and check it against the locked checksum, as aqua and github do, so a tampered or mismatched download still fails. The "No lockfile URL found" error also says when safe mode is the reason, instead of pointing to `mise lock`.

Not covered: `npm:` tools locked through aube still fail in safe mode, because the project's dependency graph is dropped, and `mise ls --missing` can report a tool as missing after a safe-mode install. Those need their own fixes.

Refs #15363

> **Medium Risk**
> Changes locked/safe-mode download and checksum verification for core runtimes (node, go, python), which are security-sensitive install paths but align with existing aqua/github behavior and add stricter locked-mode failures for python.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Safe mode + locked install** for **go**, **node**, and **python** no longer fails with “No lockfile URL found” when the lockfile only has a checksum (URLs stripped in safe mode). Those core backends now declare **`resolves_locked_url_from_checksum`**, matching **aqua/github**, so checksum-only lock entries count as valid in `--locked` mode.
> 
> **Node** treats checksum-only pins as authoritative: it downloads from the usual mirror when the lock URL is ignored, verifies against the **locked checksum** (not a freshly fetched one), and applies the same logic for locked **source** builds when the URL is missing.
> 
> **Python** returns **`resolves_locked_url_from_checksum`** only on the precompiled install path; in **locked** mode it **errors** if no precompiled artifact exists instead of falling through to compile.
> 
> The shared backend error hint now explains when **safe mode** blocks URL-less locks for backends that cannot resolve from checksum alone. E2E coverage adds **go** and **node** tampered-checksum cases under **`MISE_SAFE=1`**.

title: fix(skills): link only a project's own tools into its skills directory
body:
With `skills.auto_sync` on, a tool that only your global config declares had its agent skills linked into every project's skills directory as well as `~/.claude/skills`, so the agent saw the same skill twice. Now a project's directory gets only the tools its own config declares, and global tools are linked under your home directory.

Reported in discussion #15275, as a follow-up to #15276.

```toml
# ~/.config/mise/config.toml
[tools]
worktrunk = "latest"

[settings.skills]
auto_sync = true
```

```toml
# project/mise.toml
[tools]
node = "22"
```

```sh
mise install   # in project/
```

Before, `worktrunk`'s skills were linked into both `~/.agents/skills` and `project/.agents/skills`. Now they are linked only into `~/.agents/skills`.

- A tool the project also lists keeps whatever version is active in the project, and its skills are linked there. So does a tool selected by `MISE_<TOOL>_VERSION`.
- `mise skills sync` without `--dir` or `--global` follows the same rule as auto-sync, so a manual and an automatic sync agree. `--dir` still links every active tool, and `--global` still links the global ones.
- When the project's skills directory is the same as the home one (a project rooted at your home directory, or an absolute `skills.dir`), one pass links the tools of both, as before.
- Links already in a project's directory from global tools stay until you remove them or sync with `--prune` (or `skills.prune`).

`mise skills ls` still lists every active tool's skills.

Tested with a new e2e test (`test_skills_project_scope`) plus the existing skills e2e tests; clippy and lint pass.

> **Medium Risk**
> Changes which tools are linked during install/use/upgrade and manual sync; stale global links in project dirs remain until prune, but wrong duplicates in agents are the main user-visible behavior change.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Fixes duplicate agent skills** when `skills.auto_sync` is on: tools declared **only** in global config no longer get symlinked into each project's `skills.dir`; they stay under the home skills directory instead.
> 
> A project's directory now gets skills for tools its **local config** declares and for tools selected via **`MISE_<TOOL>_VERSION`**, while still using the **active** version when a tool appears in both project and global config. **`mise skills sync`** (without `--dir`) follows the same split as auto-sync; **`--dir`** still links every active tool, and **`--global`** still targets global tools only.
> 
> **Auto-sync** uses a new **`SkillsScope`** (project vs global vs all active) and skips a second home pass when project and home share one skills directory (via **`same_dir`**). Docs and **`settings.toml`** describe the behavior; **`test_skills_project_scope`** e2e covers global-only, project-local, explicit `--dir`, and home syn

title: fix(dotfiles): clear symlink-each state when a group is removed
body:
`mise dot unapply --group <name>` and `mise dot apply --prune` removed a dotfile group's links but left behind the per-target `symlink-each` record that tracked them, under `$MISE_STATE_DIR/dotfiles/<hash>.toml`. The files were gone while the record stayed, and nothing ever cleaned it up.

```toml
[dotfile_groups.demo]
root = "~/.dotfiles/demo"
target = "~/.demo"
mode = "symlink-each"
```

```sh
mise dot apply --yes
mise dot unapply --group demo --yes   # links removed; <hash>.toml with group = "demo" stayed
```

Removing a group's files now also drops its `symlink-each` records once none of the links they name is still in place. A record that still names a link mise left on purpose (for example a modified file) is kept, so a later run can find it.

Part of #15356 (problem 3).

## Test plan
- `mise run test:e2e test_dotfiles_groups`: new case applies a `symlink-each` group, checks the record exists, unapplies the group, and checks it is gone.

title: fix(shim): run mise, not the shim, for a due auto_update
body:
Fixes #15362.

On macOS, a shim launch with a due `tool_update.global_auto` check ran the tool with mise's internal arguments instead of updating it:

```
$ echo '{}' | ~/.local/share/mise/shims/jq -c .
jq: Unknown option --id
mise WARN  could not update aqua:jqlang/jq (exit status: 2), running the installed version
```

Without `__MISE_BIN`, mise's own path is `current_exe()`, which on macOS is the shim symlink that was run. The background update started that path, so the tool got `__tool-update <tool> --id <id>` and nothing updated. Linux resolves `current_exe()` already, so it was not affected.

The update command now resolves the path first, as the system-fallback lookup in `shim.rs` already does.

I could not reproduce this on Linux, so there is no new test; it was verified to compile only. Other places that spawn `MISE_BIN` have the same latent shape and are left alone here.

title: fix(shim): stop suggesting a reinstall when the version ships other executables
body:
Fixes #15374.

When a configured tool's name matched a binary its installed version doesn't ship, mise told users to run `mise install --force <tool>@<version>`. That reinstalls the same release and fails the same way. It also hid the more accurate "not provided by the active …, provided by …" message. This hit mprocs, which upstream renamed to dekit: 0.10.x ships only `dekit`.

Now the reinstall hint appears only when a reinstall could add the binary, meaning the version's bin dirs hold no executables yet or already include it. Otherwise:

```
mprocs@0.10.3 does not provide mprocs (it provides: dekit)
```

When another installed version provides the binary, the shim error names it first:

```
mprocs is not provided by the active mprocs@0.10.3 (set by …/config.toml)
mprocs is provided by: mprocs@0.9.6
```

`mise which` gets the same message.

Added a unit test for a version that ships only a renamed binary.

> **Overview**
> Improves shim and **`mise which`** errors when a configured, installed tool does not expose the binary you invoked—especially after upstream renames (e.g. **mprocs** → **dekit**).
>

If the active version ships other executables but not the requested name, users see **`tool@version does not provide <bin> (it provides: …)`** instead of a useless **`mise install --force`** that reinstalls the same release. title: fix(bootstrap): apply mise's own config before planning the other dotfiles
body:
`mise bootstrap` read mise's own configuration once, before the dotfiles phase. When a `[dotfiles]` entry copied a config file such as `~/.config/mise/conf.d/reviewed.toml` into place, the entries that file declares were not planned until the next run, on first placement and on every update. `mise dot apply` already avoids this by writing mise's own config first; the dotfiles phase of `mise bootstrap` now does the same.

```toml
# ~/.config/mise/config.toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.config/mise/conf.d/reviewed.toml" = { source = "~/dotfiles/reviewed.toml", mode = "copy" }

# ~/dotfiles/reviewed.toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.greeting" = { source = "~/dotfiles/greeting", mode = "copy" }
```

Before, the first `mise bootstrap` only placed `reviewed.toml` and `~/.greeting` appeared on the second run. Now one run places both. `--dry-run` previews both as well.

The config-first pass is the one `mise dot apply` uses, now shared as `apply_config_entries`. Entries already written in the first pass are not written again, and the reload commands run for them as before.

Tests: new e2e `test_bootstrap_dotfiles_config_first` (fails without the change, passes with it), plus the existing bootstrap dotfiles and `dot apply` config-first e2e tests.

Fixes discussion [#15380](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15380).

title: fix(lock): keep the vendor prefix once when moving a prefixed request
body:
`mise lock java@temurin-27` rewrote `java = "temurin-26"` in `mise.toml` to `java = "temurin-temurin"`, which then no longer installs.

```sh
cat > mise.toml <<'X'
[tools]
java = "temurin-26"
X
mise lock
mise lock java@temurin-27
cat mise.toml
```

Before: `java = "temurin-temurin"`. After: `java = "temurin-27"`, at the same precision as the original request. `java@temurin-27.0.1+0` also writes `temurin-27`, and a bare `java = "26"` followed by `java@temurin-27` moves to `temurin-27`.

A vendor switch at the same version (`java@zulu-26` over `temurin-26`) is saved too.

The command-line version's vendor prefix was taken for the version when computing the bump, so the prefix was written twice. The bump now runs on the bare version, and a vendor prefix on the command line wins over the config's.

Covered by a new unit test (`test_cli_config_bump_keeps_vendor_prefix_once`); clippy is clean. I did not run the Java repro end to end.

Fixes #15381

title: fix(completion): keep built-in descriptions when a task shares a command's name
body:
Shell completion no longer lets a task hide a built-in command's description when the two share a name.

With a task named `upgrade`, completing `mise up` offered the task's description in place of the built-in command's, because `mise` completes commands and naked task names together and shells like fish show one entry per name:

```fish
❯ mise up
up  (Upgrade outdated tools)  upgrade  (Upgrade mise and managed software, ...)   # task's description
```

`mise upgrade` runs the built-in, so that entry was misleading. The task is still reachable, and still completes, as `mise run upgrade`.

After:

```
$ mise __complete_word__ --shell fish --line 'mise up'
up	Upgrade outdated tools
upgrade	Upgrade outdated tools

$ mise __complete_word__ --shell fish --line 'mise run up'
upgrade	<the task's description>
```

At the first word after `mise` (flags skipped), a task candidate that carries a command's name or alias but not that command's description is dropped. `mise run <TAB>` is unchanged.

Fixes #15367

Tested with `e2e/cli/test_completion_dynamic` (extended with a task named `upgrade`) and `cargo clippy -p mise --all-targets -- -D warnings`.

title: fix(go): retry transient go install network failures
body:
Installing a Go tool no longer fails on a one-off network error from the Go module proxy or checksum database. The install retries instead, and when it does fail the error names the real cause.

Fixes #15378

## The problem

`go install` downloads modules itself, so `http_retries` never applied to it. A dropped stream failed the install:

```
mise go:github.com/oapi-codegen/oapi-codegen/v2/cmd/oapi-codegen@2.8.0
reading https://sum.golang.org/tile/8/0/x276/526: stream error: stream ID 59; INTERNAL_ERROR; received from peer
```

mise then retried without the `v` prefix, which is meant for modules tagged without one. That ran `go install ...@2.8.0`, which fails with an unrelated `unknown revision 2.8.0` and buries the real cause.

## The fix

- A `go install` that fails with a recognized transport error (`stream error`, `INTERNAL_ERROR`, connection reset or refused, `i/o timeout`, TLS handshake timeout, unexpected EOF, 429/502/503/504) is retried with the same version. It uses the `http_retries` setting and the same backoff as mise's own HTTP requests, and logs a warning for each retry.
- When the retries run out on a transient error, that error is returned as is. The unprefixed-version fallback only runs after a failure that is not transient.
- DNS failures (`no such host`) and errors like `unknown revision` are not retried, matching how `http_retries` treats them.

## Testing

Unit test for the stderr classifier, using the failure from the report as one case. The existing `go_install_versions` tests still pass. `cargo clippy --lib -- -D warnings` is clean.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: claude-code_2-1-309_agent.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> **Medium Risk**
> Changes Go install failure handling and version-fallback rules; behavior depends on stderr heuristics, though scoped to the Go backend with new unit and e2e tests.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Go tool installs** now retry the **same** module version when `go install` fails with a recognizable transport error (proxy/checksum stream drops, timeouts, connection issues, 429/5xx), using the existing **`http_retries`** setting and the same backoff as mise’s HTTP client. Each retry is logged as a warning.
> 
> Because `go` fetches modules on its own, mise captures **`go` stderr** (via **`never_raw`**) and classifies failures with **`is_transient_go_network_failure`**. DNS (`no such host`), bad revisions, and compile diagnostics are **not** retried.
>

title: fix(config): do not panic when a config path cannot be canonicalized
body:
Fixes #15377.

On Windows, mise panicked with `Os { code: 5, kind: PermissionDenied }` while loading project config whenever it ran inside a sandbox that denies access outside the workspace (for example Codex Desktop with Workspace write). Even `mise --version` in a fresh worktree failed.

The cause was `path.canonicalize().unwrap()` in `hashed_path_filename`, which builds the trust and ignore file names for every config. `canonicalize` needs access to every ancestor of the path, so a sandbox can make it fail. mise now falls back to the absolute path, and then to the path as given, instead of panicking. The config is then checked for trust as usual (an untrusted config gets the normal trust error).

Because the fallback path is hashed differently from the canonical one, a config trusted outside the sandbox may show as untrusted inside it. `MISE_TRUSTED_CONFIG_PATHS` works around that.

I added a unit test that hashes a path `canonicalize` cannot resolve. I did not reproduce the Windows sandbox itself.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: unavailable.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Touches config trust/ignore identity on every load; fallback hashing can diverge from prior canonical trust records in restricted environments.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes startup panics (e.g. Windows **PermissionDenied** in workspace sandboxes) when mise builds trust/ignore filenames for project config.
> 
> **`hashed_path_filename`** no longer uses **`canonicalize().unwrap()`**. It tries canonicalization first, then **`std::path::absolute`**, then the path as given, so missing or inaccessible ancestor directories cannot abort the process. Trust checks still run as before; only the on-disk trust marker name may differ from the fully canonical form when canonicalize fails.
> 
> Adds tests for uncanonicalizable paths and for relative vs absolute hashing consistency.
>

title: docs: make mise.toml reference keys findable in site search
body:
Searching the docs for a mise.toml key such as `doctor.checks` found nothing on the [mise.toml reference](https://mise.jdx.dev/configuration/reference.html), even though the page documents it at `reference.html#doctor.checks`.

The page loads its keys in the browser after it opens. The Algolia crawler that builds the site search does not run scripts, so it indexed one record for the whole page: its title. The other 421 pages in the sitemap are indexed; this page was the only gap.

After this change, the HTML the server sends contains all 1,185 keys. Each key is a heading whose `id` is the key's path (the anchor the explorer already uses), followed by its description. Once the crawler picks this up, a search for `doctor.checks` or `tasks.<name>.depends` links straight to that key in the explorer.

### How it works

- The full reference is loaded in `onServerPrefetch`, so only the server build renders the index. The page's JavaScript grows by 0.7 KB (133.9 KB to 134.7 KB), and the browser still lazy-loads the full data as before.
- The index is `display: none` and sits in a `data-allow-mismatch="children"` wrapper, so hydration removes it without errors. Browsers don't scroll to the hidden headings when the page opens with a key in the URL.
- The HTML grows from about 20 KB to 53 KB gzipped.

### Validation

- `vitepress build docs`, the social-image check and the link check pass.
- The built `reference.html` contains 1,185 `h2`/`h3` headings with ids.
- In a browser, opening `reference.html#doctor.checks` from the preview server selects `doctor.checks` in the explorer and logs nothing to the console. The empty index wrapper stays in the DOM after hydration.
- Not verified: how Algolia indexes the new headings. That will show after the next deploy and crawl.

> **Overview**
> The mise.toml reference page loads most keys in the browser, so the Algolia crawler (no JavaScript) only indexed the page title. **This change SSR-renders a hidden index of every section and nested key** so search can discover individual paths like `doctor.checks`.
> 
> During **`onServerPrefetch`**, the full **`config-reference.data.ts`** tree is flattened and emitted as **`h2`/`h3` headings** whose **`id`s match existing hash anchors**, each followed by its HTML description. The block lives in a **`.crawled`** container with **`display: none`** and **`data-allow-mismatch="children"`**, so crawlers see the content while **hydration removes it** without mismatch warnings and the interactive explorer behavior stays unchanged. Client-side lazy loading of the reference data is unchanged.

title: registry: fix blaze test for the ra-jit to blaze rename
body:
`blaze` is the new name of `ra-jit`, and releases from `v0.20261030.1` ship only `blaze`, `blaze-engine`, `blaze-proc-macro-srv` and `blaze-rustc`. The registry test still ran `ra-jit --help`, so `mise test-tool blaze` failed with `ra-jit: not found` (exit 127). That fails the `test-tool` job on the release PR once blaze's release is outside the grace period.

The test now runs the command that exists and checks the version, which blaze prints properly now (the old comment about a `ra-jit 0.0.0` nightly no longer applies):

```toml
bins = ["blaze"]
test = { cmd = "blaze --version", expected = "blaze {{version}}" }
```

`cargo-blaze`, `ra-jit` and `cargo-ra-jit` are dropped from `bins`; the current release has none of them.

Verified by installing `v0.20261030.1` and running `blaze --version`, which prints `blaze 0.20261030.1 (6560553 2026-10-30)`. I did not run `mise test-tool blaze` against a build of this branch.

title: fix(backend): keep latest on non-numeric releases under the release-age cutoff
body:
When a tool's newest release is still inside `minimum_release_age` (24 hours by default), `latest` could resolve to a release that is years old.

Odin stopped numbering its releases in 2020 and names them `dev-YYYY-MM` now. GitHub's latest release, `dev-2026-11a`, is too new for the cutoff, so mise fell back to the version list. There `latest` only matches versions that start with a digit, and Odin's last one is `0.12.0` from January 2020:

```console
$ mise latest odin
0.12.0
$ mise install odin@latest
✓ installed 1 tool in 10.8s: odin@0.12.0
$ mise which odin
mise ERROR No executable found for configured tool: odin
```

Now, when the tool's own latest release does not start with a digit, `latest` picks from every version the cutoff allows, leaving out pre-releases:

```console
$ mise latest odin
dev-2026-10
$ mise latest odin --minimum-release-age 60d
dev-2026-09
```

Tools whose latest release starts with a digit, or is a rolling channel like Rust's `stable` behind a mirror, work as before. A `nightly` or `edge` tag still does not count as `latest` for them.

Fixes #15358

title: fix(upgrade): skip out-of-range note for versions another entry already uses
body:
Fixes #15353.

When a tool is configured with several version ranges, `mise upgrade` could report a newer version that one of the entries already uses:

```toml
[tools]
python = ["3.15", "3.14"]
```

After 3.15.2 is released and installed, `mise upgrade` printed:

```
Newer versions are available but do not match the configured version ranges:
  python 3.14.10 → 3.15.2 (~/.config/mise/config.toml)
```

Because the `3.15` entry already uses 3.15.2, the note is no longer shown for it. Now `mise upgrade` prints "All tools are up to date" in this case. A version that no entry uses is still reported as before.

Added an e2e case in `e2e/cli/test_upgrade` (`dummy = ["2", "1"]`). `test_upgrade` and clippy pass.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: claude-code_2-1-309_agent.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Narrows informational out-of-range messaging in `mise upgrade` only; install and bump behavior are unchanged aside from when the note appears.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes false **out-of-range** warnings when one config entry for a tool already installed the newer release that another entry’s range would “point at.”
> 
> For multi-version tools (e.g. `python = ["3.15", "3.14"]`), a bare `mise upgrade` can still list bump-style updates that don’t fit each entry’s range. The change filters those notes when **another active entry** of the same backend already runs that **latest** version at the **same install path** (matching backend args and comparing paths on a fresh `ToolVersion`, so options that split installs are respected).
> 
> When everything in range is satisfied and the filtered list is empty, users see **“All tools are up to date”** instead of the misleading range message. Unreported versions that no entry uses behave as before.
> 
> Regression coverage was added in `e2e/cli/test_upgrade` with `dummy = ["2", "1"]`.

title: chore(deps): ignore unmaintained astral-tokio-tar and pin-utils in cargo-deny
body:
`cargo deny check` now fails `lint` on every branch. Two crates were marked unmaintained today, and both come in through rattler:

- `astral-tokio-tar`, via `rattler_package_streaming`, which the conda backend uses to unpack conda packages
- `pin-utils`, via `wasmtimer` in `rattler_repodata_gateway`

Neither advisory reports a vulnerability, and no upgrade drops either crate until rattler does. This adds ignore entries with those reasons, like the other transitive advisories in `deny.toml`.

Both advisories are still unnumbered (`RUSTSEC-0000-0000`). [rustsec/advisory-db#3497](https://github.com/rustsec/advisory-db/pull/3497) assigns them RUSTSEC-2026-0439 and RUSTSEC-2026-0437, and this ignores those IDs too. Until then, the placeholder entry is what keeps `lint` green. It ignores every unnumbered advisory, so it should be removed once the IDs are published.

## Test plan

- With a fresh advisory database, `cargo deny check advisories` fails on main with cargo-deny 0.19.4 (CI's version) and passes on this branch.

> Adds documented ignore entries in `deny.toml` for the upcoming IDs **RUSTSEC-2026-0439** and **RUSTSEC-2026-0437**, plus a **temporary** `RUSTSEC-0000-0000` ignore so CI passes while those advisories are still unnumbered in the advisory DB—intended to be removed once [rustsec/advisory-db#3497](https://github.com/rustsec/advisory-db/pull/3497) lands.

title: fix(zig): install from the lockfile URL and fix the fallback archive name
body:
When https://ziglang.org/download/index.json can't be read, `mise install` of a current zig release failed with a 404, even with a lockfile that pins the right URL. On 2026-11-03 the index was briefly invalid JSON after the 0.17.1 update, and every install of `core:zig@0.17.0` failed:

```text
INFO  zig@0.17.0      [1/3] mirror 1/17 zig-linux-x86_64-0.17.0.tar.xz
mise ERROR Failed to install core:zig@0.17.0: HTTP status client error (404 Not Found) for url (https://ziglang.org/download/0.17.0/zig-linux-x86_64-0.17.0.tar.xz)
```

Fixes #15349.

- **The lockfile URL is used.** When `mise.lock` has a URL for the platform, zig installs download it directly and don't fetch the index. The minisign signature is still checked, and the pinned checksum now applies because the URLs match. The locked URL is used only when its file name is the requested version's archive and it has no query; anything else, including the wrong `zig-{os}-{arch}-…` name an earlier fallback could have locked, is resolved through the index as before.
- **The fallback names the right file.** Zig renamed its archives from `zig-{os}-{arch}-…` to `zig-{arch}-{os}-…` in 0.14.1. The fallback that builds the URL without the index now uses the new order for 0.14.1 and later, and `.zip` on Windows. This covers installs without a lockfile and `mise lock`, which could previously write the wrong URL.
- **The index error is shown.** mise warns with the parse or fetch error before falling back, instead of leaving only the later 404.

Checked by installing `zig@0.15.1` from a lockfile URL: no request to `index.json`, and the install verified with minisign. A unit test covers the fallback names on both sides of 0.14.1 and on Windows.

Co-authored-by: Sargun Vohra <1320357+sargunv@users.noreply.github.com>

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: 2.1.309.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Touches core Zig download and lockfile URL selection, but minisign checks remain and mismatched locked URLs are rejected before use.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes Zig installs failing with **404** when `index.json` is unavailable and the lockfile already pins a good URL, and fixes the **no-index fallback** building wrong archive names (notably `zig-linux-x86_64-…` for releases ≥ **0.14.1**).
> 
> **Install path:** `download()` now uses the platform URL from `mise.lock` when `usable_locked_url` confirms the filename matches the expected archive for the version/OS/arch (no query/fragment). Otherwise it still resolves via the index. Minisign verification is unchanged; stale wrong URLs from older fallbacks are ignored and re-resolved.
> 
> **Fallback URL construction:** Shared helpers (`release_tarball_url`, `archive_name`, `arch_first`) pick **arch-os** vs **os-arch** naming and **`.zip` on Windows** by version. The same logic replaces duplicated arch/OS mapping via `index_platform`. Index fetc

title: fix(lock): leave the global lockfile alone on project installs
body:
Fixes #15345.

With the default `lockfile_mode = "generate"`, `mise install` inside a project regenerated every existing lockfile in the config hierarchy, including `~/.config/mise/mise.lock`, even when it installed only project tools. Two things went wrong:

- The global lockfile churned on every project install, picking up whatever platforms that project's `lockfile_platforms` listed.
- A global tool shadowed by the project (both declare `hk = "latest"`) was relocked under the project's locked backend. When the project still locked a backend the registry has since replaced, the global entry ended up pairing the old backend with the new backend's signer, and `mise lock --global` / `mise upgrade --global` then failed with `lockfile generation would change the recorded signer`.

Now:

- An install regenerates the lockfiles that plain `mise lock` would lock for the current config root, plus any other lockfile that a tool it installed, or a config it edited, writes to. A project install leaves the global lockfile alone unless it installs a global tool. `mise use -g` and `mise unuse -g` still update the global lockfile from inside a project.
- A request shadowed by another config is locked under the backend its own lockfile records, so `mise lock --global` from inside a project keeps the global entry on packslip while the project stays on aqua.

Settings are unchanged: when an install does touch the global lockfile (because it installed a global tool), it still uses the merged settings, including the project's `lockfile_platforms`. To refresh the global lockfile for edits to the global config, run `mise lock --global`, as the docs already describe.

## Validation

- New e2e `test_lockfile_project_install_global` reproduces the issue with hk (aqua → packslip): it fails on `main` and passes here.
- The generate-mode lockfile e2e tests and the global/shadowed lockfile tests pass. Clippy passes with `-D warnings`.
- The reporter's script (adapted to Linux with hk) now leaves the global lockfile unchanged when only project tools install, and `mise lock --global` succeeds afterwards.

Co-authored-by: Andrew <26885897+drewbitt@users.noreply.github.com>

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: 2.1.309.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes core lockfile generation paths after install and shadowed-tool resolution; mistakes could skip needed lock updates or corrupt global/project backend pairings, though behavior is covered by new e2e tests.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes unwanted **global lockfile** updates when running **`mise install`** in a project under generate-mode lockfiles.
> 
> **Install-scoped lock regeneration** no longer treats every config in the hierarchy as in scope. After an install, only lockfiles that plain **`mise lock`** would touch for the current root are regenerated, plus any lockfile tied to a tool that was act

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+# Installing in a project rewrites the global lockfile only when the install
+# changed a global tool or edited the global config, and a global request that the project shadows keeps
+# the backend the global lockfile records for it.
+#
+# hk moved from Aqua to Packslip, which serves releases from 1.58.1. The
+# project's lockfile below stands in for one written before that move: it
+# locks the same release under aqua while the global lockfile uses packslip.
+
+export MISE_LOCKFILE_MODE=generate
+export MISE_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE=0
+detect_platform
+other_platform=linux-arm64
+if [[ $MISE_PLATFORM == linux-arm64 ]]; then
+  other_platform=linux-x64
+fi
+
+cat >"$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml" <<TOML
+[settings]
+lockfile = true
+lockfile_platforms = ["$MISE_PLATFORM"]
