title: chore(config): deprecate lockfile_mode=merge, warning from 2027.4.0
body:
`lockfile_mode = "merge"` is now deprecated in favor of the default `generate` mode, which rebuilds the whole lockfile from the current requests and reuses unchanged entries.

Nothing changes for users today. The deprecation is staged on purpose:

| When | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Now | Docs mark `merge` as deprecated; no CLI warning |
| mise 2027.4.0 | Using `lockfile_mode = "merge"` (or `MISE_LOCKFILE_MODE=merge`) prints `deprecated [lockfile_mode.merge]` |
| mise 2027.10.0 | `merge` mode is removed |

To migrate, delete the setting:

```toml
[settings]
lockfile_mode = "merge" # remove this line
```

This uses a 6-month warn delay and a 6-month removal window (rather than the 12-month default), as requested by jdx.

## Changes

- `deprecated_at!("2027.4.0", "2027.10.0", "lockfile_mode.merge", ...)` in settings loading, so the removal reminder fires via `debug_assert!` once the version reaches 2027.10.0.
- Warning banner and `[deprecated]` enum description in `settings.toml`, and a banner in the lockfile reference docs.

## Validation

`cargo check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` and the `lockfile_mode` unit test pass. Running with `MISE_LOCKFILE_MODE=merge` prints no warning on the current version, as intended. `mise run render` produced no further changes.

title: perf(brew): resolve formulae from the bulk index and stop re-walking taps every run
body:
Follows #13349, which moved official casks onto the bulk index. This does the same for formulae and removes the two costs that were left on a run with nothing to do.

## Problem

`mise bootstrap packages upgrade` with nothing to upgrade still took 7 to 11 seconds on a machine declaring 79 formulae (7 from third-party taps), 144 casks (3 from taps) and 18 App Store apps. Almost none of it was work:

- **Formulae, one request each.** Every core formula, and every dependency in its closure, was a separate GET to `formulae.brew.sh/api/formula/<name>.json`: 251 requests on every run.
- **Tap casks, one after another.** Official casks answer from the bulk index, but a third-party tap cask is a chain of GitHub requests and a Ruby evaluation, about 1.3s each, and the status pass resolved them serially. Three tap casks were about 4s of the run.
- **Tap walks, repeated.** Every tap formula or cask walked the repository, its branch head, two tree listings and the raw Ruby file on every run, although everything after the branch head is addressed by a sha and cannot change.

`apply` and `status` pay the same costs, and a daily update runs `apply` and `upgrade` back to back.

## Change

- **Bulk formula index.** The cask index in `brew/cask/bulk.rs` is generalised to both documents and moved to `brew/bulk.rs`. `api/formula.json` (32,180,080 bytes) gets the same cached document, byte-range sidecar, 450s staleness window, `If-Modified-Since` revalidation, 7-day fallback window and per-entry fallback as `cask.json`; only the file stem and the fields that name an entry differ. Aliases resolve before old names across the whole document, the same answer `api::alias_map` gives the per-formula fallback. The bulk index answers only when `url_replacements` sends `formula/<name>.json` to the same place as `formula.json`; a rule that gives per-formula requests a source of their own keeps that source, as before. Exact lookups (a tap's sibling formula) do not follow aliases, and every lookup checks that the range it read is the entry it asked for. The cask sidecar keeps its on-disk format, so an existing one is not rebuilt.
- **Concurrent cask status.** `installed_with_options` resolves casks under the `jobs` limit with `buffered`, so results keep request order and the first error in that order still wins, as with the loop it replaces.
- **Tap casks evaluated once per run.** `upgrade` resolves every cask twice, once for the dependency closure and once for the plan, and a tap cask without published JSON started a sandboxed Ruby process each time. The evaluated cask is now kept for the rest of the process, so `upgrade --dry-run` runs 3 Ruby evaluations here instead of 6.
- **Sha-addressed tap cache.** Tree listings at a commit or tree sha, and raw Ruby files under the commit-pinned raw base, are kept in `system-brew/taps/`. An unchanged tap stops at its branch head; a new commit is still seen at once, because the branch head is asked every run. Entries are keyed by the URL af

title: feat(daemons): run container images as daemons with Docker or Podman
body:
## Design

**A container daemon is a custom daemon with an `image`.** mise writes its `run` command (a short POSIX shell script around `docker run`/`podman run`), and everything else (ports, exported variables, proxy, `depends`, `ready_cmd`, pitchfork supervision, `mise daemons logs`) is the existing custom-daemon path. `docker run` stays in the foreground, so its output is the daemon's log.

Why `image` rather than a `runtime = "docker"` preset-like type: presets are tied to an installed tool, a data-init step and a fixed named-port table; a container needs none of that, and a user-chosen image has no known default port. Keeping it a custom daemon means containers and native processes share one port/URL mechanism, which is the point: per-worktree application ports and URL derivation (`<NAME>_PORT`, `<NAME>_URL`, proxy hostnames) work the same for both.

Based on `main`, which now includes #15181 (preset named ports with `auto`/`base`). Container code lives in a new `container.rs` and reuses `ports::slot`; its `ports.<name>` table mirrors the `{ auto, base, stride }` shape of #15181's named ports, with a `container` key added. Folding its parser into `ports::parse_named` is a possible follow-up.

```toml
[daemons.cockroach]
image = "cockroachdb/cockroach:v25.1.0"
command = ["start-single-node", "--insecure"]
port = { auto = true, base = 26257 }
ports.http = { container = 8080, auto = true, base = 27000 }
env = { COCKROACH_SKIP_ENABLING_DIAGNOSTIC_REPORTING = "true" }
data_mount = "/cockroach/cockroach-data"
ready_cmd = "{{ runtime }} exec {{ container }} cockroach sql --insecure -e 'select 1'"
proxy = false
```

The primary checkout publishes `127.0.0.1:26257` and `127.0.0.1:27000`; a linked worktree with slot 7 publishes `26264` and `27007`, and the container keeps listening on `26257`/`8080`. Exported: `COCKROACH_PORT`, `COCKROACH_HTTP_PORT`.

## Behavior

- **Keys:** `image`, `command` (string = shell text like `run`, or argv array), `port` + `container_port` (defaults to the port's `base`), `ports.<name>` (integer, `{ container, host }` or `{ container, auto, base, stride }`), `env`, `volumes`, `data_mount` + `data_dir`, `runtime`, `runtime_args`. `init`, `depends`, `ready_*`, `proxy*` work as on any custom daemon.
- **Per-worktree:** host ports come from the existing `auto`/`base`/`stride` slot (named ports use the primary's slot). The container is named `mise-<namespace>-<daemon>`; the namespace already carries the project and worktree, so two checkouts never clash. Containers are labelled `dev.mise.daemon` and `dev.mise.project`.
- **Stale containers:** the script runs `<runtime> rm -f <name>` before `run`, so a container left by a killed run never blocks a start. Only that exact name is removed.
- **Stop:** the script traps TERM/INT/HUP and runs `<runtime> stop -t 10 <name>`, then waits for the runtime client to exit, so the image's stop signal and grace period apply. `--rm` removes the container.

title: feat(daemons): allocate preset named ports per worktree with their own base
body:
Preset named ports (`http_port` on `cockroachdb`, `monitor_port` on `nats`, ...) could not get a per-worktree port of their own. With `port = { auto = true, base = ... }` they were computed as the preset default plus the worktree slot, ignoring the primary `base`, and the only override, `ports.http_port = 8081`, was a fixed integer. With several worktrees that either collides (fixed) or lands on well-known ports such as `8080` that other local stacks already use (auto).

Named ports now accept the same allocation as the primary port:

```toml
[daemons.cockroach]
preset = "cockroachdb"
version = "26"
port = { auto = true, base = 26258 }
ports.http_port = { auto = true, base = 27000 }

[daemons.nats]
preset = "nats"
version = "2"
port = { auto = true, base = 4223 }
ports.monitor_port = { auto = true, base = 28000, stride = 2 }
```

The primary checkout gets `COCKROACH_HTTP_PORT=27000` and `NATS_MONITOR_PORT=28000`. A linked worktree adds its slot (times `stride`, default `1`) to each base, so with a slot of 7 it gets `27007` and `28014`. The daemon's command line, pitchfork's expected ports and the exported `<NAME>_<PORT_NAME>` variables all carry the resolved value, and changing the primary `base` no longer moves the named port.

## Behavior

- `ports.<name> = { auto = true }` with no `base` starts from the preset's default for that port. That also works when the primary `port` is fixed; the slot then comes from the project root, the same way `port = "auto"` derives it.
- When the primary port is `auto`, a named `auto` port uses the same slot as the primary one.
- Errors name the key: a table without `auto = true`, an unknown key, an out-of-range `base`/`stride`, or a port that would run past 65535 in a worktree (never clamped, so two worktrees can't share 65535).

## Compatibility

Everything that worked before is unchanged: integer overrides, the preset default, and defaults moving with an `auto` primary port. The JSON schema (`daemons.<name>.ports.<key>` and `daemon_providers.<name>.ports.<key>`) now accepts an integer or the `{ auto, base, stride }` table; nothing it accepted before is rejected.

## Collisions and overlapping ranges

- Within a daemon, duplicate ports were already rejected when the daemon is expanded, and that now includes allocated named ports.
- Across daemons, the existing "two daemons use one port" check (primary ports, same project root) now also covers allocated named ports: an `auto` named port that resolves to another daemon's primary port or named port in the same project fails at load with an error naming both (`daemons a (ports.http_port) and b (ports.http_port) both use port 27000 ...`). Named ports that are not `auto` (preset defaults, hand-set integers) are still not compared with each other, so two `cockroachdb` daemons that both keep the default `http_port` keep loading as before; they just fail to bind at start, as they always did.
- Within one worktree, two ports with the same stride never collide unless thei

title: fix(lock): hash file:// artifacts in place when generating lockfiles
body:
`mise install` and `mise lock` failed for an `http:` tool with a `file://` URL and no declared `checksum` whenever the lockfile was in use. Since `lockfile_mode = "generate"` became the default in 2026.10.19, this config broke even though [local files are documented as supported](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/backends/http.html#local-files):

```toml
[tools]
"http:probe" = { version = "1.0.0", url = "file:///path/to/probe", bin = "probe" }
```

Before, the tool installed and then lockfile generation failed with `builder error for url (file:///path/to/probe)`. Generate mode locks the other platforms too, and for entries without a checksum it downloaded the artifact with the HTTP client, which rejects the `file` scheme.

Now generate mode hashes the local file directly and records the URL as written, so the same config installs and locks all platforms:

```
$ mise lock
mise lock          ✓ 7 targets checked
✓ Lockfile ready at ~/workdir/mise.lock
```

The same handling applies to `download_for_verification`, which the http backend (when it strips URL credentials) and the python and ruby lock paths use. Hashing a user-supplied path also exposed a latent bug: for files over 50 MiB the external GNU `sha256sum` prefixes its output with `\` when the path contains a backslash, which would have written an invalid `sha256:\…` entry. `file_hash_sha256` now strips that prefix.

Declaring a `checksum` or using `lockfile_mode = "merge"` kept working before and is unchanged.

## Testing

- New unit tests `artifact_checksum_hashes_local_file_urls` (both functions on a local file) and `parse_sum_output_drops_the_escape_prefix`.
- `e2e/backend/test_http_local_file` now runs `MISE_LOCKFILE_MODE=generate mise lock` on a checksum-less `file://` tool and checks the lockfile keeps the URL and records the file's `sha256`. I did not confirm this e2e fails on the old code.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean.

Fixes #15177. Thanks to @hcrosse for the report and reproduction.

title: fix(pipx): share one install between tools locked with the same dependencies on different days
body:
Fixes the duplicate `pipx:`/`pypi:` installs reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15176: with `minimum_release_age` set, every repo that locked the same tool version installed its own copy of it (the reporter saw over 2GB of copies of one version).

## Cause

With a release-age cutoff, mise locks the tool's dependency graph with `uv lock --exclude-newer <cutoff>`, and uv records that cutoff in the graph:

```toml
[options]
exclude-newer = "2026-10-27T17:30:00Z"
```

mise hashed the whole graph to name the installation (`<version>~uv~<hash>`), so two repos with identical dependencies but different lock times got different directories. The cutoff only limits resolution; the install replays the graph with `uv sync --frozen` and does not use it.

## Change

The release-age cutoff is removed from the graph text before it is hashed for the installation, so a graph locked with a cutoff gets the same identity as the graph uv writes without one. A tool with a locked graph also no longer lets its own `minimum_release_age` / `install_before` options change the installation. Graphs that carry no cutoff keep exactly the identity they had, so their existing installs are untouched. The lockfile still digests the graph as written, so edit detection of the sidecar is unchanged.

Passing uv a relative time (the request in the discussion) is not needed for this and would make the lock non-reproducible, so mise keeps passing an absolute cutoff.

## Upgrading

A tool whose graph was locked with a cutoff gets one new installation the first time it is installed after this change (its old `~uv~` directory no longer matches). From then on, repos locking the same dependencies share it.

## Testing

New unit tests cover: two graphs differing only in the cutoff share an install identity (inline and sidecar), graphs without a cutoff keep their identity, other differences and other `[options]` still produce different identities, and `ToolVersion::tv_pathname`/equality for a tool locked on different days. The `ToolVersion` test fails without the fix. Related `lockfile`, `backend::pipx`, `install_layout` and `tool_version` unit tests pass and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean. I did not run an end-to-end install against PyPI.

title: fix(task): run the downloaded file of a remote task with env as a sub-task or dependency
body:
A remote file task (`file = "http://..."`) that sets its own `env` failed with exit 127 when it ran as a sub-task (`run = [{ task = "..." }]`) or a dependency (`depends`). mise also tried to run the URL joined onto the config directory as a local path, next to the correctly downloaded copy:

```toml
[tasks.remote-env]
file = "http://127.0.0.1:57275/plain.sh"
env.FOO = "1"

[tasks.fail]
run = [{ task = "remote-env hello" }]
```

Before:

```
$ mise run fail
mise WARN  could not read task file /repro/proj/http://127.0.0.1:57275/plain.sh: ...
[remote-env hello] $ /repro/proj/http://127.0.0.1:57275/plain.sh hello
sh: /repro/proj/http://127.0.0.1:57275/plain.sh: No such file or directory
[remote-env hello] ERROR task failed
```

After, `mise run fail` runs only the downloaded file, the same as `mise run remote-env hello`.

Fetching a remote task moves its own `env` out of `env` and into the overlay, which changed the task's identity in the dependency graph. The graph added the task before fetching it and the fetched copy afterwards, so the unfetched node stayed behind and ran. Without `env` the identity did not change, which is why only tasks with `env` hit this. Top-level `mise run` was unaffected because it fetches before building the graph.

Remote tasks are now fetched before they join the graph (root tasks, `depends`, and `depends_post`). Their run phase is kept across the fetch, so a remote `depends_post` task no longer comes back as a normal task. The task identity also counts the overlay env, so it is the same before and after fetching and `depends` entries that pass different env to the same remote task stay distinct.
The graph walk also de-duplicates by that identity, so each env variant of a remote task still resolves its own `depends` (previously the second variant could be left without its prerequisites).

Fixes #15175

Tested with a new e2e case in `test_task_remote_http` (sub-task and `depends` on a remote task with `env`), which fails on `main` with the error above and passes now. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean.

title: fix(brew): resolve relative install_symlink sources like Homebrew
body:
Building a tap formula from source failed whenever its `install` block linked a file by a relative name, such as `bin.install_symlink "moshi-hook" => "mh"`. The source build aborted with:

```
Error: build failed: different prefix: "" and "/opt/homebrew/Cellar/moshi-hook/0.4.0/bin"
mise ERROR failed to build moshi-hook 0.4.0 from source
```

The shim's `Pathname#install_symlink` handed the relative source straight to `relative_path_from`, which raises when one path is relative and the other absolute. Homebrew resolves the source against the receiving directory first (`Pathname(src).expand_path(dstdir)` in `extend/pathname.rb`), so `bin.install_symlink "foo" => "bar"` means "link `bin/bar` to `bin/foo`". The shim now does the same, for both the hash form and a bare relative source. Absolute sources such as `bin.install_symlink libexec/"tool"` are unchanged. A source that resolves to the link's own path (`bin.install_symlink "tool"` when `bin/tool` already exists) now fails the build with `cannot symlink ... to itself`, before anything is removed, instead of replacing the file with a link to itself. That includes the same file reached through a parent directory that links back to it (`bin.install_symlink "alias/tool" => "tool"` with `bin/alias` pointing at `bin`).

## Testing

- New unit test `shim_install_symlink_resolves_relative_sources` runs the shim against a formula that uses a relative hash source, a bare relative source and an absolute source, and checks the links it creates (`example-alias -> example`, `other -> ../libexec/other`, `tool -> ../libexec/tool`). Without the fix it fails with the same `different prefix` error, and removing the fix from either branch alone also fails it. Two more runs check that a self-referential source fails the build, both directly and through an aliased parent, and that the existing file is left in place.
- The existing shim tests pass (`cargo test --workspace --exclude mise shim_`), and `cargo clippy --workspace --exclude mise --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean.

title: feat(http): add extra_ca_certs and stop reporting unchecked tools as up to date
body:
Running mise behind a traffic-inspecting proxy whose CA is not in the system store, such as Socket Firewall (`sfw mise upgrade`), failed every version lookup, and `mise upgrade` then said everything was current (discussion #15170):

```
$ sfw mise upgrade --dry-run
mise WARN  Error getting latest version for pypi:pre-commit: error sending request: client error (Connect): One or more certificates required to validate this certificate cannot be found.
mise All tools are up to date
```

### New setting: `extra_ca_certs`

`extra_ca_certs` (`MISE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`) names a PEM bundle whose certificates mise trusts **in addition to** its usual roots, on every platform. The bundle only needs the extra CA:

```sh
MISE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/etc/ssl/proxy-ca.pem mise install
```

- It covers mise's own HTTP clients: downloads, version lookups, GitHub API calls, attestation verification, vfox plugins and the GitHub relay. The embedded npm package manager keeps reading `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`, and programs mise runs (git, uv, installers) keep their own certificate settings.
- It is `global_only`: it is read from the environment and the global config only, so a project's `mise.toml` cannot add a trusted CA. For the same reason the path must be absolute or start with `~/`; a relative path would resolve against the current directory, which may be a repository, so mise ignores it with a warning.
- If the file can't be read, holds no certificates, or holds one the TLS backend rejects, mise warns once and keeps its usual roots rather than failing every request.
- `SSL_CERT_FILE` keeps its existing meaning everywhere.

sfw sets `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` but not this variable, so until it does, pass its CA through:

```sh
sfw sh -c 'MISE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS="$NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS" mise upgrade'
```

The source build Homebrew uses compiles with `native-tls`, which did not enable mise-tls's `native-tls` feature. It does now, so that build gets the setting too.

### Failed lookups are no longer "up to date"

When a latest-version lookup fails, including the backend-wide lookup behind the out-of-range note, `mise upgrade` and `mise outdated` no longer print "All tools are up to date". They name what they could not check:

```
$ mise upgrade --dry-run
mise WARN  Error getting latest version for pypi:pre-commit@4.7.0: …
mise WARN  Could not check 1 tool for updates: pypi:pre-commit@4.7.0
```

The exit status is unchanged.

### Validation

- mise-tls unit test: a local HTTPS server with a certificate from a freshly generated CA is rejected without the setting and accepted with it, for both the rustls and native-tls backends (it fails if `build_client` stops merging the bundle). Another covers unusable bundles.
- e2e `cli/test_extra_ca_certs`: an unusable bundle is reported, and the setting in a project `mise.toml` is ignored.
- e2e `cli/test_upgrade_unchecked_lookup`: a failing `list-all`, and a working `list-all` with a failing `latest-stable`, are both reported as unchecked rather than up t

title: feat(dotfiles): resolve secret() only for the keys a merge = "missing" entry adds
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3074/changes/mise/1151
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`merge = "missing"` dotfile entries can now call `secret()`, and mise asks for a secret only when the key it fills is missing from the target. That lets you keep one private, ignored config file of API keys, populate it by prompt on a new machine, and add keys later without re-entering or exporting the ones you already have. This implements the request in [discussion #15161](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15161).

```toml
[bootstrap.secrets]
github_token = "MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN"
npm_token = "NPM_TOKEN"

[dotfiles]
"~/.config/mise/conf.d/private.local.toml/seed" = { source = "templates/private.toml", template = "tera", merge = "missing", permissions = "0600" }
```

```toml
# templates/private.toml
[env]
MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN = "{{ secret(name='github_token') }}"
NPM_TOKEN = "{{ secret(name='npm_token') }}"
```

With `mise dot apply --prompt-secrets`:

- If the file is missing, mise prompts for both tokens and creates it at `0600`.
- If a key already exists, its value is kept and its secret is neither read nor prompted for.
- If you add `PYPI_TOKEN` to the source, only that token is prompted for.

Previously `secret()` failed in merge entries because only whole-file templates registered it.

## How it works

`mise dot status` and `mise dot diff` never read or prompt for a secret. For a `missing` entry, the template is rendered once with `secret()` as a placeholder (`‹secret:name›`, which a diff shows in place of a value) so mise can tell which keys the target lacks. Apply then resolves only the secrets of those keys and puts them in place of their placeholders in that same render, so `exec()` calls in the template are not run an extra time. This happens before the apply journal begins, so an unavailable secret leaves nothing to recover.

- A placeholder has to reach the output as it is. A filter that changes or drops it, such as `secret(name='t') | upper`, is an error rather than something mise could write as the secret.

- A secret that is not declared in `[bootstrap.secrets]` is an error, even when its key is already set.
- Enforced `merge = true` entries still cannot use `secret()`, because they would overwrite a value you have since changed.
- As in other templates, the value is inserted as is. If the file no longer parses once secrets are filled in, the error says so without printing the rendered text.
- `edits::apply` now takes the `SecretValues` the callers already hold.

## Validation

- New e2e `cli/test_dotfiles_merge_secrets` covers status/diff without secrets, an unavailable secret leaving no file, creation with the declared mode, a set key being left alone, a newly added key asking only for itself, diff output containing no value, an undeclared name, a filtered placeholder being refused, the template not being rendered an extra time, and `merge = true` being refused. title: fix(install): don't fail install when a task include can't be loaded
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3073/changes/mise/1150
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Summary

`mise install` no longer exits 1 when a git task include can't be loaded. Since 2026.10.19 the default `lockfile_mode = "generate"` makes `mise install` load every task after installing, to lock the tools the tasks declare. An unreachable include, such as a private repository in a CI job with no credentials, failed that load, so the tools installed and the command then failed.

```toml
[tools]
jq = "1"

[task_config]
includes = ["git::https://github.com/jdx/does-not-exist.git//tasks?ref=v1"]
```

Before: `mise install` installs jq, prints `Received HTTP status 404`, and exits 1. After: it installs jq, warns, and exits 0:

```
mise WARN  skipping lockfile update: failed to load tasks: Transport handshake failed: ...
```

The lockfile is left as it was rather than written without the tasks, because locking with no tasks would prune the tools they declare from an existing lockfile. An explicit `mise lock` still fails on a broken include.

Fixes #15163

title: fix(shim): name the active version when it lacks the executable
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3072/changes/mise/1149
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Running a shim for an executable that the project's selected version doesn't provide used to report `No version is set for shim` and suggest `mise use -g` with an older version. A version _is_ set, so users went looking for a config bug, and following the suggestion would quietly switch the project to the wrong version. This is common with Ruby gem executables after an upgrade: `cap` and `rails` shims still exist because the older Ruby has those gems, but the new Ruby doesn't until `bundle install`.

Before:

```
mise ERROR No version is set for shim: cap
Set a global default version with one of the following:
mise use -g ruby@3.4.4
```

After, with `.ruby-version` selecting 4.0.9:

```
mise ERROR cap is not provided by the active ruby@4.0.9 (set by ~/repro/.ruby-version)
cap is provided by: ruby@3.4.4
Install it for the active version, or switch to a version that provides it.
```

The message is generic and gives no ecosystem-specific install hint, since mise can't know how a given tool adds executables to a version. When no config selects the tool at all, the existing "No version is set" message is unchanged. `mise which` has a separate message and is not touched here.

Tested with a new e2e test (`test_shim_active_version_lacks_bin`) that installs two `tiny` versions, adds an executable to only the older one, and runs its shim under a project selecting the newer one. Also added the message to the shim errors entry in `docs/errors.md`.

Fixes #15162

Co-authored-by: Matthew Zagaja <565647+mzagaja@users.noreply.github.com>

+fn active_version_lacks_bin_message(
+    ts: &Toolset,
+    bin_name: &str,
+    providers: &HashSet<&BackendArg>,
+    tvs: &[ToolVersion],
+) -> Option<String> {
+    let active = ts

+        .into_iter()
+        .map(|(_, tv)| tv)

+    if active.is_empty() {

+    }

+    }
+    // Installs are told apart by directory: the same name and version can be installed more than
+    // once with different options, and only one of them may provide the executable.
+    let others = tvs
+        .iter()
+        .filter(|tv| {
+            !active
+                .iter()
+                .any(|a| a.ba() == tv.ba() && a.install_path() == tv.install_path())
+        })
+        .map(|tv| {
+            let label = format!("{}@{}", tv.ba(), tv.version);
+            let ambiguous = active
+                .iter()
+                .any(|a| a.ba() == tv.ba() && a.version == tv.version);
+            if ambiguous {
+                format!("{label} ({})", display_path(tv.install_path()))
+            } else {
+                label
+            }
+        })
+        .collect_vec();
+    if !others.is_empty() {
+        msg.push_str(&format!(
+            "{bin_name} is provided by: {}\n",
+            others.join(", ")
+        ));
+    }
+    msg.push_str("Install it for the active version, or switch to a version that provides it.");

title: fix(lock): upgrade every lock entry of a tool declared in several config files
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3071/changes/mise/1148
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise upgrade` could leave the old version in `mise.lock` when a tool is declared in more than one config file, such as `config.toml` and `conf.d/*.toml`. It printed `Upgraded X → Y`, but the lock then held entries for both versions. With a `lockfile_version` header, the old entry kept `specifiers = ["latest"]`, so `mise outdated` offered the same upgrade again right after, and a scheduled `mise upgrade` repeated it forever.

```toml
# config.toml
[settings]
lockfile = true

[tools]
"github:cli/cli" = "latest"

# conf.d/100-extra.toml
[tools]
"github:cli/cli" = "latest"
```

Before, after `mise upgrade github:cli/cli`:

```

[[tools."github:cli/cli"]]
version = "2.103.1"
specifiers = ["latest"]

After, only the upgraded entry remains and `mise outdated` is clean.

Each declaring file contributes its own lock entry, but only the winning request is installed. The step that swaps in the freshly installed version required the entry's source file to match the installed request's, so the entries from the other files kept the old version. It now matches on tool and request (version and options) and keeps each entry's own source. Declarations that differ in version or options still don't match, as before, and so do declarations that write a different lockfile: upgrading a project's `dummy = "1"` leaves the pin of an equal global request that the project shadows untouched.

Added `e2e/lockfile/test_lockfile_upgrade_two_declarations` and `test_lockfile_upgrade_shadowed_global`, which fail without the change and pass with it. The neighbouring lockfile upgrade, shadowing, request-precedence and install e2e tests still pass, and clippy with `-D warnings` is clean.

title: fix(pypi): lock tools whose index publishes no upload times
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3063/changes/mise/1147
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise lock` failed to lock the dependency graph of a `pypi:` tool whose registry publishes no upload times, even though `mise latest` and version selection accepted that tool's release. PEP 700 upload times are optional and many self-hosted registries (Gitea/Forgejo, pypiserver, static indexes) omit them. Fixes #15146.

Before, with the default `minimum_release_age` and such a registry:

```
warning: cowsay-6.1-py3-none-any.whl is missing an upload date, but user provided: 2026-10-28T08:02:26Z
hint: `cowsay` was filtered by `exclude-newer` to only include packages uploaded before ...
mise WARN  pypi:cowsay dependency graph unavailable; keeping a version-only lock entry
```

After, the graph locks without setting `minimum_release_age = "0s"`.

## Which side moves

mise's side stays. Version selection allows a release it cannot date (`VersionInfo::filter_by_date`), and holding it back would make a tool from such a registry uninstallable by default, with the only workaround being to turn the cutoff off. uv's fail-closed rule is reasonable for uv, so mise does not change it for dependencies. For the tool being locked, `mise lock` now adds `--exclude-newer-package <name>=false` to `uv lock`, only when `minimum_release_age` is in effect and the tool's listed release has no upload time. It is a no-op for dated releases and for indexes that publish dates.

Not weakened:

- A dated release newer than the cutoff is still rejected.
- Dependencies (including `with` and `expose` requirements) keep the cutoff. A dependency without an upload time is still held back by uv, so `mise lock` falls back to a version-only entry with the same warning, and `minimum_release_age = "0s"` remains the way to lock such a graph. The docs say so.

`--exclude-newer-package` with `false` works on uv 0.12.10, the minimum for dependency locking. I checked it against the e2e fixture index: with it the tool resolves and an undated dependency is still filtered.

## Tests

New `e2e/backend/test_pypi_lock_undated_release` uses the existing fixture index (which publishes no upload times) with `minimum_release_age = "7d"`: a dependency-free tool locks its graph; a tool with undated dependencies stays version-only; `minimum_release_age = "0"` locks the full graph. The first step fails without the change, with the warning above. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `mise run lint-fix` are clean.

## Not covered

`uv tool install` for a version-only tool (no graph) also passes `--exclude-newer`, so it probably has the same mismatch; I did not check it. This PR is limited to the graph lock. It touches the same function as #15153, so a small merge is expected.

title: feat(env): add position = "append" to env._.path
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3062/changes/mise/1146
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`env._.path` entries always go ahead of tool paths. A global config that adds `~/bin` or `~/.cargo/bin` this way shadows the tools mise installs, and there was no way to put those directories behind the tools from `mise.toml`.

`_.path` entries now accept `position = "append"`. An appended entry goes after tool paths and ahead of the `PATH` mise inherited. The default is `"prepend"`, which is the existing behavior.

```toml
[env]
_.path = [
  "bin",
  { path = ["~/bin", "~/.cargo/bin"], position = "append" },
]
```

With `node` installed by mise, `mise env` now yields `PATH` in this order:

```text
<project>/bin : <node install>/bin : ~/bin : ~/.cargo/bin : <inherited PATH>
```

- `position` only orders an entry among the paths mise adds. `tools = true` does not change it.
- When several configs append paths, a nested config's entries come before its parent's, as with prepended entries.
- It applies to `mise env`, `mise exec`, `mise activate` / `hook-env`, and the env cache. The option is in the JSON schema and the `env._.path` docs.
- Only `_.path` honors it, and the schema declares it only there; like `find_up`, it is ignored on other directives. An unknown value is rejected.

Discussion: https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15149

## Validation

- New e2e test `e2e/tools/test_path_order_append` covers `mise env`, `hook-env`, `mise x`, nested configs, `tools = true`, the default, and an invalid value. The existing path-order e2e tests and the env cache tests still pass.
- Unit tests in `mise-config` (including the schema/parser option-key check) and `schema_matches_parser` pass; clippy with `-D warnings` is clean.

title: feat(pypi): add registry_index to search a tool registry ahead of PyPI when locking
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3061/changes/mise/1145
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise lock` for a `pypi:` tool with a per-tool `registry_url` runs `uv lock` with that registry as uv's *default* index, which replaces PyPI. That is right for a full PyPI mirror, but a registry that hosts only its own packages (Gitea/Forgejo, pypiserver, a static index) cannot supply the tool's dependencies. The lock fails and mise silently keeps a version-only entry:

```
Because click was not found in the package registry and all versions of black depend on click>=8.0.0 ...
mise WARN  pypi:black dependency graph unavailable; keeping a version-only lock entry
```

New tool option `registry_index` chooses how locking uses `registry_url`:

```toml
[tools]
"pypi:black" = { version = "25.9.0", registry_url = "https://gitea.example/api/packages/org/pypi/simple/{}/", registry_index = "priority" }
```

- `default` (the default, unchanged): the registry replaces PyPI.
- `priority`: the registry is passed to uv as `UV_INDEX`, ahead of the default index, which stays PyPI (or `pypi.registry_url` if set). The graph then records `black` from the registry and `click` from PyPI.

## Why this is opt-in

`priority` changes which index a package may come from, which matters for supply chain, so I did not make it the default for every `registry_url`. Today a dependency the registry lacks fails the lock. With a silent PyPI fallback, a mirror that 404s a package on purpose (a blocked package, or an internal dependency that is not published yet) would start resolving it from public PyPI, and a mirror setup that expects no PyPI traffic would start reaching for it. Users of a mirror or an air-gapped setup get exactly the behavior they have now unless they ask otherwise.

With `priority`, mise pins uv's `first-index` strategy, so each project comes only from the first index that hosts it:

- The tool itself always comes from the configured registry, even though PyPI may also host a package of that name, and even if the registry lacks the pinned version (that fails instead of falling through).
- A name on the registry cannot be taken over by PyPI.
- Only a project the registry answers 404 for falls through to PyPI.

mise sets `UV_INDEX_STRATEGY` itself because `install_env` could otherwise select `unsafe-best-match`. The option affects locking only and is not recorded in the lockfile, like `registry_url`; the sidecar `uv.lock` pins every package to the index it came from. The docs for `registry_url` now say that it replaces PyPI for dependency locking, and describe `registry_index`.

I did not take the stricter alternative from the issue (an `explicit` index with `[tool.uv.sources]` pinning only the tool), because it needs the lock to stop running `uv lock --no-config` and would break internal tools that depend on other internal packages.

## Testing

New `e2e/backend/test_pypi_lock_registry_index` serves a registry (a new `/private/simple/` route i

title: fix(prune): keep versions of tools declared in included task files
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3060/changes/mise/1144
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise prune` deleted tool versions that a project's included task files still need. It only counted a config's inline `[tasks]` as using tools, so a tool declared in a task file loaded through `task_config.includes` was reported as unused:

```toml
# mise.toml
[task_config]
includes = ["tasks.toml"]
```

```toml
# tasks.toml
[test]
run = "redis-server --version"
tools.redis = "8.10.2"
```

Before:

```text
$ mise prune --dry-run redis
redis@8.10.2 is prunable: no tracked config or tool stub requires redis
```

Now `redis@8.10.2` is kept, as it already was when the same task was written inline in `mise.toml`.

Prune now also reads the tasks a tracked project gets from its task includes:

- TOML task files named in `task_config.includes`, and TOML files inside included directories
- executable task scripts that declare tools with `#MISE tools=...`, which #14334 left uncovered
- the default task directories (`mise-tasks/`, `.mise/tasks`, …) when no config sets `includes`
- the includes of environment configs such as `mise.prod.toml`, filtered by that config's own `excludes`, even when prune runs without `MISE_ENV=prod`

It follows the include, exclude, and `task.disable_paths` rules that task loading uses. Tasks that `extends` a template resolve it the way inline tasks already did, and tasks of a monorepo project now also get the tools of a matching `[monorepo.task_defaults.<name>]` from the root config, inline tasks included. A task file that cannot be read or parsed is skipped with a warning instead of stopping the prune. Remote (`git::` / OCI) includes are not downloaded, so tools that only a remote include declares are still not protected.

Tested with a new e2e test, `test_prune_task_includes`, which fails without the fix. The existing prune e2e tests pass.

Fixes #15150

title: docs(dotfiles): show profile variants gating an entry on several active envs
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3058/changes/mise/1142
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Setup that should apply only when two config environments are both selected, such as ssh files that only the `work` machine gets, has a supported pattern for dotfiles that the docs never spelled out. This documents it, following [the question in discussion 15148](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15148).

A dotfile `profile` variant matches when its name appears anywhere in the selected `MISE_ENV` list, and an entry with no matching variant and no `default` is skipped. A variant with no `target` therefore works as a gate:

```toml
# mise.ssh.toml
[dotfiles."~/.ssh/work_key"]
source = "ssh/work_key"
mode = "symlink"
variants = [{ profile = "work" }]
```

`MISE_ENV=ssh` skips `~/.ssh/work_key`; `MISE_ENV=ssh,work` links it.

## Changes

- `docs/dotfiles/reference.md`: variant selectors state that `profile` matches any name in the selected list.
- `docs/dotfiles/managed.md`: new "Deploy an entry only for a profile" section with the example above.
- `docs/bootstrap/modules.md`: the module-combination section links to that example for dotfiles that depend on another selected module.

## Validation

Docs only. Checked with `hk run check --safe` on the three pages, `mise run docs:build` (links, anchors and redirects checked), and `tomllib` on the two new TOML fences. The gating behavior was confirmed by running `mise dot status` on a scratch project with `MISE_ENV=ssh` and `MISE_ENV=ssh,work`.

title: fix(pypi): lock the dependency graph against the selected Python
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3056/changes/mise/1141
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise lock` could not lock a `pypi:` tool's dependency graph unless a matching Python was on `PATH`. It ran `uv lock` without `--python`, so uv searched for an interpreter itself. With the Python only in mise's install dir (a CI runner without mise activated, or a per-tool `python = "3.13.5"`), the graph was skipped and only the version was locked:

```
mise WARN  pypi:black dependency graph unavailable; keeping a version-only lock entry: ... hint: A managed Python download is available for Python 3.13.5, but Python downloads are set to 'never'
```

Now `uv lock` and the `uv sync --dry-run` replay get the same interpreter, the one install binds:

- **Installed Python** (the per-tool `python` option, otherwise the configured `python`): passed by path, wherever it sits on `PATH`. Downloads stay disabled. If the lockfile pins a patch release of a per-tool `python` that is not installed, another installed release matching the selector is used.
- **Per-tool `python` not installed yet** (fresh checkout, `mise lock` before `mise install`): passed as its version, and uv may download it for the resolution only. With `offline` set, downloads stay disabled. `mise lock` still installs nothing.
- **No Python mise knows about**: unchanged, uv searches on its own without downloading.

The docs for the pypi backend describe this.

Verified with a new e2e test, `test_pypi_lock_interpreter_off_path`, that runs `mise lock` with no Python on `PATH` for both a configured and a per-tool Python. It fails on `main` with the warning above and passes here, as does a second test for the pinned-patch case (lockfile pins 3.12.10, only 3.12.11 installed), and the existing `test_pypi_lock*` tests still pass. The download path for an uninstalled Python is not covered by e2e.

Fixes #15144

title: fix(brew): skip MachO post_install steps in source builds
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3055/changes/mise/1140
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Tap formulae whose `post_install` uses Homebrew's bundled ruby-macho no longer abort the `brew:` source build with `uninitialized constant Smolvm::MachO`. This is the same class of gap as `Requirement` (#14807) and `Language::*`.

```sh
mise bootstrap packages use -g brew:smol-machines/tap/smolvm

The shim now defines `MachO` and `MachO::Tools`. During `post_install` each call warns and returns an inert value (no dylibs, no change), so the rest of the method still runs. Outside `post_install`, such as in `install`, the same calls still fail the build loudly.

title: fix(gem): skip RubyGems prereleases when resolving latest
body:
`latest` for a `gem:` tool could resolve to a prerelease instead of the newest stable release, which is not the expected behavior (most tools/backends specify that `latest` doesn't use betas or prereleases).

## Example

I have the following block in my `~/.config/mise/config.toml` configuration:

```toml
[tools]
"gem:bundler" = "latest"
```

I expect this to install Bundler v4.0.23 (the current version), but it's instead installing Bundler v4.1.0.beta3, a prerelease:

```console
$ mise latest gem:bundler
4.1.0.beta3
```

The problem is that RubyGems marks prereleases with a dotted letter segment (for example: `4.1.0.beta3` or `2.0.0.alpha1`). mise's shared prerelease pattern only recognized forms like `-beta` or `.rc`, and the versions host and the compact index don't flag prereleases themselves, so these versions were treated as stable.

The gem backend now uses RubyGems' own rule (defined under `Gem::Version#prerelease?`, where any letter in the version makes it a prerelease), so it no longer matters where the version list came from.

With the changes in this PR, the configuration mentioned above, mise installs the current non-prerelease version:

```console
$ mise latest gem:bundler
4.0.23
```

Prereleases are still available when you ask for them:

```console
$ mise latest gem:bundler@4.1.0.beta3
4.1.0.beta3
$ MISE_PRERELEASES=1 mise latest gem:bundler
4.1.0.beta3
```

A prefix that matches only prereleases, such as `gem:bundler@4.1` today, now resolves to nothing, as it does for other backends.

## Validation

- New unit tests cover the classification of RubyGems prerelease versions and `latest` resolution against Bundler's version list.
- New `e2e/backend/test_gem_prerelease` lists versions from a mock registry that flags prereleases, as rubygems.org does, and checks `latest`, exact prerelease requests and `MISE_PRERELEASES`.
- The existing gem unit tests and the `backend/test_gem_compact_index` and `backend/test_gem_source` e2e tests pass.
- I manually checked `mise latest gem:bundler` using mise built from this branch, and compared it to the output of the latest mise release (2026.10.21 linux-x64)

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: 2.1.312.*

  * RubyGems API prerelease flags are not used for this classification.

title: fix(task): allow comments in turbo.json and global.json
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3032/changes/mise/1138
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Turborepo and the .NET SDK both accept comments in their config files, but mise parsed `turbo.json` and `global.json` as strict JSON.

- A `turbo.json` with a comment logged `mise WARN failed to parse optional …/turbo.json: key must be a string at line 3 column 3` on every `mise run` and dropped the file's task suggestions (`inputs`, `outputs`, `cache`, `dependsOn`).
- A `global.json` with a comment failed to resolve the dotnet version through the idiomatic-file path.

`turbo.json` now parses as JSONC (comments and trailing commas, nothing of JSON5), the way turbo reads it. `global.json` now accepts comments but still rejects trailing commas, because the .NET host's parser does:

```jsonc
// turbo.json
{
  "$schema": "https://turborepo.com/schema.json",
  // turbo accepts comments in turbo.json
  "tasks": { "build": { "outputs": ["dist/**"] } }
}
```

This adds `from_jsonc_str` and `from_json_with_comments_str` to `mise_util::structured_merge`, reusing the JSONC options the dotfiles `merge` mode already uses. `package.json`, `.golangci.json` and other tool-owned JSON stay strict because their tools reject comments.

Not changed: whether the node provider should read `turbo.json` at all when `task.auto_infer` doesn't include `node` (the issue's second question). That's a separate behavior change.

Fixes #15140

Tests: new unit tests for a commented `turbo.json`, a commented `global.json`, and a `global.json` with a trailing comma; `cargo test -p mise --lib` for `task::workspace::node` and `dotnet` pass.

title: fix(self-update): retry replacing mise.exe on Windows while antivirus holds it
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3030/changes/mise/1136
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

On Windows, `mise self-update` could fail partway through with:

```
The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process. (os error 32)
```

Antivirus briefly holds a binary that was just written or just started, so swapping in the new `mise.exe` can fail even though it would work a moment later. This showed up as a flaky `self_update_install.Tests.ps1` failure in Windows CI ([run 40798845816](https://github.com/jdx/mise/actions/runs/40798845816/job/123203145623)).

## What changes

- **Locks are retried.** When replacing the binary fails with `ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION` (32) or `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` (5), mise retries with increasing waits, about 6 seconds in all.
- **Retries only happen while nothing has moved.** The swap starts by moving the running `mise.exe` aside, and nothing moves it back if a later step fails. So mise retries only while `mise.exe` is still at its path.
- **A failure after the move no longer leaves you without mise.** If a step fails after `mise.exe` was moved aside, mise now copies the new binary to that path and prints a warning. Before, the install directory was left with no `mise.exe` at all.

Linux and macOS are unchanged.

## Test isolation

The same CI run had a second, unrelated flake: `path.Tests.ps1` runs `mise x` ten times and expects the same PATH each time. It ran in the repo checkout, so PATH included all of the repo's tools. Earlier in the run, `npm_backend.Tests.ps1` also ran in the checkout with `MISE_NPM_PACKAGE_MANAGER` set to `bun` or `npm`. With a different package manager, mise treats installed npm tools as different installs, so the checkout's npm tools showed as missing. In the PATH test's output, one run relocked and reinstalled them, which fits one PATH coming out 323 characters longer than the first. I haven't reproduced this; the log is the evidence.

- `path.Tests.ps1` now runs in its own directory, with three `_.path` entries so mise still sets PATH for the child. It also checks that PATH was actually set.
- Each `npm_backend.Tests.ps1` case now runs in its own directory and no longer touches the checkout's config or `mise.lock`.

## Validation

- `cargo clippy -p mise --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes on Linux.
- mise can't be cross-compiled to Windows locally, so the new Windows-only functions and their four unit tests were copied into a small test crate. Clippy with `-D warnings` passes on it for `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`, and the unit tests pass when run on Linux.
- The Pester changes have not run yet; this PR's Windows CI is their first run.

title: feat(dotfiles): merge into INI files such as pip.conf and tox.ini
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3023/changes/mise/1133
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A `merge` dotfiles entry could set keys only in JSON, JSONC, TOML and YAML files, so files like `pip.conf`, `tox.ini` or `setup.cfg` had to be managed whole. Merge entries can now edit INI files too.

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.config/pip/pip.conf/shared" = { source = "pip/shared.conf", merge = true, format = "ini" }
```

With `pip/shared.conf`:

```ini
[global]
index-url = https://pypi.example/simple
retries = 3
```

and a target of:

```ini
; my pip settings
[global]
timeout = 60
index-url = https://old.example/simple
```

applying replaces the `index-url` line and adds `retries = 3` to `[global]`. The comment, `timeout`, and every other line stay as written. A section the target doesn't have yet is added at the end of the file, and a missing target is created from the source. `merge = "missing"`, `mise dot status` and `mise dot diff` work as they do for the other formats.

- An `.ini` target is detected by its extension. For any other name, set `format = "ini"`. `.cfg` and `.conf` aren't inferred, because many such files aren't INI.
- The rules follow the files Python's `configparser` reads. `[name]` starts a section, and keys before the first section belong to none. Both `key = value` and `key: value` set a key, a line with neither is a key with no value, and a line indented further than its key continues its value, blank lines in between included.
- Only lines that start with `#` or `;` are comments. `a = b ; c` sets `a` to `b ; c`, as `configparser` reads it by default.
- Keys and section names are compared as written, case included. A repeated key or section has its last value, and that's the one a merge sets.
- A new key takes the indentation of the keys already in its section, so tab-indented files such as `.gitconfig` stay consistent. CRLF line endings, a leading byte order mark, and a missing final newline are kept, and comments inside a value mise replaces stay.
- A target that doesn't parse as INI, such as an unclosed `[section`, is reported and left alone.

This also fixes a merge in any format whose target is a symlink to its own source, as left behind by switching an entry from `symlink` to `merge`. If the source is a template whose raw text doesn't parse, mise used to replace the link with a copy and then fail, leaving a regular file. It now fails first and keeps the link.

The merge is a small line-based editor in `mise-util` (`ini_merge.rs`), and it adds no dependency. `configparser`, which mise already pulls in through the conda backend, doesn't fit: it drops comments when it reads a file and rebuilds the text when it writes, so a merge built on it would strip the comments from the user's file and reformat it.

Closes the request in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15132.

Validated with new unit tests for the INI merge, the new `test_dotfiles_merge_ini` e2e test, the existing `test_dotfiles_merge_edits

title: feat(dotfiles): deploy files stored in fnox with mode = "fnox"
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3020/changes/mise/1132
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A dotfiles repository is often public or shared, so a file that holds a secret, such as `~/.npmrc` with a registry token or `~/.kube/config`, has no good place in it. This adds `mode = "fnox"`: the entry writes the file that [fnox](https://fnox.jdx.dev) stores for the same path, so the content stays encrypted in fnox and never enters the repository.

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.npmrc" = { mode = "fnox" }
```

Store the file with fnox first. fnox 1.44.0 added whole-file storage keyed by path:

```sh
mise use -g fnox
fnox set --file ~/.npmrc
```

`mise dot apply` then runs `fnox get --file ~/.npmrc` and writes the result with mode `0600`, unless the entry sets `permissions`. The entry takes no `source`, because fnox keys the file by the target path.

## Behavior

- **`mise dot edit ~/.npmrc`** runs `fnox edit --file`, which stores the change in fnox. Apply again to deploy it.
- **Dry runs** (`mise dot apply --dry-run`, `mise dot unapply --dry-run`) list fnox entries without calling fnox, since reading a file can prompt for a passphrase or a provider login.
- **`mise dot diff`** reports `content differs from the file fnox stores (not shown)` and never prints the content.
- **`mise dot status`** reads the file to compare it, as it already renders templates.
- **`mise dot unapply`** removes the target only while it still matches what fnox stores, unless `--force` is given.
- **`mise oci build`** skips fnox entries with a warning, because anyone who can pull an image can read its layers.
- **Groups and variants**: a fnox entry works inside `[dotfile_groups]` and with `permissions`. When a variant selects another `target`, fnox looks the file up by that path.
- **`mise dot add`** refuses `--mode fnox` and targets already stored in fnox, so it never copies a secret into the dotfiles root.
- mise looks for `fnox` on `PATH`. An entry that sets `source`, `exclude`, `manifest`, `encrypt = true` or a wildcard target is ignored with a warning, and the schema rejects it.

## Limitations

- Before overwriting a target, the dotfiles journal saves the previous file so `mise dot rollback` can restore it. It does the same for templates and inline content, so for a fnox entry the local state directory holds the previous plaintext.
- fnox files are UTF-8 text only, so binary files are not supported.

## Validation

- New e2e test `test_dotfiles_fnox` uses a fake `fnox` that logs its calls. It covers apply, the `0600` mode, a dry run that never calls fnox, a diff that hides both old and new content, edit, unapply, `dot add` refusals, a permissions override with a variant target, a group entry, an invalid entry, and a file fnox does not store.
- The existing dotfiles e2e tests for absent, groups, variant targets, files, permissions, edits, templates and status pass.
- `mise-system` file unit tests, `mise-config` tests and `schema_matches_parser` pass, an

title: security(secrets): refuse project grants of keys from your own fnox config
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3019/changes/mise/1131
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

fnox merges its global config (`~/.config/fnox/config.toml`, where `fnox set --global` writes) into every project, along with `fnox.toml` files in parent directories such as your home directory. Until now, any project with `[secrets.fnox]` could grant itself a key you stored there for your own use:

```toml
# a cloned repository's mise.toml
[secrets.fnox]

[tasks.build]
secrets = ["OPENAI_API_KEY"]   # your personal key, from ~/.config/fnox/config.toml
run = './build.sh'
```

Outside paranoid mode, `mise run` trusts the active config implicitly, so running one of that repository's tasks was enough.

When fnox reports where a key is defined (jdx/fnox#1059), mise now treats a key from fnox's global config, or from a file in or above `$HOME`, as yours rather than the project's:

- A task's `secrets` list or a `{{ secrets.NAME }}` reference that names such a key fails before anything is resolved:

  ```text
  task build: OPENAI_API_KEY comes from your own fnox config, so the project cannot grant it
  ```

  The error names the file that defines the key and suggests `mise run --secrets OPENAI_API_KEY build`.

- `--secrets-all` leaves such keys out and asks fnox only for the project's keys, so a signed-out provider behind one of your keys cannot fail or prompt during a project run. There are two exceptions, where mise still asks for everything and drops your keys from the answer: a project with a dynamic (`command`) lease, whose keys are only known once it runs, and a project with no keys of its own, because the call is still needed to scrub provider credentials such as `FNOX_AGE_KEY` from the task.
- `mise run --secrets NAME` and `mise x --secrets NAME` still pass them, because you named the key yourself.
- `mise secrets ls` and `mise tasks validate` report these grants as problems of kind `personal`.

To make a key the project's, define it in the project's `fnox.toml`. A project file that overrides a global key counts as the project's.

**Compatibility:** this needs the fnox release that includes jdx/fnox#1059. With an older fnox, `describe` reports no source, every key counts as the project's, and behavior is unchanged. mise secrets is still experimental.

**Not covered:** a project's own secret can reference a provider from your global fnox config, or define its own password-manager provider, and so read items your signed-in session can reach. Checking where a key is defined cannot stop that, because the key really is the project's. The protection there is config trust (`paranoid = true`).

- A new e2e test, `e2e/secrets/test_mise_secrets_personal_keys`, uses a new `FNOX_STUB_SOURCES` knob in the fnox stub. title: feat(dotfiles): apply block, line, and merge edits from a dotfile group
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3017/changes/mise/1130
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A dotfile group can now apply block, line, and merge edits alongside its whole-file entries, and those edits apply only on machines that select the group. Previously the edits had to live under `[dotfiles]`, which applies on every machine regardless of `[bootstrap] dotfile_groups`, so a `merge = "missing"` that seeds API-token placeholders could not sit next to the rest of a `common` group.

Requested in [discussion 15112](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/15112).

```toml
[dotfile_groups.common]
root = "common"
mode = "copy"

[dotfile_groups.common.entries]
"~/.config/mise/conf.d/private.local.toml/defaults" = { source = "../templates/private.toml", merge = "missing", permissions = "0600" }

[bootstrap]
dotfile_groups = ["common"]
```

With `common` selected, the first `mise dot apply` creates `private.local.toml` at `0600` from the template, and later applies add only missing keys so locally filled-in values stay. A machine that selects other groups never touches the file.

## Behavior

- An edit entry is a table keyed `<path>/<id>`, as in `[dotfiles]`. A bare string in `entries` is still a whole-file entry's source. Block, line, and merge are all accepted.
- A relative `source` starts at the group root, like the group's other entries. A `merge` without a `source` reads the same path inside the root.
- The file being edited must lie inside the group's target. The group's tree walk skips both that file and the edit's source, so the tree does not also deploy them.
- A key that only whole-file entries take (such as `mode`) is an error, and mise ignores the whole group with a warning, as it does for any bad group entry. `[dotfiles]` keeps its warn-and-skip behavior.
- A deselected group's edits are dropped before conflict checks, so they cannot conflict with anything.
- Deselecting a group leaves what its edits wrote in the file, and `mise dot unapply --group` still removes only the group's deployed files. This matches how merged keys already stay in place; to remove a block or line, run `mise dot unapply <path>` while the group is selected.

The `[dotfiles]` rule that an entry with a `group` key is invalid is unchanged; edits get their group only from the table they are declared in.

## Testing

New unit tests cover source resolution, the walk exclusions, rejected keys, and selection, and `e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_groups_edits` runs the scenario above end to end, including deselection and `unapply --group`. The existing dotfile group, edit, merge, prune, and schema e2e tests still pass, and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean.

title: fix(lockfile): keep a dotfiles checkout's lockfile URLs when it is linked into global config
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3016/changes/mise/1129
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes #15129.

If your global config includes a dotfiles checkout through a link, such as `~/.config/mise/conf.d/dotfiles → ~/dotfiles` or `~/.config/mise/config.toml → ~/dotfiles/mise.toml`, locked installs inside that checkout failed even though `~/dotfiles/mise.lock` had the URL:

```text
$ mise -C ~/dotfiles install ruby --locked --dry-run
mise ERROR Failed to install core:ruby@4.0.9: No lockfile URL found for ruby@4.0.9 on platform macos-arm64 (--locked mode)
```

The same command worked outside the checkout, and it worked inside the checkout before the link was added. Trusting the checkout did not help. This also broke `mise bootstrap` hooks that run `mise install` there.

With this change, the install inside the checkout uses the URLs from `~/dotfiles/mise.lock` and reports `ruby@4.0.9 ⇢ would install`.

## What changed

An untrusted project's lockfile keeps its versions and checksums but loses its download URLs. Only a trusted config can vouch for the lockfile beside it. Global config is trusted without asking, so the trust check excluded every config that resolved to global config. That stopped a repository from committing `mise.toml` as a symlink to your global config to get its lockfile trusted.

The check followed symlinks in both directions, so it also excluded a real file in your checkout that your global config links to. Config discovery already treats those two cases differently and keeps that file's lockfile beside it. The trust check now uses the same rule:

- **A real file you linked into your global config** (a dotfiles checkout) is your global config. Its lockfile is trusted, and the checkout does not need `mise trust`. mise already loads that `mise.toml` as global config without asking, including its templates and hooks, so trusting the lockfile beside it allows nothing new.
- **A project `mise.toml` that is a symlink to your global config** still cannot vouch for the project's lockfile.
- **Global config vouches only for the lockfile beside it.** If a dotfiles checkout sits inside a monorepo whose `[monorepo].lockfile` would route it to the shared lockfile, being global config does not make that shared lockfile trusted.

## Validation

- The new e2e test `e2e/lockfile/test_lockfile_dotfiles_global_link` covers a checkout linked as a `conf.d` folder, the same checkout untrusted, a global `config.toml` linked straight to the checkout, a linked checkout inside an untrusted monorepo with a shared lockfile, and a project `mise.toml` linked to the global config. The untrusted cases run with `MISE_SAFE=1`, because `mise install` otherwise trusts the config it runs in. The test fails without the fix.
- The non-slow `e2e/lockfile` tests and the global-symlink and dotfiles e2e tests pass (118 in all).
- The `lockfile::` and `config::` unit tests pass, and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets --

--- e2e/lockfile/test_lockfile_dotfiles_global_link (+81/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,81 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+# A dotfiles checkout linked into the global config dir keeps the lockfile
+# beside its mise.toml, and that lockfile keeps its download URLs: the user
+# made the checkout global config. A project mise.toml linked the other way, to
+# the global config, still does not vouch for the project's lockfile, and
+# global config does not vouch for a monorepo's shared lockfile.
+#
+# `mise install` trusts the config it runs in, so the arms that need an
+# untrusted project run in safe mode, which trusts nothing implicitly.
+
+export MISE_LOCKFILE=1
+export MISE_OFFLINE=1
+export MISE_TRUSTED_CONFIG_PATHS=""
+unset CI GITHUB_ACTIONS GITHUB_ACTION 2>/dev/null || true
+
+detect_platform
+PLATFORM="$MISE_PLATFORM"
+
+write_lock() {
+  cat >"$1/mise.lock" <<EOF
+[[tools.jq]]
+version = "1.7.1"
+backend = "aqua:jqlang/jq"
+"platforms.$PLATFORM" = { url = "https://example.com/jq-1.7.1.tar.gz" }
+EOF
+}
+
+mkdir -p dotfiles "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/conf.d"
+cat >dotfiles/mise.toml <<'EOF'
+[tools]
+jq = "1.7.1"
+EOF
+write_lock dotfiles
+dotfiles="$(cd dotfiles && pwd -P)"
+
+install="install jq --locked --dry-run"
+assert_fail_contains "MISE_SAFE=1 mise -C dotfiles $install 2>&1" "No lockfile URL found"
+mise trust dotfiles/mise.toml
+assert_contains "mise -C dotfiles $install 2>&1" "would install"
+
+# Linking the checkout into conf.d must not cost its lockfile the URLs.
+ln -s "$dotfiles" "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/conf.d/dotfiles"
+assert_contains "mise -C dotfiles $install 2>&1" "would install"
+
+# The link is the user's own consent, so trust is not needed on top of it.
+mise trust --untrust dotfiles/mise.toml
+assert_contains "MISE_SAFE=1 mise -C dotfiles $install 2>&1" "would install"
+
+# A global config file linked straight to the checkout behaves the same.
+rm "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/conf.d/dotfiles"
+ln -s "$dotfiles/mise.toml" "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml"
+assert_contains "MISE_SAFE=1 mise -C dotfiles $install 2>&1" "would install"
+rm "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml"
+
+# A checkout inside an untrusted monorepo with a shared lockfile keeps only its
+# own lockfile: being global config does not vouch for the monorepo's.
+mkdir -p mono/dotfiles
+cat >mono/mise.toml <<'EOF'
+monorepo_root = true
+
+[monorepo]
+lockfile = true
+config_roots = ["dotfiles"]
+EOF
+cp dotfiles/mise.toml mono/dotfiles/mise.toml
+write_lock mono
+ln -s "$(cd mono/dotfiles && pwd -P)" "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/conf.d/dotfiles"
+assert_fail_contains "MISE_EXPERIMENTAL=1 MISE_SAFE=1 mise -C mono/dotfiles $install 2>&1" "No lockfile URL found"
+rm "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/conf.d/dotfiles"
+
+# An untrusted project cannot borrow global trust by linking its mise.toml to
+# the global config: that config keeps the global lockfile, which has no URL.
+cat >"$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml" <<'EOF'
+[tools]
+jq = "1.7.1"
+EOF
+mkdir proj
+ln -s "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml" proj/mise.toml
+write_lock proj
+assert_fail "MISE_SAFE=1 mise -C proj $install 2>&1"

title: chore: release 2026.10.23
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3015/changes/mise/1128
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

### 🚀 Features

- **(dotfiles)** apply block, line, and merge edits from a dotfile group by @jdx in [#15131](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15131)
- **(dotfiles)** merge into INI files such as pip.conf and tox.ini by @jdx in [#15135](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15135)
- **(dotfiles)** deploy files stored in fnox with mode = "fnox" by @jdx in [#15134](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15134)
- **(gem)** list versions from a source's compact index, so GitHub Packages gems resolve latest by @waynehoover in [#15122](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15122)

### 🐛 Bug Fixes

- **(backend)** name the program when a command can't be found by @jdx in [#15119](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15119)
- **(lock)** keep the locks/ sidecar layout for a symlinked global config dir by @jdx in [#15125](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15125)
- **(lockfile)** keep a dotfiles checkout's lockfile URLs when it is linked into global config by @jdx in [#15130](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15130)
- **(ls)** show uninstalled lazy tools as lazy instead of missing by @jdx in [#15114](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15114)
- **(node)** keep a packageManager checksum from pinning later installs to npm by @jdx in [#15124](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15124)
- **(self-update)** retry replacing mise.exe on Windows while antivirus holds it by @jdx in [#15138](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15138)
- **(shell)** convert MANPATH to POSIX form when activating under MSYS2/Cygwin by @jdx in [#15117](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15117)
- **(shim)** keep other command wrappers active inside a wrapped command by @jdx in [#15126](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15126)
- **(uninstall)** don't remove 3.4.12 when asked to uninstall 3.4.1 by @jdx in [#15116](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15116)

### 📚 Documentation

- rewrite README with upfront config example and bootstrap guide by @jdx in [#15136](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15136)

### ⚡ Performance

- **(dotfiles)** write snapshot blobs without a git process per tracked file by @waynehoover in [#15127](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15127)

### 🧪 Testing

- **(dotfiles)** set group in the INI merge symlink test by @jdx in [#15139](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15139)

### 📦 Registry

- stop checking cargo-msrv's reported version in its test by @jdx in [#15137](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15137)

### Security

- **(secrets)** refuse project grants of keys from your own fnox config by @jdx in [#15133](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15133)

title: perf(dotfiles): write snapshot blobs without a git process per tracked file
body:
`mise dot status` and `mise dot sync` still started one `git hash-object -w` per tracked file to write its blob, so a snapshot of a home directory tracking about 860 files started about 880 git processes. This is the follow-up to #14607, which removed the per-file `ls-files` / `update-index` calls and left these behind, and it takes jdx's suggestion there to use gix.

Blobs are now written straight into the history repository's object database with gix, and the ids used to compare content without writing it are computed in-process. The number of git processes a snapshot starts no longer depends on how many files are tracked. Nothing else changes for users: the blob ids, trees, status output and failures are the same.

## Why gix rather than batching

Every blob goes through one function, `HistoryRepo::hash_blob`, and gix is already used to read this repository, so the change is that one function plus `transient_blob_id`. Batching through `hash-object --stdin-paths` or `cat-file --batch` would have meant a long-lived child, a stdin protocol to parse, and reworking each caller to hand over its files at once, including the encrypted path, which must never pass plaintext to git.

`git hash-object --stdin` hashes the bytes exactly as given (no filters, attributes or autocrlf without `--path`), and gix's `write_blob` does the same, writing the same zlib loose object read-only under `objects/`. The object format (sha1 or sha256) comes from the repository, as it does for git. On Windows, gix treats a second process writing the same loose object as success, so concurrent snapshots do not fail with `Permission denied`.

## Results

Measured on macOS (Apple Silicon) with debug builds of `main` and of this branch, each run against its own copy of the same state directory and the same 860 tracked files, `mise dot status --json`, three runs each, counting git processes with a logging wrapper on `PATH`:

| Build | Time | git processes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main` | 13.2s, 6.9s, 7.0s | 881 |
| this PR | 7.1s, 1.4s, 1.4s | 23 |

The first run of each build was slower (cold caches). The status output of the two builds was identical apart from the state directory path, and both copies ended with the same set of objects (`cat-file --batch-all-objects`). Of the 23 remaining processes, 19 are a fixed set (`write-tree`, `update-index --index-info`, `mktree`, ref and merge-base reads). The other 4 are `cat-file blob` calls that check the first bytes of a cached encrypted envelope, one per encrypted file; they stay on git because it streams just that prefix, where gix would decompress the whole blob.

## Testing

- A new unit test, `blob_ids_match_git_hash_object`, pins the ids from `hash_blob` and `transient_blob_id` to `git hash-object --stdin` in both sha1 and sha256 repositories, for an empty blob, text, CRLF text, binary bytes with NULs, a symlink target, and an 8 MiB file. It also checks that `transient_blob_id` writes nothing, that writing an existing blob again

title: fix(shim): keep other command wrappers active inside a wrapped command
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.com/gh/jdx/-/trails/3014/changes/mise/1127
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

When a `[wrappers]` entry ran its command, mise stripped the shim and `command-wrappers/bin` directories from the `PATH` that command and everything it starts inherit. That kept `mbx` from finding the `cargo` wrapper again, but it also meant a wrapped command that ran another wrapped command skipped that wrapper, silently losing its `args` and `env`. With both `pnpm` and `node` wrapped, a script run by `pnpm` got the plain `node`, not the `node` wrapper.

Now only the shims directory is stripped. mise records the wrappers whose commands are running in `__MISE_ACTIVE_WRAPPERS` (for example `["cargo","pnpm"]`), and a wrapper shim named in it runs the real tool instead of the wrapper again. Other wrappers apply normally:

```toml
[wrappers.a]
command = "wrap-a"
env = { WRAP_A = "1" }

[wrappers.b]
command = "wrap-b"
env = { WRAP_B = "2" }
```

With a real `a` that runs `a` and then `b`, `a` now prints `wrapper a:1`, `real a`, `real a` (nested, wrapper skipped), `wrapper b:2`, `real b`. Before, `wrapper b` never ran.

Things to know:
- A wrapper's `command` that is itself wrapped now runs that wrapper too (`cargo = "dummy"`, `dummy = "echo"`). Before, that lookup skipped every wrapper. Two wrappers that delegate to each other end at the real tool instead of looping. `test_exec_missing_tool_path_fallback_warning` is updated for this.
- The `mbx` → `cargo` lookup now goes through the `cargo` wrapper shim once. In a local benchmark that costs about 4 ms per call and was within noise on a warm no-op `mbx build`.
- Documented in the Command wrappers section of the shims page. Reported in jdx/mise#15108.

Validated with the new `e2e/cli/test_command_wrappers_nested` and the existing wrapper, fallback-cycle, Mr Boxington and task-shell e2e tests; clippy with `-D warnings` is clean.
