title: fix(shim): allow a few repeated fallback handoffs in one process
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/756
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

With a shim for `bash` (for example from a project that pins `conda:bash`) ahead of `/bin` on `PATH`, ordinary commands fail outside that project:

```sh
bash -c 'bash --version'
# mise ERROR shim fallback recursion detected for bash: /bin/bash keeps resolving back through mise.
```

`mise run` with `shell = "bash -e -c"` and a `#!/usr/bin/env bash` script fails the same way. Bash execs its final command in place, keeping its PID, so the shebang re-enters the shim. The fallback guard treated the second `(bash, /bin/bash)` handoff in that PID as a cycle, though the sequence is finite.

## Fix

The guard now allows up to 8 repeats of the same handoff in one process before reporting recursion. A real cycle is still caught well before the 32-entry limit.

## Docs

Shells should not be installed with mise. The shims and FAQ docs now say to install them with the system package manager, which `mise bootstrap` can manage through `[bootstrap.packages]`, and to use `shims.exclude` if one is already installed.

Closes nothing; reported in discussion #14474.

> **Medium Risk**
> Changes shim dispatch guard behavior for system fallback paths; incorrect limits could allow infinite exec loops or break legitimate nested shim use, but scope is limited to fallback tracking and is covered by e2e tests.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes false **shim fallback recursion** when a system binary (notably `bash`) **execs back into the same shim** in one process—e.g. `bash -c 'bash --version'` after a `bash` shim falls through to `/bin/bash`.
> 
> The fallback chain guard in `fallback.rs` no longer treats the **second identical handoff** as a cycle; it allows up to **8 repeats** of the same `(command, fallback path)` pair before erroring, while the **32-handoff** cap still catches real loops. Unit tests and an e2e **`repeat-tool`** scenario cover the bash-like pattern.

title: perf(outdated): resolve many registry tools with one request to the mise-versions index
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/755
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A cold `mise outdated`, `mise upgrade` or `mise install` downloads one `data/<tool>.toml` from mise-versions for each tool it has to resolve. mise now reads mise-versions' versions index (`data/index.v1.json`, jdx/mise-versions#368) instead, so many tools take one request. The answers do not change: the index is used only when it can prove the per-tool list would give the same version.

For this project, a cold `mise outdated` (empty `MISE_CACHE_DIR`/`MISE_DATA_DIR`) went from **19 requests to 14**, with identical output:

```toml
[tools]
node = "22"
python = "3.12"
go = "latest"
terraform = "1"
jq = "latest"
ripgrep = "latest"
gh = "latest"
deno = "2"
bun = "latest"
zig = "0.14"
kubectl = "latest"
helm = "3"
shellcheck = "latest"
yq = "4"
fzf = "latest"
just = "latest"
```

The six lists for node, go, bun, deno, zig and yq became one list plus the index. The other 13 requests are unchanged: aqua's `latest` shortcut (`/releases/latest`) for jq, ripgrep, gh, kubectl, shellcheck, fzf and just; kubectl's `api.github.com` lookups; and the lists for python, terraform and helm (see *What still reads its own list*). Wall time was within noise (0.8–1.3s both ways), because the requests already ran in parallel.

| Command | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mise outdated`, cold, 16 tools | 19 requests | 14 requests |
| `mise latest node`, cold | 1 request (`node.toml`) | 1 request (`node.toml`) |
| `mise latest bun`, index on disk, no `bun.toml` cached | 1 request | 0 requests |

### When the index is used

The index is about 140 KB compressed, against about 5 KB for one tool's list, so it is worth fetching only when it replaces several lists:

- A tool whose own list is already cached never consults the index. That list is complete and costs nothing.
- The first tool in a command that needs a list reads its own `data/<tool>.toml`, exactly as before. The index is fetched when a second tool needs one. A single-tool command such as `mise latest node` therefore never downloads it, and a many-tool command makes two requests instead of one per tool.
- The index is cached at `$MISE_CACHE_DIR/versions-index/` and reused for `fetch_remote_versions_cache` (1h by default), by any command, including single-tool ones. After that it is revalidated with `If-None-Match`, which returns 304 when nothing changed. A `refresh` lookup (installing a `latest` that nothing installed satisfies) reuses a copy validated in the last 5 minutes, the window a refreshed version list reuses.
- An explicit backend arg that #14459 maps to a registry tool's list, such as `aqua:jqlang/jq`, uses that tool's index entry too.
- `use_versions_host = false`, offline and `prefer_offline` never use it. Neither does any tool the per-tool list would not come from mise-versions for (local listing options, a cache context, non-default backends, tools the host does not list), and neither does

title: fix(ruby): look up the latest ruby-build release through mise-versions
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/754
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

When mise compiles Ruby with ruby-build (`ruby.ruby_install = false`, with ruby-build already installed), it checks whether ruby-build is current on every `mise ls-remote ruby` and before every source install. The check fetched `api.github.com/repos/rbenv/ruby-build/releases/latest` directly. It was the only GitHub release lookup that skipped mise-versions, so each run spent one of the 60 GitHub API requests an hour that users without a token get.

## Change

The check now goes through mise's normal GitHub release lookup, which asks mise-versions, so it no longer spends the GitHub API budget. Nothing else about how ruby-build is updated changes.

ruby-build's GitHub releases have no assets. This lookup stops reaching GitHub only once #14460 (the client accepts asset-less releases from mise-versions) and the mise-versions change that serves them have both landed. Until then it ends up at GitHub on `main`, as before.

A failed check now just warns and leaves the installed ruby-build in place. Before, it went on to delete and reinstall ruby-build, so a rate-limited lookup cost a full `git clone` on every check.

## Validation

Builds and passes clippy. This path needs an installed ruby-build with `ruby.ruby_install = false`, so it has no e2e test. #14460's mirror-only rules are covered by `backend/test_github_api_not_used`.

title: fix(github): verify attestations from mise-versions without api.github.com fallbacks
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/752
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

mise reads GitHub artifact attestations from mise-versions, but several cases still went to `api.github.com`, which allows 60 requests an hour without a token:

- **Attestations filtered by predicate type** always went to GitHub. That covers aqua packages whose `github_artifact_attestations` sets `predicate_type`, such as foundry and gleam (SPDX): every install and `mise lock` of them spent the API budget.
- **Any mise-versions hiccup** (an error, a missing bundle) sent the check to GitHub.
- **A cached set that didn't verify** was re-checked against GitHub. The set came from mise's 7-day local copy of an earlier mise-versions answer.
- **A set signed under another repository name** went to GitHub too.

## Change

When mise-versions applies (the default), attestation checks don't fall back to GitHub:

- **Predicate types:** mise-versions returns every attestation for a digest, and mise now applies the filter itself the way GitHub's `predicate_type` parameter does: an exact type, or the `provenance` / `sbom` families. The filter only chooses which attestations to verify, and verification still covers the whole signed statement.
- **A set that doesn't verify:** mise asks mise-versions once more, skipping its local copy, in case GitHub added an attestation since. If that still doesn't verify, the failure is reported. mise-versions itself refreshes a release's attestations within 30 minutes.
- **A mise-versions failure** is an error naming mise-versions and `use_versions_host = false`.
- **Attestations made by another repository** that isn't the same one renamed are a verification error.
- **What still asks GitHub:** paranoid mode, which confirms mise-versions' answers there by design, and private repositories (a 404 from mise-versions) when the user has a token. Without a token the 404 is reported with a hint.

## Merge order

Stacked on #14460, which makes mise-versions requests report failures instead of passing them off as "not found".

## Validation

- `backend/test_github_api_not_used` now also installs `aqua:goreleaser/goreleaser@2.14.1` and `aqua:foundry-rs/foundry@1.8.5` with no token, and fails on any `api.github.com` request. Locally, foundry's install logs `got 3 GitHub attestations … from mise-versions` and `✓ GitHub artifact attestations verified`.
- A unit test covers `matches_predicate_type`: exact types, the `provenance` / `sbom` families, and attestations without a bundle.
- `test_aqua_github_attestations`, `test_github_registry_attestations` and `test_lockfile_provenance` pass.

title: fix(backend): resolve packslip prefixes like `latest`
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/751
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Stacked on #14466.

For a packslip tool, `fnox@latest` and `fnox@1` could resolve to different releases for the same reason. `latest` verifies each candidate and skips a release this host cannot install: one with no artifact for this platform or `variant`, a missing stamp from a configured stamper, an unmet requirement such as glibc, or one logged after the `minimum_release_age` cutoff. A prefix such as `fnox@1` took the newest match without looking at it, so a release `latest` would have skipped got resolved and then failed at install.

A prefix now walks its matches newest first the same way, and resolves to the newest release `latest` would also accept:

```
$ mise latest 'packslip:jdx/packslip[variant=nope]@0'
mise WARN  packslip:github.com/jdx/packslip: skipping 0.3.1: no artifact for linux/x86_64/gnu with variant "nope". The release has: …
mise WARN  packslip:github.com/jdx/packslip: skipping 0.3.0: no artifact for linux/x86_64/gnu with variant "nope". …
…
mise ERROR no release of packslip:github.com/jdx/packslip matching 0 can be installed; the warnings above say why each was skipped
```

Before, the same command printed `0.3.1`, and `mise install` failed with `no artifact for linux/x86_64/gnu with variant "nope"`. When some matches are refused and an older one is fine, the older one is chosen, with a warning naming each release skipped.

When every match is refused, the request now fails with the error above. An empty match list would otherwise send resolution on to install the prefix as written (`0`), and that fails with a misleading "has no release 0". An exact version (`fnox@1.39.0`) is not walked: it names its release, and install explains why that release is refused. Offline, nothing is verified, the same as for `latest`. The listing's own dates still drop releases that are plainly too new before anything is verified, so the default 24h `minimum_release_age` does not add a warning per fresh release.

Verifying a match costs a manifest download the first time. #14466 keeps a verification that passed for a day, so a warm `fnox@1` still makes one request:

| `mise latest fnox@1` | cold | warm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| main | 112ms: `data/fnox.toml`, policy probe | 116ms: the same 2 requests |
| this PR | 497ms: `data/fnox.toml`, policy probe, `releases/v1.39.0`, the manifest | **62ms: the policy probe only** |

The cold cost is the price of checking the release before choosing it, as `latest` already does. Measured with release builds, median of 3 cold and 5 warm runs, isolated cache, data and state dirs, requests counted from `MISE_TRACE=1`.

### Tests

- Unit, on `eligible_matches` (the walk the prefix resolver runs after listing): with the newest match refused, `1` resolves to the older release `latest` also picks; an exact version is not checked; no match is not an error; every match refused is the new error; a verification failur

title: perf(backend): stop re-downloading what packslip resolution already verified
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/750
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Resolving a packslip tool (`mise latest fnox`, `mise install` of `fnox = "latest"`, and so on) downloaded and signature-verified the same release manifest on every run, and re-downloaded the version listing every time. A warm `mise latest fnox` made three requests and took about 400ms. It now makes one request and takes about 60ms.

What packslip trusts does not change. Every resolution still asks the vendor (and any configured stampers) for their signed list, so a withdrawal, a new stamp, or a removed list still applies immediately. `mise install`, `mise use` and `mise lock` still download and verify the chosen manifest from scratch.

### What changed

- **The vendor's version listing is cached.** For a GitHub project, the release listing (mise-versions' `data/<tool>.toml`, or the GitHub release list) now goes through the remote-version cache like any backend's, so it respects `fetch_remote_versions_cache`, a refresh, and offline mode. The vendor's signed list and the stamps are still applied fresh to that cached listing on every resolution. A stale listing can only hold back a new release, never admit one policy refuses.
- **A verification that passed is reused by resolution for a day.** `latest` verifies each candidate before choosing it. Resolution now keeps the verified statement and its logged and published times, keyed by everything the result depends on: the version, the signer options (`pubkey` with a key file's contents, `identity`, `identity_prefix`, `issuer`, `workflow`, `allow_unlogged`), the stamp followed and its digest, what the vendor's signed list says about the version (read fresh, including its digest pin), this machine's signer pins (all of them, since a pin left under a repository's former name also holds its releases), and the mise build. The release-age cutoff, the artifact choice for this host (`variant`, `ignore_requirements`, glibc) and requirement checks are reapplied on every read. Only passing verifications are kept. A failure is never cached, and a stale entry can at worst pick a release that install then refuses.
  - Why one day: with a signed digest from a vendor list or stamp, the key pins the exact bytes, so the result only changes with a new mise build (part of the cache file name). Two inputs cannot be in the key: a bundle with no signed digest being replaced in place, and the forge's answer for a renamed repository. A day bounds how long resolution could rely on either, and install checks both again regardless.
- **Signed release lists and stamp lists are revalidated, not re-downloaded.** The last copy is kept with its `ETag`/`Last-Modified`, and the next resolution sends `If-None-Match`. A `304` reuses the copy, which is then verified (signature, expiry, sequence) exactly like a fresh download. Within one process each list is fetched once and its signature checked once, and only the latest list per proje

title: fix(lock): download artifacts for provenance checks from github.com, not the API
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/749
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

`mise lock` downloads the current platform's artifact for each `github:` tool so it can verify the tool's attestations or SLSA provenance. For that download it used the release's API asset endpoint (`api.github.com/repos/{owner}/{repo}/releases/assets/{id}`) rather than the file's normal download URL. Each locked tool therefore spent one of the 60 GitHub API requests an hour that users without a token get, and once those ran out `mise lock` failed with a 403:

```console
$ MISE_DEBUG=1 mise lock          # github:cli/cli in mise.toml, no token
INFO  downloading artifact for lock-time provenance verification: gh_2.62.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz
DEBUG GET Downloading https://api.github.com/repos/cli/cli/releases/assets/206502108 to …
```

## Change

The lock-time download now picks its URL the same way `mise install` does: the `github.com/…/releases/download/…` URL, which isn't API-rate-limited. The API endpoint is used only when that URL can't serve the file, which is the private-repository case. Tools on a custom GitHub Enterprise, GitLab or Forgejo API still download through that API. The two install call sites and the lock call site now share one helper for this.

## Validation

New e2e test `lockfile/test_lockfile_provenance_download_url` locks `github:cli/cli@2.62.0` with no GitHub token and fails if any request goes to `api.github.com`. It fails on `main` and passes here. The existing `test_lockfile_provenance*` and `test_github_additional_assets` tests pass.

title: fix(self-update): read mise releases from mise-versions and download from github.com
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/748
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

`mise self-update` made three requests to `api.github.com`: the release lookup (`/repos/jdx/mise/releases/tags/v{version}`), then the packslip and the archive downloaded through API asset URLs. Without a GitHub token that budget is 60 requests an hour, shared with everything else mise and other tools do from the same IP, so self-update could fail with a 403 rate-limit error even though nothing about it needed the API. On Windows, refreshing `mise-shim.exe` after an update made the same API calls again.

## Change

For mise's own releases (the default `self_update.repository = "jdx/mise"` on `api.github.com`), self-update now:

- reads the release from mise-versions, which mirrors GitHub's release data, and
- downloads `packslip.sigstore.json` and the archive from `github.com/jdx/mise/releases/download/…`, which isn't API-rate-limited.

```console
$ MISE_DEBUG=1 mise self-update 2026.9.16 --yes
DEBUG GET https://mise-versions.jdx.dev/api/github/repos/jdx/mise/releases/v2026.9.16 200 OK
DEBUG GET https://github.com/jdx/mise/releases/download/v2026.9.16/packslip.sigstore.json
DEBUG GET https://github.com/jdx/mise/releases/download/v2026.9.16/mise-v2026.9.16-linux-x64.tar.gz
Updated mise to 2026.9.16
```

Trust doesn't change. The release data doesn't need to be trusted: the archive is still verified against its packslip and its zipsign signature before anything is replaced, and the download URLs mise-versions returns are pinned to `github.com/jdx/mise`.

A customised `self_update.api_url` or `self_update.repository`, or `use_versions_host = false`, keeps the direct API and API asset downloads. Those sources may be private or GitHub Enterprise.

## Validation

`cli/test_self_update_install` (real updates to 2026.9.16, 2026.9.3 and 2026.9.2) now runs the updater with debug logging and fails if it requests anything from `api.github.com`. It passes locally with the output above. The Windows-only shim path was checked with `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu`.

title: fix(packslip): fetch skills from mise-versions and raw.githubusercontent.com, not the GitHub API
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/747
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

Installing a packslip tool that declares a skill living in its repository (fnox, usage, and others) listed the skill's directory and downloaded every file through `api.github.com`'s contents API. That's at least two requests per install against the 60-an-hour budget users without a token get. Once that budget ran out, the install failed:

```console
$ mise install fnox@1.39.0
WARN  fnox@1.39.0: could not fetch skill skills/fnox from the source repository: HTTP status client error (403 Forbidden) for url (https://api.github.com/repos/jdx/fnox/contents/skills/fnox/SKILL.md?ref=cc06c75…)
mise ERROR Failed to install packslip:github.com/jdx/fnox@latest: fnox@1.39.0: declared skill(s) fnox are not installed
```

## Change

- **Skills from the source repository:** the directory listing comes from mise-versions (`/api/github/repos/{o}/{r}/contents/{path}?ref={commit}`). The listing is pinned to the commit, so mise-versions can cache it for good. The files come from `raw.githubusercontent.com/{o}/{r}/{commit}/{path}`, which isn't API-rate-limited.
- **A `url_replacements` rule** for a repository's contents API (`https://api.github.com/repos/{o}/{r}/contents`) is the source of its skill listings, as it was before.
- **Private repositories:** mise-versions doesn't know them, so they are still listed and fetched through the contents API with the user's token. Without a token the error says to set one, or to set `use_versions_host = false`.

Repository identity lookups (`repository_identity` / `canonical_repo`) stay on GitHub on purpose. They decide whether a renamed repository's attestations or packslip are trusted, and an answer from a mirror could vouch for any repository. Only renamed or transferred repositories reach them.

As in #14460, a mise-versions failure is reported as an error rather than retried against GitHub. `use_versions_host = false` and `url_replacements` for GitHub still use the API directly.

## Merge order

Stacked on #14460. It needs mise-versions to serve the `contents` endpoint first. Until then mise-versions answers 404, which this PR reads as "private repository" and turns into an error without a token. I'll confirm it with curl before marking this ready.

## Validation

- `backend/test_github_api_not_used` now also runs `mise use fnox@1.39.0` with no token and checks `mise skills ls`. It fails on any `api.github.com` request. It can only pass once the endpoints are live.
- New e2e `backend/test_packslip_skill_url_replacements` checks that a contents `url_replacements` rule is used instead of mise-versions.
- Unit tests cover the response shape and the URL encoding of contents paths.
- `test_plugins_packslip_forge`, `test_plugins_packslip_unprefixed` and `test_packslip_resources` pass. The first two use `url_replacements`, which keeps the direct-API path.

body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/746
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

Git tags were always read from `api.github.com`, with no mirror in between. That covers the 32 aqua packages with `version_source: github_tag` (tomcat, ant, aws-cli, blender, …), ubi's tag listing for repositories without releases, and go's dated tag list. Without a GitHub token, `ls-remote`, `latest`, `install`, `exec` and `lock` for those tools spend the 60-requests-an-hour budget, and fail once it's gone:

```console
$ MISE_DEBUG=1 mise latest aqua:apache/tomcat@10
DEBUG GET https://api.github.com/repos/apache/tomcat/tags?per_page=100
DEBUG GET https://api.github.com/repos/apache/tomcat/tags?per_page=100 403 Forbidden
```

## Change

Tags now come from mise-versions' tags endpoint (`/api/github/repos/{owner}/{repo}/tags?page=N`, jdx/mise-versions#369), on the same terms as release lists in #14460:

- Without `MISE_LIST_ALL_VERSIONS` mise reads the first page, as it did from GitHub. With it, mise reads every page mise-versions serves (up to 10).
- go's dated listing asks for `dates=1`, which replaces one GitHub request per tag with the dates mise-versions includes.
- A mise-versions failure is an error naming mise-versions and `use_versions_host = false`. GitHub is asked only for a repository mise-versions doesn't list, and only with a token (a private repository).

`use_versions_host = false`, `url_replacements` for GitHub and custom `api_url`s still read tags from the API directly.

## Merge order

Stacked on #14460, which adds the mirror-only rules this reuses. The tags endpoint is live on mise-versions:

```console
$ MISE_DEBUG=1 mise latest aqua:apache/tomcat@10   # no GitHub token
DEBUG GET https://mise-versions.jdx.dev/api/github/repos/apache/tomcat/tags?page=1
10.1.61
```

## Validation

- Unit tests cover the response shape from jdx/mise-versions#369, single-page vs. all-pages listing, a 404 on the first page vs. a later one, and the page limit.
- `backend/test_github_api_not_used` now also runs `mise latest aqua:apache/tomcat@10` with no token, and fails on any `api.github.com` request. It passes locally against the live endpoint.

title: fix(github): stop falling back to api.github.com when mise-versions misses
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/745
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

mise asks mise-versions for GitHub release data first, but whenever mise-versions did not answer it asked `api.github.com` instead. Without a token that budget is 60 requests an hour, and it ran out in routine cases:

- **Guessed tag spellings.** A `github:` tool is tried as `v14.1.1` and then `14.1.1`. The wrong spelling was a 404 from mise-versions and then a second 404 from GitHub.
- **Releases without assets.** kubernetes, terraform, vault and others publish binaries elsewhere. Resolving `latest` for `aqua:kubernetes/kubectl` or `terraform@latest` went to GitHub on every `latest`, `outdated`, `upgrade` and `lock`, and a 24h cache then skipped mise-versions for them entirely.
- **Any mise-versions hiccup.** A 5xx, a timeout or an unexpected answer sent the whole release list to GitHub.

```console
$ MISE_DEBUG=1 mise outdated   # terraform and kubectl in mise.toml, no token
DEBUG GET https://api.github.com/repos/hashicorp/terraform/releases/latest
DEBUG GET https://api.github.com/repos/hashicorp/terraform/releases/latest 403 Forbidden
DEBUG GET https://api.github.com/repos/kubernetes/kubernetes/releases/latest
```

## Change

When mise-versions applies (the default), it is the only source of GitHub release data:

- A mise-versions failure is an error that names mise-versions and the way out, instead of a retry against GitHub:
  ```
  failed to read GitHub release cli/cli@v2.62.0 from mise-versions.jdx.dev, which mise asks instead of api.github.com. Try again later, or set use_versions_host = false to ask GitHub directly.
  ```
- A 404 for a tag of a repository that mise-versions lists is a plain "not found", so tag-spelling guesses never reach GitHub.
- GitHub is asked only when mise-versions doesn't list the repository at all and the user has GitHub credentials (a token or a `~/.netrc` entry for api.github.com). That is the private-repository case, which mise-versions never serves. Without a token the 404 stands, with a hint to set one.
- Releases with no assets from mise-versions are used as they are, and the 24h cache that skipped mise-versions for them is gone.
- The `use_versions_host` setting docs now describe this.
- Listings past the 10 pages mise-versions serves (only reached with `MISE_LIST_ALL_VERSIONS`) end there instead of refetching everything from GitHub.

The direct API is still used with `use_versions_host = false`, with `url_replacements` that reroute GitHub, and with GitHub Enterprise or any other custom `api_url`. Attestations, tags, self-update and packslip have their own PRs.

## mise-versions endpoints

This relies on mise-versions serving releases without assets (jdx/mise-versions#378) and repository directory listings for packslip skills (#379). Both are deployed:

```console
$ curl -s https://mise-versions.jdx.dev/api/github/repos/hashicorp/terraform/releases/latest
{"tag_name":"v1.16.6", …, "assets":[

title: perf(backend): read the registry tool's version list for an explicit backend arg
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/744
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Spelling a registry tool by its backend made mise skip the small static version list on mise-versions. `jq@1.7` reads `mise-versions.jdx.dev/data/jq.toml` (1.6 KB), but `aqua:jqlang/jq@1.7` paged the GitHub release mirror (`/api/github/repos/jqlang/jq/releases?page=1`, 64 KB, fetched twice). `packslip:jdx/fnox` did the same against fnox's 157 KB release page.

Now an explicit backend arg that names the preferred backend of exactly one registry tool reads that tool's list, so `mise latest aqua:jqlang/jq@1.7`, `mise ls-remote aqua:jqlang/jq` and `mise install packslip:jdx/fnox` make the same requests as `jq` and `fnox`. Nothing changes in the config:

```toml
[tools]
"aqua:jqlang/jq" = "1.7"       # lists versions from data/jq.toml
"packslip:jdx/fnox" = "latest" # lists versions from data/fnox.toml
```

## Measurements

Debug builds of origin/main and this branch, each run with fresh cache, data, state and config dirs, counting `MISE_DEBUG` request lines:

| Command | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mise latest aqua:jqlang/jq@1.7` | 2 × `releases?page=1` (64 KB each) | 1 × `data/jq.toml` (1.6 KB) |
| `mise latest packslip:jdx/fnox@latest` | 2 × `releases?page=1` (157 KB each) + 5 others | `data/fnox.toml` (0.7 KB) + 2 × `releases/v1.39.0` (4.9 KB each) + the same 5 others |

The fnox run makes one more request than before but downloads about 300 KB less. It now matches `mise latest fnox@latest` request for request.

## When an explicit arg still lists from the source

The list on mise-versions is generated from the registry entry, including the registry's options for that backend. An explicit arg does not inherit those options, so the mapping applies only when the list describes the arg's own listing:

- **Only the preferred backend.** `github:jdx/fnox` is fnox's second backend, so it lists from GitHub as before.
- **Only one tool.** `aqua:google/go-containerregistry` is preferred by both `crane` and `go-containerregistry`, so neither list is used.
- **No registry options on that backend.** `github:tursodatabase/libsql` is preferred by `libsql-server` with `version_prefix = "libsql-server-v"`, so its list does not describe the explicit arg. This rules out 36 of 185 github-first and 6 of 666 aqua-first entries. Packslip is the exception: its catalog only proposes versions, and every one is still verified against the signed list with the arg's own options. fnox's `workflow` option does not rule it out.
- **Only the official aqua registry.** With a custom `aqua.registries` entry, which mise searches before the official registry the hosted list is generated from, an explicit `aqua:` arg lists from the source.
- **The existing rules still apply.** Local listing options, cache contexts, `use_versions_host = false` and offline/prefer-offline modes skip the versions host as before. Backends with a direct source (`cargo:`, `npm:`, `pipx:`, …) ne

title: fix(exec): ask mise-versions for GitHub releases when auto-installing from exec and shims
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/743
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

`mise x`, `mise exec`, shims and `hook-env` run in prefer-offline mode. That mode also switched off the mise-versions mirror for GitHub release and attestation metadata, but these commands still install missing tools, and the release lookup then went straight to `api.github.com`. Without a GitHub token that budget is 60 requests an hour, so auto-installing a `github:` or `aqua:` tool from a shim or `mise x` failed for users who had already used it up, while the same `mise install` worked.

```console
$ MISE_DEBUG=1 mise x github:cli/cli@2.62.0 -- gh --version
DEBUG GET https://api.github.com/repos/cli/cli/releases/tags/v2.62.0
DEBUG GET https://api.github.com/repos/cli/cli/releases/tags/v2.62.0 403 Forbidden
```

## Change

The mirror stays on under prefer-offline, so these commands get release and attestation metadata from mise-versions like every other command. Prefer-offline already caps each lookup at one short attempt with no retries, so shims and `exec` still don't stall. `--offline` still makes no requests. `use_versions_host = false` and `url_replacements` for GitHub still turn the mirror off.

New e2e test `backend/test_github_prefer_offline_versions_host` runs `mise x github:jdx/communique@1.3.5` with debug logging and fails if any request goes to `api.github.com`. It fails on `main` and passes here.

This is the first of several PRs that move normal mise usage off `api.github.com` and onto mise-versions.

title: perf(install): skip refetching version lists a cached copy already answers
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/742
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise install` downloaded version lists again even when they were already cached and could not have changed its answer. In this sample project, `mise outdated` followed by `mise install --dry-run` refetched three lists that `outdated` had written seconds earlier. The second command now makes no requests.

```toml
[tools]
node = "22"
python = "3.12"
go = "latest"
jq = "latest"
terraform = "1"
"github:BurntSushi/ripgrep" = "latest"
"npm:prettier" = "3"
"pipx:black" = "latest"
```

### `latest` no longer refreshes when the release-age cutoff makes it pointless

Installing a `latest` that nothing installed satisfies deliberately bypasses the version-list cache (#9545). That refresh stopped a list cached up to an hour ago (`fetch_remote_versions_cache`) from hiding a newer release. It predates `minimum_release_age`, which now defaults to 24h. With that cutoff, every release mise is allowed to install is more than a day old, so any list cached in the last hour already contains it. The refresh downloads the same answer again: `go.toml` and black's PyPI JSON in this project.

Resolution now skips the refresh when the cached list already holds every release the tool's cutoff (global or per tool) admits. Three conditions make that true:

- The list is still fresh, so younger than `fetch_remote_versions_cache`.
- Its file is younger than the cutoff by an hour. A mise-versions list is a snapshot republished about every 30 minutes, so its contents can be older than the file.
- Every version has a release date that parses. A version without a usable date passes any cutoff, so a backend that cannot date its versions (some asdf plugins) keeps the refresh.

The check reads the cache file and loads that same copy, so resolution uses exactly the list it approved. The 24h default qualifies. A cutoff of minutes does not. The cache lifetime itself is unchanged. A list older than an hour is fetched again as before.

A shorter cutoff, such as `minimum_release_age = 0`, still gets the refresh, with one exception: a list written in the last 5 minutes (or within `fetch_remote_versions_cache`, if that is shorter) is reused. This covers `mise outdated` immediately followed by `mise install`, where the list is seconds old. mise-versions republishes about every 30 minutes, so a refetch that soon would rarely differ.

| Setting | List cached 1 minute ago | List cached 10 minutes ago |
| --- | --- | --- |
| default (24h cutoff) | reused | reused |
| `minimum_release_age = 0` or `"10m"` | reused | fetched again |

### The release-tag lookup reads the cached list

`data/terraform.toml` was not a version listing. Installing an aqua or `github:` registry tool looks up its release **tag** in the versions-host list (#14442), and that lookup always downloaded the list again instead of reading the copy resolution had just cached. It now reads the cached list first and downloads only

body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/741
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`minimum_release_age` defaults to 24 hours, so every `latest` is checked against a release-date cutoff. On a cold cache, `mise outdated` paid for that and for its own follow-up lookups with requests whose answers it already had. For a project with these tools:

```toml
[tools]
node = "22"
python = "3.12"
go = "latest"
jq = "latest"
terraform = "1"
"github:BurntSushi/ripgrep" = "latest"
"npm:prettier" = "3"
"pipx:black" = "latest"
```

a cold `mise outdated` made 9 requests, and now makes 6. The reported versions and `release_url`s are unchanged.

| Tool | Before | After | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pipx:black` | `pypi.org/pypi/black/json` ×2 | ×1 | pipx's `latest` shortcut returned a bare version. With no date to check against the cutoff, mise listed every version, which fetches the same JSON again. The shortcut now keeps the upload date it already had. |
| `github:BurntSushi/ripgrep` | `releases/latest` + `releases?page=1` | `releases/latest` | `outdated` looked up the `release_url` in the version list first, even though `latest` came from the `/releases/latest` shortcut, which already carries the URL. It now reads a list some earlier command already cached (no request), then asks the shortcut, and fetches the list only if neither knows the version. Queries that were resolved from the list still read the list first. |
| `jq` (installed, up to date) | `releases/latest` + `data/jq.toml` | `releases/latest` | The rolling-release check (for tags like `nightly` that keep their name) listed versions for every up-to-date tool. A request that resolved to another version (`latest` → `1.8.2`) cannot be a rolling release, so that check now answers without the list. |

black's JSON also drops out of `mise install` for `latest`: a cold `mise install --dry-run` fetched it 3 times and now fetches it once, and an `install --dry-run` right after `outdated` no longer fetches it at all. The shortcut's cached answer now has a date, so the cutoff accepts it without the list that install-time resolution would otherwise refresh.

A `latest` newer than the cutoff still falls back to the full list, which is what picks the older release; a new pipx test covers both cases. Not changed: the other two refetches in `install --dry-run` (go, terraform), which are a separate cache-reuse fix.

title: perf(python): list python versions from mise-versions instead of cloning pyenv
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/740
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

With `python.compile` unset, the default, mise may compile python, so `mise ls-remote python`, `mise outdated python`, `mise upgrade` and a fuzzy `mise use python@3.12` list every python-build definition, including ones that can only be compiled. To get that list mise cloned pyenv (about 21MB) into `~/.cache/mise/python/pyenv` the first time, then ran `git pull` on it each time the version cache expired, even if you never compiled anything.

mise-versions already publishes the list `python-build --definitions` prints, with the date each definition was added. mise now reads it from there. pyenv is cloned only when mise actually compiles a python, or when the list can't come from mise-versions:

- `use_versions_host = false`, or `offline` / `prefer_offline`
- mise-versions has no list or the request fails
- `python.pyenv_repo` points at a fork, because the fork can add or remove definitions

`python.compile = false` and Windows still list precompiled builds, as before.

### Measurements

Debug build, each run using an empty isolated `MISE_CACHE_DIR`/`MISE_DATA_DIR`, with `python = "3.12"` configured:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| cold `mise ls-remote python` (5 runs) | ~2.35s, clones pyenv | ~125ms, no clone |
| cold `mise outdated python` (5 runs) | ~2.40s, clones pyenv | ~130ms, no clone |
| `mise outdated python` with an expired version cache (3 runs) | ~445ms (`git pull`) | ~145ms |

The `mise ls-remote python` output is byte-identical before and after: 1094 versions, with `3.16.0a1` hidden by `minimum_release_age` in both. In `--json` the release dates are the same instants, now written in UTC. 40 definitions that git history gave no date (for example `3.13.0`, `3.15.0`, and some `-src` pypy builds) now have one. A definition that is younger than `minimum_release_age` and previously had no date is now hidden until it is old enough, like every other tool.

### Implementation notes

Listing python still bypasses the shared versions-host path (`lists_versions_for("python")` stays false). That path would show python-build's definitions even with `python.compile = false`, which is why python was excluded in the first place. Python requests the list itself through a new `versions_host::list_python_build_definitions`. Both sources go through the same free-threaded filter and sort. `install_compiled` still clones or updates pyenv before it builds, so compiling, including the automatic fallback when no precompiled build exists, does not rely on listing having cloned it.

Tests: unit tests for picking the source (host list used, fallback on none or error, fork `pyenv_repo`, setting gates). There is also an e2e test, `e2e/core/test_python_ls_remote_versions_host`, which checks that `mise ls-remote python` lists compile-only definitions without creating `$MISE_CACHE_DIR/python/pyenv`, and that with `MISE_USE_VERSIONS_HOST=0` it clones pyenv as

title: docs: recommend committing mise.lock so CI and Docker skip version lookups
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/738
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

CI jobs and Docker builds start with no cached version lists, so a request such as `node = "24"` or `latest` makes mise fetch each tool's list of available versions on every run. A committed `mise.lock` skips that: when a tool has a matching entry, mise takes the version from the lockfile and never lists versions. The docs mentioned lockfiles for reproducibility but never said they also remove those lookups.

The docs now recommend committing `mise.lock` for CI and Docker and explain why:

```sh
mise lock --platform linux-x64,linux-arm64,macos-arm64
mise install --locked
```

- **Lockfile page:** the "Lockfiles in CI" section becomes "Lockfiles in CI and Docker". It explains the lookup each run would otherwise make, notes that a restored cache only helps until `fetch_remote_versions_cache` (1 hour by default) expires, and shows `mise lock --platform`.
- **Continuous integration page:** the intro gives the same reason with the `--platform` command, and the caching section says a cache of version lists is no substitute for a lockfile.
- **Docker cookbook:** the Debian example copies `mise.lock` and runs `mise install --locked`, with notes on locking the image's platforms, copying `.mise/locks/` when npm or PyPI dependency graphs are locked, and adapting it for projects without a lockfile.

Docs only, no generated files changed. Prettier and markdownlint pass, `mise run docs:build` succeeds, and the new links and anchors resolve in the built site.

title: ci: check R2 credentials on every prune run
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/737
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

The weekly `prune-r2-releases` job (#14445) skipped before touching the R2 bucket whenever the download stats were unavailable or incomplete. That will be every run until the stats cover a full 30-day window (around 2026-11-14), so a missing, revoked, or mis-scoped `R2_PRUNE_*` token would not show up until the first run that could actually delete something. This PR makes every run check the token first and fail if it cannot read the bucket.

## Changes

- **Credentials check on every run.** Before any stats gate, `scripts/prune-r2-releases.sh` runs `aws s3api head-object --bucket mise --key VERSION`. This is an object read, so it works with a token scoped to Object Read & Write on bucket `mise` (bucket-level calls such as `head-bucket` can be denied for such tokens). If the read fails, the job fails with exit 1 in dry-run mode too, prints the aws error, adds an `::error::` annotation that names the `r2-prune` environment secrets, and writes a "failed" job summary. Nothing is listed or deleted.
- **Clearer skip while there is no data.** The stats endpoint is live but has no complete day yet, so it returns `{"days":30,"covered_days":0,"first_covered_date":null,"last_covered_date":null,"versions":{}}`. Runs used to skip with the misleading "download stats response is not in the expected format". They now skip with:
  ```
  Skipping, nothing deleted: download stats have no covered days yet (https://mise-versions.jdx.dev/api/mise-releases/downloads?days=30).
  ```
  Only that exact shape gets the new message: integer `days`, `covered_days` equal to 0, both dates present and `null`, and `versions` absent or `{}`. Any other null or missing field, such as `versions: null`, a missing date, a date set with the other null, or a non-zero `covered_days` with null dates, still fails the strict format check.

All existing gates and their order after the check are unchanged. Missing credential env vars still fail before any `aws` call, but they now fail before the stats fetch instead of after it.

## Validation

- `shellcheck` and `shfmt` pass through `hk check`. The workflow is unchanged.
- Run against the real stats endpoint with a stub `aws`: the credentials check passed and the run skipped with the new "no covered days yet" message, exit 0.
- A stub harness (fake `aws` on `PATH` that logs every call, plus a local stats server) passed 28 cases with the new script. When head-object is denied, the run exits 1 with the `::error::` and makes no other `aws` calls, with a 404 stats endpoint, zero-coverage stats, or full valid stats in delete mode. The zero-coverage shape skips with the new message in dry-run and delete mode, with `versions` set to `{}` or absent. The near-miss shapes listed above still get the format skip. The earlier skips behave as before: HTTP 404, unreachable endpoint, HTML response, partial coverage, a window mismatch, stale or impossible

title: fix: avoid false "stack limit reached" on musl builds
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/736
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes #14449

On Ubuntu 26.04, mise 2026.10.9+ fails to parse aqua `version_filter` expressions such as `not (Version matches "-(alpha|beta|rc)")` with `stack limit reached`. Tools like kubectl then can't resolve bin paths, and their shims report "not a valid shim" even though the tool is installed.

Root cause: the release binary is static musl. musl's `pthread_getattr_np` reports only ~128 KiB for the **main thread** instead of its real 8 MiB, so `stacker::remaining_stack()` is wrong there. `pest` 2.9.3 (via `expr-lang`) started rejecting parses when that reads under 64 KiB. mise runs its async code on the main thread via `block_on`, so after a little real stack use the reading is under the limit. Ubuntu 24.04 only passed by margin (132 KB vs 126 KB reported on 26.04), which is why `ulimit -s` made no difference. I reproduced with `mise reshim` in `ubuntu:26.04`.

The fix wraps `runtime.block_on(main_())` in `stacker::maybe_grow`. When the detected space looks small it moves to a fresh stack with correct bounds; with an accurate reading (glibc) it does nothing. A musl probe reads ~130 KB before and 16 MB inside the wrapper.

I haven't run the full musl mise build in the 26.04 container; only the probe.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: unavailable.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Startup-only change via stacker::maybe_grow with a no-op fast path; no auth or data-path changes, though the whole CLI run may execute on a grown stack on affected platforms.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes false **stack limit reached** errors when **pest**/**expr-lang** parses aqua `version_filter` and similar expressions on **musl** builds, where main-thread stack detection leaves under 64 KiB reported headroom (mise#14449).
> 
> Adds the **`stacker`** dependency and runs the full Tokio **`block_on(main_)`** path inside **`stacker::maybe_grow`** (256 KiB threshold, up to 16 MiB). When remaining stack looks adequate, this is a no-op; when it looks too small, work continues on a stack with known bounds so parsing is not rejected upfront.
>

title: fix(oci): require root for apt bootstrap packages and show dpkg output on failure
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/734
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise oci build` with an apt package such as `"apt:cmake" = "latest"` fails when mise is not running as root, and the error does not say why:

```
E: Sub-process /usr/bin/dpkg returned an error code (1)
```

mise installs apt packages into the unpacked image with `dpkg --root=<rootfs>`, so dpkg chroots into the image to run package scripts. Only root can do that. The real message (`not enough privileges to change root directory with --force-not-root`) goes to apt's stdout, which mise never showed. Packages without maintainer scripts, like `zlib1g`, happened to work. Even when a non-root install succeeds, the layer keeps the builder's uid instead of root. #14296 cleared host apt hooks but did not address this, so cmake still failed.

mise now requires root for apt packages, the same way it already does for apk, and fails up front:

```
mise oci needs to run as root to install apt system packages because dpkg executes package scripts in a chroot
```

When apt-get still fails, the error now includes the last 20 lines of its stdout along with stderr. The docs say apt and apk both need root.

Reproduced the failure as uid 1000 in an ubuntu:24.04 container; added a unit test for the error output. I did not run a full `mise oci build` as root against a registry.

Fixes #14291

The install script (`curl https://mise.run | sh`, https://mise.jdx.dev/install.sh) used mise.jdx.dev only when installing the release built into the script. Any pinned `MISE_VERSION` came from GitHub Releases, which responds more slowly and adds a redirect before the download starts.

Now the release archive for every version comes from mise.jdx.dev first, and the script falls back to GitHub Releases when that download fails. Pinned versions are still always checked against checksums from GitHub Releases:

```console
$ curl -fsSL https://mise.run | MISE_VERSION=v2024.12.0 sh
mise: installing mise...
mise: could not download from mise.jdx.dev, trying GitHub Releases
mise: installed successfully to ~/.local/bin/mise
```

The fallback is needed because older release folders are being pruned from mise.jdx.dev (#14445).

## Behavior

- **Archive:** downloaded from `https://mise.jdx.dev/v<version>/<asset>`. Any failure, including a 404 or a network error, retries the same asset from GitHub Releases.
- **Checksums never come from mise.jdx.dev.** The script's built-in version uses the checksums embedded in the script, as before. Any other version is always checked against `SHASUMS256.txt` from GitHub Releases, wherever the archive came from, as it was before this PR. Because the checksum comes from a separate host, someone who compromised mise.jdx.dev could not serve a tampered archive together with a matching checksum.
- **Unverified archives are refused:** the script uses only a well-formed SHA-256 line for exactly the downloaded file. If GitHub's `SHASUMS256.txt` cannot be fetched or has no such line, the script exits with `no checksum found for <file>, refusing to install it unverified` before extracting anything. There is no fallback to mise.jdx.dev's checksums. A failed check exits with `checksum mismatch`.
- **`MISE_INSTALL_FROM_GITHUB=1`:** still downloads only from GitHub.
- **`MISE_TARBALL_URL`:** unchanged. It applies only to the built-in version, uses the embedded checksums, and has no fallback.
- **Built-in version:** the only change is the new GitHub fallback for the archive.

`installing-mise.md` now says where the script downloads archives from and where it gets checksums.

## Effect on download stats

Pinned installs will download their archives from mise.jdx.dev, so the per-platform GitHub release-asset counts behind mise-versions.jdx.dev/stats will drop unless jdx/mise-versions starts counting mise.jdx.dev (R2) downloads. Only `SHASUMS256.txt` will still come from GitHub. That mise-versions change is a separate PR that is still in progress. **I recommend merging this after that one lands.**

## Validation

- `scripts/test-install-release-age.py` (run by `scripts/test-standalone.sh` in CI) gains offline tests. They run `install_mise` against a stubbed `curl` that serves real tarballs, and they cover:
  - a pinned version downloaded

title: ci: prune unused release folders from the mise.jdx.dev CDN bucket
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/732
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

The `mise` R2 bucket behind https://mise.jdx.dev and https://mise.en.dev keeps a `v<version>/` folder for every release ever published: about 371 folders and 425 GB, growing by about 2.7 GB per release. Almost nobody fetches the old ones. The current `install.sh` downloads only its own built-in version from the CDN and gets every other version from GitHub, and mise-action uses only `mise-latest-*`. The old folders are still fetched by old saved copies of `install.sh` (for example, copies vendored into Dockerfiles), and those copies have no fallback. Folders are therefore deleted based on real download counts, not age alone.

This PR adds a weekly `prune-r2-releases` workflow and `scripts/prune-r2-releases.sh`. GitHub Releases still keeps every asset; only the CDN copy is removed.

## Rule

A top-level folder is deleted only if all of these are true:

- its name matches `^v[0-9]{4}\.[0-9]{1,2}\.[0-9]+/` (no other keys are ever touched, including `deb/`, `rpm/`, `VERSION`, `install.sh`, `mise-latest-*`, `releases.tsv`, and the docs site)
- its newest object is more than **180 days** old
- it had **zero downloads** (`binary + other`) during the last **30 days**
- it is not one of the **30 most recently uploaded** release folders
- it is not the version in `s3://mise/VERSION`

A folder's age comes from the newest `LastModified` in that folder. Uploads happen at release time, and a re-upload can only make a folder look younger, so this can never make a folder look older than its release. "Newest 30" uses the same upload order. Version strings are never compared. All thresholds can be changed with `PRUNE_*` environment variables.

## Safety gates

- **Download stats are required.** The script reads `GET https://mise-versions.jdx.dev/api/mise-releases/downloads?days=30`. If the endpoint is unreachable, returns a non-200 status (it is a 404 today), or returns an unexpected format, the run is skipped with exit 0 and nothing is deleted.
- **Matching window.** The response's `days` must equal the requested window (30), and `days` and `covered_days` must be plain non-negative integers.
- **Full coverage.** Nothing is deleted unless `covered_days` is at least the response's own `days` and at least 30 (`PRUNE_MIN_COVERED_DAYS`). Cloudflare logs start on 2026-10-14, so the first fully covered 30-day window lands around 2026-11-14. Runs before then are skipped.
- **Fresh stats.** Nothing is deleted unless `last_covered_date` is at most 3 days old (`PRUNE_MAX_STATS_AGE_DAYS`). The rollup runs daily at about 02:20 UTC for the previous day, so a stale window means the pipeline has stopped and recent downloads could be missing.
- **Valid counts only.** Only a version that is absent from the stats counts as zero downloads. If any present entry lacks non-negative integer `binary` and `other` counts (for example `{}` or `null`), the whole run is skipped.
- **Broken

title: fix(upgrade): skip version lookups for lazy tools a bare upgrade leaves alone
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/731
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

> Stacked on #14422: this branch contains its commits, so the diff shows them until that PR merges. The change for this PR is the last commit, `7e2205914`.

A bare `mise upgrade` leaves a lazy tool with nothing installed alone (#14422), but it still looked that tool up first. With the declarations below, `mise upgrade` fetched the version list for both tools, then discarded the result:

```toml [/etc/mise/conf.d/defaults.toml]
[tools]
claude = { version = "latest", lazy = true }
codex = { version = "latest", lazy = true }
```

On a machine with an unreachable backend or a slow network, that meant a delay, and a `Failed to resolve tool version list for …` warning, for tools the upgrade was never going to touch. Omarchy declares 20 such tools.

Now a bare `mise upgrade` doesn't resolve or look up a lazy tool that has nothing installed. A lazy tool with any version installed still upgrades, and one that an upgraded tool depends on is still looked up and installed with it. Naming the tool resolves it in full, as before.

## Changes

- A bare `mise upgrade` builds its toolset with the lazy-deferral that `auto_update` already uses, so missing lazy tools stay unresolved.
- The outdated check skips those requests instead of filtering them out afterward, and looks up only the ones an upgraded tool needs (transitively) via `install_dependency_declarations`.
- `Toolset::list_outdated_versions_selecting` takes an `OutdatedSelection` that adds a per-version predicate to the existing filter and exclude lists. `ToolVersion::is_unrun_lazy` is the shared check, and `mise outdated` uses it for its `[MISSING] (lazy)` note.
- `e2e/cli/test_upgrade_lazy_missing` adds a lazy tool whose backend cannot resolve (`github:mise-test/no-such-repo`): a bare `mise upgrade --dry-run` doesn't mention it, and naming it does.

## Testing

On Linux:
- `test_upgrade_lazy_missing` passes up to its final `jq` release-age assertions. This sandbox has `jq` installed system-wide, which the `jq` cases need absent. I moved the new case ahead of them and have not seen the `jq` cases pass here.
- `test_upgrade_global`, `test_upgrade_latest_stale`, `test_upgrade_bump_multiple`, `test_upgrade_bump_keeps_prefix`, `test_upgrade_no_prune`, `test_lazy_tools`, `test_lazy_tools_depends`, `test_lazy_tools_system`, `test_lazy_tools_deferred_resolution`, `test_tool_update`, `test_tool_update_missing`, `test_tool_update_lazy_neighbors`, `test_tool_update_global_auto`, and `test_outdated` pass. `test_install_before` fails here for the same system-`jq` reason.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean.

I haven't run the full unit or e2e suites, or tested on macOS or Windows.

title: perf(github): reuse mirrored attestations and skip mise-versions for asset-less latest releases
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/730
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Two kinds of GitHub API mirror (mise-versions) requests could not give mise anything new:

**Asset-less `latest` releases.** To resolve `latest`, aqua asks for a repository's latest GitHub release. Some repositories publish binaries elsewhere and their GitHub releases have no assets: `kubernetes/kubernetes` (kubectl), `hashicorp/terraform`, `hashicorp/vault`, `npm/cli`, `awslabs/amazon-ecr-credential-helper`. mise-versions answers 404 for those, and mise would refuse an asset-less answer from it anyway, so every such lookup sent a request to mise-versions before asking GitHub. Now, once GitHub has returned a latest release without assets, mise skips mise-versions for that repository's `latest` for 24 hours (kept in the cache dir). The answer still comes from GitHub, as it did before. Fixed tags are not affected.

**Attestations by digest.** mise-versions' GitHub artifact attestations for an artifact digest are now kept in the cache dir for 7 days, and an empty answer is remembered for the rest of the command. `mise lock` asked for each digest twice (once to detect provenance, once to verify it) and again for every platform that shares an artifact. A kept set gets no trust it didn't have before: every use verifies the bundles against the downloaded artifact and the repository, and falls back to the GitHub API when they don't verify, exactly as with a fresh answer. Only non-empty sets are written to disk, and `paranoid` mode always asks.

## Measured

Fresh data and cache dirs, `MISE_DEBUG=1`, counting requests to `mise-versions.jdx.dev/api/github` and `api.github.com`:

| Command | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mise use terraform@latest kubectl@latest`, run a second time | 2 mirror 404s + 2 GitHub | 2 GitHub |
| `mise lock --platform linux-x64,macos-arm64` for uv, gh, maestro | 6 attestation requests (gh: 2 per digest; maestro: 2 for its one archive) | 3 (one per digest) |

Installs from a `mise.lock` that has URLs and checksums don't request releases or attestations at all; that was already the case and is unchanged.

title: perf(backend): take release tags from the versions host instead of listing or guessing them
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/729
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Installing or locking a GitHub-hosted tool needs the release tag for the requested version, and the version alone often doesn't spell it: kustomize `5.8.1` is tagged `kustomize/v5.8.1`, maestro's version is `cli-2.6.0`, and tuist, SwiftGen, Sourcery and SwiftFormat tag without a `v`. mise worked the tag out with extra requests to the GitHub API mirror (mise-versions) and GitHub:

- **aqua tools** fetched the repository's whole release list (`/releases?page=1`) on every install and every `mise lock`, only to map the version to its tag. That is the most requested mirror endpoint (uv, pnpm, jq, gh, shellcheck, buildifier, ripgrep, actionlint, tuist), even though the versions-host list mise already reads for these registry tools records each version's release URL, tag included. When the version wasn't on the first page (older tuist releases), mise then guessed `v4.100.0`, which 404s.
- **github tools** guessed `v<version>` first, so `cli-2.6.0` and `6.6.2` each cost a 404 from mise-versions and another from GitHub. A 404 isn't cached, so every lookup of the same release in one command (resolving the pin, picking the asset, provenance, each `mise lock` platform) guessed again.

Now:

- The aqua and github backends take the tag from the versions host's `release_url` for the version, and use it only when the package (aqua) or the tool's options (github) map that tag back to the requested version, the same check their own listings apply. It is a hint, and aqua confirms it before relying on it, never with an extra GitHub API request: for packages installed from release assets it fetches the release (the lookup the install makes next, so it costs nothing), and for packages installed from URLs (terraform, kubectl, vault) it probes the artifact on its own host with one HEAD request instead of listing releases. A hint that doesn't confirm is dropped, and the tag is looked up as before, `v` alternative and URL probe included, so a stale versions-host entry costs a request, not an install. The github backend tries the hint before its usual spellings. Provenance is checked on the release the selected asset came from (for an asset reused from a lockfile, the release its URL names). Tools the versions host doesn't serve or doesn't list (non-registry tools, local `version_prefix`/`api_url` overrides, `MISE_USE_VERSIONS_HOST=0`, offline, a versions-host outage) keep the previous behavior; a miss never falls through to a full release listing.
- A tag that resolved is tried first for the rest of the command, per API host. A remembered or listed tag that fails for any reason (for example, its release lacks the wanted asset) moves on to the usual spellings.
- Without a `version_prefix`, a version that doesn't start with a digit (`cli-2.6.0`, `kustomize/v5.8.1`) is tried as written before `v` is added. Both spellings are still tried; only the order changed.

title: perf(versions-host): send install tracking and python lists to static assets
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/728
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

mise's requests to [mise-versions](https://mise-versions.jdx.dev) now all go to static assets instead of the billed Cloudflare Worker. Usage (installs, monthly active users) will be counted from Cloudflare's request logs instead of from Worker code. Installs, version lists, and Python precompiled lookups work the same for users, and the existing opt-outs (`use_versions_host`, `use_versions_host_track`, offline mode) still apply.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Don't merge this until the mise-versions changes that serve the static `/t` beacon and `/data/python-precompiled-*.gz` are deployed. Until then, install reports go to a path that doesn't count them, and Python precompiled lookups fail because mise no longer reads the old `/tools/` path.

## What changes on the wire

**Install tracking.** After a core or registry tool installs, mise used to send `POST https://mise-versions.jdx.dev/api/tools/<tool>` with a JSON body (`full`, `version`, `os`, `arch`). It now sends a GET to the static beacon, with every field as a percent-encoded query parameter:

```
GET https://mise-versions.jdx.dev/t?tool=node&full=core%3Anode&version=22.1.0&os=macos&arch=arm64
```

The set of fields is the same as before. Request URLs are logged, so mise removes any URL credentials, query string, and fragment from `full` before sending it. That works whether the URL follows a backend prefix (`http:https://user:pass@host/…`) or is the whole value (`https://user:pass@host/…`). If `full` contains a `://` URL that can't be parsed, mise leaves the `full` parameter out instead of sending the raw value. The request is still fire-and-forget. Any 2xx counts as success, and the body is ignored.

**Python precompiled lists.** `python-precompiled-<arch>-<os>.gz` now comes from `/data/` instead of `/tools/`.

**CI marking on every versions-host request.** When mise detects CI (`ci_info::is_ci()`, the same check as before), every request to mise-versions sends both of these:
- the `x-mise-ci: true` header. Version lists and the GitHub release/attestation mirror already sent it. The beacon and the Python list fetch now do too.
- a trailing ` ci` token on the User-Agent, for example `mise/2026.10.10 linux-x64 (2026-10-11) bash ci`. Logpush can't record custom headers without Enterprise, so the logs see CI through the User-Agent. The rest of the User-Agent format is unchanged, and the token is set only on mise-versions requests. Other hosts get the normal User-Agent.

## Privacy

This change is meant to reduce infrastructure costs: counting moves from a billed Cloudflare Worker to Cloudflare's request logs. Doing that requires keeping raw IP addresses for up to 35 days.

Cloudflare Logpush stores each request's raw client IP, path and query, User-Agent, and timestamp in a private R2 bucket. A nightly job aggregates the logs into counts keyed by a salted hash of the IP. The raw logs are deleted automa

title: registry: add gdal (conda:libgdal-core)
body:
Add a `gdal` shorthand so `mise use gdal` installs the GDAL/OGR command-line tools without a separate package manager:

```sh
mise use gdal@latest     # installs 3.13.3
gdalinfo --version       # GDAL 3.13.3 "Iowa City", released 2026/08/13
ogr2ogr --version
```

## Backend

`conda:libgdal-core` (tier 3). No tier 1 or 2 backend can install GDAL: the project publishes no packslip manifests, it is not in the aqua registry, and its GitHub releases contain only source tarballs. mise downloads the conda-forge package directly, so users do not need conda or mamba installed.

conda-forge splits GDAL into several outputs. `libgdal-core` ships the shared library and the command-line tools; `libgdal` is a metapackage that only adds optional format plugins, and `gdal` is the Python bindings. The entry therefore uses `libgdal-core`.

`bins` lists only the GDAL and OGR executables. The conda package also ships unrelated executables from its dependencies (`curl-config`, `openssl`, `sqlite3`, `xmllint`, ...), which should not get shims.

## Supported platforms

Linux x64 and arm64, macOS x64 and arm64, Windows x64 (every platform conda-forge builds `libgdal-core` for).

## Verification

- `mise ls-remote gdal` lists versions up to 3.13.3.
- `mise test-tool gdal` on Linux x64 installs 3.13.3 and `gdalinfo --version` prints `GDAL 3.13.3 "Iowa City", released 2026/08/13`. All 30 listed `bins` are present in the install.

## Popularity

- GitHub: 6,099 stars, 2,956 forks (OSGeo/gdal), last release v3.13.3 on 2026-08-18, active development (last push 2026-10-13)
- An OSGeo project and the de facto geospatial raster/vector library; used by QGIS, PostGIS, rasterio, GeoPandas, and MapServer, and packaged in every major Linux distribution, Homebrew, and conda-forge

<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

`system::history::shadow::tests::objects_at_finds_paths_across_several_git_calls` times out (8s) on the macOS unit job, failing unrelated PRs. It has hit at least the `release` branch, `feat/vendor-config-dir` and #14426.

Use 120 paths of ~200 characters instead. The total is still ~24 KB, above the 16 KiB `ls-tree` batch limit, so `objects_at` still splits across two git calls, but setup spawns about a tenth of the processes. Locally the test passes in ~0.5s.

title: fix(dotfiles): capture changed files of copy-mode groups with dot add --changed
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/725
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise dot add --changed` ignored files that a copy-mode `dotfile_groups` root discovers automatically. Only files declared explicitly under the group's `entries` were captured, so edits to the rest of the group's tree stayed in the target and `--changed` reported "no changed copy-mode files" while `mise dot diff` still showed differences.

```toml
[dotfile_groups.common]
root = "source"
target = "~/.config/app"
mode = "copy"
entries."~/.config/app/explicit.txt" = { mode = "copy" }
```

Before, after editing `~/.config/app/nested/config.txt` and `explicit.txt`, `mise dot add --changed` copied back only `explicit.txt`. Now it copies back both. The walk respects the group's `exclude` patterns and entry overrides, and other directory copies (outside groups) are still skipped, as documented.

Known limitation: a group with `manifest = "git"` still errors when one of its files changed, the same as capturing that path explicitly.

Tested with a new case in `e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_groups`; `test_dotfiles_groups` and `test_dotfiles_files` pass.

Fixes #14424

body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/724
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`cargo deny check` now fails on rustls 0.23.45: its `Debug` impls for `Tls12ClientSessionValue` and `Tls13ClientSessionValue` print the TLS 1.2 master secret or TLS 1.3 resumption PSK (rustls/rustls#3299, fixed in 0.23.46). The advisory is not yet numbered (`RUSTSEC-0000-0000`). This makes `trusted / lint` red on every open PR.

mise does not format those values with `Debug`; the dependency path is the AWS SDK's HTTP client, so the exposure is limited to anything that would log a custom session store's values. The bump is a lockfile-only change (`cargo update -p rustls --precise 0.23.46`; it also moves rustls's `getrandom` dependency from 0.4.3 to 0.3.4), with no `Cargo.toml` change.

Validation: `cargo check --bin mise` builds. I could not run `cargo deny` locally (the shim has no installed version here), so CI's `trusted / lint` is the check.

title: feat(bootstrap): add --upgrade to upgrade packages and tools
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/723
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise bootstrap` installs missing packages and tools but never upgrades ones that are already installed, so keeping a machine current meant a separate task running `mise bootstrap packages upgrade` and `mise upgrade`, with ordering against hooks and services left to the user.

`mise bootstrap --upgrade` does both inside the existing phases:

```sh
mise bootstrap --upgrade
mise bootstrap --adopt owner/repo --upgrade
```

- **Packages phase** (and plugin packages): installs missing packages, then runs the same upgrade as `mise bootstrap packages upgrade`. Pins are respected as that command respects them.
- **Tools phase**: installs missing tools, then runs `mise upgrade` without `--bump`, so configured version ranges hold.
- Both run before the matching post hooks and before dependent services, with no second bootstrap pass.
- `--dry-run` previews both and `--skip` applies as before. Without the flag nothing changes.
- It does not update mise itself, repositories, or container images, and does not restart services. Use `mise self-update` for mise and `--update` for repositories.

Related discussion: https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14425

Self-update and re-exec from the discussion are left out on purpose: `mise self-update --yes && mise bootstrap --upgrade` covers it without re-exec'ing before any phase runs. An automatic setting like `self_update.auto` would be a separate change.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: 2.1.295.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes bootstrap orchestration and package/tool upgrade paths; behavior is covered by e2e tests but affects real package managers and tool installs on user machines.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds **`mise bootstrap --upgrade`** so one bootstrap run can install missing items and bump what is already there, without touching mise, repos, or images.
> 
> In the **packages** phase (system and plugin packages), bootstrap still installs missing packages, then runs the same upgrade path as `mise bootstrap packages upgrade`. Package driver logic gains **`install_previewed`** so a **`--dry-run`** install pass does not trigger misleading “not installed — run apply first” warnings on the follow-up upgrade preview.
> 
> In the **tools** phase, after `mise install`, bootstrap invokes a bare **`mise upgrade`** (no `--bump`) via **`Upgrade::new_bare`**, with internal **`installed_only`** / **`yes`** so dry-run does not double-preview missing tools and **`--yes`** propagates. **`--skip`** still limits which phases run.
> 
> Docs (CLI, packages guide, man, usage KDL) and a Linux e2e test with fake zypper/rpm exercise install-then-upgrade, dry-run, and skip behavior.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 3f584ec9af982b615a41d1017e2fb762

title: fix(lock): ignore the host's implicit compile default for other lock platforms
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/722
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes #14427

`mise lock --platform linux-x64,macos-arm64` run on Alpine (or NixOS) recorded Node source builds for every platform, because those distros default `all_compile` to true. A lockfile generated there made macOS users compile Node from source even though a precompiled binary exists.

The distro default describes the machine generating the lock, not the platforms it targets. The node lock resolver now ignores it for targets other than the host platform, and only explicit settings (`node.compile` or `all_compile = true`) apply to them.

Before, on Alpine:

```toml
[tools.node."platforms.macos-arm64"]
url = "https://nodejs.org/dist/v24.21.0/node-v24.21.0.tar.gz"
install = "source"
```

After, the macOS entry records the precompiled `node-v24.21.0-darwin-arm64.tar.gz` archive with no `install = "source"` marker. The host's own entry is unchanged, since the Alpine default really does apply there. Python already behaved this way via `target.is_current()`.

Erlang has the same host-default problem plus host-derived Linux OS lookups, so it is left for a separate change. Validated with a unit test for the explicit-only helper and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`. I did not reproduce on a real Alpine host.

Cross-platform targets now use explicitly configured compile values instead of inheriting distro-derived defaults, while current-platform targets continue to use the detected compile setting. This makes lock information better reflect the intended compile behavior for each target.

title: registry: install native-sdk from npm so the native command works
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/721
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise use native-sdk@latest` installed a binary that could not run the `native` command. Since 0.4.0, the GitHub release assets (`native-sdk-*`) are only the bare runtime. The CLI is distributed as the npm package `@native-sdk/cli`, which bundles the SDK files and exposes `native` (Node 24+ required).

The registry entry now installs from npm:

```toml
backends = ["npm:@native-sdk/cli"]
test = { cmd = "native --version", expected = "native {{version}}" }
```

After this, `mise use native-sdk@latest` puts `native` on PATH. The old GitHub-asset options (per-platform patterns, `version_prefix`) are removed because they only applied to the binary download.

Validated by installing `@native-sdk/cli@0.11.0` with npm: `native --version` prints `native 0.11.0`. I could not run the registry test through mise itself, because the local mise (2026.10.4) fails npm installs on its `aube` dependency.

Fixes #14423

-# are left to autodetection so that it can pick between the glibc
-# (native-sdk-linux-x64) and musl (native-sdk-linux-musl-x64) builds; a shared
-# asset_pattern would replace autodetection and pin every Linux host to glibc.
-bin = "native-sdk"
-# The repo also tags CEF bundles (e.g. cef-144.0.6+g5f7e671+chromium-144.0.7559.59)
-# in the same release stream; those are not the CLI, so list only `v`-prefixed tags.
-version_prefix = "v"
-
-# Windows assets use a `win32` infix rather than `windows`, so they are named
-# explicitly instead of relying on autodetection.
-[backends.options.platforms.windows-x64]
-asset_pattern = "native-sdk-win32-x64.exe"
-bin = "native-sdk.exe"
-
-[backends.options.platforms.windows-arm64]
-asset_pattern = "native-sdk-win32-arm64.exe"
