title: feat(env): add --paths to list the PATH entries mise manages
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/719
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise env --paths` prints the PATH entries mise manages, one per line, instead of the environment. These are the tool bin directories and `_.path` entries that sit ahead of the inherited PATH, in the order they take in the PATH `mise env` prints.

```console
$ mise env --paths
/home/me/.local/share/mise/installs/node/24.11.0/bin
/home/me/.cargo/bin
```

A directory the inherited PATH already had, like `~/.cargo/bin` from `rust`, is listed when mise moves it forward. Before this, a caller that wanted only mise's additions had to diff the flattened `PATH` from `mise env --json` against its own, and that diff cannot tell a moved entry from an inherited one. [mise-action](https://github.com/jdx/mise-action) does this to export mise's PATH changes through `GITHUB_PATH`, and on GitHub runners it leaves `rustup` resolving to the mise shim instead of `~/.cargo/bin/rustup` (see jdx/mise-action#684 for a workaround on that side).

The list comes from the same `PathEnv` that builds the printed PATH, so the two cannot disagree. It adds `PathEnv::managed_entries` and a `Toolset::managed_path_entries` that reuses the existing PATH construction. Nothing about the printed environment changes.

Tested with a unit test for the promoted-entry ordering and `e2e/cli/test_env_paths`, which puts a `_.path` directory behind another entry on the inherited PATH and checks `--paths` and `mise env --json` agree. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes. `mise run lint` fails locally on the known cargo-check manifest warning (unused `junction` in `mise-util`), not on this change.

title: fix(pipx): preserve uv graph locking during global upgrades
body:
## Problem

`mise lock` can record a uv dependency graph for a pipx tool, exactly like it can record an aube graph for npm:

```toml
["pipx:ruff"]
version = "0.16.7"
uv = { path = ".mise/locks/pipx-ruff/0.16.7", digest = "..." }
```

Any install that resolves the version *outside* the lockfile — `mise upgrade --bump`, or a hand-edited version pin — threw that graph away. The pipx backend only computed the lockfile revision when `tv.resolved_from_lockfile()`, so the upgrade rewrote the entry without `uv`, orphaning the sidecar and leaving a fresh checkout failing hard:

```console
$ mise lock --global pipx:ruff
$ mise upgrade --bump
$ mise install --locked
mise pipx:ruff has no uv dependency graph; run `mise lock`
```

## Before

```console
$ grep -A2 pipx:ruff mise.lock   # after upgrade --bump
version = "0.17.0"
# uv graph gone; sidecar for 0.17.0 never written
```

## After

```console
$ mise upgrade --bump
$ mise lock --global --sidecars --json | jq '.[0].sidecars'
[{
  "tool": "pipx:ruff",
  "version": "0.17.0",
  "graph": "uv",
  "exists": true
}]
$ mise install --locked   # OK on a fresh MISE_DATA_DIR
```

## How it works

Follows the npm backend's fix (#14419) (`entry.aube` -> `entry.uv`), with one tier generalized to also cover hand-edited pins:

- `uv_lockfile_version` — resolved-from-lockfile requests answer to their own entry, unchanged.
- Otherwise, `graph_lockfile_version` inherits the revision of any lockfile entry that records a uv graph.
- Otherwise, `replaced_entry_lockfile_version` — a bump or a hand-edited pin rewrites the global config's selector itself, so no entry matches the new request. The install instead inherits the revision of the global entry it replaces, but only when the backend has exactly one lockfile entry *total* and that entry carries a uv graph; with zero or several entries a graph-bearing sibling must never lend its graph to a version-only request, so ambiguous or version-only predecessors leave the entry version-only — no graph is invented, and graph creation for global tools is never implicit.
- Version-only entries stay version-only, as before.

## Testing

New e2e `test_pipx_uv_global_upgrade`, mirroring `test_npm_aube_global_upgrade`:

- lock a global pipx tool, upgrade with `--bump`, assert the uv sidecar moved to the new version via `mise lock --global --sidecars --json`, then replay byte-identical from a fresh data dir with `install --locked`;
- with lockfile creation off, a version-only entry stays version-only across `--bump` — an upgrade never invents a graph;
- with an explicit `mise lock` graph and lockfile creation off, a hand-edited pin still inherits the graph: install the edited pin, assert the sidecar moved, and replay byte-identical under `install --locked`.

The positive scenarios install the toolset before running `mise lock`, so generating the graph never depends on a host-installed uv binary (the isolated e2e PATH has none).

## Scope notes

- `graph_lockfile_version` is the near-verbat

title: fix(upgrade): leave lazy tools that are not installed to their first run
body:
A bare `mise install` skips lazy tools, and since #14368 `auto_update` skips any tool with nothing installed. A bare `mise upgrade` still counted a lazy tool with nothing installed as outdated and installed it, so one `mise up` installed every lazy tool a config declares.

Now a bare `mise upgrade` leaves a lazy tool alone while no version of it is installed. It doesn't install the tool, list it in the note about versions outside the configured range, or warn about releases `minimum_release_age` holds back. Naming the tool still installs it, as `mise install node` does. A lazy tool with any version installed upgrades as before, and a missing lazy tool that an upgraded tool depends on is installed with it.

```toml [/etc/mise/conf.d/defaults.toml]
[tools]
claude = { version = "latest", lazy = true }
codex = { version = "latest", lazy = true }
```

Before: on a machine where neither has run, `mise upgrade --dry-run` prints `Would install claude@…` and `Would install codex@…`, and `mise upgrade` installs both. After: neither is mentioned or installed.

Found while testing omacom/omarchy#9596 on a fresh install. Omarchy declares 20 default tools this way, and `omarchy update` runs `mise up`, so the first system update would have installed all of them.

## Changes

- `Upgrade::leave_missing_lazy` removes a lazy request from a bare upgrade when the tool has no installed version. It then puts back any that a remaining entry depends on, using the same dependency declarations as the install graph. The out-of-range note and the `minimum_release_age` warning skip the same requests.
- `install_dependency_declarations` and `InstallDependencyDeclarations::matches` are now `pub`, so the CLI can use them.
- `mise outdated` marks a lazy tool with nothing installed as `[MISSING] (lazy)`.
- A bare `mise upgrade --bump` and the out-of-range note skip these tools too. A backend that fails to resolve is not treated as waiting for a first run, so its error still surfaces.
- The lazy tools docs say what a bare `mise upgrade` does and what `mise outdated` shows.
- New `e2e/cli/test_upgrade_lazy_missing` covers:
  - a missing lazy tool in global and system config, `--global`, and a version range;
  - naming the tool;
  - an installed lazy tool upgrading, including when its request moves past what's installed;
  - a tool that depends on a missing lazy tool;
  - a missing non-lazy tool still installing;
  - the release-age warning, using `jq` because the dummy backend has no release dates.

  On mise 2026.10.9 the test fails at the first case.

`mise outdated` still lists these tools, since it reports state rather than acting on it, but now marks them so it is clear `mise upgrade` skips them:

```
claude  latest  [MISSING] (lazy)  …  /etc/mise/conf.d/defaults.toml
```

JSON output is unchanged.

## Testing

On Linux:
- These e2e tests pass: `test_upgrade_lazy_missing`, `test_upgrade`, `test_upgrade_global`, `test_upgrade_latest_stale`, `test_upgrade_bump_multiple`, `test_up

title: fix(npm): preserve graph locking during global upgrades
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/717
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Recreates #14366 by @altendky.

A globally installed npm tool locked with a dependency graph (`mise lock --global`) lost that graph on upgrade, and the next locked install failed:

```sh
mise lock --global npm:foo        # foo@1.0.0 with an aube graph in the global lockfile
mise upgrade                      # foo@2.0.0 recorded as a version-only entry
mise install --locked             # fails: no dependency graph for npm:foo
```

Upgrades, including `mise upgrade --bump` on exact pins, now regenerate the graph for the new version in the existing global lockfile, at the same lockfile revision. Everything else stays as before:

- global graph creation remains explicit; a global tool without a graph stays version-only
- an exact pin without `--bump` keeps its existing graph and lockfile untouched
- a graph belonging to another global tool, or a temporary CLI request with no owner, never opts a request into graph installs

## How it works

An upgrade resolves its new version outside the lockfile, so the npm backend skipped the lock revision lookup that decides whether a graph is required. It now looks the revision up by selector, which covers bare and named upgrades. `--bump` rewrites the selector (`1.0.0` to `2.0.0`) before installing, so nothing in the lockfile matches it; there the backend recovers the revision from the one request in the owning global config with the same owner, backend and options, and gives up (version-only) if there is not exactly one.

Compared with #14366, this drops the extra work on the install-check path when the lockfile has no entry for the tool, documents the bump rule, and trims the e2e test to the scenarios that cover distinct behavior.

## Testing

`e2e/backend/test_npm_aube_global_upgrade` covers lock revisions 2 and 3, bare upgrades, reuse of a newer version-only install, `--bump` with aliases, environment overrides and unset automatic lock generation, plus the unlocked, unrelated-graph, exact-pin, and unowned-request boundaries. Each upgraded graph is checked for digest and dependencies, then replayed with `install --locked` into fresh data. With the whole fix disabled the test fails; with only the `--bump` recovery disabled, the non-bump scenarios pass and `bump-v2` fails.

+# any install: these commands must never touch the user's global installation.
+for path in "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR" "$MISE_DATA_DIR" "$MISE_CACHE_DIR" "$MISE_STATE_DIR"; do
+  [[ $path == "$HOME/"* ]] || fail "mise state is outside the isolated home: $path"
+done
+base_config="$MISE_CONFIG_DIR"
+base_cache="$MISE_CACHE_DIR"
+base_data="$MISE_DATA_DIR"

+# Keep a runtime on the isolated PATH when replaying into fresh mise data.
+ln -s "$(mise where node@20.11.1)/bin/node" "$HOME/bin/node"
+
+write_global_config() {
+  cat >"$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml" <<EOF

+${lockfile_setting:-lockfile = true}
+locked = true
+[tools]
+"${config_tool:-npm:mise-upgrade-fixture}" = { version = "$1", allow_low_downloads = true }

+}
+
+check_graph() {
+  mise -C "$HOME" lock --global --sidecars --json >"$PWD/sidecars.json"
+  python3 - "$PWD/sidecars.json" "$HOME" "$1" "${2:-$config_tool}" <<'PY'

+import json
+import sys
+from pathlib import Path
+listing, = json.loads(Path(sys.argv[1]).read_text())
+entry, = [item for item in listing['sidecars'] if item['tool'] == sys.argv[4]]
+version = sys.argv[3]
+assert entry['version'] == version, entry
+assert entry['graph'] == 'aube' and entry['exists'], entry
+sidecar = Path(sys.argv[2]) / entry['path']
+text = (sidecar / 'aube-lock.yaml').read_text()
+assert entry['digest'] == 'sha256:' + hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest()
+assert f'mise-upgrade-fixture@{version}' in text, text
+assert f'mise-upgrade-dep@{version}' in text, text
+assert json.loads((sidecar / 'package.json').read_text())['dependencies']['mise-upgrade-fixture'] == version
+PY
+}
+
+# Cover both lock revisions, bare and named upgrades, and reuse of a newer
+# version-only installation, including exact pins changed by --bump. Graph
+# preparation must precede the installed check.
+for scenario in bare-v3 bare-v2 preinstalled bump-v2 bump-global-env bump-aliases bump-explicit-default; do
+  export MISE_CONFIG_DIR="$base_config/$scenario"
+  export MISE_CACHE_DIR="$base_cache/$scenario"
+  mkdir -p "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR"
+  rm -rf "$MISE_DATA_DIR/installs/npm-mise-upgrade-fixture" "$MISE_DATA_DIR/installs/fixture"
+  echo 1.0.0 >"$FAKE_NPM_REGISTRY_DIR/latest"

+  config_tool=npm:mise-upgrade-fixture
+  lockfile_setting='lockfile = true'
+  [[ $scenario == bump-* ]] && selector=1.0.0

+  fi
+  if [[ $config_tool == fixture ]]; then
+    cat >>"$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml" <<'EOF'
+[tool_alias]
+fixture = "npm:mise-upgrade-fixture"
+EOF
+    [[ $scenario == bump-aliases ]] && echo 'fixture-other = "npm:mise-upgrade-fixture"' >>"$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml"
+  fi
+  if [[ $scenario == bump-aliases ]]; then
+    # Different selectors keep both aliases distinct during lock generation.
+    mise -C "$HOME" lock --global fixture fixture-other
+  else
+    mise -C "$HOME" lock --global "$config_tool"
+  fi
+  if [[ $scenario == bare-v2 || $scenario == bump-v2 ]]; then
+    sed -i.bak 's/lockfile_version = 3/lockfile_version = 2/' "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/mise.lock"
+  fi
+  check_graph 1.0.0
+  if [[ $scenario == bump-aliases ]]; then
+    check_graph 2.0.0 fixture-other
+    cp "$PWD/sidecars.json" "$PWD/aliases-before.json"
+  fi
+  mise -C "$HOME" install --locked
+  assert "mise -C '$HOME' exec -- mise-upgrade-fixture" "1.0.0:1.0.0"
+  cp -R "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR" "$PWD/$scenario-before"
+
+  if [[ $scenario == preinstalled ]]; then
+    # A global install without its explicit lock must stay version-only.
+    mv "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/mise.lock" "$PWD/saved.lock"
+    write_global_config 2.0.0
+    MISE_LOCKED=0 mise -C "$HOME" install
+    assert_succeed "test -d '$MISE_DATA_DIR/installs/npm-mise-upgrade-fixture/2.0.0'"
+    write_global_config "$selector"
+    mv "$PWD/saved.lock" "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/mise.lock"
+  fi
+
+  echo 2.0.0 >"$FAKE_NPM_REGISTRY_DIR/latest"
+  export MISE_CACHE_DIR="$base_cache/$scenario-upgrade"
+  upgrade_args=()
+  [[ $scenario == bump-* ]] && upgrade_args+=(--bump)
+  if [[ $scenario == bump-global-env ]]; then
+    MISE_FIXTURE_VERSION=1.0.0 mise -C "$HOME" --yes upgrade --global --bump
+  elif [[ $scenario == bump-explicit-default ]]; then
+    # Allow the new CLI selector through initial resolution; the existing
+    # global graph must still be maintained, without automatic lock creation.

+  else
+    mise -C "$HOME" --yes upgrade ${upgrade_args[@]+"${upgrade_args[@]}"}
+  fi
+  cp -R "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR" "$PWD/$scenario-after"

+  if [[ $scenario == bump-aliases ]]; then
+    check_graph 2.0.0 fixture-other
+    python3 - "$PWD/aliases-before.json" "$PWD/sidecars.json" <<'PY'
+import json
+import sys
+from pathlib import Path
+def other(path):
+    listing, = json.loads(Path(path).read_text())
+    entry, = [item for item in listing['sidecars'] if item['tool'] == 'fixture-other']
+    return entry
+assert other(sys.argv[1]) == other(sys.argv[2])
+PY
+  fi
+  if [[ $scenario == bump-* ]]; then
+    assert_contains "cat '$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml'" 'version = "2.0.0"'
+    if [[ $scenario == bump-aliases ]]; then
+      assert_contains "cat '$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml'" 'fixture = { version = "2.0.0"'
+    fi
+  fi
+  assert_contains "mise -C '$HOME' where '$config_tool'" '/2.0.0~aube~'

+  cp "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/mise.lock" "$PWD/replay.lock"
+  export MISE_DATA_DIR="$HOME/$scenario-replay-data"

+  assert_succeed "cmp '$PWD/replay.lock' '$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/mise.lock'"
+  export MISE_DATA_DIR="$base_data"
+done
+
+# Enabling lockfiles globally still does not opt ordinary global requests into
+# creating a lockfile, sidecars, or graph-specific installations.
+export MISE_CONFIG_DIR="$base_config/unlocked"
+export MISE_CACHE_DIR="$base_cache/unlocked"
+mkdir -p "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR"
+rm -rf "$MISE_DATA_DIR/installs/npm-mise-upgrade-fixture"

+lockfile_setting='lockfile = true'

+assert_succeed "test -d '$MISE_DATA_DIR/installs/npm-mise-upgrade-fixture/1.0.0'"
+echo 2.0.0 >"$FAKE_NPM_REGISTRY_DIR/latest"
+export MISE_CACHE_DIR="$base_cache/unlocked-upgrade"

+assert_succeed "test -d '$MISE_DATA_DIR/installs/npm-mise-upgrade-fixture/2.0.0'"
+assert_succeed "test ! -e '$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/mise.lock'"
+assert_succeed "test ! -e '$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/locks' && test ! -e '$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/.mise'"
+
+# Bumping an exact global request without a lock also stays version-only,
+# including when the newer version already exists.
+write_global_config 1.0.0
+MISE_LOCKED=0 mise -C "$HOME" --yes upgrade --bump
+assert_contains "cat '$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml'" 'version = "2.0.0"'
+assert_succeed "test ! -e '$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/mise.lock'"
+assert_fail "find '$MISE_DATA_DIR/installs/npm-mise-upgrade-fixture' -maxdepth 1 -name '*~aube~*' | grep -q ."
+
+# A graph for another global tool does not opt this request into graph installs.
+export MISE_CONFIG_DIR="$base_config/unrelated"
+export MISE_CACHE_DIR="$base_cache/unrelated"
+mkdir -p "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR"
+write_global_config 1.0.0

title: fix(npm): reinstall aube trees that lost their dependency links on Windows
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/716
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

On Windows CI, an npm tool installed by mise's embedded aube can fail at run time with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` for one of its own dependencies (#14417: `cspell` cannot find `picomatch`), even though `mise install --locked` reports `already installed`.

The reported run restores `installs/` from an `actions/cache` tar. Aube links each package's dependencies as NTFS junctions, and those do not survive the tar round trip. The package directories come back but their dependency links are gone. mise's health check only looked at the top level of `node_modules/.mise`, so it called the tree healthy.

## Fix

On Windows, the health check now also verifies that each virtual-store package has its non-optional `dependencies` present, either beside it or bundled inside it. A tree missing links is treated as not installed, so `mise install` reinstalls it from the lockfile.

The check is Windows-only so unix hook-env cost is unchanged. I could not run it on Windows here; the unit test covers the detection logic on Linux. The tar-drops-junctions cause is inferred from the cache-restore step in the reported run, not reproduced.

Fixes #14417

title: security(task): require trust before rendering a remote task file
body:
Listing the tasks of a directory you have not trusted could run a command from a remote task file. A `mise.toml` that holds only `[tasks]` loads without trust, so this is enough:

```toml
# mise.toml in a freshly cloned, untrusted repository
[tasks.build]
file = "https://example.com/build.sh"
```

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#MISE description="{{ exec(command='touch /tmp/PWNED') }}Build"
```

`mise tasks ls`, `mise tasks info build` and `mise tasks validate` downloaded `build.sh` and rendered its `#MISE` headers, so `exec()` ran with no trust prompt. The same template written in `mise.toml` itself, or in a local task file such as `mise-tasks/build.sh`, is already refused until the config is trusted.

A remote task file now follows the rule for local task includes. When its `#MISE` headers contain template syntax, the config that names it must be trusted before they render. In an untrusted directory, mise asks to trust it, or fails with `Config files in … are not trusted` when it cannot ask, and nothing renders. Only the headers are checked, because only they render: braces elsewhere in the script, such as `docker ps --format '{{.Names}}'`, need no trust. They are read the same way when a `git::` file is named `*.toml`. A remote file with no template in its headers still lists without trust, and a trusted config renders as before. `mise run` keeps trusting the config it runs, as it does for local tasks. Safe mode still waives trust, since `exec()` and `read_file()` are disabled there.

#12202 (and #11113 before it) by @risu729 reported this and proposed a wider rework of remote task metadata, which pr-closer closed. This is a narrower fix built on main's existing trust check for task includes. They are credited as co-author.

## Validation

- New `e2e/tasks/test_task_remote_http_trust`, with the remote files served from a local HTTP server:
  - In an untrusted directory, `mise tasks ls`, `mise tasks info` and `mise tasks validate` each fail with `not trusted`, and the `exec()` marker file is not created.
  - A remote file whose headers have no template still lists without trust, with `{{.Names}}` in its script body.
  - With the config trusted, a templated remote file renders.
- Unit test `test_header_checks_ignore_the_file_name`: an escaped template in the header of a file named `evil.toml` needs trust (read as a TOML document, the header is a comment), and a template in the script body does not.
- On Linux, in a `rust:1` container, the test passes with this branch's build. Run against the released 2026.10.8, the same test fails with `remote task template executed by untrusted 'mise tasks ls'`.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes.

title: perf(dotfiles): read history objects and refs through gix
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/715
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

After #14407, `mise dot pull` and `mise dot sync` no longer start git processes in proportion to the length of the history. They still started a fixed few hundred per run, though, mostly to read objects and refs. This change reads those through gix in-process.

Measured with a debug build: two machines share one origin, and machine B syncs and then pulls one incoming change. A `git` wrapper on `PATH` counts processes.

| command | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `mise dot sync` | 177 git processes | 67 |
| `mise dot pull --yes` | 460 git processes | 183 |

The counts are the same with a 2,000-commit history.

**What moved to gix.** These reads used to run one git command each:
- `ref_oid` (`rev-parse --verify`) for full ref names and `HEAD`;
- `object_at` (`ls-tree -z`), `cat_object` and `cat_object_bounded` (`cat-file -s` plus `cat-file blob`) for full object ids;
- `ls_tree` (`ls-tree -r -l`).

Any other revision syntax, such as `<oid>^{commit}`, still goes through git, so gix's `revision` feature isn't needed. Writes (`hash-object`, `update-index`, `write-tree`, `commit-tree`) and `merge-base` stay on git.

**Behavior is unchanged.** Results match git byte for byte:
- `object_at` prints modes as six octal digits, so a tree is `040000` as with `ls-tree`. Callers compare against that.
- `ls_tree` lists entries in `ls-tree -r` order, which is bytewise order of the full path.
- A tree or missing object is still refused as a blob.

A new unit test, `gix_reads_match_git`, checks each read against the git command it replaces:
- paths that are files, directories, or missing;
- commit, tree, blob and missing-object inputs;
- existing and missing refs;
- order-sensitive names such as `a-b`, `a.c`, `a/x` and `ab/y`;
- the size bound.

### Validation

The history unit tests pass, and so do all 101 dotfiles and history e2e tests.

> 
> **Overview**
> **Dotfiles history reads** now use in-process **gix** when the input is a full hex object id or a full ref name (`HEAD`, `refs/...`), instead of spawning one Git plumbing command per call.
> 
> `ref_oid`, `ls_tree`, `object_at`, `cat_object`, and `cat_object_bounded` each take a fast path: `object_id` detects raw OIDs; refs are resolved with symbolic-ref following (capped at five levels). Blob reads go through `gix_blob`, which enforces blob kind and size limits like `cat-file`. Revision expressions and non-hex specs still use Git.

title: fix(dotfiles): plan a stale pull again instead of pausing sharing
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/714
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

On a machine running the history watcher, a pull's plan can go stale while the pull is planning: another operation saves first. Every such case was recorded as a failed application, which pauses sharing:

```
could not apply incoming changes: local files were saved after enrollment planning; retry pull
application failed (…); previous files restored. Sharing is paused.
```

The watcher then stopped applying incoming changes altogether until someone ran `mise dot pull` by hand, even though nothing had been written and nothing needed fixing. This was reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14404.

**Fix.** Three checks find a stale plan before the first write:
- local saved history changed since planning;
- local files were saved after enrollment planning;
- a file changed in the complete repository merge.

These now fail only that attempt, and the next attempt plans again. Sharing is no longer paused, and the watcher keeps applying on its next pass. A manual `mise dot pull` still reports the error and can simply be rerun. Any failure after a write has started is still recorded and still pauses sharing, as before.

### Validation

A new e2e test, `test_dotfiles_pull_stale_plan`, sets up a pending incoming change on a second machine. A running `mise dot capture` saves an edit there while `mise dot pull --yes` waits for it, so the pull reports its plan as stale. Then `mise dot watch --once` must apply the change. On `main` the watcher stays paused and the file keeps its old version; with this change it applies. The history unit tests and 19 dotfiles sync, watch, adopt and conflict e2e tests pass.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: 2.1.295.*

title: feat(github): keep the OAuth refresh token behind Touch ID in the Secure Enclave
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/713
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes #14270

## What this does for users

On a Mac with Touch ID, the native GitHub OAuth refresh token (valid six months, rotating) no longer has to sit in plaintext in `github-oauth-tokens.toml`:

```toml [~/.config/mise/config.toml]
[settings.github]
oauth_cache_secure_enclave = true
```

The refresh token is sealed to the Secure Enclave and kept in `github-oauth-tokens.sealed`; the cache file holds only the 8-hour access token. Unsealing needs a fingerprint, about once per refresh and never on other invocations. A cancelled or failed prompt skips the refresh and keeps the cached token, and builds without the signed helper (Homebrew, source) or Macs without Touch ID warn and keep the token in the cache file. An existing plaintext cache migrates at the next refresh.

## How

- `src/enclave/macos.swift` is a small helper embedded in mise and built by `build.rs`, signed with the same Developer ID identity as the notification helper. `seal` / `unseal` take the token on stdin, never argv.
- The spike for the issue's open question found that no entitlement or provisioning profile is needed if the enclave key is not stored in the keychain: the helper uses CryptoKit's `SecureEnclave.P256` and keeps the key's opaque `dataRepresentation` blob in the sealed file. Keychain-stored enclave keys fail (`-34018`) or get the process killed without a profile. This is why the helper is Swift rather than Objective-C; a build without `swiftc` just reports the helper as unavailable.
- `oauth.rs` gets a `Store` enum (external commands or enclave) behind the existing refresh-token store logic, so the failure semantics from #14360 apply unchanged.

## Other platforms

Not native code, on purpose: `oauth_cache_get` / `oauth_cache_set` (#14360) already cover Linux, WSL and Windows with `pass`, `secret-tool`, 1Password, `cmdkey` and similar, and the docs now say so. Native Credential Manager, Secret Service or TPM backends can follow if there is demand.

## Testing

Verified with a Developer ID signed build against the mock OAuth server: authorize seals, a forced refresh prompts Touch ID, the rotated token is re-sealed, and the cache file never contains `ghr-`. Unsigned builds fall back with a warning (new e2e `test_token_github_oauth_enclave`).

title: fix(dotfiles): stop holding files that already have the incoming version
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/711
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Two `mise dot pull` problems reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14404. Together they left sharing paused with no command that would unpause it.

**A file that already holds the incoming version is no longer held as an unsaved edit.** An apply interrupted after it wrote a file, but before it recorded that write, leaves the file holding the incoming version, while the saved version is still the old one. mise held that file as an unsaved edit and paused sharing for the whole setup:

```
Error: sync paused: resolve all 1 conflict(s) before sharing resumes; …
```

Nobody had edited anything, and writing the incoming version over itself loses nothing. Until now, a live file was accepted as already holding the incoming version only during a fresh adoption. Now that holds everywhere:
- the conflict check, for autosaved files;
- the unsaved-edit set, for manual-save files;
- the hold check before writing, which outside an adoption also requires the file mode to match.

The same goes for the file's mode. A mode the incoming write would set anyway isn't an edit, but a mode matching neither the saved nor the incoming version still conflicts. The protective checkpoint records that mode in the manifest, so the check that nothing else was saved since planning now restores the planned paths' modes before it compares trees.

**Naming a path that an earlier pull already decided is no longer an error.** Taking the repository's version records a choice that exempts the path from the conflict check. If that pull then stopped for another reason, such as a second conflict, repeating the same command failed:

```
$ mise dot pull --yes --take-remote ~/.one   # records the choice; ~/.two still conflicts
$ mise dot pull --yes --take-remote ~/.one
Error: ~/.one is not a conflict
```

A path whose recorded choice matches the one named is now accepted.

### Validation

A new e2e test, `test_dotfiles_pull_decided_paths`, covers both fixes:
- An autosaved file, a manual-save file, and a file whose content and mode (`600`) both changed each already hold the incoming version without having saved it. The pull applies all three. It fails on `main` with the files held.
- Two conflicting files are resolved one `--take-remote` at a time, naming the first path twice.

The history unit tests and 20 dotfiles sync, adopt, conflict, permissions and bootstrap e2e tests pass.

The journal doesn't record what each write intended, so recovery can't tell its own write from a user edit. title: fix(dotfiles): recover an interrupted operation before a pull plans
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/710
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

After a `mise dot pull` (or any other history operation) was interrupted, the next `mise dot pull --yes` failed straight away:

```
mise WARN  history: recovering interrupted operation 01a13631-…
Error: local saved history changed since planning; nothing was applied; run pull again
```

Running pull again then worked, but only if nothing interrupted that run as well. In https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14404, pulls were slow enough that the user kept interrupting them. Every retry then failed this way, and each one left more commits behind.

**Cause.** A pull plans against the current local history head. It then starts its own operation, and taking the operation lock recovers any operation that died, recording its outcome as a commit. That commit landed after the plan was made. The pull's check that saved history had not changed since planning saw it as a change, and refused.

**Fix.** A pull now recovers dead operations before it plans, so the recovery commit is part of what it plans against. Nothing else changes when there's nothing to recover or another process holds the lock. Starting the operation still waits for or reports a held lock as before.

A new e2e test, `test_dotfiles_pull_after_interrupted_operation`, has one incoming change pending on a second machine. It SIGKILLs a running `mise dot capture -- sleep 60` there, then runs `mise dot pull --yes`. The test fails on `main` with the error above and passes with this change. The history unit tests and the dotfiles sync, auto-sync, take-remote and conflict e2e tests also pass.

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# A pull after an interrupted operation recovers it before planning. Recovery
+# records the dead operation as a commit; when that happened after planning,
+# the pull read it as saved history changing under its plan and refused, so a
+# pull that followed an interrupted one could never succeed.
+require_cmd git
+export MISE_HISTORY_NOTIFY=false
+# the assertions read info-level messages, whatever level the runner forwards
+export MISE_LOG_LEVEL=info
+origin="$PWD/interrupted-origin.git"
+git init -q --bare -b main "$origin"
+echo v1 >~/.native
+assert_succeed "mise dot track ~/.native"
+assert_succeed "mise dot track ~/.config/mise/config.toml --yes"
+assert_succeed "mise dot origin set file://$origin --sync manual --yes"
+assert_succeed "mise dot sync"
+
+second="$(dirname "$HOME")/second"
+mkdir -p "$second"
+export second
+b() {
+  (
+    cd "$second" || exit
+    env HOME="$second" XDG_CONFIG_HOME="$second/.config" MISE_CONFIG_DIR="$second/.config/mise" \
+      MISE_STATE_DIR="$second/.local/state/mise" MISE_DATA_DIR="$second/.local/share/mise" \
+      MISE_CACHE_DIR="$second/.cache/mise" MISE_TRUSTED_CONFIG_PATHS="$second" mise "$@"
+  )
+}
+export -f b
+assert_succeed "b bootstrap --adopt file://$origin --yes"
+echo v2 >~/.native
+assert_succeed "mise dot save"
+assert_succeed "mise dot sync"
+assert_contains "b dot sync 2>&1" "1 incoming change(s) pending"
+
+# kill an operation on the second machine while its command runs, leaving its
+# record; the command marks when it started, so no Git write is in flight
+ready="$PWD/ready"
+b dot capture -- sh -c "touch $ready; sleep 60" >/dev/null 2>&1 &
+pid=$!
+for _ in $(seq 300); do
+  [ -e "$ready" ] && break
+  sleep 0.1
+done
+assert_succeed "test -e $ready"
+pending="$second/.local/state/mise/history/index/pending"
+# SIGKILL every process under the job, deepest first, so nothing cleans up
+descendants() {
+  local child
+  for child in $(pgrep -P "$1"); do
+    descendants "$child"
+    echo "$child"
+  done
+}
+victims=()
+while read -r victim; do
+  victims+=("$victim")
+done < <(descendants "$pid")
+kill -KILL "${victims[@]}" "$pid" 2>/dev/null || true
+wait "$pid" 2>/dev/null || true
+assert_succeed "test -n \"\$(ls -A $pending)\""

title: fix(install): retain saved packslip shared-workflow pins
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/709
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Reinstalling a Packslip tool signed by a shared reusable workflow now keeps working with the trust record from its first successful install. In mise v2026.10.9, installing `packslip:github.com/suzuki-shunsuke/mkghtag@0.1.14-10` with its untouched saved pin instead rejected the unchanged signer as “not a workflow of” the tool's repository and suggested forgetting the pin.

The stored-pin recheck now uses Packslip's existing certificate-source repository check, then applies the existing signing-workflow continuity check. Unchanged shared signers keep their pins across reinstall and release refs. A changed shared signer repository, workflow path, source repository ID, or issuer is still refused; missing source evidence retains the strict fallback. This restores the existing trust model without resetting accepted trust or changing verification options.

Validation runs in a disposable Rust container: the regression tests fail before the fix and all 15 saved-pin tests and 13 related forge tests pass afterward. An all-feature build successfully reinstalls the authentic `mkghtag@0.1.14-10` release using its untouched saved pin; changed signer, changed workflow, wrong repository ID, and wrong explicit workflow are all refused, leaving pin-file bytes unchanged. Formatting and full-workspace, all-feature/all-target Clippy with warnings denied pass. The live check covers same-release reinstall; release-ref updates are covered by the unit regression.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: unavailable; version: unavailable.*

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Touches packslip trust pinning and forge verification on install; behavior change is narrow but security-relevant for who counts as the same release source.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes reinstalls failing when a packslip tool was first trusted under a **shared reusable workflow** signer: stored-pin recheck no longer treats the signing workflow as if it had to live in the tool repository.
> 
> **`check_against`** now calls **`forge::check_source`** (certificate source repository vs pinned forge ID) instead of **`forge::check`**, while the existing **signer continuity** path (`continues_signer` / same workflow path) still runs afterward. Same shared workflow and repository ID across new tags should pass without rewriting **`pins.toml`**.
> 
> Adds regression tests for shared-workflow pins: accept on reinstall/update, refuse signer/path/ID changes and wrong issuer, and reject missing source evidence.

title: perf(dotfiles): stop pull from walking history one git process per commit
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/708
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

On a long dotfiles history, `mise dot pull` could run for minutes with no output and look hung. Reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14404: about 6.5 minutes on 24,850 commits.

The time went to work that grew with the length of the whole history, not with the incoming change:

- **Manifest reads.** Reading the enrollment manifest started three git processes (`ls-tree`, `cat-file -s`, `cat-file blob`) for every commit, even though a history holds only a handful of distinct manifests.
- **Plaintext audit.** The audit before publishing ran one `git ls-tree -r` per commit, and a pull audits the whole ancestry again in each new process.
- **Index rebuild.** The checkpoint index rebuild wrote two cache files for each newly fetched commit and fsynced each one: about 18 ms per file on ext4, against 1.5 ms to read the commit.

After this change:

- Manifests and protected paths are read in-process through gix. Each distinct manifest blob, and each protected subtree, is read once.
- The rebuild renames each cache file into place whole, without a per-file fsync. A crash still never leaves a torn file. Before writing the index that names those files, it makes the batch durable with one `syncfs`. Only Linux has `syncfs`, so other platforms keep syncing each file as before.

### Measured

Measured with a debug build on ext4. Two machines share one origin with an encrypted file and a plain file. The history is padded with N empty commits that cycle through three manifest blobs. Machine B then runs `mise dot sync` and times `mise dot pull --yes` for one incoming change. A `git` wrapper on `PATH` counts processes.

| history | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 2,000 commits | 137 s, 16,504 git processes | 5.9 s, 460 git processes |
| 20,000 commits | not run (scales to ~20 min) | 44 s, 460 git processes |

The git process count no longer depends on the length of the history. Most of the remaining time is the one-time read of each newly fetched commit's metadata, which is much faster in a release build.

### Not in this PR

The discussion also reports two other problems. An interrupted pull leaves a pause that recovery reports as "local saved history changed since planning". And `--take-remote <path>` refuses a path the pause message counts as a conflict. Both need their own investigation and are not changed here.

title: fix(dotfiles): stop machines swapping ciphertext for an unchanged encrypted file
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/706
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

With `history.sync = "sync"`, machines sharing an origin and tracking an encrypted file (`encrypt = true`) could keep `mise dot watch` busy forever, publishing three commits per cycle (`before apply`, `merge origin dotfiles`, `apply: applied 0 incoming change(s)`) with no real edits. On one fleet this added about 24,000 commits to the shared branch. Reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14251.

**Trigger.** age encryption is randomized, so two machines can hold different ciphertext for the same plaintext. Machines that joined on 2026.10.8 or earlier, before #14300, already do. mise caches each machine's own ciphertext, and when the plaintext was unchanged, capture reused that cached ciphertext even after a merge had brought in the other machine's. So each machine swapped its own ciphertext back in, the other machine saw that as an incoming change and swapped it back again, and the loop never ended. Upgrading to a build with #14300 did not stop a loop that had already started.

**Fix.** When the cached ciphertext differs from what history already holds, capture now keeps the ciphertext in history if it decrypts to the same content, mode and recipients. It re-encrypts only when the content or recipients actually changed. Machines that have already diverged settle after one more sync cycle, with no manual steps.

### Example

Two machines on one origin, one encrypted tracked file, no edits, each stepped with `mise dot watch --once` (the reporter's script, with machine B joining on 2026.10.8 first):

```
# before
round 1: origin commits 5
round 2: origin commits 8
round 3: origin commits 8
round 4: origin commits 11
# after
round 1: origin commits 5
round 2: origin commits 8
round 3: origin commits 8
round 4: origin commits 8
round 5: origin commits 8
```

### Validation

- New e2e test `cli/test_dotfiles_sync_encrypted_converge`: an edit followed by a revert gives the second machine its own ciphertext for the same content. After both machines sync, origin keeps one ciphertext and further save/sync rounds publish nothing. On `origin/main` the test fails because the first machine puts its own ciphertext back.
- Existing encryption e2e tests pass: `adopt_encrypted_reuse`, `encrypted_capture`, `encrypted_diff`, `save_re_encrypt`, `sync_files_encrypted`, `profile_variant_encrypted`, `sync_stable`.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes.

This does not change two other points from the discussion: an apply that applies nothing still records one `before apply` commit and one `apply` commit, and an apply commit can carry local edits under the `applied 0` label. Both stop repeating once the ciphertext settles.

title: feat(bootstrap): add snap package manager
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/705
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Linux machines that get some tools from the Snap Store can now declare those snaps in `[bootstrap.packages]` alongside apt, flatpak, and the other host package managers, instead of scripting `snap install` in a task.

```toml
[bootstrap.packages]
"snap:jq" = "latest"
"snap:code" = { classic = true }
"snap:node" = { channel = "22/stable", classic = true }
"snap:hello-world" = { state = "absent" }
```

`mise bootstrap packages apply` installs missing snaps and removes absent ones. Snaps without options share one `snap install`; entries with `channel` or `classic` get their own command, because snap accepts those flags for one snap at a time. Commands run through sudo when mise is not root, as for apt.

**Channel drift.** With a `channel`, a snap that tracks a different one shows in `status` as `version mismatch`, for example `20.18.0 from 20/stable`. `apply` moves it with `snap refresh --channel=22/stable`. A bare risk (`edge`) means `latest/edge` and a bare track (`22`) means `22/stable`, matching how `snap list` prints the tracked channel. Without a `channel`, any tracked channel satisfies the entry. `snap list` prints a branch as `…`, so a branch channel such as `22/edge/fix-1` is checked at the track/risk level only.

**Classic confinement** is opt-in per entry with `classic = true`. Without it, snap refuses a classic snap with its own error.

**Version pins and refreshes.** snapd installs a channel's current revision and refreshes in the background, so mise cannot install or hold a version. As with flatpak, a pinned entry shows as `version mismatch` and `apply`/`upgrade` skip it with a warning. `upgrade` runs `snap refresh` now, keeping declared channels. The docs point to `snap refresh --hold` for holding a snap.

Other details:

- Available on Linux when `snap` is on `PATH`; elsewhere entries show as skipped. When snapd is not running, `status` and `apply` fail with snap's error instead of treating every snap as missing.
- Snap names are checked against the store's naming rules (which also stops a name from reaching `snap` as a flag). A malformed `channel`, including a misspelled risk such as `latest/stabel`, skips the entry with a warning rather than installing from the default channel.
- `mise bootstrap packages use snap:<name>` installs with the options of the entry it writes: an existing table entry in the target file keeps its `channel` and `classic`, and a new entry is a plain `"latest"` with none. Options declared in other config files don't apply, so `use --global` never picks up a project's channel.
- `channel` and `classic` on another manager's entry warn and are ignored, like `adopt` and `appdir`.
- `apply --update` has no effect for snap.

New page: `docs/bootstrap/packages/snap.md`. The JSON schema gains `channel` and `classic`.

## Testing

- Unit tests for `snap list` parsing, channel normalization, drift detection, comman

title: feat(bootstrap): enable COPR repositories with [bootstrap.dnf.repos]
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/704
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Packages such as Ghostty ship on Fedora from a [COPR](https://copr.fedorainfracloud.org/), and until now a bootstrap could only enable one from a `pre-packages` hook that runs `sudo dnf copr enable -y …`. Fixes #14372.

You can now declare COPRs next to the packages that come from them:

```toml
[bootstrap.dnf.repos]
ghostty = { copr = "scottames/ghostty" }
caddy = { copr = "@caddy/caddy" }

[bootstrap.packages]
"dnf:ghostty" = "latest"
"dnf:caddy" = "latest"
```

```console
$ mise bootstrap packages apply --dry-run
fetch the fedora-42 repo file for copr:scottames/ghostty into /etc/yum.repos.d/_copr:copr.fedorainfracloud.org:scottames:ghostty.repo
...
dnf install -y ghostty caddy
```

## Behavior

- **Same file as `dnf copr enable`.** mise downloads the repo file COPR publishes for this release and writes it unchanged to `/etc/yum.repos.d/_copr:copr.fedorainfracloud.org:<owner>:<project>.repo` (`group_<name>` for a group). A COPR already enabled with the plugin counts as enabled, and `dnf copr list`, `disable`, and `remove` manage the ones mise enabled. The copr plugin does not need to be installed, so this also works on Fedora Atomic hosts that use `system_packages.ostree = "layer"`.
- **Chroot.** Picked from `/etc/os-release` the way the copr plugin picks it, reading the base release from `PLATFORM_ID` when it is set: `fedora-<version>` on Fedora and derivatives such as Bazzite, `fedora-rawhide` on Rawhide, `epel-<major>` on RHEL, CentOS Stream, Rocky, Alma, Oracle Linux, and Alibaba Cloud Linux, and `amazonlinux-<version>` on Amazon Linux. If the project has no build for this release, the error lists the chroots it does build for.
- **When it runs.** Like `[bootstrap.apt.sources]`, the repositories are applied when the dnf manager runs, before its packages are installed: during `mise bootstrap`, `bootstrap packages apply`/`upgrade`, and `packages use dnf:…`. Dry runs print the plan and fetch nothing. mise only downloads the file when it is missing or disabled, so a run where everything is already enabled makes no network requests. dnf imports the COPR's signing key on the first install, as it does after `dnf copr enable`.
- **Confirmation and failures.** Without `--yes` on a terminal, mise asks once before enabling any COPR. A COPR that cannot be enabled is reported with the run's other failures, and the remaining repositories and packages still apply. On an ostree host that does not layer packages, nothing is enabled.
- **Removal.** mise does not disable or remove repositories. `mise bootstrap unapply` names the leftover file.
- **Invalid entries.** Unknown fields, bad names, and malformed projects warn, and that entry is skipped.

Only COPR is supported for now. The entry is a table, `{ copr = "…" }`, so other repository kinds can be added later without changing its shape.

## Validation

- Unit tests cover file naming for user and group

title: feat(bootstrap): adopt a branch with --adopt <url>?ref=<branch>
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/703
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise bootstrap --adopt` always took a repository's default branch. You couldn't adopt a machine's variant of your global config kept on another branch, or a setup history kept on a branch of its own. It now accepts `?ref=<branch>`, as `--from` already does:

```sh
# global config from the laptop branch, cloned and left on that branch
mise bootstrap --adopt 'you/mise-config?ref=laptop'
# a setup history kept on its own branch of the same repository
mise bootstrap --adopt 'you/mise-config?ref=history'
# the same on another host
mise bootstrap remote --host devbox --adopt 'you/mise-config?ref=laptop'
```

- `--adopt` checks the named branch for the `.mise-history/format.toml` marker, as it already did for the default branch. A setup history is restored and the machine follows that branch as its origin (`branch = "history"` in `[history.origin]`). Anything else is cloned into `~/.config/mise` and checked out on the branch.
- **The ref must be a branch.** An adopted repository is one you keep pulling and committing in, or that keeps syncing. A tag, a commit, or a branch the repository doesn't have is refused before anything is cloned: `--adopt takes a branch, and "v1" is not a branch of <url>`.
- **mise never moves an existing checkout to another branch.** A global config checkout on a different branch is refused, with or without `--update`: switch it with Git first. `--update` only fast-forwards the branch the checkout is on, as before. This applies locally and on `mise bootstrap remote` targets; without `?ref=`, an existing checkout is used as before.
- **`mise bootstrap remote --adopt`** bundles the requested branch for the target, and the target takes it as before.

The PR also clarifies how the two `--adopt` layouts relate to `mise dot origin set`, which is what #14378 asked about:

- The bootstrap overview is now three commented commands and a link. It no longer repeats the `--from`/`--adopt` table that [Bootstrap from a repository](https://mise.jdx.dev/bootstrap/from-repository.html) has. That page documents `?ref=` and says the global config row is "A Git checkout at `~/.config/mise`".
- A new sync-guide section, [The origin and your global config](https://mise.jdx.dev/dotfiles/sync.html#origin-and-global-config), covers three points:
  - `origin set` never pulls or pushes a checkout on disk.
  - The origin needs its own repository. Connecting the global config repository can put mise's history on its default branch, and after that `--adopt` restores it as a setup repository instead of cloning it.
  - To keep the history in that repository anyway, put it on a branch of its own and adopt it with `?ref=`.
- `mise dot origin set --help` now says: "The origin holds tracked-file history, not a checkout of your global config: connect a repository of its own, or a separate branch (`--branch`) of the one you adopt as global config with `mise boot

title: feat(task): add skip_if to skip a task based on current state
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/702
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Some tasks only have work to do when an external state is not reached yet, such as a workspace that another tool initializes once. Until now a task had to check for that inside its script, so mise reported it as having run even when it did nothing, and nothing in the config showed when the task does work.

Tasks now take `skip_if`, a shell command mise runs before the task. If it exits 0, mise skips the task and treats it as successful; any other exit status runs the task as usual.

```toml
[tasks.setup]
skip_if = "test -f .initialized"
run = "touch .initialized"

[tasks.deploy]
depends = ["setup"]
run = "echo deploying"
```

The first run initializes; later runs report the skip and go straight to `deploy`:

```
$ mise run deploy
[setup] $ touch .initialized
[deploy] $ echo deploying
deploying

$ mise run deploy
[setup] skip_if condition met, skipping
[deploy] $ echo deploying
deploying
```

The check can be any command, so it also covers state that only another tool knows about, e.g. `skip_if = "examplectl workspace show"`.

- The command runs in the task's directory, with the task's shell, environment and sandbox, after its `depends` and before `confirm` and the artifact cache. Its output is discarded and it gets no stdin, so it cannot prompt.
- It supports Tera templates and the task's arguments (`{{ usage.target }}`), the same as `confirm`.
- File tasks set it with `#MISE skip_if="..."`, and task templates pass it on through `extends`.
- A skipped task counts as having done no work, so a dependent task whose `sources` are fresh still skips.
- A command that cannot start, times out (it shares the task's `timeout`, which stops its whole process tree), is killed by a signal, or is interrupted with Ctrl-C fails the task.
- `mise run --force` runs the task without checking. `mise run --dry-run` prints the command (redacted) without running it, and `mise tasks info` shows it.
- The check does not receive the task's `secrets`: mise resolves those only for a task that runs.

To fail a task when a requirement is missing, such as not being logged in, keep that check in `run`. It already fails the task with the script's message.

Discussion: https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14389 (also covers https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/8698)

### Validation

- New e2e test `e2e/tasks/test_task_skip_if` covers: skipping, a dependent task still running, `--force`, the task env and arguments, `--dry-run` not running the command and redacting it, a timed-out check failing the task and leaving no child running, discarded output (binary stdout, stderr from a failed check), `tasks info`, and a file-task header.
- Ctrl-C during a check: verified by hand (SIGINT to the process group during `skip_if = "sleep 5"` exits 130 without running the task).
- Updated `test_task_info` and the `#MISE` header field test.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --al

 ## Skipping work
 
+### `skip_if`
+
+- **Type**: `string`
+
+A shell command mise runs before the task. If it exits 0, mise skips the task,
+prints `skip_if condition met, skipping`, and counts the task as successful;
+any other exit status runs the task. Use it for work that depends on state no
+file records, such as whether another tool is already set up:
+
+```mise-toml
+[tasks.setup]
+skip_if = "examplectl workspace show"
+run = "examplectl workspace init"
+```
+
+The command runs in the task's directory with the task's shell, environment,
+and sandbox, after its [`depends`](#depends) and before
+[`confirm`](#confirm). Its output is discarded and it gets no stdin, so it
+cannot prompt. It does not receive the task's
+[`secrets`](/tasks/task-configuration.html#secrets), which mise resolves only
+for a task that runs. A command that cannot start, times out (it shares the
+task's [`timeout`](#timeout)), or is killed by a signal fails the task. It supports
+Tera templates and the task's arguments, like `confirm`, and works in file
+tasks as `#MISE skip_if="..."`. `mise run --force` runs the task without
+checking, and `mise run --dry-run` prints the command without running it.
+
+A skipped task does not count as having done work, so a dependent task with
+fresh [`sources`](#sources) still skips. To make a task fail rather than skip
+when something is missing, check for it in `run`, for example
+`examplectl auth status || { echo "run examplectl login first" >&2; exit 1; }`.
+
 ### `sources`
 
 - **Type**: `string | string[]`

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+# skip_if runs a shell command before the task; exit 0 skips it, anything else runs it.
+# https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14389
+cat <<'TOML' >mise.toml
+[tasks.setup]
+skip_if = "test -f initialized"
+run = "echo initializing && touch initialized"
+
+[tasks.deploy]
+depends = ["setup"]
+run = "echo deploying"
+
+[tasks.env-check]
+env = { DONE = "1" }
+skip_if = 'test "$DONE" = 1'
+run = "echo env-check-ran"
+
+[tasks.arg-check]
+usage = 'arg "<target>"'
+skip_if = 'test "{{ usage.target }}" = skip'
+run = "echo arg-check-ran"
+
+[tasks.dry]
+skip_if = "touch condition-ran"
+run = "echo dry-ran"
+
+[tasks.slow]
+timeout = "1s"
+skip_if = "sleep 10"
+run = "echo slow-ran"
+
+[tasks.binary-check]
+skip_if = "cat binary.out"
+run = "echo binary-check-ran"
+
+[tasks.noisy-check]
+skip_if = "ls missing-file"
+run = "echo noisy-check-ran"
+
+[tasks.loud-check]
+skip_if = "echo loud-output"
+run = "echo loud-check-ran"
+
+[tasks.slow-child]
+timeout = "1s"
+skip_if = "sh -c 'sleep 3; touch late'"
+run = "echo slow-child-ran"
+TOML
+
+# The condition fails, so the task and its dependent run.
+first_run="$(mise run deploy 2>&1)"
+assert_contains_text "$first_run" "initializing"
+assert_contains_text "$first_run" "deploying"
+
+# Now the condition passes: setup is skipped and deploy still runs.
+second_run="$(mise run deploy 2>&1)"
+assert_contains_text "$second_run" "skip_if condition met, skipping"
+assert_not_contains_text "$second_run" "initializing"
+assert_contains_text "$second_run" "deploying"
+
+# --force runs the task without checking.
+assert_contains "mise run --force setup 2>&1" "initializing"
+
+# The command sees the task's env and its arguments.
+assert_not_contains "mise run env-check 2>&1" "env-check-ran"
+assert_not_contains "mise run arg-check skip 2>&1" "arg-check-ran"
+assert_contains "mise run arg-check prod 2>&1" "arg-check-ran"
+
+# --dry-run reports the condition without running it.
+assert_contains "mise run --dry-run dry 2>&1" "skip_if: touch condition-ran (not checked: dry run)"
+assert_fail "test -f condition-ran"
+
+# A condition that times out fails the task instead of choosing for it.
+assert_fail "mise run slow 2>&1" "skip_if failed"
+
+# The timeout stops the processes the check started, not just its shell.
+assert_fail "mise run slow-child 2>&1" "skip_if failed"
+sleep 4
+assert_fail "test -f late"
+
+# The check's output is discarded: binary stdout still skips, and a failing check prints nothing.
+printf '\377\376' >binary.out
+assert_not_contains "mise run binary-check 2>&1" "binary-check-ran"
+noisy="$(mise run noisy-check 2>&1)"
+assert_contains_text "$noisy" "noisy-check-ran"
+assert_not_contains_text "$noisy" "missing-file"
+
+# --raw hands tasks the terminal, but never the check: its output stays hidden.
+raw_noisy="$(mise run --raw noisy-check 2>&1)"
+assert_contains_text "$raw_noisy" "noisy-check-ran"
+assert_not_contains_text "$raw_noisy" "missing-file"
+raw_loud="$(mise run --raw loud-check 2>&1)"
+assert_contains_text "$raw_loud" "skip_if condition met, skipping"
+assert_not_contains_text "$raw_loud" "loud-output"
+
+assert_contains "mise tasks info setup" "Skip if: test -f initialized"
+
+# File tasks take it as a #MISE header.
+mkdir -p mise-tasks
+cat <<'SCRIPT' >mise-tasks/file-task
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+#MISE skip_if="test -f file-task-done"
+echo file-task-ran
+touch file-task-done
+SCRIPT
+chmod +x mise-tasks/file-task
+assert_contains "mise run file-task 2>&1" "file-task-ran"
+assert_not_contains "mise run file-task 2>&1" "file-task-ran"
+
+# The dry-run line is redacted like the task's command header.
+cat <<'TOML' >mise.toml
+redactions = ["SKIP_SECRET"]
+
+[env]
+SKIP_SECRET = "hunter2-skip"
+
+[tasks.redacted]
+skip_if = "test hunter2-skip = x"
+run = "echo redacted-ran"
+TOML
+dry="$(mise run --dry-run redacted 2>&1)"
+assert_contains_text "$dry" "(not checked: dry run)"
+assert_not_contains_text "$dry" "hunter2-skip"

title: fix(use): honor --tool-option minimum_release_age=0s when resolving latest
body:
With a global `minimum_release_age`, `mise use --tool-option minimum_release_age=0s <tool>` wrote `minimum_release_age = "0s"` to the config but installed the version allowed by the global setting. The latest lookup read tool options from the config files, which do not contain the new option until `mise use` writes them. A `0s` value disables the cutoff, so the backend saw no cutoff and fell back to the global setting. Non-zero per-tool values, inline `tool[minimum_release_age=0s]`, and `--minimum-release-age=0s` were not affected.

```sh
export MISE_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE=2023-06-01
mise use --dry-run --tool-option minimum_release_age=0s npm:prettier
# before: npm:prettier@2.8.8
# after:  npm:prettier@3.6.2
```

- Latest resolution passes the request's own tool options to the backend, so options from `mise use --tool-option` apply on the first resolution.
- New e2e test `cli/test_use_tool_option_minimum_release_age` uses the local npm fixture server. It fails without the fix.

title: fix(exec): run the original of a .mise-bins copy on Windows
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/701
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

On Windows, a tool installed with aqua's `symlink_bins`, github's `filter_bins`, or a packslip gets a `.mise-bins` directory holding only its declared executables. On Windows those entries are byte copies, and a copy runs from `.mise-bins`. A program that finds its DLLs or data next to its own executable then looks in the wrong place. For example, exiftool looks for `exiftool_files\` beside itself and fails to start.

Now each copy records which file it was copied from, and `mise x` runs that file instead. Shims go through `mise x`, so they get the fix too.

```toml
[tools]
"github:denoland/deno" = { version = "2.5.6", asset_pattern = "deno-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip", filter_bins = "deno.exe" }
```

With this config, `mise x -- deno eval 'console.log(Deno.execPath())'` used to report `...\2.5.6\.mise-bins\deno.exe`. It now reports `...\2.5.6\deno.exe`, the file the archive installed. The new Windows e2e test checks this.

Details:

- The record is a dotfile beside the copy (`.mise-bins\.deno.exe.source`) holding the original's path relative to the install, so it survives the install being moved or reached through a version link. Shim generation and `PATH` lookups skip dotfiles.
- Only originals inside the install and with the same file name are recorded. Starting a renamed original would change the name the program sees itself called by, which multi-call binaries such as uutils coreutils dispatch on. When an entry cannot be recorded, any earlier record for it is removed, and `mise x` ignores a record that names a file of another name.
- Existing installs have no record and keep running the copy until they are reinstalled (`mise install --force`).
- `mise activate` puts `.mise-bins` itself on `PATH`, so a shell that finds the copy there still runs the copy. This PR fixes `mise x` and shims only.
- Linux and macOS are unchanged: `.mise-bins` entries are symlinks there and nothing is recorded.

The aqua and github docs now describe this, and the github docs note that `filter_bins` needs the `.exe` name on Windows.

## Testing

- Unit tests cover following a record, a missing original, records that point outside the install or outside `.mise-bins`, and renamed entries.
- A new Windows Pester test (`e2e-win/backend/mise_bins_source.Tests.ps1`) installs deno with `filter_bins` and checks that `Deno.execPath()` through `mise x` and through the shim is the installed `deno.exe`, not the `.mise-bins` copy. I could not run it locally; it runs in Windows CI. `cargo clippy` passes for Linux and `x86_64-pc-windows-gnu`.

Part of discussion jdx/mise#14369.

title: feat(install): turn on the identity layout on Windows with experimental
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/697
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

On Windows, `experimental = true` now turns on the [identity install layout](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/install-layout.html) by itself. Until now it also needed `install_layout = "identity"`.

Windows is where the layout helps most. Each installation goes into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\mise\i\<label>-<hash>`, whose name has a bounded length whatever the version string is. That keeps deep npm, pipx and Java trees under the 260-character path limit. `installs\<tool>\<version>` stays as a junction to it, so IDE SDK paths keep working.

```toml
[settings]
experimental = true   # on Windows, new installs now use the identity layout
```

- Existing installations stay where they are and keep working. Only new installs use the identity layout; `mise installs migrate` moves old ones if you want.
- To opt out on Windows, set `install_layout = "legacy"` (or `MISE_INSTALL_LAYOUT=legacy`).
- Linux and macOS are unchanged: they still need `install_layout = "identity"` as well as `experimental`.

The docs for the setting and the install layout page now describe the Windows default and the opt-out.

## Testing

- A unit test covers the setting combinations (`identity`, `legacy`, unset, with and without `experimental`).
- A new Windows Pester test (`e2e-win/install_layout_default.Tests.ps1`) installs jq with `experimental` alone and checks it lands in `i\`, and checks that `install_layout = "legacy"` or `experimental` off keeps `installs\jq\1.7.1`. I could not run it locally; it runs in Windows CI.
- CI exports `MISE_EXPERIMENTAL=1`, so Windows e2e tests now run under the identity layout. Unit tests expect `installs\<tool>\<version>` paths, so the unit-test harness pins `MISE_INSTALL_LAYOUT=legacy`.

Related: discussion jdx/mise#14369.

title: fix(erlang): show a compiling phase while kerl builds from source
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/696
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

When `mise install erlang` builds from source, the install row now says `compiling with kerl` for the length of the build. Before, it kept saying `verifying checksum` (with the finished download's byte count) for the several minutes kerl spends compiling, so the install looked stuck. kerl's own output was also written straight over the progress display:

```
 erlang@29.1.1 verifying checksum  106.9/106.9 MB · 2.0 MB/s     107.7s  ███████░░░ ◟
APPLICATIONS DISABLED (See: /home/user/.cache/mise/erlang/kerl/builds/29.1.1/otp_build_29.1.1.log)
 * jinterface     : No Java compiler found
```

Now kerl runs attached to the install row. Its output lines are printed above the row, tagged with the tool, so the row keeps saying `compiling with kerl` in both the live display and plain-text output. When mise knows up front that it will compile (`erlang.compile = true`, or a source entry in `mise.lock`), the progress bar gives most of its length to the build rather than the download. With the stub kerl described below, the row reads:

```
  erlang@28.1  verifying checksum  3.0s  84.5/104.6 MB · 98.9 MB/s
mise erlang@28.1 APPLICATIONS DISABLED 1
mise erlang@28.1 Building step 1
  erlang@28.1  compiling with kerl  6.0s
```

Precompiled installs are unchanged.

Fixes #14377

## Validation

- Ran `mise install erlang@28.1` with `MISE_ERLANG_COMPILE=1` in a PTY. It downloaded the real OTP source tarball and ran a stub `kerl` that prints to stdout and stderr for six seconds. The output above comes from that run. A second run with the live display forced on (`MISE_FORCE_PROGRESS=1`) showed the row staying on `compiling with kerl` while kerl's lines printed above it.
- `cargo test --lib erlang`, plus the `test_erlang_lockfile` and `test_erlang_precompiled_strict` e2e tests.
- I did not run a real multi-minute OTP compile.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: 2.1.295.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> UX-only changes to Erlang source install progress and subprocess output handling; install logic paths are refactored but behavior for precompiled installs is unchanged.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Fixes misleading Erlang source-install progress** by treating kerl compilation as its own phase instead of leaving the row stuck on checksum verification.
> 
> Source builds now advance the install progress bar through download, checksum, and **compiling with kerl**, with custom weights (`SOURCE_BUILD_OPERATION_WEIGHTS`) so most of the bar reflects the long compile when mise knows upfront it will build from source (`installs_from_source` / `install_operation_weights`). kerl is launched via **`CmdLineRunner`** (like python-build/ruby-build): the row keeps the compile message while kerl status lines print above it via `println`, avoiding stdout overwriting

title: docs(config): explain the config search before the per-directory file names
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/695
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Read top to bottom, the [mise.toml configuration page](https://mise.jdx.dev/configuration.html) used to open its config discovery docs with "In each directory, mise reads these files" and a table of project file names. It didn't mention that mise also reads system config (`/etc/mise`) and global config (`~/.config/mise`), or that it searches every parent directory. That only came later, in "How config files combine", and that section didn't tie its directory walk back to the table.

The page now explains config discovery in this order:

1. **How config files combine** comes first. It covers system config, then global config, then every directory from the filesystem root down to the current one. It now says that each directory in that search reads the files in "Config file locations", and that the table's order decides which file wins.
2. **Config file locations** comes second. It now says it lists the file names mise looks for in each directory it searches, and links to "Global and system config" for the names used there.

The `#mise-toml` and `#configuration-hierarchy` anchors are unchanged, so existing links still work. Only these two sections moved and had their intros reworded. The tables, tree and examples are unchanged.

Fixes #14376

markdownlint and prettier pass.

title: fix(schema): reject unknown keys in env._.python and its venv options
body:
mise refuses to load an `[env]` with an unknown key in `_.python` or in its `venv` options:

```toml
[env]
_.python = { venv = { path = ".venv", bogus = 1 } }   # unknown field `bogus`, expected `path` or `create`
_.python = { venv = ".venv", bogus = 1 }              # unknown field `bogus`, expected `venv`
```

The JSON schema did not say so. An editor that validates against it, such as VS Code or tombi without strict mode, accepted both, and the mistake surfaced only when mise ran. Both objects now set `additionalProperties: false`, so the schema rejects what the parser rejects. Every option the parser reads is still listed: `path`, `create`, `python`, `uv_create_args` and `python_create_args`. This is a schema change only, and mise's behavior does not change.

This takes over the Python part of #12793 by @risu729, which pr-closer closed after 7 days of failing checks and merge conflicts. They are credited as co-author. The rest of #12793 is left out:

- **Deprecated aliases.** It modelled `value`/`values` and `[env.mise]`. mise still reads them with a deprecation warning, and listing them in the schema would invite their use.
- **`_.path` and `_.source` options.** It reshaped their option tables. mise accepts `redact`, `required` and `expand` on `_.path`, but whether each has any effect there needs its own look.

## Validation

- `e2e/config/test_schema_tombi`:
  - The valid `mise-env-directives.toml` fixture now sets `_.python.venv` with every option.
  - Four new fixtures, an unknown key in `venv` and one in `_.python`, must fail. One pair checks `schema/mise.json` and the other, set on a task, checks `schema/mise-task.json`. They carry `#:tombi schema.strict = false`, because strict mode already flags any key the schema does not list, which would make them fail with the old schema too. Without strict mode, they show what a plain JSON Schema validator sees.
- Ran tombi 0.9.22 in the test's own configuration:

  | file | `main` | this PR |
  |---|---|---|
  | `mise-env-directives.toml` | passes | passes |
  | unknown key in `venv` | passes | fails, `"bogus" is not allowed` |
  | unknown key in `_.python` | passes | fails, `"bogus" is not allowed` |
  | the same two, on a task (`mise-task.json`) | pass | fail, `"bogus" is not allowed` |

- With mise 2026.10.5, both invalid configs fail to load with the `unknown field` errors above, and `_.python = { venv = { path = ".venv", create = false } }` loads.

title: fix(rust): read the nightly manifest from RUSTUP_DIST_SERVER
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/694
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`rust@nightly` resolved the current nightly by fetching `https://static.rust-lang.org/dist/channel-rust-nightly.toml` regardless of `RUSTUP_DIST_SERVER`. With a rustup mirror such as panamax, installing `nightly` still needed access to `static.rust-lang.org` (or failed on a host that can only reach the mirror).

mise now reads that manifest from `$RUSTUP_DIST_SERVER/dist/channel-rust-nightly.toml`, falling back to `static.rust-lang.org` when the variable is unset:

```toml
[env]
RUSTUP_DIST_SERVER = "https://mirror.example.com"

[tools]
rust = "nightly"
```

`RUSTUP_DIST_SERVER` is read from the config `[env]` first, then the process environment, the same way `RUSTUP_UPDATE_ROOT` is for `rustup-init` (#14356). The lookup is used for resolving `nightly`, `mise ls-remote rust`, and `mise outdated`/`upgrade`.

The mirror from `[env]` is also handed to `rustup toolchain install`, so the toolchain download uses it even outside an activated shell, and the cached `ls-remote` listing is keyed by the mirror so switching mirrors does not reuse another mirror's nightly date.

Follow-up to https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14279.

> **Overview**

title: fix(schema): accept table forms for vars._.file and vars._.source
body:
`vars._.file` and `vars._.source` accept the same forms as `env._.file` and `env._.source`: a path, a table with options, or a list mixing the two. The JSON schema allowed only strings there, so editors and linters such as tombi or Taplo flagged a config that works:

```toml
[vars]
_.file = { path = ".env", redact = true }      # tombi: Expected a value of type String, but found Table
_.source = [{ path = "env.sh" }, "more.sh"]
```

Both now take the table form too, through the same `env_directive` definition `[env]` uses. This is a schema change only, and mise's behavior does not change.

This takes over the directive part of #12794 by @risu729, which pr-closer closed after 7 days of failing checks and merge conflicts. They are credited as co-author. Greptile's open thread on #12794 asked for fixtures with a table and with a list holding a table. The new fixture has both.

#12794 also made `[vars]` accept `false`, as a way to remove a value. That part is left out, because it does not hold on current `main`. With mise 2026.10.5, `X = false` or `X = { value = false }` in a child config leaves a parent's `X = "from-parent"` in place, so `false` does nothing. The schema keeps rejecting it, as #10774 decided. `mise-bad-vars.toml` still asserts that, and still fails. #12794's other tightening, rejecting `tools = true` in `[vars]`, is already in the schema on `main`.

## Validation

- New `mise-vars-directives.toml` fixture in `e2e/config/test_schema_tombi`, with a table for `_.file` and a list holding a table for `_.source`.
- Ran tombi 0.9.22 against the schema from `main` and from this PR:
  - The new fixture fails with `main`'s schema (`Expected a value of type String, but found Table`) and passes with this PR's.
  - `mise-vars.toml` passes with both.
  - `mise-bad-vars.toml` fails with both.
- With mise 2026.10.5, each table form takes effect:
  - `_.file = { path = "a.env" }` and `_.file = [{ path = "a.env", redact = true }]` load `A` from the file.
  - `_.source = { path = "s.sh" }` and `_.source = [{ path = "s.sh" }]` load `B` from the script.

### [`v5.1.1`](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/mise-action/releases/tag/v5.1.1): : GitHub token is no longer exported to later steps by default

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/mise-action/compare/v5.1.0...v5.1.1)

mise-action no longer exports its GitHub token as `MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN` to every later step in the job. A new `persist_github_token` input lets you turn that back on, or pass a different token to later steps. **This changes the default behavior.** If later steps need the token, see Breaking Changes below.

#### Fixed

- **The GitHub token now stays inside the action by default.** Before this release, the `github_token` input (which defaults to `${{ github.token }}`) was written to `GITHUB_ENV` as `MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN`. That let any later step read the token and call the GitHub API with the job's permissions, even if the step never asked for a credential. Now the token is set only for the mise-action step and the processes it starts. The action masks the token in logs. ([#​658](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/mise-action/pull/658) by [@​jdx](https://redirect.github.com/jdx), reported in [#​657](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/mise-action/issues/657))

#### Added

- **`persist_github_token` input (default `false`).** It takes one of three values:

  - `false`: the token stays inside the action.
  - `true`: the token the action used is exported to later steps. If `env.MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN` is already set, it takes precedence over `github_token`.
  - A token value: that token is exported to later steps instead, for example a read-only token. The action still installs tools with `github_token`, or with `MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN` if it's already set.

  Setting `false` doesn't clear a `MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN` that was already set at the job level or exported by an earlier step. ([#​658](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/mise-action/pull/658) by [@​j
