title: feat(skills): keep synced skill links out of git status
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/689
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Skill links made by `mise skills sync` are absolute and machine-local, so they must not be committed. The packslip docs say to keep them out of version control, but each link is its own path beside any handwritten skills, so every repository ended up listing every skill by name:

```gitignore
/.agents/skills/.mise-skills.json
/.agents/skills/aube
/.agents/skills/hk-configure
```

With `skills.auto_sync` set globally, a tool that starts shipping a skill adds an untracked, absolute-path symlink to every project at once.

Sync now lists the links it owns, and `.mise-skills.json`, in the repository's `.git/info/exclude`:

```gitignore
# >>> mise skills (/.agents/skills)
/.agents/skills/aube
/.agents/skills/hk-configure
/.agents/skills/.mise-skills.json
# <<< mise skills (/.agents/skills)
```

- That file belongs to your clone alone, so nothing in the repository changes, and handwritten skills in the same directory still show up in `git status`.
- The block follows the links: it is rewritten on each sync, and removed when the last link goes (for example with `--prune`). Other lines in the file are left alone.
- Linked worktrees and submodules write to the right `info/exclude`. Outside a git repository, such as `mise skills sync --global`, nothing happens.
- There is no new setting. Say so if you want one to opt out.

Covered by unit tests for the block handling and the new `cli/test_skills_git_exclude` e2e, which checks `git status` with a handwritten skill beside the links.

Stacked on the PR that makes `mise upgrade` relink skills. Both come from [discussion 14367](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14367).

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: 2.1.295.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Changes are local to each git clone’s info/exclude and only affect ignored paths; failures warn without breaking sync, with no auth or shared-repo file edits.
> 
> **Overview**
> **`mise skills sync`** now keeps machine-local skill symlinks and **`.mise-skills.json`** out of **`git status`** by maintaining a marked block in the clone’s **`.git/info/exclude`** (not **`.gitignore`**), so the repo stays unchanged and handwritten skills beside the links remain trackable.
> 
> The new **`packslip_exclude`** logic discovers the repo from the skills directory, writes anchored ignore patterns with safe escaping, locks updates, preserves unrelated exclude lines, supports multiple skill dirs via separate blocks, and skips linked worktrees and non-git contexts. **`sync_skills`** invokes this after each sync; pruning the last link removes the block. Docs describe the behavior; unit tests and **`e2e/cli/test_skills_git_exclude`** cover exclude updates and **`git status`**.

title: fix(skills): relink agent skills after mise upgrade
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/688
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

With `skills.auto_sync` on, `mise upgrade` left the skill links pointing at the version it had just replaced. With `prune` on, the old install was then removed from under them.

```toml
[tools]
probe = "latest"   # a tool that ships a skill

[settings.skills]
dir = ".agents/skills"
auto_sync = true
```

```sh
$ mise upgrade probe          # 1.0.0 -> 2.0.0
$ readlink .agents/skills/probe
.../installs/probe/1.0.0/skill    # before: still the replaced version
.../installs/probe/2.0.0/skill    # after
```

Until now you had to run `mise skills sync` by hand after an upgrade.

The sync inside the install runs before upgrade moves the `latest` links under `installs/<tool>/`. `latest` therefore resolved to the version just replaced, and the config memoized that toolset. Upgrade now syncs again once the links have moved, on a fresh config, and only when `skills.auto_sync` is on. The same sync runs after `mise upgrade --bump tool@X` when X is already installed, which only rewrites the config. The docs and the `skills.auto_sync` description now list `mise upgrade` as a sync trigger.

Reproduced with a plugin that ships a packslip skill, with and without a `mise.lock`; the new `cli/test_skills_upgrade` e2e fails without the fix and passes with it.

Reported in [discussion 14367](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14367). The other half of that discussion, keeping the links out of `git status`, is the PR stacked on this one.

title: test(bootstrap): don't depend on bc being absent in the apt sources test
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/687
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`cli/test_bootstrap_apt_sources` fails whenever it shares an e2e container with `cli/test_system_install_apt`, which is what blocked the 2026.10.9 release PR (#14297, `e2e-linux-4`).

The test asserts that `mise bootstrap packages apply --dry-run` prints `apt-get install -y -- bc`. `test_system_install_apt` ends by installing `bc`, so in a shared container the dry run correctly prints `mise apt: 1 package(s) already installed` and the assertion fails. Whether the two tests share a container depends on how the tests are split across tranches, which is why the test passed when #14306 added it.

The test now uses `apt:mise-apt-sources-test-nonexistent`, a package that is never installed, the same approach `test_bootstrap_compose` takes. Only the test changes; there is no behavior change.

Validation: `mise run test:e2e cli/test_bootstrap_apt_sources` passes locally against a fresh debug build, including the `apt-get install -y -- mise-apt-sources-test-nonexistent` assertion.

title: fix(tool): only auto_update tools that are installed
body:
Since 2026.10.7, a prompt in an activated shell starts a background update for each tool whose `auto_update` check is due. That update also installed tools that had no installed version at all. A lazy tool is meant to install the first time one of its commands runs, so a config that declares lazy tools with `auto_update` downloaded every one of them at the first prompt. A `tool-update` service pass did the same.

Now `auto_update` only moves an installed tool forward. A tool with nothing installed, lazy or not, is left alone until its first run or `mise install` installs it.

```toml [/etc/mise/conf.d/defaults.toml]
[tools]
claude = { version = "latest", lazy = true, auto_update = "4h" }
codex = { version = "latest", lazy = true, auto_update = "4h" }
```

Before: on a machine where neither is installed, the first `mise hook-env` starts a `mise __tool-update` for both and installs them. After: nothing starts. Once `claude` has run, its prompt-time updates work as before.

Found while reviewing omacom/omarchy#9596, which declares Omarchy's default agent CLIs this way in `/etc/mise/conf.d`. On a fresh install, the first prompt started installing all 11 agents, about 2.5 GB in 30 seconds.

## Changes

- `start_due_updates` (prompts) skips a tool with no installed version before claiming its check, so no process or version lookup starts for it.
- With `for_auto_update`, `Upgrade` keeps only outdated versions that have an installed `current`. This covers prompts, the service, and launches in one place.
- The automatic tool updates docs say that only installed tools are updated.
- New `e2e/cli/test_tool_update_missing` covers a lazy and a non-lazy missing tool, a declaration in system config, a service pass, and an installed tool still updating at a prompt. On `main` it fails at the first case. It uses `version = "latest"`: a prompt resolves offline, and a fuzzy version such as `"1"` with nothing installed drops out before any update starts, which hides the bug.
- `test_tool_update_hook_env` now checks `hook-env.err` with `assert_empty`. `assert "cmd" ""` reports success without comparing anything, because an empty expected value means "check the exit status only." 86 other e2e assertions use that form; this PR leaves them alone.

## Testing

On Linux: `test_tool_update_missing`, `test_tool_update`, `test_tool_update_hook_env`, `test_tool_update_service`, `test_tool_update_global_auto`, and `test_tool_update_lazy_neighbors` pass. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean. I haven't run the full unit or e2e suites, or tested on macOS or Windows.

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+# auto_update moves an installed tool forward; it never installs one. A tool
+# that is declared but missing, lazy or not, is left to the normal install paths
+# (a lazy tool's first run, `mise install`), whichever updater checks it: a
+# shell prompt (`mise hook-env`) or the tool-update service. The dummy backend
+# offers 1.0.0, 1.1.0, and 2.0.0. `latest` matters: a prompt resolves offline,
+# and a fuzzy version with nothing installed drops out before any update.
+
+export MISE_STATE_DIR="$PWD/state"
+mise uninstall dummy --all
+
+reset_checks() {
+  find "$MISE_STATE_DIR/tool-update" -type f ! -name '*.*' -delete 2>/dev/null || true
+}
+
+prompt() {
+  reset_checks
+  mise hook-env --shell bash --force >/dev/null 2>hook-env.err
+  assert_empty "cat hook-env.err"
+}
+
+# The prompt never waits, so an update it started lands later: watch for one
+# rather than sleeping a fixed time a slow machine could outlast.
+assert_stays_missing() {
+  for _ in {1..50}; do
+    [[ -z "$(mise ls --installed dummy)" ]] || break
+    sleep 0.1
+  done
+  assert_empty "mise ls --installed dummy"
+}
+
+# A prompt claims a tool's check, writing its marker (the undotted file), before
+# it starts an update. No marker means no process or version lookup started,
+# which the upgrade dropping a missing tool on its own would hide.
+markers="find '$MISE_STATE_DIR/tool-update' -type f ! -name '*.*' ! -name prompt-next-check"
+
+# A lazy tool nobody has run yet stays missing at a prompt.
+printf '[tools]\ndummy = { version = "latest", lazy = true, auto_update = true }\n' >"$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml"
+prompt
+assert_empty "$markers"
+assert_stays_missing
+
+# So does a missing tool without lazy.
+printf '[tools]\ndummy = { version = "latest", auto_update = true }\n' >"$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml"
+prompt
+assert_empty "$markers"
+assert_stays_missing
+
+# And one declared in system config, which counts as global for auto_update.
+rm "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml"
+printf '[tools]\ndummy = { version = "latest", lazy = true, auto_update = true }\n' >"$MISE_SYSTEM_DIR/config.toml"
+prompt
+assert_empty "$markers"

title: fix(packslip): keep a renamed project's lockfile signer under packslip 1.7
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/685
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Prepares mise for packslip 1.7, which would otherwise break lockfile generation for a renamed or transferred packslip project.

A lock entry records a project's signer and its forge repository ID, but not the name the project had when it was locked. packslip 1.7's `same_workflow` now treats a signer from a repository other than the pinned project as a shared reusable workflow, so a project renamed from `g/tool` to `acme/tool` (same repository ID) looked like a changed signer. `mise lock` then failed with "lockfile generation would change the recorded signer", where a rename or transfer should keep the signer.

Each lock entry's pin is now named for the repository of its own signer, so a rename or transfer still continues. The repository ID both entries must record still ties them together, and a changed ID, a changed scheme, or a changed workflow path is still refused.

One tradeoff: a lock entry can't tell a renamed own workflow from a switch between two shared workflows of the same repository ID, so mise doesn't apply packslip 1.7's stricter shared-workflow rule when comparing lock entries.

Behavior is unchanged on packslip 1.6; the next PR in the stack bumps to 1.7.0, and these tests (`lock_entries_continue_by_their_forge_ids`, `packslip_signer_follows_the_repository_id_across_a_rename`) failed there on Windows CI in the lock-file maintenance PR (#14320) before this change. Unit tests pass on both 1.6.0 and 1.7.0 locally.

title: feat(github): keep the native OAuth refresh token in a password manager or keychain
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/683
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Native GitHub OAuth (`mise token github --oauth`) caches the long-lived, rotating refresh token in plaintext in `~/.local/state/mise/github-oauth-tokens.toml`. The file is `0600`, which keeps other users out but not other programs running as you. You can now keep the refresh token in a password manager or keychain instead:

```toml
# ~/.config/mise/config.toml
[settings.github]
oauth_cache_get = "pass show mise/github-oauth"
oauth_cache_set = "pass insert -m -f mise/github-oauth"
```

With both set, the cache file keeps only the 8-hour access token. The commands work with `pass`, `op`, `bw`, fnox or anything else that stores a multi-line secret, on Linux, macOS, Windows and WSL.

- `oauth_cache_set` receives the value on stdin (never argv) each time a refresh token is issued, because GitHub rotates it on every refresh. Both settings are required together; setting one warns and keeps the file.
- The commands run only when the access token must be refreshed, about once every eight hours, not on every mise invocation.
- If `oauth_cache_get` fails at refresh time (for example a locked vault), mise skips the refresh and keeps the cached token. It is not invalidated.
- If `oauth_cache_set` fails, mise warns and keeps the rotated refresh token in the file rather than losing the session.
- When mise stores the first token, a failing `oauth_cache_get` counts as an empty store, since many tools fail on an entry that does not exist yet.
- An existing cache file with a refresh token moves into the store at the next refresh.
- Both are global-only settings, so a project's `mise.toml` cannot make mise run commands here.

This is the first step of #14270. The macOS Secure Enclave helper, native Windows/Linux credential stores and age encryption from that issue are not part of this PR; the hooks cover them for now. Requested in discussion #14260.

The commands run through the same inline shell as `credential_command`, via a small extraction in `tokens.rs`.

## Testing

New e2e test `test_token_github_oauth_store` against the mock OAuth server covers: token stored only in the store, refresh from the store, unreadable store keeps the cache file byte-identical, unwritable store keeps the refresh token in the file, only one command set, and migration of an existing plaintext cache. `test_token_github`, the oauth unit tests and clippy (`-D warnings`) pass. The hk `cargo-check` step fails here on the existing `Cargo.toml` `redundant_homepage` manifest warning, unrelated to this change.

title: feat(bootstrap): render templates in [bootstrap.repos] checkout paths
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/682
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`[bootstrap.repos]` keys can now use templates, so one shared config can let each machine choose where repositories are cloned.

```toml
[vars.repos_dir]
default = "~/src"
prompt = "Where should repositories be cloned?"

[bootstrap.repos]
"{{ vars.repos_dir }}/project-a" = { url = "git@github.com:example/project-a.git" }
```

Each machine answers `repos_dir` once (`mise vars prompt`); the answer lives in mise's state dir, not the shared config. `apply`, `update`, `status`, and `exec` all see the rendered path. Reading a var never prompts, so an unanswered one uses its `default`. A key that fails to render is warned about and skipped, like other invalid entries.

Keys without template syntax are unchanged.

Closes discussion #14257.

title: security(config): require trust for path: tool versions
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/681
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

An untrusted repository could put its own directory first on PATH without any trust prompt. A `path:<dir>` tool version needs no install step, so as soon as `mise hook-env` (run by `mise activate` on every `cd`) loaded the config, `<dir>/bin` was placed ahead of the user's PATH. A clone containing

```
# .tool-versions
node path:./local
```

plus an executable `local/bin/git` ran the attacker's `git` the next time the user typed `git`. The same worked with `node = "path:./local"` in `mise.toml`.

The cause was that the trust-free checks for `.tool-versions` and `mise.toml` only looked at the shape of `[tools]` entries (no templates, no inline options, plain strings), never at what the version string says. A `path:` version now requires trust in both, so an untrusted config is skipped, and the shell hook prints the usual warning:

```
mise WARN ~/untrusted-repo/.tool-versions is not trusted, run `mise trust` to enable it
```

After `mise trust`, `path:` versions work exactly as before. Other version forms (`20`, `latest`, `ref:`, `prefix:`) are unaffected.

Reported by Anthropic and Ada Logics (Adam Korczynski).

## Validation

- Unit tests for both checks (`.tool-versions` incl. comments, `mise.toml` string and array forms).
- New e2e `config/test_trust_path_tool_version` covers both file formats: untrusted is refused for `ls`/`env` and `hook-env` emits no repo `bin` on PATH; trusted still works.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean.

title: feat(bootstrap): layer dnf packages with rpm-ostree on Fedora Atomic hosts
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/680
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Summary

On Fedora Atomic hosts (Silverblue, Bazzite, secureblue, ...) `dnf install` cannot work because `/usr` is read-only; packages are layered with `rpm-ostree` and take effect on the next boot. This lets the `dnf` manager do that, **opt-in**, so one `[bootstrap.packages]` list keeps working on Fedora Workstation, atomic hosts, and bootc image builds:

```toml
[settings]
system_packages.ostree = "layer" # default: "error"
```

```
$ mise bootstrap packages apply --manager dnf
mise $ sudo rpm-ostree install --idempotent --allow-inactive gimp
dnf: reboot to start using the layered packages
```

With the default `"error"`, `apply` explains why it stopped and points at this setting (stacked on #14353, which adds the ostree detection).

With `layer`:

- one `rpm-ostree install --idempotent --allow-inactive` transaction for the whole batch (each call builds a new deployment); `--update` runs `rpm-ostree refresh-md` first; a reboot notice follows
- packages in the next deployment's `requested-packages` count as installed and show `pending reboot`, so later runs do not request them again
- version pins are skipped with a warning
- `state = "absent"` runs `rpm-ostree uninstall`
- `upgrade` fails with a hint to run `rpm-ostree upgrade`, since layered packages only update with the base image

Not included, left as follow-ups: `--apply-live`, calling `rpm-ostree` without sudo through polkit for local admin sessions, and `mise bootstrap packages prune` for dnf (dnf has no prune path today; declarative removal covers uninstalling).

Part of discussion [#14278](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14278).

## Test plan

- `cargo test --lib dnf` (argument building, `requested-packages` parsing, pending state)
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- Not run on a real ostree host.

title: feat(rust): download rustup-init from RUSTUP_UPDATE_ROOT
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/679
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

mise now downloads `rustup-init` from `RUSTUP_UPDATE_ROOT` when that variable is set, so rustup mirrors such as panamax can serve the bootstrap download too. Previously the URL was hardcoded to `https://sh.rustup.rs`, so installing Rust on a machine that can only reach a mirror failed before rustup ever ran.

```toml
[env]
RUSTUP_DIST_SERVER = "https://mirror.example.com"
RUSTUP_UPDATE_ROOT = "https://mirror.example.com/rustup"
```

With that config, mise fetches `https://mirror.example.com/rustup/dist/<host-triple>/rustup-init` (`.exe` on Windows). The triple comes from `rust.default_host` if set, otherwise from the current platform. Without `RUSTUP_UPDATE_ROOT`, behavior is unchanged. `RUSTUP_DIST_SERVER` already worked because mise passes the environment through to rustup; this PR documents it.

Discussion: https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14279

title: fix(shim): keep other projects' command wrappers on reshim
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/678
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes #14277.

Command wrappers (`[wrappers]`) all live in one shared folder, `$MISE_DATA_DIR/command-wrappers/bin`. A reshim, which `install`, `use` and similar commands also trigger, rebuilt that folder from only the current directory's config. Running any of them in project B deleted the wrappers defined only in project A, so `cargo` in A silently went back to plain rustup cargo.

Now the reshim also reads the wrappers from every tracked config, including the built-in `cargo` wrapper from Rust's `mr_boxington` option, and keeps them. A shim left behind for a project you are not in still falls through to the next `PATH` entry. Removing a wrapper from its own project and reshimming there still deletes its shim.

```toml
# proj-a/mise.toml
[wrappers.uname]
command = "echo"
args = ["wrapped uname"]
```

`mise reshim` in `proj-a`, then in `proj-b`: the `uname` wrapper is no longer deleted.

A tracked config that fails to load is skipped, so it can't break a reshim run from elsewhere. `mise reshim --force` still wipes the folder before rebuilding it.

Not included: having `hook-env` recreate a missing wrapper (the issue's second option).

Tested with the new `e2e/cli/test_command_wrappers_reshim_other_project`; the existing wrapper e2e tests were run too.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes shared shim sync and PATH resolution for command wrappers; mistakes could affect which binary runs or leave stale shims, but scoped to experimental wrappers and tracked configs.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Fixes cross-project command wrapper shims being wiped on `mise reshim`** (#14277). Wrappers share `$MISE_DATA_DIR/command-wrappers/bin`, but reshimming only rebuilt that folder from the current project’s config, so wrappers defined elsewhere (e.g. `[wrappers.cargo]` in another repo) disappeared.
> 
> Reshim now **merges wrappers from every tracked config** via new `tracked_command_wrappers` (explicit `[wrappers]`, plus per-project Rust/`mr-boxington` logic). Other projects’ names are kept when absent locally; bad names or unloadable configs are skipped so they don’t break your reshim. `sync_command_wrapper_shims` is **async** to support this.

> **Runtime behavior:** when a command is hit through a leftover wrapper shim and the active project doesn’t define that wrapper, shim resolution **falls through to the real system binary** even if `not_found_system_fallback` is off—unless a **missing but selected** tool version could still provide that command (`missing_version_may_provide`). `list_missing_versions` is **public** for that check.

title: feat(bootstrap): declare macOS login items
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/677
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise bootstrap` can now declare the apps that open when you log in on macOS, the list under System Settings → General → Login Items & Extensions → Open at Login:

```toml
[bootstrap.macos.login_items]
apps = [
  "/Applications/Bitwarden.app",
  "/Applications/Ghostty.app",
  "~/Applications/Example.app",
]
```

`mise bootstrap status` and `plan` report declared apps that are missing, and `mise bootstrap` / `mise bootstrap macos defaults apply` add them. Before this, the options were a LaunchAgent per app running `open -a` (which shows up as a background item and drifts from the real list) or an AppleScript hook that needs Automation permission and can't appear in `status`.

## Behavior

- The list is additive by default: apps such as Rectangle register themselves at runtime, so undeclared entries are left alone. `exclusive = true` makes the config own the whole list and removes undeclared entries.
- Paths follow the `dock.apps` rules: absolute or `~/`, ending in `.app`, no `..`, no duplicates. Invalid entries warn and are skipped.
- Across config files, `apps` are combined and the most local `exclusive` wins.
- Inert off macOS, like `defaults`.

## Implementation

`SMAppService` only registers the calling app's own bundle, so this uses `LSSharedFileList` with `kLSSharedFileListSessionLoginItems`, the API that manages other apps' entries. It has been deprecated since macOS 10.11 but still works, as discussed in jdx/mise#14284. The FFI sits in `src/system/login_items.rs` and links CoreServices directly.

## Testing

- Unit tests cover path validation and the additive and exclusive plans.
- `e2e/cli/test_system_login_items` covers the status JSON and the inert apply off macOS.
- The CoreServices FFI type-checks for `aarch64-apple-darwin` from a scratch crate, but I could not run it on macOS, so a manual check of add and remove on a real Mac is still needed.

Discussion: jdx/mise#14284

title: feat(pypi): read upload times from PEP 691 simple indexes
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/675
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Private PyPI indexes usually implement only the Simple API, not PyPI's own `/json` API. For those, `pypi:` tools listed versions from PEP 503 HTML, which has no timestamps, so `minimum_release_age` could not filter them.

When `pypi.registry_url` (or a tool's `registry_url`) is not a `/json` URL, mise now sends an `Accept` header asking for the PEP 691 JSON form and falls back to HTML:

```toml
[settings.pypi]
registry_url = "https://packages.example.com/simple/{}/"

[tools]
"pypi:my-tool" = "latest"
```

- If the index answers with PEP 691 JSON, versions come from its `files` list. Yanked files are skipped, and the earliest PEP 700 `upload-time` becomes the release time used by `minimum_release_age`.
- If it answers with HTML (PEP 503), behavior is unchanged: no timestamps.
- URLs containing `/json` still use PyPI's JSON API as before. No new setting.

Tested with a unit test for the JSON parsing; not tested against a real private index.

Closes discussion https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14281

title: feat(bootstrap): support run0 and doas for privilege elevation
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/674
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise bootstrap` elevated only with `sudo`. On hosts that don't ship it, such as secureblue (which removes sudo in favor of systemd's `run0`) or systems using `doas`, it stopped with `sudo not found. Run as root: …`. The only workarounds were copying the printed command or running all of mise as root.

mise now picks the elevation command itself:

```
$ mise bootstrap packages apply --manager dnf   # no sudo installed, run0 present
$ run0 dnf install -y gimp
```

- With nothing configured, mise uses the first of `sudo`, `run0`, `doas` found on `PATH`. If none is installed it still asks you to run the command as root.
- New setting `system_packages.elevate_with` (`MISE_SYSTEM_PACKAGES_ELEVATE_WITH`) pins the command:

  ```toml
  [settings]
  system_packages.elevate_with = "run0"
  ```

- `system_packages.sudo = false` still disables elevation entirely.

This applies to every step that elevates: apk, apt, dnf, pacman, zypper, the login shell, accounts, files, services, the firewall and Compose.

The existing guarantees hold for each command: the full command line is logged before it runs, and without a TTY mise first checks for passwordless elevation (`sudo -n`, `doas -n`, `run0 --no-ask-password`) and otherwise prints the exact command to run by hand. Other commands, such as `pkexec`, are accepted but only used in an interactive terminal, since mise has no non-interactive check for them.

The Homebrew cask shim is macOS-only and still calls `sudo` directly.

Tested with a unit test for the per-command non-interactive checks. I have not run it against a real `run0` or `doas`.

Closes https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14280

title: fix(bootstrap): don't print a stdin-only helper as a manual command
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/673
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

When `system_packages.sudo` is disabled, `mise bootstrap` fails at a privileged step with a hint like:

```
mise ERROR not running as root and system_packages.sudo is disabled. Run manually:
  sudo /path/to/mise --no-config --no-env --no-hooks bootstrap __apply-system-plan
```

That command can't work on its own: the helper reads its plan from stdin, so running it as root applies nothing.

Helpers that take their payload on stdin (system files, accounts, apt source keys, tool archives, privileged inspection) now say instead:

```
mise ERROR not running as root and system_packages.sudo is disabled. Re-run this mise command as root. The privileged helper receives its plan on stdin, so it cannot be run by itself.
```

Helpers that are plain argv commands (`apt-get`, `pacman`, …) keep the copy-pasteable `Run manually:` hint.

Reported in discussion jdx/mise#14312.

title: feat(bootstrap): embed apt source signing keys inline in .sources files
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/672
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`[bootstrap.apt.sources]` entries (PPAs and other repositories) now carry their signing key inside the generated `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/mise-<name>.sources` file, instead of a separate `/etc/apt/keyrings/mise-<name>.gpg`:

```deb822
Types: deb
URIs: https://ppa.launchpadcontent.net/git-core/ppa/ubuntu/
Suites: noble
Components: main
Signed-By:
 -----BEGIN PGP PUBLIC KEY BLOCK-----
 .
 mQINBF...
 -----END PGP PUBLIC KEY BLOCK-----
```

Deleting the one `.sources` file now removes both the repository and its trusted key, with no orphan key files left behind.

- The key is still fetched, checked against the declared fingerprints, and trimmed to those keys. It is trusted only for its own repository.
- A key already in the file that matches the declared fingerprints is kept, so it isn't re-downloaded.
- Existing sources migrate on the next apply: the `.sources` file is rewritten with the inline key and the old `/etc/apt/keyrings/mise-<name>.gpg` is removed. `--dry-run` lists both steps.

**Compatibility:** inline `Signed-By` keys need apt 2.4 or newer (Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12). Ubuntu 20.04 and Debian 11 are no longer supported for these sources.

Closes #14318

**Validation:** the `apt_sources` unit tests pass (including an armor round-trip and extraction of the inline key from a rendered stanza) and clippy is clean. I haven't run it against a real apt install.

title: fix(bootstrap): support dnf package groups
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/671
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes #14317

`dnf:@development-tools` in `[bootstrap.packages]` is now treated as a dnf package group. Before, `mise bootstrap packages status` ran `rpm -q @development-tools`, which never matches, so a group that dnf had installed successfully was always reported as missing.

```toml
[bootstrap.packages]
"dnf:@development-tools" = "latest"
```

- **Status:** checks `dnf group list --installed --hidden` for the group id (with `-v` on dnf4, which only prints ids that way).
- **Install:** `dnf install -y @development-tools`.
- **Upgrade:** `dnf group upgrade -y --refresh development-tools`, run alongside the ordinary package upgrade.
- Environment groups (`@^name`) fail `status` with a clear "not supported" error.

Unit tests cover the install/upgrade arguments and both dnf4 and dnf5 group-list output. I could not run this against a real dnf here, so the group-list parsing is checked only against sample output.

> **DNF package groups** (names like `dnf:@development-tools`) in `[bootstrap.packages]` are handled as comps groups instead of RPMs, so status no longer incorrectly reports installed groups as missing after `rpm -q`.
> 
> **Parsing:** For `dnf`, a leading `@` is treated as part of the group name, not a version pin; `@latest` on groups is ignored. Environment groups (`@^name`) are rejected with a clear error, and version pins on groups are rejected.

title: fix(brew): refuse to chown a prefix owned by another user
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/669
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise bootstrap` assumed it could take ownership of the Homebrew prefix. If `/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew` already existed but belonged to another user (for example a dedicated `linuxbrew` user managed by secureblue's brew-proxy), mise planned a `sudo mkdir -p` and `sudo chown -R <you>` over it. That would have removed the ownership boundary the setup exists to provide.

Now mise stops before touching it:

```
Error: /home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew is owned by linuxbrew and not writable by alice; mise will not change the ownership of another user's Homebrew prefix. Install the missing formulae with that prefix's own brew, or remove them from [bootstrap.packages]
```

Root-owned prefixes still get the existing one-time chown, and formulae already installed by hand are still recognised as present.

mise pours bottles into the prefix itself and does not shell out to `brew`, so this does not make brew-proxy prefixes installable by mise; it only makes the failure safe and clear. Part of discussion #14314.

Validated with a unit test, clippy (`-D warnings`), and `test_system_install_brew_linux`.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: 2.1.295.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes bootstrap ownership logic on a security-sensitive path (sudo mkdir/chown), but narrows behavior to fail safe instead of escalating privileges over another user’s prefix.
> 
> **Overview**
> **`mise bootstrap` no longer tries to take over a Homebrew prefix owned by another non-root user** (e.g. a dedicated `linuxbrew` account). It now detects that case up front and fails with a message to use that prefix’s own `brew` or drop the packages from `[bootstrap.packages]`.
> 
> Adds `foreign_owner` / `foreign_uid` helpers and an early guard in `prefix::bootstrap` before the existing mkdir/chown path. **Root-owned prefixes still follow the one-time chown flow**; only “another real user” ownership is treated as off-limits. Unit tests cover the uid/owner classification.

https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/668

On Windows, the built-in `tool-update` service opened a terminal window that stayed on screen, and closing it stopped the updater. The Scheduled Task runs `mise.exe __tool-update --watch`, which was never classified as unattended, so it kept the console Windows hands a task's console program.

[bootstrap.services.mise-tool-update]
builtin = "tool-update"

`tool-update --watch` is now treated like the dotfiles watcher, so its console is hidden right after parsing. `mise tool-update <tool>` still keeps its console so errors can be shown.

I only verified the classification on Linux (extended `only_a_starting_watcher_runs_unattended`); I haven't confirmed the window disappears on Windows 11. Discussion #13426 reports the history watcher still showing a window on build 26200.9457, so that may need separate work.

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/667
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise dot sync`, `mise dot pull`, and `mise dot apply` each write different things, and the docs and help did not say so. Users could not tell which command changes which files, or when they need more than one.

The sync guide now has a "Pull and apply" section with two comparison tables (commands, and entry modes) and a worked tracked-template example:

```sh
mise dot sync    # fetch the change
mise dot pull    # update ~/.bashrc and ~/.dotfiles/gitconfig.tera
mise dot apply   # render the template into ~/.gitconfig
```

It also says that the watcher fetches and pulls in `sync` mode but never copies or renders, so `mise dot apply` is still needed after incoming sources change.

Help text changes:

- `pull` summary: "Write fetched changes from other machines to tracked files". It no longer says "Apply" or "from the origin", which suggested a network step.
- `apply` summary: "Link, copy, and render `[dotfiles]` entries into place".
- `pull` long help says that it updates the source of a `copy` or `template` entry but never writes the target.
- `apply` long help says that it never fetches or pulls, and gives the `sync`, `pull`, `apply` order.

No behavior changes. A combined `apply --pull` is not part of this PR.

Refs #14321, #14273

Validation: docs formatted with prettier. The generated copies (`mise.usage.kdl`, `docs/cli/dotfiles/{apply,pull}.md`, `docs/public/llms.txt`, `man/man1/mise.1`) were edited by hand to match the source help rather than regenerated.

> **Overview**
> Clarifies how **`mise dot sync`**, **`pull`**, and **`apply`** divide work so users know which command touches which files and when more than one step is required.
> 
> The sync guide adds a **Pull and apply** section with comparison tables (what each command reads/writes, and how `track` vs `copy`/`template` entries behave) plus a worked example (`sync` → `pull` → `apply` after a remote template source change). It also notes that automatic sync mode pulls but does not copy or render, so **`mise dot apply`** is still needed when incoming sources change.
> 
> CLI help and generated docs are reworded: **`pull`** is described as writing fetched changes to **tracked** files (not “apply from the origin”), and **`apply`** as linking, copying, and rendering **`[dotfiles]`** locally without fetch/pull. @@ -176,6 +177,49 @@ authentication attempt fails, automatic sync retries with delays that grow

+## Pull and apply {#pull-and-apply}
+
+`sync`, `pull`, and `apply` each do one job, on different files:
+
+| Command          | Reads                              | Writes                                                                   |
+| ---------------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
+| `mise dot sync`  | The remote and your saved history  | Only saved history, never your files.                                    |
+| `mise dot pull`  | The history that `sync` fetched    | Tracked files, including the source of a `copy` or `template`.           |
+| `mise dot apply` | `[dotfiles]` and the files on disk | `[dotfiles]` targets, including edits, permission changes, and removals. |
+
+How each entry mode behaves:
+
+| Entry mode         | `mise dot pull`                                 | `mise dot apply`                            |
+| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
+| `track`            | Writes the fetched version to the tracked path. | Does nothing for the file's contents.       |
+| `copy`, `template` | Does not copy or render.                        | Copies or renders the source to the target. |
+
+A tracked path is the file an application reads when it is tracked in place,
+such as `~/.bashrc`. A template or copy source is a different path from the
+file the application reads, even when it also lives under `~/`. Track the
+source to share it between machines, and `apply` turns it into the target:
+
+```toml
+[dotfiles]
+"~/.bashrc" = { mode = "track" }
+"~/.dotfiles" = { mode = "track" }
+"~/.gitconfig" = { mode = "template", source = "~/.dotfiles/gitconfig.tera" }
+```
+
+After a change to `~/.dotfiles/gitconfig.tera` is saved on another machine:
+
+```sh
+mise dot sync    # fetch the change
+mise dot pull    # update ~/.bashrc and ~/.dotfiles/gitconfig.tera
+mise dot apply   # render the template into ~/.gitconfig
+```
+
+`~/.gitconfig` is not tracked here, so its own history is a separate choice;
+see [what history saves](/dotfiles/history.html#explicit-tracking-and-exclusions).
+If you only edit a template on this machine, `mise dot apply` alone is enough.
+In `sync` mode the watcher fetches and pulls on its own, but it does not
+copy or render, so run `mise dot apply` after incoming sources change.
+
 ## Resolve a conflict {#resolve-a-conflict}
 
 Compare the version saved on this machine with the fetched repository

title: fix(http): retry artifact downloads started by mise exec and shims
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/666
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes #14259

`mise exec`, `mise x` and shims install a missing tool with zero HTTP retries, so a single transient failure (for example a mid-body read timeout) fails the whole command. `mise install` of the same tool retries `http_retries` times (default 3). Setting `MISE_HTTP_RETRIES` had no effect under `exec`.

```
$ mise x http:tool@1.0.0 -- true   # server stalls mid-download
mise ERROR Failed to install http:tool@1.0.0: error decoding response body ...   # 1 attempt

$ mise install http:tool@1.0.0
mise WARN  HTTP GET ... attempt 1 failed ... (transient); retrying in ...        # 4 attempts
```

**Cause:** prefer-offline commands force `network::http_retries()` to 0 so shims and shell activation never stall on remote-version lookups. The artifact download loop took its retry count from the same function, so downloads lost their retries too.

**Fix:** the download loop now uses the configured `http_retries` setting. Remote-version lookups keep their single bounded attempt, so shim and activation latency is unchanged. The `http_retries` docs now say so.

**Validation:** added `test_download_retries_under_prefer_offline`, which fails without the change and passes with it. The mise-util HTTP tests and clippy pass. I did not run the issue's end-to-end reproduction script.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: unavailable.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Narrow HTTP retry behavior change limited to artifact downloads under prefer-offline; remote version lookup retry policy is unchanged.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Artifact downloads now honor `http_retries` when `mise exec`, `mise x`, or shims trigger an install**, instead of inheriting the prefer-offline “zero retries” budget meant for remote version lookups.
> 
> `retry_async` (used by the download retry loop) now passes `Settings::get().http_retries` rather than `network::http_retries()`, which forces `0` under prefer-offline fast paths. Version/metadata fetches that still call `network::http_retries()` are unchanged, so shims and activation keep a single bounded lookup attempt.
> 
> Docs for `http_retries` in `settings.toml` spell out that distinction, and **`test_download_retries_under_prefer_offline`** asserts a truncated-then-resumed download makes two server hits under prefer-offline (fixes #14259).
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 2d0dcff007be2f650c00216d50bcc235401a7d7d. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>

title: fix(schema): accept [bootstrap.groups] and [bootstrap.users]
body:
`[bootstrap.groups]` and `[bootstrap.users]` were missing from the JSON schema, so a strict schema checker such as tombi rejected any config that declared Linux accounts, even though mise reads them:

```toml
[bootstrap.groups]
deploy = { gid = 2000 }
ops = {}
old-team = { state = "absent" }

[bootstrap.users]
deploy = { group = "deploy", groups = ["ops"], exclusive_groups = true, home = "/srv/deploy", move_home = true, shell = "/bin/bash", comment = "Deploy user", create_home = true }
olduser = { state = "absent", remove_home = true }
```

The schema now describes both maps with the rules `src/system/accounts.rs` applies when it reads them:

- **Names.** Group and user names, `group` and `groups` are at most 32 characters. They are ASCII letters, digits, `_` or `-`, start with a letter or `_`, and may end in one `$`.
- **Paths.** `home` and `shell` are absolute paths, and they and `comment` contain no `:`, CR or LF.
- **Absent groups.** An absent group sets neither `gid` nor `system`.
- **Present users.** A present user (the default) needs a primary `group` and cannot set `remove_home`.
- **Absent users.** An absent user sets only `state` and `remove_home`.
- **Required pairs.** `exclusive_groups = true` needs `groups`, and `move_home = true` needs `home`.

Unknown keys are rejected. The conditional rules leave their branches open with `additionalProperties: true`, because tombi's strict mode otherwise treats a branch without it as closed, and flags `state` on `old-team = { state = "absent" }`.

This takes over the accounts part of #12529 by @risu729, which pr-closer closed after 7 days of failing checks on the fork run. They are credited as co-author. #12529 also covered services, Compose projects and managed files, which `main` has since added to the schema separately. Its open threads on accounts asked for these runtime rules: absent users carrying present-only fields, `exclusive_groups` without `groups`, `move_home` without `home`, and absolute paths. They are all included here.

One runtime rule is out of the schema's reach. A supplementary group must be declared or already exist on the machine, which depends on the machine rather than the file.

## Validation

- `e2e/config/test_schema_tombi`: the strict `mise.toml` fixture now declares the accounts above. Eight new fixtures, one per rule, must each fail.
- Ran tombi 0.9.22 against the schema from `main` and from this PR:
  - With `main`'s schema, every one of these files fails, the valid one included, with `bootstrap does not allow "groups" key` / `"users" key`.
  - With this PR's schema, the valid one passes and each invalid one fails on its own rule, for example `"group" is required`, `"home" is required`, `"srv/deploy" does not match the pattern ^/[^:\r\n]*$`, and `The value must be const value "false"`.
- With mise 2026.10.5 on Linux (Debian, in Docker), `mise bootstrap accounts status` gave these results:
  - It accepts the valid config.
  - It rejects each of the eight with the matc

title: fix(dotfiles): apply mise's own config before planning the other entries
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/664
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise dot apply` read the live mise config before applying anything. If a `[dotfiles]` entry copied an updated config over it, the rest of that run still used the old rules, so a newly added entry only took effect on a second apply.

Now the entries and edits that write mise's own configuration are applied first, the config is reloaded, and the remaining entries are planned from the new config:

```toml
# ~/.config/mise/config.toml (live copy)
[dotfiles]
"~/.config/mise/config.toml" = { source = "~/.dotfiles/config/config.toml", mode = "copy" }
# ~/.dotfiles/config/config.toml also declares "~/.gitconfig" = ...
```

A single `mise dot apply` now deploys the config and `~/.gitconfig`. `--dry-run` plans against the config file it would write, so it shows the whole result. It reuses the config simulation that the bootstrap dry run already has.

This covers the second part of #14324. The `--adopt` part is not changed, because adoption deliberately makes the repository the live configuration. Keeping a separate checkout is what `--from` is for.

Test: `e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_apply_config_first` fails without the change.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: 2.1.295.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes core dotfiles apply ordering and config reload semantics; mistakes could mis-apply files or skip entries, but behavior is covered by a dedicated e2e test.
> 
> **Overview**
> **`mise dot apply`** (and bootstrap’s dotfiles step) now runs in two passes: entries that write **mise’s own configuration** go first, then config is reloaded (or simulated on **`--dry-run`**) before the rest of the dotfiles are planned and applied. A single run can deploy an updated `config.toml` from a checkout and immediately honor new `[dotfiles]` rules it introduces.
> 
> Dry runs plan the second pass against the config **that would be written**, including when the replacement config drops entries the live file still lists. **`MISE_GLOBAL_CONFIG_FILE`** / system config paths are treated as config targets. Target filters that matched only the old config no longer error after the config pass rewrites what’s declared.
> 
> Docs and CLI help describe the behavior; **`e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_apply_config_first`** covers dry-run, full apply, targeted apply, and custom global config.

title: fix(packslip): let a workflow list carry the signer pin across a workflow move
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/663
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A machine that installed aube 2.2–2.5 could not upgrade it. aube moved its signing workflow from `release-plz.yml` to `release.yml` at 2.6.0. mise's signer pin remembered the first one, so `mise upgrade` and `latest` resolution refused every newer release. This happened even though the registry entry's `workflow` list (#14092) names both workflows:

```
$ mise upgrade
mise WARN  Error getting latest version for aube: packslip:github.com/aubepkg/aube: this release is signed by https://github.com/aubepkg/aube/.github/workflows/release.yml (sigstore-oidc), but https://github.com/aubepkg/aube/.github/workflows/release-plz.yml (sigstore-oidc) signed what mise accepted before.
mise All tools are up to date
```

A `workflow` list is the explicit trust decision the signer pin waits for. The pin now accepts a release when both the pinned signer and the release's signer are among the listed workflows, and records the new one. The same machine now upgrades without `mise packslip forget`:

```
$ mise upgrade
Upgraded 1 tool:
  aube 2.5.1 → 2.7.0
```

This applies to a list in the user's own tool options as well as a registry default:

```toml
[tools]
"packslip:github.com/example/tool" = { version = "latest", workflow = ["release-plz.yml", "release.yml"] }
```

A single `workflow`, or a list that doesn't name the pinned signer, still refuses a new signer as before.

Reported in discussion #13948.

### Validation

- New unit test in `packslip_pins.rs`: the move is refused without the list, accepted and recorded with it, and still refused when only one side is listed.
- Ran a debug build against isolated state: installed aube 2.5.1, which pinned `release-plz.yml`. Then `mise upgrade` installed 2.7.0 and moved the pin to `release.yml`, and reinstalling 2.5.1 moved it back. With `workflow = "release.yml@refs/heads/main"` alone, 2.7.0 is still refused against the old pin.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean, and the packslip unit tests pass.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: 2.1.295.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes packslip trust and pin persistence logic; scope is limited to workflow-list continuity with existing refusal paths for unrelated signers.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes upgrades that failed when a vendor moved its signing workflow (e.g. `release-plz.yml` → `release.yml`) even though the tool’s **`workflow`** list already trusted both paths.
> 
> **Signer pin continuity** now treats a multi-workflow **`workflow`** option as an explicit trust decision: if both the stored pin and the release’s signer appear in that list, the release is accepted and the pin is updated to the current workflow—no **`mise packslip forget`**. title: docs(shims): explain how to check whether a tool is installed
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/662
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

With shims on `PATH`, `command -v node` succeeds even when `node` is not installed or not active in the current directory, because the shim exists. Scripts that use `command -v` as an installed check get false positives. `which` and `whence` behave the same way. This came up in [discussion 14327](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14327).

This adds a "Checking whether a tool is installed" section to the shims page. It keeps `command -v` and asks `mise which` only when the result is a shim, so users without mise never reach that branch:

```sh
have() {
    p=$(command -v "$1") || return 1
    case $p in
    */shims/*) mise which "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1 ;;
    *) return 0 ;;
    esac
}

have prettier || echo "prettier is not installed"
```

The section also notes that an unresolved shim can still fall through to a same-named executable later on `PATH`, and that setting `not_found_system_fallback` and `not_found_auto_install` to `false` makes it fail instead.

Docs only; no behavior change. Validated with the focused hk check (prettier, markdownlint), `mise run docs:build`, and `git diff --check`. I checked the `have` branching logic against a fake shim directory but did not run it against a real mise install.

+### Checking whether a tool is installed {#command-v}
+
+With shims on `PATH`, `command -v node` succeeds even when `node` is not
+installed or not active in the current directory, because the shim exists. A
+script that uses `command -v` as its installed check therefore gets a false
+positive. `which` and `whence` behave the same way.
+
+Keep `command -v`, and ask mise only when it finds a shim. A shim is a symlink
+to the `mise` binary, wherever
+[`shims_dir`](/configuration/settings.html#shims_dir) or `system_shims_dir` puts
+it. `command mise` skips the `mise` shell function that `mise activate` defines.
+`mise which` exits non-zero unless the tool resolves in the current directory:
+
+```sh [have.sh]
+have() {
+    p=$(command -v "$1") || return 1
+    if [ -L "$p" ] && [ "$(basename "$(readlink "$p")")" = mise ]; then
+        command mise which "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1
+    else
+        return 0
+    fi
+}
+
+have prettier || echo "prettier is not installed"
+```
+
+Users without mise never take the `mise which` branch, so the same script works
+for a team where only some people use mise. This example assumes symlink shims, so
+it does not cover Windows. [Command wrappers](#command-wrappers) are also
+symlinks to `mise`, and `mise which` does not resolve their names, so `have`
+reports a wrapped command as missing even though running it works.
+
+An unresolved shim can still run another executable with the same name later on
+`PATH`, so `have` may report a tool as missing that the shim would run anyway.
+Set `not_found_system_fallback` and `not_found_auto_install` to `false` to make

body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->

`mise upgrade` with an aqua package that has no GitHub repo, such as `aqua:codeberg.org/mergiraf/mergiraf` (an `http`-type registry entry), printed "does not have repo_owner and/or repo_name" about ten times, once per version lookup.

The warning now prints once per run and says what to do:

mise WARN  aqua package codeberg.org/mergiraf/mergiraf has no repo_owner and/or repo_name, so its versions cannot be listed. Pin an exact version to install it.

Pinned versions of these packages still install as before. `latest` and prefix requests still cannot resolve, so the generic "No versions found" warnings from `mise upgrade` remain.

title: fix(prune): keep a uv-locked pipx tool's installs for every Python
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/660
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise prune` no longer removes a global `pipx:`/`pypi:` tool's install just because another directory uses a different Python.

A uv-locked `pipx:`/`pypi:` install is named `<version>~uv~<digest>`, and the digest includes the Python it was built with. That Python comes from the directory mise runs in, so a global tool ends up with one install per Python. Prune only resolved the Python of the current directory, so it marked the install for the other Python as prunable:

```toml
# ~/.config/mise/config.toml
[tools]
python = "3.14.6"
ansible-core = "2.21"   # pipx:ansible-core
# a project's mise.toml sets python = "3.13.11"
```

```
$ cd ~ && mise prune --dry-run
mise ansible-core@2.21.5~uv~<3.13 digest> is prunable: ansible-core is required at ... 2.21.5~uv~<3.14 digest> by ~/.config/mise/config.toml
```

Running the same command from the project flipped it to the 3.14 install, and `mise install` brought back whichever one prune had removed.

Now, when a tracked config needs a uv-locked tool, prune also keeps every installed `<version>~uv~*` directory of that same version, in both the legacy and identity layouts. Prune from either directory leaves both installs alone.

Tradeoff: variants aren't narrowed to Pythons that are still in use, so after permanently changing a global Python, the install built with the old one stays until the tool's version changes.

Validation: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean. I did not add a regression test (it needs uv and two Pythons) and did not run an end-to-end prune against two Pythons.

Reported in discussion #14323.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: claude-code_2-1-295_agent.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes prune retention logic for pipx/pypi uv installs; wrong matching could leave extra disk use or, in edge cases, prune the wrong variant, but scope is limited to `collect_needed_versions`.
> 
> **Overview**
> **`mise prune`** no longer treats alternate on-disk installs of the same uv-locked **`pipx:`/`pypi:`** version as unused when only one Python-specific digest is resolved from the current directory.
> 
> When building the set of versions tracked configs still need, **`collect_needed_versions`** now calls **`keep_uv_python_variants`**, which—for tools with a uv install identity—also protects every installed directory matching `<version>~uv~*`, in both legacy version names and identity-layout install dirs.
> 
> **Tradeoff:** installs built with a Python you no longer use are kept until the tool version changes; targeted **`mise prune <tool>`** behavior for fully unneeded tools is unchanged.

title: fix(prune): keep versions of task-scoped tools
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/659
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise prune` treated a tool as unused when a tracked config referenced it only through a task, so it deleted versions that `mise run` would need again.

```toml
[tasks.hello]
run = "true"
tools = { dummy = "1.0.0" }
```

Before, `mise prune --dry-run` listed `dummy@1.0.0` as prunable. Now the config's task tools count as needed and the version is kept; unreferenced versions are still pruned.

Tools declared in file-based task scripts (`#MISE tools=...`) are not covered yet, only tasks defined inline in config files.

Fixes #14325

Tested with a new e2e test (`test_prune_task_tools`).

> **Overview**
> **`mise prune` now treats inline task `tools` as in-use** for tracked configs, so versions only referenced by tasks (including via `extends` task templates) are no longer marked prunable.

title: fix(dotfiles): show per-file diffs for directory copy entries in dot diff
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/658
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise dot diff` now shows the differing hunks for directory copy entries, such as those created by `[dotfile_groups.*]` with `mode = "copy"`. Previously it only printed the entry's summary line, so you couldn't tell what had drifted.

Before:

```
$ mise dot diff
dotfile differs: ~
  desired directory contents: ~/.config/dotfiles/home -> ~
```

After:

```
$ mise dot diff
dotfile differs: ~
  desired directory contents: ~/.config/dotfiles/home -> ~
  content differs: ~/.config/dotfiles/home/dot-config/app/a.conf -> ~/.config/app/a.conf
--- ~/.config/app/a.conf (current)
+++ ~/.config/dotfiles/home/dot-config/app/a.conf (desired)
@@ -1 +1 @@
-changed
+alpha
```

A file missing from the target prints `missing: <path>`, and a symlink or directory in the way prints `file type differs`. Unchanged files are not listed. Template-mode directories still print only the summary line.

Reported in [discussion 14330](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14330).

Added `e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_diff_directory_copy`, which passes. Clippy and the wider e2e suite were not run.

title: refactor: replace serde_yaml with serde-saphyr
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/657
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`serde_yaml` is deprecated, and the C-translated parser underneath it, `unsafe-libyaml`, is now flagged as unmaintained (RUSTSEC-2024-0449). mise's own YAML reading and writing now goes through [`serde-saphyr`](https://crates.io/crates/serde-saphyr), a maintained YAML parser written in safe Rust.

This covers every place mise itself reads YAML: the aqua registry (vendored and custom), YAML env files, sops-encrypted YAML, aube lockfile data in `mise.lock`, `pnpm-lock.yaml` for task change detection, `gh`/`glab` host files, and structured config merges.

### One visible change: YAML env files keep values as written

Unquoted values in a YAML env file used to go through YAML's number parsing, so some were silently rewritten. They are now passed through exactly as written:

```yaml
# .env.yaml, loaded with _.file = ".env.yaml"
VERSION: 1.10
PORT_HEX: 0x1F90
```

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `VERSION` | `1.1` | `1.10` |
| `PORT_HEX` | `8080` | `0x1F90` |

Booleans stay `true`/`false`, `yes`/`on` stay strings as before, and null, list or mapping values are still errors. The env docs and `e2e/env/test_env_file` cover this.

### What this does not do

`unsafe-libyaml` stays in `Cargo.lock`. `rattler_conda_types` (conda backend) depends on `serde_yaml` unconditionally, and `rops` uses it for sops YAML files, so the `deny.toml` ignore for RUSTSEC-2024-0449 from jdx/mise#14326 is still needed.

### Implementation

- `mise-util` has a new `yaml` module: `from_str`/`to_string` with mise's parser options, plus an order-preserving `Value`/`Mapping` for code that reads YAML without a fixed schema. Its options make only `true`/`false` booleans when a value has no declared type, matching `serde_yaml`; by default `serde-saphyr` would also read `yes`, `on` and `y` as `true`.
- Structured config merges (`src/system/edits.rs`) compare and prune YAML on `yaml-edit`'s lossless syntax tree, so tags such as `!include` and `!secret` count when comparing values and keep their place when missing keys are filled in. When either document uses anchors, aliases or `<<` merge keys, which the syntax tree does not resolve, both are compared as parsed values instead, as before. A pair using both tags and aliases is an error. `serde-saphyr` still validates the syntax first.
- An in-place YAML merge now has to produce exactly the target with the source merged in, or it is refused. Previously, on `main` too, merging `kid: {y: 2}` into `base: &b {x: 1}` / `kid: *b` replaced the alias and silently dropped `kid.x`.
- A non-finite float with no declared type (`.inf`, `.nan`, `1e999`) is a parse error. Without that, `serde-saphyr` would hand it over as the string `".inf"`. Typed fields, including env file values, are not affected.
- `aqua-registry` reads scalar strings and string maps (`replacements: {386: i686}`) through serde visitors and exposes `RegistryYaml::from_yaml`, whi

Fixes the two CI failures blocking the 2026.10.9 release PR (jdx/mise#14297) and every other open PR. Only a test and the `cargo deny` config change; mise's behavior is unchanged.

**Aqua registry test fixture.** `test_baked_registry_numeric_replacement_keys` checks that a numeric replacement key (`386`) survives baking the aqua registry, using `sharkdp/hyperfine`. It reaches mise only through `serde_yaml` (mise, mise-util, the aqua-registry build, rattler, rops), and there is no safe upgrade. It is added to the `deny.toml` ignore list alongside the existing `proc-macro-error2` entry. Moving off `serde_yaml` is a separate change.

**Validation.** All seven `test_baked_registry*` tests pass with `main`'s vendored registry and with the release branch's `vendor/aqua-registry` swapped in. `cargo deny check advisories` fails on RUSTSEC-2024-0449 without the ignore and passes with it.

title: fix(schema): accept [bootstrap.secrets]
body:
`[bootstrap.secrets]` was missing from the JSON schema, so a strict schema checker such as tombi rejected any config that used it, even though mise reads it:

```toml
[bootstrap.secrets]
github_token = "GITHUB_TOKEN"
"deploy.key" = { env = "DEPLOY_KEY", description = "Deploy key", allow_empty = true }
```

The schema now describes it the way `src/system/secrets.rs` reads it:

- **The key is the secret name.** It uses ASCII letters, digits, `.`, `_` or `-`.
- **The value is an environment variable name**, either as a string or as a table with `env`, `description` and `allow_empty`.

The table form rejects unknown keys. mise silently ignores a misspelled option such as `allow_emty = true`, which leaves `allow_empty` at its default, so the schema is where that typo can be caught.

This takes over #12789 by @risu729, which pr-closer closed after 7 days of failing checks on the fork run. They are credited as co-author. CodeRabbit and Greptile both left the same open thread on #12789: add `additionalProperties: false` to the table form. This PR does that.

## Validation

- `e2e/config/test_schema_tombi`:
  - The strict `mise.toml` fixture now declares both forms above.
  - Three new fixtures must each fail:
    - an unknown key: `"allow_emty" is not allowed`;
    - an invalid variable name `1BAD`: `does not match the pattern ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$`;
    - an invalid secret name `bad name`: `does not match the pattern ^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$`.
- Ran tombi 0.9.22: with `main`'s schema the `mise.toml` fixture fails, and with this PR's it passes. The three invalid fixtures fail with the messages above.
- With mise 2026.10.5, `mise bootstrap secrets status` gave these results:
  - It lists both secrets above.
  - It accepts `allow_emty` without a word.
  - It rejects `1BAD` (`invalid environment variable name`) and `bad name` (`invalid bootstrap secret name`). These are the same rules the schema now applies.

title: fix(task): bump gix so remote tasks work in git hooks
body:
## Problem

I ship a few tools as remote mise tasks ([qctl](https://github.com/victor-software-house/qctl), [verctl](https://github.com/victor-software-house/verctl), [forkctl](https://github.com/victor-software-house/forkctl)) and run them from git hooks. On a fresh machine, or with a stale cache, the first commit fails while mise fetches them:

```text
error: invalid object 100644 8f8c4eb for '.ctl/operator/SKILL.md.jinja'
error: Error building trees
```

Git sets `GIT_INDEX_FILE` for hooks, and gix has honored it when cloning since 0.87, so the clone writes over the commit's index.

## Fix

I fixed it in gitoxide with its maintainer ([GitoxideLabs/gitoxide#3035](https://github.com/GitoxideLabs/gitoxide/pull/3035)), and it shipped in gix 0.89.0. This PR updates mise to it:

- `cargo update -p gix --precise 0.89.0` (only `Cargo.lock` changes)
- drops six `map_err(gix::Exn::into_error)` calls that 0.89 no longer needs
- adds an e2e case where a pre-commit hook runs an uncached remote task and the commit should only contain the staged file

## Verification

The new e2e case fails on gix 0.88 and passes on 0.89. The other remote task e2e tests, the related unit tests, clippy (`-D warnings`), `cargo deny` and the MSRV check all pass. I also reproduced the original failure on macOS with mise 2026.10.7.

## Author review

I used AI assistance writing the code, and I have manually reviewed and validated the solution. Happy to change anything you'd like done differently, and any blunders left are on me.

Thanks for mise, love your work!

title: fix(dotfiles): restore config entries when adopting under a symlinked home
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/654
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes the problems reported in discussion #14287 on machines where `/home` is a symlink (Fedora Atomic / secureblue: `/home` → `/var/home`).

## What was wrong

- **`mise dot origin set` warned "Not portable for setup sharing: ~/.config/mise/config.toml"** even though the file is under the mise config directory. The path was compared unresolved against resolved roots.
- **`mise bootstrap --adopt` restored `home/` entries but none of the `config/` entries** on a fresh machine whose `~/.config/mise` did not exist yet. That directory was resolved lexically (`/home/user/.config/mise`) while `$HOME` was resolved (`/var/home/user`), so incoming `config/...` files were filed as `home/.config/mise/...` and dropped.
- **`mise bootstrap --adopt https://user:TOKEN@host/repo.git` silently fell back to a plain clone** into `~/.config/mise`, leaving the token in `.git/config`.

## After this change

- The warning is gone; the normal "Not enrolled … `mise dot track`" hint is shown instead.
- Adopting from a repo that tracks `config/config.toml`, `config/files/x` and `~/.gitconfig` under a symlinked home now writes all 3 files (before: 1).
- A credentialed `--adopt` URL fails without cloning or echoing the token:

```
Error: setup repository URLs must not contain credentials, query parameters, or fragments; use a Git credential helper or SSH agent
```

This is a behavior change: `--adopt` with a credentialed URL on an ordinary (non-setup) repository used to work through the plain clone and now fails.

## Validation

Reproduced both symlink problems with a symlinked `$HOME`; added a unit test for `normalize` and the e2e `test_bootstrap_adopt_rejects_credentials`. `cargo test --lib system::history`, clippy with `-D warnings`, and the existing `--adopt` e2e tests pass. I did not reproduce the reporter's `reconcile repository conflicts first: config/config.toml` error; it may have come from state left by their credentialed attempt.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: 2.1.295.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes path normalization used during adopt/sync and makes credentialed `--adopt` URLs fail where they previously fell back to a plain git clone.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes **bootstrap `--adopt`** and **origin enrollment checks** when `$HOME` (or ancestors) are symlinks, and blocks credentialed adopt URLs from being cloned into config.
> 
> **Path resolution:** `normalize` now falls back to `normalize_target` when the leaf path does not exist, so a missing `~/.config/mise` resolves through the same symlinked home as an existing tree. `mise dot origin set` prerequisite checks use `normalize_target` before `would_capture` / `branch_path`, fixing wrong “not portable” warnings and restoring **`config/`** entries during adopt ins

title: fix(brew): preserve protected post-install copy destinations
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/653
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Homebrew serializes protected `copy` steps with `overwrite: false`. mise previously ignored that setting, so a post-install step could replace a file Homebrew would protect.

Copy steps now resolve the same destination Homebrew checks, including when the target is an existing directory, and refuse an existing protected destination. Absent file and recursive-directory destinations continue to be copied.

Compatibility note: Homebrew’s current executor guards this case with `destination.exist?`; its `Pathname#exist?` is false for dangling symlinks. mise intentionally preserves that source behavior rather than treating a dangling link as an existing protected destination.

Validation: the focused post-install unit tests passed in a disposable Rust 1.95 container (7 passed). The dangling-symlink compatibility behavior was verified in a disposable Ruby 3.4 container.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: openai/GPT-5; version: unavailable.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes file-write behavior during brew bottle post-install; incorrect logic could skip needed copies or still clobber user config, though scope is limited to declarative copy steps with explicit overwrite semantics.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Homebrew post-install `copy` steps** now honor **`overwrite: false`**, matching Homebrew instead of always replacing the destination.
> 
> Copy resolves the real destination path via **`copy_destination`** (when the target is a directory, the protected path is `target/source_basename`). If `overwrite` is explicitly `false` and that path already exists, the step errors and leaves the file unchanged; omitting `overwrite` still allows overwrite, unlike `move`/`write`. Protection uses `exists()` (dangling symlinks are not treated as existing, per Homebrew).
> 
> Four unit tests cover protected vs default overwrite, file targets, recursive copies into directories, and existing children under a directory target.

title: docs: self-host DM Sans and JetBrains Mono so they load on mise.jdx.dev
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/652
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

mise.jdx.dev was not showing its intended fonts. Body text fell back to the reader's system font (San Francisco on macOS, Segoe UI on Windows) instead of DM Sans, which jdx/mise#14302 made the reading font. Code fell back to SF Mono or Consolas instead of JetBrains Mono.

**Cause.** Cloudflare's font optimization rewrites the Google Fonts `<link>` in the served HTML into inline `@font-face` rules, and it keeps only Cormorant Garamond. The live HTML has no DM Sans or JetBrains Mono faces, and the browser registers neither. Local and CI builds aren't served through Cloudflare, so they looked correct. JetBrains Mono has been missing in production since before #14302; DM Sans only became visible once the site started using it.

**Fix.** Both families are now served from `docs/public/fonts`, like Roc Grotesk, and dropped from the Google Fonts request:

- **DM Sans:** Google's variable font (weights 100–1000, with optical sizing), upright and italic, latin and latin-ext subsets, about 210 KB in all. A page downloads only the files its text needs, and the upright latin file (63 KB) is preloaded.
- **JetBrains Mono:** the upstream 2.304 webfonts at weights 400, 500, 600 and 700, about 94 KB each, each downloaded only when a page uses that weight. Unlike Google's build, they include the `✓` and box-drawing characters mise prints.
- Both are under the SIL Open Font License 1.1; the license texts sit next to the files.

Cormorant Garamond still loads from Google Fonts, which Cloudflare handles.

In a local production build, "Running tasks" loads DM Sans and JetBrains Mono 400 and 500 from `/fonts/`, with no other Google Fonts request than Cormorant's. hk's markdownlint and prettier pass.

title: fix(npm): give unlocked requests their own install under the identity layout
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/651
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

This follows up on #14307, which fixed the npm tool reported missing in discussion https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14276. A project with a `mise.lock` installs the tool from its locked dependency graph, which is stored as `<version>~aube~<digest>`. Another config with no lockfile then resolves `latest` against installed versions. #14307 made that config report the npm version, but with `install_layout = "identity"` it also made the config run the project's lockfile-built installation:

```
$ mise -C global current npm:inflight
1.0.6
$ mise -C global where npm:inflight
~/.local/share/mise/installs/inflight-p54rj3gd   # the project's graph install
```

The identity layout keeps a graph install to the lockfile that made it. It already did that for a pinned version: `npm:inflight@1.0.6` in the global config never used the project's install, but `npm:inflight@latest` did. Now an unlocked request stands for the npm version and gets its own plain installation. If that plain install is missing, mise reports it as missing and `mise install` adds it, separate from the project's. The project keeps running its graph install, and later lockfile changes in the project no longer change what the global config runs. The legacy layout is unchanged from #14307: it reports the npm version and keeps using the directory that was found.

Requests by version prefix (`"npm:inflight" = "1.0"`), an installed fuzzy match, and package.json semver ranges also resolve against installed versions. Before this change they still took the private name as the version:

```
$ mise -C global current npm:inflight   # "npm:inflight" = "1.0"
1.0.6~aube~883b3ea0f0f63119
```

They now get the same handling as `latest`. pipx tools installed from a uv graph (`~uv~`) are treated the same way.

Note that `mise where npm:inflight` with no version re-resolves the configured request without reading `mise.lock`. Inside a locked project under the identity layout, it can therefore print the plain install while `mise ls --current` and the shims use the graph install. This was already true for pinned versions and is not changed here.

### Validation
- `backend/test_npm_aube_unlocked_latest` now runs `latest` and a `1.0` prefix in an unlocked config under both layouts, next to a project locked with `mise lock`. Identity layout: the version is reported without `~aube~`, the unlocked config is missing until `mise install` adds a separate plain install, the prefix request uses that plain install, and the project still runs its graph install. Legacy layout: both requests use the found directory. The test fails on `main`. With only the fuzzy-match path left unconverted, the prefix case fails with `1.0.6~aube~883b3ea0f0f63119`.
