title: fix(go): read an exact go line in go.mod as the toolchain version
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/650
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

With `go` in `idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools`, a `go.mod` like this triggered the `go`-directive deprecation warning:

```text [go.mod]
module example.com/app

go 1.27.1
```

The warning said to add a `toolchain go1.27.1` line, but `go mod tidy` deletes a `toolchain` line that matches the `go` line ([golang/go#75331](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/75331)). So following the advice left a `go.mod` that tidy rewrote, `go mod tidy` CI checks failed, and the warning came back ([discussion](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14286)).

Go treats those two files as the same. Its [toolchain docs](https://go.dev/doc/toolchain) say "a `go.mod` that says `go 1.21.0` with no `toolchain` line is interpreted as if it had a `toolchain go1.21.0` line." mise now reads them the same way: with no `toolchain` line, an exact `go X.Y.Z` line selects that Go version without a warning. This applies to `go.mod` and `go.work`.

| File | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `go 1.27.1` | 1.27.1, deprecation warning | 1.27.1, no warning |
| `go 1.27.0` + `toolchain go1.27.1` | 1.27.1 | 1.27.1 |
| `go 1.27` | latest 1.27.x, deprecation warning | unchanged; stops being read in 2026.11.0 |
| `go.work` with only `go 1.27.1` | nothing | 1.27.1 |
| `go 1.27.1` + `toolchain default` | 1.27.1, deprecation warning | unchanged |

`idiomatic_version_file_ignore_minimum_versions` still skips `go 1.27`, but it no longer skips an exact `go 1.27.1`.

## Why an exception to the minimum-version rule

mise doesn't read fields that only declare a minimum, such as `package.json` `engines`. Strictly, Go treats both `go` and `toolchain` as minimums: with the default `GOTOOLCHAIN=auto` it runs a newer local toolchain when one is installed. mise reads these lines anyway because the `go` command writes the version it runs into them (`go mod init`, `go get`, `go work init`), so they record the Go the project was last developed with. `go 1.27` without a patch names no release, so it stays deprecated. A `toolchain` line that isn't a release, such as `toolchain default`, cancels the implied toolchain, as it does in Go.

## Validation

- Unit tests for `go.mod` and `go.work` parsing cover exact and partial `go` lines, with and without a `toolchain` line, and with the ignore setting.
- `e2e/core/test_go_from_gomod` and `e2e/core/test_go_from_gowork` check the resolved version and that no deprecation warning is printed.

title: fix(npm): resolve unlocked latest to the npm version of a graph-locked install
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/649
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Discussion https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14276 reports this bug. Suppose a project with a lockfile installs an npm tool. mise builds that install from the locked dependency graph and stores it as `<version>~aube~<digest>`. Another config that asks for the same tool as `latest` without a lockfile (typically the global config) resolves `latest` to the newest installed version. It used that private directory name as the version:

```
PS (global)> mise ls
Tool            Version                              Source                      Requested
prettier        3.9.9 (missing) [prettier-djym7d3g]  ~\.config\mise\config.toml  latest
prettier        3.9.9 [prettier-zk2ialuk]
mise WARN  missing: prettier@3.9.9~aube~b9c537a2e2590f84
PS (global)> prettier -h
mise ERROR Tool not installed for shim: prettier
```

With `install_layout = "identity"`, the suffixed name was hashed into an installation identity that nothing has. The tool showed as missing and its shims failed even though it was installed. With the legacy layout the tool still ran, but the private name leaked into `mise current`, env and warnings as if it were the version.

Now, when `latest` resolves to an installed version, mise uses the npm version (`3.9.9`) and keeps pointing at the installation it found. This is the same normalization `mise lock` got in #13542. In the identity layout the found name is a compatibility link, so the installation is looked up through that link rather than by re-hashing the name. Pinning `prettier@3.9.9` in the global config was the workaround and is no longer needed.

### Validation
- New e2e `backend/test_npm_aube_unlocked_latest`: installs `npm:inflight@latest` from a lockfile in one directory, then resolves `latest` without a lockfile in another. It checks `mise current`, `ls --missing`, `ls` and `env` show no `~aube~` name or missing tool, and `where` points at the graph install. It runs under both layouts. Before the fix it failed in both (identity layout: `1.0.6 (missing) [inflight-jfo7ej4u]`). With the compatibility-link lookup removed, the identity-layout `where` check fails.
- `test_npm_aube*`, `cli/test_install_layout*`, and the `tool_version`/`lockfile`/`install_layout`/`npm` unit tests pass. One `tool_version` unit test, `has_linked_version_ignores_mise_managed_absolute_targets`, fails in this sandbox with and without this change. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes.

title: feat(bootstrap): add apt repositories and PPAs with [bootstrap.apt.sources]
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/648
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Ubuntu's own git, fish, and many other packages lag well behind upstream, and vendor tools such as Docker ship from their own apt repositories. Until now, getting either into a bootstrap meant a `pre-packages` hook that ran `add-apt-repository` or wrote source files and keys by hand ([discussion](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14290)).

You can now declare those repositories next to the packages that come from them:

```toml
[bootstrap.apt.sources]
git-core = { ppa = "git-core/ppa" }
fish = { ppa = "fish-shell/release-4" }

[bootstrap.apt.sources.docker]
uris = "https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu"
components = "stable"
key = "https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg"
fingerprint = "9DC8 5822 9FC7 DD38 854A E2D8 8D81 803C 0EBF CD88"

[bootstrap.packages]
"apt:git" = "latest"
"apt:fish" = "latest"
"apt:docker-ce-cli" = "latest"
```

```console
$ mise bootstrap packages apply --dry-run
fetch the signing key for ppa:git-core/ppa into /etc/apt/keyrings/mise-git-core.gpg
write /etc/apt/sources.list.d/mise-git-core.sources
...
apt-get update
apt-get install -y -- git fish docker-ce-cli
```

On Ubuntu 24.04 this installs git 2.55 from the PPA (noble ships 2.43), fish 4.9, and docker-ce-cli.

## Behavior

- **Files.** Each source becomes `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/mise-<name>.sources` (deb822) with `Signed-By` pointing at `/etc/apt/keyrings/mise-<name>.gpg`. apt trusts that key only for that repository, unlike a key dropped into `trusted.gpg.d`.
- **PPAs.** mise reads the signing key fingerprint from the Launchpad API and downloads the key from `keyserver.ubuntu.com`. `software-properties-common` is not needed. A `fingerprint` pins the key and skips the Launchpad lookup. PPAs are added only on Ubuntu or on releases that set `UBUNTU_CODENAME` (for example Linux Mint, which uses its Ubuntu base codename). Elsewhere they are skipped, so one config also works on Debian.
- **Other repositories.** These need `uris`, `key`, and `fingerprint`. `suites` defaults to the release codename (on derivatives such as Mint, the Ubuntu base codename), and `components` defaults to `main` (none for a flat `.../` suite). `architectures` is optional.
- **Key checking.** From the downloaded key, mise keeps only the certificates whose fingerprints you declared, and fails if one is missing. Short key IDs are rejected. A key that is already on disk and matches is not downloaded again. If it is missing or has changed, it is replaced on the next apply. A PPA without a pinned fingerprint gets its key again whenever its source changes, for example when the name is pointed at another PPA. A PPA entry accepts at most one fingerprint.
- **Package lists.** Sources are applied when the apt manager runs: during `mise bootstrap` (after the `pre-packages` hook), `mise bootstrap packages apply`/`upgrade`, and `packages use apt:…`. Dry runs included. When a source changes, m

title: fix(docker): install libatomic1 in the Debian image so Node.js 26 runs
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/645
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Node.js 26's Linux build links against `libatomic.so.1`, which `debian:trixie-slim` does not ship. In the official `-debian` image (`ghcr.io/jdx/mise:<version>-debian`, `jdxcode/mise:<version>-debian`), `mise install node@26` downloaded Node and then failed its post-install check:

```console
$ docker run --rm jdxcode/mise:2026.10.7-debian mise install node@26.9.0
mise ERROR Failed to install core:node@26.9.0: /mise/installs/node/26.9.0/bin/node exited with non-zero status: exit code 127; last stderr: /mise/installs/node/26.9.0/bin/node: error while loading shared libraries: libatomic.so.1: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory

title: docs(bootstrap): explain when to use --from versus --adopt
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/643
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

The [Start from a repository](https://mise.jdx.dev/bootstrap.html#starting-from-a-repository) docs said which flag matches which repository layout, but not when you would want each one. Readers could not tell that `--from` is for applying a separate setup project, such as a team's workstation repository, while `--adopt` makes the repository this machine's own configuration from then on.

Both the bootstrap overview and [Bootstrap from a repository](https://mise.jdx.dev/bootstrap/from-repository.html) now open with that distinction:

- `--from` keeps a checkout of the project in `$MISE_DATA_DIR/bootstrap-repo`, runs bootstrap from it, and does not clone anything into `~/.config/mise`.
- `--adopt` makes the repository your global mise config, or restores a setup repository of tracked dotfiles and keeps it in sync.

The `--from` section also states two facts the page left out:

- The checkout stays for later runs. The table said "Rerun the same command to apply the project again", but a rerun without `--update` reuses the old checkout. It now says to rerun with `--update` to apply new commits.
- Your global config still loads during a `--from` run, so its `[bootstrap.packages]` and hooks apply alongside the project's. I checked this with an isolated `HOME` whose global config and project each declared a `pre-packages` hook: `mise bootstrap --from` ran both.

Fixes #14292

title: fix(dotfiles): keep existing ciphertext when an encrypted file is unchanged
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/642
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A machine that adopted a dotfiles setup could no longer sync once another machine edited an encrypted file. `mise dot sync` failed with:

```
repository application paused: reconcile repository conflicts first: home@work/.secret
```

**Trigger.** Encrypted files (`encrypt = true` with `[history.encryption] recipients`) are encrypted with age, which produces different ciphertext every time. mise keeps a local cache so an unchanged file reuses its ciphertext, but a fresh machine has no cache. After `mise bootstrap --adopt`, the second machine's first checkpoint encrypted the unchanged file again and wrote new ciphertext into history. When the first machine then edited and synced the file, Git saw both sides changing it and paused sync. This showed up most clearly for a profile variant that was inactive on the second machine, because mise did not merge that path for it.

**Fix.** When the cache has no entry for a file, mise now checks the ciphertext already in history. If it decrypts to the same content and mode for the same recipients, mise reuses it and seeds the cache. If anything differs, or this machine cannot decrypt it, mise encrypts as before. Changing recipients still re-encrypts.

### Example

```bash
# machine A
mise -E work dot save        # "~/.secret" = { mode = "track", encrypt = true, variants = [{ profile = "work" }] }
mise -E work dot sync
# machine B
mise -E work bootstrap --adopt <origin>
mise dot save                # profile inactive
# machine A edits ~/.secret, saves, syncs
mise dot sync                # machine B: before, paused on a conflict; now succeeds
mise -E work dot pull --yes  # machine B: receives the edit
```

### Validation

- New e2e test `cli/test_dotfiles_adopt_encrypted_reuse` runs the steps above. It also checks that, after the adopt, the second machine's history holds the same blob as the origin. On `origin/main` that check fails, and so does the `dot sync` step.
- Existing encryption e2e tests pass: `save_re_encrypt`, `encrypted_capture`, `encrypted_diff`, `sync_files_encrypted`, `destination_variants`, `history_bootstrap`, and `adopt_take_remote`.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes, and so does `cargo +1.95 check --all-features`.

title: feat(http): add libc() and avx2() template functions
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/641
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Some tools publish one download per libc or CPU level: bun, opencode and others name their Linux builds `-musl` and their no-AVX2 x64 builds `-baseline`. A `url` template could not choose between them, because it only had `os()` and `arch()`, so an `http:` registry entry could only cover glibc machines with AVX2.

Two template functions fix that. Like `os()` and `arch()`, they take keywords that rename the value:

```toml
url = "https://example.com/my-tool-{{ os() }}-{{ arch() }}{{ avx2(yes="", no="-baseline") }}{{ libc(gnu="", musl="-musl") }}.tgz"
```

- `libc()` returns `gnu` or `musl`. It uses the same detection as the platform key and honors the `libc` setting.
- `avx2()` returns `yes` or `no`. Only x86-64 CPUs can report `no`.

Both are deferred at config load and resolve for the target during `mise lock`, from the target's `musl` / `baseline` qualifier, the same way `os_family()` does. An `http:` tool whose URL uses either function now locks every variant (`linux-x64`, `-baseline`, `-musl`, `-musl-baseline`), and a no-AVX2 host looks up the `-baseline` key, so install and lock agree on the artifact.

> **Medium Risk**

> **Overview**
> Adds **`libc()`** and **`avx2()`** Tera helpers (like `os()` / `arch()`) so HTTP download URLs can suffix **musl** and **no-AVX2 baseline** builds. Host install uses runtime libc detection and `host_has_avx2()`; **`mise lock`** and **`get_tera_for_target`** map lock qualifiers (`musl`, `baseline`, `musl-baseline`) to those values, and deferred config templates preserve the calls for later rendering.

> The **HTTP backend** detects `libc()` / `avx2()` in URL templates, expands lock **platform variants** accordingly, and uses a **`baseline`** (or **`musl-baseline`**) platform key on x64 hosts without AVX2 so locked installs pick the right artifact. **`get_platform_key_for`** / **`platform_variants_for`** on the backend trait wire lock, install, and stub generation to per-request options. title: fix(oci): ignore host apt hooks when installing apt bootstrap packages
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/639
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise oci build` with `[bootstrap.packages]` apt entries such as `"apt:cmake" = "latest"` failed for non-root users with:

```
debconf: DbDriver "passwords" warning: could not open /var/cache/debconf/passwords.dat: Permission denied
touch: setting times of '/var/lib/update-notifier/dpkg-run-stamp': Permission denied
E: Sub-process /usr/bin/dpkg returned an error code (1)
```

mise runs the host's `apt-get` against the unpacked image rootfs. apt reads the host's `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d` before `-o` overrides apply, so host hooks (debconf's `dpkg-preconfigure`, update-notifier's stamp `touch`, PackageKit notifications) ran against the host system instead of the image. Packages that trigger them, like cmake, failed; simple ones like `zlib1g` did not.

mise now passes apt a `-c` config file that clears the pre/post-invoke hook lists (`-o` cannot empty a list option), so only the image's own package scripts run.

Fixes #14291

Validation: added a unit test that the config removes a host hook; `cargo clippy --lib --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean. I could not run a full `mise oci build` with cmake (needs network and an apt mirror), so the reporter's config is unconfirmed end to end.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: 2.1.293.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Scoped to OCI apt bootstrap invocation arguments; no auth or data-path changes, with a targeted regression test.
> 
> **Overview**
> OCI apt bootstrap installs now pass a temporary **`-c`** config that **`#clear`s** host `DPkg`/`APT` pre- and post-invoke hook lists before `apt-get update`/`install` run against the image rootfs.
> 
> That stops debconf, update-notifier, and similar hooks loaded from the host’s `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d` from touching host paths (which broke non-root `mise oci build` for packages like cmake). **`-o` alone could not empty those list options**, so the dedicated config file is required.
> 
> `apt_root_args` takes the config path and prepends `-c`; a unit test uses `apt-config dump` to assert a simulated host hook disappears when `APT_CLEAR_HOST_HOOKS` is applied.
>

title: registry: install opencode 2 from npm
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/638
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise use opencode@latest` stayed on OpenCode 1 (1.18.35) because the `opencode` shorthand only used `aqua:anomalyco/opencode`, which installs from GitHub releases. OpenCode 2 is not published there; it ships on npm as `@opencode/cli`.

The shorthand now lists `npm:@opencode/cli` first with `min_version = "2.0.0"`, and keeps aqua for older versions, the same way hk and dagu handle packslip:

```console
$ mise latest opencode
2.0.26
$ mise latest opencode@1
1.18.35
$ mise x opencode@latest -- opencode --version
opencode v2.0.26
```

`allow_builds` is set for `@opencode/cli` because its postinstall script links the platform binary; without it the install fails with "postinstall script was not run".

Users on `opencode@latest` will move to v2 on their next upgrade; `opencode@1` keeps v1.

Fixes #14294

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: 2.1.293.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Brew changes run post-install subprocesses and mutate prefix `etc`/`var` during every pour; failures are softened to warnings, which can leave formulae half-configured. The opencode registry switch affects default installs for users on `opencode@latest`.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Bootstrap `brew` pours now mirror more of `brew install` after the bottle lands.** Formula metadata gains `post_install_steps` from the Homebrew API. During pour, mise copies `etc`/`var` from the keg’s `.bottle` tree into the prefix (existing files are kept; the bottle copy is written as `*.default`), then runs declarative post-install steps while still holding the commit lock. A new `post_install` module implements generic step types (`symlink`, `copy`, `move`, `remove`, `mkdir_p`, `touch`, `write`, `set_permissions`, `run`); unsupported or failing steps warn and do not fail the install. Docs and a Linux e2e (`openssl@4` / `ca-certificates`) cover cert bundles and re-pour behavior.
> 
> **Separately, the `opencode` registry shorthand prefers OpenCode 2.x from npm** (`npm:@opencode/cli` with `min_version = "2.0.0"` and `allow_builds`), with `aqua:anomalyco/opencode` kept for 1.x; `bins = ["opencode"]` is declared.
>

title: test(http): stop the allow_html test waiting out the https retry
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/637
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`test_text_request_allow_html_returns_the_page` (added in #14253) times out on every run, which fails `unit-macos` on main (run 38058688044) and reproduces locally on Linux.

Its second half checks that an HTML page is still rejected without `allow_html()`. For an `http://` URL, `TextRequest::send` retries as `https://` first. That retry sends a TLS hello to the plain-HTTP canned server, which drains until `\r\n\r\n` and so blocks until the 2s client timeout. nextest's CI ceiling is 1s, so both attempts are killed.

The test now uses a small inline listener for that half: it answers the first connection with the HTML and drops the second, so the https retry fails immediately. The test goes from timing out to 0.03s, and all 34 `http::tests::retry` tests pass. No production code changes.

title: fix(dotfiles): stop a newly selected profile from deleting its shared file
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/635
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A tracked file with a profile variant can lose its shared copy when a second machine turns that profile on.

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.work-settings" = { mode = "track", variants = [{ profile = "work" }] }
```

**Before:**

1. Machine A saves `~/.work-settings` under the `work` profile and syncs.
2. Machine B runs `mise bootstrap --adopt` with the profile inactive, so the file is not restored there. That's expected.
3. On B, `mise -E work dot pull` says "nothing to apply", and `mise -E work dot status` reports `~/.work-settings` as an unsaved change.
4. The next `mise -E work dot sync` on B publishes a **deletion**, and the file disappears from the shared repository.

This was reported in [omacom/omarchy discussion 3796](https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/discussions/3796#discussioncomment-18850236). Switching a profile off, letting another machine edit the file, and switching it back on reverted that edit the same way.

The cause: B's local history carries every stream, including one another machine wrote while it wasn't selected on B. Once the profile was selected, B treated that saved version as its own. The missing (or older) live file then looked like an edit made on B.

**After:**

- `mise -E work dot status` on B shows `not applied here: ~/.work-settings (saved by another machine while not selected here); mise dot pull applies them`, not "unsaved changes".
- Saves leave that file's saved version alone until it is applied. An explicit `mise dot save` says so.
- `mise -E work dot pull` applies it. If B left the profile at an older version and hasn't changed the file since, the pull applies the newer one as an ordinary update.
- If B has a different copy of its own, the pull stops with a conflict. `--take-remote <path>` takes the shared version. `--keep-local <path>` followed by `mise dot save <path>` publishes B's.

## Limitations

- `--keep-local` works only on a tracked file. Inside a tracked directory that another machine saved while the profile was inactive here, take the shared version with `--take-remote`, then copy yours back and save it. Keeping a single file would otherwise save the directory's other files too.
- `--take-remote` on such a file cannot be undone, because this machine never saved its own copy. The docs say to copy the file aside first.

## How it works

mise now keeps a small per-machine record in the history index (`held.json`): the streams that were selected at the last save, and the version each one had when it was last deselected. A selected stream counts as held when:

- it stayed selected,
- its saved version is unchanged since it was last selected here,
- nothing is saved for it, or
- its live files already match the saved version.

For a stream that isn't held, a save carries the saved version forward, the way manual-save entries are carried. Sync uses the live file as this machine's side, with no shared baseli

title: fix(backend): keep decoded download file names inside the download directory
body:
Several backends name a download after the last segment of its URL and save it under the tool's download directory, using `get_filename_from_url`. aqua does this for artifacts and for checksum, signature and provenance files. That name could point outside the directory:

| URL ends with | file name before | file name now |
|---|---|---|
| `tool%2F..%2Fpwned.tar.gz` | `tool/../pwned.tar.gz` | `tool%2F..%2Fpwned.tar.gz` |
| `pkg%00x.tar.gz` | `pkg` + NUL + `x.tar.gz` | `pkg%00x.tar.gz` |
| `C%3Atool.zip` (Windows) | `C:tool.zip` | `C%3Atool.zip` |
| `C:payload` (Windows, literal) | `C:payload` | `download` |

Joined under the download directory, `tool/../pwned.tar.gz` lands outside it. On Windows, a name with `:` names a drive, so `Path::join` discards the directory altogether.

Two rules now apply:

- **The decoded name cannot be one path component.** That means an empty name, `.`, `..`, a `/` or NUL, and on Windows its reserved characters, control characters and a trailing space or dot. The encoded segment is kept instead, because it is inert. These are the same rules brew casks already use for their staged downloads, after #13431 (`is_unusable_file_name` in `src/system/packages/brew/cask/state.rs`).
- **The encoded segment itself would also leave the directory.** That is a literal `.`, `..`, `/`, NUL, or on Windows a `\` or `:`. The name falls back to `download`, as for a URL with no file name.

Ordinary escapes still decode: `We%2DAre%2DThe%2DChampions.zip` is still `We-Are-The-Champions.zip`, and `my%20tool.zip` is still `my tool.zip`.

The name also keys checksum lookups, so these rules change it only when the decoded name is unusable. A Windows name with a literal trailing dot, such as `tool.`, comes out the same as before. One written as `tool%2E` now stays encoded.

This takes over #13438 by @hktitof, which pr-closer closed after 7 days without contributor activity. They are credited as co-author. Review threads on #13438:

- **CodeRabbit (Major, path traversal).** A literal `C:payload` segment fell back to itself and escaped the directory on Windows. Fixed by the second rule above.
- **Greptile (checksum names).** Its concern was that rewriting a name breaks checksum matching. That is why a usable name, and a literal trailing dot, are left as before.
- **CodeRabbit (Windows device names).** It covered names like `CON.exe` and their superscript-digit variants. Not taken up: they do not leave the directory, casks do not handle them either, and they belong in a separate change.

## Validation

- `test_get_filename_from_url` gains a row for each case in the table. It also covers a bare `..` and `%2E%2E`, and checks that an ordinary escape still decodes. Inside a URL, the parser already drops an encoded dot segment, so that path yields `download`.
- A standalone copy of the old and new function, built with the same `url` 2.5.8 and `urlencoding` 2.1.3, gave the results in the table on Windows. Every pre-existing row came out unchanged, and so d

title: fix(brew): install bottle etc files and run post_install_steps when pouring
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/634
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Formulae poured by `mise bootstrap packages apply` (brew) skipped two things `brew install` does, so some tools broke at runtime. For example, with

```toml
[bootstrap.packages]
"brew:openssl@4" = "latest"
```

neither `etc/ca-certificates/cert.pem` nor `etc/openssl@4/` was created, so anything linked against the poured `openssl@4` failed certificate verification (`Verify return code: 20`) and `openssl req` couldn't find `openssl.cnf`. Reported in discussion #14254.

## What changes

- **Bottle `etc`/`var` files** are copied into the prefix, as brew does. A file you already have is never overwritten; the bottle's copy lands beside it as `<file>.default`.
- **`post_install_steps`** from the Homebrew API now run after linking. The generic types are implemented: `symlink`, `copy`, `move`, `remove`, `mkdir_p`, `touch`, `write`, `set_permissions`, `run`, with the `on`/`if_exists`/`unless_exists` guards and the common path templates. For `openssl@4` this builds the CA bundle (via `ca-certificates`) and symlinks `etc/openssl@4/cert.pem` to it.
- Tool-specific step types (`compile_gsettings_schemas`, `init_data_dir`, ...) and glob-source steps are skipped with a warning that points at `brew postinstall <formula>`.
- As in Homebrew, a failing step warns and stops the remaining steps; it does not fail the install.

Already-installed kegs are not retroactively fixed; re-pour them or run `brew postinstall`.

## Validation

- Poured `openssl@4` into a scratch prefix on Linux: `etc/ca-certificates/cert.pem`, the `cert.pem` symlink and `etc/openssl@4/openssl.cnf` match the `brew postinstall` output in the report, and `openssl s_client -CAfile etc/openssl@4/cert.pem` to github.com returns 0.
- New unit tests and e2e `test_system_install_brew_post_install` (incl. the `.default` behavior). Clippy `-D warnings` is clean.
- Not run on macOS. 6 `cask_shim_*` unit tests fail in my sandbox; they're in the cask module, which this change doesn't touch.

body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/633
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

IDEs and other programs that can't run mise need a stable installation path that survives version changes. Each tool's install directory now has a `global` link to the version global and system config select:

```text
~/.local/share/mise/installs/maven/
├── 3.9.13/
├── 3.9.16/
└── global -> ./3.9.16
```

Point an IDE's Maven or JDK home at `.../installs/maven/global` and it follows `mise use -g maven@3.9.13`.

- Updated with the other runtime symlinks (`latest`, `3`, ...), so after `mise use -g`, `mise install`, and `mise upgrade`.
- Only global and system config count. Project config and `MISE_*_VERSION` do not change it.
- A tool no global config selects has no link; an existing one is removed.
- A real directory named `global` is left alone.
- Always on; there is no setting to disable it.

Implements discussion [#14263](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14263).

Tested with a new e2e (`test_runtime_symlinks_global`: create, retarget, project override, removal) and `test_install_failure_runtime_symlinks`; clippy is clean.

title: feat(github): add oauth_copy_code to copy the device code to the clipboard
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/632
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise token github --oauth` opens the browser, but you still have to copy the one-time device code by hand. A new setting copies it for you, like `gh auth login --clipboard`:

```toml
[settings.github]
oauth_copy_code = true
```

With the setting left unset in a terminal:

```
$ mise token github --oauth
Open https://github.com/login/device and enter code ABCD-1234 to authorize GitHub access.
? Copy the code to your clipboard? Yes
Copied the code to your clipboard.
```

Only the device code is copied, never the token. mise pipes it to `pbcopy` on macOS, `clip.exe` on Windows and WSL, and `wl-copy`, `xclip` or `xsel` elsewhere. title: registry: test ansible, azure and dvc against python 3.14
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/631
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Python 3.15.0 became the latest release, so every registry test that pulls in `python` unpinned now runs on it. `ansible`, `ansible-core`, `azure` and `dvc` fail there, which fails `test-tool-1/2/3` and `registry-ci` on every PR:

```
error: Distribution `pyyaml==6.0.3` can't be installed because it is marked as `--no-build` but has no binary distribution
fatal error: git2.h: No such file or directory   (building pygit2 for dvc)
```

`pyyaml` and `pygit2` publish wheels only up to cp314, and mise installs from the dependency graph with `--no-build`, so no mise change can make these four install on 3.15 until upstream ships wheels. Every other Python tool installs fine on 3.15.

## Changes

- `registry/{ansible,ansible-core,azure,dvc}.toml`: their tests now declare `tools = ["python@3.14"]`.
- `mise test-tool`: a test that names a dependency itself (such as `python@3.14`) now replaces the unpinned dependency instead of installing `latest` beside it. Without this the pin had no effect.

Drop the pins once those packages publish 3.15 wheels.

## Testing

`MISE_LOCKFILE=1 mise test-tool ansible ansible-core azure dvc` on a clean data dir: all four pass on Python 3.14.8. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` are clean.

title: docs(dotfiles): add a recommended setup and a readable modes-and-keys table
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/630
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Feedback from a chezmoi user trying `mise dot` ([omacom/omarchy discussion 3796](https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/discussions/3796#discussioncomment-18850236)) said two things got in the way:

- **No clear starting point.** The overview covers tracking, symlinks, copies, templates, groups, and edits equally, so `mise dot` looks larger than it needs to be on first read.
- **An unreadable table.** The [modes-and-keys table](https://mise.jdx.dev/dotfiles/reference.html#modes-and-keys) had nine columns and did not fit on screen.

Changes:

- **Recommended setup.** [Dotfiles](https://mise.jdx.dev/dotfiles.html) now opens with a short "Recommended setup" section. It covers the `history-watch` service table, then `mise dot track …`, `mise bootstrap services apply`, `mise dot origin set <url> --sync sync`, and `mise bootstrap --adopt` on the next machine. It links to [Set up a machine](https://mise.jdx.dev/bootstrap/setup.html) for the full walkthrough and says the rest of the pages are optional.
- **Modes and keys.** The table is transposed to one row per kind of entry, with three columns: the entry, the keys it accepts, and the keys it accepts without effect. Every cell of the old table carries over, including the conditions on the source kind (for example, `copy` accepts `manifest` only with a directory source). `track-local` now has its own row instead of a sentence.

Docs only; Prettier passes on both pages.

title: feat(dotfiles): show tracked entries that no variant selects in status
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/629
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A tracked entry can declare variants, so that each machine saves its own version, or only some machines track the file at all:

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.work-settings" = { mode = "track", variants = [{ profile = "work" }] }
```

When no variant matches the machine, for example because the `work` profile is not active, mise neither saves nor pulls that entry here. `mise dot status` still listed it as plain `tracked`, so nothing showed that it was being skipped. A user testing profile variants on two machines could not tell why a file never arrived.

`mise dot status` now names the variants the entry is waiting for:

```console
$ mise dot status
~/.shared         track  ~/.config/mise/config.toml  tracked
~/.work-settings  track  ~/.config/mise/config.toml  not on this machine (variants: work)
$ mise -E work dot status
~/.shared         track  ~/.config/mise/config.toml  tracked
~/.work-settings  track  ~/.config/mise/config.toml  tracked
```

In `--json`, the entry keeps `"state": "tracked"` and gains `"reason": "no variant matches this machine: work"`, so scripts that read `state` are unaffected. The status-states reference documents the new row.

Validation: a new e2e test, `test_dotfiles_status_unselected_variant`, covers the plain and JSON output with the profile on and off.

Reported in [omacom/omarchy discussion 3796](https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/discussions/3796#discussioncomment-18850236).

title: fix(schema): accept outputs = { auto = false } on tasks
body:
The JSON schema allowed only `true` for a task's `outputs = { auto = … }`. `false` loads and runs fine in mise, but editors and linters such as tombi or Taplo flagged it:

```toml
[tasks.build]
run = "cargo build"
outputs = { auto = false }   # tombi: The value must be one of [true], but found false
```

The schema now accepts both booleans. Its description now says what `false` actually does. The parser maps `auto = false` to the same value as leaving `outputs` unset (`src/task/task_sources.rs`). So `false` is not a separate "disable tracking" switch. This is a schema change only, and mise's behavior does not change.

This takes over #12797 by @risu729, which pr-closer closed after 7 days of failing checks on the fork run. They are credited as co-author. #12797 described `false` as disabling automatic tracking. Greptile's open thread there noted that a task inheriting global inputs still gets automatic tracking with `auto = false`. I did not reproduce that, but the parser code above already shows that `false` only means "unset", so the new description says that and nothing more.

## Validation

- `e2e/config/test_schema_tombi` now sets `outputs = { auto = false }` in two places:
  - the `mise.toml` fixture, checked against `schema/mise.json`;
  - the standalone task fixture, checked against `schema/mise-task.json`.
- Ran tombi 0.9.22 on both:
  - With `main`'s schemas, both fail with `The value must be one of [true], but found false`.
  - With this PR's schemas, both pass.
- With mise 2026.10.5, a task with `outputs = { auto = false }` and one with `{ auto = true }` both run.

title: chore(ci): switch to jactionlint v2 and drop zizmor
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/627
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Workflow linting now runs jactionlint v2 with its default profile, which includes the security and policy audits the separate zizmor workflow ran. The zizmor workflow is gone, so contributors have one linter for `.github/`.

To check or fix workflows locally:

```sh
hk check --all --step jactionlint   # or: jactionlint
hk fix --all --step jactionlint     # applies jactionlint --fix
```

## What changed

- `jactionlint` is pinned to `2` in `mise.toml` (lockfile refreshed, same platforms).
- The hk step runs `jactionlint {{ files }}` as the check and `jactionlint --fix {{ files }}` as the fix, and also covers `.github/actions/**/action.y*ml` and `.github/dependabot.y*ml`.
- `.github/workflows/zizmor.yml` is removed. It is not a required check in the `main` ruleset. `registry/zizmor.toml` stays: that is the registry entry for the tool, not our use of it.
- The 7 `# zizmor: ignore[dangerous-triggers]` comments became `# jactionlint ignore=dangerous-triggers` (via `jactionlint --migrate-ignores`, keeping their explanations). The 7 `cache-poisoning` comments on `Swatinem/rust-cache` were stale (nothing is reported without them) and are deleted.

## Findings fixed

The default profile reported 123 findings and now reports 0:

- `jactionlint --fix`: 33 `persist-credentials: false` on checkouts, 4 `concurrency:` blocks, 1 `permissions:`. I reverted one fix: `release-plz.yml` pushes tags with the persisted credential (see below).
- `timeout-minutes` on 24 jobs (10 minutes for small jobs, 15 to 60 for publish, docker and plugin jobs).
- `permissions:` on 23 jobs: `contents: read` at workflow level for the build, test and publish workflows. The `dockerhub` and `merge` docker jobs get `contents: read` plus `packages: write`, because they push to ghcr.io. The repository default token permission is `write`, so these jobs were running with write-all before.
- `set -o pipefail` in 18 scripts that pipe `gh`, `curl`, `jq` and similar, so a failing left-hand command no longer passes silently.
- `concurrency:` on the remaining workflows. Release-event workflows (`copr-publish`, `ppa-publish`, `winget`, `test-plugins`, `auto-merge-release`, `notify-release-failure`) use `cancel-in-progress: false`, so a running publish is never cancelled.
- The concurrency groups of `test-impl.yml`, `test-vfox-impl.yml`, `registry-impl.yml` and `docs-impl.yml` moved to their calling workflows with the same groups and cancel behavior (the rule wants the limit on a workflow whose jobs only call a reusable one).
- `cache-binary: false` on the two `setup-buildx-action` steps that run on release events.

## Ignored on purpose (`.github/jactionlint.yaml`)

Each entry is scoped to a file (and job) and carries a reason:

- `artipacked` in `release-plz.yml`: the release-plz task pushes tags with the checkout's credential.
- `unverified-download` in `cloudflare-deploy.yml`, `npm-publish.yml

title: fix(brew-cask): support generate completions in evaluated casks
body:
The generated completions artifact is parsed, installed, and documented as supported.

However, it is only true when the metadata comes from the Homebrew API. For casks evaluated by mise, `unsupported cask metadata DSL` is raised instead, as neither of the Ruby shims implemented support for the stanza.

This implements support for the stanza on both Ruby shims:

- The metadata shim now emit the artifact in the shape the Rust parser reads. Specifically, casks pass options as symbols, so values have to be stringified alongside the keys as the parser expects strings.
- The lifecycle shim gets an inert stub as all the other completion stanzas.

## Validation

- `cargo check --bin mise`
- `cargo clippy --all-features --tests` (clean)
- `cargo test --lib system::packages::brew::tap` (15 passed, 1 new)
- Verified against a real tapped cask:
  `brew-cask:entireio/tap/entire` fails to evaluate on `2026.10.6` and resolves on this branch.

title: fix(http): retry when a response body drops mid-stream
body:
A request whose response body dropped partway through failed on the first try, even with `http_retries` set. mise already counts a broken body read as transient, and #14049 extended that to an HTTP/2 stream reset during the read. But the retry loop ended once the response headers arrived, and callers read the body afterwards, outside it:

```rust
let resp = self.get_async(url).await?; // retried
let json = resp.json().await?;         // not retried
```

So a version list or release page cut off mid-transfer failed with `error decoding response body`, with no retry.

The retry loop now takes a reader and runs it inside each attempt. These callers read the whole body inside the retry:

- `json` / `json_headers` / `json_headers_with_headers`
- `get_text` and everything built on its request, including the cached variants
- `get_bytes`
- a version list read with `version_regex`. It used to fetch the response and read it outside the loop, so it bypassed `get_text`'s HTML check. It now goes through `get_text` with a new `allow_html()`, which keeps the HTML pages that regex parsing expects.

Callers that need the response itself, such as HEAD, streamed downloads and error-body inspection, pass the response through unchanged, so their behavior is the same. `get_html` is unchanged too: it checks `Content-Type` before reading, and reading inside the retry would download bodies it currently discards.

This takes over #12974 by @Binlogo, which pr-closer closed after 7 days of failing checks. The HTTP client has since moved to `crates/mise-util/src/http.rs`, so this ports the change and does not replay it. They are credited as co-author. The original description gives background: a 27 MB GitHub releases page in `mise-versions` that drops mid-stream. As it says, retrying alone will not always rescue a response that large.

Review threads on #12974:

- **Greptile: the `version_regex` path was still unretried.** Fixed, as described above.
- **CodeRabbit: `json_headers` resolves auth headers before checking offline mode.** Not changed here. That order predates this PR: `get_async` resolved the headers before `get_async_with_headers` checked offline mode. It is a separate fix.

## Validation

- New unit tests in `crates/mise-util/src/http/tests/retry.rs`:
  - `get_text`, `json` and `get_bytes` each get a response cut off before its `Content-Length` on the first attempt and a full one on the second. Each returns the second body after two connections.
  - `allow_html()` returns an HTML page, which is still rejected without it.
- `cargo test -p mise-util --lib -- http::tests::retry` passes all 33 tests with this change, the four new ones among them.
- The three retry tests, run against `main`'s code, fail with `error decoding response body`, the symptom this fixes.

title: fix(lock): decode percent-encoded release tags when checking a locked URL
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/626
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise install` no longer refuses a lockfile entry whose release tag contains `@`.

`mise lock` writes such tags percent-encoded, e.g. `.../download/cli%400.46.0/sentry-darwin-arm64` for getsentry/toolkit's `cli@0.46.0`. The locked-URL check added in #13401 read the raw path, so `%40` glued a `40` onto the version (`400.46.0`) and the install failed against its own entry, with no way to repair it by re-running `mise lock`. The check now percent-decodes the path first, so `cli@0.46.0` matches version `0.46.0`.

Fixes #14250

title: fix(history): skip rewriting unchanged checkpoint metadata on index rebuild
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/625
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Every history index rebuild (after each apply, save and so on) rewrote every file in `$MISE_STATE_DIR/history/index/meta/` through a temp file, rename and fsync, even when the content was identical. On a history with tens of thousands of checkpoints this meant minutes of sustained disk writes per pass, and `mise dot save` failed with `another history operation is running` meanwhile (see #14248).

The rebuild now reads the existing metadata file and only writes it when the bytes differ, so a rebuild with nothing new touches no files.

This does not fix the other half of #14248: machines on a shared origin exchanging empty `apply: applied 0 incoming change(s)` commits forever. I have not found the cause of that yet, so this PR deliberately does not close the issue.

## Test plan

- `cargo test --lib system::history::checkpoint` passes.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Localized I/O optimization in metadata cache writes; behavior is unchanged when content or permissions need updating.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Index rebuilds no longer rewrite every checkpoint metadata file when nothing changed**, which was causing heavy disk I/O (and related lock contention) on large histories.
> 
> `write_meta_cache_in` now goes through `write_json_if_changed`, which compares the serialized JSON to the existing file and **skips the atomic temp-file write/fsync** when the bytes match. JSON writing is centralized in `write_json_text` with a `skip_unchanged` flag; ordinary `write_json` callers behave as before.
> 
> On Unix, **chmod to `0600` is also skipped** when the file is already private, so unchanged metadata files avoid extra inode updates during rebuilds.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 3df8814ce45efc066d62c2440679f0474a56f888. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>

  * Metadata-cache files are left untouched when their contents already match, avoiding unnecessary file updates.
* **Reliability**
  * JSON files are written atomically when contents need updating. Parent directories are created as needed, and Unix files are set to secure permissions when written.

title: fix(schema): reject env required combinations that mise rejects
body:
The JSON schema accepted three `[env]` entries that mise refuses to load, so an editor or linter such as tombi or Taplo showed no error, and the problem only appeared when mise ran:

```toml
[env]
A = { value = "x", required = true }       # error: cannot have both 'value' and 'required'
B = { value = "x", required = "set B" }    # same error
C = { required = false }                   # error: has no value
```

The schema now matches mise:

- **A variable with its own `value`** accepts only `required = false`.
- **A variable without a value** must be `required = true` or a help string.

The `env_required` description now says the same. `{ value = "x", required = false }`, `{ required = true }` and `{ required = "help" }` are still accepted, as they are by mise. This is a schema change only, and mise's behavior does not change.

This takes over #12531 by @risu729, which pr-closer closed after 7 days of failing checks and merge conflicts. It was rebuilt on current `main`. They are credited as co-author.

Review threads on #12531:

- **`age` forms (CodeRabbit, Major).** It asked to reject `required = true` on `age` forms too. Not done, because mise does not reject it: `{ age = "…", required = true }` and `{ age = { value = "…", required = "help" } }` load the same as without `required`, and fail only at decryption, as any undecryptable value does. Rejecting them would make the schema stricter than mise. The `age` branches are unchanged.
- **Separate invalid cases (CodeRabbit).** It noted that putting all invalid cases in one fixture lets one of them hide a regression in another. So each case gets its own file.
- The other threads were about a wider earlier revision and are outdated.

## Validation

- `e2e/config/test_schema_tombi`:
  - The valid `mise-age.toml` fixture had `VALUE_OBJECT = { value = 123, …, required = "set VALUE_OBJECT" }`, a combination mise rejects. It now uses `required = false`, and gains `REQUIRED_HELP = { required = "set REQUIRED_HELP", tools = true }`.
  - Three new fixtures, one per invalid case above, must each fail.
- Ran tombi 0.9.22 against the schema from `main` and from this PR. All three invalid fixtures pass with `main` and fail with this PR, and the valid `mise-age.toml` passes with both.
- With mise 2026.10.4, `mise env` gave these results:
  - `A`, `B` and `C` above fail with the errors shown.
  - `{ value = "x", required = false }`, `{ required = true }` and `{ required = "set X" }` load.

title: feat(npm): warn when a package installs no executables
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/624
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Installing an `npm:` package that has no `bin` used to succeed silently. For example, `mise use npm:lodash` downloaded the package, added it to `mise.toml` and listed it in `mise ls`, but created no shim and put nothing on `PATH`. Project code could not `require` it either, so the tool did nothing. New users can do this when they mix up dev tools and project dependencies.

mise now warns right after such an install:

```console
$ mise use npm:lodash@4
mise WARN  npm:lodash@4.18.1 installed no executables, so mise created no shims for it. npm: tools are for command-line programs; add a library to your project's package.json instead.
mise ✓ npm:lodash@4.18.1  1.5s
```

It is a warning, not an error, because `bin` can change between versions and a package may be installed on purpose just for its files. The warning appears only when an install actually runs, not when the tool is already installed. Packages with a `bin`, such as `npm:prettier`, install exactly as before.

This applies only to `npm:`. The `pipx:`, `cargo:` and `go:` installers already fail on a package that has no binaries.

Requested in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14245.

### Validation

- A new unit test covers the executable check. It uses the same lister that shim generation uses, so the warning matches whether shims get created.
- Ran a real install with an isolated data dir: `npm:lodash@4` warns, while `npm:prettier@3` does not warn and creates its shim.

title: fix(doctor): show dotfiles repo and origin when history is disabled
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/623
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

With `history.enabled = false`, `mise doctor` left out the `dotfiles:` section entirely, so the `repo:` and `origin:` lines added in #14173 never appeared. Now doctor shows a short section when anything is tracked, the history repo exists, or a setup repository is connected:

```
dotfiles:
  1 tracked entry, history disabled (history.enabled = false): nothing is saved or synced
  repo: ~/.local/state/mise/history/repo.git
  origin: file://~/workdir/origin.git (branch main, sync manual)
```

When history is disabled, doctor reads only the declared tracking and never opens or creates the history store. It skips watcher, capture and sync health checks, since none of them run while history is off. If the tracking declaration cannot be read, for example an encrypted entry with an empty `[history.encryption].recipients`, the section reports that error instead of counting zero entries. If nothing is tracked, no history exists and no setup repository is connected, there is still no section.

`mise doctor --json` adds `dotfiles.history_enabled` and `dotfiles.tracking_error`. When `history_enabled` is `false`, `watcher` and `notifications` are `"disabled"`.

Fixes #14241

## Testing

The new e2e test `test_doctor_dotfiles_history_disabled` covers the enabled and disabled text output, the JSON fields, an unreadable tracking declaration, and an empty state that shows no section. `test_dotfiles_watch_cache` and `test_dotfiles_sync_stable` still pass, and clippy with `-D warnings` is clean.

title: feat(upgrade): add --global so self-updating tools can update through mise
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/622
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Coding agents and other tools that update themselves don't know when mise installed them. Their updaters either overwrite the binary inside `installs/<tool>/<version>/` (Copilot CLI, goose, Jules, and pi with the npm backend do this), so mise reports one version while the directory holds another, or they install a second copy outside mise (gemini-cli, Cursor Agent, qwen-code). In both cases mise later offers an update that is already installed. There was also no mise command such a tool could call to update itself without touching the project it happens to be running in.

This adds `--global` to `mise upgrade` and `mise outdated`, alongside the existing `--local`:

```sh
# inside a project whose mise.toml pins claude = "2.1.0"
mise outdated --global claude --json   # reports the global config's request: "latest": "2.1.5"
mise upgrade --global claude           # installs 2.1.5 for the global request
mise x -- claude --version             # still 2.1.0 here; 2.1.5 everywhere else
```

`--global` works on the requests in the global and system config (`~/.config/mise/config.toml`, `/etc/mise/config.toml`), even where a project config or a `MISE_<TOOL>_VERSION` variable sets its own version of the tool. Like an `auto_update` upgrade, the command reruns itself from the filesystem root with the environment mise's activation started from, so a project's config, lockfile, and `[env]` are neither read nor changed, wherever it is run. The upgrade stays within the request and respects `minimum_release_age`, and an exact global version is never moved. A version installed with `mise install --system` is upgraded in the system installs directory. `--bump` writes the global config. A tool the global config doesn't list reports `{}` and installs nothing. `--global` conflicts with `--local` and `--inactive`.

A new docs page, [Self-updating tools](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/self-updating-tools.html), sets out the integration for tool authors:

- **Detect** a mise install from the real path of the executable: an ancestor directory holding `.mise.backend.toml` (default layout) or `.mise-install.toml` (identity layout) names the tool. Environment variables aren't used because child processes inherit them.
- **Check** with `mise outdated --global <tool> --json`, so the tool's "update available" notice agrees with what mise will install.
- **Update** with `mise upgrade --global <tool>` instead of the tool's own updater.
- **Switch a running session** at a safe point by exec'ing `mise x -- <tool> <resume args>`. Re-exec'ing your own path or looking it up on the inherited `PATH` would land back on the old version under shell activation. mise already keeps the old version installed while a process runs from it.

Next, I'll open PRs and issues with the agent projects pointing at this page.

## Validation

- New e2e test `e2e/cli/test_upgrade_global` covers a projec

+---
+description: How a tool that updates itself, such as a coding agent, checks for and installs updates through mise and switches running sessions to the new version.
+socialDescription: Let mise update your tool, and move running sessions onto the new version.
+---
+
+# Self-updating tools
+
+This page is for authors of tools that update themselves, such as coding
+agents, editors, and long-running CLIs. When mise installed your tool, update
+it through mise instead of your own updater.
+
+A built-in updater doesn't know about mise's install directory. It either
+writes the new version over the files in `installs/<tool>/<version>/`, so the
+directory names one version and holds another, or installs a second copy
+elsewhere that mise doesn't manage. mise then reports the old version, offers
+an update that is already installed, and can't verify the files against the
+lockfile. Updating through mise avoids all of that, and the update follows
+the user's version request,
+[`minimum_release_age`](/security.html#minimum-release-age), and `locked`
+setting.
+
+Users who want mise to update tools on its own can set
+[`auto_update`](/dev-tools/#automatic-tool-updates) instead. The steps below
+work with or without it.
+
+## Detect a mise install
+
+Resolve the real path of your executable (for a script, of the script, not of
+its interpreter) and walk up its parent directories. mise installed it if one
+of them contains either file:
+
+| File                 | Layout                                                          | Tool name              |
+| -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
+| `.mise.backend.toml` | `installs/<tool>/<version>/`; the file is in `installs/<tool>/` | the `short` key        |
+| `.mise-install.toml` | the [identity layout](/dev-tools/install-layout.html)           | the `requested_as` key |
+
+Pass that tool name to the commands below. Don't detect mise from environment
+variables: child processes inherit them, so a tool started by yours would think
+mise installed it too.
+
+## Check for an update
+
+```sh
+mise outdated --global claude --json
+```
+
+```json
+{
+  "claude": {
+    "name": "claude",
+    "requested": "latest",
+    "current": "2.1.3",
+    "bump": null,
+    "latest": "2.1.5",
+    "source": {
+      "type": "mise.toml",
+      "path": "/home/me/.config/mise/config.toml"
+    }
+  }
+}
+```
+
+An entry for the tool means a newer version is available within the global
+config's request; `{}` means it is up to date, or that the global config
+doesn't list the tool. `--global` checks the request in
+the user's global config even inside a project that sets its own version, which
+is the request `mise upgrade --global` moves. Show your own "update available"
+notice from this answer rather than from your release server, so it agrees with
+what mise will install.
+
+## Install the update
+
+```sh
+mise upgrade --global claude
+```
+
+This installs the newest version the request in the global or system config
+allows, into the system installs directory if the current version was
+[installed there](/dev-tools/system-installs.html), and moves the global
+lockfile entry if one pins the tool. It runs as if from outside any project, so
+a project's config, lockfile, and `[env]` are neither read nor changed.
+Progress goes to stderr and a summary to stdout, and the command exits non-zero
+if the update fails. Run it non-interactively, with stdin closed. Updates run
+one at a time; one started from a hook of another mise update skips with a
+warning.
+
+The version you upgraded from stays installed while any process still runs from
+it, and for [`upgrade.prune_after`](/configuration/settings.html#upgrade.prune_after)
+after that, so running sessions keep working.
+
+## Switch a running process to the new version
+
+A process can't change its own code while it runs, but it can replace itself.
+To move a long-running session onto the new version:
+
+1. Find the executable mise runs in the session's directory:
+   `mise which claude`. If it is the one you are running from, stop here. This
+   is also how a project that pins its own version shows up: the global update
+   doesn't change what runs there.
+2. Wait for a safe point, such as between turns with no tool call running, and
+   save the session.
+3. Replace the process with `mise x -- claude <resume arguments>`, started in
+   the session's working directory. On Unix, `exec` it so the process ID and
+   terminal stay the same. Windows has no `exec`: start it as a child and exit.
+
+Start the new version through `mise x`, not through your own path, `argv[0]`,
+or a `PATH` lookup. Those all lead back to the old version: with
+[shell activation](/shell-setup.html), the `PATH` your process inherited names the
+old version's directory. `mise x` resolves the version again, and the
+processes the new session starts (MCP servers, hooks, subagents) get the new
+`PATH`.
+
+Guard against loops: if the version you land on is the one you left, don't
+switch again.
+
+## Summary
+
+- Don't write into mise's install directories, and don't install a second copy
+  of the tool.
+- Check with `mise outdated --global <tool> --json`, and update with
+  `mise upgrade --global <tool>`.
+- Don't bypass `minimum_release_age`: it is the user's security policy.
+- Switch sessions with `mise x -- <tool> <resume arguments>` at a safe point.

title: feat: trust a restored download cache with --locked and make its size configurable
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/621
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Restoring a CI cache of installed tools is fast but unverified: mise can't check an installed tree against `mise.lock`. Caching the download store instead is verified, and this PR makes that a supported setup (follow-up to the download cache in #14222).

**What changes**
- **`--locked` and `paranoid` reuse only pinned downloads.** A kept download is used, or even stored, only when a pinned checksum will be checked against it afterwards. A restored or shared `downloads-cas` can then save downloads but can't change what gets installed. Unpinned downloads (no checksum) skip the store in these modes.
- **Core tools pin and link like the other backends.** The precompiled archives of Node, Go, Bun, Deno, Zig, Java, Python, Ruby, Erlang, Elixir and Swift pass the checksum in `mise.lock` to the download, and are installed from the stored file linked into place (a copy across devices). Node's source tarball is kept the same way and compiled each time. Source builds through `ruby-build`, `python-build` and `kerl` fetch their own sources, so those are not kept.
- **`download_cache_max_size`** (default `2GiB`, `MISE_DOWNLOAD_CACHE_MAX_SIZE`, `0` for no limit) replaces the fixed 2 GiB cap. An unreadable value falls back to 2 GiB.
- **Docs.** A "Cache downloads, not installs" section in the CI guide shows the GitHub Actions setup:

```yaml
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v7
  - uses: actions/cache@v6
    with:
      path: ~/.cache/mise/downloads-cas
      key: mise-downloads-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('mise.lock') }}
  - uses: jdx/mise-action@v5
    with:
      cache: false
```

Tools are unpacked on every run, so this is slower than restoring installs, and tools compiled from source still compile.

**Tested.** New unit tests for the size setting and for locked mode keeping only pinned downloads; a new e2e test (`test_http_locked_download_cache`) that does a locked reinstall from the store alone with the server stopped, and refuses a changed stored file. The core-tool and http e2e tests pass; clippy with `-D warnings` is clean. I did not run the full e2e suite or the VitePress build.

title: fix(backend): stop list() and get() panicking while the tool map reloads
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/620
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise run` could crash intermittently with:

```
The application panicked (crashed).
Message:  called `Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value
Location: src/backend/mod.rs:541
```

Running the same command again usually worked.

mise reloads its tool list after it installs tools, for example when `mise run` installs a task's missing tools. The reload emptied the shared list and then rebuilt it. If another part of mise read the list during the rebuild, it found it empty and panicked.

The reload now builds the new list before replacing the old one, so readers always see either the old list or the new one. Readers also no longer panic if the list has not been loaded yet.

Fixes #14238

## Validation

- New unit test `test_list_and_get_survive_concurrent_reset` runs 200 reloads while four threads read the list. Without the fix it panics within milliseconds; with the fix it passed three runs in a row.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes.
- Five task and install e2e tests pass, including `test_task_tools` and `test_install_concurrent_via_exec`.
- Seven other unit tests fail in this sandbox for reasons unrelated to this change: the brew cask shim tests need Ruby, and `has_linked_version_ignores_mise_managed_absolute_targets` cannot write to `/usr/local/share`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: 2.1.293.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Touches global tool-cache initialization, listing, lookup, and reset paths used across installs and task runs; behavior changes are intentional but concurrency-sensitive.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes intermittent panics when `list()` or `get()` ran while the shared backend tool map was reloading (e.g. after installs during `mise run`).
> 
> **`reset()`** now calls **`build_tools()`** and only then swaps the cached `TOOLS` / `TOOLS_SEEDED` entries, so concurrent readers always see the previous or the new map—not an empty slot. Seed-map construction is extracted into **`build_tools()`** so **`load_tools()`** and **`reset()`** share the same build path.
> 
> **`list()`** goes through **`installed_tools()`**, which returns the extended map under one lock (avoiding a gap where **`reset()`** could clear the cache between extend and read) and yields an **empty list** if **`load_tools()`** has not run yet instead of unwrapping `None`. **`get()`** skips caching into `TOOLS` when the map is missing, so a pre-init lookup cannot poison the seed map **`load_tools()`** would adopt.

title: feat(tool): update auto_update tools in the background at a shell prompt
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/619
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`auto_update` only ran when a shim or `mise exec` was about to launch a tool. In a shell with `mise activate`, tools run straight from `PATH`, so nothing triggered an update unless you also ran the `tool-update` service.

Now, when the shell prompt appears and an opted-in global tool's check is due, `mise hook-env` starts the update in a detached background process. The prompt does not wait, the next command after it finishes uses the new version, and nothing prints to the terminal.

```toml
# ~/.config/mise/config.toml
[tools]
node = { version = "24", auto_update = "6h" }
```

With the shell activated, a prompt after six hours now upgrades `node` within `24.x` in the background.

- It reuses the existing launch rules: global config only, not for exact versions, not offline, in CI, or with `locked`, honors `minimum_release_age`, and one check per interval through the same claim marker.
- While the `tool-update` service runs, prompts leave updates to it, like launches do.
- A failed background update is recorded and shows in `mise doctor`, like a launch's update.
- Prompts with no opted-in tool pay nothing beyond an in-memory check.

Tested with a new e2e `test_tool_update_hook_env` (updates in the background without output, no recheck within the interval, deferral to the service, projects that pin their own version, failure shown in `mise doctor`). I changed two assertions in `test_tool_update` that assumed hook-env never checks. clippy with `-D warnings` is clean. `mise run lint` fails locally on the existing `Cargo.toml` manifest warning, which is not from this change.

> **Medium Risk**
> Changes tool upgrade timing, background process spawning, and locking around `hook-env`, which runs on every prompt for activated users, though behavior mirrors existing launch-time updates and is heavily covered by new e2e tests.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Opted-in global tools with `auto_update` can now upgrade at the shell prompt** in activated shells, not only when a shim or `mise exec` launches a tool. On each prompt, `mise hook-env` may spawn a detached `mise __tool-update --background` for due tools; the prompt does not block, update output is discarded, and failures surface in `mise doctor`.

title: feat(upgrade): add tool_update.global_auto to update every global tool
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/618
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Automatic tool updates were opt-in one tool at a time: every entry in global config needed its own `auto_update = true`. The new `tool_update.global_auto` setting turns them on for every tool in global config at once. It takes the same values as `auto_update`: `true` checks every `tool_update.check_duration` (24h by default), and a duration such as `"12h"` sets the interval.

```toml
# ~/.config/mise/config.toml
[settings]
tool_update.global_auto = "12h"

[tools]
claude = "latest"                                   # checked every 12h
node = { version = "24", auto_update = "6h" }       # its own interval wins
python = { version = "3.13", auto_update = false }  # opted out
```

A tool's own `auto_update` takes precedence, so `auto_update = false` opts a tool out. The existing rules still apply: only global (and system) config counts, so a project can't set this, and a project's own version of a tool is never updated. Exact versions such as `node = "24.11.1"` stay put, and nothing updates offline, in CI, or with `--locked`. `MISE_TOOL_UPDATE_GLOBAL_AUTO` sets it from the environment.

`self_update.auto` now accepts an interval too: `self_update.auto = "1d"` checks for a new mise release every day, overriding `self_update.check_duration`. `true` and `false` work as before.

### Also fixed

A global tool with `auto_update = false` used to create `$MISE_STATE_DIR/tool-update` every time it launched, because the service-lock check ran before the value was read. mise now reads the value first and returns before touching the disk.

### Testing

- New e2e `test_tool_update_global_auto`: `true` and an interval, shims, the env var, a per-tool opt-out, exact versions, a project-set version, and a project trying to turn the setting on.
- Existing `test_tool_update*` and `test_settings_self_update_aliases` still pass.
- Unit tests cover parsing a bool or an interval, and `self_update.auto = "6h"` overriding `check_duration`.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes.

> **Medium Risk**
> Changes when mise self-updates and may auto-upgrade global tools on launch; scope is gated by global-only settings, CI/offline/locked rules, and per-tool opt-out.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds **`tool_update.global_auto`** so every tool in global config can auto-update without per-tool `auto_update`, using the same bool-or-duration values. Per-tool `auto_update` still wins (including `false` to opt out), and project config cannot enable it.
>

title: fix(schema): accept a single dependency table and reject empty nested dependencies
body:
A task's `depends`, `depends_post` and `wait_for` can be a single table instead of a list, and mise runs it:

```toml
[tasks.main]
depends = { task = "greet", args = ["world"], env = { GREETING = "hi" } }
depends_post = { task = "greet", args = ["post"] }
wait_for = { task = "greet" }
run = "echo main"
```

The JSON schema allowed only a string or an array there, so editors and linters such as tombi or Taplo flagged a config that works. The schema also let through `depends = [[]]`, an empty nested list, which mise rejects when it loads the config.

The schema now matches mise:

- **A single table.** `depends`, `depends_post` and `wait_for` accept it, with the same `task`, `args`, `env` and `optional` keys a table inside the list already allows. The definition is shared as `task_dependency_table`.
- **No empty nested list.** A nested list has to name at least one item.

This is a schema change only, and mise's behavior does not change.

This takes over #12521 by @risu729, which pr-closer closed after 7 days of failing checks on the fork run. Greptile scored it 5/5. Its one CodeRabbit thread was about `rust_cache.verify` text from an earlier, wider revision, and is outdated. They are credited as co-author. `schema/mise.json` is edited, and `schema/mise-task.json` is regenerated by `mise run render:schema`.

## Validation

- `e2e/config/test_schema_tombi`:
  - The strict-schema `mise.toml` fixture now uses a table for `depends`, `depends_post` and `wait_for`.
  - A new `mise-bad-task-deps-empty.toml` with `depends = [[]]` must fail.
  - The standalone task schema (`schema/mise-task.json`) gets the same checks: `mise-task-deps.toml` uses a table and a non-empty nested list and must pass, and `mise-bad-task-file-deps-empty.toml` with `depends = [[]]` must fail.
- Ran tombi 0.9.22 against the schemas from `main` and from this PR. `mise.json` and `mise-task.json` gave the same results:

  | file | `main` | this PR |
  |---|---|---|
  | table `depends`/`depends_post`/`wait_for` | fails, `Expected a value of type String, but found Table` | passes |
  | `depends = [[]]` | passes | fails |

- With mise 2026.10.4, the table example above runs both dependencies with their args and exits 0. `depends = [[]]` fails to load with `data did not match any variant of untagged enum StringOrValue`.

title: docs: explain auto_update's release delay and prefer mise settings KEY=VALUE
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/617
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Two docs clarifications, plus a consistency pass on how mise tells people to set a setting.

**`auto_update` and `minimum_release_age`.** Auto-updates already honor `minimum_release_age` (default `24h` for most backends), but the docs didn't say so. A release becomes eligible 24 hours after publishing, and mise only notices it at the next check (`tool_update.check_duration`, also 24h by default). For a tool launched at least once per interval, an update can land 24 to 48 hours after a release. The "Automatic tool updates" section now explains this and shows how to wait longer for one tool:

```toml
[tools]
node = { version = "24", auto_update = "6h", minimum_release_age = "3d" }
```

**`mise settings KEY=VALUE`.** Docs, `settings.toml` descriptions and runtime hint messages (the upgrade prune hint, the node flavor and mirror hints, the python precompiled hint) told users to run `mise settings set KEY VALUE`. They now use the shorter `mise settings KEY=VALUE`, which `mise settings` already accepts:

```sh
mise settings self_update.auto=true
mise settings --local jobs=2
```

The `mise settings set` subcommand itself, its own help and its tests are unchanged, and release notes are left as written.

Docs and message text only. I ran `mise run render` (clean apart from the regenerated `llms.txt`, which is committed) and `prettier --check`, and checked `mise settings --local jobs=2` and `mise settings disable_backends=asdf,vfox` write the expected TOML. I updated the `test_upgrade_prune_hint` e2e assertion for the new hint text but did not run it.

> **Low Risk**
> Docs and hint-string changes only; no behavior change to settings parsing or the `mise settings set` subcommand.
> 
> **Overview**
> Documentation and user-facing messages now recommend **`mise settings KEY=VALUE`** (and **`mise settings --local KEY=VALUE`**) instead of **`mise settings set`**, across configuration guides, `settings.toml` help text, `llms.txt`, and runtime hints (upgrade auto-prune, Node flavor/mirror, Python precompiled). The **`mise settings set`** subcommand is unchanged.
> 
> The **automatic tool updates** section adds a tip that **`minimum_release_age`** (default **24h**) plus the check interval can delay visible updates by **24–48h**, with a **`minimum_release_age`** per-tool example. The upgrade-prune e2e assertion matches the new hint wording.

title: fix(self-update): keep showing the auto-update hint until it is disabled
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/616
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise version` and `mise self-update` show a hint about enabling automatic updates, but it was only printed the first time. After that it was recorded in the state dir and never shown again, so most people never saw it a second time.

The hint now appears on every run until the user acts on it:

```
hint keep mise updated automatically with mise settings self_update.auto=true
```

It stops when `self_update.auto` is enabled or when the user disables it:

```sh
mise settings add disable_hints auto_update
```

To support this, `hint!` gets an `always` form, `hint!(always, id, message, cmd)`. It skips the show-once marker file and respects `disable_hints` and the terminal checks like any other hint. The default `hint!` form is unchanged, so other hints still show once. Anyone who already has an `auto_update` marker file will see the hint again.

Tested with `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`. Hints are suppressed under tests, so there is no automated coverage of the output.

Follow-up to #14218, stacked on it (base is a copy of that PR's head, since its branch does not allow maintainer edits). Retarget to `main` once #14218 merges.

`mise lock` no longer clones the aqua package once per version candidate for packages whose version overrides have no `version_prefix`, which is nearly every package. In that case every candidate resolves to the root prefix, so there is nothing to disambiguate and the ambiguity pass is skipped.
