title: fix(env): join adjacent quoted and unquoted dotenv value parts again
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/614
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Since 2026.10.3, mise reads a dotenv value as exactly one of single-quoted, double-quoted, or unquoted. Before that, values were read like a shell word: quoted and unquoted parts next to each other were joined and their quotes removed. Common `.env` lines broke:

```sh
A='it'\''s'
B=a'b c'd
C="one"'two'three
```

| | before 2026.10.3 | 2026.10.3–2026.10.6 | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `A` | `it's` | syntax error | `it's` |
| `B` | `ab cd` | `a'b c'd` (quotes kept) | `ab cd` |
| `C` | `onetwothree` | syntax error | `onetwothree` |

The syntax error hurt most under the `env_file` setting (`MISE_ENV_FILE=.env`): mise warned and dropped every line after `A`. In `_.file`, it failed the whole config.

This PR joins value segments again, as before 2026.10.3. These stay the same:

- Single-quoted parts are fully literal: no escapes, no `$VAR` substitution (#14228).
- Variables resolve against the file's own earlier assignments first.
- A `${...}` expression is one unit, so quotes in a default (`${NAME:-"a b"}`) don't split the value, and a brace inside a quoted default (`${NAME:-"{}"}`) doesn't end the expression.

### Compatibility notes

- Quotes inside an unquoted value are now removed again. A JSON value that must keep its quotes needs single quotes: `CONFIG='{"debug": true}'`. Before 2026.10.3, `CONFIG={"debug":true}` gave `{debug:true}`; 2026.10.3–2026.10.6 kept the quotes. Unquoted JSON with spaces was a syntax error before 2026.10.3, so files written for older mise are unaffected.
- A quote partway through a value opens a quoted part only when its partner comes later on the same line. Otherwise it's a literal character, so `NAME=O'Brien` and `GREETING=it's great` read as written, as they did in 2026.10.3–2026.10.6 (dotenvy rejected both). Only a value's opening quote may span lines, as before. Quotes and comments are read left to right, so a partner inside a trailing comment still counts (as in dotenvy, `a'x #y'` is `ax #y`): write `NAME="O'Brien" # owner's name`.
- Text after a closing quote is now part of the value (`KEY="a"b` gives `ab`), so `mise_dotenv::ParseErrorKind::TrailingCharacters` no longer occurs and is removed.

### Validation

- New unit tests cover concatenation, the quote/comment interactions, substitution across segments, and dotenvy 0.15.7's own `test_parse_value_escapes` cases (e.g. `KEY4='sweet $\fgs'\''fds'` → `sweet $\fgs'fds`). Existing tests that asserted literal quotes in unquoted values now expect dotenvy's results.
- `render_value` now quotes any value containing `'` or `"`. Its round-trip property tests pass with 20,000 cases.
- New e2e test `e2e/env/test_env_file_quote_concatenation` covers `_.file` and `MISE_ENV_FILE`. It fails without this change with the old syntax error.
- A differential fuzz against dotenvy 0.15.7 compared ~936k single-line values that dotenvy accepts. With the divergences that predate th

title: fix(schema): accept task references in a task array
body:
A task written as an array can mix scripts with references to other tasks, and mise runs them in order:

```toml
[tasks]
hello = "echo hello"
bye = "echo bye"
ci = ["echo first", { task = "hello" }, { task = "bye", args = [], env = { CI = "1" } }, { tasks = ["hello", "bye"] }]
```

The JSON schema allowed only strings in that array. So editors and linters that use it, such as tombi or Taplo, flagged the tables as errors even though `mise run ci` works. Each array item now uses the same `task_run_entry` definition as a task's `run` key. That definition allows a script string, `{ task, args, env }`, or a parallel `{ tasks = [...] }` group. This is a schema change only, and mise's behavior does not change.

This takes over #12796 by @risu729, which pr-closer closed after 7 days of failing checks on the fork run. Greptile scored it 5/5, with no open threads. They are credited as co-author. As before, `schema/mise.json` is edited and `schema/mise-task.json` is regenerated by `mise run render:schema`.

## Validation

- `e2e/config/test_schema_tombi` now lints a `mise-task-array.toml` with the example's mix of entries under the strict schema.
- Ran tombi 0.9.22 on that file:
  - With the schema from `main`, it fails with `Expected a value of type String, but found Table` at each of the three tables.
  - With this PR's schema, it passes.
- `mise run ci` with the example above runs every entry with mise 2026.10.4 and exits 0, so the schema now matches what mise accepts.

title: fix(env): keep backslashes literal in single-quoted dotenv values
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/612
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Since 2026.10.3, mise has processed backslash escapes inside single-quoted `.env` values. That broke Windows paths loaded through `[env] _.file` and the `env_file` setting:

```sh
# .env
UNC_PATH='\\fileserver\data\share'
DIR='C:\temp\'
```

| | 2026.10.3–2026.10.6 | Now (and 2026.10.2 and earlier) |
|---|---|---|
| `UNC_PATH` | `\fileserver\data\share`. On Windows this resolves to `D:\fileserver\...` on the current drive | `\\fileserver\data\share` |
| `DIR` | parse error: unterminated quote | `C:\temp\` |

Single-quoted values are literal again, as they are in shell, Node's `dotenv`, and the `dotenvy` parser mise used before 2026.10.3. Double-quoted and unquoted values still process escapes.

title: fix(dotfiles): replace a junction target when a symlink source changes
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/611
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

On Windows, changing the `source` of a `mode = "symlink"` dotfiles entry whose target is a directory junction made `mise dot apply` fail:

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/x/dir" = { source = "b/dir", mode = "symlink" }  # was a/dir
```

```
Error: failed rm: C:\Users\me\x\dir   (os error 5)
```

Windows refuses to delete a junction with a plain file removal, so the old link could not be replaced. Replacing a target now removes a symlink or junction as a link (never the directory it points to), so `mise dot apply` re-points it at `b/dir`. Unix behavior is unchanged.

Fixes #14224

## Validation

Added `remove_existing_removes_a_directory_link_not_its_target`. On a Windows 11 machine it fails without the fix with `failed rm: ...\link` and passes with it; it also passes on Linux.

title: fix(bootstrap): stop reporting freshly cloned repos as dirty with core.autocrlf
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/610
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

On Windows with `core.autocrlf=true`, `mise bootstrap repos status` reported every freshly cloned repo as `dirty` even though `git status` was clean.

`repos apply` clones with the user's git config, so files are checked out with CRLF line endings. Every later git call mise made on the repo forced `-c core.autocrlf=false`, so git compared the CRLF files against LF blobs and saw them all as modified. This removes the override from the repo git helpers (and the printed dry-run command), so checks read the repo under the same config it was cloned with.

Added a unit test that clones with `core.autocrlf=true` and expects the repo to be `current`.

Fixes #14223

title: feat: reuse downloads the server confirms are unchanged
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/609
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Every backend that downloads through mise's HTTP client fetched its artifact again on each install, and nothing checked what a restored or shared cache handed back (discussion 14217). This PR adds one content-addressed download store, `$MISE_CACHE_DIR/downloads-cas`, that re-hashes what it holds before using it, and says plainly what that does and doesn't protect.

**Revalidated downloads (all HTTP-client callers, on by default).** A finished download is kept with the `ETag` or `Last-Modified` value the server sent. The next request for the same URL is conditional; on `304 Not Modified` mise uses the kept file after hashing it again, so nothing is transferred. A file that no longer matches is dropped and downloaded again. This covers github, aqua, http, the core tools, plugin archives, the registry, brew, remote task files and the rest without per-backend wiring. Servers that send no validator aren't cached.

**Pinned reuse, no network (`http`, `github`, `aqua`, `packslip`).** A checksum a tool pinned, in its options, in `mise.lock`, or as a packslip's signed digest, names the stored file, which is used without any request even if the URL changed. The pin is still verified after the download as before.

**No extra copy.** Files are stored once, by hash, under their own file name (installers read the format and the binary's name from it). The four pinning backends download into the store and the file in `downloads` is a hard link to it, so the archive takes no extra space; across devices it falls back to a copy. I checked that these install paths only read the downloaded file (raw binaries are copied and the copy is made executable), and a stored file is hashed again before every reuse, so an in-place change would cost a re-download, never a wrong install. Partial downloads now resume from the store's staging area.

Turn it all off with `download_cache = false` (`MISE_DOWNLOAD_CACHE=0`). The store holds up to 2 GiB, least recently used first. `always_keep_download` is deprecated (warns from 2026.11.0, removed 2027.11.0): downloads are kept in the store instead.

**Trust.** The recorded hash lives beside the file, so it catches damage but not a cache whose file and metadata were both replaced; without a pinned checksum a writable cache is trusted, and the docs say so. The extracted `http-tarballs` tree from `shared_extraction` (opt-in) is still trusted as is.

**Docs.** A "Restored caches and installed tools" section in the lockfile docs explains why mise can't validate an installed tree (installs are mutable on purpose, and source-built tools differ from their tarball) and what to do instead, with warnings on the `http` shared-extraction note and the GitHub Actions section.

Tested with unit tests of the 304 path, a tampered stored file, pinned reuse and the linked download, plus e2e tests for pinned and unpinned reinstalls with the server sto

title: fix(rust): treat rustup profile aliases like their full names
body:
rustup accepts `m`, `d` and `c` (and an empty value) for its `minimal`, `default` and `complete` profiles, but mise compared the profile against `"default"` literally. With

```toml
[tools]
rust = { version = "1.81.0", profile = "d" }
```

rustup installed the default profile. mise, though, did not count clippy, rust-docs and rustfmt as required. So when one of them went missing from the toolchain, `mise install` reported the tool as installed and did not restore it. That restoring is the reconciliation from #12771, and with `profile = "default"` it already worked.

mise now maps the aliases to the full names before it decides which components the profile needs, matching rustup's own parser:

```rust
// rustup src/dist/mod.rs, impl FromStr for Profile
"minimal" | "m" => Ok(Self::Minimal),
"default" | "d" | "" => Ok(Self::Default),
"complete" | "c" => Ok(Self::Complete),
```

Only mise's own comparisons use the normalized name. rustup still receives the profile as configured. An unknown profile name now fails in mise with rustup's list of valid names, where before it reached rustup.

This takes over #12814 by @risu729, which pr-closer closed after 7 days without contributor activity. Its CI had passed, and CodeRabbit and Greptile had no findings. They are credited as co-author, and the change is theirs, unchanged.

## Validation

- Unit test `profile_aliases_match_rustup` covers each full name, alias and the empty value, plus an unknown name.
- `e2e/core/test_rust_components_reconcile` now installs with `profile = "d"`, removes `rustfmt` from the toolchain, and checks that `mise install` sees the gap and puts it back. It uses a fake `rustup`, so it needs no network.
- Ran that e2e in Docker:
  - With mise 2026.10.4, it fails at the new step. `mise install rust --dry-run-code` reports `profile = "d"` as already installed with `rustfmt` missing.
  - With this PR's CI build on Ubuntu 24.04, it passes. `mise install` reinstalls the toolchain (the fifth `toolchain install`) and `rustfmt` is back.

title: fix(cargo): lock the same rust homes the rust plugin resolves
body:
## Problem

#14042 made the cargo backend take the rust-state lock before `cargo install` fallbacks. But it resolved *which* homes to lock from `CARGO_HOME`/`RUSTUP_HOME` in the child environment only, while the rust plugin resolves the same homes from more sources. When a user configures homes through either of these, the two take different lock files and the race #14041 described is still live:

- settings `rust.cargo_home` / `rust.rustup_home` — `settings.toml` documents these as the way to "keep mise's toolchains apart from another rustup installation" (env alias `MISE_CARGO_HOME` / `MISE_RUSTUP_HOME`)
- `MISE_CARGO_HOME` / `MISE_RUSTUP_HOME` set in `[env]`

The failure is silent: nothing errors, the lock just doesn't cover the plugin's homes.

## Example

`.config/mise/settings.toml`:

```toml
[rust]
cargo_home = "~/.mise-rust"
rustup_home = "~/.mise-rustup"
```

Two parallel installs that both fall back to source builds: the plugin locks `~/.mise-rust`/`~/.mise-rustup` while the cargo backend locks the default `~/.cargo`/`~/.rustup` — different locks, both installs may run rustup on the shared state at once, and the install fails with `could not rename 'component' ... Directory not empty (os error 39)` like #14041. Before this change the lock only protected users who set plain `CARGO_HOME`/`RUSTUP_HOME`; after, the same lock covers the settings- and `[env]`-configured homes too.

## Fix

Lock the union of two sets of homes, in sorted order:

- **What the rust plugin locks**: resolved by `RustHomes::from_config_env`, the resolver `RustHomes::resolve` uses. `config.env()` forms the config tier, `rust.cargo_home` / `rust.rustup_home` settings are the configured tier, and the process env is the ambient tier. Other tools' exec env is excluded because the plugin never sees it.
- **What the spawned `cargo` uses**: the process env, overridden by the toolset env and then by `install_env`, including removals.

The two differ when `install_env` removes or changes a home, or when a settings home never reaches the child. Both go through the same normalization (`resolve_rust_home`), so tilde and relative paths resolve the same way on both sides.

## Tests

Each test holds the cargo-fallback lock, then probes the expected locks with `LockFile::try_lock`:

- settings-configured homes (fails on the #14042 code)
- `MISE_*_HOME` from `[env]` (fails on the #14042 code)
- a settings home that `install_env` removes: covers both the plugin's settings home and the child's default home
- an ambient home that `install_env` removes
- a `CARGO_HOME` exported by another tool alongside a settings home: covers both
- tilde paths, kept as a regression guard

Fixes #14041 (gap follow-up to #14042)

title: fix(lock): apply aqua version prefixes before selecting overrides
body:
`mise lock codex --platform windows-x64` can now lock Codex 0.154.0 when the release-tag listing does not contain that pinned version. Previously, override selection received only `0.154.0` and `v0.154.0`, so the aqua registry's `rust-` prefix rejected every override. The empty asset name became `.exe`, and the Windows platform entry was skipped. It now resolves `codex-package-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.tar.gz` and records its checksum.

Reuse the prefix-aware candidate selection already used during installation before applying lock-time version overrides. Exact release tags remain authoritative, and overrides still use the requested target platform. When tag lookup misses and multiple prefix families match, warn and skip that platform entry instead of choosing a release by registry order. Disjoint version constraints that select one prefix remain supported. This extends the installation metadata fix in #11499 to lock generation.

Validation: all 122 aqua backend unit tests and three focused lockfile end-to-end tests passed. The regression covers both the Codex-shaped Windows package and ambiguous prefixes with reachable archives; the ambiguity case fails against the previous PR binary. The real Codex 0.154.0 Windows lock reproduction succeeds with the expected archive and checksum. Strict workspace Clippy (`cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`) passed. Scoped hk checks passed; the full `mise run lint-fix` task could not finish because the local environment lacks `npm:markdownlint-cli@0.49.1`.

title: fix(npm): build the open-file limit raise on 32-bit targets
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/608
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

mise failed to compile on 32-bit Linux targets such as `armv7-unknown-linux-gnueabihf`, which broke the `build-tarball-linux-armv7` job and blocked the 2026.10.6 release PR (#14186).

#14174 added a startup step that raises the soft open-file limit. It hardcoded the target as `u64`, but `rlim_t` is `u32` on 32-bit glibc, so `hard.min(TARGET)` failed with `E0308: mismatched types`. The target is now typed as `nix::libc::rlim_t`, which matches the platform on every target. Behavior on 64-bit platforms is unchanged.

Validation: `cargo check --bin mise` passes on x86_64 Linux. I did not build for armv7 locally; the armv7 tarball job is the check for that.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: unavailable.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Single constant type change in Unix startup; no logic change on 64-bit and no security or data-path impact.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes a **compile failure on 32-bit Unix** (e.g. `armv7-unknown-linux-gnueabihf`) in the startup `raise_nofile_limit()` helper added for parallel installs.
> 
> The open-file cap constant was `u64`, but `getrlimit` returns `rlim_t` (often `u32` on 32-bit glibc), so `hard.min(TARGET)` no longer type-checks. **`TARGET` is now `nix::libc::rlim_t`**, matching the limit APIs on all platforms; 64-bit behavior stays the same (still caps at 10240).

title: feat(task): include working-tree changes in --affected and drop the experimental gate
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/607
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise run --affected` only looked at committed changes, so you had to commit before you could see which projects an edit touched. It now also counts staged and unstaged edits and untracked files, so the selection reflects what is in your working tree:

```sh
# Run build in projects changed by HEAD or by anything you have not committed yet
mise run --affected build

# Only what you have not committed yet
mise run --affected --affected-uncommitted --affected-untracked build

# Reproducible: the committed range only, as before
mise run --affected --affected-committed build
```

The three sources are `--affected-committed` (the `base...head` range), `--affected-uncommitted` (staged and unstaged edits to tracked files, against `HEAD`), and `--affected-untracked` (untracked files that `.gitignore` does not exclude). With none of them, all three count. Naming any of them limits the selection to those, and they combine. Each also has an environment variable (`MISE_AFFECTED_COMMITTED`, `MISE_AFFECTED_UNCOMMITTED`, `MISE_AFFECTED_UNTRACKED`).

- The working tree only counts when the head revision is the commit you have checked out. With a different `--affected-head` the result stays a pure commit range, and asking for `--affected-uncommitted` or `--affected-untracked` there is an error.
- CI checkouts are normally clean, so the default there is unchanged. A CI job that writes untracked, unignored files before running `--affected` would now see them. `--affected-committed` restores the old behavior.
- A pnpm lockfile edited in the working tree is still attributed per project, by comparing the merge base with the working-tree file.

## Experimental gate removed

The workspace project graph and everything built on it no longer requires `experimental = true`: `mise run --affected`, `mise tasks graph`, `[monorepo.task_defaults]`, `[monorepo.projects]`, and `task.auto_infer`. Setups that already enable experimental features are unaffected. Docs, help text, the usage spec, man page, and schema no longer mark them experimental.

Closes the request in discussion jdx/mise#14213.

## Testing

`test_task_affected` covers untracked, staged, unstaged, and ignored files, each source flag alone and combined, a working-tree lockfile edit, and a non-checkout head. The graph e2e tests now run without `MISE_EXPERIMENTAL`. Unit tests cover the same cases against a temporary repository.

--- .oss-scanner/threat_model.md (+53/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,53 @@
+# Threat model
+
+## What this project does and where untrusted input enters
+
+mise is a Rust CLI that installs developer tools, manages per-directory environment variables and runs tasks.
+Treat these as attacker-controlled:
+
+- Files in a cloned repository that mise reads before the user has trusted it. Config files are only
+  executed or templated once trusted (`mise trust`); a way to run code, read secrets or write files from an
+  untrusted config is a real bug.
+- Network responses from tool sources: GitHub/GitLab/Forgejo releases, HTTP and S3 downloads, the aqua
+  registry, packslip manifests, npm/cargo/pip/gem/go registries, and the mise-versions mirror.
+- Downloaded archives (tar, zip, 7z) and the filenames inside them.
+- Version strings, tool names and backend options from config or the network.
+- Shell input to `mise activate`, shims and hook-env (directory names, env var values, PATH).
+
+Out of scope as inputs: the user's own trusted config, their own shell, and anything that already requires local code execution as that user.
+
+## Components that matter most / least
+
+Most: download and extraction (path traversal, symlink and hardlink escapes), checksum, signature and
+provenance verification (a bypass or downgrade is a bug), trust handling, template rendering, shell
+activation output (quoting and injection), shims, lockfile handling, credential and token handling
+(leaks into logs, env, URLs, or sending a token to the wrong host).
+Least: docs/, e2e/, benchmarks/, scripts/, xtasks/, and CI workflow files. `crates/vfox` Lua plugins
+run with the user's privileges once installed, so installing a plugin is trusted; report only sandbox or
+trust-boundary escapes beyond that.
+
+## How to exercise it
+
+`target/debug/mise` is already built. `cargo test` runs unit tests; `e2e/` holds bash tests (run through `mise run test:e2e <file>`).
+Use a throwaway `HOME`, `MISE_DATA_DIR`, `MISE_CONFIG_DIR` and `MISE_STATE_DIR` so a proof of concept does not touch real state.
+
+## How you rate severity
+
+- Critical: code execution or arbitrary file write from untrusted config without trust, from a malicious
+  or tampered download that passes verification, or from a crafted archive escaping the install dir.
+- High: bypass of trust or of checksum/signature verification; credential disclosure to a third party;
+  injection into emitted shell code. Rate by demonstrated impact: a bypass that leads to code execution
+  or arbitrary file write is Critical, and the highest applicable level wins.
+- Medium: denial of service from untrusted input (crash, unbounded memory or disk), local-only
+  information disclosure.
+- Low: hardening gaps with no demonstrated exploit.
+
+## Anything to leave alone
+
+- Behavior that requires the user to run `mise trust`, install a plugin, or add a tool source they chose.
+- A malicious tool being malicious after it is correctly installed.
+- Reports that need a pre-compromised machine, an attacker-controlled `PATH` or `HOME`, or root.
+- Panics reachable only through `unwrap` on trusted internal state that untrusted input cannot trigger or
+  influence. A panic an attacker can trigger stays in scope (Medium, see above).
+
+Reports should include a runnable reproducer; a minimal patch is preferred over a large refactor.

title: fix(dotfiles): don't credit rollback to a checkpoint past a truncated change list
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/605
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Follow-up to #14207, which merged just before this fix was pushed to its branch.

`mise dot rollback <path>` names the checkpoint that saved the version it restores. It finds it by walking back from the checkpoint restored from to the newest one whose list of changed paths includes `<path>`. Those lists are capped, though. A checkpoint that changed many files records only the first ones and is marked truncated, so it can't say whether it changed `<path>`. The search walked past such a checkpoint and could name an earlier one even when the truncated checkpoint was the one that saved the version.

The search now stops at a truncated change list and names the checkpoint restored from, which does hold the version. What gets restored is unchanged.

## Validation

New unit test `saved_in_names_the_checkpoint_that_changed_the_path`. It covers the ordinary lookup and the fallback when nothing changed the path. Its truncated-list case would name checkpoint 1 without the fix and now names checkpoint 3. The rollback e2e tests pass.

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Messaging-only fix in rollback attribution logic; restore behavior is unchanged and covered by new unit tests.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes **incorrect rollback success messages** when dotfile history walks backward through checkpoints whose change lists are **capped and marked truncated**.
> 
> `saved_in` now takes checkpoint id + `Changes` pairs instead of full entries. While scanning newest-to-oldest up to the restore target, it **stops at a truncated list** and credits the **restore checkpoint** (which actually holds the version), instead of continuing and naming an older checkpoint that merely listed the path. **Restored file content is unchanged**—only which checkpoint id appears in the “rolled back … to checkpoint N” message.
> 
> Adds unit test `saved_in_names_the_checkpoint_that_changed_the_path` for normal attribution and the truncated-list fallback.
>

title: feat(dotfiles): add `mise dot save --re-encrypt`
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/604
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

After you change `[history.encryption] recipients`, a save re-encrypts only the files it reads from disk. Encrypted files the save carries forward keep their old encryption: entries with `autosave = false` that the save doesn't name, and variants for other platforms. A machine added to the list then can't read them, and `mise bootstrap --adopt` fails with `cannot unlock <path>` until each file is edited and saved again.

`mise dot save --re-encrypt` saves as usual, then re-encrypts every file in the new checkpoint that was encrypted to a different recipient list:

```sh
mise dot save --re-encrypt
# mise history: re-encrypted 2 files to the current recipients
# mise history: saved checkpoint 3: re-encrypted 2 files to the current recipients
```

- It re-encrypts the **saved** version of each file. A manual-save file's unsaved edits are never captured just to change its keys.
- If this machine can't unlock some files, nothing is saved, and the error lists every one: ``cannot re-encrypt ~/.manual, ~/.other: no age identity on this machine unlocks them; nothing was saved. Run `mise dot save --re-encrypt` where they can be unlocked``
- With nothing to do, it prints `history: every encrypted file already uses the current recipients` and records no checkpoint.
- Older checkpoints are not rewritten. As before, a machine added later can only read versions saved after the change.

The "Change recipients" section of the encryption docs now explains which files a plain save leaves behind and when to run `--re-encrypt`.

Reported in https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/discussions/3796#discussioncomment-18824990.

## Validation

New `e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_save_re_encrypt`:
- After adding a second recipient, a plain save leaves the manual-save file's ciphertext unchanged, and adopting from a machine that has only the second key fails.
- `--re-encrypt` without a usable identity fails, names both files and leaves history untouched.
- After `--re-encrypt`, that machine adopts and gets the saved contents, while the unsaved edit stays only on disk.
- A second `--re-encrypt` has nothing to do.

With the re-encrypt step disabled, these assertions fail. The existing encrypted-history e2e tests and the `history::` unit tests pass.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: 2.1.293.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Touches encrypted dotfiles history commits and recipient handling; failures are all-or-nothing, but a bad re-encrypt could block saves until keys are fixed.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds **`mise dot save --re-encrypt`** so dotfiles history can rotate age recipients for encrypted files that a normal save only carries forward (manual-save / `autosave = false`, other-platform variants, etc.).
> 
> A save still re-encrypts files it reads live

title: feat(dotfiles): show unsaved changes in `mise dot status`
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/603
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

With the watcher stopped, or for an entry tracked with `--no-autosave`, an edit nothing had saved yet was invisible in `mise dot status`. Only `mise dot history diff` showed it. Status now compares the tracked files with the latest checkpoint and lists what changed:

```
History: tracking 2 entries (3 files); 1 checkpoints recorded.
  latest checkpoint 1 (track, …): …
  unsaved changes: 2 path(s) since the latest checkpoint (~/.config/app/added.toml, ~/.zshrc); `mise dot history diff` shows them, `mise dot save` records them.
```

`mise dot status --json` reports the same paths as `history.unsaved`: an empty list when nothing changed, or `null` when it couldn't be determined: there's no checkpoint yet, a tracked file or directory couldn't be read, or an encrypted file's ciphertext changed and this machine can't decrypt it without prompting to compare the contents.

It works the way `history diff` does, the same work `git status` does: every tracked file is read and hashed. It never prompts for a passphrase. A file the credential guard leaves out is never reported. An encrypted file is compared by its decrypted contents, so re-encrypting unchanged contents doesn't count as a change.

Reported in https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/discussions/3796#discussioncomment-18824990.

## Validation

- New `e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_status_unsaved` covers: nothing to report right after a save; an edit and a new file in a tracked directory; a removed file; an unchanged versus an edited encrypted file, including with the encryption cache deleted; and unreadable files and directories.
- All 39 e2e tests that run `mise dot status` pass.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: 2.1.293.*

* **Documentation**

--- e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_status_unsaved (+91/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,91 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# `mise dot status` says when tracked files changed since the latest
+# checkpoint, so unsaved edits are visible without `history diff`.
+require_cmd git
+echo one >~/.zshrc
+mkdir -p ~/.config/app ~/.config/mise
+echo one >~/.config/app/config.toml
+echo key >~/.config/app/secrets.key
+# with no checkpoint yet there is nothing to compare against
+assert "mise dot status --json | jq -c .history.unsaved" 'null'
+assert_succeed "mise dot track ~/.zshrc ~/.config/app"
+
+# right after a save there is nothing to report, and a credential the
+# guard leaves out is not an unsaved change
+assert_not_contains 'mise dot status' 'unsaved changes'
+assert "mise dot status --json | jq -c .history.unsaved" '[]'
+
+echo two >~/.zshrc
+echo new >~/.config/app/added.toml
+assert_contains 'mise dot status' 'unsaved changes: 2 path(s) since the latest checkpoint (~/.config/app/added.toml, ~/.zshrc)'
+assert "mise dot status --json | jq -c .history.unsaved" '["~/.config/app/added.toml","~/.zshrc"]'
+# status only reports; the edits are still unsaved afterwards
+assert_contains 'mise dot status' 'unsaved changes: 2 path(s)'
+
+assert_succeed 'mise dot save'
+assert_not_contains 'mise dot status' 'unsaved changes'
+
+rm ~/.zshrc
+assert "mise dot status --json | jq -c .history.unsaved" '["~/.zshrc"]'
+
+# an unchanged encrypted file is not reported, and an edited one is
+export MISE_AGE_KEY="AGE-SECRET-KEY-142E7VJ8GUWR94MXDCYQJ7ZTQZRXKQSP9PUJU8HUQJ206QN7QPV4SM5QRL8"
+cat >>"$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml" <<'TOML'
+[history.encryption]
+recipients = ["age1fuvsfq02qr5ju0nhh3rulrwracymjljlr5j49kres24ltd3fjq0s9z9d8l"]
+TOML
+echo private >~/.private
+assert_succeed 'mise dot track --encrypt ~/.private'
+assert_succeed 'mise dot save'
+assert "mise dot status --json | jq -c .history.unsaved" '[]'
+echo changed >~/.private
+assert "mise dot status --json | jq -c .history.unsaved" '["~/.private"]'
+
+# the encryption cache is only a cache: without it, an unchanged encrypted
+# file encrypts to a new ciphertext and is still not reported
+assert_succeed 'mise dot save'
+rm -f "$MISE_STATE_DIR/history/index/encryption.json"
+assert "mise dot status --json | jq -c .history.unsaved" '[]'
+# nor is it guessed at when this machine cannot decrypt to compare
+rm -f "$MISE_STATE_DIR/history/index/encryption.json"
+assert "MISE_AGE_KEY= mise dot status --json | jq -c .history.unsaved" 'null'
+
+# a tracked file or directory that cannot be read is unknown, not removed
+# (root reads through the permissions, so only an ordinary user can check)
+mkdir -p ~/.config/app/sub
+echo nested >~/.config/app/sub/nested.toml
+assert_succeed 'mise dot save'
+if [ "$(id -u)" != 0 ]; then
+  chmod 000 ~/.config/app/config.toml
+  assert "mise dot status --json | jq -c .history.unsaved" 'null'
+  chmod 644 ~/.config/app/config.toml
+  chmod 000 ~/.config/app/sub
+  assert "mise dot status --json | jq -c .history.unsaved" 'null'
+  chmod 755 ~/.config/app/sub
+fi
+
+# a saved file the walk now omits (here, replaced by a special file) is
+# carried by the next save, so it is not an unsaved removal either
+echo saved >~/.config/app/fifo
+assert_succeed 'mise dot save'
+rm ~/.config/app/fifo
+mkfifo ~/.config/app/fifo
+assert "mise dot status --json | jq -c .history.unsaved" '[]'
+
+# but one the rules no longer retain (a credential whose encryption was
+# turned off) is a removal the next save records, so status reports it
+echo token >~/.secret-token
+assert_succeed 'mise dot track --encrypt ~/.secret-token'
+assert_succeed 'mise dot save'
+sed -i.bak 's|^"~/.secret-token" = { mode = "track", encrypt = true }|"~/.secret-token" = { mode = "track" }|' "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml"
+assert_contains "cat $MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml" '"~/.secret-token" = { mode = "track" }'
+assert "mise dot status --json | jq -c .history.unsaved" '["~/.secret-token"]'
+assert_contains 'mise dot save 2>&1' 'removed ~/.secret-token'
+assert "mise dot status --json | jq -c .history.unsaved" '[]'
+
+# turning encryption off for an ordinary file is a change the next save
+# records, not a reason to give up on the whole list
+echo other-edit >~/.zshrc
+sed -i.bak 's|^"~/.private" = { mode = "track", encrypt = true }|"~/.private" = { mode = "track" }|' "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml"
+assert_contains "cat $MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml" '"~/.private" = { mode = "track" }'
+assert "mise dot status --json | jq -c .history.unsaved" '["~/.private","~/.zshrc"]'

title: fix(dotfiles): list every encrypted file a sync cannot unlock
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/602
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

When a machine couldn't decrypt some of a shared setup's encrypted files (its age key wasn't a recipient when they were saved), `mise bootstrap --adopt`, `mise dot pull` and `mise dot sync` stopped at the first such file and named only that one. A stale recipient list was then fixed one file per retry.

These commands now try every incoming encrypted file and fail once, listing them all:

```
mise ERROR cannot unlock 2 encrypted files: home/.config/app/first, home/.config/app/second
mise ERROR cannot unlock home/.config/app/first; run mise dot pull interactively with a matching age identity
mise ERROR No matching keys found
```

A single locked file reports exactly as before. A damaged file isn't one another key would open, so it still stops the sync immediately with `<path> is not a readable encrypted file`. That covers an envelope or age header that doesn't parse or fails its integrity check. Every file is tried with the caller's prompting setting, so a hardware age identity can still open the files it holds keys for.

Reported in https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/discussions/3796#discussioncomment-18824990.

## Validation

New `e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_adopt_locked_files`: a second machine whose key is not a recipient adopts a setup with two encrypted files and gets both in one error, and nothing is written. `test_dotfiles_sync_files_encrypted`, `test_dotfiles_adopt_take_remote` and the `history::` unit tests pass.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: 2.1.293.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Touches dotfiles/history decryption and upstream loading used by bootstrap, pull, and sync; behavior change is intentional but could affect error handling and partial-failure paths.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Dot sync/adopt/pull** no longer stops at the first encrypted file this machine cannot open. Upstream reconciliation tries every encrypted path, collects unlock failures, and returns one error listing all of them (single-file behavior is unchanged). That lets you fix a stale age recipient list in one pass instead of retrying per file.
> 
> Decryption errors are split so **corrupt or tampered age envelopes** (invalid header/MAC/format) surface immediately as unreadable ciphertext, while **missing/wrong identity** is tagged as `Locked` and can be aggregated. `agecrypt` maps those structural age failures to `DecryptError::Corrupt` so they are not mistaken for “try another key.”
>

title: fix(dotfiles): name the checkpoints rollback and undo restore and record
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/601
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise dot rollback ~/.zshrc` named a checkpoint that `mise dot history --path ~/.zshrc` didn't list. Without `--to`, rollback picks the newest checkpoint holding a different version of the file, and that is often an unrelated save that only carried the version along. The listing showed checkpoints 6 and 8, while rollback said "rolled back to checkpoint 7". Undo then referenced checkpoint 10, with 9 nowhere in the listing.

Rollback now names the checkpoint that saved the version it restored. Rollback and undo also name the two checkpoints every operation records: the result, and the one holding the state before it. For the case above:

```
history: rolled back ~/.zshrc to checkpoint 6; recorded as checkpoint 10, with checkpoint 9 holding the state before it
```

What gets restored is unchanged, as is the checkpoint recorded as the operation's `to`. `--to <ref>` still names the checkpoint you passed. The history docs now explain the two checkpoints per operation.

Reported in https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/discussions/3796#discussioncomment-18824990.

## Validation

`e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_rollback` covers both messages: rolling back past three unrelated saves now names the baseline (checkpoint 1) instead of checkpoint 4, and `history --path` lists that same checkpoint. The other rollback and history e2e tests and the `history::` unit tests pass.

title: fix(dotfiles): ask the plaintext question only of a terminal
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/599
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise dot track` asks before saving a credential-named file in plaintext. It asked whenever stderr was a terminal, and the prompt reads a piped answer from stdin. In a script that loops over a file list, the next line of the list became the answer:

```sh
while read -r f; do mise dot track "~/$f"; done < files.txt
# mise ERROR expected y/yes or n/no, got ".config/starship.toml"
```

Piping `y` in also approved the file, though `--yes` deliberately does not. The prompt now needs a terminal on stdin too. Without one, `mise dot track` fails with the existing pointer to `--allow-plaintext`:

```
~/.api-token: use --encrypt for credentials or --allow-plaintext to save this file in plaintext without a terminal
```

Other `mise dot` confirmations still accept piped answers.

Reported in https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/discussions/3796#discussioncomment-18824990.

## Validation

`e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_credential_omissions` runs `printf 'y\n' | mise dot track ~/.api-token` under `script(1)`, so stderr is a terminal and stdin is a pipe, and asserts it fails without saving the file. The same assertion fails on main, where the piped `y` approves the file.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: 2.1.293.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes credential plaintext approval for `mise dot track`, which affects whether secrets can enter Git history; behavior is stricter and better matches script safety expectations.
> 
> **Overview**
> **`mise dot track`** no longer treats piped stdin as consent when a credential-named file would be saved in plaintext. The interactive prompt now runs only when **both** stderr and stdin are terminals, so scripts that feed paths on stdin (e.g. `while read … | mise dot track`) cannot accidentally answer “yes” with the next path line—or with `printf 'y\n' | …` while stderr is still a TTY.
> 
> Without a fully interactive terminal, tracking those files still requires **`--allow-plaintext`** or **`--encrypt`**; **`--yes`** remains unable to bypass that guard. Docs in `history.md` spell out that piped answers do not approve plaintext tracking, and the credential-omissions e2e test covers the `script` + piped-`y` case.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 1c9f13361af8b90a4711583511f55cbae91ca9e3. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>

title: fix(dotfiles): stop re-warning about approved plaintext files
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/598
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Once you approve a credential-named file for plaintext tracking (`mise dot track --allow-plaintext` or answering yes at the prompt), mise no longer warns about it on every save. Before, the warning came back on every save, and because watcher saves queue their notices, on every `mise dot` command too:

```
mise WARN  history: ~/.config/app/secrets.sh.example: explicitly allowed for plaintext tracking; this credential-like file may be shared with an origin; `encrypt = true` saves it encrypted instead
```

Approving the file was already the user's answer, and there was no way to silence the warning. Approved files are still listed as `plaintext:` in `mise dot paths`. Files an `include` list sweeps in were never asked about, so they still warn on every save, which is what the [capture warnings docs](https://mise.jdx.dev/dotfiles/history.html#capture-warnings) already described.

Names ending in `.example`, `.sample` or `.template` (such as `secrets.sh.example`) no longer match the credential name rules (`*secret*`, `*token*`, …). These are templates that ship with placeholder values. The content scan that runs before publishing to an origin still checks them.

Reported in https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/discussions/3796#discussioncomment-18824990.

## Validation

- New unit tests: an approved file produces no capture warning, and template suffixes are not credentials while `token.example.age` still is.
- `e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_credential_omissions`: a save of an approved file no longer warns, and a `secrets.fish.example` under a tracked directory is captured.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: 2.1.293.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes dotfiles capture and credential filtering behavior that affects what is saved and what users see on every save/sync, though scope is limited to warning policy and filename heuristics.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Dotfiles credential handling** is tightened in two ways: repeated save noise is reduced, and template filenames stop being treated as secrets.
> 
> Files you explicitly approve for plaintext tracking (`--allow-plaintext` / `allow_plaintext = true`) are **no longer warned on every save** about sharing with an origin. That warning still applies on each capture for credential-like paths pulled in by an **`include`** list (unchanged policy). Approved paths remain listed as `plaintext:` in `mise dot paths`.
> 
> Built-in credential name rules **ignore** basenames ending in `.example`, `.sample`, or `.template` (e.g. `secrets.fish.example`), so templates can be saved without matching `*secret*` / `*token*`. Names like `token.example.age` still match.
> 
> Docs in `history.md` describe both behaviors; unit and e2e tests cover template capture and silent re-saves after approval.

title: fix(shim): skip other missing lazy tools when a lazy tool installs on first use
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/596
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Launching a lazy tool for the first time no longer looks up remote versions for the other lazy tools that are not installed.

Stacked on #14197. The first run of a lazy tool through its shim installs it, and afterwards mise resolved the whole config again, so every other missing lazy tool queried its version list. With a config like this, running `dummy` for the first time also tried to resolve the second entry:

```toml
[tools]
dummy = { version = "latest", lazy = true, lazy_bins = ["dummy"] }
codex = { version = "latest", lazy = true }
```

Now the launch installs `dummy`, runs it, and leaves `codex` unresolved until it is launched itself. Where `codex`'s lookup failed, the launch used to print "Failed to resolve tool version list" warnings, and offline it waited for each timeout.

Resolving again after an install now has its own `after_install_resolve` field on `InstallOptions`. #14197 reused `resolve_options` for this, which also decides which versions get installed; deferring a lazy tool there made the first lazy launch install the literal version `latest` in my first attempt. Keeping them separate means a command can leave other missing lazy tools unresolved without touching the install. `mise x`, the `auto_update` flow, and the lazy shim install set the new field; `mise install`, `mise upgrade` and `mise use` resolve everything after an install as before.

The new `test_lazy_tools_first_launch_neighbors` installs a lazy tool through its shim while another missing lazy tool is configured. It fails on #14197 and passes with this change, and also checks the installed version is a real one, not `latest`.

> **Medium Risk**

> 
> **Overview**
> **Fixes first launch of a lazy tool** so installing one lazy shim no longer triggers remote version resolution (and offline timeouts / “Failed to resolve tool version list” warnings) for other configured but not-yet-installed lazy tools.
> 
> `InstallOptions` gains **`after_install_resolve`**, separate from **`resolve_options`**: the latter still drives which versions to install; the former controls only the post-install re-resolve. That avoids incorrectly deferring lazy tools during install (e.g. pinning `latest` literally) while still skipping neighbor lazy tools after a first-use install. **`ResolveOptions::for_side_effect_resolve`** is removed in favor of cloning **`after_install_resolve`**.

title: fix(oci): write a tool with several versions once in the embedded config
body:
`mise oci build` writes the project's resolved tools into the image as `/etc/mise/config.toml`. A tool pinned to several versions got one `name = "version"` line per version. That is a duplicate key, so mise inside the container could not read its own config:

```toml
[tools]
java = ["liberica-25", "liberica-17"]
maven = "3.9.16"
```

became

```toml
# Auto-generated by `mise oci build`. Do not edit.
[tools]
java = "liberica-25.0.4+9"
java = "liberica-17.0.20+10"
maven = "3.9.16"
```

and `mise tools` in the container failed with `Invalid TOML in config file … duplicate key`.

Now each tool is written once. A tool with several versions becomes an array, in the order they were resolved, because the first one takes precedence on PATH. A tool with one version is still a string, and the keys keep the short tool name, as before.

This takes over #12732 by @nitschSB, which pr-closer closed after 7 days of failing checks. Those were GitHub API rate limits on the fork run. They are credited as co-author, and the change is theirs. They later re-opened it as #13761, keyed by the full backend name instead (`core:java`), and closed that one themselves. Greptile and CodeRabbit both flagged that variant: the image keeps installs under the short name's directory, so a full-name key would make mise look in the wrong place. This keeps #12732's short-name keys.

Greptile's remaining finding on #12732 was that its tests built the grouped map by hand, so the grouping step itself went untested. The new `repeated_tool_versions_group_into_one_key` test feeds resolved tool versions through the grouping and checks two things: a repeated version collapses, and first-seen order holds.

## Validation

- Unit tests in `src/oci/builder.rs`: a single version renders as a string, several versions render as an ordered array, and repeated resolved versions group into one key.
- With mise 2026.10.4 in a Debian container, `jq = ["1.7.1", "1.6"]` and `mise oci build --from scratch --no-mise` embedded `jq = "1.7.1"` followed by `jq = "1.6"`. The fixed build is covered by the unit tests above on CI; the end-to-end build was not run with it.

Release notes and `CHANGELOG.md` had two link problems (#14198).

**Wrong "Full Changelog" base.** The link at the bottom of GitHub release notes compared against the wrong tag. For v2026.10.5 it was `compare/vfox-v2026.10.4...v2026.10.5` instead of `compare/v2026.10.4...v2026.10.5`, because communique auto-detects the previous tag and the repo also carries `vfox-v…`, `mise-settings-v…` and `mise-util-v…` tags. **CHANGELOG.md headings link to the release.** Each new version heading now links to its GitHub release instead of the commit range, e.g. `## [2026.10.6](…/releases/tag/v2026.10.6) - 2026-10-09`. The two documents stay intentionally different: `CHANGELOG.md` is the terse commit log and the release is the long-form write-up.

title: fix(exec): skip lazy tools that are not installed when resolving after an install
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/594
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

When `mise x` or a shim installs a missing tool version, it no longer looks up remote versions for lazy tools that are not installed.

#14195 stopped an `auto_update` check from resolving every lazy tool, but a launch that actually installs an update still did: after the install, `mise x` resolved the whole toolset again, and each missing lazy tool queried its version list.

```toml
[tools]
dummy = { version = "1", auto_update = true }
codex = { version = "latest", lazy = true }
```

With a newer `dummy` available, `mise x -- dummy` installed it and then looked up `codex`'s versions, which printed warnings and waited on the network if it was unreachable. It now runs the updated `dummy` and leaves `codex` unresolved until it is launched.

The update itself (`mise __tool-update`) gets the same treatment in the three places it resolved the config again after installing: its install options, the symlink rebuild, and the check for versions other projects still need. A lazy tool with nothing installed has nothing to keep or remove there.

Only the commands that run a tool opt in (`mise x` and shims); `mise install`, `mise upgrade`, and `mise use` still resolve everything after an install. It applies where mise already skips these lookups, under `prefer_offline`.

Not covered: the install of a lazy tool on its first launch through a shim still resolves the other missing lazy tools after installing. I tried the same change there and it did not stop the lookups, so I left it out.

The new `test_tool_update_lazy_neighbors` runs an `auto_update` that installs a newer version while a missing lazy tool is configured; it fails without this change.

> **Overview**
> **`mise x` and shims** no longer resolve remote version lists for **configured lazy tools that are not installed** after an install triggered by `auto_update` (or other missing-version installs on launch). title: fix(upgrade): skip remote lookups for missing lazy tools during auto_update
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/592
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Launching a tool with `auto_update = true` while offline no longer waits tens of seconds on remote version lookups for other lazy tools that are not installed.

2026.10.5 stopped a shim from resolving every lazy tool in the config (#14063), but the update it runs before launching an `auto_update` tool still did. That update resolved the whole global config, so with a cold version cache each missing lazy tool waited for its own network timeout before the launch could continue. With Omarchy's defaults (omacom/omarchy#9596), where the agent CLIs set `auto_update`, an installed agent stalled on every launch until the machine was back online.

```toml
[tools]
cursor-agent = { version = "latest", lazy = true, auto_update = true }
codex = { version = "latest", lazy = true }
claude = { version = "latest", lazy = true }
gh = { version = "latest", lazy = true }
```

With `cursor-agent` installed and the others not, an empty version cache, and every connection refused (to simulate offline), `cursor-agent --version`:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 2026.10.5 and this change, `auto_update = true` | 41 s | 8.7 s |
| No `auto_update` | 0.26 s | 0.26 s |

The remaining 8.7 s is the retry backoff on `cursor-agent`'s own failed lookup, after which the installed version runs, as before. The update now resolves only the tool it updates; lazy tools that are not installed stay at their requested version, and installing one through its shim resolves it as before. Nothing changes for a tool that is the update's target, for installed lazy tools, or for `mise upgrade`.

After a successful update, mise still resolves the whole global config once to prune old versions, so an online update that installs something can still look up other missing lazy tools. That doesn't stall offline launches, because nothing was installed.

The new check in `e2e/cli/test_tool_update` fails without the change and passes with it.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: 2.1.293.*

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes toolset resolution during auto_update launches; behavior is scoped to `for_auto_update` but affects upgrade timing and which lazy tools get resolved.
> 
> **Overview**
> **`auto_update` pre-launch upgrades** no longer trigger remote version lookups for **uninstalled lazy tools** in the same global config, even when online (not only under `prefer_offline`).
> 
> Adds **`defer_missing_lazy_online`** on `ResolveOptions` and **`ToolsetBuilder::with_deferred_lazy_resolution_online()`**, used when `mise upgrade` runs with **`for_auto_update`**. body:

Shims and `mise which` no longer resolve a tool's bin name to a directory in another tool's bin path.

Before, with `hunk` (which ships a `skills/` directory next to its binary) ahead of `npm:skills` in the toolset:

mise use -g hunk npm:skills

After, the shim skips the directory and runs `npm:skills`' real binary, matching what shells do through `mise activate`.

Same symptom as #12541 (fixed by #12545), but on the tool bin path rather than the system `PATH` fallback. Reported in discussion #14192.

title: chore(ci): lint workflows with jactionlint
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/590
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Workflow files under `.github/workflows/` are now linted by [jactionlint](https://github.com/jdx/jactionlint), a maintained fork of actionlint, both from `mise run lint` and the hk pre-commit hook. It catches unknown `with:` inputs, `${{ }}` type errors, script injection, bad runner labels and shellcheck problems in `run:` blocks before CI does.

- New `jactionlint` step in `hk.pkl`, and `jactionlint` added to `[tools]` in `mise.toml`.
- `mise.lock` now pins jactionlint 1.8.2 for nine platforms (additions only). CI already runs `mise run lint` (hk) in the `lint` job of `test-impl.yml`, so the new step is exercised without workflow changes.
- New `.github/jactionlint.yaml` declares the self-hosted and Namespace runner labels (`namespace-profile-*`, `jdx-*`) and ignores two style-only shellcheck notes (SC2129 on grouped `>> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"` redirects, SC2016 on the intentional `sh -c '...'` in `test-impl.yml`).

The hk builtin for jactionlint is not in an hk release yet, so this uses an inline step.

Verified: `hk check --all --step jactionlint` passes on the current workflows; without the config file it reports the label and shellcheck findings above.

title: feat(vars): ask once and remember [vars] answers per machine with mise vars prompt
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/589
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A `[vars]` entry can now ask for its value once per machine, offer a default, and remember the answer without putting it in a config file or dotfiles history. Use case: sharing one dotfiles setup while each machine picks its own Git identity (discussion #14183).

```toml
[vars.git_name]
default = "Ada Lovelace"
prompt = "Git author name"

[vars.git_email]
required = "Run mise vars prompt to set git_email"
prompt = "Git email"
```

```sh
mise vars                       # list every var and where it comes from
mise vars git_name=Ada          # save a value on this machine, no terminal needed
mise vars git_name              # print the value templates see
mise vars prompt                # ask for every unanswered prompt var (or name some)
mise vars unset git_name        # forget a saved value, to be asked again
mise bootstrap --prompt-vars    # the same prompting, inside a bootstrap run
```

Enter accepts the default. Every answer, accepted defaults included, is saved in `$MISE_STATE_DIR/vars.toml` (mode 0600, written under a lock), so it is asked once and is then available to templates (`{{ vars.git_name }}`), tasks and tools.

- **Only two things ask:** `mise vars prompt` and `mise bootstrap --prompt-vars`. Shell activation, `mise run`, background sync and runs without a terminal use the saved answer, then `default`, and a `required` var with neither fails with its usual error.
- **Why `--prompt-vars` on bootstrap too:** with `mise bootstrap --adopt owner/dotfiles` the config that declares the vars only exists after the checkout is fetched, so `mise vars prompt` cannot run first. The flag is passed through to the full run in the checkout. It is rejected with a bootstrap subcommand.
- **Precedence**, highest first: process environment, a value in a higher-precedence config file such as `mise.local.toml`, the saved answer, the `default`.
- **Why `[vars]`:** it is what templates, tasks and dotfiles already read, so no second lookup is needed. `prompt` in `[env]` is an error.

Limitations: answers are keyed by var name, so projects using the same name share one answer on a machine. Prompting is eager, so it asks about every unanswered prompt var in the loaded config, used or not; naming vars to `mise vars prompt` narrows that. A `--dry-run` that prompts still saves the answers. A follow-up could ask only for vars the run actually uses.

Tested with terminal runs (Enter on the default, a typed value, only the named var, later `mise run` reusing the answers with no prompt), unit tests for the touched area, and a new e2e test for the non-interactive paths.

 file, source, and plugin directive forms. Under `[vars]`, these directives fill
 `vars` instead of exporting environment variables.
 
+## Ask once and remember {#prompt}
+
+`prompt` makes a var a per-machine answer. Pair it with a `default` to offer a
+suggestion, or with `required` when there is none:
+
+```mise-toml
+[vars.git_name]
+default = "Ada Lovelace"
+prompt = "Git author name"
+
+[vars.git_email]
+required = "Run mise vars prompt to set git_email"
+prompt = "Git email"
+```
+
+Run `mise vars prompt` to be asked for each of these vars that has no answer
+yet; name vars to ask only for those (`mise vars prompt git_name`). Enter accepts
+the default. mise saves every answer, including an accepted default, in
+`$MISE_STATE_DIR/vars.toml`, so it is never asked again, never lands in your
+config or dotfiles history, and is available to every command that reads vars from then on.
+
+```sh
+mise vars                       # list every var and where it comes from
+mise vars git_name=Ada          # save a value on this machine, no terminal needed
+mise vars git_name              # print the value templates see
+mise vars prompt                # ask for every unanswered prompt var
+mise vars unset git_name        # forget a saved value, to be asked again
+```
+
+`mise bootstrap --prompt-vars` does the same inside a bootstrap run, which is how
+a fresh machine answers them with `mise bootstrap --adopt owner/dotfiles`: the
+config that declares the vars only exists once the checkout has been fetched. A
+`--dry-run` still saves the answers it asks for.
+
+Only `mise vars prompt` and `--prompt-vars` ever ask. Everything else, including
+shell activation, tasks, and runs without a terminal, uses the saved answer and
+otherwise falls back to `default`, or fails as any other `required` var does.
+
+A var resolves in this order, highest first: the process environment, a value
+in a higher-precedence config file such as `mise.local.toml`, the saved answer,
+the `default`. Answers are keyed by var name alone, so projects that use the same
+name share one answer on a machine. A value saved with `mise vars NAME=VALUE`
+works for any var name, with or without a `prompt`, and replaces that var's
+`default` on this machine. `prompt` works only in `[vars]`, not `[env]`.
+

title: fix(dotnet): validate the SDK being installed, not the active one
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/588
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Installing an isolated .NET SDK failed when a different mise-managed SDK was already ahead of the mise shims directory on `PATH`, even though the install itself succeeded:

```text
mise ERROR Failed to install core:dotnet@8.0.425: dotnet SDK 8.0.425 was not found in `dotnet --list-sdks` output:
10.0.401 [.../installs/dotnet/10.0.401/sdk]
```

The post-install check ran `dotnet` from `PATH`. With `activate_aggressive=false`, entries before the shims directory stay ahead of the SDK being validated, so the already-active SDK answered. The check now runs the new SDK's `dotnet` by absolute path, so install success no longer depends on what was active beforehand.

Adds an e2e case that installs a second isolated SDK with the first one ahead of the shims on `PATH`; it fails with the error above without the fix and passes with it.

Fixes #14181

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: 2.1.293.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Narrow change to post-install SDK verification for core dotnet; runtime-only installs are unchanged and an e2e test covers the regression.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes false **dotnet** SDK install failures when another mise-managed SDK is already earlier on `PATH` than the shims (e.g. with `activate_aggressive=false`). The post-install check now runs `dotnet --list-sdks` via the **new install’s** binary path from `list_bin_paths`, instead of whatever `dotnet` resolves on `PATH`, so validation targets the version just installed.
> 
> Adds an e2e scenario: isolated install with an older SDK prepended to `PATH`/`DOTNET_ROOT`, then installing a newer SDK must succeed and report the correct version.
>

title: feat(bootstrap): offer to install git and ssh before cloning a repository
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/587
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise bootstrap --from` and `--adopt` clone with the host's `git`, and an SSH URL also needs `ssh`. On a fresh machine that has neither, the command failed on a spawn error, and the repository's own `[bootstrap.packages]` couldn't help because it hadn't been cloned yet.

Now mise checks first and offers to install what's missing with the host package manager:

```
$ mise bootstrap --adopt git@github.com:you/dotfiles.git
git and ssh must be installed to clone git@github.com:you/dotfiles.git. Install git openssh-client with apt? [Y/n]
```

- `--yes` accepts the offer, so unattended bootstraps work: `mise bootstrap --adopt you/dotfiles --yes`.
- Without a terminal and without `--yes`, it stops with a message saying to re-run with `--yes` or install the tools yourself.
- `ssh` is only required for `ssh://` and `user@host:path` URLs. HTTPS and local paths need git alone.
- Supported managers: apt, dnf, pacman, apk, zypper, Homebrew, scoop, winget. macOS and Windows ship an SSH client, so only git is installed there. With no usable manager, the error says so.
- `--dry-run` reports what is missing and what would be installed, and installs nothing.

Discussion: https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14161

Validation: unit tests for SSH URL detection and manager selection, an e2e test (`test_bootstrap_missing_git`) with git off `PATH`, and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`. I didn't run an actual apt install of git end to end.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: 2.1.293.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Runs host package-manager installs and shells out to system tools before clone; behavior differs by OS (e.g. macOS git stub) and URL scheme, but scope is limited to bootstrap entry paths.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Bootstrap clone prerequisites:** `mise bootstrap --from` and `--adopt` now verify that `git` is available (and `ssh` when the remote is SSH/scp-style) *before* cloning, instead of failing on a spawn error on a bare machine.
> 
> When tools are missing, mise can prompt to install them via a detected host package manager (apt, dnf, pacman, apk, zypper, Homebrew, scoop, winget), with `--yes` / `MISE_YES` skipping the prompt and `--dry-run` only reporting what would be installed. Repo `[bootstrap.packages]` still cannot cover this step because the repo is not cloned yet. macOS treats the `/usr/bin/git` stub as “not installed” until Command Line Tools work.
> 
> Docs for repository bootstrap are updated; unit tests cover SSH URL detection and manager selection, plus an e2e test for `--dry-run` when `git` is off `PATH`.

title: test(upgrade): cover auto_update from system config
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/584
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Distros that ship default tools in a system config such as `/etc/mise/conf.d` (Omarchy does) can opt those tools into `auto_update`, so agent CLIs like `codex` and `claude` stay current without `mise upgrade`:

```toml
# /etc/mise/conf.d/defaults.toml
[tools]
codex = { version = "latest", lazy = true, auto_update = true }
```

This already works, because system config counts as global config. This adds e2e coverage so it stays that way: a system-config entry upgrades before `mise x` and before a shim launches it.

No behavior change.

title: fix(config): do not panic for a config file at the filesystem root
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/583
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes #14168

A config file at the filesystem root (`/mise.toml`, common when a Dockerfile copies just the config into the image) made `mise install` and `mise exec` abort with `called Option::unwrap() on a None value` in `config_root`.

```dockerfile
RUN printf '[tools]\n' > /mise.toml
RUN mise trust /mise.toml
RUN mise install   # panicked on 2026.10.4
```

The trust check computes the config root (`/`) and then passes that root back into `config_root`. `/` has no parent, so the unwrap panicked. The parent steps in `config_root` now stop at `/` instead of unwrapping. A config nested under a directory named `mise` directly below `/` (such as `/mise/config.toml`) is fixed too.

title: fix(go): install tools whose published go.mod is not tidy
body:
A `go:` tool failed to install when its published `go.mod` was missing a requirement that one of its packages needs. mise ran `go install -mod=readonly <pkg>@<version>`, and Go refuses to fix up the module graph in that mode:

```
mise ERROR Failed to install go:example.com/untidy/cmd/untidy@v0.1.0: go exited with non-zero status: exit code 1; last stderr: go mod tidy
```

Go's full message is `updates to go.mod needed, disabled by -mod=readonly`. The original report found it with `go:tailscale.com/cmd/tailscale`: the client imports a package whose dependency is not in tailscale's `go.mod`, while `tailscale.com/cmd/tailscaled` from the same module installs fine.

mise now passes `-mod=mod`, so Go resolves the missing requirement and the tool installs. The flag exists so a project's `GOFLAGS=-mod=vendor` does not reach these installs (#7052), and `-mod=mod` still keeps it out. The tool's module sits in the read-only module cache, so nothing on disk is rewritten. The `go list` calls that list versions keep `-mod=readonly`.

This takes over #13203 by @JuanJoseGonGi, which pr-closer closed after 7 days of a failing check. That was an unrelated flaky unit test. They are credited as co-author, and the flag change is theirs. Both CodeRabbit and Greptile pointed out on #13203 that its new test passed with `-mod=readonly` too, because `github.com/jdx/go-example` is tidy. So this replaces that test with one that installs an untidy module.

## Validation

- `e2e/backend/test_go_install` now builds a local `GOPROXY` with two modules. `example.com/untidy` imports `example.com/dep` without requiring it. The test installs the untidy module with `GOFLAGS=-mod=vendor` set, so it covers the untidy module and #7052 together.
- With mise 2026.10.3 (`-mod=readonly`) in a Debian container, that step fails with the error above.
- With Go 1.24 on the same proxy, run directly:
  - `go install -mod=readonly` fails with `updates to go.mod needed`.
  - `go install -mod=mod` installs, and does so with `GOFLAGS=-mod=vendor` too.
  - Without an explicit `-mod`, `GOFLAGS=-mod=vendor` fails with `cannot query module due to -mod=vendor`.
- CI: `backend/test_go_install` passed in the Linux `e2e` job with this change. `backend/test_go_install_error` checks the exact `go install` arguments, so its expected `-mod=readonly` is now `-mod=mod`.

title: fix(use): create config.toml instead of writing global tools to config.<env>.toml
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/582
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

With an environment active (`MISE_ENV=work` or `env = ["work"]` in a miserc) and no `~/.config/mise/config.toml` yet, `mise use -g` wrote the new tool into `config.work.toml`. If that file is a work-only module (for example symlinked from a dotfiles repo), a machine-local tool ends up in it.

```sh
export MISE_CONFIG_DIR=$(mktemp -d)
echo 'env = ["work"]' > "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/miserc.local.toml"
touch "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.work.toml"
mise use -g jq   # before: updates config.work.toml; after: creates config.toml
```

Environment-specific files for the active environments are no longer picked as the default global write target, so `mise use -g` creates `config.toml`, matching the docs and `mise use --help`. Once `config.toml` exists nothing changes, and `--path` and `write_targets` still win.

Discussion: https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14175

title: feat(config): allow local paths in include
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/581
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`include` in `mise.toml` now accepts a local file path, not just `git::` and `oci::` references, matching what `task_config.includes` already allows.

```toml
include = ["./config/tools.toml", "/etc/mise/team.toml"]

[tools]
node = "24" # this file's own entries still win
```

A local include is relative to the including file (or absolute) and is merged the same way as a remote one: it ranks just below the including file, a later entry overrides an earlier one, and the same key allowlist and no-nesting rules apply. It is read on every load, so edits take effect immediately; there is no cache or TTL.

Paranoid mode rejects a local include, because the including file's trust hash does not cover a file that can change without it. Safe mode still skips all includes for project config.

Discussion: https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14144

title: fix(brew): detach a DMG left attached by an interrupted install
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/580
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes #14151

## Problem

If \`mise bootstrap\` is killed while installing a \`.dmg\` cask, the cached image stays attached at its temporary mountpoint. Every later run then fails with \`hdiutil ... exited with code 1\` (\`Resource busy\`, hidden by \`-quiet\`) until the user runs \`hdiutil detach\` by hand.

## Fix

Before attaching, \`un_dmg\` now looks for the same image in \`hdiutil info\` and force-detaches its disk. The next run installs the cask with no manual cleanup. If \`hdiutil info\` or the detach fails, mise logs it at debug level and continues to the attach.

## Notes

- Not changed: surfacing hdiutil's stderr (\`-quiet\` suppresses it) and detaching on SIGINT/SIGTERM. The pre-attach check recovers from a killed run.
- Tested with a unit test for parsing \`hdiutil info\` output (sample modeled on the issue). Not run against a real macOS \`hdiutil\`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: unavailable.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes macOS DMG attach behavior with force-detach of disk devices; failures are non-fatal but wrong parsing could detach the wrong image in edge cases.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes DMG installs failing with **Resource busy** when a prior run was killed mid-extract and left the image attached.
> 
> **`un_dmg`** now takes a per-archive lock (`<canonical-archive>.lock`) so concurrent extractions of the same DMG are not treated as stale, then runs **`detach_stale_dmg`**: it parses **`hdiutil info`** via **`dmg_attached_devices`** to find the whole-disk `/dev/diskN` for that image path and **`hdiutil detach -force`** it. Info/detach failures are logged at debug and attach still proceeds.
>

title: feat(config): merge [bootstrap] from config includes
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/579
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`[bootstrap]` in a config `include` used to be rejected with "`bootstrap` is not supported in a config include", so a shared baseline could not declare bootstrap packages for the repos that include it. It now merges in.

```toml
# shared baseline (git:: or oci:: include)
[bootstrap.packages]
"brew:jq" = "latest"
"brew:fd" = "latest"
```

```toml
# project mise.toml
include = ["git::https://github.com/myorg/platform.git//mise.toml?ref=<sha>"]

[bootstrap.packages]
"brew:jq" = "1.7"   # this file wins; brew:fd comes from the include
```

The included `[bootstrap]` ranks below the including file, key by key: a key the including file declares keeps its own value, lists get the shared entries first, and unset options take the shared value. Every `[bootstrap]` field is accepted, including hooks, users, services and files. They run with the including file's trust, as other included content does (paranoid mode still requires a pinned include).

Fixes #14157

## Validation

Added a unit test merging a fragment's `[bootstrap]` into files with and without their own; it and the existing include merge test pass, and clippy with `-D warnings` is clean. No end-to-end `mise bootstrap` run against a real include.

title: fix(npm): raise the soft open-file limit at startup
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/578
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Summary

Parallel `npm:` installs could fail with `Too many open files (os error 24)` when mise ran under macOS's default launchd soft limit of 256 (e.g. started from a LaunchAgent), because aube's store import keeps many files open at once. mise now raises its soft `RLIMIT_NOFILE` toward the hard limit at startup (capped at 10240, which macOS requires even when the hard limit is unlimited), so no `ulimit -Sn` workaround is needed. Raising the soft limit is unprivileged; the limit is only raised, never lowered.

Fixes #14152

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: unavailable.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Startup-only, best-effort ulimit bump on Unix with no lowering of limits; low blast radius aside from child processes inheriting the new soft limit.
> 
> **Overview**
> On Unix, **mise now raises the soft open-file limit (`RLIMIT_NOFILE`) at the very start of `main`** before other startup work, targeting up to **10240** (macOS `OPEN_MAX`) or the process hard limit if lower. The soft limit is only increased when it is below that target; already-higher limits are unchanged, and failures to read or set the limit are ignored.
> 
> This addresses parallel installs (notably npm/aube store import) failing with **“Too many open files”** under launchd’s default soft limit of 256. The `nix` crate gains the **`resource`** feature for `getrlimit`/`setrlimit`, and a new **e2e test** checks that `mise x` inherits the raised limit from a low parent ulimit while preserving a higher one.
