title: fix(cli): accept yes/no booleans, prefix: in latest, and warn log level
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/544
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

This PR fixes four small CLI problems.

**`mise config set --type bool` rejected `yes`, `no`, `1`, and `0`**, even though settings accept those spellings from the environment. `--type bool` and boolean settings now accept true/yes/1 and false/no/0, in any case:

```console
$ mise config set settings.experimental yes      # before: error: provided string was not `true` or `false`
$ mise config get settings.experimental
true
```

For keys that are not settings, such as `env.*`, `vars.*`, or a task's env, inference stays strict. Only the words `true` and `false` become booleans; anything else is stored as a string. `env.DEBUG = false` unsets `DEBUG`, so reading `0` as a boolean would change what the value means. These commands used to fail with an error; now they store the value as written:

```console
$ mise config set env.DEBUG 0     # writes DEBUG = "0"
$ mise config set env.PORT 1      # writes PORT = "1"
$ mise config set --type bool env.FLAG yes   # writes FLAG = true
```

**`mise latest tool@prefix:X` failed with "invalid version".** It now resolves through the backend's version matching, the same way a bare prefix does:

```console
$ mise latest node@prefix:20
20.19.5
```

**`--log-level warn` was rejected.** Before, the flag only took `warning`, and the logger read that as `info`. The flag now takes the names the `log_level` setting documents: `trace`, `debug`, `info`, `warn`, and `error`. `warning` still works as a hidden alias and now really means warn.

**`mise doctor` hid why config or the toolset failed to load.** It printed only the top-level error. It now prints the full error chain, so the cause appears in the report, for example that the config files are not trusted or that a field is unknown.

### Tests

There are unit tests for boolean parsing, strict inference for keys that are not settings, and the log-level names. There are e2e tests for `config set`, `latest`, and `--log-level` (checking that warn hides info output), plus a new `test_doctor_config_error`.

title: fix(edit): do not overwrite an existing config without a terminal
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/543
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

When `mise edit` or `mise generate config` runs without a terminal (a script, CI, an editor task) or with `-y`, it skips the interactive editor and writes a commented starter template. That template is a new file, not an edit of the existing one, so it silently replaced an existing config and exited 0:

```console
$ cat mise.toml
[tools]
node = "22"
$ mise edit -y
mise writing to mise.toml
$ head -1 mise.toml
# mise config files are hierarchical. mise will find all of the config files
```

Now both commands refuse to write the template over an existing file, and the file is left untouched:

```console
$ mise edit -y
Error: mise.toml already exists; to edit it, run this command in a terminal without --yes, or pass --force to replace it with the starter template
```

A new `-f/--force` flag on both commands asks for the replacement explicitly (`mise edit -y --force`, `mise generate config -y --force`). The interactive editor, `--dry-run` and `--tool-versions` (which merges into the existing file) work as before, and so does creating a config that does not exist yet.

**Migration:** scripts that used `mise edit -y` or `mise generate config -y` to reset an existing config to the template must now add `--force`.

Tested with a new e2e test, `e2e/cli/test_edit_existing`, which fails without the fix. The existing `test_edit_global` and `test_generate_config` still pass.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: claude-code_2-1-289_agent.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes default CLI behavior for scripts/CI using `-y` without `--force`, and touches config file creation with symlink edge cases; scope is limited to edit/generate config template writes.
> 
> **Overview**
> **`mise edit` and `mise generate config` no longer silently overwrite an existing config** when they take the non-interactive path (no TTY or `--yes`). They now error with guidance to use a real terminal or pass **`--force`** to apply the starter template.
> 
> A new **`-f/--force`** flag restores the old overwrite behavior for that template path only; interactive edit, **`--dry-run`**, and **`--tool-versions`** are unchanged. Template writes to a missing file go through **`write_new_config`**, which uses **`create_new`** (and symlink-aware targeting) so existing configs and racing writers are not clobbered.
> 
> Docs, usage metadata, and man pages are updated; behavior is covered by **`e2e/cli/test_edit_existing`** and unit tests on **`write_new_config`**.
> 
> **Migration:** scripts that relied on `mise edit -y` / `mise generate config -y` to reset a file must add **`--force`**.

title: fix(cli): print the invoked command name in help
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/542
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise dotfiles` is also available as `mise bootstrap dotfiles`. Help for its subcommands always showed the `bootstrap` path, whichever one you typed:

```console
$ mise dot add --help
Usage: mise bootstrap dotfiles add [FLAGS] [TARGET]…
```

Help now follows the path you actually used:

```console
$ mise dot add --help
Usage: mise dotfiles add [FLAGS] [TARGET]…

$ mise bootstrap dotfiles add --help
Usage: mise bootstrap dotfiles add [FLAGS] [TARGET]…
```

This applies to `--help`, `-h`, `mise help <command>`, the page printed when required arguments are missing, and `--help-all` where a command supports it. Any subcommand mounted in two places now shows the path you typed. Aliases are shown by their canonical name (`dot` shows as `dotfiles`), as before.

The cause was that help looked the command up by its address, and a subcommand mounted in two places has a single address, so the first mount always won. mise now renders the page from the route the parser took through the command line, using usage-rs's `help::page`. When that route can't be rebuilt, it falls back to the old lookup.

No migration needed.

Validation: a new e2e test (`e2e/cli/test_help_shared_subcommand`) fails on main and passes with this change. The existing help e2e tests and the `cli` unit tests pass.

title: fix(task): report unmatched sources, show depends_post, and load global tasks
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/541
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Warn when a task's `sources` match no files

mise has a warning for a task whose `sources` globs match nothing, but it never fired: the task's config file is always added as a source, so there was always at least one match. A typo in `sources` now produces the warning when mise checks whether the task is up to date.

```toml
[tasks.build]
sources = ["src/**/*.rss"]  # typo
run = "cargo build"
```

```
mise WARN  no files match sources for task build: src/**/*.rss
```

With a task that has `depends_post`, `mise tasks deps <task>` left out the post tasks, though `mise tasks deps` with no arguments showed them:

```toml

```

one (post)

```

## Global file tasks load without a global config file

Scripts in `$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/tasks` (by default `~/.config/mise/tasks`) only loaded when a global config file such as `~/.config/mise/config.toml` existed. Without one, they were missing when you ran mise from outside `$HOME`. They also never loaded from a `MISE_CONFIG_DIR` other than `~/.config/mise`. Both cases now work:

```sh

```

Without a global config file, only `$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/tasks` is global. The other task directories in `$HOME` (`~/.mise/tasks`, `~/mise-tasks` and so on) are still loaded as local tasks, so a `~/mise.toml` `[task_config]` (`dir`, `includes`, `excludes`, env, inputs) still applies to them. A `MISE_CONFIG_DIR` whose path contains glob characters such as `[` is treated as a literal path.

title: fix(task): skip fresh raw and interactive cached tasks when their cache key is unchanged
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/540
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

If a task had `cache` enabled and ran with `raw = true`, `interactive = true`, or `mise run --raw`, it ran every time, even when nothing had changed. The artifact cache skips these tasks because their output goes straight to the terminal and cannot be captured or replayed. The usual "sources up-to-date, skipping" check was skipped along with it.

```toml
[tasks.build]
run = "./build.sh"
raw = true
sources = ["input.txt"]
outputs = ["dist"]
cache = { enabled = true, env = ["PROFILE"] }
```

**Before:** each `PROFILE=debug mise run build` ran `./build.sh` again.

## Fix

mise now computes the cache key for raw and interactive tasks. It skips one only when its sources are fresh (or it declares `outputs = []`) **and** its cache key matches the key from its last successful run. The key covers sources, `cache.env`, `cache.command_inputs`, tool versions and dependency keys.

**After:**

```console
$ PROFILE=debug mise run build     # runs
$ PROFILE=debug mise run build     # sources up-to-date, skipping
$ PROFILE=release mise run build   # runs again: cache.env changed
```

- A failed run clears the recorded key, so the next run executes instead of keeping the failed run's outputs.
- The task passes its cache key to dependents whether it runs or is skipped, so a cached dependent does not reuse outputs built from an earlier upstream key.
- `--force` still runs the task.
- Raw and interactive tasks still store and restore no artifact, so their output is never replayed.
- `--task-cache-explain` reports the key for these tasks even when they are skipped.

## Behavior change

Because the key is now computed, a raw or interactive task's `cache.command_inputs` run on every invocation, as they already do for other cached tasks. Dry runs still do not run them.

title: fix(task): resolve mise run ./script relative to the current directory
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/539
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise run` accepts a path to a script, such as `./build.sh` or `../scripts/release.sh`. That relative path was resolved against the project root instead of the directory you ran mise from. From a subdirectory, this either ran a different script with the same name at the project root, or failed because the file was not found:

```console
$ cd project/sub
$ mise run ./x.sh        # sub/x.sh exists, project/x.sh does not
mise WARN  could not read task file /…/project/./x.sh: No such file or directory (os error 2)
sh: 0: cannot open /…/project/./x.sh: No such file
[] ERROR task failed

$ mise run ../x.sh       # also looked for /…/project/../x.sh
```

Now a `./` or `../` path is resolved from the current directory, the same way a shell resolves it:

```console
$ cd project/sub
$ mise run ./x.sh
[] $ /…/project/sub/x.sh
```

Behaviour that does not change:
- The script still runs with the project root as its working directory.
- `MISE_TASK_NAME` still comes from the path as typed.
- Absolute paths and `file = "./x"` entries in `mise.toml` (which are relative to the config root) work as before.

`MISE_TASK_FILE` and `MISE_TASK_DIR` now point at the script that actually runs. Nothing needs migrating, unless you relied on `./name` from a subdirectory running the copy at the project root. In that case, use `mise run ../name` or an absolute path.

Validation: the new e2e test `e2e/tasks/test_task_run_relative_path` fails without the fix and passes with it. The neighbouring task e2e tests still pass.

> **Overview**
> **`mise run` with a relative script path** (e.g. `./build.sh`, `../scripts/x.sh`) now resolves that path from the **current working directory**, matching shell behavior. Previously the same argument was resolved against the **project/config root**, so running from a subdirectory could pick the wrong file or fail with “file not found”.
> 
> Implementation: when the run argument looks like a filesystem path and the file exists, the path is **absolutized from CWD** before `Task::from_path`, while the **task name** still reflects the path as typed. **`MISE_TASK_FILE`** and **`MISE_TASK_DIR`** now refer to the script that actually runs. Unchanged: cwd for execution stays the project root, absolute paths, and `file = "./x"` in `mise.toml` (config-root-relative).
> 
> Adds e2e coverage in `e2e/tasks/test_task_run_relative_path`.
>

title: fix(vfox): do not fail every command for an env plugin with no source
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/538
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

An `[env]` module names a vfox env plugin. If that plugin was not installed and mise had nowhere to install it from, every `mise` command failed while loading config. That included `mise plugins install` and `mise plugins link`, the commands that would fix it. "Nowhere to install it from" means no registry entry, no `[plugins]` URL, and a name that is not owner/repo or a URL.

```toml
[env]
_.my-env-plugin = {}
FOO = "bar"
```

Before, every command failed:

```
$ mise ls
Error: Invalid version: my-env-plugin
```

Now mise skips that module, keeps the rest of `[env]`, and tells you how to fix it:

```
$ mise env -s bash
mise WARN  skipping env plugin my-env-plugin: it is not installed and has no source (a registry name, owner/repo, or URL)
Install it with `mise plugins install my-env-plugin <git-url>`, or set its URL in [plugins]
export FOO=bar
```

`mise doctor` lists each skipped module as a problem and exits 1. After you install or link the plugin, the next command uses it. The skipped result is never cached.

Only a plugin with no source at all is skipped. If the source is known but the install fails, mise still errors as before, and `mise run` and `mise exec` stop instead of running without the env. Examples of that are a missing repository, a network error, paranoid or safe mode, or a declined community-plugin prompt. Env plugins often provide secrets, so a deploy task does not run without its credentials. An installed plugin whose hook raises an error is still an error too.

The error for a name mise cannot resolve now says `no plugin source for <name>` instead of `Invalid version`.

An e2e test (`e2e/env/test_env_module_not_installed`) covers:
- the skip, the warning and the doctor report
- linking the plugin afterwards
- an installed plugin whose hook raises an error
- a known source that cannot be installed (a local path and an owner/repo clone), which keeps failing and does not run the task

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: claude-code_2-1-289_agent.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes config/env resolution behavior for missing env plugins—mostly safer UX—but misclassified “no source” vs “failed install” could still let commands run without expected secrets or skip modules incorrectly.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Unconfigured `[env]` vfox modules no longer brick the whole CLI.** If `_.<name>` points at a plugin that is not installed and has no install source (registry, `[plugins]`, `owner/repo`, or URL), mise **warns**, **skips** that module, still applies the rest of `[env]`, and marks the result uncacheable—so `mise plugins install` / `mise plugins link` keep working.
> 
> **`mise doctor`** now errors on each skipped module (with install hints), except under **safe mode**, where project env module

title: fix: replace panics on bad input with errors
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/537
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Several kinds of bad input crashed mise with a panic instead of an error you could act on. This PR turns each one into a clear error.

### Invalid plugin cache key
An asdf plugin whose `mise.plugin.toml` has an invalid cache-key template used to panic. mise now reports the template parse error.

### Unknown setting values
An unknown value for `status.missing_tools` panicked in `hook-env`, which runs at every prompt in an activated shell. An unknown `windows_shim_mode` panicked during reshim. Both are now rejected when settings load, the same way `lockfile_mode` already is:

```
$ MISE_STATUS_MESSAGE_MISSING_TOOLS=sometimes mise hook-env -s bash
Error: invalid status.missing_tools value "sometimes"; expected one of: never, if_other_versions_installed, always
```

`mise settings set` now refuses these values before writing them. Before, it saved the bad value, and then every command failed until you edited the config by hand:

```
$ mise settings set windows_shim_mode copy
Error: invalid windows_shim_mode value "copy"; expected one of: exe, file, hardlink, symlink
```

If one of these settings already holds a bad value in a config file, you can fix it with `mise settings set <key> <value>` or `mise settings unset [--local] <key>`, because those commands no longer need to load settings first. The allowed values for `status.missing_tools` and `windows_shim_mode` are now also listed in the JSON schema, so editors can flag a typo.

### `mise unset` with no config file
`mise unset FOO` failed with "Is a directory" when the directory had no config file. It now creates `mise.toml`, as `mise set` does and as its help text says. If the config file exists but isn't valid TOML, `mise unset` reports the parse error instead of overwriting the file.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: claude-code_2-1-289_agent.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Settings validation runs on every load and changes CLI repair behavior for strict-choice keys; plugin cache init now fails on bad templates instead of crashing.
> 
> **Overview**
> Replaces several **panic-on-bad-input** paths with clear errors users can fix.
> 
> **Strict enum settings** (`lockfile_mode`, `status.missing_tools`, `windows_shim_mode`) are validated at settings load and blocked by `mise settings set` via codegen’d `setting_choices` from `settings.toml`, with `STRICT_CHOICE_SETTINGS` and repair-mode `mise settings set`/`unset` so broken values in config can still be corrected without loading settings. `status.missing_tools` parsing no longer panics on unknown strings; Windows shim code returns errors instead of panicking on invalid modes.
> 
> **External plugin cache** template rendering for cache keys now propagates parse failures instead of panicking inside lazy cache ini

title: fix(plugins): stop mise plugins uninstall --purge from panicking
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/536
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

`mise plugins uninstall --purge` panicked for a vfox backend plugin, a plugin that provides `plugin:tool` tools. The plugin itself was removed, but every `plugin:tool` install, its downloads and its cache were left behind:

```console
$ mise plugins uninstall my-backend --purge
thread 'main' panicked at src/cli/plugins/uninstall.rs:...
```

The command looked up a backend by the plugin's name after removing the plugin. No tool has that name, so the lookup came back empty, and that empty result was unwrapped.

## Fix

`--purge` now works out what to remove before it removes the plugin:

- **Backend plugins:** every installed tool the plugin backs, for example `my-backend:foo` and `my-backend:bar`, has its installs, downloads and cache removed. So does a tool that config declares with the plugin but whose last version was already uninstalled, since its cache and kept downloads remain.
- **asdf and vfox plugins:** the tool with the plugin's name is purged, as before.

Directories are never removed by name alone. Two tools can map to the same directory name (`acme:extra` and a plugin `acme-extra` both use `acme-extra`), so a tool whose directory another installed or configured tool also uses is skipped with a warning:

```console
$ mise plugins uninstall acme --purge
mise WARN  not purging acme:extra: another tool uses its directory
```

`--purge` only removes the user's own installs. An install found in a shared or system install dir (`MISE_SHARED_INSTALL_DIRS`, `/usr/local/share/mise/installs`) is left in place, because other users may rely on it. Only the user's own cache and downloads for that tool are removed.

```console
$ mise plugins uninstall my-backend --purge
mise plugin:my-backend remove ~/.local/share/mise/installs/my-backend-foo
mise plugin:my-backend remove ~/.cache/mise/my-backend-foo
mise plugin:my-backend remove ~/.local/share/mise/downloads/my-backend-foo
mise plugin:my-backend ✓ uninstalled
```

Other backend plugins' tools are not affected.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: claude-code_2-1-289_agent.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes destructive `--purge` behavior and filesystem deletion rules for multi-tool backend plugins, with collision and shared-dir safeguards but still a high-impact uninstall path.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes a panic when running `mise plugins uninstall --purge` on a **vfox backend** plugin (tools named `plugin:tool`). Purge targets are computed **before** the plugin is removed, instead of looking up a backend by the plugin name afterward (which no longer exists and used to `.unwrap()`).
> 
> For backend plugins, `--purge` now removes installs, downloads, and cache for every tool that plugin backs—installed `plugin:tool` entries and tools still declared

+assert_directory_exists "$MISE_CACHE_DIR/purge-backend-extra"

title: fix(cli): replace unimplemented!() in --monorepo flags with an error
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/535
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise outdated`, `mise prune` and `mise upgrade` accepted a `--monorepo` flag that was only a placeholder. Passing it crashed mise with a Rust panic and exit code 101, and `--help` listed the flag as if it worked.

Before:

```
$ mise upgrade --monorepo
The application panicked (crashed).
Message:  not implemented: mise upgrade --monorepo is not implemented yet
Location: src/cli/upgrade.rs:227
$ echo $?
101
```

After:

```
$ mise upgrade --monorepo
mise ERROR --monorepo is not supported by mise upgrade yet
$ echo $?
1
```

`mise outdated --monorepo` and `mise prune --monorepo` behave the same way. The placeholder flags are now hidden from `--help` and the CLI reference until monorepo support exists for these commands. They are still accepted, so scripts that pass them get the clear error instead of an unknown-flag error. `mise install --monorepo`, `mise ls --monorepo` and the other monorepo flags that work are unchanged.

Validation: a new e2e test, `cli/test_monorepo_unsupported_flags`, checks the error, the absence of a panic, and the hidden help entry for all three commands. It fails on main and passes with this change. The existing outdated and prune e2e tests still pass.

> **Overview**
> **Placeholder `--monorepo` on `outdated`, `prune`, and `upgrade` no longer panics.** Those commands still accept the flag for forward compatibility, but they now exit with a normal `mise ERROR` (`--monorepo is not supported by mise <cmd> yet`) instead of Rust `unimplemented!()` (exit 101).
>

title: fix(watch): pass watchexec flags through to watchexec
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/534
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise watch` lists about 17 watchexec flags in its help, but it parsed them and never passed them to watchexec. So `mise watch --shell bash build`, `--notify`, `--color never`, `--timings`, `--bell`, `--fs-events create,modify`, `--filter-file`, `--emit-events-to` and the rest did nothing.

All of them except `--workdir` now reach watchexec:

```sh
mise watch --timings --color never --fs-events create,modify build
# runs: watchexec --color never --timings --fs-events create,modify ... -- mise run build
```

Flag defaults are not forwarded, so watchexec still applies its own.

### Flags that need special handling

- **`--env` and `--quiet`.** watchexec's `-E/--env` and `-q/--quiet` used to shadow mise's global `-E/--env` and `-q/--quiet` after `watch`. They are now spelled `--watchexec-env KEY=VALUE` and `--watchexec-quiet`. `mise watch -E dev build` still selects the `dev` environment, as it does for every other command.
- **`--manual`.** `mise watch --manual` prints watchexec's manual page. It no longer needs a task to resolve.
- **`--only-emit-events`.** `mise watch --emit-events-to json-stdio --only-emit-events build` watches `build`'s sources and prints the matching events. It does not run the task. watchexec refuses both `--manual` and `--only-emit-events` when a command follows, so mise adds no `-- mise run ...` for these two.
- **`--project-origin`.** A user-supplied `--project-origin` replaces the origin mise derives from the task sources, and the source filters are made relative to it. An origin that does not contain every watched source is an error, because watchexec would silently drop the filter for the source outside it.
- **`--workdir`.** It is hidden and not forwarded, and `mise watch` warns that it has no effect. mise runs each task from its own `dir`, so the flag could only change where the nested `mise run` looks up tasks, and it would find the wrong ones or none.
- **`--glob`.** It is now shown in `mise watch --help`.

### Validation

- Unit tests check the watchexec argv built for the forwarded flags. They also check that the defaults add nothing, that `-E`/`-q` after `watch` stay mise's own, and that `--only-emit-events` gets no command.
- e2e tests `test_watch_forwarded_flags` and `test_watch_without_command` run real watchexec 2.8.0. They check the logged command line, that creating a matching file reruns the task and a non-matching file does not, that the task sees `--watchexec-env` and `-E dev`, that `--manual` prints the man page, and that `--only-emit-events` prints events without running the task.

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+# The watchexec flags `mise watch` accepts must reach the watchexec command
+# line it builds; several used to be parsed and then dropped. We assert on the
+# `$ watchexec ...` line that mise logs (with MISE_DEBUG=1) right before
+# spawning watchexec, and on what the task itself sees.
+#
+# `-E dev` after `watch` is mise's environment flag, not watchexec's `--env`,
+# which is spelled `--watchexec-env` instead.
+
+mise use -g watchexec@latest
+mkdir -p src
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[tasks.example]
+run = 'echo "task saw FOO=$FOO MISE_ENV=$MISE_ENV"'
+sources = ["src/**/*.txt"]
+EOF
+
+output_file=.watch_forwarded_output
+
+MISE_DEBUG=1 mise watch -E dev --watchexec-env FOO=bar --watchexec-quiet --timings \
+  --color never --fs-events create,modify --project-origin src --workdir /tmp example >"${output_file}" 2>&1 &
+PID_TO_KILL=$!
+# Stop watchexec as well as mise, also when an assertion below fails.
+stop_watch() {
+  pkill -P "$PID_TO_KILL" 2>/dev/null || true
+  kill "$PID_TO_KILL" 2>/dev/null || true
+}
+trap stop_watch EXIT
+
+runs() { tr -d '\0' <"${output_file}" | grep -c '^task saw FOO=bar' || true; }
+wait_for_runs() {
+  for _ in $(seq 1 40); do
+    [ "$(runs)" -ge "$1" ] && return
+    sleep 0.5
+  done
+}
+wait_for_runs 1
+
+# The filters must match real changes: a new .txt file under the origin
+# reruns the task, and a file the filter excludes does not.
+sleep 1
+touch src/ignored.md
+sleep 2
+[ "$(runs)" = 1 ] || fail "src/ignored.md reran the task: $(tr -d '\0' <"${output_file}")"
+touch src/changed.txt
+wait_for_runs 2
+[ "$(runs)" = 2 ] || fail "src/changed.txt did not rerun the task: $(tr -d '\0' <"${output_file}")"
+
+# Stop watchexec as well as mise; killing mise alone leaves watchexec running.
+stop_watch
+
+assert_contains "cat ${output_file}" "--env FOO=bar"
+assert_contains "cat ${output_file}" "--color never --timings --quiet"
+assert_contains "cat ${output_file}" "--fs-events create,modify"
+assert_contains "cat ${output_file}" "--project-origin $(pwd -P)/src "
+assert_contains "cat ${output_file}" "-f **/*.txt"
+assert_not_contains "cat ${output_file}" "--env dev"
+# --workdir is accepted but not forwarded, so the nested `mise run` still
+# finds the task in this project (the output below).
+assert_contains "cat ${output_file}" "--workdir has no effect"
+assert_not_contains "grep -F '\$ watchexec' ${output_file}" "--workdir"
+assert_contains "cat ${output_file}" "task saw FOO=bar MISE_ENV=dev"
+
+# An origin that does not contain every source is rejected: watchexec would
+# drop the filter for the source outside it.
+mkdir -p shared
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[tasks.example]
+run = 'echo ran'
+sources = ["src/**/*.txt", "shared/**/*.txt"]
+EOF
+assert_fail_contains "mise watch --project-origin src example" "does not contain the watched source"
+
+# An exclusion outside the origin excludes nothing inside it, so it is not
+# rejected: the check fails only on the positive source. A gitignore-style
+# exclusion such as `!**/*.tmp` starts above the origin but still matches
+# files inside it, so it is rebased onto the origin and keeps working.
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[tasks.example]
+run = 'echo ran'
+sources = ["src/**", "!shared/**", "!**/*.tmp"]
+EOF
+# The `src/**` filter matches any file watchexec sees, so the log goes outside
+# the watched directory or every write to it would retrigger the task.

+MISE_DEBUG=1 mise watch --project-origin src example >"${output_file}" 2>&1 &
+PID_TO_KILL=$!
+runs() { tr -d '\0' <"${output_file}" | grep -c '^ran$' || true; }
+# `mise run` skips the task when its own sources are unchanged, so count the
+# times watchexec starts it rather than the times the task prints.
+triggers() { tr -d '\0' <"${output_file}" | grep -c '^\[Running: ' || true; }
+wait_for_runs 1
+[ "$(runs)" = 1 ] || fail "the task did not run on start: $(tr -d '\0' <"${output_file}")"
+sleep 1
+touch src/excluded.tmp
+sleep 2
+[ "$(triggers)" = 1 ] || fail "src/excluded.tmp retriggered the task: $(tr -d '\0' <"${output_file}")"
+touch src/included.txt
+wait_for_runs 2
+[ "$(triggers)" = 2 ] || fail "src/included.txt did not rerun the task: $(tr -d '\0' <"${output_file}")"

+assert_contains "grep -F '\$ watchexec' ${output_file}" "--ignore **/*.tmp"
+assert_not_contains "grep -F '\$ watchexec' ${output_file}" "shared"

title: fix: require experimental for remote task sources, OpenTelemetry and spinel
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/533
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

These features are documented as experimental but worked without `experimental = true`. They now need it at the point of use. Config that only mentions them still loads.

**Breaking for anyone already using them:** add `experimental = true` under `[settings]`, or set `MISE_EXPERIMENTAL=1`, if you use any of these:

- `git::` remote task files (`file = "git::..."`)
- `git::` or `oci::` entries in `task_config.includes`
- OpenTelemetry export of `mise run` (`otel.enabled`/`otel.logs` with an OTLP endpoint)
- the `spinel:` backend's installs

### Before / after

```toml
[tasks.deploy]
file = "git::https://github.com/org/tasks.git//deploy"
```

Before, with experimental off: `mise run deploy` fetched and ran the remote file.

After:

```
$ mise run deploy
mise ERROR loading task `deploy` from a `git::` file is experimental. Enable it with `mise settings experimental=true`
```

The rule: only running a task enforces the experimental gate on remote (`git::`) task files. Commands that only inspect tasks (list, show, validate, dependency trees, completion, docs generation, and similar) never fetch a gated remote file; they show the task with a one-time warning that its remote file is experimental and was not fetched.

```
$ mise tasks info deploy
mise WARN  task `deploy` has a `git::` file, which is experimental and was not fetched. Enable it with `mise settings experimental=true`
Task: deploy
...
```

- Runs, so refuses: `mise run` (including a `git::` task pulled in as a dependency), `mise watch`, and `mise run --dry-run`. A dry run executes nothing, but it plans the execution from the fetched file, so it stays strict.
- Inspects, so shows the task from its TOML metadata and warns once: `mise tasks ls`, `mise tasks info`, `mise tasks deps` (tree and `--dot`), and `mise generate task-docs`. `mise tasks ls --complete` and `mise tasks --usage` (the `mise run` completion spec) do the same without the warning, since a shell reads their output. `mise tasks validate` reports a validated `deploy` as a validation warning instead, and says nothing about a gated task it was not asked to validate. A TOML `usage` default that feeds `depends` still resolves, so `mise tasks deps` shows the full graph.
- `mise generate task-docs` previously never fetched remote task files and warned that it could not read `git::...` as a local path. It now fetches them like `mise tasks info` does, so with experimental on a remote task's `#USAGE` header is documented. Hidden tasks are dropped before fetching, so a hidden task's unreachable file cannot fail the command.
- `mise cache task` and `mise cache clear --task` use the inspecting fetcher too, but task artifact caching is itself experimental, so they still refuse with experimental off.
- `mise generate task-stubs`, `mise tasks edit` and the MCP `mise://tasks` resource never fetch remote task files, so the gate does not apply

@@ -0,0 +1,129 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+# Remote `git::` task files, `git::`/`oci::` task includes and OpenTelemetry
+# export are experimental: with experimental off, a config that mentions them
+# still loads, and nothing is fetched or exported.
+
+export MISE_EXPERIMENTAL=0
+
+# Nothing listens on port 9 here, so a missing gate shows up as a fetch error.
+cat <<'TOML' >mise.toml
+[tasks.local]
+run = "echo local-ok"
+
+[tasks.remote]
+description = "a remote task"
+file = "git::https://127.0.0.1:9/org/repo.git//tasks/hello"
+
+[tasks.uses-remote]
+depends = ["remote"]
+run = "echo uses-remote"
+TOML
+
+# Only running a task enforces the gate, dry runs and dependencies included.
+assert "mise run local" "local-ok"
+assert_fail_matches "mise run remote" "loading task .remote. from a .git::. file is experimental"
+assert_fail_matches "mise run uses-remote" "loading task .remote. from a .git::. file is experimental"
+assert_fail_matches "mise run --dry-run remote" "loading task .remote. from a .git::. file is experimental"
+
+# Commands that only inspect tasks never fetch the remote file: they show the
+# task from its TOML metadata and warn that its file was not fetched.
+assert_contains "mise tasks ls" "local"
+assert_contains "mise tasks ls" "a remote task"
+assert_matches "mise tasks ls 2>&1" "task .remote. has a .git::. file, which is experimental and was not fetched"
+assert_contains "mise tasks info remote" "a remote task"
+assert_contains "mise tasks info remote 2>&1" "was not fetched"
+assert_contains "mise tasks info remote --json" '"description": "a remote task"'
+assert_contains "mise tasks deps uses-remote" "remote"
+assert_contains "mise tasks deps uses-remote 2>&1" "was not fetched"
+assert_contains "mise tasks deps --dot" "uses-remote"
+assert_contains "mise generate task-docs" "a remote task"
+assert_contains "mise generate task-docs 2>&1" "was not fetched"
+assert_not_contains "mise generate task-docs 2>&1" "could not read task file"
+assert_contains "mise tasks ls --complete" "local:"
+assert_contains "mise tasks ls --complete" "remote:a remote task"
+assert_not_contains "mise tasks ls --complete 2>&1" "experimental"
+assert_contains "mise tasks --usage" 'cmd local'
+assert_contains "mise tasks --usage" 'cmd remote'
+assert_not_contains "mise tasks --usage 2>&1" "experimental"
+
+# Validation does not fetch the remote file either: it reports it as a warning
+# and still validates the other tasks.
+assert_succeed "mise tasks validate local"
+assert_succeed "mise tasks validate"
+assert_contains "mise tasks validate 2>&1" "is experimental; not fetched"
+assert_not_contains "mise tasks validate 2>&1" "not found"
+# Validate reports a validated remote task as an issue, not also as a warning,
+# and says nothing about a remote task it was not asked to validate.
+assert_not_contains "mise tasks validate 2>&1" "was not fetched"
+assert_not_contains "mise tasks validate local 2>&1" "remote"
+
+# A remote task's TOML usage defaults still resolve its dependencies.
+cat <<'TOML' >mise.toml
+[tasks.child]
+run = "echo child"
+
+[tasks.remote-usage]
+usage = 'arg "[target]" default="child"'
+depends = ["{{usage.target}}"]
+file = "git::https://127.0.0.1:9/org/repo.git//tasks/hello"
+TOML
+
+assert_contains "mise tasks deps remote-usage" "child"
+assert_not_contains "mise tasks deps remote-usage 2>&1" "could not read task file"
+
+# Hidden tasks are never documented, so an unreachable remote file on one does
+# not stop docs for the others.
+cat <<'TOML' >mise.toml
+[tasks.local]
+description = "a local task"
+run = "echo local-ok"
+
+[tasks.hidden-http]
+hide = true
+file = "http://127.0.0.1:9/hidden.sh"
+TOML
+
+assert_contains "mise generate task-docs" "a local task"
+
+cat <<'TOML' >mise.toml
+[task_config]
+includes = ["git::https://127.0.0.1:9/org/repo.git//tasks"]
+
+[tasks.local]
+run = "echo local-ok"
+TOML
+
+# The remote include is skipped with a warning; the config's own tasks still
+# list, complete and run.
+assert_succeed "mise config ls"
+assert "mise run local" "local-ok"
+assert_matches "mise run local 2>&1" "skipping task include .git::https://127.0.0.1:9/org/repo.git//tasks.: including tasks from a .git::. source is experimental"
+assert_contains "mise tasks ls" "local"
+assert_contains "mise tasks ls --complete" "local:"
+
+cat <<'TOML' >mise.toml
+[task_config]
+includes = ["oci::127.0.0.1:9/org/tasks:v1"]
+
+[tasks.local]
+run = "echo local-ok"
+TOML
+
+assert "mise run local" "local-ok"
+assert_matches "mise run local 2>&1" "including tasks from an .oci::. source is experimental"
+
+cat <<'TOML' >mise.toml
+[settings.otel]
+enabled = true
+
+[tasks.local]
+run = "echo local-ok"
+TOML
+
+# Without an endpoint nothing is exported, so the setting alone is fine.
+assert "mise run local" "local-ok"
+assert_fail_contains "OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:9 mise run local" "OpenTelemetry export is experimental"
+
+export MISE_EXPERIMENTAL=1
+assert "OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:9 OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT=100 mise run local" "local-ok"

title: fix(bootstrap): warn on legacy command spellings and mise direnv
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/532
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Several old spellings kept working with no sign that they were deprecated. Users had no reason to move off them before they are removed:

- `mise bootstrap launchd`, `mise bootstrap systemd` and `mise bootstrap macos-defaults` (and their `apply`/`status` subcommands), which moved under `mise bootstrap macos` and `mise bootstrap linux`
- the old part names in `--only`/`--skip`: `launchd`, `systemd`, `defaults` and `shell`
- `mise direnv`, deprecated in #3464 (December 2024) but never warned

Each one now still works but prints a deprecation warning that names its replacement:

```console
$ mise bootstrap launchd status
mise WARN  deprecated [bootstrap.launchd]: `mise bootstrap launchd` is deprecated. Use `mise bootstrap macos launchd-agents` instead. This will be removed in mise 2027.10.4.

$ mise bootstrap --skip launchd,shell
mise WARN  deprecated [bootstrap.part_aliases]: Legacy bootstrap part names in --only/--skip are deprecated. Replace `launchd` with `macos-launchd-agents`, `shell` with `mise-shell-activate`. This will be removed in mise 2027.10.4.

$ mise direnv activate
mise WARN  deprecated [cli.direnv]: `mise direnv` and the `use mise` direnv integration are deprecated. Use `mise activate`, and move .envrc settings into mise.toml `[env]` (see https://mise.jdx.dev/direnv.html). This will be removed in mise 2027.10.4.
```

## Migration

| Old | New |
| --- | --- |
| `mise bootstrap launchd …` | `mise bootstrap macos launchd-agents …` |
| `mise bootstrap systemd …` | `mise bootstrap linux systemd-units …` |
| `mise bootstrap macos-defaults …` | `mise bootstrap macos defaults …` |
| `--only`/`--skip` `launchd`, `systemd`, `defaults`, `shell` | `macos-launchd-agents`, `linux-systemd-units`, `macos-defaults`, `mise-shell-activate` |
| `mise direnv` / `use mise` in `.envrc` | `mise activate`, with `.envrc` settings moved into mise.toml `[env]` |

`mise bootstrap remote --only/--skip` warns the same way. Behavior does not change otherwise: the old spellings run exactly as before until they are removed in 2027.10.4. Only `mise direnv` and `mise direnv activate` warn. The `use_mise` hook in an existing direnv setup calls the internal `mise direnv exec` on every reload, and that stays quiet, so the warning does not repeat on each directory change.

## Validation

New e2e tests (`e2e/cli/test_bootstrap_legacy_spellings`, `e2e/direnv/test_direnv_command_deprecated`) check that each old spelling warns, each new one does not, and the internal `mise direnv exec` and `envrc` commands stay quiet. A unit test checks that `--skip` records the alias that was typed. The existing `test_bootstrap*` e2e tests still pass, and the help text and usage spec are unchanged.

title: chore(settings): deprecate settings that have no effect
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/531
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Three settings are accepted without complaint but do nothing:

- `task.cache.stats_report` has done nothing since the built-in action cache was removed in #12509.
- `sops.age_recipients` does nothing because mise never encrypts sops files. To encrypt values, use `mise set --age-encrypt --age-recipient ...`.
- `plugin_autoupdate_last_check_duration` was never implemented.

Setting one of them in config or through its environment variable currently does nothing and prints no warning. People who set one may think it is working.

They are now hidden from the settings docs and marked deprecated in `schema/mise.json`, so editors flag them. From mise 2026.10.5, setting one prints a warning. They will be removed in 2027.10.5.

```toml
# mise.toml
[settings]
task.cache.stats_report = "stats.json"
```

```
$ mise run build
mise WARN  deprecated [setting.task.cache.stats_report]: This setting has no effect since the built-in action cache was removed. Remove it from your config. This will be removed in mise 2027.10.5.
```

**Migration:** delete these keys from `mise.toml`, and unset `MISE_TASK_CACHE_STATS_REPORT`, `MISE_SOPS_AGE_RECIPIENTS` and `MISE_PLUGIN_AUTOUPDATE_LAST_CHECK_DURATION`. Since none of them did anything, removing them changes nothing else.

**Validation:**
- A new unit test checks that all three settings are deprecated and have a warn and removal version. It fails on main.
- I confirmed the warnings by building with the warn version lowered to the current one.
- The settings and sops e2e tests pass.

title: feat(mcp): implement install_tool and require a trusted project for run_task
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/530
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

The MCP server (`mise mcp`) had three problems:

- **`run_task` trusted projects on the client's behalf.** It ran `mise run` with `MISE_YES=1` and implicit trust, so an AI client could run tasks, and render templates, from a project you had never trusted. Trusting it as a side effect meant later commands trusted it too.
- **`install_tool` was a stub** that always returned "Tool installation not yet implemented".
- **The `mise://tasks` resource reported an empty `env`** for every task.

## What changes

**Trust.** `run_task` and `install_tool` now refuse to act in a project whose config is not trusted, and tell the client which command to show you:

```text
Refusing to act on untrusted config. The MCP server does not trust config on a client's behalf. Ask the user to review it and run:
  mise trust /path/to/project
```

The `mise` processes the server starts never trust anything themselves. This covers config the early check does not look at, such as a templated task include in a subdirectory or a nested `mise` call from a task: it fails with the usual "not trusted" error rather than being trusted silently. Refusing does not trust anything. Run `mise trust` yourself and the request goes through.

**`install_tool`** now installs the way `mise install` does:

```json
{"tool": "node", "version": "22"}
```

returns

```json
{"tool": "node@22", "version": "22.11.0", "install_path": "/home/me/.local/share/mise/installs/node/22.11.0", "output": "..."}
```

With no `version`, it installs the version configured for that tool, or latest if the tool is not configured. A failed install comes back as an error result that includes mise's output. Installs have no time limit; `run_task` still respects `task_timeout`.

**`mise://tasks`** reports each task's env directives, using the same format as `mise tasks ls --json`. This changes the `env` field's type from an object to an array of strings:

```json
"env": ["MCP_TASK_ENV=task_value", "_.file = \".env\""]
```

Clients that read `env` as an object need to update.

title: fix(config): ignore project bootstrap and dotfiles config in safe mode
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/529
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

Safe mode (`MISE_SAFE=1`) loads a project's `mise.toml` without asking whether to trust it. It already skips the project's `[env]`, `[settings]`, hooks and tasks, but it still applied the project's `[bootstrap]`, `[dotfiles]` and `[dotfile_groups]`. So an untrusted repository could make `mise bootstrap` link files into `$HOME`, clone repositories or install packages:

```toml
# untrusted mise.toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.bashrc" = "evil-bashrc"

[bootstrap.repos]
"~/src/thing" = { url = "https://example.com/thing.git" }
```

```sh
MISE_SAFE=1 mise bootstrap --yes   # before: linked ~/.bashrc and cloned the repo
```

## Change

In safe mode, mise now ignores `[bootstrap]`, `[dotfiles]` and `[dotfile_groups]` from project config, the same way it ignores the project's `[env]` and `[settings]`. Config you own still applies:

- global and system config (`~/.config/mise/config.toml`, `/etc/mise/config.toml`)
- the folders that global config selects with `[bootstrap].config_roots`

A `config_roots` set in a project's config is still ignored.

Both `mise bootstrap` and `mise dotfiles` list the project config files whose sections were skipped:

```
mise WARN  [bootstrap], [dotfiles] and [dotfile_groups] in these config files were skipped because safe mode (MISE_SAFE=1) ignores project config:
  ~/src/project/mise.toml
```

Outside safe mode nothing changes. `mise dotfiles add --changed` in an untrusted project under safe mode now shows this warning instead of failing with "--changed requires trusted configuration".

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: claude-code_2-1-289_agent.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes security behavior in safe mode for home-directory writes and repo cloning; incorrect filtering could break legitimate global/config_roots workflows or leave a residual bypass.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Safe mode (`MISE_SAFE=1`) no longer applies project `[bootstrap]`, `[dotfiles]`, or `[dotfile_groups]`**, closing a gap where untrusted project config could still link files into `$HOME`, clone repos, or install packages while automation loads that config without a trust prompt.
> 
> Global and system config still apply, including dotfiles/bootstrap declared under **`[bootstrap].config_roots` chosen from global config**; project-selected `config_roots` stay ignored. `mise bootstrap` and `mise dotfiles` warn once per process listing skipped project files; **`mise dotfiles apply --prune` is blocked** when safe mode hides declarations that would make deployed files look orphaned. **`mise dotfiles add --changed`** under safe mode surfaces the skip warning instead of requiring trusted configuration.
> 
> Docs (`docs/security.md`, `settings.toml`) and e2e coverage document and exercise the new behavior.
>

title: fix(env): honor redact = false exclusions in mise env --redacted
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/528
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise env --redacted` listed variables that were exempted from redaction with `redact = false`. Task output and CI masking already leave those variables unmasked, so `--redacted` disagreed with the rest of mise. Any script that feeds `mise env --redacted` into a secret masker (for example `::add-mask::` in GitHub Actions) masked values the config says are not secret.

```toml
redactions = ["*_TOKEN"]

[env]
SECRET_TOKEN = "s3cret"
TEST_TOKEN = { value = "not-sensitive", redact = false }
```

Before:

```console
$ mise env --redacted --json
{
  "SECRET_TOKEN": "s3cret",
  "TEST_TOKEN": "not-sensitive"
}
```

After:

```console
$ mise env --redacted --json
{
  "SECRET_TOKEN": "s3cret"
}
```

This applies to every output format (`--json`, `--json-extended`, `--dotenv`, `--values`, and shell output) and to `tools = true` variables. A later `tools = true` assignment to a variable overrides an earlier `redact = false`, the same way it does when task environments are redacted. No migration is needed. Configs that don't use `redact = false` get the same output as before.

Validation: added a case to `e2e/cli/test_env_redacted_flags`. It fails without the fix and passes with it. The existing task redaction e2e tests still pass.

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Scoped bugfix to `mise env --redacted` filtering; behavior changes only for configs using `redact = false`, with e2e validation.
> 
> **Overview**
> **`mise env --redacted`** now aligns with task output and CI masking: keys exempted via **`redact = false`** are omitted even when they match a **`redactions`** pattern.
> 
> Redaction selection is refactored into a **`RedactedKeys`** helper that unions redaction patterns (config, tools pass, global keys) and subtracts **`redaction_exclusions`**, with the same override rule as tasks—a later **`tools = true`** assignment clears a config-level exemption. title: fix(env): skip watch_files runs in safe mode and with --no-hooks
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/527
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`[[watch_files]]` entries are hooks: when shell activation sees a matching file change, mise runs their `run` command or `task`. But unlike every other hook, they still ran when hooks were turned off with `--no-hooks`, `MISE_NO_HOOKS=1`, or the `no_hooks` setting. They also ran in safe mode (`MISE_SAFE=1`), which is supposed to stop project config from running code.

With this config:

```toml
[[watch_files]]
patterns = ["watched.txt"]
run = "echo WATCH_FILES_RAN"
```

after `watched.txt` changes:

```console
# before
$ MISE_SAFE=1 mise hook-env -s bash
...
WATCH_FILES_RAN

# after
$ MISE_SAFE=1 mise hook-env -s bash
...            # no watch_files output
```

`mise --no-hooks hook-env`, `MISE_NO_HOOKS=1`, and `no_hooks = true` now skip watch_files runs as well, just as they skip `enter`, `cd`, `preinstall`, and the other hooks. With hooks enabled, nothing changes.

title: fix(sandbox): clear inherited variables for --deny-env on Windows
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/526
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

On Windows, `mise x --deny-env` and a task's `deny_env` never cleared the inherited environment, so the child process saw every variable mise had, including any secrets in the parent shell. `mise x --deny-env` could also fail outright. The check for the variables deny_env always keeps was case-sensitive, so mise's `Path` was dropped and the program could not be found.

Before, on Windows:

```toml
[tasks.denied]
run = 'echo [%DEPLOY_KEY%]'
deny_env = true
```

```
> $env:DEPLOY_KEY = 'secret'; mise run denied
[secret]
```

After:

```
> mise run denied
[%DEPLOY_KEY%]
```

## What changes

- `mise x --deny-env` and task `deny_env` now clear the inherited environment on Windows, as on Linux. The child sees only what mise computed, variables allowed with `--allow-env` / `allow_env`, and what a Windows process needs to start: `SystemRoot`, `SystemDrive`, `windir`, `ComSpec`, `PATHEXT`, `TEMP`, `TMP`, `USERPROFILE` and `USERNAME`, alongside the usual `PATH`, `HOME`, `USER`, `SHELL`, `TERM`, `COLORTERM` and `LANG`.
- This also covers tasks with a `timeout`, which Windows starts through a helper process that interrupts them when time runs out.
- On Windows, variable names match case-insensitively: `Path` is `PATH`, `allow_env = ['appdata*']` matches `APPDATA`, and `cache_env` names match whatever spelling the environment uses.
- The "sandbox is not supported" warning on Windows now appears only when file, network or process restrictions are requested. Windows still does not enforce those. Environment-only sandboxing runs without a warning.
- Task environment clearing now also applies on FreeBSD and other non-Linux unix platforms, matching what `mise x --deny-env` already did there. macOS is unchanged.

## Validation

- New Pester tests in `e2e-win/sandbox_deny_env.Tests.ps1` cover `mise x` with and without `--deny-env`, the variables Windows keeps, the PATH mise builds, `--allow-env`, and tasks with `deny_env`, with `deny_env` plus a `timeout`, and with `allow_env`.
- Unit tests cover the Windows essentials, case-insensitive matching, and the sandbox marking the environment as cleared so the timeout helper does not pass it on.

title: fix(sandbox): reject allow_net on macOS instead of writing invalid rules
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/525
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

On macOS, a command or task using `--allow-net=<host>` (or task `allow_net`) never actually ran. mise turned each host into a Seatbelt rule like `(allow network* (remote ip "1.2.3.4:*"))`, but Seatbelt only accepts `*` or `localhost` as the host there. So `sandbox-exec` rejected the whole generated profile, and the error was a confusing one:

```
sandbox-exec: host must be * or localhost in network address
```

macOS now rejects `allow_net` before building the profile, with the same clear error Linux already gives:

```console
$ mise x --allow-net=registry.npmjs.org -- npm install
Error: per-host network filtering (--allow-net=<host>) is not supported on macOS. Use --deny-net to block all network, or remove --allow-net.
```

Linux and macOS now share one check, for both `mise x` and tasks, and the macOS profile builder no longer resolves hostnames or writes host rules. The `--allow-net` help text now says per-host filtering is unsupported on Linux and macOS.

**Migration:** nothing that worked before breaks: on macOS, `allow_net` already stopped the command from starting. Use `deny_net` / `--deny-net` to block network, or drop `allow_net` if the command needs network access.

**Validation:** I added a cross-platform unit test for the rejection and replaced the macOS profile test that expected the invalid host rule. Sandbox unit tests and workspace clippy pass on Linux. macos.rs was type-checked and linted for `aarch64-apple-darwin` in a stub crate, but none of the tests have been run on macOS.

title: fix(config): verify .monorepo markers in paranoid mode
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/524
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Paranoid mode ties config trust to file content: `mise trust` stores a hash, and editing the file makes it untrusted again. Configs inside a monorepo skipped that check. Trusting a root with `monorepo_root = true` in normal mode leaves a marker, and paranoid mode honored it, so every config below the root loaded by path with no hash. Those configs also kept loading after edits.

Before, with a root trusted in normal mode and then trusted again in paranoid mode:

```console
$ MISE_PARANOID=1 mise -C sub trust --show
~/repo/mise.toml: trusted
~/repo/sub/mise.toml: trusted      # never reviewed in paranoid mode, no hash
```

After:

```console
$ MISE_PARANOID=1 mise -C sub trust --show
~/repo/mise.toml: trusted
~/repo/sub/mise.toml: untrusted
$ MISE_PARANOID=1 mise -C sub env
mise ERROR ... not trusted
```

Paranoid mode now ignores the monorepo marker. Each subproject config needs its own `mise trust`, and editing it requires approving it again, like any other config. Normal mode is unchanged: trusting a monorepo root still trusts the configs below it.

**Migration:** if you use paranoid mode and relied on a monorepo root to trust subprojects, review each subproject's config and run `MISE_PARANOID=1 mise trust` in each one.

Validation: a new e2e test, `e2e/config/test_paranoid_monorepo_trust`, fails on main and passes with this change. The existing trust and monorepo e2e tests and the `config::config_file` unit tests also pass.

title: fix(task): keep secret values out of remote cache keys
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/523
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

With a remote task cache configured (`task.cache.remote_url`), mise uploads the action a task's cache key is hashed from. That action used to contain the plaintext values of the task's `env`, its `cache.env` variables, `[vars]` and the task's args, including env values marked `redact = true`. Args can carry secrets too: dependency args are rendered from templates such as `{{env.TOKEN}}`, and CLI args are whatever you pass to `mise run`.

For example, with this config the uploaded action contained `"args":["s3cr3t"]`:

```toml
[env]
TOKEN = { value = "s3cr3t", redact = true }

[tasks.release]
depends = [{ task = "publish", args = ["{{env.TOKEN}}"] }]
```

Now every env, var and arg value is recorded as a `blake3:<hex>` digest. Variable names and whether a variable is set stay readable. The cache key still changes when a value changes, but the value never leaves the machine. `mise run --explain` output is unchanged.

The action format version is unchanged. Existing remote and local cache entries miss once after upgrading, because their keys change.

The digests are not salted, so someone with access to the cache server could still confirm a guessed low-entropy value. This was already true before, because the old key hashed the same plaintext. Keep values that must not be guessable out of `cache.env` and use `pass_through_env` instead.

title: fix(prune): skip a tracked config whose tool version no longer parses
body:
`mise prune` reads every tracked config, so it can keep the versions those projects use. If any one of them had a tool version that no longer parses, the whole prune stopped with that error. That happens even when the project is unrelated or abandoned. With mise 2026.10.3:

```toml
# ~/old-project/mise.toml, tracked from an earlier `mise use`
[tools]
node = "-bad"
```

```
$ mise prune --dry-run
mise ERROR invalid version for node in ~/old-project/mise.toml
mise ERROR invalid tool version "-bad": must not start with '-'
```

A tracked config that does not parse at all was already skipped with a warning (`error loading tracked config file …`). A tracked tool stub that cannot be resolved is skipped too, so it does not stop the prune. A config that parses, but whose tool version fails later, is now handled the same way. prune warns with the same `error loading tracked config file <path>: <error>` message, leaves that config out, and goes on.

As with an unparseable config, the skipped config protects nothing. The versions it would have needed are pruned like any other unused version. The same function decides which old versions `mise upgrade` keeps for other projects (`src/cli/upgrade.rs:918`), so a broken tracked config no longer stops that step either. That is from reading the code; it was not run.

## Validation

- New `e2e/cli/test_prune_tracked_config_invalid_version` tracks a project and then breaks its version. It checks three things:
  - `mise prune --dry-run` warns and names the file.
  - The prune still protects another tracked project's `dummy@2.0.0`.
  - The prune still lists the unused `dummy@3.0.0`.
- Before: on Windows 11, with mise 2026.10.3 and the config above among 28 tracked configs, `mise prune --dry-run` exited 1 with the error shown (the path above is shortened).
- After: the CI-built mise from this PR, in the same environment, warned once for each of the two broken tracked configs, listed the other prunable versions, and exited 0.

title: fix(github): percent-encode the tag in gitlab release lookups
body:
TL:DR Simple fix to encode nested / for gitlab

Installing a GitLab release whose tag contains a slash, such as the `admin-cli/v0.34.783` tags that monorepo-style projects use, failed with a 404:

```
mise install gitlab:group/project@admin-cli/v0.34.783
```

mise percent-encoded the project path when it looked up the release but put the tag into the URL as-is, so it requested `.../releases/admin-cli/v0.34.783`. GitLab only resolves such tags when they are encoded in the path, as `admin-cli%2Fv0.34.783`. The tag is now encoded the same way as the project.

**Before / after**, against a real private GitLab project with slash tags:

```
GET .../projects/<group>%2F<project>/releases/admin-cli/v0.34.783    -> 404 (before)
GET .../projects/<group>%2F<project>/releases/admin-cli%2Fv0.34.783  -> 200 (after)
```

With the fix, `mise install gitlab:<group>/<project>@admin-cli/v0.34.783` downloads and extracts the matching OS/arch asset. Tags without a slash are unaffected.

**Validation:** added `test_get_release_encodes_slash_in_tag`, which fails without the change and passes with it. The existing gitlab tests pass, and `cargo clippy -p mise-util --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean. I also confirmed the install end to end against the project above. I did not run the e2e suite.

title: docs(agents): treat 12 months as the default deprecation window
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/521
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

AGENTS.md said every deprecation is removed 12 months after its warning starts. Some deprecations in mise use shorter windows on purpose (for example 6 months for `tera_v1`, the `task_*` setting aliases, `task.cache_remote_*` and `shorthands_file`). An agent reading the old wording would flag those as policy violations, or lengthen them.

The policy now says 12 months is the default for new deprecations, not a hard rule, and that existing shorter windows stay as they are.

title: docs: rewrite CLI help and settings descriptions
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/520
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

The CLI reference, the man page and the settings page are generated from the help text in `src/cli` and the descriptions in `settings.toml`. This PR applies the documentation rewrite to those sources, so `mise <command> --help`, `mise settings` and the generated pages say the same thing as the guides.

## What changes for users

- **Help text matches behaviour.** Text the audit found wrong or stale is fixed. For example:
  - `--allow-net` claimed per-host filtering that no platform supports.
  - `--deny-write` did not mention the paths that stay writable.
  - Safe mode said hooks are refused; they are skipped.
  - Several settings said wrong things about defaults or flags that do not exist, such as `offline` pointing at an `--offline` flag and `node.verify` described as GPG.
- **Consistent help.**
  - Command summaries are short imperative phrases ("Remove stale cache files").
  - Flag help is a fragment without a period.
  - Examples use `example(...)` attributes with a one-line description, so they render the same in `--help` and on the website.
  - Long help links the guide page for the feature.
- **Setting descriptions** are one sentence that says what the setting does. The longer text links the guide instead of repeating the type, environment variable and default, which the settings page already shows.
- **Less noise in help output.**
  - Flags that are parsed but have no effect are hidden: `completion --include-bash-completion-lib`, `generate task-docs --root/--style`, `generate tool-stub --http`, and the `PATH` argument of `mise dot pull`. Each still parses, so scripts that pass it keep working.
  - The `launchd`, `systemd` and `macos-defaults` compatibility spellings under `mise bootstrap` keep working but no longer get their own reference pages; the old pages redirect to `macos launchd-agents`, `linux systemd-units` and `macos defaults`.
  - The `--skip`/`--only` part aliases are accepted but no longer listed.
- `mise daemons providers` gains the `[experimental]` label its parent command has.

No command behaviour changes. In a smoke test with the built binary, the compatibility spellings, the `shell` part alias and the hidden flags all still work.

## Generated files

`mise.usage.kdl`, `docs/cli`, `man/man1/mise.1`, `cli_commands.ts`, the JSON schemas and `llms.txt` are regenerated from the new sources. The man page also matches the committed spec when rendered with the pinned usage 6.12.1. Three e2e tests that assert help or setting text are updated (`test_dotfiles_files`, `test_generate_tool_stub`, `test_settings_ls`).

## Validation

- Clippy with `--all-features --all-targets -D warnings` passes.
- `cargo test --workspace` passes except 7 tests in code this PR does not touch that fail in this sandbox: 6 brew cask shim tests, which need a Ruby shim, and 1 toolset test.
- I ran the 170 e2e tests matching the files that assert help

title: docs: restructure and rewrite the documentation site
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/519
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A full pass over the hand-written documentation, the README and the contributor pages. Two problems drove it. Many pages had drifted from what mise does today. Most topics were explained in three to five places that no longer agreed. The site is now reorganized so each topic has one home, and every page was rewritten against the code.

## What readers will notice

- **Navigation.**
  - The sidebar groups are now: Start here, Dev tools, Languages, Environments, Tasks, Daemons, Bootstrap, Dotfiles, Configuration, Security, Plugins, Help, Cookbook, About, Contributing and CLI reference. Only "Start here" opens by default.
  - Eight pages that were not in the sidebar now are: `lang/dotnet`, `backends/s3`, `bootstrap/firewall`, flatpak, winget, contact, `mise-cookbook/neovim` and the Docker page.
  - The top nav gains Bootstrap and a Reference menu for CLI commands, `mise.toml`, settings, `MISE_*` variables, task configuration, the registry, troubleshooting and errors. mise-versions stays in the nav.
- **One canonical page per topic**, linked from everywhere else:
  - shell activation: new `/shell-setup.html`
  - activate vs shims vs `mise exec`: `/dev-tools/shims.html`
  - version requests and version files: new `/dev-tools/versions.html`
  - trust, safe mode and minimum release age: `/security.html`
  - `MISE_*` variables: new `/configuration/environment-variables.html`
  - task discovery and includes: new `/tasks/task-discovery.html`
- **Long pages split into focused ones:**
  - daemons: presets, worktrees, sharing, data
  - dotfiles: managed files, groups, edits, history, sync, encryption, reference
  - bootstrap: from a repository, modules, the GitHub relay
  - also `mise.lock`, task caching, monorepo, Homebrew casks, `macos-app`, contributing and packaging
- **Corrected content.** An audit checked every concrete claim against the source, the e2e tests and a built binary. About 650 verified errors are fixed. Examples:
  - The dnf/COPR instructions named Fedora and RHEL versions the COPR does not build.
  - The CI page pinned old `mise-action` and `checkout` majors, and claimed the generated wrapper uses the generating version.
  - Safe mode was described as refusing hooks; it skips them.
  - The netrc token was described as an override; it is a fallback.
  - The landing page called the `pypi` backend `pipx` and left out packslip.
  - Several pages said GitHub Issues are disabled.
- **Prose.** Pages follow one style:
  - plain, present tense
  - no em dashes, bold-label bullet lists or recap sections
  - examples that run (I ran the README and landing-page quickstarts in a sandbox)
- **Front pages.**
  - The README, landing page, hero and site description tell one story in the same words. asdf no longer appears in that copy; the "Migrating from asdf" page stays.
  - The README and landing page share the four-step quickstart that getting starte

title: chore(docs): keep moved pages reachable and fail on dead anchors
body: https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/518 The docs site is static files in an R2 bucket, so when a page is renamed or deleted, its old URL keeps serving stale HTML until the periodic purge, and then it 404s. VitePress checks links to pages, but not links to `#anchors`, so a link to a section that was renamed or moved fails silently. This PR adds the redirect mechanism and link checking that the docs rewrite stacked on top of it relies on. **Redirect stubs for moved pages.** `docs/.vitepress/redirects.mjs` holds `pageRedirects`. For each entry, the build writes a small HTML page at the old URL with a meta refresh, `rel=canonical` and `noindex`. A script on that page also maps old section hashes to their new homes: ```js export const pageRedirects = { "/team.html": { to: "/about.html#who-makes-mise" }, "/history.html": { to: "/dotfiles/history.html", hashes: { "sharing-across-machines": "/dotfiles/sync.html" }, }, }; ``` **Redirects for moved sections.** `anchor-redirects.mjs` maps `"/page.html#old-id"` to the section's new location. When a page opens with a hash that matches nothing on it, the theme loads this map (a separate chunk, fetched only then) and forwards the reader. **Link checker.** `check-links.mjs` runs at the end of `docs:build`. The build fails on: - a link to an anchor that does not exist - a link to a page that only exists as a redirect stub - a redirect whose source still exists or whose target is gone `check-social-images.mjs` skips the stubs. The checker found six same-page links on main whose anchors never existed, because VitePress turns `_` into `-` in heading ids. They now link the page path, which markdownlint's MD051 does not check and `check-links.mjs` does. Both maps are empty in this PR. Tests cover path normalization, stub rendering, hash mapping and the checker. In a local build with temporary entries, I confirmed in headless Chromium that old URLs, old hashes and client-side navigation all land on the new pages. *AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: claude-code_2-1-289_agent.* 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- Stack created with GitHub Stacks CLI • Give Feedback 💬 ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Links to moved documentation pages and sections now redirect to their updated destinations, including links with section anchors. title: fix(config): report an invalid tool version in config ls instead of panicking
body:
`mise config ls` crashed when a config file had a tool version mise cannot parse. Every other command reports the problem as an error and names the file. `config ls` is often the first thing to run when a config misbehaves, so this is when it should work.

```toml
[tools]
tiny = "bogus:1.0"
```

Before, with mise 2026.10.3, `mise config ls` panicked (exit code 101):

```
The application panicked (crashed).
Message:  called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value:
...
Location: src\cli\config\ls.rs:62
```

`mise config ls --json` panicked the same way at `ls.rs:106`. Now both report the error, as `mise ls` does:

```
mise ERROR invalid version for tiny in ~/project/mise.toml
mise ERROR invalid tool version request: bogus:1.0
```

This takes over the `config ls` part of #12212 by @risu729, which pr-closer closed after 7 days of merge conflicts. They are credited as co-author. The rest of #12212 changed places where `install`, `lock`, `upgrade`, `outdated` and task tool installation dropped this error. On current main those commands already stop with the error above before reaching those places: with the config above, `ls`, `install`, `install tiny@3.1.0`, `run`, `outdated`, `upgrade`, `upgrade --bump`, `lock`, `env` and `tool` all exit 1 with it. So those changes are left out. The review findings on #12212 were about those left-out parts: CodeRabbit's `Option` nitpick on `lock.rs`, and Greptile's P1 on #12198's concrete-version check.

## Validation

- `e2e/config/test_tool_version_vars` now checks that both `mise config ls` and `mise config ls --json` exit with status 1, and that the error names `tiny` and `mise.toml`. It checks the exit status because the old panic printed the same message.
- On Windows 11, the new check fails with mise 2026.10.3 (`expected exit code 1, got 101`) and passes with this branch's CI build. On that build, both commands exit 1 with `invalid version for tiny in …\bad-tools\mise.toml`.

title: feat(packslip): accept a list of signing workflows
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/517
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`workflow` pins the one workflow file that signs a tool's releases. A project that moved its signing workflow can't use it: aube's 2.2.11–2.5.1 releases were signed by `release-plz.yml` and 2.6.0 onward by `release.yml`, so pinning either breaks the other half of the versions the registry covers. `workflow` now also takes a list, and a release signed by any one of the named workflows on a tag is accepted:

```toml
[tools]
"packslip:github.com/aubepkg/aube" = { version = "latest", workflow = ["release-plz.yml", "release.yml"] }
```

A single name behaves exactly as before. A list rejects an empty list, non-strings, paths, and `@` refs, and it still can't be combined with `pubkey`, `identity`, `identity_prefix` or `issuer`. Each listed workflow is held to the tag namespace and the GitHub Actions issuer, so the list is wider than one workflow but still narrower than the repository-wide default. A rejection with several candidates reports every identity's refusal.

Stacked on #14091. The schema (`mise.json`, `mise-task.json`) and the packslip backend docs accept and describe the list. Unit tests cover list parsing, de-duplication, and the any-one-verifies behavior; `cargo clippy --lib --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean.

title: registry: pin packslip tools to the workflow that signs their releases
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/516
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Packslip registry defaults accept a release signed by any workflow of the vendor's repository. This pins each tool to the workflow, and ref, that actually signs its releases, so a signature from another workflow or ref is rejected for `mise use hk` and the other shorthands.

Stacked on #14093 (a list of workflows, and a ref on an entry), which sits on #14091 (a user's own signer options replace these defaults). Worktrunk is handled by #14073.

| Tool | Pin |
|---|---|
| dagu, timoni | `workflow = "release.yaml"` |
| helmfile | `workflow = "releaser.yaml"` |
| fnox, hk | `workflow = "release.yml"` |
| usage | `workflow = "publish-cli.yml"` |
| communique, mr-boxington, pitchfork | `workflow = "release.yml@refs/heads/main"` |
| aube | `workflow = ["release-plz.yml@refs/heads/main", "release.yml@refs/heads/main"]` |

communique, mr-boxington, pitchfork and aube sign from `main`, not from a tag, so their entries name the ref. For them the protection is only as strong as `main`'s branch protection. aube's releases 2.2.11–2.5.1 were signed by `release-plz.yml` and 2.6.0 onward by `release.yml`, hence the list.

Verified against every release at or above each entry's `min_version`: I read the certificate identity in each `packslip.sigstore.json` and it matches the pin. I also built this branch and installed the `min_version` and latest release of every pinned tool, and aube 2.2.11, 2.5.1, 2.6.0 and 2.7.0, with isolated data and state dirs. All succeeded in a fresh dir.

**Known limit:** packslip's existing signer continuity still applies on top. A machine that has installed aube 2.7.0 and then installs 2.2.11 (or the reverse) is refused because the signing workflow path changed, and has to run `mise packslip forget github.com/aubepkg/aube`. That happens without this PR too; the list only makes either era installable on its own.

Tag-based pins are only as strong as the vendor's tag protection (anyone who can push a tag can run a modified workflow). They still reject other workflows and branch or PR runs, so they are no weaker than the repository-wide default.

title: fix(packslip): let a user signer option replace a registry workflow default
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/515
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A registry entry that sets the Packslip `workflow` option (as in #14073) would break for anyone who pins their own signer on the shorthand. `workflow` can't be combined with `pubkey`, `identity`, `identity_prefix` or `issuer`, but tool options merge key by key, so the user's key landed next to the registry's `workflow` and the install failed:

```toml
[tools]
# registry default: workflow = "release.yaml"
worktrunk = { version = "latest", pubkey = "RWQ..." }
# before: packslip:… `workflow` cannot be combined with `pubkey`, …
# after: the registry `workflow` is dropped and the key is used
```

Now a signer option from config, the command line or an install manifest removes a `workflow` that came from the registry. A `workflow` the user sets themselves next to another signer option is still rejected. Unrelated user options such as `variant` leave the default in place.

Prerequisite for pinning the signing workflow in the registry entries for Packslip tools.

Tests: three unit tests in `tool_version_options.rs` (user signer drops the default for each of the four keys; unrelated options keep it; a user-set `workflow` is kept). `cargo clippy --lib --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean.

A user-defined `workflow` beside another user signer is left intact for Packslip to reject; `list_identity_prefix` alone does not clear the registry bundle signer.
> 
> Docs note that an explicit signer on shorthand overrides a registry `workflow` default. Unit tests cover the merge and override paths.
