title: fix(backend): only warn about a backend switch when the backend kind changes
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/476
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A registry entry that moves to another repo or org within the same backend no longer triggers the "registry now installs it from …" warning, and no longer appears in `mise backends switch` or `mise doctor`.

Before, a tool locked or installed on `vfox:mise-plugins/vfox-lua` was reported as superseded once the registry listed `vfox:jdx/vfox-lua`:

```
lua is locked to vfox:mise-plugins/vfox-lua, but the registry now installs it from vfox:jdx/vfox-lua. Run `mise backends switch lua` to switch.
```

There is nothing for the user to switch: the tool installs the same way from the same kind of backend. Now only a change of backend kind counts (`aqua:` to `github:`, `asdf:` to `vfox:`, …). A repo or org rename within a kind, such as `mise-plugins/*` to `jdx/*` or one `aqua:` package name to another, is ignored.

The check is shared by the runtime warning, `mise backends switch`, and `mise doctor`.

title: fix(outdated): don't bump vendor-only requests like java@temurin
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/475
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise upgrade` and `mise outdated --bump` suggested switching Java vendors for a vendor-only request. With `java = "temurin"` in `~/.config/mise/config.toml` and Temurin 27 installed:

```
$ mise upgrade
mise Newer versions are available but do not match the configured version ranges:
  java temurin-27.0.0+35 → 27.0.0 (~/.config/mise/config.toml)
Run `mise outdated --bump` ... `mise upgrade --bump` to update the configuration and upgrade.
```

Running `mise upgrade --bump` would have rewritten the config to `java = "27"`, which resolves through `java.shorthand_vendor` (OpenJDK by default), silently dropping Temurin.

A request like `temurin` (or `nightly`) contains no version, so there is no range to move out of; plain `mise upgrade` already tracks the latest release. The latest lookup for it also has no vendor prefix, which is how it landed on OpenJDK's `27.0.0`. Bump suggestions are now skipped for requests that contain no version. After the fix, `mise outdated --bump` shows `[NONE]` for `java = "temurin"`, while `java = "20"` still bumps to `27` and `temurin-27.0.0+35` is unaffected.

Reported in jdx/mise#13987.

Tested with the new unit test and by running the built binary against `java = "temurin"`, `"temurin-27.0.0+35"` and `"20"`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

> **Medium Risk**
> Changes config-bump behavior for `outdated --bump`/`upgrade --bump`; wrong heuristics could still skip valid bumps or allow unwanted rewrites, but scope is limited to outdated bump logic with new unit tests.
> 
> **Overview**
> **`mise outdated --bump` / `mise upgrade --bump`** no longer propose config rewrites for **vendor- or channel-only** tool requests (e.g. `java = "temurin"`) that contain no version digits.
> 
> Bump calculation now goes through **`bumped_request_version`**, which skips bumping when the request string has no version component (`request_names_a_version`), so a latest lookup that returns an unprefixed release (e.g. OpenJDK `27.0.0`) cannot replace a moving-target vendor pin. **Version-bearing** requests and **pinned** full versions keep the previous semver bump behavior.

title: feat(prune): add prune.exclude to keep chosen tools from being pruned
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/474
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise prune` removes every version that no tracked config uses. That is wrong for a tool that something outside mise resolves through its install path (a virtualenv built from a mise Python, an editor SDK entry), or whose old versions you keep on purpose. The only way to protect such a version was to reference it in a tracked config or lockfile.

The new `prune.exclude` setting names tools that are never pruned:

```toml
[settings]
prune.exclude = ["node", "aqua:BurntSushi/ripgrep"]
```

or `MISE_PRUNE_EXCLUDE=node,ripgrep`. Versions of those tools are kept by `mise prune`, `mise ls --prunable`, and by `mise upgrade`, which neither schedules nor (with `--prune`) removes the old version, even when no config uses them and even when the tool is named on the command line (`mise prune node` does nothing for an excluded `node`). Tools are matched the way they are named elsewhere: `node` and `core:node` are the same tool, as are `ripgrep` and `aqua:BurntSushi/ripgrep`. `mise uninstall` is unaffected.

## Notes

- The exclusion is applied where prune builds its list of deletable versions, which `mise prune`, `ls --prunable` and the deferred removal after an upgrade share, and again where `mise upgrade` picks the old versions to remove or schedule, which does not go through that list.
- It excludes whole tools, not single versions. Pinning one version is still done by referencing it in a tracked config or lockfile.
- Tests: an e2e test covers the environment variable, the config file with a full backend name, an explicit `mise prune <tool>`, `ls --prunable`, the excluded install staying on disk after a real prune, and `mise upgrade --prune` (dry run and real) leaving the old version; a unit test covers short and full name matching. The existing prune e2e tests and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` pass. `schema/mise.json` is regenerated.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: 2.1.288.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes shared prune and upgrade cleanup paths; misconfiguration could leave unused installs on disk, but it does not weaken explicit uninstall or broaden deletion.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds **`settings.prune.exclude`** (and **`MISE_PRUNE_EXCLUDE`**) so named tools are never treated as prunable, even when no tracked config references them and even when you pass the tool to **`mise prune`**.
> 
> Excluded tools are filtered out of the shared prunable-version logic used by **`mise prune`**, **`mise ls --prunable`**, and post-upgrade removal; **`mise upgrade --prune`** also skips uninstalling old versions for those tools. Matching accepts short and full backend names (e.g. `node` / `core:node`, `ripgrep` / `aqua:…`). **`mise uninstall`** is unchanged.
> 
> Documentation/schem

title: fix(bootstrap): don't create history state or fail on its lock unless writing files
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/473
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise bootstrap` could fail with `another history operation is running` even when no history was being recorded. Every bootstrap took an exclusive lock in `$MISE_STATE_DIR/history` (and created the history store) before it knew whether it would write anything, so two bootstraps sharing a state dir (parallel CI jobs on one runner, or a cached state dir) serialized, and the second failed after waiting 30 seconds. This was reported in discussion #13325.

```
$ mise bootstrap          # while another bootstrap holds the lock
mise history: waiting for another history operation to finish
mise ERROR another history operation is running      # after 30s
```

Now a bootstrap that records no file history (nothing tracked, no enrollment, no existing history) opens its history journal lazily, at the first dotfile or edit it is about to rewrite:

- A bootstrap that rewrites none (no `[dotfiles]` or edits to apply, which is most CI re-runs) never takes the lock and never creates `history/` in the state dir.
- One that does rewrite files still journals them for crash recovery, exactly as before, when the lock is free.
- If another process holds the lock at that moment, it no longer fails. It warns and runs without the recovery journal for that run:

```
mise WARN  history: another history operation is running; continuing without recovery data for this run
mise files: copied ~/proj/src.txt to ~/out.txt
```

Runs that do record history (tracked files, enrollment, existing history), and every other history operation (apply, undo, saves), behave as before: they take the lock up front, wait up to 30 seconds, and then fail. A bootstrap that starts with nothing to record but ends up declaring tracking (for example from a pulled configuration) still takes the lock at the end so its outcome is recorded. `history.enabled = false` still skips all of this.

The tradeoff is that a contended bootstrap with nothing to record loses crash recovery for the files it rewrites in that run. Running bootstrap writes without recovery data is already an accepted mode (it warns and continues when it cannot save a recovery copy).

The history docs (`docs/history.md` and the `history.enabled` setting) now also explain that history activates only once you track files or adopt a setup repository, however that config arrives (including a plain `git clone`, a dotfile manager, or Nix), that `history.enabled = false` stops automatic capture and explicit saves, and that CI jobs sharing a runner can use a per-job `MISE_STATE_DIR` or `MISE_HISTORY_ENABLED=false`.

Validation: unit tests cover the typed lock-busy error, that nothing to record creates no history store, and that existing history counts as recording; the existing history unit tests pass (267). With the built binary I checked that a bootstrap with nothing to write leaves no `history/` dir, that a dotfile write creates the store and

title: fix(http): don't retry a 429 whose Retry-After outlasts the backoff
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/471
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

When `mise-versions.jdx.dev` rate-limits a client, mise retries the 429 on its normal ~200ms/1s/4s/15s backoff. The limiter was blocking the client for far longer than that, so every retry failed and still counted against the limit. In CI this turned a brief limit into hundreds of extra requests per job (python/pipx installs failing with `GET .../tools/python-precompiled-*.gz -> 429`).

## Change

A 429 carrying `Retry-After` (seconds) is now handled by the HTTP retry loop:

- `Retry-After` over 30s: not retried. The 429 is returned right away, so callers that fall back (the versions-host list, GitHub metadata) do so immediately instead of after the full backoff.
- `Retry-After` of 30s or less: the retry waits at least that long.
- No `Retry-After`, a non-429 status, or an HTTP-date value: unchanged.

`http::error_code` still reports 429, so existing 429 handling keeps working. The error message gains `(retry-after: Ns)`.

## Context

The matching Cloudflare rule on the zone was changed separately: its mitigation drops from 3600s to 60s and `/data/` and `/tools/` are exempt from it.

## Tests

Three new tests in `crates/mise-util/src/http/tests/retry.rs` (long `Retry-After` makes one request and keeps code 429; short `Retry-After` is retried; header parsing). `cargo clippy -p mise-util --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: unavailable.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes shared HTTP retry and error-classification behavior for all requests; mis-parsing Retry-After could affect rate-limit recovery, though behavior is narrowly scoped to 429 with numeric headers.
> 
> **Overview**
> HTTP retries now respect **429** responses that include a numeric **`Retry-After`** (seconds), instead of blindly reusing the normal backoff and hammering rate-limited hosts.
> 
> When **`Retry-After` is over 30 seconds**, the client **does not retry** and returns the **429** immediately (with `(retry-after: Ns)` in the message) so callers can fall back without extra requests. Shorter values still retry, sleeping at least as long as the header asks. Non-429 statuses, missing headers, and HTTP-date **`Retry-After`** values behave as before.
> 
> **`error_code`** now prefers the real **`reqwest`** status over substring heuristics, so a 429 whose wait is **404** seconds is not misread as a 404. New tests cover long vs short **`Retry-After`**, delay math, and header parsing.
>

title: feat(upgrade): update global tools before they run with auto_update
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/470
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Tools you install globally, such as an AI CLI or a formatter, can now keep themselves up to date without anyone remembering to run `mise upgrade`. Set `auto_update` on the tool's entry in your global config:

```toml
# ~/.config/mise/config.toml
[tools]
claude = { version = "latest", auto_update = true }
node = { version = "22", auto_update = "6h" }
```

When a shim or `mise x` is about to run the tool and mise hasn't checked for an update within the interval, it upgrades the tool first, showing the usual install progress on stderr, then runs the new version:

```console
$ mise x -- dummy        # global: dummy = { version = "1", auto_update = true }, 1.0.0 installed
mise by @jdx – installing 1 tool
mise ✓ dummy@1.1.0  243ms
mise ████████████████ 1/1 · installed 1 tool in 247ms
This is Dummy 1.1.0!
```

(Output from the e2e test's non-interactive run; only the last line is on stdout.)

If the update fails or you're offline, mise warns and runs the version you already have.

- **The configured version is the range.** `node = "22"` updates to the newest 22.x, never 23. Exact versions (`node = "22.11.0"`) are never updated.
- **Interval:** `true` checks every 24 hours, set by the new global setting `tool_update.check_duration`. A duration such as `"6h"` sets that tool's own interval. Anything under one hour is raised to one hour, with a warning.
- **Only the tool being run is checked.** `mise x -- npm test` never stops to update `claude`. Tasks, `mise hook-env`, and shell activation never update tools; with activation, run the tool through its shim or `mise x`. A follow-up adds a `mise bootstrap` service that updates in the background instead.
- **Global config only.** A project config can't turn it on. When a project sets its own version of the tool, runs in that project don't update it. The upgrade runs as `mise __tool-update <tool>` from the filesystem root, with the environment your shell had before mise's activation changed it, plus the active `-E`/`MISE_ENV` environments. So a project's config, lockfile and `[env]` (PATH included) are never read or written. If a global lockfile (`mise lock --global`) pins the tool, its entry moves to the new version.
- **Per version.** In a multi-version entry, only the versions with `auto_update` enabled are upgraded. `mise use -g --tool-option auto_update=true node@22` saves the option, and rewriting an entry keeps it.
- **Never runs** offline, in CI, or with `locked = true`.
- **Failures:** if a tool's last update failed, `mise doctor` shows the error, until an update succeeds or the tool's global entry stops enabling `auto_update`.
- The previous version is pruned on the usual `upgrade.auto_prune` schedule, which waits until no running process is using it.

### Implementation notes

- Eligibility is checked in memory first: the request must come from a global `mise.toml`, with `auto_update` written in

@@ -0,0 +1,216 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+# auto_update on a global [tools] entry upgrades the tool, within its
+# configured version, before a shim or `mise x` launches it. The dummy backend
+# offers 1.0.0, 1.1.0, and 2.0.0. Each case gets its own state dir, so its
+# first check is always due.
+
+fresh_state() {
+  export MISE_STATE_DIR="$PWD/state-$1"
+}
+
+global_config() {
+  printf '[tools]\n%s\n' "$1" >"$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml"
+}
+
+reset_dummy() {
+  mise uninstall dummy --all
+  mise install dummy@1.0.0
+}
+
+assert_not_checked() {
+  assert_fail "test -e '$MISE_STATE_DIR/tool-update'"
+}
+
+# `mise use` writes the option, and rewriting the entry keeps it.
+global_config '# no tools'
+mise use -g --tool-option auto_update=true dummy@1
+assert_contains "cat $MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml" "auto_update = true"
+mise use -g --tool-option auto_update=12h dummy@1
+assert_contains "cat $MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml" 'auto_update = "12h"'
+mise use -g dummy@1
+assert_contains "cat $MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml" 'auto_update = "12h"'
+printf '[tools.dummy]\nversion = "1"\n' >"$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml"
+mise use -g --tool-option auto_update=true dummy@1
+assert_contains "cat $MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml" "auto_update = true"
+
+# `mise x` updates within the range first and runs the new version, with
+# nothing added to the tool's stdout.
+fresh_state exec
+global_config 'dummy = { version = "1", auto_update = true }'
+reset_dummy
+assert "mise x -- dummy" "This is Dummy 1.1.0!"
+assert_not_contains "mise ls --installed dummy" "2.0.0"
+
+# Within the interval it runs what is installed without checking again.
+mise uninstall dummy@1.1.0
+assert "mise x -- dummy" "This is Dummy 1.0.0!"
+
+# Another version of the tool that doesn't opt in is left alone.
+fresh_state mixed
+reset_dummy
+cat >"$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml" <<'EOF'
+[tools]
+dummy = [{ version = "1", auto_update = true }, { version = "latest", auto_update = false }]
+EOF
+assert "mise x -- dummy" "This is Dummy 1.1.0!"
+assert_not_contains "mise ls --installed dummy" "2.0.0"
+global_config 'dummy = { version = "1", auto_update = true }'
+
+# Shims update the same way.
+fresh_state shim
+reset_dummy
+mise reshim
+assert "$MISE_DATA_DIR/shims/dummy" "This is Dummy 1.1.0!"
+
+# Only the tool being launched is checked.
+fresh_state other-command
+reset_dummy
+assert_succeed "mise x -- true"
+assert_not_checked
+
+# A project config can't turn it on, and a project that sets its own version
+# of the tool doesn't update the global entry's tool.
+fresh_state project-option
+global_config '# no tools'
+cat >mise.toml <<'EOF'
+[tools]
+dummy = { version = "1", auto_update = true }
+EOF
+reset_dummy
+assert "mise x -- dummy" "This is Dummy 1.0.0!"
+assert_not_checked
+
+fresh_state project-version
+global_config 'dummy = { version = "1", auto_update = true }'
+cat >mise.toml <<'EOF'
+[tools]
+dummy = "1"
+EOF
+assert "mise x -- dummy" "This is Dummy 1.0.0!"
+assert_not_checked
+rm mise.toml
+
+# Exact versions are never updated; nothing is checked offline or from hook-env.
+fresh_state pin
+global_config 'dummy = { version = "1.0.0", auto_update = true }'
+assert "mise x -- dummy" "This is Dummy 1.0.0!"
+assert_not_checked
+
+global_config 'dummy = { version = "1", auto_update = true }'
+fresh_state locked
+mise lock --global dummy
+assert "mise --locked x -- dummy" "This is Dummy 1.0.0!"
+assert_not_checked
+rm "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/mise.lock"
+fresh_state offline
+assert "MISE_OFFLINE=1 mise x -- dummy" "This is Dummy 1.0.0!"
+assert_not_checked
+fresh_state hook-env
+assert_succeed "mise hook-env -s bash >/dev/null"
+assert_not_checked
+
+# A per-tool interval is accepted; one under an hour is raised with a warning.
+fresh_state interval
+global_config 'dummy = { version = "1", auto_update = "1m" }'
+assert_contains "mise x -- dummy 2>&1" "below the 1h minimum"
+assert_contains "mise ls --installed dummy" "1.1.0"
+
+# A failed update warns, runs the installed version, and shows in doctor
+# until an update succeeds.
+fresh_state failed
+global_config 'dummy = { version = "1", auto_update = true }'
+reset_dummy
+global_config 'dummy = { version = "1", auto_update = true, postinstall = "exit 1" }'
+assert_contains "mise x -- dummy 2>&1" "could not update asdf:dummy"
+assert "mise x -- dummy" "This is Dummy 1.0.0!"
+assert_contains "mise doctor 2>&1 || true" "the last auto_update of asdf:dummy failed"
+# A shell override of the version still shows it; a tool that no longer opts
+# in does not, since nothing would clear it.
+assert_contains "MISE_DUMMY_VERSION=1.0.0 mise doctor 2>&1 || true" "the last auto_update of asdf:dummy failed"
+global_config 'dummy = { version = "1", auto_update = false }'
+assert_not_contains "mise doctor 2>&1 || true" "auto_update of asdf:dummy failed"
+global_config 'dummy = { version = "1", auto_update = true }'
+printf '[tools]\ndummy = "1"\n' >"$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.local.toml"
+assert_not_contains "mise doctor 2>&1 || true" "auto_update of asdf:dummy failed"
+rm "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.local.toml"
+global_config 'dummy = "1"'
+assert_not_contains "mise doctor 2>&1 || true" "auto_update of asdf:dummy failed"
+global_config 'dummy = { version = "1", auto_update = true }'
+find "$MISE_STATE_DIR/tool-update" -type f ! -name '*.*' -delete
+assert "mise x -- dummy" "This is Dummy 1.1.0!"
+assert_not_contains "mise doctor 2>&1 || true" "auto_update of asdf:dummy failed"
+
+# A check whose version lookup fails is a failure, not "up to date".
+fresh_state lookup-failed
+reset_dummy
+global_config 'dummy = { version = "1.0", auto_update = true }'
+MISE_CACHE_DIR="$PWD/empty-cache" RTX_FAILURE=1 mise x -- dummy 2>/dev/null || true
+assert_contains "mise doctor 2>&1 || true" "the last auto_update of asdf:dummy failed"
+global_config 'dummy = { version = "1", auto_update = true }'
+
+# In an activated shell the project's [env] is exported, but the update runs
+# with the environment activation started from.
+fresh_state activated
+reset_dummy
+cat >"$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml" <<'EOF'
+[tools]
+dummy = { version = "1", auto_update = true, postinstall = "echo FOO=$FOO >> $HOME/postinstall.log" }
+EOF
+cat >mise.toml <<'EOF'
+[env]
+FOO = "project"
+EOF
+eval "$(mise activate bash)" && _mise_hook
+assert "printenv FOO" "project"

+fresh_state nested

+needs-dummy = { version = "1", auto_update = true }

title: fix(prune): snapshot what templated tool versions render to in the identity layout
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/469
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

With the experimental identity install layout (`install_layout = "identity"`), `mise prune` and `mise ls --prunable` now work for projects whose tool versions are templates, and still delete the versions nothing uses.

```toml
# project/mise.toml
[vars]
tool_version = "1.0.0"

# project/child/mise.toml
[tools]
node = "{{vars.tool_version}}"
```

Run from another directory, prune rendered the child's template without the parent's vars and failed (maplibre/maplibre-native-ffi#771). Rendering it from there is also unsafe in general, because a version can depend on inputs prune cannot see: `mise --no-env`, a `[settings] env_file`, the active `MISE_ENV`, shell exports. A wrong render makes prune delete the version the project uses.

## What changes

When a command resolves tools in a project, the catalog saves a snapshot of what that project's templated versions rendered to, under `installs/.mise/snapshots/`. `mise prune` reads the snapshot instead of rendering, and treats the recorded versions as a literal config. Any template works, because prune never evaluates one: vars, env and the tera functions.

The rule prune relies on is that a version may be removed on the strength of a snapshot only if the snapshot is complete and current:

- **Complete.** A snapshot is the config's whole rendered tool list for one context (the `MISE_ENV` plus the set of loaded config files), taken from the requests a command resolved, and only when that command resolved every templated tool of the config that no other source replaces. A command that resolved fewer (`mise exec node@22`) records nothing, and prune and `ls --prunable` never record. A newer snapshot of the same context replaces the old one outright, so a version a project stopped using becomes prunable.
- **Current.** A snapshot stores a hash of every config file it loaded. If one is gone, that context cannot occur again and is dropped. If one changed, or the config has no snapshot, prune keeps every installation of the config's templated tools until a command runs in the project again. Prune never fails for it.

Without the identity layout nothing changes.

## Limits

- A snapshot cannot see anything that is not a config file. A changed shell variable or flag is noticed at the next command in the project, not before.
- Only the newest snapshot per context is kept, so a project run with alternating env values keeps only the last. To keep a version a snapshot no longer lists, reference it in a tracked config or lockfile.

## Notes

- Replaces #14008, which tried to rebuild each project's environment and could not reproduce install-time inputs, and builds on the report in #13993 by @sargunv.
- An earlier revision of this PR recorded individual installs. Each review round needed another coverage rule, because observing that an install was used cannot show that it is no longer needed. Snapshots replace that w

title: fix(pypi): build uv tool venvs on mise's python
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/468
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A `pypi:`/`pipx:` tool installed with uv could end up with a venv whose `python` links to a CPython that uv downloaded into `~/.local/share/uv/python`, even when mise manages Python. CI that caches only the mise data dir (for example with `jdx/mise-action`) then restores the tool without its interpreter, and it fails with `couldn't exec process`.

uv's default preference is `managed`, so `uv tool install` picks an earlier uv download over the mise Python that mise only puts first on `PATH`. `fix_venv_python_symlink` leaves such a link alone because it does not point into the mise installs dir, so nothing flagged it.

Version-only installs now pass `--python <mise python>` to `uv tool install` when mise manages Python, the same way graph-locked installs already bind their interpreter. A `--python`/`-p` in `uvx_args` still wins, and nothing changes when mise has no Python for the tool (a `PATH` interpreter is not pinned).

```toml
[tools]
python = "3.12"
uv = "latest"
"pypi:cowsay" = "6.1"
```

With `UV_PYTHON_PREFERENCE=only-managed`, the venv for `pypi:cowsay` used to link to `~/uv-pythons/cpython-3.13.5-.../bin/python3.13`; it now resolves under `installs/python/`.

Tradeoff: an explicit `--python` is a hard requirement, so a package whose `requires-python` excludes mise's Python now fails instead of getting a uv download. Override with `--python` in `uvx_args` if needed.

Not covered: with no mise-managed Python, uv still uses a `PATH` or downloaded interpreter outside the data dir. That is documented in the discussion, not changed here.

Discussion: https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13984

## Test plan

- New `e2e/backend/test_pipx_uv_python_binding` fails without the change (venv links to the uv download) and passes with it.
- `e2e/backend/test_pipx_uvx` passes.

title: fix(dotfiles): skip legacy link discovery for group entries
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/467
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes #14021.

## Problem

With dotfile groups, the first `mise dot apply` (before any symlink-each state is recorded) could delete a pre-existing link to an entry, such as a stow-migrated `~/.config/demo`, and not recreate it until a second apply. Before state exists, every group also walked its whole target (e.g. `~`) on each command, so many groups targeting `~` made `status` and `apply --dry-run` take minutes.

## Fix

Legacy pre-state link discovery is skipped for group requests. Groups postdate the state file, so there is no legacy deployment to discover. Ordinary entries are unchanged.

Tradeoff: a dangling link left by a removed group source is not cleaned up on the first apply.

Adds a unit test covering the excluded entry link for plain vs group requests.

title: feat(http): add headers option for bearer and API-key auth
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/466
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

The `http:` backend could only authenticate with netrc Basic auth, so tools hosted behind a bearer token or API-key header could not be installed. A common case is a binary stored as an OCI blob on `ghcr.io`, which rejects Basic auth on `/v2/` blob requests and wants `Authorization: Bearer base64(token)`. Previously a `headers` entry in the tool options was silently ignored and the install failed with a 401.

The `http:` backend now takes a `headers` table. Values are templates, so the secret can come from the environment:

```toml
[tools."http:polaris"]
version = "0.9.2"
headers = { Authorization = "Bearer {{ env.GITHUB_TOKEN | b64_encode }}" }

[tools."http:polaris".platforms]
linux-x64 = { url = "https://ghcr.io/v2/acme/polaris/blobs/sha256:...", format = "tar.gz" }
```

The headers are sent with the artifact download, the `version_list_url` request, and the `checksum_url` requests `mise lock` makes.

- Header values are marked sensitive so they stay out of debug output, and `headers` is ignored for install identity, so changing a token does not reinstall the tool.
- An undefined env var fails the install rather than sending the literal template.
- Headers are sent to the host in `url` only. On a redirect to another host, port, or scheme, every credential header is dropped for the rest of the chain, which is what GHCR's signed blob URLs need. This includes `X-Api-Key`-style headers, which reqwest would otherwise forward (it only strips `Authorization`, `Cookie` and `Proxy-Authorization`). To support that, requests carrying such a header follow redirects themselves; other requests are unchanged.

- To send a header to another host after a redirect (for example a CDN that needs the same key), list the hosts per header with `headers_forward`:

  ```toml
  headers = { X-Api-Key = "{{ env.KEY }}", Authorization = "Bearer {{ env.TOKEN }}" }
  headers_forward = { X-Api-Key = ["cdn.example.com", "*.assets.example.com"] }
  ```

  Here only `X-Api-Key` reaches those hosts; `Authorization` stays with the `url` host. Hosts are exact names or `*.` plus a suffix (no bare `*`), forwarding never steps down to plain HTTP, and a name that is not in `headers` is an error.

Not included: built-in GHCR token handling and a bearer-token credentials file, which the original request listed as alternatives.

Tested with the new `e2e/backend/test_http_headers` (401 without the header, success with it, `version_list_url`, unset variable, cross-host redirect for `Authorization` and `X-Api-Key`, same-host redirect keeps the header), plus the existing `test_http_lock_checksum` and `test_http_ls_remote_current_opts`. Clippy with `-D warnings` is clean. `mise run lint` still stops on an unrelated pre-existing `unused dependency junction` warning in `crates/mise-util`.

Relates to discussion #14014.

title: fix(prune): keep versions that a running process was started from
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/465
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise prune` treats a version as unused when no tracked config or tool stub resolves to it. A program started before its version was replaced can still be running from that version — a terminal session still on `claude@2.1.289` after `claude@2.1.291` is selected, for example — and pruning deletes files out from under the live process. This also applies to the deferred pruning after `mise upgrade` once `upgrade.prune_after` has passed. Some setups turn automatic pruning off entirely because of this, and old versions pile up instead.

Pruning now keeps a version while a process is running from it, and says which process kept it. This works on Linux, macOS and Windows:

```console
$ mise prune --tools --dry-run
mise claude@2.1.289 is kept: still running as pid 3445962 (claude)
mise claude@2.1.263 is prunable: claude is required at 2.1.291 by ~/.config/mise/config.toml
mise claude@2.1.263 [dryrun]             uninstall
...
```

Once the process exits, the version becomes prunable again.

## What counts as running from a version

A process runs from an install directory when either of these is inside it:

- its executable, which covers native tools such as `claude`, `gh` or `node`
- an absolute path in its command line, which covers interpreted tools whose executable is an interpreter from another install, such as an `npm:` or `pipx:` tool

Install paths are matched both as mise names them and with symlinks resolved. On Windows, matching ignores case.

A command-line path can also go through one of the tool's runtime links. mise puts `installs/<tool>/latest/bin` on `PATH` for a `latest` request, so an `npm:` tool started that way has `installs/npm-foo/latest/...` in its command line, and an upgrade later retargets `latest` while the process keeps running from the old version. If the link has not changed since the process started, it is followed to the version it names. If it changed after the process started, the version the process started from cannot be known, so every prune candidate of that tool is kept until the process exits.

Processes are read from `/proc` on Linux, `libproc` and `sysctl` (`KERN_PROCARGS2`) on macOS, and the Toolhelp and `NtQueryInformationProcess` APIs on Windows. Processes that cannot be inspected, such as another user's, are skipped, and a debug line reports how many there were. On Windows this also avoids a prune that fails partway through because the OS refuses to delete a running executable.

## Where it applies

The check is part of `toolset::prunable_tools`, so every command that decides what is unused agrees: `mise prune`, `mise unuse --prune`, `mise ls --prunable`, and the deferred pruning after `mise upgrade`, which keeps the receipt and checks again at most once a day. `mise uninstall` and `mise upgrade --prune` are unchanged; they remove what they are told to remove.

The scan runs only when there are prune ca

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# A version that no tracked config or tool stub needs any more can still be in
+# use: a long-running process started from it before it was replaced keeps
+# loading files from its install directory. Pruning keeps such a version until
+# the process exits. Windows has its own test in e2e-win.
+
+held=""
+trap '[[ -n $held ]] && kill "$held" 2>/dev/null' EXIT
+
+# Stand in for a program started from the version before it stopped being
+# needed: a copy of sleep inside the version's own install directory. The copy
+# keeps its name because multi-call coreutils and busybox pick the program to
+# run from it, and stays out of bin/ so mise does not create a shim for it.
+start_held_process() {
+  mkdir -p "$1/libexec"
+  cp "$(command -v sleep)" "$1/libexec/sleep"
+  if [[ "$(uname -s)" == "Darwin" ]]; then
+    # A copy of a system binary is killed on launch until it is signed again.
+    codesign --force --sign - "$1/libexec/sleep" 2>/dev/null
+  fi
+  "$1/libexec/sleep" 120 &
+  held=$!
+  # Wait until the copy is the running program so the checks below do not
+  # race its exec, and stop here if it could not start.
+  local expected attempt running
+  expected="$(realpath "$1/libexec/sleep")"
+  for attempt in {1..50}; do
+    if [[ -e /proc/$held/exe ]]; then
+      running="$(readlink -f "/proc/$held/exe" 2>/dev/null)"
+    else
+      running="$(realpath "$(ps -o comm= -p "$held" 2>/dev/null)" 2>/dev/null)"
+    fi
+    if [[ $running == "$expected" ]]; then
+      return
+    fi
+    sleep 0.1
+  done
+  fail "the stand-in process did not start after $attempt checks"
+}
+
+stop_held_process() {
+  kill "$held"
+  wait "$held" 2>/dev/null || true
+  held=""
+}

+
+echo "=== mise prune keeps a version a process is running from ==="
+# Installed on its own, so no tracked config mentions dummy at all.
+assert "mise install dummy@1.0.0"
+start_held_process "$install"
+
+assert_not_contains "mise ls --prunable" "1.0.0"

+assert_not_contains "mise prune --tools --dry-run 2>&1" "[dryrun]"
+# Nothing is left to prune, so --dry-run-code succeeds.
+assert_succeed "mise prune --tools --dry-run-code"
+MISE_YES=1 assert_contains "mise prune --tools 2>&1" "dummy@1.0.0 is kept"
+assert "ls $install"
+
+# Once the process exits, the version is unused again.
+stop_held_process
+MISE_YES=1 assert_not_contains "mise prune --tools 2>&1" "is kept"
+assert_fail "ls $install"
+
+echo "=== deferred pruning after an upgrade waits for the process ==="
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml

+dummy = "1"
+
+[settings]

+EOF
+
+mise install dummy@1.0.0
+start_held_process "$install"

title: fix(deps): update rust crate sigstore-verify to 0.14
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/464
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Summary

Updates `sigstore-verify` from 0.11 to 0.14 and ports `mise-sigstore` to the new API. This replaces the Renovate PR #13995, which can't compile on its own because 0.14 is a breaking release. There is no user-visible behavior change: attestation, cosign and SLSA verification keep the same trust decisions.

API changes handled:

- **TUF mirror override** — `TufConfig::custom` now takes a `TufBootstrap`; the mirror still bootstraps from the embedded production root (`SigstoreInstance::PublicGood.tuf_root()`). `DEFAULT_TUF_URL` is no longer exported, so `mise-sigstore` defines it.
- **Verification policy** — `VerificationPolicy` has no `Default`; mise uses `any_identity()` and keeps authorizing the signer itself via the existing workflow check. `skip_tlog` is now `skip_tlog_unsafe`, applied only when the bundle has no inclusion proof (same as before). `verify_with_key` takes an explicit `PublicKeyVerificationPolicy::default()` (tlog verified, as before).
- **DSSE / keys** — envelopes carry exactly one signature (`envelope.signature`, `payload.as_bytes()`); key type detection uses `KeyAlgorithm::from_spki`, still accepting only Ed25519 and ECDSA P-256.

## Testing

`cargo test -p mise-sigstore` (54 pass) and `cargo +stable clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` are clean.

Supersedes #13995.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: unavailable.*

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes sit on attestation, cosign, and SLSA verification paths; the diff is mostly an API port, but reviewers should confirm policy choices still match 0.11 behavior.
> 
> **Overview**
> Bumps **`sigstore-verify`** from **0.11** to **0.14** in `mise-sigstore` (with matching **`Cargo.lock`** churn for the sigstore crate graph and transitive bumps like **`windows-sys`**). This is a compile-fix for the breaking 0.14 release, not a feature change.
> 
> **`mise-sigstore`** is updated to match the new API while keeping the same verification rules: **`VerificationPolicy::any_identity()`** plus the existing workflow identity check; **`skip_tlog_unsafe()`** only when a bundle has no Rekor inclusion proof; **`skip_sct()`** for GitHub-internal certs; and **`PublicKeyVerificationPolicy::default()`** on **`verify_with_key`**. TUF mirror overrides now use **`TufConfig::custom(url, TufBootstrap::trusted(...))`** instead of **`with_root(PRODUCTION_TUF_ROOT)`**, and **`DEFAULT_TUF_URL`** is defined locally because 0.14 no longer exports it.
> 
> DSSE handling follows the new envelope shape (**`payload.as_bytes()`**, single **`envelope.signature`**), cosign key detection uses **`KeyAlgorithm::from_spki`**, bundle validation uses **`ValidationOptions::new()`**, and **`TrustedRoot::fulcio_certs()`** is used without the old **`Re

title: feat(config): add global section write targets
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/463
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Summary

- add opt-in global `settings.write_targets` for tools, bootstrap packages, and dotfiles
- write new global declarations to their configured section file while preserving existing declarations in place
- require an explicit `--path` for ambiguous fragments or mixed entries that resolve to different targets
- document the behavior and regenerate the JSON schema

## Example

```toml
[settings.write_targets]
tools = "~/.config/mise/conf.d/10-tools.toml"
packages = "~/.config/mise/conf.d/20-packages.toml"
dotfiles = "~/.config/mise/conf.d/30-dotfiles.toml"
```

Existing entries are never migrated; local and `--env` writes are unchanged.

## Validation

- `cargo test --lib write_target_tests`
- `cargo check --all-targets --all-features`
- `cargo test -p mise-settings`
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `e2e/run_all_tests cli/test_global_section_write_targets`

> **Overview**
> Adds opt-in **`settings.write_targets`** so global `[tools]`, `[bootstrap.packages]`, and `[dotfiles]` can be written to separate `conf.d` fragments instead of the main global config.
>

title: fix(oci): stream large blob uploads in one PATCH
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/462
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes #14016.

Large `mise oci push` layers previously crossed the 64 MiB threshold into multiple ranged `PATCH` requests. GHCR rejects the later non-empty patch with `416 Range Not Satisfiable`, so the image could not be pushed.

Large blobs now stream from disk in one `PATCH` without `Content-Range`, followed by the existing zero-byte `PUT ?digest=` finalization. This keeps memory bounded and matches the single-PATCH flow accepted by GHCR and ECR. Small blobs continue to use the existing monolithic `PUT` path.

## Compatibility

This intentionally trades the previous 64 MiB per-request cap for compatibility with registries that do not support more than one non-empty PATCH. Registries or proxies with a smaller request-body limit may still reject an oversized single PATCH; this PR adds no new configuration or fallback behavior.

## Validation

- Added a credential-free >64 MiB protocol fixture that requires exactly one range-free PATCH and the digest-finalizing PUT.
- Expanded the real Distribution-compatible registry E2E test with a >64 MiB tar layer and independent `crane validate` coverage.
- Passed containerized `cargo fmt --check`, the focused protocol regression test, and `bash -n` for the E2E script.
- The local real-registry E2E execution did not start because Docker shared-volume I/O stalled while cross-building the Linux test binary; normal PR CI is the remaining compatibility gate.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: OpenAI/GPT-5; version: unavailable.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes OCI push networking and HTTP client timeout behavior for large uploads; mistakes could affect registry compatibility or hang/retry semantics, but scope is mostly push paths with added regression coverage.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Large OCI layers (>64 MiB) now upload via one disk-streamed `PATCH` without `Content-Range`, then the existing zero-byte `PUT ?digest=` finalize** — replacing multi-chunk ranged PATCHes that GHCR rejects with `416`.
> 
> To support slow streaming bodies, the HTTP layer adds **`HTTP_UPLOAD`** (connect timeout only, no reqwest read timeout) and an **`UploadWatch`** that extends the deadline as upload bytes flow and fails stalled uploads with retryable `TimedOut` I/O errors. Registry push uses **`send_upload`** so 401 auth retries rebuild a fresh stream body.
> 
> **Tests and CI:** protocol regression for the single PATCH path, upload-watch unit tests, a streaming-upload HTTP test, a longer nextest override for the large-blob test, and OCI push E2E extended with a ~65 MiB layer plus updated push expectations.

title: feat(dotfiles): add merge entries that own only some keys of a config file
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/461
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Tools like Codex, Claude Code, and oh-my-pi write their own state into the same JSON, TOML, or YAML file that holds your settings. A `symlink` or `copy` dotfile entry fights them for the whole file, and a `block` can't survive an application that rewrites the file. A new `merge` edit entry owns only the keys in its source and leaves the rest to the application:

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.codex/config.toml/shared" = { source = "codex/shared.toml", merge = true }
"~/.claude/settings.json/shared" = { source = "claude/shared.json", merge = true }
"~/.omp/agent/config.yml/shared" = { source = "omp/shared.yml", merge = true }
```

With `codex/shared.toml` holding `model = "gpt-5"` and `[tui] theme = "light"`, `mise dot apply` sets those two keys in `~/.codex/config.toml` and leaves the app's `[plugins.*]` tables, `notify`, and comments exactly where they were. The format comes from the target's extension, and a missing target is created from the source.

- Tables merge recursively; scalars and arrays are replaced. Keys only the target has are never touched, and keys removed from the source are not removed from the target.
- `mise dot status` and `mise dot diff` report drift only in owned keys, so keys the application adds never show up.
- TOML and YAML keep comments, order, and formatting of untouched keys. JSON keeps key order and indent. A target that does not parse (including JSON with comments) is reported and never overwritten.
- `template = "tera"` renders the source first, like other edit entries. `mise dot unapply` leaves merged keys in place because the application may have changed them.

Also teaches the whole-file entry parsers (`files.rs`, dotfile groups) that `merge` marks an edit. Without that a merge entry was also read as a whole-file symlink at `~/.codex/config.toml/shared`, which the new e2e test caught. Adds `merge` to `schema/mise.json` and a section to `docs/dotfiles.md`.

Open design questions from the discussion, answered conservatively and easy to change: removing a key from the source does not remove it from the target, and arrays are replaced rather than merged. A modify-script entry (chezmoi's `modify_`) is not part of this PR.

Verified with the new `e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_merge_edits` (create, drift, in-place apply across all three formats, unapply, bad extension, unparseable target), the existing dotfiles edit/files/groups/absent e2e tests, unit tests, and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`.

Closes nothing directly; addresses the request in jdx/mise#13986. Stacked on #14011.

body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/459
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Adds an internal helper that sets keys on a YAML document by editing its syntax tree in place, so comments, key order, quoting, and flow/block style on everything else survive. Nothing calls it yet; it is the foundation for the `merge` dotfile entries stacked on top (jdx/mise#13986).

```rust
merge_yaml("# note\ntheme: dark  # ui\nkeep: 1\n", "theme: light\n")
// => "# note\ntheme: light  # ui\nkeep: 1\n"
```

- Mappings that exist on both sides merge recursively; any other value, including a sequence, is replaced by the source's. A value that already equals the source's is left untouched, formatting included.
- An empty or comment-only target is an empty mapping. A non-mapping root or a multi-document file is an error.

It is built on [`yaml-edit`](https://crates.io/crates/yaml-edit) (pure Rust on `rowan`, MSRV 1.70). aube's comment-preserving path uses `yamlpatch`/`yamlpath`, which are pinned below their latest releases for MSRV and pull in tree-sitter; this avoids both. `yaml-edit` adds `rowan 0.16` and nothing else new to `Cargo.lock`.

Verified with unit tests, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`, and `cargo +1.95 check`.

title: feat(dotfiles): report notification availability and add notify command
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/458
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

`history.notify` reads like a general alert channel, but it only announces sync conflicts that pause sharing. Users who hit another failure, such as a watcher that cannot save checkpoints, get no notification and nothing tells them why. On macOS the permission prompt only appears with the first conflict, so "mise" is absent from System Settings > Notifications until then. Unofficial builds such as Homebrew can never notify, and the only hint is a one-time warning when connecting a setup repository. See discussion jdx/mise#13861.

## Changes

- `mise doctor` now includes a `notifications:` line in the dotfiles section, in text and JSON:
  - `disabled (history.notify = false)`
  - `unavailable (unofficial macOS build such as Homebrew)` or `unavailable (`notify-send` not found)`
  - otherwise it points to `mise dot notify`
- `mise dot status` shows the same `notifications:` line under the setup repository.
- New `mise dot notify` sends a test notification. On macOS it triggers the permission prompt on demand, and it turns the helper's denied and timed-out exits into readable errors.
- The `history.notify` setting docs and `docs/history.md` now state that notifications cover sync conflicts only, that the macOS prompt appears with the first notification, and that Homebrew builds never notify.

```
$ mise dot notify   # Homebrew build
Error: desktop notifications are unavailable: unofficial macOS build such as Homebrew
```

Only the signing and `notify-send` checks are static. macOS permission state can only be learned by sending, which is why doctor points at `mise dot notify`.

title: fix(pypi): lock from <root>/simple/ for JSON URLs
body:
uv_index_url turns a `<root>/pypi/{}/json` registry template into
 `<root>/pypi/simple/`. PyPI and JFrog Artifactory serve the simple
 index at `<root>/simple/`, so `mise lock` fails for every pypi: tool
 on such a registry.

 Change the unit test to expect `<root>/simple/`, and add an
 Artifactory-shaped case and a case showing that only a `pypi` path
 segment is dropped. Give the notpypi.org case a path prefix so that a
 host check matching it as pypi.org fails.

 Stop the e2e fixture from serving the simple index at `/pypi/simple/`.
 Because it served both paths, test_pypi_lock passed with either
 mapping.

### Out of scope

A registry template for a simple index whose path does not end in `simple`, such as devpi's
`https://devpi.example.com/root/pypi/+simple/{}/`, still gets `/simple/` appended, so uv is
pointed at `.../+simple/simple/`. That behaviour predates this PR and this PR does not change it.

title: fix(config): keep global config when a project ignore resolves onto it via symlink
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/456
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A project `.miserc.toml` that sets `ignored_config_paths` no longer hides your global config when `~/.config/mise` is a symlink into that project.

Example: with `~/.config/mise` -> `~/dotfiles/mise/dot-config/mise` and this in `~/dotfiles/.miserc.toml`:

```toml
ignored_config_paths = ["mise"]
```

`mise config ls` from `~/dotfiles` used to list nothing, because the ignore entry resolves to `~/dotfiles/mise` and the global config's symlink target is under it. It now still lists `~/.config/mise/config.toml`, while the project copy stays ignored.

Global and system configs are now matched against `ignored_config_paths` as discovered, without resolving symlinks. Ignoring `~/.config/mise` by its own path still works, and non-global configs match exactly as before, so the Windows matching from #11818 is unaffected. The one behavior change: a global config can no longer be ignored only through its symlink target.

Reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14001. That report also showed duplicate rows in `mise ls --all-sources`, which I could not reproduce and this PR does not touch.

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes how ignored and trusted config paths are resolved for global/system files, which affects config loading and trust gating, though behavior for non-global configs is preserved.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes a case where a project **`ignored_config_paths`** entry (e.g. `["mise"]`) could unload the **global** config when `~/.config/mise` is a symlink into that project, because ignore matching followed the symlink target.
> 
> **Global and system configs** are now checked against `ignored_config_paths` using the path as discovered (**without** symlink resolution). Project configs still match via trust root and the existing canonical rules. Ignoring `~/.config/mise` by its literal path still works; you can no longer ignore a global config *only* through its symlink target.
> 
> Call sites that filtered ignored configs now use **`is_config_ignored_via_setting`** instead of pairing trust-root and path checks with **`is_ignored_via_setting`**. Config discovery applies **`unique_by(desymlink)`** after the ignore filter so deduping does not mask ignore behavior.

> Adds an **e2e** script covering dotfiles-style symlinks and the case where the global symlink target is the same directory the project names as `mise/`.

### Release Notes

<details>
<summary>jdx/renovate-config (jdx/renovate-config)</summary>

### [`v1.0.2`](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/renovate-config/releases/tag/v1.0.2): : Lockfile workflows recover when mise.lock is stale

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/renovate-config/compare/v1.0.1...v1.0.2)

The `aube-lock` and `mise-lock` reusable workflows no longer leave Renovate PRs red when a mise tool bump leaves `mise.lock` with stale platform entries. The preset also stops delaying `jdx/workflows` updates.

#### Fixed

- **Lockfile workflows now handle a stale `mise.lock`.** When Renovate's mise manager bumps a tool, it rewrites only the `version =` line in `mise.lock`, so the per-platform URLs and checksums still point at the old release. On [jdx/usage#1520](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/usage/issues/1520) (aube 2.6.0 → 2.6.1), this broke both workflows. ([#​34](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/renovate-config/issues/34), [@​jdx](https://redirect.github.com/jdx))

  - `aube-lock` crashed during setup: `mise install --locked` failed with `aube@2.6.1 is locked to a download URL from 2.6.0`. The workflow now refreshes a copy of `mise.lock` on the runner before installing tools. It never commits that copy, because committing `mise.lock` is `mise-lock`'s job. Repos with no tracked `mise.lock` still get a plain `mise install`.
  - `mise-lock` could exit successfully but leave a just-published tool's entries on the previous release, then push a lockfile that still failed CI.
  - Both workflows now check the result with `mise install --dry-run`. If it reports stale entries, they re-run `mise lock` up to 4 times, waiting 30, 60, then 90 seconds between attempts, and fail with the dry-run output if the entries are still stale. Any other dry-run failure only produces a warning in `mise-lock` and goes on to the normal install step in `aube-lock`, so repos that worked before aren't blocked.

  Callers pin these workflows by SHA, so the fix takes effect once Renovate bumps your pin to v1.0.2.

#### Changed

- `jdx/workflows` is now on the preset's list of jdx-owned packages exempt from the 7-day `minimumReleaseAge`, so Renovate bumps it right after each release. ([#​33](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/renovate-config/issues/33), [@​jdx](https://redirect.github.com/jdx))

**Full Changelog**: <https://github.com/jdx/renovate-config/compare/v1.0.1...v1.0.2>

</details>

---

> Some dependencies could not be looked up. Check the warning logs for more information.

---

### Release Notes

<details>
<summary>cijiugechu/nodejs-semver (nodejs-semver)</summary>

### [`v7.0.0`](https://redirect.github.com/cijiugechu/nodejs-semver/blob/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md#700-2026-09-25)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/cijiugechu/nodejs-semver/compare/v6.0.0...v7.0.0)

##### Bug Fixes

- **range:** compound ranges no longer silently drop tokens that the fast parser rejects but loose parsing accepts; `^1.0.0 v1.2.3` now yields `>=1.0.0 <2.0.0-0||1.2.3` instead of discarding `v1.2.3` ([fbd593c](https://redirect.github.com/cijiugechu/nodejs-semver/commit/fbd593c10858120270875459bb2f8aa5f7f4ca62))

- **range:** `||` disjunctions following a comparator set are no longer parsed twice ([fbd593c](https://redirect.github.com/cijiugechu/nodejs-semver/commit/fbd593c10858120270875459bb2f8aa5f7f4ca62))

##### Performance

- **parser:** share number, identifier, and whitespace scanning across the fast and loose parsers; remove the garbage-token fallback stage and make loose parsing allocate only when a range actually spans multiple `||` branches ([fbd593c](https://redirect.github.com/cijiugechu/nodejs-semver/commit/fbd593c10858120270875459bb2f8aa5f7f4ca62))

##### **BREAKING CHANGE**

All parsers now use a single whitespace definition matching JavaScript's `\s` ([fbd593c](https://redirect.github.com/cijiugechu/nodejs-semver/commit/fbd593c10858120270875459bb2f8aa5f7f4ca62)).

`Range::parse` trims leading and trailing whitespace before parsing, so inputs such as `" <v 1"` or `"<v 1 "` no longer change meaning based on edge whitespace. Non-space whitespace now also acts as a token separator, so `"foo\n1.2.3-beta"` parses as `1.2.3-beta` instead of failing.

Loose parsing keeps tokens it accepts even when the fast parser cannot handle them, and tilde ranges accept `~1.x.3` with a prerelease suffix to match the fast parser.

Callers relying on the exact set of accepted or rejected inputs, or on the displayed form of parsed ranges for inputs containing unusual whitespace or mixed loose and strict tokens, may observe different results.

</details>

> Some dependencies could not be looked up. Check the warning logs for more information.

---

### Release Notes

<details>
<summary>jdx/mise-action (jdx/mise-action)</summary>

### [`v5.0.0`](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/mise-action/releases/tag/v5.0.0): : Default minimum release age of 24 hours for mise

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/mise-action/compare/v4.3.0...v5.0.0)

If you don't pin a `version`, mise-action now installs the newest stable mise release that is at least 24 hours old. Upgrading mise on a runner that already has it is also less likely to hit GitHub API rate limits.

#### Breaking Changes

##### `minimum_release_age` now defaults to `24h` ([#​632](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/mise-action/pull/632) by [@​jdx](https://redirect.github.com/jdx))

Before this release, `minimum_release_age` was an opt-in setting. It now defaults to `24h`. If you don't set `version`, the action picks the highest-numbered stable mise release published at least 24 hours ago. A mise release that just shipped won't be installed until it's a day old.

To get the latest stable release right away, as in v4, set the delay to `0s`. You can also choose a longer delay:

```yaml
- uses: jdx/mise-action@v5
  with:
    minimum_release_age: 0s   # or e.g. 7d
```

- An explicit `version` input still takes precedence and skips the delay.
- The setting applies only to the mise binary, not to tools installed by mise.
- The action now gets the release list from a public CDN index (`releases.tsv` on mise.jdx.dev) instead of paging through the GitHub Releases API. Picking a release doesn't use GitHub API quota, even when an installed binary is reused. If the index is missing or malformed, the action fails instead of skipping the release-age check.
- Replacing an older installed binary still runs `mise self-update`, which may call the GitHub API to fetch that exact release.

#### Fixed

- `mise self-update` now runs with `MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN`. When a runner already had a different mise version installed, the action runs `mise self-update` to switch versions. That GitHub API call used to go out without authentication, so busy shared or self-hosted runners could hit the rate limit and fail with `HTTP 403 RateLimitedError`. If you already set a token in your environment, the action leaves it unchanged. ([#​619](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/mise-action/pull/619) by [@​hegde5](https://redirect.github.com/hegde5))

#### New Contributors

- [@​hegde5](https://redir

title: fix(uninstall): report each version once in a dry run
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/445
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes the confusing output in discussion #13988: `mise uninstall --dry-run java --all` printed the same `remove <path>` row several times per version, plus a row for a version that isn't installed.

```
$ mise uninstall --dry-run java --all
java@temurin-11.0.30+7 remove ~/.local/share/mise/installs/java/temurin-11.0.30+7
java@temurin-11.0.30+7 remove ~/.local/share/mise/installs/java/temurin-11.0.30+7
java@temurin-27.0.0+35 remove ~/.local/share/mise/installs/java/temurin-27.0.0+35
...
java@27.0.0     remove ~/Library/Caches/mise/java/27.0.0
```

- A dry run now collects the install, download and cache paths and reports them in one message per version, instead of one progress-row update per path.
- `mise uninstall --all` skips a listed entry whose install directory doesn't exist (a configured request like `27` standing for `temurin-27.0.0+35`), so it no longer shows up as a second removal that only touches cache.

I reproduced the output on Linux without a TTY (clean there) and couldn't reproduce the repeated rows themselves, so the TTY redraw is read from the code rather than observed. The e2e test covers the one-row-per-version output.

title: fix(backend): read a repository's packslip release list once per command
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/444
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A repository may keep a signed release list at `.well-known/packslip.json`, and most do not. mise fetched it on every lookup, so one `mise up` sent 22 requests for the same two 404s (`jdx/hk` and `jdx/mr-boxington`).

The fetch is now reused for 30 seconds, with a 404 cached as "no list". That covers one command and no more: a long-running process such as `mise mcp` or `mise watch` fetches the list again, so a withdrawal is still noticed. Other errors are not cached and are still reported.

Measured with `mise --debug up` in a home directory with about 15 tools: `packslip.json` requests went from 22 to 2, one per repository, and the command output was unchanged. Unit tests cover repeated and concurrent callers, a 404, and a failed fetch that is retried.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: 2.1.288.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Scoped HTTP caching in packslip GitHub list loading; behavior for missing lists and errors is preserved, with a short TTL so long-lived processes still refresh.
> 
> **Overview**
> Packslip resolution was hitting `raw.githubusercontent.com` for the same `.well-known/packslip.json` on every release lookup, so a single command could repeat identical requests (including slow 404s when a repo has no list).
> 
> **`fetch_github_list`** deduplicates fetches per URL: concurrent callers share one in-flight request via `OnceCell`, and successful bodies plus **404 → no list** are reused for **30 seconds**. Non-404 errors are not cached, so a later call can retry. **`github_list`** now routes through this helper instead of inline HTTP.
> 
> Unit tests assert one network call for parallel/repeated success and missing-list cases, and that a 500 is retried after the cache is cleared by failure.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 77c3c1b44f623a88ba2ba5bb8220f58049f8c147. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>
<!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Performance**
  * Repeated requests for the same GitHub release list can return faster for up to 30 seconds, including when the list is missing. Concurrent requests for the same list are handled together.
* **Reliability**
  * Temporary fetch failures aren’t reused, allowing a later request to try again. Missing lists continue to be handled as before.

title: fix(http): fetch a cached GitHub release once when callers race
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/443
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise up` asked mise-versions for every tool's latest release twice. When two callers wanted the same release at once, each saw an empty cache and each made the request, so the cache only helped the later of two sequential calls.

`CacheManager::get_or_try_init_async_if` now holds a per-cache lock across the fetch and re-checks the cache once it has it, so racing callers share one request. A new test runs three concurrent callers and asserts a single fetch; it fails without the lock.

Measured with `mise --debug up` in a home directory with about 15 tools (duplicates counted as repeated `GET` lines). Alongside the packslip change in the sibling PR, requests fell from 66 to 46; the output was identical.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5; version: 2.1.288.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Localized concurrency fix in the async cache helper; behavior change is limited to coalescing duplicate in-flight fetches for the same cache instance.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes a **cache stampede** in `CacheManager::get_or_try_init_async_if`: when several tasks miss the in-memory cache at once, they no longer each run the same async fetch.
> 
> Each `CacheManager` now carries an **`Arc<tokio::sync::Mutex<()>>`** (`fetch_lock`). After the fast path misses, callers **await the lock**, **re-check** `cache_async`, then only the first proceeds to disk/network fetch while others reuse the populated value.
> 
> A new **`concurrent_callers_share_one_fetch`** tokio test runs three parallel `get_or_try_init_async_if` calls and asserts the fetch closure runs **once**.
>

title: test(go): disable minimum_release_age in go install e2e
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/442
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

`backend/test_go_install` fails whenever `jdx/go-example` has a commit less than 24 hours old. The test installs `go:github.com/jdx/go-example/deep/cmd/tool/v2@latest`, which resolves to a pseudo-version minted from the latest commit. mise's default `minimum_release_age` (24h) hides it, so the install fails with "no versions found ... matching minimum_release_age (24h)". This broke CI on #13972, which doesn't touch the Go backend.

Set `minimum_release_age = "0s"` in the test's `[settings]`. No CLI behavior changes.

`mise run test:e2e backend/test_go_install` passes locally.

title: fix(ruby): keep Gemfile reload watches out of executable hooks
body:
A Gemfile such as `ruby file: ".ruby-version"` makes mise watch that file so shell activation can reload the selected Ruby version. Changing it currently prints `watch_file hook has neither run nor task set, skipping`, even though the internal watch intentionally has no command.

Keep idiomatic version-file watches in environment invalidation, but exclude them from executable watch hooks. Ruby activation still reloads the referenced file; explicit `[[watch_files]]` commands still run, and a user hook missing both `run` and `task` still warns.

The regression test changes the active Ruby executable using local linked fixtures. It covers `.ruby-version`, `.tool-versions`, and a nested custom version file with environment caching enabled and disabled, plus explicit user hooks watching the same file. Each case uses its own state directory, and cache-enabled cases assert that an encrypted environment cache was actually created.

Fixes #13982.

Validation ([Ubuntu 22.04 ARM CI](https://github.com/DahanItamar/mise/actions/runs/37373338337)): the regression reproduces the warning against official v2026.10.3; the patched version passes formatting, shell syntax/lint, workspace Clippy with all features and targets, the all-features build, all three affected E2E tests, and 45 affected unit tests. The full upstream CI suite is tracked separately in the PR checks.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: OpenAI/unavailable; version: unavailable.*
author: DahanItamar
diff:
--- e2e/core/test_ruby_gemfile_watch_files (+80/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,80 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+mise settings set idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools ruby
+mise settings add idiomatic_version_file_disable_files ruby:.ruby-version
+
+# Direct hook-env calls need a session key to enable encrypted environment caching.
+export __MISE_ENV_CACHE_KEY="dGVzdGtleXRlc3RrZXl0ZXN0a2V5dGVzdGtleXRlc3Q="
+
+# Link local fixtures so activation can demonstrate the Ruby PATH change without
+# downloading or building Ruby.
+for version in 3.3.6 3.4.7; do
+  mkdir -p "$HOME/ruby-$version/bin"
+  printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\necho "%s"\n' "$version" >"$HOME/ruby-$version/bin/ruby"
+  chmod +x "$HOME/ruby-$version/bin/ruby"
+  mise link "ruby@$version" "$HOME/ruby-$version"
+done
+
+check_gemfile_watch() (
+  local reference=$1
+  export MISE_ENV_CACHE=$2
+  unset __MISE_SESSION __MISE_DIFF
+  mkdir -p "case-$2-${reference//\//-}"
+  cd "case-$2-${reference//\//-}"
+  export MISE_STATE_DIR="$PWD/state"
+  mkdir -p versions
+  printf 'ruby file: "%s"\n' "$reference" >Gemfile
+  if [[ $reference == .tool-versions ]]; then
+    printf 'ruby 3.3.6\n' >"$reference"
+  else
+    printf '3.3.6\n' >"$reference"
+  fi
+
+  eval "$(mise hook-env -s bash)"
+  assert "ruby" "3.3.6"
+  if [[ $MISE_ENV_CACHE == 1 ]]; then
+    assert_not_empty "find \"$MISE_STATE_DIR/env-cache\" -type f"
+  fi
+
+  sleep 1
+  if [[ $reference == .tool-versions ]]; then
+    printf 'ruby 3.4.7\n' >"$reference"
+  else
+    printf '3.4.7\n' >"$reference"
+  fi
+  mise hook-env -s bash >hook-env.out 2>hook-env.err
+  assert_not_contains "cat hook-env.err" "watch_file hook has neither run nor task set"
+  assert_contains "cat hook-env.out" "__MISE_SESSION"
+  eval "$(cat hook-env.out)"
+  assert "ruby" "3.4.7"
+)
+
+# The disabled .ruby-version and custom nested file rely on the Gemfile's watch,
+# rather than independently discovered version files. Exercise env caching too.
+for cache in 0 1; do
+  for reference in .ruby-version .tool-versions versions/ruby; do
+    check_gemfile_watch "$reference" "$cache"
+  done
+done
+
+# Explicit user hooks must still run and warn when their command is missing,
+# even when they watch the same file as the internal Gemfile watch.
+printf '3.3.6\n' >.ruby-version
+printf 'ruby file: ".ruby-version"\n' >Gemfile
+cat >mise.toml <<'EOF'
+[[watch_files]]
+patterns = [".ruby-version"]
+run = "echo USER_WATCH_RAN"
+
+[[watch_files]]
+patterns = [".ruby-version"]
+EOF
+eval "$(mise hook-env -s bash)"
+sleep 1
+printf '3.4.7\n' >.ruby-version
+mise hook-env -s bash >hook-env.out 2>hook-env.err
+assert_contains "cat hook-env.err" "USER_WATCH_RAN"
+assert_contains "cat hook-env.err" "watch_file hook has neither run nor task set, skipping"
+assert "grep -c 'watch_file hook has neither run nor task set' hook-env.err" "1"
+eval "$(cat hook-env.out)"
+assert "ruby" "3.4.7"
--- src/config/mod.rs (+2/-0)
@@ -1744,6 +1744,8 @@ impl Config {

             .config_files

title: fix(python): create the auto uv venv with mise's python during install
body:
With `python.uv_venv_auto = "create|source"` and a `pipx:`/`pypi:` tool installed through uv, `mise install` created the project venv without telling uv which Python to use. uv then picked any Python on `PATH` or downloaded its own, even though mise had just installed the configured one.

For example, with `.python-version` set to `3.14.7`:

```toml
[settings]
idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools = ["python"]
python.uv_venv_auto = "create|source"

[tools]
uv = "0.12.19"
"pipx:pre-commit" = "4.6.2"
```

Before, `mise install` ran `uv venv .venv`. uv downloaded CPython 3.14.7 into `~/.local/share/uv/python`. Because uv prefers its managed Pythons, `uv tool install pre-commit` then built the tool on that download too. In CI this breaks restored caches: the tool lives in the mise data dir, its interpreter does not, and the next run fails with `couldn't exec process`.

Now `mise install` runs `uv venv .venv --python <mise python>`, and both the project venv and the tool use mise's Python.

`mise install` passes each backend its toolset before resolving it, and `mise install <tool>` leaves python out of it entirely. Either way, venv creation treated python as provided outside mise. In both cases it now resolves python and uv from the config, as the `_.python.venv` directive already does.

A new e2e test, `core/test_python_uv_venv_install`, covers `mise install` and `mise install pipx:cowsay`. Both fail without the fix (the venv used the system Python) and pass with it. The existing uv venv and pipx e2e tests pass.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: 2.1.289.*

title: feat(lock): preserve shared lockfile entries on request
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/441
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Summary

Adds `settings.lockfile_auto_prune`, which defaults to `true`.

- Full lock runs prune top-level tools absent from the active configuration by default.
- Set `lockfile_auto_prune = false` for a shared lockfile where profiles intentionally configure different tools.
- This applies to `mise lock --global` in both `merge` and `generate` modes. Configured tools still refresh, and their stale versions, option variants, and native dependency graphs are pruned. Retained unreferenced entries keep their graph sidecars.
- Filtered commands retain their existing scoped behavior.

This addresses the profile-shared lockfile pruning portion of #13976. It deliberately does not change the separate `allow_builds` report.

## Validation

- `cargo test --all-features lockfile::generate::tests --lib` (Docker)
- `e2e/run_test lockfile/test_lockfile_global_preserve_unreferenced` (Docker; default pruning, filtered locks, `lockfile_auto_prune = false`, aube references/sidecars, and empty-profile upgrades in merge and generate modes)
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` (Docker)
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `shfmt -i 2 -d -s`, schema rendering, and `git diff --check`

*AI-assisted — Tool: GitHub CLI; model: OpenAI/GPT-5; version: unavailable.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes core lockfile mutation and generate-mode skip logic; wrong defaults could leave stale entries or skip needed regeneration, but behavior stays opt-in via an explicit setting with default matching today.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds **`settings.lockfile_auto_prune`** (default **`true`**, env **`MISE_LOCKFILE_AUTO_PRUNE`**) so a full **`mise lock`** can keep lock entries for tools that are not in the **active** configuration when profiles share one committed lockfile.
> 
> With **`lockfile_auto_prune = false`**, unfiltered runs in **merge** and **generate** modes (including **`mise lock --global`**) no longer drop top-level tools from other profiles; configured tools still refresh, stale versions/option variants still prune, and **`mise lock --upgrade`** can upgrade format even when the active config resolves no tools. Generate-mode **`is_current`** skips the tool-count check when auto-prune is off, and generation carries forward unselected tools (including **aube** sidecars) while only clearing **aube** metadata for npm tools in the current run.
> 
> Default behavior is unchanged: full locks still prune unconfigured tools; filtered **`mise lock <tool>`** still preserves entries outside the filter. Documentation, JSON schema, and an e2e test cover global shared-lockfile pruning, retention, and upgrade paths.
>

title: perf(secrets): read cached fnox secrets from the fnox daemon
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/440
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

<!-- ccr-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"jdx"} -->
_Requested by **Jeff**_

> **Merge gate satisfied.** This needed fnox's daemon protocol 6 (jdx/fnox#937, merged), `fnox-client` published to crates.io, and an fnox release containing it. fnox 1.39.0 is released and `fnox-client` 1.39.0 is on crates.io, so the dependency is now `fnox-client = "1"` from crates.io.

mise secrets (experimental) resolves fnox secrets when a granted task or `mise x --secrets` is about to run.

## Before

Every `mise run` with grants spawned `fnox env --json`, even when fnox's daemon already had every value cached.

## After

When the project's fnox config enables the daemon, a daemon is running, and the terminal is interactive, a cache hit is one Unix-socket round trip and no fnox process:

```toml
# fnox.toml
root = true
[daemon]
enabled = true
```

```
$ MISE_DEBUG=1 mise run deploy
...
secrets: fnox daemon hit (1 keys)
```

A miss runs the fnox CLI in the foreground on your terminal, exactly as before; fnox resolves, stores into the daemon, and the next run hits. mise never starts the daemon and never stores into it, and CI never touches it. `mise secrets ls` adds `daemon: running (protocol 6)` or `daemon: not running` to its header (it never starts a daemon).

### mise follows fnox's setting

| fnox says | mise does |
| --- | --- |
| daemon enabled, running, all keys cached | one socket round trip, no process |
| key not cached, or needs a lease, or resolves to nothing | fnox CLI on the terminal (stores into the daemon) |
| `[daemon] enabled = false` or `FNOX_DAEMON=0` | fnox CLI, daemon never contacted |
| no daemon running | fnox CLI (fnox may start it if its config enables it; mise never does) |
| different protocol, or socket not owned by you | fnox CLI (a one-time hint, or a warning for the ownership case) |
| CI, no TTY, MCP, Windows | fnox CLI with `--non-interactive --no-daemon` (Windows has no daemon) |

A daemon from an older fnox is ignored until it exits (protocol 6 moved the socket). Docs: "Caching with the fnox daemon" in `docs/environments/secrets/fnox.md`.

## Implementation notes

- New `src/secrets/fnox/daemon.rs` using `fnox-client`; the broker asks a new `SecretSource::resolve_cached` for missing keys before taking the terminal. The resolve document now uses `fnox_client::document::EnvDocument` on both the CLI and daemon paths; describe, error and schema pre-check parsing keep their lenient types. The socket key and the CLI's global flags both come from `fnox_client::CliFlags`.

## Validation

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo +1.95 check --all-targets`: clean.
- Unit tests: `plan()` for every `EnvOutcome`, a non-interactive run never builds a client, fake Unix-socket daemon (hit, miss, disabled, protocol mismatch, silent close, rejection, no socket creates nothing),

+### Caching with the fnox daemon
+
+When fnox's daemon is running and has your values cached, mise reads them straight from the
+daemon's socket. A hit skips the resolving `fnox env --json` call: no provider calls and no
+prompt. mise still runs `fnox env --json --describe` once per run to check the grants.
