title: ci: retry unit tests once so a one-off runner stall doesn't fail unit-macos
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/261
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`unit-macos` keeps failing on a single fast unit test that happens to stall on the runner. In the 13 most recent failed `unit-macos` jobs (Sep 26–27), 11 failed with exactly one timeout out of ~4,200 tests. It was a different test each time, and each was pure computation that normally runs in ~10 ms. For example, `backend::aqua::lock_candidate_tests::test_select_github_release_asset_prefers_musl_variant` hit 1.6s on jdx/mise#13705, while the tests around it took 12 ms. Other tests that timed out include `args::tool_arg::tests::test_tool_arg_with_version`, `backend::aqua::tests::cargo_warning_uses_crate_name` and `backend::asset_matcher::tests::test_archive_preference`. Nothing in those tests can take a second. The 1–2.6s stalls come from the runner, and the strict no-retry `ci` profile turns each one into a red build.

This change gives the `ci` profile one retry, after a fixed 1s delay:

- **A one-off stall** passes on the second try. Nextest still labels it `FLAKY` in the summary.
- **A test that is actually over budget** times out on both attempts and still fails CI, so #13120's per-test ceiling still does its job.

I checked both cases with a throwaway crate using this config under `--no-fail-fast`. A test that stalls only once gave `FLAKY 2/2 ... PASS`, and a test that always sleeps 1.5s gave `TRY 2 TMT` and failed the run.

**Tradeoff:** nextest can't retry only timeouts, so this retry also covers a test whose assertion fails intermittently. Such a test is still flagged `FLAKY` in the log rather than hidden. `flaky-result = "fail"` would bring the stall failures back, so I didn't set it. `ci-shared` inherits the retry, which does nothing there because that profile never kills a test.

title: perf(shim): skip rustup checks on shim calls for tools that won't be installed
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/260
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes #13698.

Since #12771, every shim call ran rustup's install check when `rust` was in the config, even for shims of other tools. With this config, `go version` through its shim ran two `rustup` commands (`rustup show profile` and `rustup component list --installed`) before starting `go`. The reporter measured the `go` shim at about 31 ms, compared with about 12 ms without `rust` in the config.

```toml
[tools]
go = "latest"
rust = "1"
```

Now mise runs backend-specific install checks, such as rustup's check for missing components and targets, only for tools it may install on this call. Other tools get the cheap install-marker check that `hook-env` already uses. In practice:

- **Shims** skip the rustup check for all configured tools. A shim auto-installs only explicit tool arguments, and it has none.
- **`mise exec` with auto-install disabled** skips it too. This covers `MISE_EXEC_AUTO_INSTALL=0` and `MISE_AUTO_INSTALL=0`, which previously did not help.
- **`mise install`, `mise exec` with auto-install on, and task auto-install** still detect a rustup toolchain that has lost components or targets, and repair it.

## Validation

`e2e/core/test_rust_components_reconcile` now checks that a `rustc` shim and `MISE_EXEC_AUTO_INSTALL=0 mise exec -- rustc -V` do not call rustup. Without this change the new check fails. The test's `sed -i` calls now use `-i.bak` so the test also runs on macOS. The related lazy-tool, auto-install, and rust e2e tests and clippy pass.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: 2.1.274.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes when install satisfaction is evaluated on hot paths; full rustup reconciliation is intentionally skipped for tools that cannot be auto-installed on that invocation, which could delay detecting a broken rust install until an explicit install/exec with auto-install.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes slow shim/exec paths when **rust** is configured alongside other tools: mise no longer runs backend **full satisfaction** checks (e.g. spawning **rustup** for components/targets) for every configured tool on every missing-version scan.
> 
> **`list_missing_versions_checking`** selects per tool whether to use the expensive **`is_install_satisfied_or_false`** path or the cheap install-marker check. **`install_missing_versions`** applies full checks only for tools **`may_auto_install`** would actually install on that call (same filters as before, now centralized). Explicit **`mise install`**, exec with auto-install on, and similar flows still full-check rust so broken toolchains/components are detected and repaired.
>

title: feat(packslip): keep packslip tools installing after a repository is renamed
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/257
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

When a GitHub repository that publishes packslips is renamed, its new releases are signed by the workflow under the new name. Until now mise pinned the signer by name, so a config that still said the old name refused every new release. It also meant the name was all that was trusted: if a repository was deleted and someone else created one under its name with a workflow at the same path, its releases would have matched the pin.

mise now pins GitHub and GitLab packslip projects by the **repository ID** that GitHub Actions and GitLab CI signing certificates record, which a rename does not change.

## Example

`old/tool` is renamed to `new/tool` on GitHub. This config keeps working:

```toml
[tools]
"packslip:github.com/old/tool" = "latest"
```

`mise install` installs the new release, which is signed as `github.com/new/tool`, and warns once:

```
packslip:github.com/old/tool was renamed to github.com/new/tool; mise followed it by its repository ID. Change the tool to packslip:github.com/new/tool in your config
```

The signer pin and the `mise.lock` commitment follow the repository, so you do not need `mise packslip forget`. mise does not rewrite your config. Releases from before the rename, signed under the old name, still install after you switch the config to `new/tool`.

The pin is found by the repository ID in the release's certificate, whichever name changed first. If you switch the config to `new/tool` before any release signed under the new name was accepted, or another machine's `pins.toml` still has the old name, the release is still held to the old name's pin (signer, owner, provenance, attestor) instead of being treated as a first install, and the pin, its release-list sequence, and the "a list was accepted" state then move to the new name. One repository keeps one pin.

## What is refused

- **A transfer to another owner.** mise does not follow the repository to its new owner, because trusting the old owner says nothing about the new one. The error explains this. To accept the transfer, run `mise packslip forget` for the old name and name the repository as it is called now (for example `packslip:github.com/new-owner/tool`); the old pin is found by repository ID under the new name too, so renaming the config alone is not enough.
- **A different repository under a pinned name.** This is what a deleted repository whose name someone else took looks like. It is refused even though the name and workflow path match:

  ```
  packslip:github.com/o/tool: this release was signed by github.com/o/tool as GitHub repository ID 555, but mise pinned GitHub repository ID 922514152 for it. The name now belongs to a different repository, ...
  ```

  If the vendor re-created the repository itself, `mise packslip forget` plus removing the tool's `mise.lock` entries accepts it.

## Where the IDs come from

- `packslip/pins.toml` stores the repository

title: feat(aqua): add per-tool libc option to choose glibc or musl builds
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/256
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

On a glibc Linux host, mise prefers a release's glibc (`gnu`) build even when the aqua registry names the musl one (added in #12093 so tools like ruff get the glibc build). For some tools the musl build is the one to use. `aqua:domcyrus/rustnet` is one: its registry entry names `unknown-linux-musl`, and aqua installs that. mise installs `unknown-linux-gnu` instead, which dynamically links `libpcap.so.0.8`, `libelf.so.1` and `libz.so.1`, so it won't start on a host without them. The musl build is fully static. Until now the only way out was the global `libc = "musl"` setting, which also forces musl for every other tool.

Aqua tools now accept a `libc` option for a single tool:

```toml
[tools]
"aqua:domcyrus/rustnet" = { version = "latest", libc = "musl" }
```

- Accepts `glibc` (or `gnu`) and `musl`. Selection is strict for that tool, like the global setting: mise never falls back to the other libc's build.
- Overrides `libc = "glibc"` in settings. It never overrides a platform that names a libc (a musl host, or a `linux-x64-musl` lockfile platform), because a gnu build cannot run there and the lockfile entry would be wrong for musl machines. `libc = "musl"` in settings makes the host a musl platform (for example `linux-arm64-musl`), so under that setting a per-tool `glibc` has no effect.
- Recorded in the lockfile's tool options (`libc = "musl"`), so changing it resolves the tool again.
- Applies to install, `mise lock`, and the checksum, signature and provenance lookups that follow, so they all use the same libc build. A registry var named `libc` must be set as `vars.libc`.

Tools without the option behave as before.

Limitations:

- A version that is already installed keeps its build until `mise install --force`, as with other install-affecting options.
- The full version list (`mise ls-remote`) shares one cache across a tool's configurations, so it still uses the host libc. Resolving `latest` from the release GitHub marks as latest honors the option.

Fixes #13700

## Validation

- `mise lock --platform linux-arm64` for rustnet 1.6.0 locks `rustnet-v1.6.0-aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz` without the option and `…-aarch64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz` with `libc = "musl"`. With `libc = "glibc"`, `linux-x64-musl` still locks the musl build. This is covered by the new e2e test `e2e/backend/test_aqua_libc`.
- Unit tests cover option parsing and normalization, rejection of unknown values, keeping `libc` out of aqua vars, and libc precedence.
- On Linux, the e2e test also installs with `libc = "musl"` and runs the installed musl build. That part runs only in Linux CI; I ran the test on macOS, where it is skipped.

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+# The registry names rustnet's static musl build. The release also ships a gnu build,
+# which mise prefers on an unqualified Linux platform unless the tool sets `libc`.
+export MISE_LOCKFILE=1
+export MISE_AQUA_BAKED_REGISTRY=0
+
+REGISTRY_DIR="$PWD/aqua-registry-local"
+mkdir -p "$REGISTRY_DIR"
+
+cat <<'EOF_REGISTRY' >"$REGISTRY_DIR/registry.yml"
+packages:
+  - type: github_release
+    repo_owner: domcyrus
+    repo_name: rustnet
+    files:
+      - name: rustnet
+        src: "{{.AssetWithoutExt}}/rustnet"
+    asset: rustnet-{{.Version}}-{{.Arch}}-{{.OS}}.{{.Format}}
+    format: tar.gz
+    replacements:
+      amd64: x86_64
+      arm64: aarch64
+      darwin: apple-darwin
+      linux: unknown-linux-musl
+EOF_REGISTRY
+
+export MISE_AQUA_REGISTRY_URL="file://$REGISTRY_DIR"
+RELEASE_URL="https://github.com/domcyrus/rustnet/releases/download/v1.6.0"
+
+cat <<'EOF_MISE' >mise.toml
+[tools]
+"aqua:domcyrus/rustnet" = "1.6.0"
+EOF_MISE
+touch mise.lock
+mise lock --platform linux-arm64
+assert_contains "cat mise.lock" "url = \"$RELEASE_URL/rustnet-v1.6.0-aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz\""
+
+cat <<'EOF_MISE' >mise.toml
+[tools]
+"aqua:domcyrus/rustnet" = { version = "1.6.0", libc = "musl" }
+EOF_MISE
+rm -f mise.lock
+touch mise.lock
+mise lock --platform linux-arm64
+assert_contains "cat mise.lock" 'libc = "musl"'
+assert_contains "cat mise.lock" "url = \"$RELEASE_URL/rustnet-v1.6.0-aarch64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz\""
+assert_not_contains "cat mise.lock" "unknown-linux-gnu"
+
+# A platform that names its libc keeps it: a gnu build cannot run on a musl target.
+cat <<'EOF_MISE' >mise.toml
+[tools]
+"aqua:domcyrus/rustnet" = { version = "1.6.0", libc = "glibc" }
+EOF_MISE
+rm -f mise.lock
+touch mise.lock
+mise lock --platform linux-arm64,linux-x64-musl
+assert_contains "cat mise.lock" 'libc = "gnu"'
+assert_contains "cat mise.lock" "url = \"$RELEASE_URL/rustnet-v1.6.0-aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz\""
+assert_contains "cat mise.lock" "url = \"$RELEASE_URL/rustnet-v1.6.0-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz\""
+
+# Install the musl build on a Linux host and run it: it is statically linked, so it does
+# not need libpcap. Changing `libc` for an installed version needs `--force`.
+if [[ "$(uname -s)" == "Linux" ]]; then
+  cat <<'EOF_MISE' >mise.toml
+[tools]
+"aqua:domcyrus/rustnet" = { version = "1.6.0", libc = "musl" }
+EOF_MISE
+  rm -f mise.lock
+  mise install --force aqua:domcyrus/rustnet@1.6.0
+  assert_contains "mise which rustnet" "unknown-linux-musl/rustnet"
+  assert_succeed "mise x -- rustnet --version"
+fi

title: fix(task): apply run --no-cache to Git task includes and remote dependencies
body:
`mise run --no-cache` is documented as "Do not use cache on remote tasks", but remote `git::` task includes (`[task_config] includes`) ignored it: once the repository had been cloned, every run loaded the tasks from that clone, so a branch `ref` stayed at the commit cloned first.

The same gap affected [remote tasks](https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/toml-tasks.html#remote-tasks) (`file = "git::..."` or `file = "https://..."`) that run as a dependency of another task: `mise run --no-cache build` fetched `build` again, but not a remote task `build` depends on. This is fixed as well.

For example, with a Git include like the one in the docs, where `lint` is a task from the included directory:

```toml
[task_config]
includes = ["git::https://github.com/myorg/shared-tasks.git//tasks?ref=main"]
```

- Before: `mise run --no-cache lint` loads `lint` from the cached clone.
- After: it clones the include again, as `MISE_TASK_REMOTE_NO_CACHE=true mise run lint` already did. The same holds for `mise tasks run --no-cache`.

`--no-cache` is now declared with `setting = "task.remote_no_cache"`, the way `--truncate` binds its setting, so the flag enters the CLI settings layer when arguments are parsed and every reader of that setting sees it. The registry in `src/cli/mod.rs` gains that entry, and the helper that read only `truncate` from the parsed layer now builds a `SettingsPartial` holding both bound settings, which `Cli::settings_layer` extends with the global flags.

A smaller alternative is to call `Settings::override_with` in `Run::run`, as `ls-remote --prerelease` does. It is 6 lines in `run.rs`, but it sets the setting partway through `Run::run` and only works while it stays before the first task lookup: [that version](https://github.com/irisTa56/mise/compare/4f06646d92e30a92be94bb9e93e534535628b712...31df46b9eccd96ef829beb5c044a55840bc4b275). Happy to switch to it if you prefer.

Propagating the flag to includes was also one of the goals of #12206, which was auto-closed.

Tests:

- `e2e/tasks/test_task_remote_git_includes` checks that after the served branch advances, `mise run --no-cache` and `mise tasks run --no-cache` each clone a Git include again and run the updated task, and that `mise run --no-cache` fetches a remote Git `file =` dependency again while a plain `mise run` keeps using the cache.
- A unit test checks that `run --no-cache` and `tasks run --no-cache` set `task.remote_no_cache`, and that `oci build --no-cache` does not.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: 2.1.281.*

title: perf(config): load config faster by building plugin shorthands without walking every tool's backends
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/254
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Every mise command that loads config builds the table of asdf/vfox plugin shorthands from the registry. That walked every registry tool through `RegistryTool::backends()`. For each tool, `backends()` first checks for a `MISE_BACKENDS_<TOOL>` override, which means converting the tool name to SHOUTY_SNAKE_CASE, formatting the variable name, taking a lock and reading the environment. It then filters every backend the tool lists by platform, disabled backends and experimental status. Only `asdf:` and `vfox:` backends become shorthands, so almost all of that work was thrown away, and it cost about 7.5 million instructions on each config load.

`backends()` is now split into the override lookup and a `registry_backends_where(keep)` that applies `keep` before the other filters. When no `MISE_BACKENDS_*` variable is set, `get_shorthands` asks each tool for its plugin backends directly. When one is set, or one was already read in this process, it still goes through `backends()` as before. The resulting shorthands are the same.

## Measurements

Instructions retired (callgrind, Linux x86_64, release build, same source with and without the change):

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `get_shorthands` | 7.49M | 2.39M |
| `mise env -s bash`, project with one tool | 52.3M | 48.7M (−6.7%) |
| `mise env -s bash`, mise repository | 104.8M | 102.7M (−2.0%) |
| `mise run noop`, project with one tool | 93.9M | 93.2M (−0.8%) |

`get_shorthands` itself drops by 5.1M in both commands. In `mise run`, where about 20 runtime threads are active, the total moves much less than that: other functions grow by a similar amount between the two builds. Repeated runs give the same result, but I could not pin the difference to one function, so the `run` row is reported as measured.

## Validation

A new test builds the shorthands the previous way, through `backends()` for every registry tool, and checks that `get_shorthands` returns exactly the same table. The existing shorthand tests and the registry unit tests pass.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: unavailable.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Refactor of registry backend resolution and shorthand building with an equivalence test; override behavior is unchanged when MISE_BACKENDS_* is set.
> 
> **Overview**
> Config load builds asdf/vfox plugin shorthands by scanning the whole registry. That used to call **`RegistryTool::backends()`** for every tool, which always looked up **`MISE_BACKENDS_<TOOL>`** (locks, env formatting) and filtered all backends even though only **`asdf:`** / **`vfox:`** entries matter.
> 
> **`backends()`** is split into **`env_backend_override()`** and **`registry_backends_where(keep)`**, which applies **`keep` first** so callers can narrow backends before platform/disab

title: perf(config): stop re-resolving symlinks for every tool when checking global configs
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/253
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Resolving a toolset asks, for every tool, whether its config file is a global config. That check tolerates symlinked path prefixes (for example Fedora Atomic's `/home` → `/var/home`), so when the path is not literally one of the global config files it resolves the path, and then every global config file, through `canonicalize`. Nothing was cached, and `canonicalize` is expensive on macOS (a `getattrlist` per path component). `mise run` resolves the toolset many times per task, so this repeated resolution was about 17% of its CPU time on macOS.

Resolutions of existing paths are now cached until config is reloaded. A path that does not exist yet is resolved again on every call, so a config file created later in the same command is still seen correctly. `Config::reset()`, which already rediscovers the global config files, now also clears this cache. A long-running process therefore follows a global-config symlink that was retargeted since the last load, instead of classifying files by its old destination.

## Measurements

`mise run noop` in a project with one tool and a one-line task, macOS arm64, release build from the same source with and without the change. samply, 60 runs, CPU time summed over all threads:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| CPU per run (median) | 55.0 ms | 41.1 ms |
| share of CPU in `desymlink_path` | 16.9% | 0.9% |

The machine was busy with other builds, so these are CPU rather than wall-clock numbers. On Linux, `canonicalize` is much cheaper and the gain is small.

## Validation

A new unit test checks three things. The cached lookup returns what `desymlink_path` returns. A retargeted link keeps its cached destination until the cache is cleared, then follows the new one. And a missing path is not cached: once it becomes a symlink, the next call follows it. The existing `desymlink_path` and config tests pass.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: unavailable.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Performance-focused caching with explicit invalidation on config reset; behavior is intended to match prior symlink-aware global config checks, with tests for retargeting and late-created paths.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Adds a process-wide cache for symlink-resolved absolute paths** used when deciding whether a config file counts as global. `config_set_contains` now calls `desymlink_path_cached` instead of re-running `canonicalize` on every tool during toolset resolution—this was a large share of CPU on macOS for repeated `mise run` work.
> 
> The cache only stores resolutions for paths that already exist; missing paths are resolved on each call so configs created mid-command still match. **`Config::reset()` clears the cache** so retargeted global-config symlinks are picked up after reload without serving

title: perf(backend): resolve fuzzy versions like `node = "24"` without compiling regexes
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/252
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Whenever mise resolves a fuzzy version request (`latest`, a prefix like `node = "24"`, `lts`, a vendor prefix like `temurin-`), it matched the installed versions against a regex built from the request. Each of those compiled one or two regexes, and each compilation cost about 1.4 million instructions, more than the rest of resolving the tool. `mise env`, `mise x`, `mise run`, shims and a `hook-env` after `cd` all resolve every configured tool, and `mise run` resolves the toolset many times per task, so these compilations were a large share of their CPU time.

The matching rules are simple enough to write as string comparisons, and they are unchanged:

- `latest` matches a version starting with a digit, after an optional `v`.
- A request ending in `-` (a vendor prefix like `temurin-`) matches any version it prefixes.
- Otherwise the version must equal the request or continue it with a separator and at least one more character. For numeric requests like `1.2` the separators are `+`, `-` and `.`, so `1.2` matches `1.2.3` and `1.2+build` but not `1.20`. For names they are `-` and `.`, so `truffleruby` does not select `truffleruby+graalvm`.
- A numeric request also matches a `v`-prefixed version, and a `v`/`V`-prefixed request also matches the version without the prefix.

The aqua backend's filter gets the same treatment for everything except `latest`, whose pattern is fixed and is now compiled once.

## Measurements

Instructions retired (callgrind, Linux x86_64, release build, same source with and without the change), in a project with `node = "24"`, a one-line task, and a global config with a few `latest` tools:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `mise env -s bash` | 52.3M | 46.7M (−10.6%) |
| `mise run noop` | 94.0M | 77.3M (−17.8%) |

Projects that pin exact versions resolved through `mise.lock` see little change, since they skip fuzzy matching; in the mise repository `mise env` drops 1.3%.

## Validation

A new test runs the previous regex matcher and the new one over 1,204 query/version pairs, including `v`/`V` prefixes, vendor prefixes, flavour names with `+`, trailing separators, empty strings, non-ASCII text and embedded newlines, and requires them to agree. The existing fuzzy-matching tests and all 746 backend unit tests pass.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: unavailable.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Fuzzy version resolution is on the critical path for every tool; behavior is intended to be identical but the matching logic is non-trivial and heavily refactored.
> 
> **Overview**
> Replaces **per-request regex compilation** during fuzzy version resolution with **string-prefix rules**, because resolution runs this path for every configured tool on commands like `mise env`, `mise x`, and `mise run`

title: test(dotfiles): wait for the Windows history watcher to exit before cleanup
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/250
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`e2e-win/dotfiles_watch.Tests.ps1` sometimes fails on `windows-e2e` even when every `It` passes. Pester can't delete TestDrive afterwards:

```
Exception calling "Delete" with "2" argument(s): "The process cannot access the file
'\\?\C:\Users\runneradmin\AppData\Local\Temp\<guid>' because it is being used by another process."
```

In [run 36290081924](https://github.com/jdx/mise/actions/runs/36290081924) it failed this way on both attempts inside the job.

This changes only the test. The watcher itself is unchanged.

## Why it happens

The cases stop watchers with `Stop-Process -Force` (for the watcher started on its own), `taskkill /T /F` (for the watcher started under `cmd.exe`) and `schtasks /end` (for the Task Scheduler service). Then they wait for `mise bootstrap dotfiles status` to stop reporting `running`. That only shows the watch lock is free. It doesn't show that the watcher process has exited, or that anything the watcher started (such as a `git` plumbing call) has exited:

- `Stop-Process` kills only the watcher, so a `git` child it was running is left behind.
- `schtasks /end` requests termination and returns without waiting. The watcher dies only when the launcher's job object closes.

Nearly every process this file starts inherits TestDrive as its working directory. The delete fails on the TestDrive root, not on a file inside it, which is what a process whose working directory is still there looks like. Pester deletes TestDrive right after `AfterAll`, so any such process still running at that moment causes the failure.

## What changes

- A new `Stop-Tree` helper finds a process and all of its descendants, including orphans whose parent has already exited. It checks start times so a reused pid is never mistaken for one of ours. It kills them all, waits up to 30 s with `Wait-Process` for them to exit, and prints a warning naming anything still running.
- Case 3 stops both watchers with `Stop-Tree` and asserts that the tree exited before it checks the lock.
- Case 4 calls `Stop-Tree` on the service launcher right after `schtasks /end`, and asserts it. The launcher lookup now also requires the TestDrive path in its `--launch` argument. Without that, on a machine that runs a real `mise-history` service, the case could pick up and kill the real launcher.
- `AfterAll` first moves the working directory out of TestDrive, as before. Then it runs `Stop-Tree` over everything the test host started since the file began, plus any process whose command line names a TestDrive path. This covers a case that failed before its own cleanup ran.

## Verification

I don't have a Windows machine, so this PR's `windows-e2e` job is the real check. The CI log doesn't say which process held the directory. If this ever fails again, `Stop-Tree`'s warning will list what was still running.

Locally, the file parses with PowerShell 7.6. I also ran the tree wal

+        # A process by pid and start time, so a pid Windows has since handed
+        # to something else is never taken for it.
+        function script:Get-ProcessRoot([int]$Id) {
+            $process = Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "ProcessId = $Id"
+            if ($null -eq $process) { return $null }
+            return [pscustomobject]@{ Id = $Id; StartTime = $process.CreationDate }
+        }
+
+        # Pester deletes TestDrive as soon as AfterAll returns, and Windows
+        # refuses while any process still has its working directory there —
+        # which everything started from this file does, down to the `git` a
+        # watcher runs. The watch lock going free, which is all Wait-Watcher
+        # sees, says neither that the process holding it has exited nor that
+        # what it started has. So this ends `$Roots` and every descendant
+        # still running, then waits for all of them to exit. An orphan still
+        # names its dead parent's pid, so it is found too; start times keep a
+        # reused pid, and whatever that new process started, out.
+        #
+        # The tree is walked again after every kill: a watcher can start a
+        # `git` between one walk and the kill, and only a walk that finds
+        # nothing running says the tree is gone. Everything found stays
+        # known, so a process whose parent has since died is still reached.
+        function script:Stop-Tree([object[]]$Roots, [int]$TimeoutSec = 30) {
+            $known = @{}
+            foreach ($root in $Roots) { if ($null -ne $root) { $known[$root.Id] = $root } }
+            $isTree = {
+                $member = $known[[int]$_.ProcessId]
+                $null -ne $member -and [int]$_.ProcessId -ne $PID -and
+                [math]::Abs(($_.CreationDate - $member.StartTime).TotalSeconds) -lt 1
+            }
+            $deadline = (Get-Date).AddSeconds($TimeoutSec)
+            while ($true) {
+                $all = @(Get-CimInstance Win32_Process)
+                $walked = @{}
+                $pending = [System.Collections.Generic.Queue[object]]::new()
+                foreach ($member in @($known.Values)) { $pending.Enqueue($member) }
+                while ($pending.Count -gt 0) {
+                    $node = $pending.Dequeue()
+                    if ($walked.ContainsKey($node.Id)) { continue }
+                    $walked[$node.Id] = $true
+                    if (-not $known.ContainsKey($node.Id)) { $known[$node.Id] = $node }
+                    # the pid's next owner, if it has one: what started after
+                    # it is that process's, not this one's
+                    $next = $all | Where-Object {
+                        $_.ProcessId -eq $node.Id -and $_.CreationDate -gt $node.StartTime.AddSeconds(1)
+                    } | Select-Object -First 1
+                    foreach ($child in $all) {
+                        if ($child.ParentProcessId -ne $node.Id) { continue }
+                        if ($child.CreationDate -lt $node.StartTime) { continue }
+                        if ($next -and $child.CreationDate -ge $next.CreationDate) { continue }
+                        $pending.Enqueue([pscustomobject]@{
+                                Id = [int]$child.ProcessId; StartTime = $child.CreationDate })
+                    }
+                }
+                $live = @($all | Where-Object $isTree |
+                        ForEach-Object { Get-Process -Id $_.ProcessId -ErrorAction Ignore })
+                if ($live.Count -eq 0) { return $true }
+                $remaining = [int][math]::Ceiling(($deadline - (Get-Date)).TotalSeconds)
+                if ($remaining -le 0) { break }
+                $live | Stop-Process -Force -ErrorAction Ignore
+                $live | Wait-Process -Timeout $remaining -ErrorAction Ignore
+            }
+            foreach ($process in $all | Where-Object $isTree) {
+                Write-Warning "still running: $($process.ProcessId) $($process.CommandLine)"
+            }
+            return $false
+        }

+            $treeStopped = Stop-Tree @($launcherRoot)
             mise bootstrap services remove mise-history 2>&1 | Out-String | Out-Null
             schtasks /delete /tn $task /f 2>&1 | Out-Null
             $watcherStopped = Wait-Watcher $false
             $env:MISE_EXPERIMENTAL = '0'
         }
+        $treeStopped | Should -BeTrue
         $watcherStopped | Should -BeTrue

title: fix: compare v-prefixed semver versions correctly
body:
Fix outdated checks and upgrade warnings offering an older release when a complete SemVer version has a leading `v` or `V`. For example, `v2.1.280 → 2.1.278` and `v0.156.0 → 0.155.1` now return false, while `2.1.278 → V2.1.280` remains an update. The first downgrade pair reproduced the bug in a unit test before the fix; both pairs pass afterward.

The shared comparison removes one leading `v` or `V` for strict SemVer parsing, preserves prerelease ordering, and treats build metadata differences as equal. This also makes bare `17.0.7+7 → 17.0.7+8` and `1.36.4+k3s1 → 1.36.4+k3s2` equal for outdated detection. Original version strings are preserved. Other version formats continue through the existing comparison, and backends continue to select candidates.

The comparison helper lives in `crates/mise-util/src/semver.rs` and is exposed through the existing `src/semver.rs` re-export. The util crate now declares the existing `semver` dependency directly. Tests cover the helper's precedence and unsupported-format behavior, alongside the seven regression assertions in the outdated test.

Validation: 12 outdated tests, 16 mise-util semver tests, and the hidden-release test passed. Changed-file cargo-check and cargo-fmt, workspace Clippy with all features and targets and warnings denied, and the existing outdated and upgrade E2E tests passed.

title: test: keep aube cache out of the test home directory
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/248
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Running the unit tests on macOS (for example `cargo test --lib aube`) left an untracked `test/Library/Caches/aube/adaptive-state.json` in the working tree. That file was committed by accident once and removed again in jdx/mise#13685.

The test harness points `HOME` at the repo's `test/` fixture tree. The embedded aube crate saves its adaptive concurrency state to `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/aube/`. When that variable is unset, aube falls back to `~/Library/Caches/aube/` on macOS. On Linux the fallback is `~/.cache/aube/`, which `test/.gitignore` already ignores, so only macOS was affected.

`mise::testing::init` now sets `XDG_CACHE_HOME` to `test/.cache`, so the state file goes to the same ignored directory on every platform. The same setting keeps unit tests from writing into a developer's real cache when their shell sets `XDG_CACHE_HOME`. mise's own cache location doesn't change, because the tests already set `MISE_CACHE_DIR` explicitly.

The change affects only the test harness. mise's runtime behavior is unchanged.

## Validation

- On macOS, `cargo test --lib aube` created `test/Library/` before this change. After it, `git status` stays clean and the state file is written to the ignored `test/.cache/aube/`.
- `cargo test --lib --bins`: 3870 passed, 1 failed. The failing test is `system::defaults::tests::test_sandboxed_round_trip_writes_container`, and it fails the same way without this change.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes.

title: perf(config): halve settings load time by skipping globs for missing conf.d directories
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/247
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Every mise command loads settings, and that starts by finding config files in the current directory and every ancestor. For each directory, discovery globs a dozen `conf.d` patterns: `.config/mise/conf.d/*.toml`, `.mise/conf.d/*/mise.toml`, `mise/conf.d/*.toml`, their `local` and per-environment variants, and so on. Each glob compiles its pattern and walks the path, even though almost no directory has any of those `conf.d` folders. In a checkout eight levels deep that is close to a hundred globs before any config is read.

Now each glob first checks that the directory named by the pattern's literal prefix (for example `.mise/conf.d`) exists. If it does not, nothing can match and the glob is skipped. Results are unchanged: a pattern component with any glob metacharacter, escaped ones included, ends the literal prefix, so a pattern that could match is never skipped. The check is an ordinary path lookup, so case-insensitive filesystems behave as before.

## Measurements

macOS arm64, release builds from the same source, in the mise repository (`src/`, eight directories deep):

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| settings load (`MISE_TIMINGS` logger phase, median of 40) | 1.7 ms | 0.85 ms |
| `mise current` (hyperfine, 500 runs, two rounds) | 19.4 / 19.7 ms | 18.7 / 18.5 ms |
| `mise hook-env -s bash --force` | 31.2 ms | 30.1 ms |

The saving grows with directory depth. Commands and shims that load settings but little else gain proportionally more.

A unit test covers patterns under a missing directory, matches under an existing one, and a fully literal pattern (which names a file, so it is never checked as a directory). The existing config discovery tests pass.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: unavailable.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Behavior-preserving performance change in config discovery; edge cases (invalid patterns, literal file patterns) are explicitly tested.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Config file discovery** now avoids running full `glob::glob` when the pattern’s literal directory prefix (e.g. `.mise/conf.d` before the first `*`) does not exist under the search directory. In that case it returns an empty match set after still validating the pattern with `glob::Pattern::new`, so malformed globs error the same way as before.
> 
> A new `glob_parent_exists` helper walks path components until a glob metacharacter appears, then checks whether that prefix is a directory. Fully literal patterns (no wildcards) are unchanged because the prefix check does not treat a lone filename as a directory to skip.

title: perf(release): start mise about 3 ms faster on Linux by linking non-PIE
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/246
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Every mise command on Linux paid about 3 ms before `main` even ran: shims, `mise x`, and the `hook-env` that runs before every shell prompt. mise was linked as a position-independent executable (PIE). A PIE can be loaded at any address, so at every launch the dynamic loader patches every absolute pointer stored in the binary to match where it was placed. mise has a lot of them: panic locations, CLI and settings metadata, the embedded registries, and vtables. A plain release build carries about 330k relocations, and applying them copies about 2,200 pages (8 MB) of the binary into private memory on every run.

The Linux GNU release binaries (x64, arm64, armv7) are now linked non-PIE, at a fixed address. The pointers are final in the file, so the loader has almost nothing to do (20k relocations, left over from static C libraries).

## Measurements

Linux x86_64 (32 cores), plain release build, same source linked both ways, hyperfine in the mise repository:

| | PIE | non-PIE |
|---|---|---|
| `mise hook-env` with nothing changed (every prompt) | 6.6 ms | 3.5 ms |
| `mise hook-env --force` | 22.0 ms | 18.4 ms |
| page faults before `main` | 2,201 | 334 |

## Tradeoff

A non-PIE executable is always loaded at the same address, so address space layout randomization (ASLR) no longer applies to mise's own code and data. The heap, stack and shared libraries are still randomized. This is the same way Go builds on linux/amd64 by default, including tools like `gh`. mise is written in Rust, so the memory-corruption bugs ASLR mitigates are rare, but the mitigation is weaker than before.

## Scope

- This is an opt-in for release builds only. `scripts/build-tarball.sh` sets `MISE_NO_PIE=1` for `*-linux-gnu*` targets, and `build.rs` then adds `-no-pie` to the `mise` executable's link. Source builds, `cargo install`, and distro packages (which enforce PIE themselves) are unchanged.
- The flag reaches only bin targets. Dependencies stay position-independent, and no shared library is linked with it; a global `-no-pie` in `RUSTFLAGS` breaks the `slug` crate's cdylib.
- musl builds stay static-PIE. Linking them with `-no-pie` produces a binary that segfaults at startup, because musl's static-PIE start code relocates itself; they would need `-C relocation-model=static`, which a build script cannot set. macOS is unaffected; arm64 macOS requires PIE.
- `build-tarball.sh` fails the build if the result is not `ET_EXEC`, so a lost env var cannot silently ship a PIE.

## Validation

- `MISE_NO_PIE=1 cargo build --release` on Linux produces an `ET_EXEC` mise with 20k relative relocations, down from ~330k.
- The pinned cross images (`x86_64`, `aarch64`, `armv7` GNU 0.2.5, GCC 5.4) link a PIE-compiled program with `-pie ... -no-pie` into an `ET_EXEC`.
- `cross -v` shows `MISE_NO_PIE` passed into the container through the new `Cross.toml` passthrough.
- A full `cross` relea

title: perf(hook-env): cut per-prompt cost when nothing changed
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/245
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

With `mise activate`, `mise hook-env` runs before every shell prompt. Almost always nothing has changed, and mise exits early without printing anything. That early exit still did two expensive things first:

- **It loaded all settings** to read two values, `hook_env.chpwd_only` and `hook_env.cache_ttl`. Loading settings looks for every supported config filename (about 30, including `conf.d` globs) in every ancestor directory and parses the ones it finds. That was about 75% of the time spent inside mise on each prompt.
- **It started the async runtime**, which spawns 8–16 worker threads and tears them down again, about 1 ms per prompt, for a check that never uses them.

Now the full run records in `__MISE_SESSION` whether both of those settings were unset, which is the default. When they were, the per-prompt check skips loading settings entirely. When either is set, it reads them live, exactly as before. The check also runs before the runtime is created. If it finds that something changed, mise continues exactly as before.

## Measurements

`mise hook-env -s bash --reason precmd` with an unchanged session in the mise repository, plain release builds from the same source, hyperfine:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Linux x86_64 (32 cores) | 6.6 ms | 4.9 ms |
| macOS arm64 | 8.1 ms | 6.9 ms |

Time spent inside `main` on macOS dropped from about 2.9 ms to 0.66 ms. Most of what is left is process startup before `main`.

## Behavior

- With neither shortcut configured, turning one on edits a config file or a `MISE_*` variable. The per-prompt check notices either and forces a full run, which records the new state.
- With either shortcut configured, settings are read live on every prompt, as before. So turning `chpwd_only` or `cache_ttl` off takes effect on the next prompt.
- A session written by an older mise has no record, so it also reads settings live.
- When the early check falls through, `mise` no longer loads `.miserc.toml` a second time.
- A new e2e test covers `chpwd_only` on a prompt vs. a directory change, turning `chpwd_only` off without changing directories, and `cache_ttl` skipping the file checks. The existing hook-env e2e tests pass.

title: perf(npm): make cd and hook-env faster when npm tools are installed
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/244
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Every `cd` in a shell with mise activated was spending most of its time checking npm tool installs. Each time mise asks whether an npm tool version is installed, it checks the install's `node_modules/.mise` (and `.aube`) virtual store for dangling links, and it did that by calling `stat` on every package in the tree. A single `hook-env` run asks about the same install about eight times, so a project with a few npm tools, or a global tool with a large dependency tree, ran thousands of `stat` calls per directory change. With `npm:openclaw` installed globally (327 packages, checked through two paths) that came to roughly 6,000.

Now:

- Only virtual-store entries that are symlinks can dangle, so the entry type from the directory listing settles every other entry without a `stat`. Current embedded-aube installs contain plain directories, so for them the check is a single directory read.
- A prefix whose virtual store holds only real directories is remembered for the rest of the process: nothing outside the prefix can break it. Trees that link into a shared store are checked again on every call, since another process can prune that store, and broken trees are never cached, so a repair or reinstall in the same command is still seen. An uninstalled prefix already fails the earlier existence check.

The dangling-link detection added in #12570 is unchanged; its tests still pass.

## Measurements

title: fix(shim): stop native shim copies recursing through mise x
body:
On Windows, a native shim could start an unbounded process chain whenever a second copy of `mise-shim.exe` was on PATH. The reported case: running `C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Local\Programs\mise\bin\mise-shim.exe` with no arguments. The shim treats its file stem as the tool to run, so it ran `mise x -- mise-shim`; that resolved to the copy winget also puts at `WinGet\Links\mise-shim.exe`, which ran `mise x -- mise-shim` again, and so on:

```
mise.exe            "mise" x -- mise-shim
WinGet\Links\mise-shim.exe
mise.exe            "mise" x -- mise-shim
Programs\mise\bin\mise-shim.exe
mise.exe            "mise" x -- mise-shim
...
```

The same happens under any tool name when two shim copies are on PATH outside mise's own shims directory. The existing `__MISE_SHIM_PATH` guard skips only the shim that called `mise x`, and `mise x` clears it before running what it resolved, so two copies hand the call back and forth.

Now:

- Run as `mise-shim` itself (any case, with or without `.exe`), the shim exits 1 without starting `mise`:
  ```
  mise-shim: refusing to run as `mise-shim`: …\mise-shim.exe is the template mise copies to create tool shims (e.g. node.exe), not a tool
  ```
- When `mise x` dispatches for a shim on Windows, it records what it resolved in `__MISE_SHIM_TARGET`. A native shim that finds its own path there was picked instead of the tool, so it stops at the first hop:
  ```
  mise-shim: `mise x` resolved mytool to C:\…\copy-b\mytool.exe, which is another shim, not the tool. Remove that directory from PATH.
  ```
  A stray shim copy ahead of the real tool on PATH is therefore an error naming the copy to remove, rather than being skipped. A real tool's children inherit the tool's own path in `__MISE_SHIM_TARGET`, so shims they start (legitimate nesting) are unaffected, and task launchers take the `mise run` path before the check.

## Validation

On Windows 11 with this branch's debug `mise` and `mise-shim`:

- 10 levels of legitimate nesting (`t0` run through a shim, each real `tN.cmd` calling `tN+1` through its own shim copy) exit 0 and reach the end; each real tool sees `__MISE_SHIM_TARGET` set to its own path.
- Two copies ahead of the real tool on PATH: the second copy exits 1 with the message above after one hop.
- `mise-shim.exe` run by its own name with a second copy on PATH: exits 1 with the refusal.
- `e2e-win/shim_recursion.Tests.ps1`: all 7 cases pass, including `native shim stops when mise x resolves it to another copy of itself`. Its runs happen in a job object with a 60 s limit, so a regression fails instead of hanging the job.
- `crates/mise-shim/tests/recursion.rs`: `refuses_to_run_as_its_own_name` and `stops_when_mise_x_resolved_to_this_shim` fail against the previous `main.rs` and pass now; `a_target_elsewhere_still_runs_mise` is the control.

`__MISE_SHIM_TARGET` is set only in the Windows `exec_program`: `exe`-mode native shims exist only on Windows.

Step 1 of #13678, which moves install directories to names based on the backend's full identifier, for example `installs/aqua-yarnpkg-berry/4.18.1` instead of `installs/yarn/4.18.1`. This PR changes no behavior and no paths. It makes the tool's `BackendArg` the only thing that decides where a tool's files live, so the follow-up can change that decision in one place.

- **Path fields are private.** `BackendArg`'s `installs_path`, `cache_path` and `downloads_path` are now read through accessors, about 140 call sites across 28 files. The few places that override them get explicit setters, `set_installs_path` and `set_downloads_path`:

  - staged plugin downloads (packslip)

- **Locks and markers key off `BackendArg`.** Incomplete-install markers and tool-version install locks took a short name and recomputed `cache/<kebab(short)>` on their own. `incomplete_file_path`, `lock_tool_version`, `lock_tool_version_with_notice` and `clear_incomplete_marker` now take the tool's `BackendArg` and use its cache dir, which is the same directory today.

The lockfile's dependency sidecar directory (`src/lockfile/graph.rs`) still derives its name from the short. It belongs to the lockfile layout next to `mise.lock`, not to install state.

title: feat(registry): add max_version for version-dependent backends
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/240
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Registry backends could already set `min_version` to serve only newer releases (hk uses it: Packslip from 1.58.1 on, Aqua before that). There was no way to say that a backend only serves *older* releases. A frozen 1.x line published from a separate repository needs that: the backend for 2.x and later can't install 1.x, and the 1.x backend has nothing newer.

Registry entries can now set an exclusive `max_version`, alone or together with `min_version`:

```toml
version_order = "semver"
backends = [
  { full = "aqua:example/tool-next", min_version = "2.0.0" },
  { full = "aqua:example/tool-legacy", max_version = "2.0.0" },
]
```

With this entry, `tool@1` and `tool@1.9.9` install from `tool-legacy`, while `tool@2`, `tool@2.0.0` and `tool@latest` install from `tool-next`. It follows the same rules as `min_version`:

- It must be a complete semantic version and requires `version_order = "semver"`.
- A prefix entirely at or above the boundary (such as `2`) skips the backend. A prefix overlapping it keeps the preferred backend.
- `latest`, channels and unresolved aliases keep normal backend priority.
- When a backend sets both bounds, `min_version` must be lower than `max_version`. Both the bundled and the floating registry reject invalid entries.

## Lockfiles

A locked backend stays in use only for versions it serves. The same check already applies to `min_version`. For example, if `mise.lock` records `tool-legacy` for `tool = "1"` and the config changes to `tool = "2"`, mise now selects `tool-next`. Without an upper bound it would have kept asking the legacy backend for a 2.x release, and the install would fail with a 404.

No registry entry uses `max_version` yet. The first planned user is yarn, where v1 and later releases are published from different repositories.

## Tests

Unit tests cover the boundary (including prefixes, pre-releases and build metadata), combined bounds, validation errors, `backends_for_version`, and the lock check. The docs in `docs/contributing.md` and `schema/mise-registry-tool.json` are updated.

title: perf(install): scan installed versions in a single pass
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/239
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Commands that list every installed tool (`mise ls`, `mise prune`, and the shim rebuild after `mise install`) scan each tool's install directory for versions. That scan listed the subdirectories and then, for every entry, checked whether it was a runtime symlink such as `latest -> ./1.2.3`. For a plain version directory that check alone cost two filesystem calls, only to find it was not a link.

The scan now decides each entry from its directory entry's file type in one pass. Plain version directories cost nothing beyond the existing incomplete-install check. Only symlinks are read, to skip runtime symlinks and to keep links from `mise link` whose target is gone. What gets listed is unchanged.

## Performance

A/B on macOS (arm64): release builds of `main` and this branch, 194 installed tools, 1,282 entries in their install directories.

| | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `full_scan_tools` (`MISE_TIMINGS=1 mise ls`, median of 21) | 8.9 ms | 7.3 ms |
| `mise ls` end to end (`hyperfine -N`, 40 runs) | 35.5 ms ± 0.8 | 34.2 ms ± 1.4 |

A standalone benchmark that replays the scan's filesystem calls against a copy of the same directory layout took 5.1 → 3.6 ms on macOS (APFS) and 4.3 → 2.7 ms on Linux (btrfs). `hook-env` and `mise exec` don't do this full scan, so they aren't affected.

## Notes

- `file::dir_subdirs_keeping_broken_links` had no other callers, so it's removed. Its broken-link test moved to `scan_versions`, including the check that a Windows junction is reported as a symlink.

title: perf(prune): back off re-checking in-use tool purgatory receipts
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/238
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

After `mise upgrade` schedules an old version for deferred pruning, every later mise command checks whether that receipt is due. Once it was due but a tracked config still referenced the version, mise kept the receipt unchanged. The next command then loaded every tracked config and scanned all installed versions again, found the same reference, and kept it again. This repeated on every command until the reference went away. Unrecognized receipts looped the same way and printed a warning on every run.

With one such receipt (`github:jdx/tak@0.0.12`, due ~16h earlier and still referenced by a tracked config), a trivial `mise x -- true` took about 9x longer than it did without the receipt.

## What changes

- When pruning keeps a due receipt (still in use, or unrecognized), it moves the receipt's `remove_after` a day ahead, under the state-file lock. The expensive check now runs at most once a day per receipt, not on every command.
- The receipt is kept, so the version still gets pruned automatically after the last reference goes away. Tradeoff: that can now happen up to a day later than before. The `upgrade.auto_prune` docs now say this.
- The "is anything due?" pre-check reads the state file without taking the cleanup or state locks, so a pending receipt that isn't due costs one file read. Saves are atomic renames, so an unlocked read always sees a whole file. If that read fails, mise falls back to the locked path.

## Performance

Measured on macOS (arm64) with `hyperfine -N --warmup 3 'env MISE_STATE_DIR=<dir> mise x -- true'`, using copies of a real state directory with and without the receipt above:

| binary | state | time |
|---|---|---|
| mise 2026.9.12 | due, in-use receipt | 308.5 ms ± 11.7 ms |
| this branch (`--release`) | same receipt, after the first run backed it off | 33.6 ms ± 1.8 ms |
| this branch (`--release`) | no receipt | 34.4 ms ± 2.6 ms |
| mise 2026.9.12 | no receipt | 30.5 ms ± 3.0 ms |

The first command after a receipt comes due still does the full evaluation once, then skips it for a day. The ~3 ms gap between the two "no receipt" rows comes from comparing a local `--release` build with the distributed 2026.9.12 binary. It isn't caused by this change.

## Tests

- New unit tests: kept receipts move to the re-check time and become due again after it, untouched receipts keep their time, and a receipt rescheduled by a concurrent upgrade during the pass is neither removed nor backed off.
- `e2e/cli/test_upgrade_no_prune` now checks that the in-use receipt is evaluated once and then skipped by the next command. It then sets the receipt due again to show the version is pruned once nothing references it.

https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/237
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

On Windows, `[wrappers.*]` command wrappers (including the one `rust = { mr_boxington = true }` generates for `cargo`) were silently skipped under the default `windows_shim_mode = "exe"` and under `"file"`. Both `mise x -- cargo …` and running `cargo` through a shim ran the real tool instead of the wrapper.

```toml
[wrappers.cargo]
command = "mbx"
env = { MBX_CARGO_SHIM_MODE = "1" }
```

Before, on Windows with `exe` or `file` shims, `cargo build` ran cargo directly and `mbx` never saw it. Now it runs `mbx build` with `MBX_CARGO_SHIM_MODE=1`, the same as on Unix and with `hardlink`/`symlink` shims.

## Cause

`exe`- and `file`-mode shims aren't mise itself. They run `mise x -- <name>` and set `__MISE_SHIM_PATH` to their own path. Only `handle_shim` applied wrappers, and it only runs when mise is invoked *as* `<name>`. So `mise x` looked up `cargo`, found the wrapper's own shim first, skipped it as the active shim (that check exists to prevent recursion), and ran the real cargo.

## Fix

When `mise x -- <name>` comes from a native shim whose file name is `<name>`, it now looks up the wrapper for that name and runs it the way `handle_shim` does: it installs a missing wrapper command, prepends the wrapper's `args`, adds its `env`, and strips the mise dispatch directories from `PATH` so the wrapper reaches the real tool. Like `handle_shim`, it also resolves the tools of the task that ran the shim, so a wrapper that only a task's tool declares (for example `tools = { rust = { version = "1.81.0", mr_boxington = true } }`) applies too. On Windows the wrapper name matches case-insensitively, since a shim can be invoked as `Cargo`. The wrapper lookup is moved out of `which_shim` so both paths share it.

## Tests

- `e2e/cli/test_command_wrappers` simulates the native dispatch on Linux by setting `__MISE_SHIM_PATH` to the wrapper shim. That assertion fails without this change (the real cargo runs) and passes with it.
- `e2e/core/test_rust_mr_boxington` runs the same simulated dispatch from a task whose own `rust` tool enables `mr_boxington`. It also fails without the task-tools change.
- New `e2e-win/command_wrappers.Tests.ps1` checks `mise x -- <tool>` and the wrapper shim run directly, in both `exe` and `file` modes. I couldn't run it locally; Windows CI will be its first run.

Fixes #13671

title: fix(task): fail `tasks validate` when a file task's #USAGE spec does not parse
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/236
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise tasks validate` passed a file task whose `#USAGE` spec didn't parse. `mise run` then ran that task with its declared arguments silently ignored. Reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13669.

```sh
printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\n#USAGE arg "<x" {{{\necho hi\n' > mise-tasks/bad
chmod +x mise-tasks/bad
mise tasks validate --errors-only
```

**Before:** mise printed a `WARN invalid usage spec` diagnostic, then `✓ All 1 task(s) validated successfully`, and exited 0. The same happened with `flag "--v" default=true` (a KDL bool written as `true` instead of `#true`).

**After:** the task fails validation with a `usage-parse-error` **error** that includes the KDL diagnostic, and the command exits 1, including with `--errors-only`:

```
1 task(s) validated with 1 issue(s):

  ✗ 1 error(s)

Task: bad
  ✗ Failed to parse usage specification [usage-parse-error]
      invalid usage spec in task file …/mise-tasks/bad
        × Found child block instead of node name
        …
```

There were two causes:

- Loading a task still falls back to an empty spec when its `#USAGE` doesn't parse, so one broken task doesn't break every other one. Validation used that same lenient path, so it always saw a successful parse. Validation now parses the spec strictly. An unreadable task file still only warns, because validation already reports a missing file as its own issue.
- `usage-parse-error` was a warning, which `--errors-only` drops. It's now an error. This also applies to TOML tasks whose `usage` field doesn't parse.

**Compatibility:** a project whose task specs don't parse will now fail `mise tasks validate` in CI, where before it only showed warnings. `mise run`, `mise tasks ls`, and other commands behave the same as before.

## Validation

- New e2e cases in `e2e/tasks/test_task_validate` cover both malformed specs from the discussion, the non-zero exit with `--errors-only`, and `"severity": "error"` in `--json` output.
- `cargo test --bin mise task::` passes. Clippy runs clean with `-D warnings`.

> **Medium Risk**
> CI and local workflows that relied on `mise tasks validate` passing with only warnings for bad usage specs will now fail; runtime `mise run` behavior is unchanged.
> 
> **Overview**
> **`mise tasks validate` now fails** when a task’s usage spec (including `#USAGE` in file tasks) does not parse, instead of succeeding after a runtime-style warn-and-empty-spec path hid the problem.
> 
> Validation calls a new **strict** parse path (`parse_usage_spec_for_validation` / `parse_task_script_usage_checked`) so broken KDL is surfaced as an error. **Task loading is unchanged**: invalid specs still warn and fall back to an empty spec so one bad task do

title: feat(oci): package vfox plugin tools in mise oci images
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/235
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise oci build` (experimental) used to reject every tool installed by a vfox plugin, so projects using a vfox plugin or a custom backend plugin couldn't be packaged. vfox tools are now built into the image like other tools, and the plugin comes along with them. asdf plugins are still rejected.

```toml
[tools]
"vfox:version-fox/vfox-kotlin" = "2.1.0"
"my-plugin:formatter" = "1.0.0"   # custom vfox backend plugin
```

```sh
mise oci build -o ./img
```

Before: `mise oci build does not support asdf/vfox plugins in v1 ...`
After: the image gets one layer per tool plus one layer per plugin, and the image env has the variables and PATH from the plugin's env hook.

## Behavior

- **Plugin layers.** Each plugin that installed a tool goes into its own layer at `/mise/plugins/<name>/` (annotated `dev.mise.plugin`). `.git` is left out. Symlinked plugins (`mise plugins link`, git subdirectories) are copied from where the link points. A symlink inside a plugin that points outside the plugin fails the build rather than copying a host file into the image. The build logs which plugin directory it copies. With this layer, the mise inside the image can resolve the tool without cloning the plugin. That includes plugins declared by URL in a project `[plugins]` section, which the image config doesn't carry. Plugins built into the mise binary are not copied.
- **Env comes from the build host.** The plugin's `EnvKeys` / `BackendExecEnv` hook runs on the host when the image is built. Paths under the host install dir are rewritten to the in-image path; other values are baked in as-is. mise warns when a value points under the build host's home directory (e.g. `GOPATH=$HOME/go`), since that path usually doesn't exist in the container. `[oci].env` can override it.
- **Layer reuse follows the plugin.** Tool layers from plugins get a `dev.mise.tool.plugin` annotation holding the plugin layer's content digest. That digest is now part of the `mise oci push` reuse key, so updating a plugin rebuilds its tools' layers instead of reusing stale ones. Tools not installed by a plugin get no annotation, so existing images still match.
- **asdf stays rejected.** Its bash install scripts commonly write outside the install dir, and its `exec-env` scripts need bash at runtime. The error now suggests switching to a vfox plugin or another backend.

## Limitations

- `PostInstall` / `BackendInstall` hooks can run arbitrary commands. Only files they write inside the tool's install directory end up in the image.
- When `mise oci push` reuses a vfox tool's layer from the registry and the tool isn't installed locally, the env hook runs against a missing install directory. Plugins whose hook reads files there may produce incomplete env. The docs' existing `--no-cache` caveat now names this case.

## Validation

- New e2e test `e2e/oci/test_oci_vfox_plugin`. It uses a local backend plugin (no

title: feat(vfox): let plugins update installs that no longer match tool options
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/234
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

vfox plugins can now tell mise that an installed version no longer matches its tool options. mise then brings that install up to date in place, without downloading the tool again. The rust core plugin already works this way for rustup components.

## Why

Some plugins install extra pieces based on tool options. The motivating case is gcloud components (mise-plugins/vfox-gcloud#12): a project wants to check in the components it needs:

```toml
[tools]
gcloud = { version = "latest", components = ["gke-gcloud-auth-plugin"] }
```

Until now mise considered a vfox tool installed as soon as its version directory existed. Adding a component to that list did nothing for anyone who already had the version installed, until they ran `mise install --force`, which downloads the whole ~150 MB SDK again.

## What changes

Plugins get a new optional hook, `hooks/mise_install_satisfied.lua`:

```lua
function PLUGIN:MiseInstallSatisfied(ctx)
    local file = require("file")
    for _, name in ipairs(ctx.options.components or {}) do
        if not file.exists(file.join_path(ctx.path, "components", name)) then
            return {satisfied = false, reason = "missing component " .. name}
        end
    end
    return {satisfied = true}
end
```

- **When it runs:** whenever mise decides whether a tool needs installing: `mise install`, `mise install --dry-run`, and auto-install (for example `mise x`).
- **What the hook sees:** `ctx` contains `version`, `path` and the current `options`.
- **What it can return:** a table with `satisfied` (a boolean) and an optional `reason` string (shown with `MISE_DEBUG=1`), a boolean, or `nil`, which counts as satisfied.
- **What happens when it returns `false`:** mise runs the plugin's `PostInstall` again on the existing install. It doesn't run `PreInstall`, download anything, or remove the install directory. Afterwards, as after a fresh install, it runs the tool's `postinstall` script from `mise.toml` and refreshes activated shells. Then it runs the check again. If the install still doesn't match, mise fails with the plugin's `reason` and leaves the existing install in place. `mise install --force` still reinstalls from scratch.
- **When the hook itself fails:** mise warns and keeps the existing install, both on the first check and on the check after a repair, so a broken check can't cause work on every command or fail the install.
- **Plugins without the hook** behave exactly as before. mise checks whether the hook file exists without loading the plugin's Lua, so those plugins don't slow down `mise x`.
- Backend plugins (`BackendInstall`) aren't covered yet.

Plugin authors need to know two things, both covered in `docs/tool-plugin-development.md`:
- **Keep the check cheap.** It runs often, so it should inspect files rather than start the tool or make network requests.
- **Make `PostInstall` safe to rerun.**

body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/232
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

The comment in `registry/gcloud.toml` said gcloud has no Python dependency because it bundles its own Python since v352.0.0. That holds only for Google's Linux x86_64 archive. The other platforms rely on the vfox plugin to handle Python:

- **Windows x86_64:** the plugin uses Google's separate bundled-Python archive unless `bundled_python = "false"` is set.
- **macOS:** the exact Python minor version gcloud requires must already be installed (for example `brew install python@3.14`). The plugin finds it and passes it as `CLOUDSDK_PYTHON`. For v352.0.0 and later, if it is missing, the plugin warns and skips gcloud's own Python setup, which would otherwise install Python with `sudo` and hang on an invisible password prompt.

The old comment made it look as if a plain HTTP registry entry could replace the plugin. This came up in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13405.

This PR changes only the comment; install behavior is unchanged.

title: fix(plugins): warn when an installed plugin drifts from its [plugins] pin
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/231
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Pinning a plugin with `#<ref>` in `[plugins]` could leave it at a different commit than the config names, without saying so (reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13656). `[plugins]` still applies only when a plugin is installed. Editing a pin doesn't move a plugin that's already installed, but mise now reports the mismatch, and the reinstall command it suggests honors the pin.

### Drift warnings

When an installed git plugin's origin URL differs from its `[plugins]` entry, or the entry's ref isn't what's checked out, `mise install`, `mise plugins install`, and `mise doctor` (including `-J`) now warn:

```toml
[plugins]
vfox-1password = "https://github.com/mise-plugins/vfox-1password#14b79c56651d7d22cdb0909263a82686cd908bf3"
```

```
$ mise plugins install --all
mise WARN  all plugins already installed
mise WARN  plugin vfox-1password is checked out at 1f22e02, but [plugins] pins 14b79c56651d7d22cdb0909263a82686cd908bf3; run `mise plugins install --force vfox-1password` to reinstall it from [plugins]
```

The check uses only local git state (`rev-parse <ref>^{commit}` compared with `HEAD`), so it makes no network calls. A branch pin counts as matching while the local branch is checked out. New upstream commits on that branch don't count as drift; `mise plugins update` still moves it. Packslip, zip, and local-directory plugins are skipped.

### Fixes

- **`mise plugins install --force <name>` dropped the pin.** It reinstalled from the existing checkout's `origin` URL, which has no `#ref`, so the plugin landed on the default branch. For plugins that are also embedded in mise (such as `vfox-1password`) it did nothing at all. It now reinstalls from `[plugins]`.
- **A failed ref checkout left an unpinned clone.** When the clone succeeded but checking out the ref failed, the default-branch clone stayed installed, and later commands reported it as already installed. The clone is now removed.
- **Short SHAs failed with a confusing error.** `#1f22e02` failed with `fatal: couldn't find remote ref 1f22e02`, because servers can't resolve abbreviated SHAs in a fetch. It now fails with `1f22e02 is not a branch or tag on the remote, and abbreviated commit SHAs are not supported; use the full commit SHA`. Hex-only branch or tag names still resolve, because this check only runs after `ls-remote` finds no ref by that name.

- **Shorthand pins lost their ref.** A shorthand entry like `owner/repo#v1.2.0` expanded to `https://github.com/owner/repo#v1.2.0.git`, which turned the ref into `v1.2.0.git`. The ref is now kept outside the expansion: `https://github.com/owner/repo.git#v1.2.0`.

A plain `mise plugins install <name>` without `--force` behaves as before, including the prompt for untrusted plugins and the paranoid-mode refusal. Credentials in URLs are removed before they appear in a drift warning.

The `[plugins]` docs now describe the full-SHA

title: fix(task): run conf.d folder fragment tasks in the folder
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/230
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Tasks in a `conf.d` folder fragment now run in the folder, as the [conf.d folders docs](https://mise.jdx.dev/configuration.html#conf-d-folders) describe. This works in global, system, and project `conf.d` directories. Reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13652.

Given `~/.config/mise/conf.d/demo/mise.toml`:

```toml
[task_config]
includes = ["tasks"]

[tasks."demo:inline"]
run = 'echo "{{config_root}}"; pwd'
```

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `{{config_root}}` and cwd of `demo:inline` | `$HOME` | `~/.config/mise/conf.d/demo` |
| cwd and `MISE_CONFIG_ROOT` of a file task in `demo/tasks/` | `$HOME` | `~/.config/mise/conf.d/demo` |
| cwd and `MISE_CONFIG_ROOT` of a file task in a project's `.mise/conf.d/<name>/tasks/` | project root | the folder |
| `~/.config/mise/tasks/*` when a fragment sets `task_config.includes` | no longer listed | still listed |

`[env]` and `[dotfiles]` in a fragment already used the folder as their root; tasks now do too.

### Behavior

A folder fragment is now its own task root:

- Its `[task_config]` (`includes`, `dir`, `shell`, env, and cache defaults) applies only to tasks the folder defines. Previously, a fragment and the config around it shared one `task_config`, so a fragment's `includes` replaced the default task directories (`~/.config/mise/tasks`, `.mise/tasks`, …), and settings from the surrounding config reached the fragment's tasks.
- The folder counts as a config root inside its directory, so `[task_config]` that the directory's own config or a parent sets with `cascade = true` (`shell`, `dir`, cache, inputs, `excludes`) applies to the folder's tasks. Cascaded `includes` do not, since the enclosing directory already loads them.
- With no `includes`, the folder's own default task directories (for example `<folder>/mise-tasks/`) are searched, as for a project root.
- When a folder and other config define the same task name, the task from the higher-precedence file wins, the same order as `[env]`: `config.toml` beats folder fragments, which beat single-file fragments such as `conf.d/tools.toml`. A task found only in a default task directory (such as `.mise/tasks`) loses to any task a config defines, as it already did within one root. Metadata-only blocks still overlay across the boundary: a `[tasks.x] description = "…"` in `config.toml` or in a folder applies to a same-named task from the other. The overlaid task keeps its own root's `[task_config]` defaults: a block with no command that overlays a task defined elsewhere does not carry its root's `dir`, `shell`, cache, or input defaults onto it. A block with no command that stands alone, such as a group of `depends`, still gets its root's defaults.

### Implementation

Before, global task loading put every user-global file into one group rooted at `MISE_GLOBAL_CONFIG_ROOT`. Project loading grouped a fragment's `mise.toml` with its projec

title: fix(bootstrap): name the config behind an unresolvable brew formula in prune
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/229
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise bootstrap packages prune` keeps every package declared by the current config **and** every tracked config, so it won't remove something another project still needs. When one of those other configs has a stale or mistaken `brew:` entry, prune stops because it can't look up that formula. Before this change, the error didn't say where the entry came from. In #13655, the reporter's own `mise.toml` correctly listed `brew-cask:1password-cli`, but prune failed with:

```
mise ERROR failed to fetch Homebrew formula '1password-cli'
mise ERROR HTTP status client error (404 Not Found) for url (https://formulae.brew.sh/api/formula/1password-cli.json)
```

That made it look like mise was treating casks as formulae. I reproduced it by adding a second tracked config that contains `"brew:1password-cli" = "latest"`. The config from the issue alone prunes fine.

The same situation now reports:

```
0: brew:1password-cli is declared in ~/old-dotfiles/mise.toml
1: '1password-cli' is a Homebrew cask, not a formula; declare it as "brew-cask:1password-cli"
2: failed to fetch Homebrew formula '1password-cli'
3: HTTP status client error (404 Not Found) for url (https://formulae.brew.sh/api/formula/1password-cli.json)
```

- **Prune names the declaring config file(s).** It searches the current config and the tracked configs for the failing `brew:` entry. Prune still stops instead of pruning with an incomplete keep-list.
- **Cask hint.** When a homebrew/core formula lookup returns 404 and no alias matches, mise checks whether a cask with that name exists and suggests `brew-cask:<name>`. The hint also appears in `mise bootstrap packages apply`, for example when someone writes `brew:1password-cli`. The extra request only happens after a lookup has already failed.

Not covered: a stale `brew-cask:` entry in another tracked config still fails without naming its file.

### Notes for reviewers
- The formula-fetch error is now a typed `FormulaFetchFailed` context, so prune can recover the failing name with `downcast_ref`. Its message text is unchanged.
- `HTTP_FETCH.json_cached` turns the underlying reqwest error into a string, so the 404 check matches the `(404 Not Found)` text instead of downcasting. `http::error_code` already relies on the same text.

### Validation
- New mockito unit test: a 404 formula that is a cask gets the hint, a missing non-cask gets the plain error, and the failing name can be recovered in both cases. New unit test for finding the declaring config file.
- `cargo test --bin mise -- system::` passes (1148 tests). `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean.
- Checked by hand on macOS with a debug build, running `prune --dry-run` and `apply --dry-run` against the issue's config plus a tracked config with the stale entry. No e2e tests were run.

Fixes #13655
