title: fix(release): package every file mise reads at compile time
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/174
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

On 2026.9.12, installing mise from crates.io for a Windows target fails:

```
cargo install --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu --no-default-features \
  --features rustls,vfox/vendored-lua --locked mise
error: couldn't read `.../mise-2026.9.12/src/../crates/mise-shim/native-shim-marker`: No such file or directory
```

`src/shims.rs` embeds `crates/mise-shim/native-shim-marker` on Windows, but that file is not in the published crate. Cargo leaves another package's directory out of a crate even when `include` names the file, so listing it does not help. The marker moves to `src/assets/`, which is already packaged, and `mise-shim` (not published) reads it from there. `.gitattributes` keeps it marked `binary`, which stops Git from changing its line endings on Windows checkouts. `mise-shim` is now marked `publish = false`, because it reads the marker from outside its own package and was never published.

Two more files that have not been released yet would have broken `cargo install mise` on **every** platform in the next release:

- `build/registry_url.rs`, needed by `build.rs` since #13533. `include` now lists `/build/*.rs`.
- `schema/mise.json`, read by `src/cli/config/keys.rs` since #13551. It is now in `include`.

Release publishes with `cargo publish --no-verify`, so nothing caught these before users hit them.

Fixes #13572

### Validation

- I copied only the files `cargo package --list` reports into a clean tree, added the workspace crates, and ran `cargo check --locked --bin mise`. It failed on `build/registry_url.rs` before this change and passes after it.
- The marker constant also compiles under `cfg(test)`, so `cargo check --tests` on that tree reaches the Windows include on Linux. The marker read no longer fails. The only failures left are test-only fixtures, which `cargo install` does not compile.
- The 39 `shims::` unit tests pass.
- Not run: a real `x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` build (target not installed locally).

title: fix(task): retain dependencies when optional usage values are omitted
body:
Tasks now keep their declared dependencies when an optional usage flag or argument is omitted, even without an explicit default. Previously, an empty parsed usage map left dependency templates unresolved; mise silently dropped those dependencies and could exit successfully without doing their work. Structured `run` calls instead failed with `Variable usage is not defined`.

For example:

```toml
[tasks.compile]
run = "echo compiling"

[tasks.build]
usage = 'flag "--release"'
depends = ['compile {% if usage.release %}--release{% endif %}']
```

`mise run build` now runs `compile`, and `mise run build --release` still forwards the flag. Adding `default=#false` is no longer necessary to make the dependency run. Optional string arguments similarly receive an empty string. This follows #9062, which covered no-argument invocations with explicitly declared defaults.

Dependency and structured-call templates now share the typed fallback context already used by inline task scripts, with the selected command path overriding sibling fallbacks and parsed values taking precedence. Same-named optional values use the selected subcommand’s defaults or typed empty values, including aliases and nested commands. Existing cross-command template keys remain available. This also resolves omitted values in usage-dependent source/output paths. Required-argument validation and intentional omission of dependency names that render empty are preserved.

Validation:
- The new dependency regression fails on unmodified HEAD and passes with this fix.
- All 40 task-script parser unit tests and eight focused e2e suites pass, covering omitted values, dependencies, source/output freshness, usage maps, subcommands, validation, double-dash handling, and environment isolation.
- Scoped hk fix/check and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` pass.

The freshness test's line-count assertions also normalize BSD/GNU `wc` whitespace so they work on macOS and Linux.

title: fix(daemons): fail early when a postgres daemon would start as root
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/173
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

PostgreSQL's `initdb` and `postgres` refuse to run as root. Before this change, starting a PostgreSQL daemon or daemon provider as root (common in containers and CI) first installed PostgreSQL. Only then did it fail, with initdb's error buried in the daemon log:

```
[mise-provider-pg/server] initdb: error: cannot be run as root
  0: daemon initialization failed running initdb; existing data was preserved
```

Now mise refuses before it installs or starts anything, and says what to do:

```
$ mise daemons providers start pg   # as root
Error:
   0: daemon provider pg cannot run as root: the postgres preset's server refuses root privileges. Run mise as a regular user, for example by adding one and switching to it with `USER` in a Dockerfile or with `su - <user>`
```

This applies to `mise daemons start`, `mise daemons providers start|restart`, and tasks that require a PostgreSQL daemon. `mise daemons register` and `ls` still work as root. Other presets (Redis, CockroachDB, NATS, SpiceDB) are unaffected.

### Why not run PostgreSQL as an unprivileged user?

That would mean dropping to an account such as `nobody`. That account usually cannot reach root's tools: mise installs PostgreSQL under `/root/.local/share/mise`, and `/root` is mode 0700. So root users would swap one confusing failure for another, and mise would also have to chown data directories as root. A clear error is the honest behavior.

### Tests
- `test_daemons_providers_slow` drops the root skip that #13565 added. Instead of skipping, it is marked `# e2e:non-root`, the existing harness marker that `test_daemons_databases` already uses. In the CI Docker container it runs as `nobody`, so CI exercises the real PostgreSQL lifecycle again. `test_daemons_resources_slow` and `test_daemons_resources_proxy_slow` (from #13536) start real PostgreSQL too and had the same latent failure, so they get the marker as well.
- `test_daemons_providers` (fast, runs as root in CI) now asserts the new error when it runs as root, and that nothing was installed or created.

### Validation
- `TEST_ALL=1 mise run test:e2e cli/test_daemons_providers_slow` passes as a regular user.
- `test_daemons_providers` passes as root (via `sudo`). As root, `test_daemons_providers_slow` stops in 5s with the new error instead of failing after the install. A project `[daemons] postgres = "18"` start as root fails the same way, before anything is installed.
- Daemon unit tests, `mise run lint`, and clippy with `-D warnings` pass.
- I couldn't run the Docker `--user nobody` path locally because the local Docker daemon can't see this worktree. CI is the first run of that path for the providers test.
- `cli/test_daemons_pitchfork` fails locally on this branch and on unmodified origin/main alike (`pitchfork project list` count). It's unrelated.

title: fix(install): extract .tar.zst archives compressed with a long window
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/172
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Since 2026.8.9, mise prefers a release's `.tar.zst` asset over `.tar.xz`. For LLVM, that broke installs:

```
$ mise use -g github:llvm/llvm-project
Error: Failed to install github:llvm/llvm-project@latest: failed to extract tar: …/LLVM-23.1.2-Linux-X64.tar.zst to …: Frame requires too much memory for decoding
```

LLVM compresses its `.tar.zst` releases with a 1 GiB window (`zstd --long=30`). libzstd refuses any window above 128 MiB unless the decoder raises its limit, and the `zstd` CLI (and `tar --zstd`) fails on these files the same way unless you pass `--long`. mise now raises that limit to 1 GiB when it extracts `.tar.zst` and `.zst` archives, so these archives install again. It goes no higher, which bounds the memory a crafted archive can make the decoder allocate. The decoder only allocates the larger buffer when a frame declares a large window, so ordinary archives use the same memory as before.

Reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13563.

## Validation

- A new unit test extracts a `.tar.zst` whose frame declares a 1 GiB window. It fails with "Frame requires too much memory for decoding" without the fix.
- With a local debug build, `mise install github:llvm/llvm-project@llvmorg-23.1.2` selected `LLVM-23.1.2-Linux-X64.tar.zst`, installed it, and the extracted `clang --version` ran.

The OCI layer decoders in `src/oci/` still use the default limit. This PR does not change them.

> **Medium Risk**
> Raises zstd decoder memory limits for install/archive extraction paths; bounded to 1 GiB but large-window frames can allocate more than before. OCI zstd decoders are unchanged.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes installs that fail on **LLVM-style** `.tar.zst` releases with *"Frame requires too much memory for decoding"* after mise started preferring `.tar.zst` over `.tar.xz`.

That path is used for standalone `.zst` decompression and for **`.tar.zst`** when opening tar archives. The cap stays at 1 GiB so memory use from malicious frames is bounded; normal archives are unchanged.

title: test(e2e): skip the postgres daemon provider test as root
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/171
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`cli/test_daemons_providers_slow` (added in #13534) starts a real Postgres server through the `postgres` daemon provider preset. The e2e job runs as root, and `initdb` always refuses to run as root, so the test fails every time slow tests run:

```
[mise-provider-pg/server] initdb: error: cannot be run as root
  0: daemon initialization failed running initdb; existing data was preserved
```

Normal PR runs skip `_slow` tests, so #13534 merged green. The first run to hit it was the release PR, #13425, and this failure blocks that release.

The test now exits early when it runs as root, as `test_bun_cross_device_install` and other tests already do for unavailable preconditions. Everything below the guard is unchanged, so the test still runs for non-root contributors.

The downside: CI will no longer exercise this test at all. Running the provider as root (for example, starting Postgres as an unprivileged user) is a real product gap. Root users hit the same `initdb` error, so that fix should go in a separate PR.

### Validation
- `hk check` (shellcheck + shfmt) passes on the file.
- The root branch, checked with a fake `id` that reports uid 0, prints `skipping: postgres initdb cannot run as root` and exits 0. I didn't rerun the full non-root test locally because it installs Postgres.

title: test(task): check OpenTelemetry export end to end
body: https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/170 Adds `e2e/tasks/test_task_otel_export`. It runs tasks against a ~20-line Python OTLP/HTTP receiver and checks what actually reaches the wire: - nothing is sent with only an endpoint set; `otel.enabled` is required - root, setup and task spans are parented correctly, and a nested `mise run` joins the outer trace under the task that invoked it (one trace ID) - on a fail-fast run, the failing task is `Error` with `process.exit.code=3`, and the sibling it stopped is `Unset` with `mise.task.cancelled=true` - logs are off by default. With `otel.logs`, each line is exported once, against the task that printed it, including nested-run output The receiver speaks OTLP/JSON, so this also enables the exporter's `http-json` feature. Users can choose it with `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=http/json` (documented). With that feature on, the exporter's own fallback would switch to JSON, so mise sets the protocol explicitly and protobuf stays the default. The test checks the default request's content type first. The test runs in the normal e2e suite in ~4s with no Docker. It replaces the OATs + Grafana LGTM compose job from #9069, which needed its own Docker CI job and a new global dev tool. --- Part of the OpenTelemetry stack rebuilt from jdx/mise#9069 by @MatthiasGrandl (with @zeitlinger), who are co-authors on these commits. *AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: unavailable.* 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) Stack created with GitHub Stacks CLI • Give Feedback 💬 ## Summary by CodeRabbit - **New Features** - OpenTelemetry data can be exported using OTLP HTTP/JSON or HTTP/protobuf. HTTP/protobuf remains the default; set `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL` to `http/json` to use JSON. Signal-specific protocol settings take precedence over the general setting. - **Documentation** - OpenTelemetry setup guidance now lists `http/protobuf` as the default, `http/json` as an alternative, and notes that gRPC is unsupported. --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Changes OTLP exporter configuration and dependency features for telemetry export; behavior is gated by opt-in settings but default encoding choice affects all enabled exports. > > **Overview** > Adds an **e2e test** (`e2e/tasks/test_task_otel_export`) that runs `mise run` against a small local OTLP/HTTP receiver and asserts trace shape (gating on `MISE_OTEL_ENABLED`, span parenting, nested runs in one trace, fail-fast error vs cancelled siblings) and optional log export with `MISE_OTEL_LOGS`. > > To exercise JSON on the wire without Docker, the PR turns on the OTLP exp

--- e2e/tasks/test_task_otel_export (+154/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,154 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+# Exports traces and logs from `mise run` to a local OTLP/HTTP JSON receiver
+# and checks what arrives on the wire: span parenting, status, nested-run
+# propagation, and log correlation.
+
+cat <<'EOF_SERVER' >collector.py
+import http.server
+import pathlib
+
+
+class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
+    def do_POST(self):
+        body = self.rfile.read(int(self.headers["Content-Length"]))
+        signal = self.path.rsplit("/", 1)[-1]
+        with open("content-types.log", "a") as f:
+            f.write(f"{signal} {self.headers['Content-Type']}\n")
+        with open(f"{signal}.jsonl", "ab") as f:
+            f.write(body.replace(b"\n", b"") + b"\n")
+        self.send_response(200)
+        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
+        self.send_header("Content-Length", "2")
+        self.end_headers()
+        self.wfile.write(b"{}")
+
+    def log_message(self, *_args):
+        pass
+
+
+server = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
+pathlib.Path("collector.port").write_text(str(server.server_port), encoding="utf-8")
+server.serve_forever()
+EOF_SERVER
+
+# Prints one line per span: "<name> parent=<parent name> status=<code> [attrs]",
+# and one per log record: "log <task span name>: <body>".
+cat <<'EOF_SUMMARY' >summary.py
+import json
+import pathlib
+import sys
+
+signal = sys.argv[1]
+path = pathlib.Path(f"{signal}.jsonl")
+if not path.exists():
+    sys.exit(0)
+batches = [json.loads(line) for line in path.read_text().splitlines()]
+spans = [
+    span
+    for batch in (json.loads(l) for l in pathlib.Path("traces.jsonl").read_text().splitlines())
+    for rs in batch.get("resourceSpans", [])
+    for ss in rs.get("scopeSpans", [])
+    for span in ss.get("spans", [])
+] if pathlib.Path("traces.jsonl").exists() else []
+names = {s["spanId"]: s["name"] for s in spans}
+
+
+def attrs(item, keys):
+    out = []
+    for kv in item.get("attributes", []):
+        if kv["key"] in keys:
+            value = next(iter(kv["value"].values()))
+            if not isinstance(value, str):
+                value = json.dumps(value)
+            out.append(f"{kv['key']}={value}")
+    return " ".join(out)
+
+
+if signal == "traces":
+    for s in spans:
+        parent = names.get(s.get("parentSpanId", ""), "-")
+        status = s.get("status", {}).get("code", 0)
+        extra = attrs(s, {"process.exit.code", "mise.task.cancelled", "mise.span_type"})
+        print(f"{s['name']} parent={parent} status={status} {extra}".rstrip())
+    print("traces=" + str(len({s["traceId"] for s in spans})))
+else:
+    for batch in batches:
+        for rl in batch.get("resourceLogs", []):
+            for sl in rl.get("scopeLogs", []):
+                for rec in sl.get("logRecords", []):
+                    body = rec["body"]["stringValue"]
+                    print(f"log {names.get(rec.get('spanId', ''), '?')}: {body}")
+EOF_SUMMARY
+
+python3 collector.py &
+collector_pid=$!
+trap 'kill "$collector_pid" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
+wait_for_file collector.port "OTLP collector port" 30 "$collector_pid"
+
+port="$(cat collector.port)"
+export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT="http://127.0.0.1:$port"
+
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[tasks.a]
+run = "echo from-a"
+[tasks.b]
+run = "echo from-b; mise run inner"
+[tasks.inner]
+run = "echo from-inner"
+[tasks.all]
+depends = ["a", "b"]
+[tasks.fail]
+run = "sleep 1; exit 3"
+[tasks.slow]
+run = "sleep 30"
+[tasks.fail-fast]
+depends = ["fail", "slow"]
+EOF
+
+# An endpoint alone is not enough: nothing is exported until otel.enabled.

title: feat(task): export task output as OpenTelemetry logs
body: https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/169 Adds `otel.logs`: task stdout/stderr lines are exported as OTLP log records linked to the task span that produced them. In the backend you can go from a slow or failing span straight to its output. ```toml [settings] otel.enabled = true otel.logs = true # separate opt-in; also needs a logs endpoint ``` - **Separate opt-in:** shipping task output crosses a different trust boundary than span metadata. Anything a task echoes, including secrets from env vars, leaves the machine. `otel.logs` defaults to `false` and is gated on `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` / `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_LOGS_ENDPOINT` independently of traces. - **Redaction applies** before lines are forwarded, and to the task args attached to each record. `--raw` bypasses capture, so nothing is exported for that task. - **Severity:** stdout is `INFO` and stderr is `WARN`. Failure is carried by the span status, not by log severity, since plenty of tools write progress to stderr. - **Nested runs report their own output once.** When a task calls `mise run`, the inner run's output also flows through the outer task's pipe. Each nested run registers a claim while it is alive, and the outer run stops exporting until the last claim is released, so each line is exported once, against the inner task that actually printed it. This works for concurrent nested runs too (`mise run a & mise run b & wait`). Output the outer task writes before and after is still attributed to the outer task. - **Works with the task cache:** command output observers now chain instead of replacing each other, so a task that writes to the artifact cache still exports its logs. - **Trade-off (documented):** in `interleave` / `quiet` output modes mise normally hands the task the terminal directly. With `otel.logs` on, it keeps a pipe so it can read the lines, so those tasks no longer see a TTY (colors, progress bars and prompts may change). Use `--raw` for a task that needs a real TTY. **Validation:** unit tests for the forwarder and the claim handoff (including a claim left behind by a SIGKILLed nested run). Checked by hand against `otelcol-contrib`: `mise run all` with a nested `mise run inner` exported each line once, with the right span ID. --- Part of the OpenTelemetry stack rebuilt from jdx/mise#9069 by @MatthiasGrandl (with @zeitlinger), who are co-authors on these commits. *AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: unavailable.* 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) Stack created with GitHub Stacks CLI • Give Feedback 💬 ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Added experimental OpenTelemetry export for task stdout and stderr, linked to task spans. title: feat(task): cover setup in the OpenTelemetry root span
body: https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/168 The root span of a `mise run` trace used to start only after tools were installed and deps providers had run. On a fresh CI runner, a two-minute tool install showed up as a trace whose first task started late for no visible reason. Telemetry now starts as soon as the requested tasks are known. Each setup phase gets its own child span of the root, tagged `mise.span_type = "setup"`. That includes `fetch tasks` when any requested task is remote: ``` mise run withtool 40.9s ├── resolve tasks 0ms ├── install tools 38.6s ← github:BurntSushi/ripgrep ├── deps 0ms ├── start daemons 0ms └── withtool 33ms ``` (Real timings from a local collector with an empty `MISE_DATA_DIR`.) If a phase fails (for example a tool that can't be installed), its span and the root span are marked `Error` and the trace is still flushed. Phases with nothing to do still emit a near-zero span. That keeps the trace shape predictable, at the cost of four small spans per run. **Validation:** unit tests cover phase parenting, error status, and the no-telemetry passthrough. Checked by hand against `otelcol-contrib`. --- Part of the OpenTelemetry stack rebuilt from jdx/mise#9069 by @MatthiasGrandl (with @zeitlinger), who are co-authors on these commits. *AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: unavailable.* 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) Stack created with GitHub Stacks CLI • Give Feedback 💬 ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * OpenTelemetry traces now cover the full `mise run` lifecycle, including remote task fetching, task resolution, tool installation, dependency setup, and daemon startup. * The root span is named for the requested tasks and includes setup work, scheduling, queueing, and tool and environment resolution. Failed setup phases and runs are marked as errors. * **Documentation** * Updated OpenTelemetry guidance to describe the expanded trace coverage and how setup work, scheduling, and queueing are represented. --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Changes when traces start and what `mise run` exports to collectors; behavior is gated on existing OTEL enablement but alters trace shape and timing semantics for anyone relying on the old root span boundaries. > > **Overview** > **OpenTelemetry traces for `mise run` now cover the full invocation**, including setup that used to sit outside the root span (so long tool installs on CI no longer look like dead time before the first task). > > Telemetry

title: feat(task): export OpenTelemetry traces for task runs
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/167
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Adds experimental OpenTelemetry trace export for `mise run`. Each run becomes one trace in Jaeger, Tempo, SigNoz, Honeycomb or any other OTLP backend, so you can see which task is slow, which one failed, and which monorepo package it belongs to.

```toml
# mise.toml
[settings]
otel.enabled = true
```

```bash
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4318
mise run build ::: test ::: lint
```

```
mise run build test lint          ← root span
├── packages/frontend             ← monorepo group span (per config_root)
│   └── build                     ← task span
└── test                          ← task span
```

- **Opt-in twice:** nothing is exported unless `otel.enabled = true` (`MISE_OTEL_ENABLED=1`) *and* an `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` / `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT` is set. CI environments that set the endpoint for other tools stay silent.
- **Standard configuration:** headers, service name and resource attributes come from the usual `OTEL_*` env vars. OTLP over HTTP (protobuf). `service.name` defaults to `mise` unless `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` or `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES` sets it.
- **Stays out of the way:** each export times out after 3s unless `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT` says otherwise, so an unreachable collector adds at most that to the end of a run. Offline mode turns export off, and an empty endpoint counts as unset.
- **Task spans** carry `mise.task.*` attributes plus the CLI semantic conventions `process.command_args` and `process.exit.code`.
- **Failures:** when a failing task stops its siblings, only the one that failed has status `Error`. Siblings mise stopped with a signal are marked `mise.task.cancelled = true`, so searching for errored spans finds the cause. A sibling that fails on its own is still an `Error`. A run cut off by `--timeout` still exports its root span as an error.
- **W3C trace context both ways:** a run joins an upstream trace from `TRACEPARENT`/`TRACESTATE` (CI, an outer `mise run`), and each task receives a `TRACEPARENT` for its own span. Nested `mise run` and any OTel-instrumented tool a task calls then nest under that task.

Task args are exported in span names and attributes after mise's configured redactions are applied. An unredacted secret passed as an argument would still leave the machine, and the new docs page (`docs/tasks/opentelemetry.md`) says so. Task output is **not** exported here (see the logs PR above).

**Dependencies:** `opentelemetry` / `opentelemetry_sdk` / `opentelemetry-otlp` 0.33 with default features off. The OTLP exporter uses the reqwest 0.13 mise already has, and nothing new beyond `prost` appears (no tonic, no second reqwest).

**Validation:** unit tests with an in-memory exporter cover the hierarchy, group spans, error vs. cancelled status, drop/timeout behavior and propagation round-trips. Checked by hand against `otelcol-contrib` 0.140, including a nested `mise

title: fix(task): only report the task that failed as an error
body: https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/166 When several tasks run in parallel and fail together (the first failure SIGTERMs the rest), mise is meant to print the error chain only for the task that actually caused the stop. It decided that by checking whether the run was already stopping and recording the failure afterwards, so two tasks failing at the same moment could both pass the check and both print themselves as the cause. Recording a failure now also returns whether an earlier one was already there, under a single lock, and only the first failure prints its error chain. Exit codes and the final failure summary are unchanged. The OpenTelemetry layer above reuses this to mark only the originating task as an error and its siblings as cancelled. **Validation:** a unit test covers the first-vs-later return value. Existing fail-fast e2e tests pass. --- Part of the OpenTelemetry stack rebuilt from jdx/mise#9069 by @MatthiasGrandl (with @zeitlinger), who are co-authors on these commits. *AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: unavailable.* 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) Stack created with GitHub Stacks CLI • Give Feedback 💬 ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * When multiple tasks fail during a run, the first failure is now consistently reported as the cause. Later failures no longer replace the initial error report.

title: chore(backend)!: remove the experimental pkgx backend
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/165
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Removes the experimental `pkgx:` backend, which installed packages from the [pkgx pantry](https://github.com/pkgxdev/pantry) without the pkgx CLI. pkgx looks largely unmaintained, so mise no longer carries a backend for it. The backend was always gated behind `MISE_EXPERIMENTAL`, and no registry entries used it.

**If you used it:** a tool such as `"pkgx:stedolan.github.io/jq" = "1.7.1"` in `mise.toml` no longer resolves. Mise now treats `pkgx:` like any other unknown prefix, so the error is the generic `plugin not installed`, not a pkgx-specific message. Switch to the tool's registry shorthand (`jq`) or another backend such as `aqua:` or `github:`. Tools already installed through pkgx stay on disk until you uninstall them.

**Lockfiles:** existing `mise.lock` files that contain pkgx data still load. The `[pkgx-packages…]` section and the `pkgx_deps` / `pkgx_provides` / `pkgx_runtime_env` platform keys are ignored and dropped the next time mise writes the lockfile.

The `pkgx` registry entry for installing the pkgx CLI itself (via `aqua:pkgxdev/pkgx`) is unchanged.

This also closes #13147, which fixed OpenSSL-style `1.1.1w` versions in pkgx dependency resolution.

## Validation

- `cargo build` and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` are clean.
- `cargo test --bin mise lockfile` (205 passed), `backend::` (729 passed) and `cli::lock` (27 passed).
- New test `test_legacy_pkgx_lockfile_sections_are_ignored` loads a lockfile with pkgx sections and checks that saving drops them.
- `mise run lint` is clean. Deletes `e2e/backend/test_pkgx`, the pkgx docs page, and `licenses/pkgx-LICENSE.txt`, which came in with the backend.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: unavailable.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

> 
> **Overview**
> **Removes the experimental `pkgx:` backend** that installed pantry packages without the pkgx CLI. `pkgx:` tool entries no longer resolve (they behave like an unknown backend prefix), and pantry install, lock resolution, and wrapper generation are gone from the codebase.
> 
> **Lockfiles:** existing `mise.lock` files still load tool entries that used pkgx, but `[pkgx-packages]` and platform keys such as `pkgx_deps` are no longer read or written; the next save strips that metadata while keeping other fields like checksums where present.

title: test(e2e): serve npm metadata from a local fake registry
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/164
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Internal test change: no user-facing behavior changes. The goal is fewer calls to npm (and a few other registries) on every PR's e2e run, and fewer flakes from them.

## Fake npm registry

`e2e/fixtures/npm/server.py` is a small metadata-only npm registry, following the same pattern as the existing `e2e/fixtures/pypi/server.py`. It serves packuments for `prettier`, `aws-cdk`, `request` and `left-pad`. Those packuments carry the publish dates, `latest` dist-tags and deprecations the tests depend on: prettier's cutoff dates, aws-cdk's accidentally published and deprecated 3.0.0, and request with every release deprecated.

A test opts in with:

```bash
source "$ROOT/e2e/fixtures/npm/start.sh"
# ... mise latest / ls-remote npm:... ...
assert_fake_npm_registry_used prettier aws-cdk request
```

`start.sh` sets `NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY`, which both mise's HTTP client and `npm view` (`npm.shell_out`) respect. `assert_fake_npm_registry_used` checks the server's request log, so a lookup that bypasses the fixture fails the test instead of quietly going to the network. I checked this by removing the export: `test_ls_remote` then failed against the real left-pad metadata.

Tests moved to it:
- `backend/test_npm_install_before`: all ~15 `mise latest` lookups, which included repeated full fetches of aws-cdk's very large packument with fresh caches. It still installs node for the `npm view` cases.
- `cli/test_ls_remote`: the npm `created_at` check now asserts an exact value. Previously it sat inside `if …; then` and was skipped whenever the network failed.
- `backend/test_backend_missing_deps`: the two `left-pad` lookups.

## Other reductions

- **ajv schema tests merged:** `test_schema_{daemons,doctor,bootstrap_file_phases,bootstrap_file_permissions_only,bootstrap_file_remove_empty}` and the ajv half of `test_schema_bootstrap_services` each ran `mise use -g node@24 npm:ajv-cli@5.0.0` in a fresh HOME. They are now one `config/test_schema_ajv` file with the same assertions, so node and ajv-cli install once instead of six times.
- **`test_ls_remote` cargo/pipx probes removed:** the `cargo:eza` and `pipx:black` `created_at` checks were skipped whenever the network request failed, so they cost network calls without reliable coverage. Unit tests in `cargo.rs` and `pipx.rs` already cover `created_at` parsing for both backends.

## Notes for reviewers

- npm labels `npm view` output with `_id`, so the fixture includes `_id` at both the package and version level. Without it, the shell-out deprecation lookup saw no deprecated versions and resolved aws-cdk to 3.0.0.
- The fixture serves metadata only, not tarballs. Tests that install npm packages still use the real registry; adding tarballs is a possible follow-up.

## Validation

`mise run test:e2e backend/test_npm_install_before config/test_schema_ajv config/test_schema_bootstrap_services cli/test_ls_remote backend/tes

title: test(e2e): share one HTTP test server via start_http_server
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/163
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Internal test-suite change; no effect on mise itself.

About 40 e2e tests each started their own Python HTTP server. Every copy repeated the same code: a heredoc server on port 0, a port file, `wait_for_file`, and a `trap kill`. Two helper scripts, `http_test_server.py` and `tool_stub_test_server.py`, also did the same job with different routes.

This PR replaces all of that with one helper in `e2e/assert.sh`:

```bash
# Serve fixture files
start_http_server --dir "$FIXTURES"
url="http://127.0.0.1:$HTTP_PORT/tool.tar.gz"

# Or supply custom behavior
start_http_server --handler - <<'PY'
class Handler(TestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        ...
PY
```

- `start_http_server` starts `helpers/scripts/http_test_server.py`, waits until it is listening, and sets `HTTP_PORT` and `HTTP_SERVER_PID`. The server exits by itself when the test shell does, so tests need no cleanup. If it fails to start, the test prints the server's log instead of timing out on a missing port file.
- Without `--handler`, the server answers the fixed routes the old helpers provided (`/test/mytask`, `/status/200`, `/tool`, …) and serves any other path from `--dir`. `--headers-log` keeps the request-header logging that `test_netrc` and `test_github_versions_host_no_api` rely on.
- `--handler` loads a `Handler` class from a file or a heredoc, with `TestHandler` available to extend. A handler whose request ordering matters sets `SERVER_CLASS = HTTPServer` to stay single-threaded (aqua resume, bun checksums, the GitHub OAuth mock).

**Converted:** the 9 callers of the old helpers, 17 inline static-file servers, 9 inline custom servers, and `e2e/fixtures/mock-github-oauth.py`, which is now a handler file. `tool_stub_test_server.py` is merged into `http_test_server.py` and deleted.

**Not converted:**
- `git_http_backend_server.py`, because it speaks git's smart-HTTP protocol.
- `test_install_resolve_progress` and two macOS brew-cask tests, which run the whole scenario in Python with the server built in.
- The daemon tests, where the server is the daemon under test.

**Behavior change for reviewers:** `test_lockfile_aqua_http_v_prefix` only passed because the old helper answered `HEAD` with 200 for every path, so the check for a v-prefixed download always succeeded. Against a server that returns 404 for missing files it failed. It now serves a real `tool-v1.2.3` file and no unprefixed one, so the test actually checks that mise finds the v-prefixed download.

## Validation

- All 38 converted tests pass locally on Linux.
- `mise run lint` passes.
- No server processes were left running after the test run.
- Not run on macOS or in the Docker CI mode.

@@ -113,6 +113,58 @@ wait_for_file() {
   fail "$description did not appear within ${attempts}s: $file"
 }
 
+# Start the e2e HTTP server (helpers/scripts/http_test_server.py) in the
+# background and wait until it listens. Sets HTTP_PORT and HTTP_SERVER_PID.
+#
+#   start_http_server [--dir DIR] [--bind ADDR] [--headers-log DIR] \
+#     [--handler FILE|- [ARGS...]]
+#
+# Without --handler it serves the script's fixed routes, then files under DIR
+# (default: the current directory). --handler - reads the handler module from
+# stdin; see the script's docstring for what the module must define.
+#
+# The server exits with the test shell, so there is nothing to clean up. Call
+# this from the test shell itself: a server started in a subshell or command
+# substitution exits with that subshell.
+start_http_server() {
+  local state_dir
+  state_dir="$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/http-server.XXXXXX")"
+  local args=(--port-file "$state_dir/port")
+  while (($# > 0)); do
+    if [[ $1 == --handler ]]; then
+      if [[ ${2:-} == - ]]; then
+        cat >"$state_dir/handler.py"
+        args+=(--handler "$state_dir/handler.py")
+      else
+        args+=(--handler "${2:?--handler needs a file}")
+      fi
+      shift 2
+      args+=("$@")
+      break
+    fi
+    args+=("$1")
+    shift
+  done
+
+  python3 "$TEST_ROOT/helpers/scripts/http_test_server.py" "${args[@]}" >"$state_dir/log" 2>&1 &
+  HTTP_SERVER_PID=$!
+  local i
+  for ((i = 0; i < 600; i++)); do
+    if [[ -s "$state_dir/port" ]]; then
+      # shellcheck disable=SC2034 # read by the calling test
+      HTTP_PORT="$(cat "$state_dir/port")"
+      return 0
+    fi
+    if ! kill -0 "$HTTP_SERVER_PID" 2>/dev/null; then
+      cat "$state_dir/log" >&2
+      fail "HTTP test server exited before listening"
+    fi
+    sleep 0.05
+  done
+  cat "$state_dir/log" >&2
+  fail "HTTP test server did not listen within 30s"
+}

title: fix(lock): refuse to lock a version that a failed listing never confirmed
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/162
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

When mise can't fetch an aqua tool's version list (GitHub rate limit, network failure, a mirror that is down), a request like `4` resolves to itself, because without the list mise can't tell a version selector from a short exact version. mise then trusted that string:

```
$ mise lock                                  # tfcmt = "4", listing unreachable
✓ Lockfile written to mise.lock              # exit 0
$ grep version mise.lock
version = "4"

$ mise install aqua:suzuki-shunsuke/tfcmt@4
Error: Failed to install aqua:suzuki-shunsuke/tfcmt@4: error sending request: ... Connection refused
```

The lockfile got a version that may not exist, and the install error never mentioned that the version list was missing.

**`mise lock`** now refuses to record a version that only resolved to its own request string after that tool's listing failed, unless the version is installed:

```
$ mise lock
Error: cannot lock aqua:suzuki-shunsuke/tfcmt@4: unable to fetch versions for aqua:suzuki-shunsuke/tfcmt: error sending request: ... Connection refused
```

Versions already in the lockfile are unaffected, because they resolve from the lockfile and don't need the list.

**`mise install`** still tries the request as written, since a short exact version can be valid: aqua's `nektro/zigmod` maps `100` to its `r100` tag. When that fails, the error now says the version was never checked against its version list and why:

```
Error: Failed to install aqua:suzuki-shunsuke/tfcmt@4: error sending request: ... Connection refused
note: aqua:suzuki-shunsuke/tfcmt@4 was not checked against its version list, which could not be fetched: ...
```

Only backends that record a failed fetch are affected, and today that's aqua.

`e2e/backend/test_aqua_version_listing_fetch_failure` now also covers `install …@4` and `mise lock` with a prefix selector, with the listing hosts unreachable. The new install check fails without this change. The aqua and lock e2e tests, the unit tests and clippy with `-D warnings` pass.

title: feat(config): complete keys for `mise config get` and `mise config set`
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/161
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise config get` and `mise config set` now complete their dotted key argument, with descriptions in shells that show them (fish, zsh, PowerShell). Before this, pressing Tab after `mise config set` offered file paths.

```
$ mise config set settings.jo<TAB>
settings.jobs    How many jobs to run concurrently such as tool installs. …

$ mise config get tools.node.v<TAB>
tools.node.version        version of the tool to install
tools.node.version_order  ordering applied to remote versions: …

$ mise config set tasks.build.dep<TAB>
tasks.build.depends       tasks.build.depends_post
```

Where the keys come from:

- **Keys mise defines** (top-level sections, `settings.*`, a tool's options, a task's fields) come from `schema/mise.json`. Completion follows `$ref`, `allOf`, `oneOf` and `anyOf`, so `tools.<name>.` and `tasks.<name>.` resolve to the tool and task options. Deprecated keys are left out.
- **Keys you choose** (tool names, task names, env vars) come from the file the command would read or write. `--file`, `--global` and `--system` are respected, so `mise config set --file other.toml tools.<TAB>` lists the tools in `other.toml`.

Closes #3908. The issue suggested adding a separate TOML schema file for this. The existing JSON schema was enough, so this PR doesn't add one.

### Implementation notes

- The completer is a typed usage-rs completer (`#[usage(complete = …)]`), so it gets the half-parsed command and can read `--file`.
- **Upstream usage bug, worked around here:** the `run=` that usage-rs 6.11.1 emits for typed completers passes `--line=LINE`, but `CompletionRequest::parse` only accepts `--line LINE`. The completer therefore received an empty line. `completion_request` now splits the joined form before parsing. This can be removed once usage handles `--line=` itself (jdx/usage#1487).
- That `run=` path also returns values only. When the cursor is on a typed completer, mise now answers from its compiled tables, which is how the descriptions survive.
- `config get` and `config set` now share one target-file resolver, which the completer also uses.
- The schema (~227 KB) is embedded with `include_str!`. It is only parsed when a key is being completed.

### Validation

- Unit tests cover the schema walk, file keys, the `--line=` form, and descriptions.
- New e2e test `e2e/cli/test_completion_config_keys`. Disabling the `--line=` rewrite makes it fail.
- These existing e2e tests still pass: `test_config_set`, `test_config_target_aliases`, `test_completion_dynamic`, `test_completion_avoids_project_config`.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `mise run lint` are clean.

title: feat(search): search package registries by backend prefix or with --all
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/160
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise search` only knew about the mise registry, aqua, and installed vfox backend plugins, so a package like `typescript-language-server` returned nothing even though `mise use npm:typescript-language-server` installs it fine. You had to go to npmjs.com (or crates.io, rubygems.org, nuget.org) to find the exact package name.

Now, prefixing the query with a backend also searches that backend's package registry:

```
$ mise search npm:typescript-language
npm:typescript-language-server            Language Server Protocol (LSP) implementation for TypeScript using tsserver
npm:typescript-eslint-language-service    TypeScript language service plugin for ESLint
npm:typescript-prettier-language-service  TypeScript language service plugin for Prettier
...

$ mise search cargo:jaq
cargo:jaq            Just another JSON query tool
cargo:jaq-parse      Parser for the jaq language
...
```

Supported prefixes:

| Prefix | Registry |
| --- | --- |
| `npm:` | the default registry from `~/.npmrc` / `NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY` (npmjs.org by default), via `/-/v1/search` |
| `cargo:` | crates.io (skipped when `cargo.registry_name` points installs elsewhere) |
| `gem:` | rubygems.org |
| `dotnet:` | the NuGet feed in `dotnet.registry_url`, filtered to .NET tool packages |

Each registry returns up to 20 results, and those go through the same `--match-type` filtering as other search results (`mise search -m equal npm:prettier` returns just `npm:prettier`). Results are cached for `fetch_remote_versions_cache` and bounded by `fetch_remote_versions_timeout`. A failed request logs a warning and returns no registry results.

## Searching every backend with `--all`

`mise search --all <query>` searches every source for an unprefixed query: the mise registry, aqua packages (which normally appear only when the registry has no match), installed backend plugin catalogs, and all four package registries. Everything runs concurrently. A cold `mise search --all jq` took 0.32s here and returned 41 rows across the registry, aqua, `cargo:`, `npm:`, `gem:`, and `dotnet:`, all sorted by match score. Each package registry adds at most 10 results in `--all` mode, so rubygems can't flood the table. Duplicate ids are merged: aqua's `tokei` translates to `cargo:tokei`, which also comes back from crates.io, so it appears once.

```
$ mise search --all --match-type equal typescript-language-server
cargo:typescript-language-server  A high-performance TypeScript and JavaScript language server implemented in Rust
npm:typescript-language-server    Language Server Protocol (LSP) implementation for TypeScript using tsserver
```

## What doesn't query package registries

- **Unprefixed searches without `--all`** (`mise search prettier`) behave exactly as before.
- **Shell completion** (`--complete` / `--complete-ids`) never queries package registries, so tab completion never waits on the network.
- **`

title: fix(aqua): report only the provenance and signature checks mise performs
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/159
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise tool`, `mise registry --json --security`, and [mise-versions](https://mise-versions.jdx.dev) could list SLSA, Cosign, or Minisign for an aqua tool that mise never verifies. The aqua backend guessed those checks from the latest release's asset names. Any `.sig`, `cosign`, `.intoto.jsonl`, `provenance`, or `.minisig` file was enough, whether or not the aqua registry configured a verification mise runs.

For example, syft configures keyless Cosign through CLI `opts`. mise's native Cosign verifier ignores `opts` and uses only a `key` or signature `bundle`, so installing syft never checks a Cosign signature. syft still showed up as signed:

```console
$ mise registry syft --json --security | jq -c .security
[{"type":"checksum","algorithm":"sha256"},{"type":"cosign"}]
```

With this change, SLSA, Cosign, and Minisign come only from the registry config that install-time verification uses. That is the same rule GitHub artifact attestations already follow. syft now reports `checksum` only.

Checksums still use the release assets. mise verifies the GitHub API asset digest even when a package has no checksum config, so a release with checksum files still reports `checksum`.

The feature detection moved into a synchronous `AquaBackend::security_features` so it can be unit-tested without network access. New tests cover signature-named assets without config, Cosign `opts` compared with a `bundle`, and config that only appears in `version_overrides`.

Related: #13548 shows this security info on the registry docs page.

title: docs(registry): show verification badges and link each tool to mise-versions
body:
The [registry page](https://mise.jdx.dev/registry.html) listed each tool's backends but said nothing about how mise verifies a download. You could not tell from the docs whether a shorthand would verify a signature or only a checksum.

The tool table now shows that in two ways:

- **Badges on each backend** for the signature and provenance checks mise runs when it installs through that backend:
  - **packslip**: every `packslip:` backend, since a signed release manifest is always verified.
  - **attestations**, **SLSA**, **cosign**, **minisign**: `aqua:` backends whose package config in the bundled aqua registry enables that check for at least one version.
- **A "details ↗" link on each tool** to its [mise-versions](https://mise-versions.jdx.dev/tools) page. That page lists the tool's versions and the security info mise reports for every backend, including `github:` and core tools, which have no badges here.

For example, `aqua:goreleaser/goreleaser` shows `attestations` and `cosign`, and `packslip:github.com/jdx/hk` shows `packslip`. A checkbox, also reachable as `registry.html?verified=1`, limits the table to tools with at least one badge. The page text explains the badges and also points to `mise tool <name>` and `mise registry --json --security`.

Current counts: 57 attestations, 41 cosign, 19 SLSA, 8 packslip, 4 minisign.

## How the badges are computed

The docs loader reads `vendor/aqua-registry/registry.yml`, the same snapshot mise bundles. It applies the registry-config rules from `AquaBackend::security_info`: it checks the base package, every version override, and checks nested under `checksum`. Cosign counts only when the config has a `key` or `bundle`, because mise does not run Cosign `opts`. The docs build makes no network calls.

These rules match #13549, which stops `security_info` from inferring SLSA, Cosign, and Minisign from release asset names. Until #13549 lands, `mise registry --json --security` and mise-versions can still report those inferred checks. For example, they show syft as `cosign`, and this page does not.

Seven registry tools have no mise-versions page yet: aws-cli, chromedriver, daemon-presets, mole, sui, tiny, and vim. `docs/registry.data.ts` lists them so they get no details link. Remove a name from that list once its page exists.

This also fixes the loader's `watch` globs. VitePress resolves them relative to the loader file, so `./registry` pointed at a nonexistent `docs/registry`, and editing `registry/*.toml` never reloaded the docs dev server.

The CLI side of the issue was already covered by `mise registry --json --security` (#9364) and the `Security:` row in `mise tool`.

Closes #3985

## Validation

- `vitepress build docs` succeeds. The built `registry.html` contains the badge counts above and 998 details links, one for every registry tool except those seven.
- `hk run check` passes on the changed files (prettier, markdownlint).

This adds `yaml` as a docs dev dependency to parse the aqua registry.

title: fix(lock): lock global requests shadowed by the project config
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/157
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise lock --global` silently skipped a tool from `~/.config/mise/config.toml` whenever the current project's `mise.toml` declared a tool with the same short name. The global `mise.lock` entry was left without checksums or URLs, both for `mise lock --global` and `mise lock --global hk`.

For example, with a global `hk = "1"` locked at 1.58.1 (with an empty `[tools.hk."platforms.linux-x64"]` table) and a project `hk = "1.58.1"`:

```
$ mise lock --global --platform linux-x64
```

**Before:** nothing was locked; the global lockfile was unchanged. It only worked after deleting the project's `mise.toml`.

**After:**

```
mise lock            hk@1.58.1 linux-x64
✓ Updated 1 platform entries (0 skipped)
✓ Lockfile written to ~/.config/mise/mise.lock
```

and the global entry gets its `checksum`, `url`, and `signer`, still at 1.58.1.

This also fixes a related case: when the global and project configs both request `hk = "2"` but their lockfiles pin different versions (say 2.0.0 globally, 2.1.0 in the project), `mise lock --global` used to overwrite the global pin with the project's 2.1.0. It now keeps 2.0.0.

## How

`mise lock` collects tools from the merged toolset, where the project's request wins, and then has a second pass over the target config files to pick up overridden requests. That pass had two problems:

- It matched overridden requests against the resolved toolset by version string alone, so an identical request from another config handed over a version pinned by that config's lockfile. It now only reuses a resolved version when it was resolved through the lockfile being written.
- It only re-resolved an overridden request when it was `latest` or came from an idiomatic version file. It now also resolves a request that is overridden by a config writing a *different* lockfile, for the tools being locked (all tools, or the ones named on the command line). Those requests resolve through their own lockfile entry, so an existing pin is kept and `--bump` still bumps.

A request overridden by another config that writes the *same* lockfile (for example `conf.d/01-base.toml` under `conf.d/02-override.toml`) is still left out: the winning request alone describes that lockfile.

A shadowed request that fails to resolve is logged at debug level and skipped, as before.

This unblocks removing the shadowed-entry skip in `BackendsSwitch::drop_shadowed` from #13543.

## Validation

- New e2e `e2e/lockfile/test_lockfile_global_shadowed` pins a global `hk = "2"` at 2.0.0. Under a project `hk = "1.58.1"` it checks that `mise lock --global` and `mise lock --global hk` keep 2.0.0 and record checksums, and that `--bump` moves it to the newest 2.x without editing either config. title: security(bootstrap): don't follow untrusted parent symlinks when changing directories as root
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/156
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

When mise changes a `[bootstrap.directories]` entry as root (declared `owner`/`group`, `recursive = true`, or any change the invoking user is refused), it no longer follows a symlink that another user could have planted in the directory's path. This extends #13539, which did the same for `[bootstrap.files]`, to directories.

## What changes

Before, root created, replaced, and removed directories by path. If a user could write any directory along that path, they could swap a component for a symlink and redirect the change. For example, a recursive removal of `/srv/app/cache` could be pointed at `/etc` (CWE-59).

Now, when the change runs as root:

- **Removal** opens the parent one component at a time and removes the directory relative to it. `recursive = true` walks the tree by descriptor. It unlinks symlinks, sockets, and other non-directories inside the tree but never follows a symlink, and it removes directories bottom-up.
- **`replace = true`** unlinks the existing non-directory entry relative to the strictly opened parent before creating the directory.
- **Status and dry-run** report the untrusted symlink for directories, so they agree with apply. Changes to a user-level directory that resolve the path strictly are flagged too, because directory creation and metadata updates already walk the path that way for every user.

A symlink is still followed when it sits in a root-owned directory that no other user can write, such as `/var -> /private/var` on macOS. Declaring the resolved path makes the change go through:

```toml
[bootstrap.directories."/home/me/linked/cache"]   # ~/linked is a symlink
state = "absent"
recursive = true
```

```
$ mise bootstrap files apply --yes
Error: refusing to remove directory /home/me/linked/cache: its path crosses symlink /home/me/linked, which root does not follow outside a root-owned directory no other user can write; declare the resolved path instead
```

Changes the invoking user makes without elevation behave as before. For example, a plain `state = "absent"` rmdir of an empty directory the user can remove still follows parent symlinks.

**Compatibility note:** `recursive = true` removals always run as root. A recursive removal whose path crosses a symlink in a user-writable directory is now refused, even under `$HOME`. Declare the resolved path instead.

## Implementation notes

- The descriptor-relative `remove_all_at`, which brew-cask already used for safe tree removal, moves to `crate::file` so both callers share it.
- The inspection request sent to the privileged helper gains `directory` and `recursive` fields (both default to `false`).

## Validation

- New unit tests call the strict directory functions as an unprivileged user. They check that a symlinked parent is refused and nothing outside it changes, that a recursive removal doesn't follow symlinks inside the tree, and that normal behaviour

--- src/file.rs (+48/-0)
@@ -184,6 +184,54 @@ pub(crate) fn remove_all<P: AsRef<Path>>(path: P) -> Result<()> {
     Ok(())
 }
 
+/// Remove `name` under `parent` and, for a directory, everything below it,
+/// without following a symlink anywhere in the tree. Every entry is resolved
+/// relative to a descriptor for the directory holding it: a symlink is
+/// unlinked, never descended into, and a directory is opened with
+/// `O_NOFOLLOW`, so an entry swapped for a symlink mid-walk fails the open
+/// instead of redirecting the removal. Directories are removed bottom-up. A
+/// missing `name` is not an error.
+#[cfg(unix)]
+pub(crate) fn remove_all_at<Fd: std::os::fd::AsFd>(
+    parent: Fd,
+    name: &std::ffi::OsStr,
+) -> Result<()> {
+    let stat =
+        match nix::sys::stat::fstatat(&parent, name, nix::fcntl::AtFlags::AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW) {
+            Ok(stat) => stat,
+            Err(nix::errno::Errno::ENOENT) => return Ok(()),
+            Err(err) => return Err(err.into()),
+        };
+    // Compare the whole type field: sockets and block devices share the
+    // directory bit.
+    let kind = nix::sys::stat::SFlag::from_bits_truncate(stat.st_mode & nix::libc::S_IFMT);
+    if kind == nix::sys::stat::SFlag::S_IFDIR {
+        let fd = nix::fcntl::openat(
+            &parent,
+            name,
+            nix::fcntl::OFlag::O_RDONLY
+                | nix::fcntl::OFlag::O_DIRECTORY
+                | nix::fcntl::OFlag::O_NOFOLLOW
+                | nix::fcntl::OFlag::O_CLOEXEC,
+            nix::sys::stat::Mode::empty(),
+        )?;
+        let mut directory = nix::dir::Dir::from_fd(fd)?;
+        let entries = directory
+            .iter()
+            .map(|entry| entry.map(|entry| entry.file_name().to_owned()))
+            .collect::<std::result::Result<Vec<_>, _>>()?;
+        for entry in entries {
+            if entry.as_bytes() != b"." && entry.as_bytes() != b".." {
+                remove_all_at(&directory, std::ffi::OsStr::from_bytes(entry.to_bytes()))?;
+            }
+        }
+        nix::unistd::unlinkat(parent, name, nix::unistd::UnlinkatFlags::RemoveDir)?;
+    } else {
+        nix::unistd::unlinkat(parent, name, nix::unistd::UnlinkatFlags::NoRemoveDir)?;
+    }
+    Ok(())
+}
+

 /// [`fs::remove_dir_all`] is running.

title: test(lockfile): make the python provenance-skip test use its locked tarball
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/155
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes the `e2e/lockfile/test_lockfile_python_skip_provenance_verify` failure on main's "trusted / e2e" job (first seen at 7cd93453c and 13a2fe350) and on #13539. This is not a regression in mise, and CI credentials are not the cause.

**What was wrong:** the test sets `python = { version = "3.13.5", patch_sysconfig = false }`. Since #10161, `patch_sysconfig = false` has been part of Python's lock identity, but the lockfile the test seeds had no `options`. The entry never matched, so mise ignored the locked local URL and checksum. It downloaded real CPython 3.13.5 from GitHub instead and verified its attestations through mise-versions, which does not need the test's deliberately invalid token. The real binary also prints `Python 3.13.5`, so the test passed without ever running the skip path it is named for.

On 2026-09-23 the mise-versions attestation endpoint began returning 503. mise fell back to the GitHub API with `MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN=invalid` and got a 401. The only change between the passing and failing commits (#13518) is a dotfiles change.

**Fix (test only):**
- Add `options = { patch_sysconfig = "false" }` to the seeded lockfile entry so it matches the request.
- Make the fake interpreter print `Python 3.13.5 (fake lockfile tarball)` and assert that string. The test now proves the locked tarball was installed and cannot pass by installing upstream CPython.

Attestations stay enabled in the test.

**Validation**
- The test now passes locally in about 2s with no GitHub or mise-versions attestation request.
- Mutation check: I forced `install_precompiled` to always verify provenance. The test then fails with the attestation 401, so it covers the skip path.
- `hk` check (shellcheck, shfmt) passes. No Rust changes.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: unavailable.*

title: fix(lock): make --bump check remote versions and fail when it can't
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/154
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise lock --bump` could leave a lockfile at old versions and exit 0 when it had not actually checked for newer releases. For packslip tools, the check itself was also the easiest thing to break: every resolution called `api.github.com` several times, so a user out of GitHub rate limit got a screen of `403 Forbidden` warnings instead of a bump.

### `--bump` now checks the remote for every selector

Before, `--bump` only asked the remote about `latest` and rolling channels. A prefix such as `usage = "6"` resolved to the newest **installed** 6.x, so with only 6.10.0 installed:

```
$ mise lock --bump usage          # 6.11.0 is published
$ grep version mise.lock
version = "6.10.0"                # exit 0, nothing bumped; --dry-run --json reported []
```

Now the same command locks 6.11.0. `--dry-run --json` agrees with the real run, because both use the same remote resolution. When the remote version list can't be fetched, `--bump` fails with the cause instead of keeping the locked version:

```
$ mise lock --bump usage          # GitHub rate limit exhausted
Error:
   0: failed to resolve usage@6 for lockfile mise.lock
   1: fetching the release list of packslip:github.com/jdx/usage
   2: HTTP status client error (403 Forbidden) ...
```

`mise lock --bump tool@version` used to log the same failure at debug level and continue. It fails too now. Plain `mise lock` without `--bump` is unchanged: it keeps the locked versions and stays tolerant of network failures. An exactly pinned version that is already installed still resolves to itself under `--bump`, without contacting the remote.

### packslip tools no longer call api.github.com in normal use

For a registry tool whose preferred backend is packslip (usage, hk, communique, fnox, pitchfork, mr-boxington, aube), `latest`, `ls-remote`, `lock` and `install` now make no `api.github.com` requests:

- **Candidate versions** come from the mise-versions catalog. Its update job builds that catalog with `mise ls-remote`, which runs the same packslip listing.
- **GitHub's "latest release"** and the **release holding a version's `.packslip` asset** come from the mise-versions release mirror. If the mirrored release is missing the `.packslip` asset, mise falls back to GitHub's release listing.
- **The signed `.well-known/packslip.json` list** and **repository files a packslip names** (man pages, completions) come from `raw.githubusercontent.com`. That's GitHub's CDN, which the API rate limit doesn't cover. A token is still sent for private repositories.

Trust decisions stay on the client: the signed list, stamps and every manifest are still fetched and verified on each resolution. A stale catalog can only delay a new release; it can't admit one that policy refuses.

`api.github.com` is still used:
- for packslip projects that aren't the registry's preferred backend for their name (for example `packslip:owne

title: feat(lock): keep locked backends when the registry moves a tool, and add `mise backends switch`
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/153
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

When the registry moves a tool to a new backend, mise used to follow it silently, even when `mise.lock` recorded the old one. This showed up with communique and hk, which now install from `packslip:` but were locked as `github:jdx/communique` and `aqua:jdx/hk` in many projects:

- `mise lock --bump` moved the tool to the new backend without saying so.
- `mise lock --bump communique` (or `mise lock --bump github:jdx/communique`) printed nothing, exited 0, and left the old version in place. The tool argument resolved to the locked backend while the configured tool resolved to the registry's, so the filter matched nothing.

A locked tool now stays on its locked backend for any version that backend can serve, so a registry update never changes where it installs from:

```sh
# mise.toml: communique = "latest"; mise.lock: communique 1.4.0 on github:jdx/communique
$ mise lock --bump communique
mise WARN  communique is locked to github:jdx/communique, but the registry now installs it from packslip:github.com/jdx/communique. Run `mise backends switch communique` to switch.
# mise.lock: communique 1.4.2, still on github:jdx/communique
```

`mise install` (for versions it installs) and `mise lock` print that warning when a tool configured by its short name is locked to a backend the registry no longer prefers. Tools configured with an explicit backend (`"github:jdx/communique" = "latest"`), an environment backend override, or a `[tool_alias]` backend are the user's choice and don't warn.

### `mise backends switch`

The new `mise backends switch [TOOL@VERSION]...` adopts the registry's backend:

```sh
$ mise backends switch --dry-run
mise would switch communique@1.4.2 from github:jdx/communique to packslip:github.com/jdx/communique in ~/proj/mise.lock
$ mise backends switch communique
$ mise backends switch --global        # the global config's lockfile
```

For each locked tool whose backend the registry has replaced, it:

1. Moves the lock entries to the registry's backend at the same versions. With version-dependent registry backends, each version goes to the backend the registry picks for it.
2. Relocks each lockfile on its own, for the platforms it already covered, to record the new backend's checksums, URLs and dependency graphs.
3. Reinstalls installed versions from the new backend. Installs are keyed by tool and version, so an install from the old backend would otherwise keep satisfying the new entry.

With no arguments it switches every configured tool with a replaced backend. A tool argument can be the short name or the locked backend, and `@VERSION` limits the switch to one version. The command covers the lockfiles `mise lock` writes: the current project's by default, or the global config's with `--global`. Tools come from every config source, including idiomatic version files.

The switch is all-or-nothing per run:

title: fix(lock): lock the npm version, not the aube install directory name
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/152
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

With an npm tool requested as `latest` and already installed through the embedded aube package manager, `mise lock` failed:

```toml
[tools]
prettier = "latest"
```

```
$ mise lock prettier
→ Processing 3 tool(s): ... prettier@3.9.6~aube~de4f77e9115401ed
mise ERROR aube install failed: failed to resolve dependencies
  caused by: no version of prettier matches range `3.9.6~aube~de4f77e9115401ed`
```

Without `--bump`, `mise lock` resolves `latest` to the newest installed version, and installed versions are directory names. Installs made with an aube dependency graph are stored in `<version>~aube~<digest>`, so that directory name was treated as the version, sent to aube, and would have been written to `mise.lock`. `mise lock --bump` worked because it resolves against the registry.

Now `mise lock` locks `prettier@3.9.6` and resolves its dependency graph for that version. The same applies to pipx tools installed with a uv graph (`<version>~uv~<digest>`) and to lockfile updates made during `mise install`/`mise use`. The resolved tool still points at the installed directory it came from.

### Validation
- New e2e `backend/test_npm_aube_lock_installed_latest`: installs `npm:inflight@latest` with a graph (creating `1.0.6~aube~…`), deletes the lockfile, and runs `mise lock npm:inflight`. It failed before this change and now writes `version = "1.0.6"` with no `~aube~`. A full `mise lock` followed by `mise install --locked` also succeeds.
- `test_npm_aube`, `test_npm_aube_cli_trampoline`, `test_lock_global_sidecar_symlinks`, lock/tool_version unit tests, and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` pass.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes how versions are written during lock and lockfile updates for npm/pipx graph installs; behavior is scoped and covered by new e2e and unit tests, but incorrect stripping could affect locked installs.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes **`mise lock`** when a tool is configured as **`latest`** but already installed via a graph-locked npm (aube) or pipx (uv) layout. Installed scans were using directory names like **`3.9.6~aube~<digest>`** as the version, which broke dependency resolution and would have polluted **`mise.lock`**.
> 
> Adds **`ToolVersion::strip_install_path_identity()`**, which rewrites those path identities to the **logical semver** while **keeping the same install directory**. That normalization runs when collecting tools to lock, when merging installed versions during **`mise lock`**, and when **`update_lockfiles`** builds lock entries (including post-**`mise use`** / **`mise up`** updates).

title: security(bootstrap): refuse untrusted parent symlinks when writing or removing files as root
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/149
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`[bootstrap.files]` writes and removals that run as root now refuse to follow a symlinked parent directory that another user could have planted. Status and dry-run report such a file as `unknown`, so they agree with what apply does.

## Problem

When a file change needs root (a declared `owner`/`group`, or a write or removal in a directory the user can't modify), mise runs it through its privileged helper. #13511 made permissions-only changes walk the parent directories one component at a time. Writes (temp file + rename), removals, and path inspection still resolved the parent by path as root. A user who can write any ancestor directory could swap it for a symlink between plan and apply, and the root write, rename or unlink would then land somewhere else, such as `/etc` (CWE-59).

## What changes

When mise acts as root, whether in the privileged helper or under `sudo mise …`, it now opens the file's parent with the same no-follow walk that `[bootstrap.directories]` already uses. On Linux the walk opens directories with `O_PATH`, so a `0711` home still resolves. A symlink is followed only when the directory that holds it is owned by root and no one else can write it, so `/etc → /private/etc` on macOS still works. Everything after the walk happens relative to that directory handle:

- **write:** `openat` a temp file (`O_EXCL|O_NOFOLLOW`), `fchown`/`fchmod`/`fsync` it, check the existing entry with `fstatat`, then `renameat` it into place and fsync the directory
- **remove:** `fstatat` + `unlinkat`
- **inspect:** `fstatat(AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW)`, then read content through an `openat` handle

Changes made as the invoking user are unchanged: they follow parent symlinks like `[dotfiles]`, so `~/.config → ~/dotfiles/config` keeps working for user-level files.

```toml
# ~/linked is a symlink to ~/real
[bootstrap.files."/home/me/linked/app.conf"]
content = "…"
owner = "me"          # declared ownership → applied as root
```

```
$ mise bootstrap files status
unknown  file:/home/me/linked/app.conf  unknown (its path crosses symlink /home/me/linked, which root does not follow outside a root-owned directory no other user can write; declare the resolved path instead)  file mode 0644 owner me
$ mise bootstrap files apply --yes
Error:
   0: refusing to write file /home/me/linked/app.conf: its path crosses symlink /home/me/linked, which root does not follow outside a root-owned directory no other user can write; declare the resolved path instead
```

title: feat(daemons): isolate shared NATS consumers with accounts
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/148
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

NATS consumers can share one named server while retaining separate subject and JetStream namespaces. Each checkout gets a stable account by default; matching explicit resource names intentionally share an account and its messages.

```toml
# Global mise configuration
[daemon_providers.local-nats]
preset = "nats"
version = "2"
port = "auto"

```

```toml
# Project mise configuration
[daemons.messages]
provider = "local-nats"
# resource = "shared_events"
```

This builds on #13536, which builds on #13534; provider sharing remains experimental. Mise persists private account credentials and exports an authenticated `NATS_URL`. Daemon inspection omits passwords. Resolving connection settings may create credential files, but does not start a server or provision a live account.

Consumer startup validates and reloads provider-owned NATS configuration, preserving existing accounts and connections. Credentials and JetStream data survive provider restarts. Automatic accounts require managed loopback configuration; custom NATS files and TLS/certificate authentication are rejected for providers. Ordinary local NATS daemons retain those options.

Validation: real-server integration tests on macOS and Linux verify subject and stream isolation, explicit account sharing, a connected client's survival across adding an account, consumer stop isolation, credential privacy and restart persistence. Unit coverage verifies stable, distinct credentials with private file permissions.

No Entire configuration changes, automatic account deletion, migrations, server upgrades or releases are included.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: unavailable; version: unavailable.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Adds credential generation, private on-disk secrets, and live NATS config reload on a shared server; scope is experimental loopback providers, with validation before replacing active configuration.
> 
> **Overview**
> Shared **NATS daemon providers** now provision a separate account per `resource`, so multiple checkouts can reuse one `nats-server` without sharing subjects or JetStream data. Consumers get a stable authenticated **`NATS_URL`** (credentials are created on first resolve, including `mise env`, and are **not** shown in `mise daemons ls`).
> 
> Provider startup writes mise-managed loopback **`server.json`**, validates candidates with `nats-server -t`, and **reloads** when a new consumer account is added while leaving existing connections up. Explicit matching `resource` names still share one account and its messages; **`options.jetstream = false`** keeps isolation on core NATS only. Custom provider `config`/TLS paths are **rejected** so mise does not rewrite external NATS setups.
> 
> Docs and JSON schema describe NATS resource sharing; a slow e2e script exercises isolation, shared resources, invalid-config rejection, consumer stop, p

+import json
+import os
+import socket
+import subprocess
+import urllib.parse
+import uuid
+from pathlib import Path
+
+base = Path.cwd()
+
+def mise(project, *args):
+    return subprocess.check_output(["mise", "--cd", str(base / project), *args], text=True)
+
+def start(project):
+    subprocess.run(["mise", "--cd", str(base / project), "daemons", "start", "bus"], check=True)
+
+def url(project):
+    return json.loads(mise(project, "env", "--json"))["NATS_URL"]
+
+class Client:
+    def __init__(self, url):
+        parsed = urllib.parse.urlparse(url)
+        self.socket = socket.create_connection((parsed.hostname, parsed.port), timeout=5)
+        self.file = self.socket.makefile("rb")
+        assert self.file.readline().startswith(b"INFO ")
+        self.events = []
+        connect = json.dumps({"verbose": False, "user": parsed.username, "pass": parsed.password})
+        self.send(f"CONNECT {connect}\r\n".encode())
+        self.ping()
+    def send(self, data):
+        self.socket.sendall(data)
+    def frame(self):
+        line = self.file.readline()
+        if line.startswith(b"PING"):
+            self.send(b"PONG\r\n")
+            return self.frame()
+        if line.startswith(b"MSG "):
+            fields = line.split()
+            data = self.file.read(int(fields[-1]))
+            assert self.file.read(2) == b"\r\n"
+            if fields[2] == b"1":
+                self.events.append(data)
+                return b"EVENT", data
+            return b"MSG", data
+        assert not line.startswith(b"-ERR"), "NATS rejected the account or operation"
+        assert line, "NATS closed an existing connection"
+        return line.strip(), b""
+    def ping(self):
+        self.send(b"PING\r\n")
+        while self.frame()[0] != b"PONG":
+            pass
+    def publish(self, subject, payload):
+        self.send(f"PUB {subject} {len(payload)}\r\n".encode() + payload + b"\r\n")
+    def request(self, subject, value):
+        inbox = "_INBOX." + uuid.uuid4().hex
+        data = json.dumps(value).encode()
+        self.send(f"UNSUB 99\r\nSUB {inbox} 99\r\nPUB {subject} {inbox} {len(data)}\r\n".encode() + data + b"\r\n")
+        while True:
+            kind, payload = self.frame()
+            if kind == b"MSG":
+                result = json.loads(payload)
+                assert "error" not in result, "JetStream rejected the request"
+                return result
+    def close(self):
+        self.file.close()
+        self.socket.close()
+

+first_url = url("one")
+a = Client(first_url)
+a.send(b"SUB events 1\r\n")

+start("two")

+b = Client(second_url)
+# Reject an invalid candidate before replacing or reloading the live config.
+broken_url = urllib.parse.urlparse(url("broken"))

+credentials = provider / "credentials" / (broken_url.username + ".json")

+    ["mise", "--cd", str(base / "broken"), "daemons", "__resource", str(provider.parent), broken_url.username],
+    capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=60,
+)
+assert rejected.returncode != 0, "invalid account configuration was accepted"
+assert "NATS configuration command failed" in rejected.stderr, "candidate was not rejected by validation"
+assert (provider / "server.json").read_bytes() == live_config, "invalid candidate replaced live config"
+a.ping()
+b.ping()
+credentials.write_bytes(original_credentials)
+start("broken")
+Client(url("broken")).close()
+b.publish("events", b"other account")
+b.ping()
+a.ping()
+assert not a.events, "subjects leaked between accounts"
+a.publish("events", b"own account")
+a.ping()
+assert a.events == [b"own account"]
+for client in [a, b]:
+    client.request("$JS.API.STREAM.CREATE.proof", {"name": "proof", "subjects": ["proof"], "storage": "file"})
+a.request("proof", {"n": 41})
+assert b.request("$JS.API.STREAM.INFO.proof", {})["state"]["messages"] == 0
+b.request("proof", {"n": 42})
+assert a.request("$JS.API.STREAM.INFO.proof", {})["state"]["messages"] == 1
+start("three")
+start("four")
+assert url("three") == url("four")
+c = Client(url("three"))
+c.request("$JS.API.STREAM.CREATE.shared", {"name": "shared", "subjects": ["shared"], "storage": "file"})
+c.request("shared", {"n": 73})
+d = Client(url("four"))

+    client.close()
