+assert url("two") == second_url
+for endpoint in [first_url, second_url]:
+    client = Client(endpoint)
+    assert client.request("$JS.API.STREAM.INFO.proof", {})["state"]["messages"] == 1

+assert urllib.parse.urlparse(second_url).password not in rows

title: feat(daemons): share SQL servers with isolated checkout databases
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/147
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Projects can opt into a named global PostgreSQL or CockroachDB provider while keeping a database per checkout. The default resource identity includes the canonical checkout path and local daemon name, so unrelated projects and Git worktrees share a server without sharing data. An explicit resource name intentionally shares a database.

```toml
[daemons.db]
provider = "local-postgres"
# resource = "shared_app" # opt into sharing data too
```

This builds on #13534. Providers own server versions, ports and storage; consumers cannot override them. Connection exports point at the selected database and preserve existing environment precedence. This remains experimental and uses trusted local SQL authentication; separate databases are development isolation, not a security boundary.

Provisioning runs after server readiness for explicit starts, task dependencies and hostname-triggered application starts. Concurrent provisioning is serialized, existing databases are preserved, and registration stays cold. Stopping or pruning a consumer leaves the provider and other consumers running. No databases are automatically deleted, migrated or upgraded.

Validation: focused macOS and Linux integration tests cover unrelated projects, Git worktrees, concurrent first starts, explicit shared resources, cold registration, hostname startup, task dependencies, consumer stop/prune and persistence across provider restarts. Daemon unit tests and scoped checks also pass.

Known upstream behavior: Pitchfork may print a dependency-order warning when stopping a consumer whose provider is outside its project configuration. The integration tests verify that the provider and other consumers remain functional.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: unavailable; version: unavailable.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes daemon loading, Pitchfork dependencies, and live SQL provisioning against shared local servers; mistakes could affect multi-project dev databases, though scope is experimental and local-only.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds a **provider-backed daemon** shape so projects can attach to a globally defined PostgreSQL or CockroachDB server while getting their own database by default. Consumers declare only `provider` and optional `resource`; server version, ports, and storage stay in `[daemon_providers]`.
> 
> **Default isolation:** omitting `resource` derives a database name from the canonical checkout path and daemon name, so worktrees and unrelated checkouts share one server but not data. **Opt-in sharing:** the same explicit `resource` name points multiple consumers at one database.
> 
> Runtime wiring installs/prepares referenced providers before consumer registration, injects a Pitchfork dependency on the shared server, and runs a hidden `mise daemons __resource` readiness process that waits for SQL, creates the database under lock, and ex

+### Choose what to share
+
+Keep an ordinary preset declaration for a server and data owned by this checkout.
+To share a server while keeping a separate database, select a global provider:
+
+```toml
+[daemons.db]
+provider = "local-postgres"
+```
+
+Mise derives a database name from the canonical checkout path and daemon name.
+Each worktree or unrelated project gets its own database on the same server.
+Symlinked paths to the same checkout keep the same database. Moving the checkout
+changes that identity; the previous database remains on the provider.
+
+To share the database too, choose the same resource name in each consumer:
+
+```toml
+[daemons.db]
+provider = "local-postgres"
+resource = "shared_app"
+```
+
+Resource names start with a lowercase letter and contain at most 63 lowercase
+letters, digits or underscores. This is development isolation between trusted
+local projects, not a security boundary: SQL clients use the preset's existing
+local superuser authentication.

+Use a local configuration or profile override to opt into sharing. Mise never
+selects a provider automatically, and a missing provider is an error. A provider
+reference accepts only `provider` and `resource`; server versions, options and
+storage belong in global configuration.

+PostgreSQL and CockroachDB resources export their usual preset connection
+variables, pointing at the selected database. Explicit `[env]` values still win.
+The provider's tool version does not become a tool requirement for the consumer.

+with `depends = ["db"]` waits for both the server and database provisioning.
+`mise daemons register` prepares this dependency chain without starting the server
+or creating databases, including for later hostname-triggered application starts.

+Each consumer has a small readiness process managed by Pitchfork. Stopping or
+pruning that consumer stops its readiness process, leaving the shared server and
+its data intact. Starting another consumer provisions additional databases even
+when the provider's data directory already exists. Concurrent provisioning is
+serialized and existing databases are preserved. Mise does not run application
+migrations or automatically delete databases.
+

+`mise daemons ls --json` to inspect `provider`, `resource` and `ownership`; use
+`mise daemons providers ls --json` for the server's port and storage location.

Removes the Entire trail runners under `.entire/runners/` (`trail-review`, `trail-summary`, `trail-confidence`, `trail-risk`, `trail-security`, `trail-drift`). Branches will no longer get automated Entire review comments, summaries, or confidence/risk/security/drift scores, and the "Entire Gates" check stops running.

Entire itself stays enabled: `.entire/settings.json` (session checkpoints) is unchanged. Configuration only; no code or runtime behavior changes.

title: feat(daemons): add user-owned shared server providers
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/145
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Shared development servers can now live in global mise configuration instead of being owned by a disposable checkout. Each provider has independent tools, ports, persistent storage and explicit lifecycle commands.

```toml
# ~/.config/mise/config.toml
[daemon_providers.local-postgres]
preset = "postgres"
version = "18"
port = "auto"
```

Run `mise daemons providers start local-postgres` to start it, `ls --json` to inspect it, and `stop` or `restart` with its name to manage it. PostgreSQL, CockroachDB and NATS presets are supported. This is experimental and requires Pitchfork.

Providers do not join project groups or shell sessions. Their processes and probes use an isolated, frozen environment. A running provider rejects changed configuration or a changed tool environment until explicitly restarted. Data defaults to the provider's user-state directory and survives checkout deletion.

This is the first part of a stack. Consumer database and account selection will follow in dependent PRs; this PR supplies provider configuration and management only.

Validation: provider unit tests, cold-listing/configuration e2e checks, scoped formatting/schema/lint checks, and a real PostgreSQL lifecycle test on macOS and Linux. The lifecycle test covers automatic tool installation, consumer environment isolation, project stop, profile changes and explicit provider restart.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: unavailable; version: unavailable.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Introduces long-running shared database services and Pitchfork lifecycle management with deliberate isolation, but misconfiguration or supervisor identity bugs could still affect local dev environments.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds **experimental shared server providers** configured only in global `[daemon_providers]`, separate from project `[daemons]`. You can declare PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, or NATS presets with fixed or auto ports and optional `data_dir`, then manage them with **`mise daemons providers`** (`ls`, `start`, `stop`, `restart`).
> 
> Providers run under their own Pitchfork namespace and state under `$MISE_STATE_DIR/daemon-providers/<name>/`. They **do not** join project daemon groups or shell hook start/stop. Management uses global config and a frozen tool/runtime environment via a hidden **`daemons __provider-exec`** wrapper, so consumer project env, profiles, or PATH cannot redirect the supervisor or server process.
> 
> **Safety rules** include rejecting project-local `[daemon_providers]`, templated versions/tools, unknown declaration keys, and starting when config or execution env changed while the server is still running (restart required). List/stop can still see providers left in state after config removal or damaged `definition.json`.
> 
> Supporting changes: JSON schema for `daemon_providers`, usage/man/docs/llms.txt, port helper **`resolve_

title: feat(registry): add a url field for a tool's project homepage
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/144
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Registry entries can now set a `url` for the tool's project homepage or repository. Closes #4284.

Before this change, the [registry page](https://mise.jdx.dev/registry.html) could only link each backend to a URL guessed from its slug, and `mise tool` showed no project link. The guesses leave `http:`-only tools such as dart, flutter, and julia without a link, and produce wrong links for some slugs, e.g. `aqua:x.ai/cli/grok` → `https://github.com/x.ai/cli`.

```toml
# registry/dart.toml
description = "An approachable, portable, and productive language for high-quality apps on any platform"
url = "https://dart.dev"
```

```
$ mise tool dart
Backend:            http:dart
URL:                https://dart.dev
...

$ mise tool dart --url
https://dart.dev

$ mise registry dart --json | jq -r .url
https://dart.dev
```

- **Registry page:** each tool name now links to its `url`, or to the first backend URL that can be inferred when `url` is unset.
- **`mise tool`:** shows a `URL:` row and a `url` field in `--json` output (`null` when unset). A config alias of a registry tool shows the target tool's URL. `mise tool <name> --url` prints only the URL, or `[none]`.
- **`mise registry --json`:** includes `url` when set.
- **Validation:** the build, the floating registry, and the registry schema all reject anything that isn't an `http(s)` URL, and reject `{{ … }}` templates, so a backend download `url` put in the wrong table doesn't get picked up as the project URL.
- **Seeded:** URLs for 11 `http:`-only tools (android-cli, cursor-agent, dart, flutter, julia, neo4j, nomad-pack, oc, openshift-install, sentinel, tfc-agent), each checked to load. I left out grok, muse, and twg because I couldn't confirm a canonical homepage for them. grok still shows the wrong guessed link.

`docs/contributing.md` documents the field.

## Validation

- `cli/test_registry` and `cli/test_tool` e2e tests cover `url` being present and absent, including `--url` with and without `--json`. The dynamic-registry unit test covers runtime parsing.
- `mise run lint` and `cargo clippy --all-features --all-targets -D warnings` pass.

title: fix(shim): install a wrapper command's missing provider before dispatching
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/143
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A command wrapper such as `[wrappers.cargo] command = "mbx"` ran its command without first installing the tool that provides it. When a project pinned a version of that tool that wasn't installed, every `cargo` call failed. Calling the command's own shim in the same directory worked, because it auto-installed the missing tool.

The wrapper now installs a missing provider the same way the command's own shim does:

- **Lazy providers** are always installed on first use.
- **Other providers** are installed when `not_found_auto_install` is on, which is the default.
- With `MISE_NOT_FOUND_AUTO_INSTALL=0`, a non-lazy provider is still not installed and the wrapper fails as before.

**Trigger:** only `mr-boxington` 1.14.0 is installed, and the project's `mise.toml` pins 1.10.0:

```toml
[tools]
mr-boxington = "1.10.0"

[wrappers.cargo]
command = "mbx"
```

Before:

```console
$ cargo --version
mise ERROR "mbx" couldn't exec process: No such file or directory
$ mbx --version
mise ████████████████ 1/1 · installed 1 tool in 2.6s
mbx 1.10.0
```

After:

```console
$ cargo --version
mise ████████████████ 1/1 · installed 1 tool in 4.1s
mbx 1.10.0
```

This happened in real CI. jdx/packslip runs release-plz, which runs `cargo package` in a temp checkout of the last released commit. That commit's `mise.toml` pinned an older `mr-boxington` than the one mise-action installed, so the release-PR workflow failed on every push to main (jdx/packslip#129 works around it).

**Validation:** the new `e2e/cli/test_command_wrappers_install_provider` checks three things:
- a pinned but uninstalled provider (`dummy` 2.0.0, with 1.0.0 installed) is installed and run through the wrapper;
- with `MISE_NOT_FOUND_AUTO_INSTALL=0`, the wrapper still fails for a non-lazy provider;
- a lazy provider is installed even with that setting off.

The existing `test_command_wrappers`, `test_exec_wrapper_recursion*` and `test_rust_mr_boxington` tests still pass. I reproduced the mbx case above with isolated mise data and config directories, against 2026.9.12 and against this branch.

title: feat(ls): filter and group tools by backend
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/142
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Users who install many small binaries through mise (go tools, cargo crates, npm CLIs) want to see them apart from their runtimes. Until now, `mise ls` had no way to filter by backend, and the only workaround was parsing its output (#4442).

`mise ls` gets two new flags:

**`-b, --backend <BACKEND>`** shows only tools from the given backend. Repeat it to include several backends. Registry shorthands count as the backend they resolve to, so a plain `jq` entry is listed under `aqua`. The filter works with `--json`, `--current`, `--installed`, `--prunable` and the other existing filters.

```
$ mise ls --current -b ubi -b core
go             1.25.12             ~/.config/mise/config.toml  1.25.12
node           22.23.2             ~/src/app/mise.toml         22
ubi:jqlang/jq  jq-1.8.1 (missing)  ~/src/app/mise.toml         jq-1.8.1
```

**`--grouped`** prints one section per backend, headed by the backend's name and sorted alphabetically:

```
$ mise ls --grouped --current
aqua
gh      2.101.0          ~/.config/mise/config.toml  latest
jq      1.7.1 (missing)  ~/src/app/mise.toml         1.7.1

cargo
cargo:usage-cli  6.11.0 (missing)  ~/src/app/mise.toml  latest

core
go    1.25.12  ~/.config/mise/config.toml  1.25.12
node  22.23.2  ~/src/app/mise.toml         22

ubi
ubi:jqlang/jq  jq-1.8.1 (missing)  ~/src/app/mise.toml  jq-1.8.1
```

`--grouped` conflicts with `--json`. Use `--backend` to filter JSON output instead. `--backend` accepts the same backend names as `mise registry --backend`. Entries from vfox backend plugins (`plugin:tool`) count as `vfox`.

This doesn't implement grouping tools inside config files, which the issue discussion ruled out.

Closes #4442

## Validation
- New assertions in `e2e/cli/test_ls` cover `--backend` for aqua, ubi, cargo, repeated flags, JSON output and an invalid backend name. They also cover `--grouped` section headings and contents, and the `--json` conflict.
- `test_ls_all_sources`, `test_ls_cache`, `test_config_ls`, the `cli::ls` unit tests and `cargo clippy --all-features --all-targets -D warnings` pass.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: unavailable.*

> 
> **`--grouped`** prints tools in alphabetically sorted sections headed by backend name; it cannot be used with **`--json`** (use **`--backend`** for JSON instead). Vfox

title: fix(backend): keep .exe when bin renames a raw Windows download
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/141
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

On Windows, setting `bin` on a tool that downloads a single `.exe` installed the file without its extension, so Windows could not run it. This is the setup a cross-platform tool stub uses:

```toml
#!/usr/bin/env -S mise tool-stub
version = "2.18.0"
bin = "cloud-sql-proxy"

[platforms.windows-x64]
url = "https://storage.googleapis.com/cloud-sql-connectors/cloud-sql-proxy/v2.18.0/cloud-sql-proxy.x64.exe"
```

**Before:** mise saved the file as `cloud-sql-proxy`, and running the stub failed with `Tool 'http:cloud-sql-proxy' does not have an executable named 'cloud-sql-proxy'`. The only workaround was renaming the file by hand.

**After:** mise saves it as `cloud-sql-proxy.exe`, and the stub runs.

On Windows, when the downloaded file ends in `.exe`, `.cmd` or `.bat` and `bin` doesn't, mise now adds that extension. Archives already worked this way. The change covers raw and compressed single-binary downloads (e.g. `.exe.gz`) in the `http:`, `github:` and `gitlab:` backends. A `bin` that already includes the extension is left alone, and nothing changes on Linux or macOS.

The http extraction cache is keyed on the installed filename, so affected tools get a new cache entry and don't reuse the old extension-less file. Windows users who already installed an affected tool need to reinstall it once with `mise install -f <tool>`.

Fixes #13523

## Testing

- Unit tests cover the naming rule and the http backend's `dest_filename` for raw and `.exe.gz` downloads. I also ran them on Linux with `cfg!(windows)` temporarily forced to true, so the Windows branch is exercised, not just the no-op path.
- New `e2e-win/backend/raw_bin_exe_extension.Tests.ps1` installs `docker-compose-windows-x86_64.exe` with `bin = "docker-compose"` through the `http:` and `github:` backends, checks that `docker-compose.exe` exists, and runs it. This test runs only in Windows CI; I haven't run it locally.
- Existing Linux e2e tests for `bin` on the http and github backends still pass.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: unavailable.*

> **Medium Risk**
> Changes install-time binary naming on Windows for tools using `bin` with single-file downloads; behavior is platform-scoped but affects http/github/gitlab install paths and extraction cache keys.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes Windows installs where **`bin`** names a tool without an extension but the download is a raw **`.exe`** (common for cross-platform tool stubs). mise used to write **`cloud-sql-proxy`** instead of **`cloud-sql-proxy.exe`**, so Windows could not run it.
> 
> The change adds **`bin_name_for_download`**: on Windows only, when the artifact ends in **`.exe`**, **`.cmd`**, or **`.bat`** and **`bin`** does not, the installed filename keeps that extension. This is wired into the

title: docs(agents): move task procedures into skills and fix stale guidance
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/140
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

AGENTS.md (also loaded as CLAUDE.md) goes into every agent session in full. Some of it only matters for occasional tasks, and a few statements no longer matched the repo. This PR moves three task-specific procedures into skills and fixes the stale guidance.

## Procedures moved into skills

These now live in `.agents/skills/`. `.claude/skills` is a symlink to that directory, so both Codex and Claude Code find them. AGENTS.md keeps a short summary of each rule and links to the full `SKILL.md` for agents without skill support.

- **`registry-submission`**: the popularity bar, the required warning to the user and popularity check, the `## Popularity` PR section, and the backend tiers. The summary at the top of AGENTS.md still states the bar and the accepted backends, so agents see the warning even without loading the skill.
- **`pr-description`**: the release-note guidance for PR titles and descriptions. This also merges a separate paragraph under "GitHub Interactions" that repeated the same advice. The AI disclosure requirement stays in AGENTS.md.
- **`update-aube`**: the checklist for bumping the embedded aube crates.

AGENTS.md goes from 406 to about 320 lines.

## Stale guidance fixed

- **Clippy**: `mise run lint` does not run clippy (the step in `hk.pkl` is commented out), but CI does. The guide now says to run `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` yourself before pushing Rust changes.
- **Workspace crates**: the guide said the workspace was only `crates/vfox`. It now lists all seven member crates.
- **Windows modules**: the guide described only `*_windows.rs`. It now documents both conventions the code uses:
  - `*_windows.rs` replaces a same-named module on Windows through `cfg_attr(path)`, e.g. `fake_asdf_windows.rs`.
  - `windows_*.rs` is one module compiled on every platform, e.g. `windows_posix.rs` and `windows_console.rs`.

markdownlint and prettier pass on all changed files.

The main guide keeps short summaries and links; full rules live in each skill’s `SKILL.md`.

--- .agents/skills/pr-description/SKILL.md (+52/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,52 @@
+---
+name: pr-description
+description: How to write or revise a mise pull request title and description. PR titles and bodies feed the release notes, so use this whenever opening a PR, editing a PR body, or after review feedback changes what a PR does.
+---
+
+# Writing PR Titles and Descriptions
+
+Communique uses PR titles and descriptions to generate release notes. Write them
+for a mise user who has not read the diff or this conversation.
+
+- **Describe the final result.** Before requesting review and again after feedback
+  changes the implementation, compare the title and body with the complete current
+  diff. Rewrite both when the scope changes. Remove abandoned approaches, stale
+  requirements, and claims that the final code or validation no longer supports.
+- **Lead with the user-visible change.** Keep the conventional commit format, but
+  name the affected behavior and outcome in the title. Open the body with the
+  problem or use case and what users can now do. Avoid titles such as "address
+  feedback" or "fix CI" when the PR's actual purpose is a feature or behavior fix.
+  For internal-only work, explain the concrete maintainer or contributor benefit
+  without inventing a user-facing impact.
+- **Make the change concrete.** For new configuration or commands, include a small,
+  valid example and explain its result. For a bug fix, describe the trigger and
+  before/after behavior. For visible UI or output changes, include actual before/after
+  screenshots or a short recording when they help reviewers assess the change;
+  CLI input/output snippets are often clearer than screenshots of a terminal.
+  Use measured results for performance claims and state how they were measured.
+- **Keep the essential facts in text.** Caption screenshots and explain examples.
+  A reader or release-note generator should understand the change without opening
+  an image, following an external link, or reading the diff. Do not fabricate
+  screenshots, output, measurements, or validation results.
+- **State adoption details when relevant.** Include new flags or settings, defaults,
+  supported platforms, experimental status, required dependency versions, and any
+  compatibility changes or migration steps that affect using the feature. Distinguish
+  current behavior from planned follow-ups; do not advertise unfinished work.
+- **Keep review details proportionate.** Summarize meaningful validation and its
+  limitations. Include implementation details only when they explain behavior or a
+  tradeoff reviewers need to assess. Omit agent work logs, intermediate commit
+  summaries, and exhaustive test-command lists. A small fix can be a short paragraph
+  and a test result; screenshots and sections are not mandatory for every PR.
+
+For example, prefer `fix(task): install missing tools before running referenced tasks`
+over `fix(task): address review feedback`. Its description should explain which
+command previously failed, show the same command succeeding with automatic tool
+installation, and mention any relevant prerequisites. This guidance does not replace
+the AI disclosure that AGENTS.md requires on GitHub content.
+
+## Use cases and tradeoffs
+
+For user-facing behavior, explain materially different use cases or tradeoffs
+(for example, bounded catalogs versus query-driven search). Write the description
+for users and reviewers, not as a list of files or implementation steps; keep
+implementation details and test commands in secondary sections.
--- .agents/skills/registry-submission/SKILL.md (+60/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,60 @@
+---
+name: registry-submission
+description: Rules for adding a new tool or shorthand to mise's `registry/` — the popularity bar, the required user warning and popularity check, the PR's Popularity section, and which backends are accepted. Use before creating any new registry entry or registry PR. Not needed for maintenance of existing entries.
+---
+
+# Registry Submissions
+
+**Most new registry additions from agents get rejected.** Before adding a new tool to `registry/`, understand the rules:
+
+- **mise does not host self-written, personal, niche, or low-popularity tools.** The registry is curated for tools that are _already_ widely used. "It works" or "it has tests" is not the bar.
+- **There is a high bar for new registry additions: tools generally need thousands of GitHub stars, not hundreds.** jdx will reject projects that do not meet this popularity bar and will not give a reason. Per [contributing.md](../../../docs/contributing.md): "@jdx won't explain why a given tool wasn't accepted." There is no appeal, no checklist, no second chance — the PR is closed and that's it.
+- **Wasted PRs are the default outcome** for tools the agent or user has not vetted against this bar. Do not submit one speculatively.
+
+## Required check for new registry additions
+
+Before adding a new tool or shorthand to `registry/`, ALWAYS do the following. This check does not apply when editing an existing registry entry; do not ask the user about popularity for maintenance or fixes to tools already in the registry.
+
+1. **Warn the user clearly and ask:** "New registry additions have a high popularity bar: jdx generally rejects projects without thousands of GitHub stars and will not give a reason. Is this tool already widely used outside your own projects and does it meet that bar?" If it's the user's own tool, a fork, an internal/company tool, or something with a small audience, **stop and tell them the PR will be rejected.** Do not submit.
+2. **Actively check popularity for every new registry addition — no exceptions.** Look up real numbers; do not guess. Useful sources:
+   - GitHub stars and fork count (`gh repo view owner/repo --json stargazerCount,forkCount`)
+   - Recent release activity / last commit date (`gh repo view owner/repo --json pushedAt,latestRelease`)
+   - Download counts on relevant package registries (npm `npmjs.com/package/x`, crates.io, PyPI, Homebrew analytics, etc.)
+   - Whether the project shows up in third-party docs, awesome-lists, or other tools
+3. **Apply the bar.** Rough signals — very low numbers are disqualifying:
+   - GitHub stars in the thousands, not hundreds
+   - Active maintenance (recent releases, not abandoned)
+   - Real third-party usage (referenced in docs, blog posts, other tools, package registries)
+   - Recognizable in its ecosystem
+4. **Include the popularity data in the PR description.** Every PR adding a new registry tool or shorthand MUST contain a short section like:
+
+   ```
+   ## Popularity
+   - GitHub: 12.3k stars, 480 forks, last release 2026-04-12
+   - crates.io: 1.2M downloads
+   - Used by: <project A>, <project B>
+   ```
+
+   This is non-negotiable for new additions — it lets the maintainer evaluate the submission without re-doing the research. New-tool PRs without it look speculative and are more likely to be rejected.
+
+5. **If the tool is borderline or numbers are low, warn the user clearly** that the PR is likely to be rejected without reason, and ask if they still want to proceed. Do not soften this — users have repeatedly been surprised when their PR was closed, and the agent should have warned them up front.
+6. **Suggest the alternative:** users can install any tool themselves via explicit backend syntax (`mise use aqua:owner/repo`, `mise use github:owner/repo`, `mise use cargo:name`, `mise use npm:name`, etc.) or by writing a [tool plugin](https://mise.jdx.dev/tool-plugin-development.html). The registry is _only_ for shorthand convenience for popular tools — not for enabling installation.
+
+## Backend choice: packslip (preferred), then aqua, github, or gitlab
+
+For registry entries the backend tiers are:
+
+- **Version listing is mandatory.** Before adding a registry entry, run `mise ls-remote <backend>` and confirm it returns installable versions. A backend that can install only an explicitly pinned version is not sufficient, even if the package exists in an upstream registry. If the preferred backend cannot list versions, use another accepted backend (for example, a custom `http:` backend with a reliable `version_list_url`) or stop.
+- **Tier 1 — preferred:** `packslip:`. Use it when the project publishes signed release manifests; mise verifies the signer and artifact digests without requiring a plugin or separate package manager.
+- **Tier 2 — routinely accepted:** `aqua:`, `github:`, and `gitlab:`.
+  - **Prefer `aqua:`** when the project does not publish packslips and the tool is in the [aqua registry](https://github.com/aquaproj/aqua-registry). Better UX, SLSA verification, and per-version logic.
+  - **Use `github:`** when the tool isn't in aqua but ships GitHub releases.
+  - **Use `gitlab:`** for tools released through GitLab.
+- **Tier 3 — high bar, but lower than tier 4:** `conda:`. Potentially acceptable when the tool can't be supported via packslip/aqua/github/gitlab. The bar is lower than tier 4 because **the conda backend in mise does not require a separately-installed package manager** — mise downloads and extracts packages directly from anaconda.org via rattler, so users don't need conda/mamba on PATH. Still requires a popular, well-maintained tool.
+- **Tier 4 — extremely high bar, almost never accepted:** `npm:`, `pipx:`, `gem:`, `cargo:`, `go:`, `dotnet:`. These all rely on a separately-installed runtime/toolchain being present on PATH (`node`, `python`, `ruby`, `cargo`, `go`, `dotnet`), which is fragile — the wrong version, a missing install, or PATH ordering quirks all break them. `npm:`/`pipx:`/`gem:` are particularly painful because tools installed via them silently bind to whichever `node`/`python`/`ruby` was on PATH at install time. Don't reach for these for a registry PR unless the user has explicitly confirmed @jdx wants it that way for this specific tool.
+- **Not accepted at all:**
+  - **New `asdf:` plugins** — supply-chain security. Use packslip/aqua/github/gitlab instead.
+  - **New `vfox:` plugins** — same reason. Use packslip/aqua/github/gitlab instead.
+  - **`ubi:`** is deprecated and will not be accepted under any circumstances.
+
+Users can still install via any backend themselves with explicit syntax (`mise use vfox:...`, `mise use cargo:...`, etc.) — they just don't get a registry shorthand for it.
--- .agents/skills/update-aube/SKILL.md (+15/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,15 @@
+---
+name: update-aube

title: fix(completion): exit quietly when the completion reader closes stdout
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/139
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Shell completion no longer crashes mise when the completion is cancelled mid-flight. Before this fix, as-you-type completion drivers such as [flyline](https://github.com/HalFrgrd/flyline) re-run completion on every keystroke and kill the previous run. Every cancelled `mise run <TAB>` then aborted mise with SIGABRT, leaving a coredump and, on desktops, a "process crashed" notification. See https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13520.

**Before** (2026.9.12, reader closes early):

```
$ mise __complete_word__ --shell bash --line 'mise run ' --bash-word '' | (sleep 0.02; exit)
The application panicked (crashed).
Message:  failed printing to stdout: Broken pipe (os error 32)
$ echo ${PIPESTATUS[0]}
134
```

**After:** the same command exits 0 with nothing on stderr. Completion output to a reader that stays open is unchanged.

### Two bugs, same symptom

1. The completion protocol printed with `print!`, which panics on `EPIPE`. It now uses `miseprint!`, which returns the error instead. `handle_err` already turns a `BrokenPipe` error into a quiet exit 0, and the rest of mise's output uses the same path.
2. Any error from the completion fast path crashed too. `handle_err` initialises the logger, which reads `env::ARGS`, and that fast path returns before `ARGS` is ever set. Errors therefore panicked with `index out of bounds: the len is 0` instead of being reported. For example, `mise __usage_complete_word bogus` on 2026.9.12 exits 134. It now prints `mise ERROR Invalid input length: 5` and exits 1.

### Why not restore the default SIGPIPE disposition

The discussion suggests `signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_DFL)` as a global fix. mise relies on getting `EPIPE` back as an error when writing to a child process's stdin:
- `git.rs` ignores it so git's exit status reports the real failure.
- `oci/docker_archive.rs` adds it to the `docker load` error message.

With the default disposition, mise would be killed silently by signal 13 in both places, and those error messages would be lost.

### Testing

New `e2e/cli/test_completion_broken_pipe`:
- A reader that closes stdin before mise writes must see exit 0 and no panic.
- An open reader still receives the candidates.
- An unreadable spec produces a normal error.

The test fails on `main` (exit 101, the debug build's unwinding panic) and passes with this change. The existing completion e2e tests still pass.

Other commands still use raw `print!`/`println!`, for example `hook-env`, `which` and `run --help`. Nothing cancels their readers routinely, so they are left for a follow-up.

title: feat(bootstrap): support PartOf, BindsTo, Before, Conflicts and ExecStartPre/Post in systemd units
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/138
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Several things from existing systemd user units could not be moved into `[bootstrap.linux.systemd.units]`, especially units tied to the graphical session. Keys such as `part_of` and `exec_start_pre` triggered an `unknown field` warning and were dropped (discussion #13501). mise now writes these directives to the unit file:

| TOML key | systemd directive | Section | Units |
|---|---|---|---|
| `before` | `Before=` | `[Unit]` | services and timers |
| `binds_to` | `BindsTo=` | `[Unit]` | services and timers |
| `part_of` | `PartOf=` | `[Unit]` | services and timers |
| `conflicts` | `Conflicts=` | `[Unit]` | services and timers |
| `exec_start_pre` | `ExecStartPre=` | `[Service]` | services only |
| `exec_start_post` | `ExecStartPost=` | `[Service]` | services only |
| `exec_stop_post` | `ExecStopPost=` | `[Service]` | services only |

All seven keys take a list of strings. For the three exec keys, each entry is written on its own line, in order. A timer that sets one of them gets the existing "cannot set service-only directive(s)" error, and an empty or whitespace-only command is rejected.

```toml
[bootstrap.linux.systemd.units.panel]
part_of = ["graphical-session.target"]
after = ["graphical-session.target"]
exec_start_pre = ["~/.local/bin/panel --check-config", "-~/bin/optional-check"]
exec_start = "~/.local/bin/panel"
wanted_by = ["graphical-session.target"]
```

The service now stops and restarts along with `graphical-session.target`. Before this change, `wanted_by` only started it with the session. If a precondition check fails, systemd skips `ExecStart`, and `systemctl --user status` shows which check failed. Previously the check had to be wrapped in `sh -c '<check> && exec …'`.

### `~` expansion with exec prefixes

systemd lets exec commands start with prefix characters (`-`, `@`, `:`, `+`, `!`, and combinations such as `-+` or `!!`). Before this change, `~` expansion only worked when `~` came first, so `-~/bin/check` was written unexpanded and systemd rejected the unit because the path wasn't absolute. mise now keeps the prefixes in front of the expanded home path. This applies to every exec key, including the existing `exec_start` and `exec_stop`.

Commands without a prefix render exactly as before, so units that don't use the new keys produce the same file and are not reported as changed.

### Not included

`.path` units (`PathExists=`, `PathChanged=`, …) were also raised in the discussion. They need a third unit type alongside services and timers, so they are left for a separate change.

### Validation

- New unit tests cover the full rendered output with every new directive, the exec prefixes combined with `~` in both bare and quoted forms, rejection of the service-only exec keys on timers (while `part_of` is still allowed there), and rejection of empty commands.
- `e2e/cli/test_bootstrap_unit_templates` now also checks that tem

title: fix(aqua): create .mise-bins for registry files listed by name only
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/137
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Some aqua registry entries list a binary by name only, with no `src`. `mvdan/sh` does this (`files: [{name: shfmt}]`), and so does `astral-sh/uv` in its Windows override (`files: [{name: uv}, {name: uvx}]`). With `symlink_bins = true`, mise skipped these files when building `.mise-bins`. The directory was never created, but mise still put it on PATH:

```toml
[tools]
"aqua:mvdan/sh" = { version = "latest", symlink_bins = true }
```

```
$ mise install && mise which shfmt
Error: shfmt is not a mise bin. Perhaps you need to install it first.
```

On Windows, the same bug means `mise reshim` makes no shims for `uv`, `uvx` or `uvw`.

A file with no `src` is now found at its `name`. That matches aqua, and matches what mise's own install step already assumes when it places the binary. With this change, `.mise-bins/shfmt` is created, `mise which shfmt` resolves to it, and shims are generated. For packages without `symlink_bins` nothing changes: the bin-path directory is still the install root.

Installs made before this fix have no `.mise-bins` directory, and mise does not repair them. Run `mise install -f <tool>` to rebuild them.

Fixes discussions #13459 and #13460.

## Validation
- New unit test `test_srcs_default_src_to_file_name` covers the Windows uv layout. All aqua unit tests pass.
- `e2e/backend/test_aqua_symlink_bins` now installs `aqua:mvdan/sh@3.12.0` with `symlink_bins` and checks `mise which` and `mise x`. The test passes.
- New Windows test `e2e-win/backend/aqua_symlink_bins.Tests.ps1` installs `aqua:astral-sh/uv@0.8.22` with `symlink_bins`, runs `mise reshim --force`, and runs `uv` and `uvx` through their shims. It runs in the Windows CI job; I haven't run it on Windows myself.
- I reproduced #13459 on Linux before the fix, then confirmed it is fixed for `mvdan/sh` and `JohnnyMorganz/StyLua`.

- `.github/workflows/issue-closer.yml` is removed. It closed every issue opened by anyone other than jdx with "issues may only be created by maintainers", so issues were still effectively disabled.

title: feat(vfox): add BackendUninstall hook for backend plugins
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/135
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Backend plugins had no way to run custom logic during uninstall. mise skipped `PreUninstall` for them and only deleted the install directory. Some tools change things outside that directory, such as registry entries created by a Scoop manifest's `uninstaller`, and a plugin couldn't undo those changes.

Backend plugins can now define `hooks/backend_uninstall.lua`:

```lua
function PLUGIN:BackendUninstall(ctx)
    -- ctx.tool, ctx.version, ctx.install_path, ctx.download_path, ctx.options
    -- install_path still exists here, so the plugin can read files it installed
    local cmd = require("cmd")
    cmd.exec(ctx.install_path .. "/uninstall.cmd")
    return {}
end
```

The hook is optional; plugins without it behave as before.

## Behavior

title: chore(deps): group all usage crates in one Renovate update
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/134
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Renovate opened #13516 to move `usage-lib` to 6.11.1 but left `usage-rs`, `usage-derive` and `usage-cli` at 6.11.0. `usage-argv` 6.11.1 moved most `CommandMeta` and `FlagMeta` fields into a new `extra` struct. `usage-rs` 6.11.0 only sets a caret requirement on `usage-argv`, so its derive output stopped compiling and every build job failed.

The shared `jdx/renovate-config` preset lists only `usage-cli` and `usage-lib` as jdx crates. `usage-rs` therefore fell into the general `rust crates` group and the 7-day release-age delay. This rule puts every `usage-*` crate in the `jdx crates` group and turns off that delay, so one PR moves the whole family.

Checked with `renovate-config-validator`. Adding `usage-rs` to the shared preset would fix this for other repos too.

> The rule sets `minimumReleaseAge` to `null` and `schedule` to **at any time**, so `usage-rs` and related crates are no longer split from `usage-cli`/`usage-lib` by the default rust-crate delay—avoiding mismatched versions that broke builds when only part of the family updated.

title: feat(dotfiles): remove directories mise created once they are empty
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/133
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

When mise writes a dotfile into a directory that does not exist yet, it creates the missing parents. Until now those directories stayed behind after mise removed the file, so a work-only config like `~/.config/newapp/sub/work.toml` left an empty `~/.config/newapp/sub/` tree once it was switched off or unapplied. This addresses the "remove directories left empty" part of https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13410.

mise now records the parent directories it creates for a single-file target, and removes them with the target once they are empty:

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.config/newapp/sub/work.toml" = { source = "work.toml.tera", mode = "template", remove_empty = true }
```

With `~/.config` present and `~/.config/newapp` absent:

```console
$ WORK=1 mise dot apply --yes     # creates newapp/ and newapp/sub/, writes work.toml
$ mise dot apply --yes            # WORK unset: the template renders empty
mise files: removed ~/.config/newapp/sub/work.toml (template rendered empty)
```

`work.toml`, `newapp/sub/`, and `newapp/` are gone; `~/.config` stays.

The same applies to `mise dot unapply` for `symlink`, `copy` (single file), `template`, and inline `content` entries, and `--dry-run` lists the directories it may remove:

```console
$ mise dot unapply --dry-run
rm ~/.config/copyapp/deep/copied
rmdir ~/.config/copyapp/deep (if empty)
rmdir ~/.config/copyapp (if empty)
```

## What is kept

The walk goes upward from the target's parent and stops at the first directory that fails any of these checks:

- **mise created it.** Directories that already existed when mise first wrote the target (`~/.config` above) are never removed.
- **It is empty.** A directory holding anything else, such as a file you added next to the target, stays, and so does everything above it.
- **No other entry needs it.** A directory that is another active entry's target, or one a `symlink-each` or directory `copy` entry places files in, stays.
- **It is physically inside `$HOME`.** Your home directory, everything above it, and everything outside it are never removed, even if mise created them. A target such as `/opt/newapp/app.toml` leaves `/opt/newapp` in place, because directories outside home may be shared with other software. The check resolves symlinks, so with `~/.config -> /opt/config`, `~/.config/app` is kept too. Symlinked parents still work for apply.

Pruning runs once every target in an apply or unapply is gone. Only the first entry written into a new directory records it, so each walk counts the directories recorded by any target removed in the same run. Two sibling files in a directory mise created therefore take it along, whichever is removed first. Unapplying an entry whose target is already gone still clears its record and removes the recorded directories once they are empty. That covers a file you deleted by hand, and a directory a `remove_empty` apply kept be

+assert_succeed "WORK=1 mise dot apply --yes"
+echo "mine" >"$notesapp/notes.txt"
+assert_succeed "mise dot apply --yes"
+assert_fail "test -e $notesapp/sub"
+assert_contains "cat $notesapp/notes.txt" "mine"
+# the record keeps the directory it could not remove and adds the ones a
+# later apply creates, so both go once the user's file is gone
+rm "$notesapp/notes.txt"
+assert_succeed "WORK=1 mise dot apply --yes"
+assert_succeed "mise dot apply --yes"
+assert_fail "test -e $notesapp"
+
+# a directory a removal had to keep is retried by a later apply, even though
+# the target is already gone and nothing else changes
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[dotfiles]
+"~/.config/retryapp/sub/work.toml" = { source = "dotfiles/work.toml.tera", mode = "template", remove_empty = true }
+EOF
+retryapp="$HOME/.config/retryapp"
+assert_succeed "WORK=1 mise dot apply --yes"
+echo "mine" >"$retryapp/notes.txt"
+assert_succeed "mise dot apply --yes"
+assert_fail "test -e $retryapp/sub"
+rm "$retryapp/notes.txt"
+assert_contains "mise dot status" "applied"
+assert_succeed "test -d $retryapp"
+assert_succeed "mise dot apply --yes"
+assert_fail "test -e $retryapp"
+
+# unapplying a target that is already gone still removes the directories
+# mise created for it once they are empty
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[dotfiles]
+"~/.config/leftapp/sub/work.toml" = { source = "dotfiles/work.toml.tera", mode = "template", remove_empty = true }
+EOF
+leftapp="$HOME/.config/leftapp"
+assert_succeed "WORK=1 mise dot apply --yes"
+echo "mine" >"$leftapp/notes.txt"
+assert_succeed "mise dot apply --yes"
+assert_fail "test -e $leftapp/sub"
+rm "$leftapp/notes.txt"
+assert_succeed "mise dot unapply --yes"
+assert_fail "test -e $leftapp"
+
+# a target mise cannot read is removed with --force, and its created
+# directories go with it
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[dotfiles]
+"~/.config/lockedapp/sub/work.toml" = { source = "dotfiles/work.toml.tera", mode = "template", remove_empty = true }
+EOF
+assert_succeed "WORK=1 mise dot apply --yes"
+chmod 000 "$HOME/.config/lockedapp/sub/work.toml"
+assert_succeed "mise dot apply --yes --force"
+assert_fail "test -e $HOME/.config/lockedapp"
+
+# a record written before mise recorded directories removes none
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[dotfiles]
+"~/.config/oldapp/sub/work.toml" = { source = "dotfiles/work.toml.tera", mode = "template", remove_empty = true }
+EOF
+assert_succeed "WORK=1 mise dot apply --yes"
+for record in "$MISE_STATE_DIR"/dotfiles/targets/*.toml; do
+  awk '/^created_dirs/ { exit } { print }' "$record" >"$record.old"
+  mv "$record.old" "$record"
+done
+assert_succeed "mise dot apply --yes"
+assert_fail "test -e $HOME/.config/oldapp/sub/work.toml"
+assert_succeed "test -d $HOME/.config/oldapp/sub"
+
+# sibling targets removed in one apply take their shared parent along,
+# whichever of them created it and whichever is removed first. Only a.toml
+# exists at first, so it alone records the directory.
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[dotfiles]
+"~/.config/pair1/a.toml" = { source = "dotfiles/work.toml.tera", mode = "template", remove_empty = true }
+"~/.config/pair2/a.toml" = { source = "dotfiles/work.toml.tera", mode = "template", remove_empty = true }
+EOF
+assert_succeed "WORK=1 mise dot apply --yes"
+# pair1 removes its creator first, pair2 removes it last
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[dotfiles]
+"~/.config/pair1/a.toml" = { source = "dotfiles/work.toml.tera", mode = "template", remove_empty = true }
+"~/.config/pair1/b.toml" = { source = "dotfiles/work.toml.tera", mode = "template", remove_empty = true }
+"~/.config/pair2/b.toml" = { source = "dotfiles/work.toml.tera", mode = "template", remove_empty = true }
+"~/.config/pair2/a.toml" = { source = "dotfiles/work.toml.tera", mode = "template", remove_empty = true }
+EOF
+assert_succeed "WORK=1 mise dot apply --yes"
+assert_contains "cat $HOME/.config/pair1/b.toml" "work = true"
+assert_contains "cat $HOME/.config/pair2/b.toml" "work = true"
+assert_succeed "mise dot apply --yes"
+assert_fail "test -e $HOME/.config/pair1"
+assert_fail "test -e $HOME/.config/pair2"
+
+# unapplying a copy into a fresh nested directory removes what mise created
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[dotfiles]
+"~/.config/copyapp/deep/copied" = { source = "dotfiles/copied", mode = "copy" }
+EOF
+assert_succeed "mise dot apply --yes"
+assert_contains "cat $HOME/.config/copyapp/deep/copied" "copied"
+assert_succeed "mise dot track ~/.config/copyapp/deep/copied"
+assert_contains "mise dot unapply --dry-run" "rmdir ~/.config/copyapp/deep (if empty)"
+assert_contains "mise dot unapply --dry-run" "rmdir ~/.config/copyapp (if empty)"
+assert_succeed "test -d $HOME/.config/copyapp/deep"
+assert_succeed "mise dot unapply --yes"
+assert_fail "test -e $HOME/.config/copyapp"
+assert_succeed "test -d $HOME/.config"
+# and undo restores them
+assert_succeed "mise dot undo --yes"
+assert_contains "cat $HOME/.config/copyapp/deep/copied" "copied"
+
+# a copy the user deleted by hand: unapply still removes the directories mise
+# created for it and clears its record
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[dotfiles]
+"~/.config/handapp/deep/copied" = { source = "dotfiles/copied", mode = "copy" }
+EOF
+assert_succeed "mise dot apply --yes"
+rm "$HOME/.config/handapp/deep/copied"
+assert_contains "mise dot unapply --dry-run" "rmdir ~/.config/handapp/deep (if empty)"
+assert_succeed "mise dot unapply --yes"
+assert_fail "test -e $HOME/.config/handapp"
+# the record went with it: nothing is left to unapply
+assert_contains "mise dot unapply --yes 2>&1" "all files are unapplied"
+
+# a copy changed to mode = "absent": the file goes and so do the directories
+# mise created for it
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[dotfiles]
+"~/.config/goneapp/deep/copied" = { source = "dotfiles/copied", mode = "copy" }
+EOF
+assert_succeed "mise dot apply --yes"
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[dotfiles]
+"~/.config/goneapp/deep/copied" = { mode = "absent" }
+EOF
+assert_succeed "mise dot apply --yes"
+assert_fail "test -e $HOME/.config/goneapp"
+assert_succeed "test -d $HOME/.config"
+
+# a directory another entry still needs stays, even when mise created it
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[dotfiles]
+"~/.config/claimapp/deep/copied" = { source = "dotfiles/copied", mode = "copy" }
+EOF
+assert_succeed "mise dot apply --yes"
+cat <<'EOF' >>mise.toml
+"~/.config/claimapp/deep" = { source = "dotfiles/empty", mode = "symlink-each" }
+EOF
+assert_succeed "mise dot unapply --yes ~/.config/claimapp/deep/copied"
+assert_fail "test -e $HOME/.config/claimapp/deep/copied"
+assert_succeed "test -d $HOME/.config/claimapp/deep"

title: feat(dotfiles): remove a template's target when it renders empty
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/130
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A `[dotfiles]` template can now decide whether its target exists at all. With `remove_empty = true`, a render that is empty or whitespace-only removes the target instead of writing an empty file. This addresses the "remove the target when a template renders empty" part of https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13410.

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.config/app/work.toml" = { source = "work.toml.tera", mode = "template", remove_empty = true }
```

```jinja
{% if env.WORK == "1" %}
[proxy]
url = "http://proxy.example.com"
{% endif %}
```

```console
$ WORK=1 mise dot apply --yes
mise files: rendered ~/work.toml.tera to ~/.config/app/work.toml
$ mise dot status
~/.config/app/work.toml  template  …  differs (template renders empty, target will be removed)
$ mise dot diff
dotfile differs: ~/.config/app/work.toml
  template renders empty: remove ~/.config/app/work.toml
  …
-work = true
$ mise dot apply --yes
mise files: removed ~/.config/app/work.toml (template rendered empty)
```

Setting `WORK=1` again and applying recreates the file.

## Ownership rule

mise removes a target without `--force` only when the file is empty or whitespace-only, or when it still holds exactly the content mise last wrote there. Otherwise the apply stops with the usual "refusing to overwrite existing files" conflict and leaves the file in place. `status` explains why: "template renders empty, but it changed since mise last wrote it; use --force to remove it". `mise dot apply --force` removes it anyway. A directory or symlink at the target is always a conflict, and so is a file mise cannot read (for example one written with `permissions = "0200"`). `--force` removes any of them. A target that already holds exactly the rendered content is recorded as written by mise, because removing it loses nothing the template cannot produce again. `mise dot diff` reports a conflicted target as kept, not as a removal. mise checks ownership again right before removing the file, so an edit made while the confirmation prompt is open is not deleted without `--force`.

To know what it last wrote, mise now keeps a small per-target record under `$MISE_STATE_DIR/dotfiles/targets/`. The record holds a sha256 digest of the rendered content. mise records it for **every** template, not only `remove_empty` ones. It is also filled in for templates that are already up to date, so turning on `remove_empty` later still allows a safe removal. The record is local state. On a machine that never wrote the file, an existing non-empty target is a conflict.

The record is versioned, and new fields default when read. A follow-up PR (directories mise created are removed once they are empty) will add the parent directories mise created to it.

## Other behaviour

- `remove_empty` is valid only with `mode = "template"`, or with the default mode when `dotfiles.default_mode = "template"`. On any other entry, preflight reje

title: feat(dotfiles): set target file permissions with a permissions key
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/129
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`[dotfiles]` entries can now set a target's permissions with a new `permissions` key. You can also manage the permissions of a file whose contents mise does not own, such as `~/.ssh/config`. Before this change a template always took its source file's mode, inline content was always `0600`, and mise had no way to make sure a file you edit by hand stays private.

This addresses the "permissions without content" item in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13410.

```toml
[dotfiles]
# override what the entry would otherwise set
"~/.netrc" = { source = "netrc.tera", mode = "template", permissions = "0600" }
"~/.config/token" = { content = "secret\n", permissions = "0400" }

# manage only the permissions of files that already exist
"~/.ssh" = { permissions = "0700" }
"~/.ssh/config" = { permissions = "0600" }
```

```
$ chmod 644 ~/.ssh/config
$ mise dot status ~/.ssh/config
~/.ssh/config  permissions  -  ~/.config/mise/config.toml  differs (permissions differ)
$ mise dot diff ~/.ssh/config
dotfile differs: ~/.ssh/config
  permissions differ: 0644 (current) -> 0600 (desired)
$ mise dot apply --yes
mise files: set permissions of ~/.ssh/config to 0600
```

`mode` already names the entry kind in `[dotfiles]`, so the new key is `permissions` rather than `mode`. It takes an octal string such as `"0600"` or `"0o600"`, the same syntax `[bootstrap.files]` accepts for `mode`.

## Behavior

- **With `copy`, `template`, or inline `content`:** `permissions` replaces the source's mode (copy and template) or the `0600` default (content).
  - `mise dot status` reports drift, `mise dot diff` shows it, and apply repairs it.
  - A declared mode that denies the owner read access, such as `0200`, is checked by mode alone, because the content cannot be read back.
  - A target that drifts to an unreadable mode, such as `0000`, is reported as `permissions differ` and rewritten by apply.
  - OCI images built from these entries carry the declared mode.
- **On its own (no `source`, `content`, or `mode`):** the entry manages only the permissions of an existing file or directory.
  - mise never creates the target and never changes its content. It never infers a source from `dotfiles.root`.
  - **A missing target counts as satisfied.** Apply warns and skips it. Status reports it as `applied (target absent; permissions not applied)`, the JSON has a matching `reason`, and `mise dot status --missing` does not fail. This matches how `[bootstrap.files]` handles a metadata-only entry whose target is missing.
  - If another entry in the same apply creates the directory, the chmod runs after that entry, so the new directory gets its mode.
  - A symlink at the target is never followed. Status reports it, and apply skips it with a warning.
  - The chmod goes through a descriptor opened with `O_NOFOLLOW`, so a link swapped in while mise runs is refused. A `0000` target cannot be open

title: feat(dotfiles): remove targets with mode = "absent"
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/128
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

When you retire a tool, its old config file stays on every machine that already has it. You can delete it by hand on each machine, but nothing in `[dotfiles]` could say "this file should not exist". This PR adds `mode = "absent"`, which addresses the declarative-removal request in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13410.

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.oldrc" = { mode = "absent" }

# remove a file on some machines only
[dotfiles."~/.bash_profile"]
mode = "absent"
variants = [{ os = "macos" }]
```

```console
$ mise dot status
~/.oldrc  absent  -  ~/.config/mise/config.toml  would remove (present)
$ mise dot apply --dry-run
rm ~/.oldrc
$ mise dot apply --yes
mise files: removed ~/.oldrc
mise files: applied ~/.oldrc
$ mise dot status
~/.oldrc  absent  -  ~/.config/mise/config.toml  absent
```

(The history summary lines that `status` prints after the table are left out.)

## Behavior

- `apply` removes a regular file or a symlink at the target. It does not compare content first, because the declaration is the instruction; `[bootstrap.files] state = "absent"` works the same way. For a symlink, only the link is removed, never the file or directory it points to; on Windows this includes directory symlinks and junctions, which are removed as links. Once the target is gone, `apply` does nothing more.
- **Only regular files and symlinks are removed.** If the target is a directory, or a FIFO, socket, or device node, `status`, `diff`, and `apply` report an error that names it. This happens even with `--force`, so absent never deletes recursively and never unlinks a service's socket. `status` shows these as errors, not as "would remove".
- An absent entry takes no `source`, `content`, `exclude`, `manifest`, `permissions`, or `encrypt = true`, and cannot be combined with block or line edit keys (`block`, `line`, `template`, `comment`, `position`). Such an entry is rejected instead of turning into a removal of the file it meant to edit. A separate edit entry (`"~/.oldrc/id" = { line = … }`) on a file an absent entry removes is also rejected, by `mise dot apply` and by `mise bootstrap` before any file is written, since the two would undo each other on every apply. Config preflight rejects these combinations, and the schema flags them.
- An absent target counts as a leaf in the composed footprint, so no other entry can place a file beneath it, and a permissions-only entry cannot name the same target.
- Destination `variants` work. A machine that matches no variant skips the entry.
- History: when the target is under a tracked path, the removal is journaled like any other apply (the target is captured in full), so `mise dot undo` restores the file.
- `unapply` skips absent entries. Undoing an absence would mean recreating a file mise never wrote, the same rule as `declares_absence` for `[bootstrap.files]`.
- `status` shows `absent` when the target is gone and

title: feat(install): explain checksum mismatches caused by re-uploaded GitHub assets
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/127
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

When a maintainer re-uploads a GitHub release asset after publishing, any lockfile or cached release metadata that recorded the original digest makes `mise install` fail with a bare checksum mismatch. The error doesn't say whether the download was corrupted, tampered with, or legitimately replaced upstream.

This happened with rvben/rumdl v0.2.76, which was published at 01:45Z on 2026-09-23 and had every asset re-uploaded at 08:25Z. It broke the registry test job on #13504. The stale digest was fixed on the mirror in jdx/mise-versions#323.

## What changes

When a `github:` or `aqua:` install fails with a checksum mismatch on a github.com release asset (primary or additional), mise now makes one GitHub API request for that release. The request skips mise's release cache and mise-versions, because either could still hold the old digest. If GitHub's current digest for the asset matches the downloaded file, mise adds a hint to the error:

```console
$ mise install   # mise.lock still holds the pre-re-upload digest
Error:
   0: Failed to install github:rvben/rumdl@0.2.76: lockfile entry for github:rvben/rumdl@0.2.76 on linux-x64 locks https://github.com/rvben/rumdl/releases/download/v0.2.76/rumdl-v0.2.76-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz: Checksum mismatch for file .../rumdl-v0.2.76-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz:
      Expected: sha256:3a02b5677a7a3f6e7a8f6cc09d93bb384ee56f4da0273865f4ddf94594382785
      Actual:   sha256:90a8589a34cdc9aa50c9cf9a2b1e41837afe16bb11b2a7ace2e05dfb56a51176
      hint: GitHub's current digest for rumdl-v0.2.76-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz in rvben/rumdl v0.2.76 matches this download (asset updated 2026-09-23T08:25:23Z, release published 2026-09-23T01:45:05Z), so the expected checksum is out of date: the maintainer likely re-uploaded the asset. If you trust the new upload, update the checksum in mise.lock.
```

Before this change, the output was the same without the `hint:` line.

- **The install still fails.** mise never accepts the new digest automatically, because a changed digest is exactly what checksum verification is meant to catch.
- **No extra calls on success.** The lookup runs only after verification has failed. A successful install from the same lockfile makes no request to the release endpoint.
- **Only for checksum mismatches.** Checksum mismatches are now a typed `hash::ChecksumMismatch` error with the same message. Size mismatches, I/O errors, and malformed checksums pass through with no lookup.
- **Advice depends on where the checksum came from.** When `mise.lock` held the expected checksum, the hint says to update it. When the checksum came from release metadata (no lockfile entry), the hint says that metadata refreshes within about an hour and that `mise cache clear` drops mise's local copy.
- **Otherwise unchanged.** If the lookup fails, is rate-limited, or GitHub's digest doesn't match the downl

title: feat(bootstrap): manage a file's permissions without its contents
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/126
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Some files need specific permissions, but their content comes from somewhere else: a package, an installer, or the user. Examples are `~/.ssh/config`, `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`, and a credentials file an installer wrote. Until now, `[bootstrap.files]` required `source` or `content`, so the only way to fix a file's mode was to take over its content too. This PR addresses part of https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13410.

An entry with neither `source` nor `content` now manages only the metadata it declares:

```toml
[bootstrap.files."/etc/ssh/sshd_config"]
mode = "0600"
owner = "root"
```

```console
$ mise bootstrap files apply --dry-run
would set permissions on file /etc/ssh/sshd_config
```

`mise bootstrap files status --json` reports the entry's desired state as `file mode 0600 owner root (content unmanaged)`.

## Behavior

- **What it requires and compares.** The entry must declare at least one of `mode`, `owner`, or `group`. Only the declared fields are compared and changed. Without `mode`, the mode is left alone rather than defaulting to `0644`.
- **How the path is resolved.** This depends on who makes the change:
  - **A mode change to the user's own file** is made as that user. mise opens the file with `O_NOFOLLOW` on the final component only, so symlinked parents are followed, the same as the `[dotfiles]` `permissions` key. For example, `~/.ssh/config` works when `~/.ssh` is a symlink.
  - **A change made as root** is a declared `owner`/`group`, or a mode change to another user's file. mise walks the parent directories one component at a time, opening them for search only (`O_PATH` on Linux). It follows a symlink only when the link sits in a root-owned directory that nobody else can write, such as `/etc` on macOS. It then opens the file relative to that parent with `O_NOFOLLOW`. A user who can write an ancestor directory therefore cannot redirect root's `fchown`/`fchmod` to a file such as `/etc/shadow`. CodeRabbit reported that risk in review 5294192767.
  - **Status and dry-run** use the same rule. An entry whose root-level change would cross an untrusted symlink shows as `unknown` with the reason, and apply warns and leaves it unchanged.
- **How the change is made.** mise checks it is a regular file with `fstat`, then calls `fchown` and `fchmod`. The content and inode stay the same. This goes through the same retry-with-privilege path as other file changes, including the `__apply-system-plan` helper. Declaring `owner` or `group` goes straight to the privileged helper, as it already does for content-managed files. On Linux and macOS, the owner can fix the mode of a file it cannot read (for example mode `0000`) without sudo:
  - On Linux, mise opens an `O_PATH|O_NOFOLLOW` descriptor and makes the change through its `/proc/self/fd` entry.
  - On other Unix systems, mise refuses a symlink, then calls `fchmodat`/`fchownat` with `AT_SY

title: feat(bootstrap): remove a templated file when it renders empty
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/125
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A templated `[bootstrap.files]` entry could only ever write its target. To make a system file conditional on a var or environment variable, you needed two declarations and some way to switch between them. Now a template can switch its own file on and off. This covers part of the chezmoi-style requests in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13410.

Set `remove_empty = true` beside `template = true`. If the template renders to empty or whitespace-only content, mise removes the target instead of writing it:

```toml
[vars]
proxy_host = "proxy.internal:3128"

[bootstrap.files."/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/95proxy"]
template = true
remove_empty = true
content = """
{% if vars.proxy_host %}Acquire::http::Proxy "http://{{ vars.proxy_host }}";
{% endif %}"""
```

With `proxy_host` set, `mise bootstrap files apply` writes the file. Set `proxy_host = ""` and the next apply removes it. `mise bootstrap files status` / `mise bootstrap plan` show the row as a removal whose desired value is `absent (template rendered empty)`, and `--dry-run` prints `would remove file /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/95proxy`. Restoring the var recreates the file.

## Rules and limits

- Only an empty render removes a file. It is removed the same way as a `state = "absent"` file. Nothing records ownership, because this table already overwrites its target unconditionally.
- If the target is a directory, mise refuses to remove it and reports it as `unknown`, the same as for `state = "absent"`.
- If a secret the template needs is unavailable, mise can't know whether the render would be empty, so it never removes the file. Status reports it as "not inspected: required secret unavailable", and apply fails as it does for any other template.
- `notify` services fire when the file is removed, as for any other file removal.
- Validation still treats the file as declared present. Parent-directory rules therefore don't change with what the template renders: a `remove_empty` file under an absent managed directory is still an error, and phase ordering is checked as for a present file.
- `mise bootstrap unapply <env>` does nothing for an entry that currently renders empty, just as it does for `state = "absent"`. With `--verbose` it says `template rendered empty, nothing was applied for it`. `--force` doesn't change this: it only overrides drift from what the module wrote, and an empty render wrote nothing.
- mise rejects `remove_empty` without `template = true` (`remove_empty requires template = true`) and on `state = "absent"` entries. The JSON schema enforces the same rules, so editors flag these combinations too.

## Validation

- Unit tests cover: empty, whitespace-only and `{% if false %}` renders becoming removals; non-empty content being kept; the validation errors; plan text, remove action, notification, and the refused-directory case; and parent-structure validation using the declared state.
- New

title: fix(bootstrap): run history reload commands for dotfiles bootstrap writes
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/124
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`[history.reload]` commands already run after `mise dot apply` writes a matching dotfile (#13414), but the dotfiles phase of `mise bootstrap` applies the same entries and ran none of them. A bootstrap that changed `~/.config/hypr/hyprland.conf` or `~/.ssh/config` therefore left the application on its old configuration, or skipped a fixup such as `chmod 700 ~/.ssh`, unless you ran `mise dot apply` separately.

`mise bootstrap` now runs the matching reload commands for the targets its dotfiles phase wrote, each once, after that phase's writes and before the `post-dotfiles` hooks. This is the same point at which `mise dot apply` runs them.

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.config/app/settings.toml" = { source = "dotfiles/app/settings.toml", mode = "copy" }

[history.reload]
"~/.config/app/**" = "app --reload"
```

```sh
$ mise bootstrap --only dotfiles --yes
mise bootstrap: dotfiles
mise files: copied ~/.config/mise/dotfiles/app/settings.toml to ~/.config/app/settings.toml
mise files: applied ~/.config/app/settings.toml
mise history: reload: app --reload
```

Behaviour matches `mise dot apply`:

- The reload map is read from the trusted system and global configuration layers after the `pre-dotfiles` hooks and before the phase writes anything. A dotfile that the phase writes cannot change which commands run. For example, a bootstrap that first links a global config containing `[history.reload]` runs those commands on the next run, not this one.
- `--dry-run` writes nothing and runs no reload commands. A phase with nothing left to write runs none either.
- `--skip dotfiles` or an `--only` that excludes dotfiles runs no reload commands.
- If a later entry fails or the edit prompt is declined, the commands matching the targets written before it still run. The error or declined result is then reported as before.

Bootstrap and `mise dot apply` now call the same helper, so the two cannot drift apart. The phase now loads its edit entries before writing whole-file entries, as `mise dot apply` already does. An invalid edit entry is therefore reported before any file is written, instead of after the whole-file entries have been applied.

This addresses part of https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13410.

## Validation

- New e2e test `e2e/cli/test_bootstrap_dotfiles_reload` runs `mise bootstrap --only dotfiles --yes` and checks these cases:
  - Copy and edit entries each run their command once, and an unmatched glob runs nothing.
  - A dry run creates no marker, and neither does `--only shell`.
  - A second run with nothing to write creates no marker.
  - A changed source runs only its own command.
  - A second entry fails on an unwritable parent: the first entry still reloads and bootstrap exits non-zero.
- Without this change, bootstrap writes no marker, so the test would fail at its first apply. I worked this out from the code and did not run the test on `ori

title: test(bootstrap): cover the bootstrap task on adoption and later updates
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/123
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

When you share your setup through a setup repository, some machine setup can't be written as a file: installing shell plugins, fixing permissions, and similar steps. #13435 and #13485 proposed an adoption-only hook for this. They were closed in favour of the ordinary, repeatable `bootstrap` task, which should handle both the first adoption and later shared updates. This PR adds a test for that workflow and documents it. The test found no bug.

Put the setup in the shared global configuration:

```toml
[tasks.bootstrap]
run = "chmod 700 ~/.ssh"
```

- **Adopting:** `mise bootstrap --adopt you/setup` restores the files, then bootstraps from the restored configuration. The task runs in the same command.
- **Later updates:** `mise dot pull` (or the watcher) restores the new files but runs no setup. `mise dot status` shows `declarations changed: run mise bootstrap` until a complete `mise bootstrap` has run, and that run executes the updated task. A partial run such as `--only task` runs the task but leaves the reminder in place.
- **Held adoption:** when a local file differs, adoption stops with "nothing was bootstrapped" and runs no task from either configuration. After `mise dot pull --take-remote-all`, `mise bootstrap` runs the adopted task.
- **`[history.reload]` is no substitute:** mise reads reload commands before the restore, so a reload table that arrives in the same update, including the first adoption, doesn't run for it.

The task runs on every bootstrap, so it must be safe to repeat. The docs now say so in `docs/bootstrap.md` (shared dotfile history, and what goes where), `docs/bootstrap/setup.md` (sharing changes, setting up another machine) and `docs/history.md` (reload commands, adoption).

This addresses the first-adopt setup request in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13410.

## Validation

`e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_bootstrap_task` passes locally. It sets up machine A with a `[tasks.bootstrap]` that appends to a marker, tracks the task and pushes it to a local bare origin, then checks three machines with separate HOMEs:
- **B, adoption:** a full `mise bootstrap --adopt --yes` runs v1.
- **B, update:** after A edits and syncs the task, B runs `mise dot sync` and `mise dot pull`. The pull writes v2 but doesn't run it, and the status reminder appears. `--only task` runs v2 but keeps the reminder. A full `mise bootstrap` runs v2 again and clears the reminder.
- **C, held adoption:** C starts with a differing config. Adoption fails without running a task. After `--take-remote-all` and `mise bootstrap`, v2 runs.

The PR changes no code, so the test also passes on `main`. `mise run lint` passes.
