 the origin. Once conflicts are resolved, it runs bootstrap to install
-packages, tools, and services and render templates. The configuration and
-required sources must have been tracked and shared for those steps to work.
+packages, tools, and services, render templates, and run the shared
+`bootstrap` task. The configuration and required sources must have been
+tracked and shared for those steps to work. Later pulls restore files
+without running setup; run `mise bootstrap` to apply a shared update, which
+runs the task again.
 See [repository bootstrap](/bootstrap.html#starting-from-a-repository) for
 how this differs from cloning a global configuration repository.
 
--- e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_bootstrap_task (+86/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,86 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# Machine setup that files alone cannot express lives in the ordinary,
+# repeatable `bootstrap` task of the shared configuration. Adopting a setup
+# repository runs the task from the configuration that just arrived, and a
+# later shared change reaches an existing machine through a pull followed by
+# `mise bootstrap`, which runs the updated task.
+# shellcheck disable=SC2016
+
+require_cmd git
+
+origin="$PWD/origin.git"
+git init -q --bare -b main "$origin"
+
+# ---- machine A publishes a configuration whose bootstrap task sets a
+# machine up
+cat <<'EOF2' >"$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml"
+[tasks.bootstrap]
+run = 'echo v1 >>"$HOME/setup.log"'
+EOF2
+assert_succeed "mise bootstrap dotfiles track $MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml"
+assert_succeed "mise bootstrap dotfiles origin set file://$origin --yes"
+
+# other machines are other HOMEs reached through wrapper scripts
+wrapper() {
+  local home="$1" script="$2"
+  mkdir -p "$home"
+  cat <<EOF2 >"$script"
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+export HOME="$home" XDG_CONFIG_HOME="$home/.config" MISE_CONFIG_DIR="$home/.config/mise" \\
+  MISE_STATE_DIR="$home/.local/state/mise" MISE_DATA_DIR="$home/.local/share/mise" \\
+  MISE_CACHE_DIR="$home/.cache/mise" MISE_TRUSTED_CONFIG_PATHS="$home"
+cd "\$HOME" && exec mise "\$@"
+EOF2
+  chmod +x "$script"
+}
+
+# ---- machine B: a fresh HOME
+B="$(dirname "$HOME")/b-home"
+wrapper "$B" "$PWD/b"
+b="$PWD/b"
+
+# adoption restores the configuration, then runs its task in the same run
+assert_fail "test -e '$B/setup.log'"
+assert_succeed "$b bootstrap --adopt file://$origin --yes"
+assert "cat $B/setup.log" "v1"
+
+# ---- A changes the task (keeping the rest of the configuration) and
+# shares it
+config="$(cat "$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml")"
+printf '%s\n' "${config/echo v1/echo v2}" >"$MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml"
+assert_contains "mise bootstrap dotfiles sync 2>&1" "published"
+
+# a sync fetches it and a pull restores the new configuration, but neither
+# runs setup: the status says to bootstrap
+assert_succeed "$b dot sync"
+assert_succeed "$b dot pull --yes"
+assert_contains "cat $B/.config/mise/config.toml" "v2"
+assert "cat $B/setup.log" "v1"
+assert_contains "$b bootstrap dotfiles status" "declarations changed"
+
+# a partial run of the task alone runs the updated version but applies
+# only part of the setup, so the reminder stays
+assert_succeed "$b bootstrap --yes --only task"
+assert "cat $B/setup.log" $'v1\nv2'
+assert_contains "$b bootstrap dotfiles status" "declarations changed"
+
+# the complete bootstrap runs it again (it must be safe to repeat) and
+# clears the reminder
+assert_succeed "$b bootstrap --yes"
+assert "cat $B/setup.log" $'v1\nv2\nv2'
+assert_not_contains "$b bootstrap dotfiles status" "declarations changed"
+
+# ---- machine C already has a differing configuration: adoption holds it
+# and runs no task from either version; once the conflict is decided, the
+# ordinary bootstrap runs the adopted task
+C="$(dirname "$HOME")/c-home"
+wrapper "$C" "$PWD/c"
+c="$PWD/c"
+mkdir -p "$C/.config/mise"
+printf '[env]\nC_ONLY = "1"\n' >"$C/.config/mise/config.toml"
+assert_fail "$c bootstrap --adopt file://$origin --yes 2>&1" "nothing was bootstrapped"
+assert_fail "test -e '$C/setup.log'"
+assert_succeed "$c dot pull --take-remote-all --yes"
+assert_fail "test -e '$C/setup.log'"
+assert_succeed "$c bootstrap --yes"
+assert "cat $C/setup.log" "v2"

title: docs(bootstrap): remove files in the home directory with state = "absent"
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/122
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

If you retire a dotfile, removing its entry from `[dotfiles]` leaves the file in place on every machine that already applied it. `[bootstrap.files]` can already remove it, but the docs said targets must be absolute paths, so nobody would try a home-directory path. Targets that begin with `~/` already resolve from the home directory, for both present and absent files.

```toml
[bootstrap.files."~/.oldrc"]
state = "absent"
```

`mise bootstrap files apply` (or `mise bootstrap`) removes `~/.oldrc` whatever its content. Once it is gone, apply reports `already converged`. A file you own in your home directory is removed without `sudo`. As with other absent file declarations, a directory at the target is refused rather than deleted, and a bare `~` stays a relative path and is rejected.

This PR changes docs and tests only:

- `docs/bootstrap/files.md` says targets may begin with `~/` and adds the home-directory example under "Removing resources".
- `docs/dotfiles.md` "Conflicts" now links to this for removing a file that machines still have from an old entry.

This addresses part of https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13410, which asks for declarative removal.

## Validation

`e2e/cli/test_bootstrap_system_files_no_sudo` now covers the following, with sudo disabled:
- A `~/` present target is written with the requested mode.
- A `~/` absent target is planned as `remove` and then removed.
- A second status on the removed target reports `noop`, and a second apply reports `already converged`.

That test and `test_bootstrap_system_files` pass locally, and `mise run lint` passes.

title: chore(deps): refresh Cargo.lock and handle build metadata from versions 8.0.1
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/121
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Brings in the Cargo crate updates from lockfile maintenance (#13443), rebuilt on current `main`. It also fixes a `mise upgrade --bump` regression that one of those updates would otherwise cause.

## The regression

`versions` 8.0.1 now includes SemVer build metadata when it converts a version (`to_mess()`). mise already works around the older behavior by appending that metadata itself in `chunkify_version`, so with 8.0.1 it's added twice:

```
mise upgrade --bump metatest   # pinned to 1.36.4+k3s1
# with versions 8.0.1, before this PR:
metatest = "1.37.0+k3s1+k3s1"
# after:
metatest = "1.37.0+k3s1"
```

`attach_meta` now skips metadata that the version already ends with. This works on both 8.0.0 and 8.0.1.

## Why not merge #13443

That branch is 12 commits behind `main` and still has `quick-xml` 0.38.4, which cargo-deny now rejects (RUSTSEC-2026-0194/0195). `main` already moved to patched versions through the rattler update. Under the new Renovate config it won't be rebased unless it conflicts. So this PR applies the 41 same-major-version upgrades it contained onto `main` with `cargo update --precise` (for example tera 2.4.0, toml_edit 0.25.15, uuid 1.26.1, versions 8.0.1, plus `synstructure` 0.14.0), keeping Renovate's 7-day release-age cutoff. `bun.lock` and `mise.lock` maintenance are left to next week's run.

## Validation

- `semver::` and `outdated_info::` unit tests: 26 passed with `versions` 8.0.1 and also with 8.0.0
- `e2e/cli/test_upgrade_bump_build_metadata` passes
- `cargo clippy --bin mise -- -D warnings`: clean

title: fix(release): build Windows with panic=unwind so vfox Lua errors don't abort
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/119
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes the Windows crash reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12646. Since 2026.8.9, `mise upgrade`, `mise install`, and other commands can abort on Windows with:

```
The application panicked (crashed).
Message:  panic in a function that cannot unwind
thread caused non-unwinding panic. aborting.
```

Every report involves a vfox plugin (`vfox:php`, the `winget` plugin). 2026.8.8 works.

## Cause

#12146 moved the Windows release build to the `serious` profile, which sets `panic = "abort"`. Lua reports errors with `longjmp`, and mlua deliberately longjmps across its `extern "C-unwind"` callback trampolines. This happens whenever a Rust-implemented Lua function that a plugin calls returns an error. MSVC implements `longjmp` as an SEH unwind (`RtlUnwindEx`), so under `panic=abort` the first Rust frame it crosses aborts the process. That matches the reported stack: `RtlUnwindEx → _CxxFrameHandler3 → abort`.

The `aws_lc_…_jent_entropy_switch_notime_impl` frames in the report are a symbolization artifact. The release binary ships without a PDB, so each address resolves to the nearest exported symbol. AWS-LC and jitter entropy are not involved. On Unix, `longjmp` doesn't unwind, so the Linux and macOS builds are unaffected and keep `panic=abort`.

Windows CI builds with the dev profile, which unwinds, so it never exercised this path.

## Fix

`scripts/build-tarball.ps1` sets `CARGO_PROFILE_SERIOUS_PANIC=unwind`, so Windows release builds keep fat LTO but use unwinding panics. The build output path stays the same.

## Validation

- Release builds now run a smoke test on the packaged Windows x64 binary (`scripts/smoke-test-vfox-lua-error.ps1`). A local vfox plugin `pcall`s a failing Rust-backed `json.decode` and must report that it caught the error. That is the longjmp-through-Rust path that aborted, and the Windows e2e suite can't exercise it because it uses debug builds. arm64 is skipped because the x64 runner can't execute it.
- The smoke test passes on Linux. I haven't run it on Windows, because release tarballs aren't built on ordinary PRs. It will first run on the next release PR.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5; version: unavailable.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes Windows release binary panic/unwind semantics and release CI; behavior is intentional for vfox/Lua but alters crash characteristics on that platform only.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes Windows release crashes when vfox plugins hit Lua errors raised from Rust (e.g. `json.decode`), which under MSVC + `panic=abort` abort with *panic in a function that cannot unwind* (#12646).
> 
> **`scripts/build-tarball.ps1`** overrides the `serious` profile on Windows only by setting `CARGO_PROFILE_SERIOUS_PANIC=unwind`, keeping LTO and other release set

diff:
--- .github/workflows/release.yml (+4/-0)
@@ -305,6 +305,10 @@ jobs:
         env:
           OS: windows
           ARCH: ${{matrix.arch}}
+      # The runner is x64 and cannot execute the arm64 binary.
+      - name: Smoke-test vfox Lua errors
+        if: matrix.arch == 'x64'
+        run: scripts/smoke-test-vfox-lua-error.ps1 dist/mise/bin/mise.exe
       - uses: actions/upload-artifact@043fb46d1a93c77aae656e7c1c64a875d1fc6a0a # v7
         with:
           name: tarball-${{matrix.target}}
--- scripts/build-tarball.ps1 (+8/-0)
@@ -17,6 +17,14 @@ $BaseName = "mise-v$Version-$Env:OS-$Env:ARCH"
 # OpenSSL was compiled into every release and never called.
 $Features = "rustls-native-roots,self_update,vfox/vendored-lua"
 
+# The serious profile sets `panic = "abort"`, which Windows cannot use. Lua
+# raises errors with longjmp, and mlua deliberately longjmps across its
+# `extern "C-unwind"` callback trampolines. MSVC implements longjmp as an SEH
+# unwind, so under panic=abort those frames abort the process with "panic in a
+# function that cannot unwind" whenever a vfox plugin hits a Lua error.
+# On Unix, longjmp does not unwind, so the other targets keep panic=abort.
+$Env:CARGO_PROFILE_SERIOUS_PANIC = "unwind"
+
 cargo build --profile=serious --ignore-rust-version --no-default-features --features "$Features" --target "$Target"
 cargo build --profile=serious -p mise-shim --target "$Target"
 mkdir -p dist/mise/bin
--- scripts/smoke-test-vfox-lua-error.ps1 (+49/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,49 @@
+Set-StrictMode -Version Latest
+$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
+
+# Runs a packaged mise binary through a vfox hook that catches an error raised
+# by a Rust-backed Lua function. Lua raises errors with longjmp, which MSVC
+# implements as an SEH unwind across mise's Rust frames. A release profile with
+# panic=abort turns that into "panic in a function that cannot unwind" (#12646),
+# and the debug builds the Windows e2e suite uses cannot catch it.
+
+$Mise = (Resolve-Path $args[0]).Path
+
+$Root = Join-Path ([System.IO.Path]::GetTempPath()) "mise-smoke-$([guid]::NewGuid())"
+$PluginDir = Join-Path $Root "plugin"
+New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path (Join-Path $PluginDir "hooks") | Out-Null
+
+foreach ($dir in "DATA", "CACHE", "CONFIG", "STATE") {
+    Set-Item "Env:MISE_${dir}_DIR" (Join-Path $Root $dir.ToLower())
+}
+
+# Run outside the checkout so the repository's untrusted mise.toml stays out.
+Set-Location $Root
+
+@'
+PLUGIN = {}
+PLUGIN.name = "lua-error-smoke"
+PLUGIN.version = "0.1.0"
+PLUGIN.description = "release smoke test for Lua errors raised through Rust callbacks"
+'@ | Set-Content (Join-Path $PluginDir "metadata.lua")
+
+# json.decode is implemented in Rust, so its error is raised from a Rust
+# callback frame. pcall catches it, and the hook reports whether it did.
+@'
+function PLUGIN:Available(ctx)
+    local ok = pcall(require("json").decode, "{")
+    return {
+        { version = "caught-" .. tostring(not ok) },
+    }
+end
+'@ | Set-Content (Join-Path $PluginDir "hooks/available.lua")
+
+& $Mise plugins link lua-error-smoke $PluginDir
+if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "mise plugins link exited with $LASTEXITCODE" }
+
+$Output = & $Mise ls-remote lua-error-smoke
+if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "mise ls-remote exited with $LASTEXITCODE" }
+if ($Output -notcontains "caught-true") {
+    throw "expected the hook to catch the Lua error, got: $Output"
+}
+Write-Output "vfox Lua error smoke test passed"

title: feat(tool-stub): lock stubs in their project's mise.lock
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/118
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Locked tool stubs now actually lock. `mise generate tool-stub --lock` records the stub in its project's `mise.lock`, like any `mise.toml` tool. Installs then use the recorded URLs and verify the recorded checksums, and locked mode (`--locked` / `MISE_LOCKED=1`) accepts the stub.

Reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13499.

## The bug

`--lock` used to write platform URLs and checksums into a `[lock]` section in the stub, but they were never used. The data was attached to the resolved version and then dropped, because installation resolves each request again. So:

- **Checksums were never verified.** A stub with a zeroed-out checksum installed without complaint. This has been true since the feature shipped.
- **Locked mode rejected locked stubs.** On a machine without the tool installed (a fresh CI runner, say), `MISE_LOCKED=1 ./bin/pnpm` failed with `pnpm@10.33.4 is not in the lockfile`. Putting a `mise.lock` next to the stub didn't help, because stubs had no lockfile at all.

## Stubs lock into their project's `mise.lock`

```bash
mise generate tool-stub bin/pnpm --lock
```

The stub keeps its version request, and `mise.lock` records the resolution:

```toml
# bin/pnpm
#!/usr/bin/env -S mise tool-stub
tool = "pnpm"
version = "10"
```

```toml
# mise.lock
tool-stubs = ["bin/pnpm"]

[[tools.pnpm]]
version = "10.33.4"
specifiers = ["10"]
# ...platform URLs and checksums
```

- **Finding the lockfile.** A stub walks up from where the stub file lives to the nearest project config. The directory it's run from never matters, and a symlinked stub is followed to its real location. Local and environment configs are skipped, so a committed stub locks the same way on every machine. In a monorepo with a root lockfile, the root is also worked out from where the stub lives.
- **`tool-stubs`** lists the stubs whose entries the lockfile holds. No config declares those tools, so this is how `mise lock` knows to keep their entries, refresh them (`--bump` re-resolves them too), and prune them once the stub is deleted. `mise lock <tool>` reaches stubs as well.
- **Locked mode.** A stub needs an entry for the current platform, like any other tool. Stubs no longer skip locked mode's install-time URL check (the #7729 exemption).

## Changes to `generate tool-stub --lock`

- It errors when no project config sits above the stub (`no project config found above …`). It used to write a `[lock]` section into the stub.
- It no longer pins the stub's `version` to the exact release. The pin lives in `mise.lock`.
- A `[lock]` section written by an older mise is ignored, and `--lock` removes it. Its data was never used for installs, so no lock behavior that worked is lost. Stubs whose `version` an older `--lock` already pinned keep that pin.

A mise release without this change ignores `tool-stubs` when reading a `mise.lock`, and drops it when writing one. Its

title: fix(task)!: let both spellings of a file task take it over
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/117
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Stacked on #13458 — review that one first; this PR's diff is just the convergence.

## The problem

`[tasks.hello]` and `[tasks."hello.sh"]` name one script. Since #13448 every field configures it identically under either spelling — description, env, depends, alias. A command was the one exception, and the two spellings did different things:

```bash
mkdir -p mise-tasks
printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\necho script\n' > mise-tasks/hello.sh
chmod +x mise-tasks/hello.sh
printf '[tasks.hello]\nrun = "echo inline"\n' > mise.toml
mise tasks ls --no-header
```

Before — the script is still a task, shadowed by exact-name matching:

```
hello
hello.sh
```

Under the full name (`[tasks."hello.sh"]`) it took the script over instead. The stem is what `mise tasks ls` shows and what `mise run` takes, so the spelling a config happened to use decided what it did.

After, under either spelling:

```
hello
```

## What changed

A block that declares a `run`, `run_windows`, or `file` says what its name runs, and the scripts that name reaches stop being tasks of their own. The name reaches scripts exactly as it does when configuring them, so the two spellings stay different in the one way they should be — how much they cover:

```toml
[tasks."hello.sh"]  # claims hello.sh only
[tasks.hello]       # claims every script with that stem: hello.sh and hello.js
```

Claiming is resolved before the duplicate-name bookkeeping, so the result does not depend on which block the merge loop reaches first, and a block spelling a claimed script still finds the task it became — `[tasks."hello.sh"] description` configures what `[tasks.hello] run` now runs.

Unchanged: a script the command does not outrank is left alone and decorated instead, which is what a `conf.d` fragment layering onto a script found by the config above it relies on.

## Compatibility

`[tasks.hello] run = ...` beside `mise-tasks/hello.sh` used to leave the script runnable as `mise run hello.sh`; it is now claimed. `mise run hello` already ran the inline command, so what changes is only whether the script survives beside it. To keep both, give the command a name of its own.

## Validation

- unit tests for both spellings, the multi-script stem, and a block written with a claimed script's name; three existing tests that asserted the old asymmetry are updated, including two from #13448
- new e2e test `e2e/tasks/test_task_file_task_toml_command_both_spellings`
- 429 e2e tests under `e2e/tasks/` and `e2e/config/` (non-slow), all passing
- `mise run lint`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5; version: 2.1.270.*

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

+cat <<'EOF' >mise-tasks/build.sh

title: fix(install): align per-tool progress bars in interactive installs
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/115
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

In the interactive install view, each tool's progress bar sat in the middle of the row, followed by the elapsed time and artifact name. Those vary in width (`850ms` vs `12.3s`, different artifact names), so the bars started in a different column on every row and looked ragged.

The bar is now the last cell on the row, next to the spinner, so every tool's bar lines up:

```
 aqua:BurntSushi/ripgrep@14.1.1 downloading                   2.7s  ███░░░░░░░ ◠
 node@22.23.2                   downloading                   4.2s  ███░░░░░░░ ◞
 node@22.23.2                   verifying checksum            9.2s  ████████░░ ◡
```

Rows without a bar get blank space where the bar would go, so elapsed times also end in the same column. The narrow-terminal rules for when the row bar is shown are unchanged. Text/CI output and the header bar are unaffected.

Tested by capturing a forced-TTY `mise install` of jq, node, ripgrep and go; the `tty_install_progress` unit tests pass.

> 
> The right-hand cell is now built in **`row_right`**: optional artifact, then elapsed time, then the bar (or a fixed-width blank when `layout.row_bar` is on but the tool has no weights), so bars and elapsed-time endings line up when the row template right-aligns that cell. **`refresh`** delegates to that helper instead of inlining the string.

This PR contains the following updates:

| Package | Type | Update | Change |

| [jdx/packslip](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/packslip) | action | minor | `v1.1.1` → `v1.2.0` |

---

> [!WARNING]
> Some dependencies could not be looked up. Check the Dependency Dashboard for more information.

---

### Release Notes

<details>
<summary>jdx/packslip (jdx/packslip)</summary>

### [`v1.2.0`](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/packslip/releases/tag/v1.2.0): : Shell completions and a man page

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/packslip/compare/v1.1.1...v1.2.0)

This release adds native shell completions and a man page to the packslip CLI, both shipped as signed, verifiable release resources, and fixes two problems the first releases hosted on packslip.dev turned up: an unreliable major-tag move and a CDN that answered every download with a malformed 206.

#### Added

- `packslip completion <shell>` generates self-contained completion scripts for Bash, Zsh, Fish, and PowerShell. The scripts and the CLI specification are generated from the release binary, shipped as release assets, and declared and verified as `completion/<shell>` resources in the signed inventory published at packslip.dev. ([#​84](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/packslip/issues/84), [@​jdx](https://redirect.github.com/jdx))

  ```sh
  packslip completion zsh > _packslip
  ```
- Each release now ships a generated `packslip.1` man page, attested alongside the other assets and declared and verified as a `man` resource in the signed inventory. ([#​105](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/packslip/issues/105), [@​jdx](https://redirect.github.com/jdx))

#### Fixed

- The release workflow now moves the `v1` major tag through the Git refs API instead of `git push -f`. A forced push sent the tag's tree, and GitHub's built-in token refused it because the tree touches `.github/workflows` without `workflows` permission; when the retry loop exhausted, the failing job also skipped publishing the release index. Moving the ref pushes no objects and sidesteps the check entirely. ([#​83](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/packslip/issues/83), [@​jdx](https://redirect.github.com/jdx))
- The packslip.dev Worker no longer answers plain downloads with a 206. It previously forwarded request headers to R2 as a range unconditionally, so every response was a range response with no `content-range` (malformed under RFC 9110), genuine range requests were malformed the same way, and immutable release files were re-read from R2 on every request instead of being cached. The range is now requested only when the client asks for one, `content-range` is set when it does, and immutable files are cached as intended. ([#​83](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/packslip/issues/83), [@​jdx](https://redirect.github.com/jdx))

#### Changed

- The landing pag

title: fix(activate): make bash `mise` function work without $__MISE_EXE
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/112
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes the `bash: command not found:` error reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13473.

## Problem

The `mise` function from bash activation runs `command "$__MISE_EXE" ...`. If a shell has the function but not the variable, the command expands to `command "" ...` and fails with an empty command name.

This happens in agent tools that copy shell functions into later non-interactive shells, such as Claude Code's Bash tool. Those tools copy the function definition but not ordinary environment variables. On Windows, if Claude Code starts from PowerShell (pwsh activation never sets `__MISE_EXE`), every `mise ...` call in the Bash tool fails:

```
$ mise ls
bash: command not found:
```

#9081 exported `__MISE_EXE`, but that only helps when a parent bash shell with the variable already set starts the child shell.

## Fix

The bash `mise` function now has the absolute mise path written into it at activation time. zsh, fish and bash's own `command_not_found` handler already work this way. `export __MISE_EXE=...` is still emitted for anything else that reads it.

## Tests

- Updated the bash activate snapshot.
- Extended `e2e/cli/test_activate_export`: it copies the `mise` function into `env -u __MISE_EXE bash -c ...` and checks that `mise --version` runs.

title: chore(deps): bump locked dev tools and fix communique 1.4.1 lock entry
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/111
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Renovate's communique update (#13465) failed CI in every job that installs the repo's dev tools. Renovate changed `version = "1.4.0"` to `"1.4.1"` in `mise.lock` but kept the platform blocks, so their download URLs and checksums still pointed at the v1.4.0 release. mise refuses to install when a lockfile's URLs belong to a different version than the one it names:

```
communique@1.4.1 is locked to a download URL from 1.4.0:
  https://github.com/jdx/communique/releases/download/v1.4.0/communique-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz
```

This PR rebuilds the lockfile with `mise lock --bump`, which updates the versions and their download URLs and checksums together:

- communique 1.4.0 → 1.4.1, now using the `packslip:github.com/jdx/communique` backend, which is what CI already resolves it to
- cargo-nextest 0.9.144 → 0.9.145
- git-cliff 2.14.1 → 2.14.2
- gh 2.100.0 → 2.101.0

I also ran `mise lock --upgrade`. It changed nothing, because the lockfile is already on format v2.

On macOS arm64, `MISE_LOCKED=1 mise install` installed all four bumped tools from the new lockfile. This replaces #13465.

title: fix(deps): update rattler to rattler_conda_types 0.53
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/110
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Moves the conda backend onto the rattler set released on 2026-09-17: `rattler_conda_types` 0.53.0, `rattler` 0.49.0, `rattler_virtual_packages` 7.0.0, `rattler_solve` 9.0.8, `rattler_repodata_gateway` 0.33.5, `rattler_package_streaming` 0.27.6, and the transitive `rattler_shell`, `rattler_menuinst`, `rattler_cache` and `rattler_networking` bumps they require.

These crates pin each other to exact versions, so they have to move together. Lock file maintenance (#13443) moved `rattler_solve` alone to 9.0.8 and ended up with two copies of `rattler_conda_types`, which broke the build. That PR now keeps `rattler_solve` at 9.0.7 until this one lands. Renovate hasn't opened a grouped rattler PR for this release.

## Behavior change

In 0.53, `Platform::current()` returns `Option<Platform>` and no longer assumes a known host. The conda backend now returns the error `conda backend does not support this platform` on hosts rattler doesn't recognize, where it used to rely on rattler's old behavior. Supported platforms (linux/macos x64+arm64, windows x64) behave exactly as before.

## Validation

- `cargo clippy --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean
- `cargo test --bin mise conda`: 29 passed
- e2e `backend/test_conda`, `test_conda_activation`, `test_conda_url_replacements`: all pass

title: fix(github): don't abort when a forge token has an invalid header character
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/109
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

If a resolved GitHub token contains a character that is illegal in an HTTP header — a newline is the easy way to get one — mise aborts the whole process instead of reporting a bad credential:

```console
$ MISE_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE=0 mise up
The application panicked (crashed).
Message:  called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: InvalidHeaderValue
Location: src/github.rs:924
Aborted (core dumped)
```

`src/github.rs` built the `Authorization` header with `HeaderValue::from_str(..).unwrap()`, so a malformed token became a SIGABRT with a coredump rather than an error message.

## After

```console
$ GITHUB_TOKEN=$'dummy\nvalue' mise latest 'github:jdx/mise@latest'
Error:
   0: invalid GitHub token: it contains characters that cannot be sent in an HTTP header (token redacted)
```

Exit code 1, no panic, no coredump, and the token is not echoed back.

## What changed

- All four Authorization-header sites — two in `src/github.rs`, one each in `src/gitlab.rs` and `src/forgejo.rs` — now go through a shared `tokens::bearer_header`, which maps `InvalidHeaderValue` to the redacted error above. The GitLab and Forgejo sites carried an `// Avoid panicking here. See #3547.` comment directly above the `unwrap()`; `get_headers` in those two modules now returns `Result<HeaderMap>` so the error has somewhere to go.
- `bearer_header` also calls `HeaderValue::set_sensitive(true)`, so reqwest redacts the credential from its own debug output.
- Tokens read from `github_tokens.toml`, `gitlab_tokens.toml` and `forgejo_tokens.toml` are now trimmed and dropped when blank. The environment-variable sources already did this in `env::scoped_var`, so a token with a trailing newline worked from `GITHUB_TOKEN` but panicked from the config file.
- `packslip::repo_file_request` used `github::get_headers(..).ok()?`, which would have turned this error into the misleading warning "comes from the source repository, which mise cannot read files from". It returns `Result<Option<..>>` now, so a real failure propagates and `None` still means only "unsupported forge".

No behavior change for well-formed tokens: header contents and token-source reporting are unchanged.

## Validation

- Added unit tests covering the redacted error (newline, carriage return and NUL tokens), the sensitive flag, the TOML trim, and a regression test that `github::get_headers` returns an error rather than panicking.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean; `mise run lint` clean.
- Unit suite: 4532 passed. 23 tests fail identically on this branch and on unmodified `main` in my local sandbox (pacman, `system::remote*`, `tera` path tests) — pre-existing and unrelated.
- Verified the reporter's exact reproduction no longer aborts, and that a normal `mise latest github:jdx/mise@latest` still resolves.

Reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13471

title: fix(npm): run npm_execpath scripts through aube, not the task runner
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/105
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes the `npm:` install failure reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13451.

## The problem

Every package manager exports `npm_execpath`, the executable that ran a lifecycle
script, and packages use it to re-enter *that same* manager.
`install-artifact-from-github` (2.5M weekly downloads, used by `re2` among others)
checks a prebuilt native binary it just downloaded with
`${packageManager} run verify-build`.

Embedded aube had no aube executable to name, so it named the running one — mise.
The check became `mise run verify-build`, which means "run the mise task
`verify-build`":

```
$ cat mise.toml
[tools]
"npm:re2" = { version = "1.26.1", allow_builds = ["re2"] }

$ mise install
mise npm:re2@1.26.1 Trying https://github.com/uhop/node-re2/releases/download/1.26.1/linux-x64-137.br ...
mise npm:re2@1.26.1 The verification has failed: building from sources ...
mise npm:re2@1.26.1 mise ERROR no tasks defined in …/node_modules/re2. Are you in a project directory?
mise npm:re2@1.26.1 The rebuild has failed: exit code 1.
```

The artifact was fine — it was never tested. re2 fell back to compiling from
source, which needs a working C++ toolchain. A package with no source-build
fallback fails the install outright.

## After

Same config, same machine:

```
$ mise install
mise npm:re2@1.26.1 Trying https://github.com/uhop/node-re2/releases/download/1.26.1/linux-x64-137.br ...
mise npm:re2@1.26.1 Writing to build/Release/re2.node ...
mise npm:re2@1.26.1 Done.
mise ✓ npm:re2@1.26.1  4.3s
```

The verification runs and passes, the prebuilt binary is kept, and nothing is
compiled (no object files under the install tree). 4.3s including the download,
against ~9s of C++ plus a toolchain before.

## How

aube 2.3.0 exports a shim for `npm_execpath` that re-enters aube's CLI through
the host, marked with a private `__aube-cli` argv token
(aubepkg/aube#1565). mise answers it the way it already answers
`__node-gyp-bootstrap`, forwarding the argv to `aube::cli_main`, which strips the
token — so the package script gets aube's `run` (and `exec`, and `install`)
instead of mise's task runner.

No new user-facing surface: `__aube-cli` is private to the shim, and nothing
changes for `npm.shell_out = true`.

The aube bump moves every aube workspace crate together. `aube` requires its
siblings at `"2"`, so bumping `aube` alone leaves `aube-scripts` — the half that
stamps the shim — on 2.2.17 and the fix inert.

## Validation

`cargo check --locked`, `cargo test --locked --bin mise aube` (37 tests) and
`… task::workspace::node::tests` (29) pass. `e2e/backend/test_npm_aube_cli_trampoline`
covers the trampoline running a package script and the re2 install asserting the
`no tasks defined` signature is gone — with stderr folded in, since the e2e
assert helpers capture stdout only.

+# Regression for embedded-aube lifecycle scripts that re-invoke their package
+# manager (jdx/mise#13451).
+#
+# Every package manager exports npm_execpath, and packages use it to re-enter
+# the same one. Embedded, aube points it at a shim that calls:
+#   $AUBE_CLI_EXE __aube-cli <args>
+# mise must intercept that before naked-run rewriting, or a package verifying
+# its prebuilt binary with `${npm_execpath} run verify-build` runs
+# `mise run verify-build`, fails with "no tasks defined", and concludes a
+# perfectly good artifact is broken.
+

+{
+  "name": "aube-cli-trampoline-probe",
+  "version": "1.0.0",
+  "private": true,
+  "scripts": { "verify-build": "echo verified-by-aube" }
+}
+JSON
+
+# The trampoline reaches aube's own run, not mise's task runner. The bug
+# signature lands on stderr, which the success-path assertions do not capture
+# on their own, so fold it in.
+assert_contains "mise __aube-cli run --no-install verify-build" "verified-by-aube"
+assert_not_contains "mise __aube-cli run --no-install verify-build 2>&1" "no tasks defined"
+
+# Going through the task runner is the bug path (naked-run rewrite).
+assert_fail "mise run __aube-cli run --no-install verify-build"
+
+# The reported case: re2's install script downloads a prebuilt binary and
+# checks it with `${npm_execpath} run verify-build`. The check has to run as a
+# package script — if it lands in mise's task runner the install still
+# succeeds, just after an unnecessary source build, so assert the failure
+# signature rather than the exit status.
+cat >mise.toml <<'TOML'
+[tools]
+node = "24"
+"npm:re2" = { version = "1.26.1", allow_builds = ["re2"] }
+TOML
+
+# One install, both guarantees: `assert_not_contains` fails the test when the
+# command exits non-zero, so this covers the install succeeding *and* the
+# verification never reaching mise's task runner.
+assert_not_contains "mise install 2>&1" "no tasks defined"

title: feat(dotfiles): deliver warnings from background captures
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/104
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Dotfiles commands now deliver capture warnings that would otherwise remain in background watcher logs. This covers credential-named files selected for plaintext storage and files left out of new checkpoints after an include list is narrowed.

Explicit saves and tracking report warnings in their output. Bootstrap reports them during its run. The watcher and automatic application keep pending notices for the next `mise dot` command other than `watch`, or a bare `mise bootstrap`:

```sh
mise dot watch --once
mise dot paths
```

The second command delivers pending notices and shows the current selection. Non-watch dotfiles commands and bare `mise bootstrap` also deliver notices generated while they run, including on failure. Matching plaintext warnings are deduplicated within the process, and repeated background observations do not add duplicate pending notices. Protective checkpoints retain their warnings if the operation fails before reporting them. Capture and selection-narrowing warnings are delivered once the Git snapshot is durable, before metadata-cache, index, or enrollment writes that can fail. Failed snapshots and failed commits do not generate notices claiming files were saved. Scan warnings are delivered even when a save finds no changes or cannot create a snapshot.

Include patterns also select files created later. With this configuration, a new `~/.config/fish/functions/secrets.fish` is captured in plaintext even if it did not exist when tracking began:

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.config/fish" = { mode = "track", include = ["**"] }
```

Background capture can save and share the file before the queued warning is read. Warnings do not block capture or publication. To encrypt the selected contents, configure encryption before capturing private files:

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.config/fish" = { mode = "track", include = ["**"], encrypt = true }
```

This changes warning delivery, not file selection or encryption. Narrowing a list leaves earlier versions in history; selecting a credential-named file without encryption still stores it in plaintext and can share it with the origin.

Tests cover pending-notice storage, single delivery, watcher deferral, bootstrap output, and include-list narrowing. A regression test creates a credential-named file after configuring a broad include and verifies plaintext capture, deferred warning delivery, and clearing the pending notice.

Regression coverage also checks warning delivery after a metadata-cache failure, silence for failed snapshots and commits, and pending notices delivered by a failed bootstrap. Validation includes checkpoint and reconciliation unit tests, focused dotfiles end-to-end tests, linting, and the full documentation build.

+### Capture warnings
+
+Saves warn when an include list selects a credential-named file for
+plaintext storage. They also report when a changed include list leaves
+out files that an earlier checkpoint contained. The latter notice means
+those paths stop appearing in new checkpoints; their earlier versions

+capture stores that warning for a later command; the file can already be
+saved and shared with the origin before you see it. Warnings do not block
+capture or publication.

+before capturing private files:

+"~/.config/fish" = { mode = "track", include = ["**"], encrypt = true }
+```

+protects selected contents; it does not remove earlier plaintext versions
+from history. See [remove plaintext from history](#remove-plaintext-from-history).
+
+Warnings appear according to how the capture runs:
+
+| Capture                    | Where to read the warning                                              |
+| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
+| Explicit save or tracking  | In that command's output                                               |
+| Bootstrap                  | During the bootstrap command                                           |
+| Watcher or automatic apply | At the next `mise dot` command other than `watch`, or `mise bootstrap` |
+
+For example, after the watcher applies a narrower include list, run:
+
+```sh
+mise dot paths
+```

+A notice about a narrowed include list names the earlier checkpoint that
+holds the omitted paths.
+Non-watch dotfiles commands and `mise bootstrap` also deliver notices produced while they run, including
+when the command fails. Matching plaintext warnings are shown once per
+process, even if both a stored notice and the command's capture report them.
+A background condition can be reported again after its previous notice
+has been delivered.
+
+Warnings from protective checkpoints are kept until they can be reported.
+If an operation fails after saving its protective checkpoint, its pending
+notices remain available to a later dotfiles command. These notices do not
+change selection or encryption settings; use `encrypt = true` for private
+contents and review [existing plaintext history](#remove-plaintext-from-history)

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/103
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Third in a series decoupling `src/system` from `src/cli`. Stacked on #13480 — review that one first.

## Why

`declaration_file` and `read_document` lived in `cli::dotfiles::track`, but neither is specific to dotfiles or to the CLI:

- `mise settings set` and `mise settings unset` both call `declaration_file` to find the config file to edit.
- `system::history::sync::origin` called both, reaching up into `cli`.

`declaration_file` answers "which global config file do commands write to — `config.toml`, or `config.local.toml` for machine-only entries". That's a config concern.

## What changes

Both move to a new `config::edit` module. `cli::dotfiles::track` re-exports them, so `super::track::read_document(...)` in `untrack.rs` and the other dotfiles subcommands is unchanged.

## Effect

`system -> cli` references drop from **5 to 2**:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `cli::dotfiles::track` | 3 | **0** |
| `cli::args::ToolArg` | 2 | 2 |

## What's left

The last two are `cli::args::ToolArg` in `system/packages/brew/source.rs`. `ToolArg` isn't really a CLI argument type — `toolset` (18 refs), `task` (14), `shims` (7), `config` (3), `env` and `daemons` all depend on it too. Moving it out of `cli::args` would take `system -> cli` to zero *and* decouple those five modules, so it deserves its own PR rather than being tacked on here.

## Notes

No behaviour change. `hk fix` clean; `config::` (323), `system::history::sync` (67) and `cli::dotfiles::` (9) tests pass.

Placement of `config::edit` is the one judgment call here — happy to move these elsewhere if you'd rather they sat in `config/mod.rs` or kept a dotfiles-specific name.

Second in a series decoupling `src/system` from `src/cli`, following #13457.

## Why

`open`, `resolve` and `short` lived in `cli::dotfiles::history`, but they're domain logic rather than presentation — that module already imports `Store`, `Entry` and `TrackedSet` from `crate::system::history`. `display_arg` and `local_time` stay in `cli` — those are genuinely display helpers.

title: registry: add nim
body:
Adds `nim` to the mise registry via the `http:` backend using official precompiled release tarballs from [nim-lang.org](https://nim-lang.org).

## Popularity

- GitHub: 18.2k stars, 1.5k forks, active development ([nim-lang/Nim](https://github.com/nim-lang/Nim))
- Ecosystem: The official compiler and toolchain for the Nim programming language ([nim-lang.org](https://nim-lang.org))

## Implementation Details

- **Backend**: Native `http:nim` backend downloading official prebuilt archives directly from `https://nim-lang.org/download/`.
- **Platforms Supported**:
  - `linux-x64`
  - `linux-arm64` (versions >= 2.2.8)
  - `macos-x64` (versions >= 2.2.8)
  - `macos-arm64` (versions >= 2.2.8)
  - `windows-x64`
  - `windows-arm64` (runs x64 under emulation)
- **Version Discovery**: Scraped directly from `https://nim-lang.org/install.html`, avoiding GitHub API rate limits.
- **Checksums**: Verifies SHA-256 against upstream `.sha256` files.
- **Project Detection**: Detects `*.nimble`, `nimble.lock`, `nim.cfg`, and `config.nims`.
- **Idiomatic Version File**: Supports `.nim-version`.
- **Binaries**: Installs `atlas`, `nim`, `nimble`, `nimgrep`, `nimpretty`, `nimsuggest`, and `testament`.

## Verification

```sh
mise use nim@latest
nim --version
nimble --version
```

+url = "https://nim-lang.org/download/nim-{{ version }}-macosx_x64.tar.xz"
+
+[backends.options.platforms.macos-arm64]
+checksum_url = "https://nim-lang.org/download/nim-{{ version }}-macosx_arm64.tar.xz.sha256"
+url = "https://nim-lang.org/download/nim-{{ version }}-macosx_arm64.tar.xz"

+checksum_url = "https://nim-lang.org/download/nim-{{ version }}_x64.zip.sha256"
+url = "https://nim-lang.org/download/nim-{{ version }}_x64.zip"

title: fix(task): allow TOML commands to replace file tasks
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/87
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## The problem

A `[tasks.<name>]` block whose name matched an auto-discovered [file task](https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/file-tasks.html) could not give it a command, and what happened instead depended on which spelling you used.

```bash
mkdir -p mise-tasks
printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\necho script\n' > mise-tasks/hello.sh
chmod +x mise-tasks/hello.sh
```

With `[tasks."hello.sh"] run = "echo inline"`, the `run` was **silently discarded** and the script ran anyway — no warning, nothing in `mise tasks`:

```
[hello] $ /tmp/demo/mise-tasks/hello.sh
script
```

With `[tasks.hello] run = "echo inline"`, the command ran but the script stayed a second task, shadowed by exact-name matching:

```
$ mise tasks ls --no-header
hello
hello.sh
```

Since #13448 every other field — description, env, depends, alias — configures the script identically under both spellings. A command was the one exception, and the stem is the spelling `mise tasks ls` shows and `mise run` takes.

## What changed

A block that declares `run`, `run_windows`, or `file` says what its name runs, and the discovered scripts that name reaches stop being tasks of their own. Both spellings now do this:

```toml
[tasks.hello] # or [tasks."hello.sh"]
run = "echo hi" # runs instead of mise-tasks/hello.sh
```

```
$ mise tasks ls --no-header
hello
```

The name reaches scripts the same way it does when configuring them, so the spellings differ only in how much they cover: `[tasks."hello.sh"]` claims that script, `[tasks.hello]` claims every script sharing the stem — both `hello.sh` and `hello.js`, if both exist.

Claiming is resolved before the duplicate-name bookkeeping, so the result does not depend on which block the merge reaches first, and a block written with a claimed script's name still configures the task it became — `[tasks."hello.sh"] description` decorates what `[tasks.hello] run` now runs.

### Precedence is unchanged

A script is in the running because some config's `task_config.includes` found it, so taking it over needs that config's standing or better. A command from further down the chain decorates the script and leaves it running, under either spelling — which is what a `conf.d` fragment layering onto a script found by the config above it relies on. ## Why

`src/system` — the largest module in the crate at ~92k LOC — depends on `crate::cli::version` for platform constants and version identity. Meanwhile `cli` already depends on `system` in roughly 200 places. The arrow points the wrong way, and that cycle blocks extracting `system` into its own crate later.

None of the moved items are CLI concerns.

## What moves

**To `src/platform.rs`** (alongside the existing `Platform`, `LinuxOsRelease`, `detect_libc`):

- `OS`, `ARCH`
- `normalize_os`, `normalize_arch`
- `os_selector_matches`, `is_os_family_selector`

**To a new `src/version.rs`** (following the precedent of `src/build_time.rs`):

- `V`, `VERSION_PLAIN`, `VERSION`

`cli::version` keeps what is genuinely CLI: the `Version` command, `print_version_if_requested`, `show_latest`, `check_for_new_version` and the update hints.

The three tests covering the moved functions (`test_normalize_os`, `test_normalize_arch`, `test_os_selector_matches`) move to `platform.rs` with them.

## Effect

`system -> cli` references drop from **23 to 11**:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `cli::version` | 12 | **0** |
| `cli::dotfiles` | 9 | 9 |
| `cli::args` | 2 | 2 |

The remaining 11 need logic relocated rather than a straight move, so they're left for follow-ups:

- **9 × `cli::dotfiles`** — `history::{open, resolve, short}` and `track::{declaration_file, read_document}`, all called from `system/history/`. These belong in `system::history` with `cli` as a thin caller.
- **2 × `cli::args::ToolArg`** — in `system/packages/brew/source.rs`.

## Notes

No behaviour change — this is a pure move plus import updates across 30 files.

`cargo check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets` and `cargo fmt` are clean; the 17 `platform::tests` pass, including the three moved ones.

title: test: don't reset the shared fixture tree in --list invocations
body:
## The problem

`cargo nextest run` can abort during its list phase, before a single test has
run:

```
thread '<unnamed>' panicked at src/test.rs:93:28:
called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: "No such file or directory" }

thread '<unnamed>' panicked at .../core/src/panicking.rs:225:5:
panic in a function that cannot unwind
...
13: mise::test::init::_::__ctor_private
command `.../deps/mise-<hash> --list --format terse --ignored` aborted with signal 6 (SIGABRT)
```

nextest lists each test binary by executing it twice — `--list --format
terse`, with and without `--ignored` — and those two processes run
concurrently. Both run the test ctor, which resets the shared fixture tree:

```rust
file::remove_all(&*env::HOME.join("cwd")).unwrap();
file::create_dir_all(&*env::HOME.join("cwd").join(".mise").join("tasks")).unwrap();
env::set_current_dir(env::HOME.join("cwd")).unwrap();
// ... a dozen fixture writes, one via env::current_dir()
```

`$HOME` in tests is the compile-time `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR/test`, shared by
every process of the same build. One process's `remove_all()` unlinks the
directory the other just `set_current_dir()`'d into; that process is left on
a dead inode and aborts at the ctor's next `current_dir()` call. The window
is only the dozen writes between the chdir and that call, so CI usually wins
the timing — a loaded machine doesn't. A nix-sandbox build on aarch64-darwin
hit it on the first attempt.

## Now

Invocations that only list tests skip the ctor. Listing enumerates
compiled-in test names; it needs neither the fixture tree nor a cwd.

The run phase is unchanged: nextest executes tests in per-test processes with
no `--list` argument, and `.config/nextest.toml`'s `test-threads = 1` already
serializes those against the shared fixture path — the listing pair was the
one concurrent execution left.

## Validation

- With the guard, a from-scratch nix-sandbox build on aarch64-darwin running
  `cargo nextest run --all-features --no-fail-fast` (profile `ci-shared`)
  completes: `Summary [ 154.579s] 4163 tests run: 4163 passed (8 slow), 348
  skipped`. The same build without the guard aborts in the list phase as
  above.
- Context: found while moving nix packaging (nixpkgs and downstream) onto
  cargo-nextest, the runner this suite is written for — under plain `cargo
  test`'s single shared process, a dropped-tempdir cwd strands ~23 unrelated
  `current_dir()`-calling tests, which process-per-test resolves.

title: fix(self-update): fail before downloading when the install dir is not writable
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/84
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## The problem

`mise self-update` on an install the current user cannot write to downloads the entire release and *then* fails, with a message that names a temp file nobody has seen and no directory at all:

```
Downloading...
[00:00:03] [========================================] 40.91 MiB/40.91 MiB (0s) Done
Verifying downloaded file...
Extracting archive... Done
Replacing binary file... mise ERROR IoError: Permission denied (os error 13) at path "/usr/local/bin/.mise.__temp__XKV5Oz"
```

This is the ordinary shape of a root-owned install being updated by a normal user: a `/usr/local/bin/mise` left by the install script, or an install under `/opt`. Replacing the binary goes through `self-replace`, which renames the running mise out of its directory and writes the new one in its place — both are writes to the *directory*, not to the file — so the failure arrives at the last step, after everything has been fetched.

## Now

The install directory is probed once the update is known to be needed, before anything is downloaded:

```
$ mise self-update
mise ERROR cannot replace /usr/local/bin/mise: /usr/local/bin is not writable by the current user

Either run `sudo mise self-update` to update this install, or update mise the same way you installed it.
```

Naming the binary matters as much as naming the directory: the install that is stuck is often not the one the user thinks they are running. The report this came from was a `/usr/local/bin/mise` at 2026.9.1 shadowing a package-managed `/usr/bin/mise` at 2026.9.12 — the path is what gives that away.

Two details of the placement:

- **After the up-to-date comparison**, so `mise self-update` on a read-only install with nothing to update still reports "mise is already up to date" rather than a permission problem it was never going to hit.
- **Only for permission and read-only-filesystem errors.** Any other probe failure is ignored and left to the update itself, which reports the real operation rather than a probe standing in for it.

When the install also ships packager instructions, those are appended to the message.

## Validation

- New e2e test `e2e/cli/test_self_update_not_writable`: a mise in a mode `a-w` directory reports the directory, the binary, and the `sudo` suggestion, and still reports "already up to date" when asked for the version it has. Skipped under a root test runner, which ignores the mode bits, in the same shape `e2e/backend/test_packslip_resources` already uses.
- Unit tests for the probe (writable directory leaves nothing behind, unwritable one classifies as fatal), the error classification, and the message.
- `mise run lint-fix`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`.

title: chore(ci): comment on a discussion when the PR implementing it merges
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/83
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

GitHub links merged pull requests to **issues** through `Closes #N`, but discussions have no equivalent. A discussion that asks for a feature stays open and unlinked after the pull request implementing it merges, so the person who filed it is never told it shipped and the thread has to be closed by hand.

This adds a workflow that runs when a pull request merges, scans its body for discussion references, and comments on each referenced discussion with a link back to the pull request.

| In the PR body | Effect on the discussion |
|---|---|
| `Closes #N`, `Fixes #N`, `Resolves #N` | Comment, then close as `RESOLVED` |
| `Refs #N`, `Discussion: #N` | Comment only |

A PR titled `feat(status): show the last cron start and next scheduled time` whose body ends in `Closes #901` posts this on discussion #901 the moment it merges:

> Implemented in [#902](https://github.com/jdx/pitchfork/pull/902): feat(status): show the last cron start and next scheduled time

Numbers that turn out to be issues or pull requests are skipped, so GitHub's native issue linking is unaffected, and a pull request whose body references no discussion does nothing at all. Only same-repository references (`#42`) are recognized, not `owner/repo#42`.

The action is pinned to `jdx/link-discussion-action@38e7537` — a fork of [`gaojunran/link-discussion-action`](https://github.com/gaojunran/link-discussion-action) v0.1 (MIT) taken at that same commit, so the code that runs against this repository's token is not controlled by a third-party account. It authenticates with the automatic `GITHUB_TOKEN` scoped to `discussions: write` and `pull-requests: read`; no new secrets are required.

This has been running in [jdx/pitchfork](https://github.com/jdx/pitchfork) since [#596](https://github.com/jdx/pitchfork/pull/596).

> **Overview**

>

title: feat(cli): colour the help page mise prints, and give it a logo
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/81
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Colour

mise handles `usage::Error::Help` itself rather than letting `parse()` exit, so the colour policy `parse()` would have applied has to be applied here — and it was not. Every help page mise printed was monochrome, while the same page from a CLI that lets `parse()` handle it came out coloured.

Each of the six places that print a page now renders through `Style::auto()`, or `auto_stderr()` for the one that goes to stderr. A page is coloured on a terminal, plain in a pipe, and `NO_COLOR` is respected.

## Logo

mise's mark — the chef's toque and the wink — in block characters, using the `logo` node [usage 6.11](https://github.com/jdx/usage/releases/tag/v6.11.0) adds. It is a text file (`src/cli/logo.txt`) so it can be edited by looking at it.

Where it lands is decided by the terminal's width, not the spec: in the right margin when there is room, above the page as a banner when there is not, and nowhere at all on a terminal narrower than the art. It appears on `mise` and `mise --help` only, never on subcommand pages, and it is not part of generated docs or man pages.

## Two fixes that need no code here

usage 6.11 also brings these, and mise gets them by upgrading:

**Help is laid out at the terminal's real width.** Width used to come from `COLUMNS` alone, which no POSIX shell exports, so mise wrapped at 80 columns however wide the terminal was.

**A list of examples has a blank line between entries.** mise's front page has twenty; they used to read as a wall of commands.

At 140 columns, `mise` now prints:

```
Dev tools, env vars, and tasks in one CLI                                                     ▄▄  ▄▄▄  ▄▄
                                                                                             ▟  ▙▟   ▙▟  ▙
Usage: mise [FLAGS] [TASK] [SUBCOMMAND]                                                      ▜▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▛
                                                                                              ▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀
Commands:                                                                                      ▗▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▖
  activate      Print the script to activate mise in an interactive shell                      ▌ ▀   ▔ ▐
  backends      Manage backends [aliases: b, backend, backend-list]                            ▝▄ ▀▄▀ ▄▘
  bin-paths     List all the active runtime bin paths
```

against the previous 80-column monochrome page with no logo.

## Adoption

The three `usage` crate floors move from `6.8` to `6.11`, and the `usage` tool from `6.10.0` to `6.11.0`.

**Worth a look:** relocking switched the `usage` tool's backend from `aqua:jdx/usage` to `packslip:github.com/jdx/usage`, and dropped its `url_api` fields. That is mise's own resolution now that the usage release publishes a packslip, and it matches `aube` and `mr-boxington`, which already use that backend in this lock — but it is a backend change riding inside a

title: fix(task): preserve script execution and dependencies in metadata overlays
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/80
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes metadata-only task definitions that could make `mise run` exit successfully without running the intended script or dependencies. Reported in #13446.

For an executable script at `mise-tasks/hello.sh`, you can now configure its description and environment using the same name you pass to `mise run`:

```toml
[tasks.hello]
description = "Say hello"
env = { GREETING = "hi" }
```

Previously, this created an empty `hello` task that shadowed the script. Now `mise run hello` runs `hello.sh` with `GREETING=hi`, and `mise tasks ls` shows the description. The full spelling, `[tasks."hello.sh"]`, continues to work.

### Both spellings behave the same

`[tasks.hello]` and `[tasks."hello.sh"]` name one script, so the spelling you pick never changes what the block does. Dependencies work under either:

```toml
[tasks.hello] # or [tasks."hello.sh"]
description = "Say hello after linting"
depends = ["lint"]
```

`mise run hello` runs `lint` and then the script, whichever name the block used. Previously only the full name could do this; under the extension-free name a `depends` made a separate group that shadowed the script — so the name `mise tasks ls` shows and `mise run` accepts was the one that silently did something else.

Only a block declaring its own `run`, `run_windows`, or `file` still defines a separate task. If an inline command already uses the name `hello` elsewhere, metadata under `[tasks.hello]` applies to that task, and the script stays reachable as `mise run hello.sh`.

A script takes only its highest-precedence definition, and because the two spellings name one script they compete for that single slot: a `[tasks.hello]` in `mise.local.toml` replaces a `[tasks."hello.sh"]` in `mise.toml` rather than adding to it. Lower-precedence blocks contribute nothing, not even additive fields such as `env` or `alias` — the rule from #11103, now applied across spellings as well as within one. A block using the extension-free name applies to all scripts sharing that name; the full name targets one. Matching preserves monorepo path prefixes.

### Preserve dependencies when layering task groups

A group such as `[tasks.check] depends = ["lint", "test"]` now keeps its dependencies when `mise.local.toml` adds a description. Previously, the group could be dropped during merging, leaving an empty task. Blocks that add dependencies to an existing inline command continue to extend that command.

The docs now separate script configuration, dependency groups, and config layering, with examples of each naming rule. Warnings for unmatched metadata-only blocks remain outside this change.

### Validation

- Regression coverage includes script execution, task listing and validation, inline-task precedence, mixed name spellings, shared script names, monorepo paths, and dependency-group layering.
- 330 task e2e tests pass, plus lint and Clippy, re-run against the fin

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+# A file task's name keeps its extension ("hello.sh") while `mise run` and
+# `mise tasks ls` both address it by the stem ("hello"), so `[tasks.hello]` is
+# the block people write to attach metadata to `mise-tasks/hello.sh`. Keyed on
+# the exact name it used to become a separate task with no executable content
+# that shadowed the script, and `mise run hello` exited 0 having run nothing.
+
+mkdir -p mise-tasks
+cat >mise-tasks/hello.sh <<'SCRIPT'
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+echo "ran-hello-marker GREETING=$GREETING"
+SCRIPT
+chmod +x mise-tasks/hello.sh
+
+cat >mise.toml <<'TOML'
+[tasks.hello]
+description = "overlaid description"
+env = { GREETING = "hi" }
+TOML
+
+mise trust
+
+# The block overlays the script instead of shadowing it, so there is one task.
+assert "mise tasks ls --no-header" "hello  overlaid description"
+
+out="$(mise run hello)"
+assert_contains_text "$out" "ran-hello-marker GREETING=hi"
+
+count="$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -c 'ran-hello-marker' || true)"
+if [[ $count != "1" ]]; then
+  echo "FAIL: expected the script to run exactly once, but 'ran-hello-marker' appeared $count time(s):"
+  printf '%s\n' "$out"
+  exit 1
+fi
+
+# The name carrying the extension keeps working.
+assert_contains "mise run hello.sh" "ran-hello-marker GREETING=hi"
+
+# The merged task is a real task, not the "no executable content" shape.
+assert_contains "mise tasks validate" "validated successfully"
+
+# The spelling must not change what a block does, so a `depends` under the
+# extension-stripped name reaches the script exactly as it does under the full
+# name: the dependency runs and then the script does.
+for spelling in hello hello.sh; do
+  cat >mise.toml <<TOML
+[tasks.lint]
+run = "echo lint-ran"
+
+[tasks."$spelling"]
+depends = ["lint"]
+TOML
+
+  out="$(mise run hello)"
+  assert_contains_text "$out" "lint-ran"
+  assert_contains_text "$out" "ran-hello-marker"
+  # One task: the script is not listed separately under its full name.
+  assert_not_contains "mise tasks ls --no-header" "hello.sh"
+done
+
+# An inline block with its own command still wins over the file task, and a
+# metadata-only block at higher precedence overlays that inline base rather
+# than the script.
+cat >mise.toml <<'TOML'
+[tasks.hello]
+run = "echo inline-ran"
+TOML
+cat >mise.local.toml <<'TOML'
+[tasks.hello]
+description = "from local"
+TOML
+
+mise trust
+
+assert_contains "mise tasks ls --no-header" "from local"
+out="$(mise run hello)"
+assert_contains_text "$out" "inline-ran"
+assert_not_contains_text "$out" "ran-hello-marker"
+
+# A lower-precedence block of the other spelling must neither overwrite the
+# higher-precedence one nor survive as a task shadowing the script.
+rm -f mise.local.toml
+cat >mise.toml <<'TOML'
+[tasks.hello]
+description = "low precedence"
+TOML
+cat >mise.local.toml <<'TOML'
+[tasks."hello.sh"]
+description = "high precedence"
+TOML
+
+mise trust
+mise trust ./mise.local.toml
+
+assert "mise tasks ls --no-header" "hello  high precedence"
+assert_contains "mise run hello" "ran-hello-marker"
+
+# A script takes only its highest-precedence definition, so the `depends` in
+# `mise.toml` does not survive the description in `mise.local.toml`. The two

title: test(daemons): make the port-slot test deterministic
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/79
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`daemons::ports::tests::every_worktree_of_a_bare_repository_is_offset` fails at
random on unrelated pull requests — twice so far on `trusted / unit-macos`, most
recently on #13432, which touches nothing under `src/daemons`.

`slot()` maps a linked worktree's canonical root into 511 slots, so two roots
under a random `tempfile::tempdir()` collide about once in 511 runs. Three tests
asserted that two such slots differ, which is not a property the code provides:

```rust
assert_ne!(slots[0], slots[1]);        // every_worktree_of_a_bare_repository_is_offset
assert_ne!(slot(&one), slot(&two));    // linked_worktrees_are_stable_and_distinct
assert_ne!(slot(&nested), slot(&sibling));  // nested_project_roots_inherit_their_checkout
```

Nothing is wrong with port allocation itself. A bounded slot space means
collisions are expected; what the allocator guarantees is that a given root
always lands on the same slot, in `1..SLOTS`, and never on slot 0, which belongs
to the primary checkout.

## What changed

`slot()` now delegates its hashing step to a private `hashed_slot(root)`, and
the tests pin what the slot is derived from rather than comparing two roots to
each other:

```rust
assert_eq!(slot(&root), expected_slot(&root), "{name} hashes its root");
```

`expected_slot` works the slot out in the test — `1 + hash % (SLOTS - 1)` —
rather than calling `hashed_slot`, so a changed formula fails instead of moving
both sides of the assertion together. It still reads the hash through
`hash::hash_to_str`: a golden hex digest would pin `Path`'s `Hash`
implementation, which std does not promise to keep stable across releases and
which `PortClaim` persistence is designed to tolerate changing.

That keeps the coverage the `assert_ne!`s were really providing — a `slot` that
ignored the path, returned a constant, or hashed the enclosing checkout instead
of the project root still fails, which is the regression the sibling-project
assertions guarded against. A new `distinct_roots_spread_across_the_slot_range`
covers the spread over 64 fixed synthetic paths, needing no filesystem and no
tempdir, so its inputs are identical on every run and every platform.
`linked_worktrees_are_stable_and_distinct` is renamed to
`linked_worktrees_get_their_own_stable_slot` to match what it now asserts.

Port values are unchanged: `hash_to_str(&PathBuf)` and `hash_to_str(&&Path)`
both reach `Path::hash`, so no existing worktree moves ports.

## Validation

The bare-repository test body was temporarily wrapped in a 4000-iteration loop
over real tempdirs, counting the old assertion instead of asserting it:

```
old assert_ne! would have failed 7/4000 times
```

0.175%, matching the predicted 1/511. The new assertions held in all 4000
iterations. The oracle was checked by mutation: dropping the `1 +` from
`hashed_slot` and widening its modulus to `SLOTS` fails 4 of the 9 tests, where

title: feat(bootstrap): remove module resources with unapply
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/77
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Removing a bootstrap module from `env` leaves its resources on the machine. `mise bootstrap unapply <ENV>…` removes the managed files, directories, user services, and dotfile entries and edits contributed by one or more modules.

Remove the module from `env` in `miserc.toml`, keep its configuration file on disk, then preview and confirm cleanup:

```sh
mise bootstrap unapply ssh --dry-run
mise bootstrap unapply ssh
```

The command temporarily selects the named environments alongside the remaining selection, so it works after a module has been deselected. To remove several modules together, use `mise bootstrap unapply ssh gpg`.

## Removal behavior

Mise compares the current configuration with and without the named environments; it does not maintain a history of applied resources. Keep the module declarations until cleanup is complete.

- Resources still declared present by the base configuration or another selected environment are preserved.
- Changed targets are skipped with a reason unless `--force` is supplied. Directories must be empty after the planned removals; unreadable directories and managed paths with an unexpected type are kept even with `--force`.
- Source files and configuration entries are preserved. Declarations of `state = "absent"` are not reversed.
- Removal requires confirmation. `--yes`, the global `--yes`, `MISE_YES`, and the `yes` setting approve it without a prompt; mise enables `yes` in CI.

Packages, repositories, and Compose projects require separate cleanup, with guidance printed for those declarations. Package pruning is not limited to one module. Other bootstrap sections, including system services, are outside the command's scope. `--prompt-secrets` supports configurations that require secret inputs.

## Validation

The PR adds e2e coverage for previews, shared resources, changed targets, deselected environments, directory and path safeguards, confirmation, and repeated removal, plus unit coverage for environment argument forwarding and service-status classification.

Editorial validation: `mise run lint-fix`, `cargo check --all-features`, VitePress build, six TOML examples, 58 rendered internal links and anchors, and consistency between source help, the usage specification, CLI reference, and man page. Runtime tests were not rerun for the editorial update.

Closes the manual-cleanup gap described in [#13437](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13437); builds on the module documentation in #13439.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5; version: 2.1.270.*

> Destructive filesystem and user-service removal with conservative planning, but mistakes or `--force` could delete user data; confirmation defaults to no in non-interactive runs.

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/75
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Document how to organize optional machine setup into modules using existing config environments. Each module groups its packages, dotfiles, and services in one file; each machine selects the modules it needs.

For example, keep shared setup in `~/.config/mise/config.toml`, define SSH and GPG setup in `config.ssh.toml` and `config.gpg.toml`, then select both by default:

```toml
# ~/.config/mise/miserc.toml
env = ["ssh", "gpg"]
```

Run `mise bootstrap --dry-run` to preview the combined setup and `mise bootstrap` to apply it. Use `mise -E ssh,gpg bootstrap` for one invocation, or each remote host's `mise_env` list for host-specific selection.

The guide includes a Linux SSH module example, explains same-directory environment precedence and resource origins, and distinguishes optional modules from always-loaded configuration. It also explains that deselecting a module does not undo its resources: dotfiles must be unapplied while selected, and package pruning has manager-specific scope.

Docs only; no runtime behavior change. Addresses the composition use case in [#13437](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13437).

## Validation

Documentation build and focused Markdown checks passed. All 11 TOML examples in the changed pages parse, and the module section's links and rendered anchors resolve. Precedence and cleanup guidance were checked against the implementation; the Linux SSH service was not run on this macOS host.

+## Modules
+
+Use [config environments](/configuration/environments.html) to group optional
+machine setup by application or role. Each environment file can declare its
+packages, dotfiles, and services together. These files act as modules using
+mise's existing configuration system.
+
+### Define a module
+
+Keep shared setup in `~/.config/mise/config.toml` and put optional setup in
+`config.<name>.toml` alongside it. For example, this SSH module targets a Linux
+machine using apt and a systemd user session. It installs the client, links an
+existing SSH config from your dotfiles checkout, and runs an agent:
+
+```toml [~/.config/mise/config.ssh.toml]
+[bootstrap.packages]
+"apt:openssh-client" = "latest"
+
+[dotfiles]
+"~/.ssh/config" = "~/src/dotfiles/ssh/config"
+
+[bootstrap.services.ssh-agent]
+scope = "user"
+command = "ssh-agent -D -a %t/ssh-agent.socket"
+```
+
+Create the source file at `~/src/dotfiles/ssh/config` before applying this
+module. To use the agent from your shell, set `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` to
+`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/ssh-agent.socket`.
+
+For a [bootstrap project](#a-bootstrap-project), use `mise.toml` and
+`mise.ssh.toml` in the project directory instead.
+
+### Select and preview modules
+
+Choose a machine's default modules in
+[`miserc.toml`](/configuration/environments.html#setting-mise-env-in-miserc-toml).
+For example, after defining `config.ssh.toml` and `config.gpg.toml`:
+
+```toml [~/.config/mise/miserc.toml]
+env = ["ssh", "gpg"]
+```
+
+The base `config.toml` still loads. Preview the combined setup, then apply it:
+
+```sh
+mise bootstrap --dry-run
+mise bootstrap
+```
+
+To select modules for a single invocation, use `mise -E ssh,gpg bootstrap`.
+For [remote bootstrap](/bootstrap/remote.html), set each host's `mise_env` list
+in the inventory. One repository can then describe machines with different
+combinations of modules.
+
+### How modules combine
+
+Declarations with different keys contribute to the same run. Within the same
+directory, the environment listed later takes precedence when both declare
+the same key. For example, with `env = ["ssh", "gpg"]`, a service declared in
+both files uses the definition from `config.gpg.toml`.
+
+Use `mise config` to inspect the loaded files. `mise bootstrap plan --json`
+includes `origin.config` and `origin.environment` for each managed file and
+service, so you can trace those resources back to their declarations.

+[`conf.d`](/configuration/environments.html#conf-d-environments) fragment
+without an environment suffix, such as `conf.d/ssh.toml`.

+### Remove a module's resources
+
+Removing a module from `env` stops loading its declarations; it does **not**
+undo an earlier bootstrap. Remove resources explicitly before dropping the
+module:
