title: feat(dotfiles): select tracked files with include lists
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/73
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Tracked directories can specify which files to save, keeping new caches and session directories out of history by default:

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.codex" = { mode = "track", include = ["config.toml", "rules/**"] }
```

This selects `config.toml` and files beneath `rules/`. The selection rules are:

- No `include` field: consider the whole tree with built-in credential filtering.
- `include = []`: select no files.
- A populated list: select matches, with equal authority for literals and globs.
- Explicit exclusions always win. `.git`, machine-local configuration, and nested repositories retain their capture boundaries.

Includes use the same relative matching rules as per-entry exclusions. `include = ["**"]` selects credential-named files too. Tracking warns about these files before enrollment, and previews and path listings label them `plaintext:`. Set `encrypt = true` to encrypt selected contents; changing selection or encryption does not remove plaintext from earlier commits.

An omitted local include list preserves a selection published by another machine. Removing a list previously declared locally restores the default selection. Selections are recorded in checkpoint coverage and shown by `mise dot history show`. Narrowing a list stops managing the excluded paths without asking other machines to delete them; deleting a still-selected file continues to propagate normally.

Include lists apply only to tracked directories. Invalid patterns, lists on deployment entries, and lists on existing file targets are rejected during incoming-config preflight. Re-tracking an unreadable declaration refuses instead of silently replacing it with a broader selection. Explicitly track a nested repository's root to capture its working files.

Previews skip subdirectories that no include pattern can reach. `mise dot include <glob>` continues to remove a global exclusion; edit the `[dotfiles]` entry to change its include list.

## Compatibility

Includes are stored in shared enrollment metadata and checkpoint coverage. Older clients reject manifests containing this field. All new checkpoints use schema version 2, so older clients also cannot roll them back even when no include list is configured. Upgrade the machines sharing the setup before adopting the feature.

## Validation

Validated with the standalone include-list end-to-end test, multi-machine selection tests, history unit tests, and scoped formatting and lint checks. Documentation validation includes TOML example parsing and a full site build at the stack tip.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: OpenAI/unavailable; version: unavailable.*

> **Medium Risk**
> Changes dotfile history selection, sync deletion semantics, and checkpoint schema version 2, but adds preflight, reconcile safeguards, and explicit plaintext warnings to limit accidental over-capture or rollba

title: fix(brew-cask): percent-decode artifact filenames from cask URLs
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/72
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Installing a cask whose download URL percent-encodes characters that are literal in the artifact name failed:

```console
$ mise system install brew-cask:font-m-plus-1-code
mise ERROR brew-cask: font artifact 'MPLUS1Code[wght].ttf' was not found
```

Google Fonts casks are the common case. Homebrew's cask definition pairs an escaped URL with an unescaped artifact name:

| cask | URL basename | declared artifact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `font-m-plus-1-code` | `MPLUS1Code%5Bwght%5D.ttf` | `MPLUS1Code[wght].ttf` |
| `font-ar-one-sans` | `AROneSans%5BARRR%2Cwght%5D.ttf` | `AROneSans[ARRR,wght].ttf` |

`archive_filename` returned the last URL path segment verbatim. These are raw (non-archive) downloads, which are staged under that name, so the file landed as `MPLUS1Code%5Bwght%5D.ttf` while the artifact lookup searched for `MPLUS1Code[wght].ttf` and missed. It is not font-specific — any raw-download cask with an escaped URL basename, including a bare `binary`, hit the same mismatch.

`archive_filename` now percent-decodes the segment, matching Homebrew, which unescapes the same basename in its download strategy. Both casks above install after the change.

Decoding can produce a name that would escape the staging directory (`%2F`, `%2E%2E`) or that no filesystem accepts, so an unusable result falls back to the encoded segment — the value the function returned before this change, and inert as a path component. A URL basename with no escapes therefore decodes to itself and is unaffected.

One adoption note: the decoded name is also part of the download cache path, so an affected cask re-downloads once.

## Validation

Three unit tests in `src/system/packages/brew/cask/tests.rs`: decoding of both reported casks plus an escaped space, the traversal invariant for names that decode to a separator, `..` or a NUL, and an end-to-end check that the staged name is what `stage_font`'s lookup then finds. Reverting the decode makes the first and third fail. Full cask suite passes (324 tests); `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean.

Reported in #11879.

title: fix(bootstrap): stop running Windows user services through cmd.exe
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/71
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Stacked on #13428 — review that one first; this PR's own change is the single commit on top.

On Windows, a user service that set `environment` ran behind a terminal window, and closing that window killed the service. Task Scheduler's task XML has no environment block, so mise registered such a service as `cmd.exe /c set "K=V" && <command>`, and that `cmd.exe` stayed attached to the console Task Scheduler allocated for as long as the service lived. #13428 gives the history watcher's own console up, but it cannot help here: `cmd.exe` is attached alongside it, so the console still has a reader and the window stays.

The same wrapper meant the environment and the command line went through a shell, so mise had to reject `"`, `%`, `&`, `|`, `<`, `>`, `^`, and newlines in environment keys, values, and commands rather than pass them through as something different.

## What changes

mise carries the environment itself. Nothing changes in how you declare a service:

```toml
[bootstrap.services.mise-history]
builtin = "history-watch"
environment = { GIT_SSH_COMMAND = "ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_mise" }
```

```sh
mise bootstrap services apply
```

The registered action is now mise rather than `cmd.exe`:

```
<Command>C:\Users\me\AppData\Local\mise\bin\mise.exe</Command>
<Arguments>bootstrap __service-exec --launch C:\Users\me\AppData\Local\mise\state\user-services\mise-history.launches\5f2b….json --digest 5f2b… -- mise-history</Arguments>
```

That process applies the environment, starts the service without a console window, and stays for its lifetime as the process Task Scheduler tracks, so `MultipleInstancesPolicy`, `schtasks /end`, and restart-on-failure keep working. A wrapper that exited after applying the environment would take all three with it.

The environment and the command line travel beside the definition in `$MISE_STATE_DIR/user-services/<name>.launch.json` and never reach a command line, so **the character restrictions are gone** — keys, values, and commands are passed through as written. The command line is handed to the program verbatim rather than re-quoted, so it sees exactly what Task Scheduler used to give it.

A service that sets no `environment` is registered exactly as before: its own program, no wrapper, no extra process.

## Drift detection

The action names the stored launch by absolute path and digest, so changing `environment` changes the registered definition and `mise bootstrap services status` still detects drift with one comparison. The digest is staleness detection, not a security boundary — the state directory and the task are writable by the same user — but it does mean a launch left over from a replaced definition is refused rather than run under a task registered for something else.

The path is absolute because Task Scheduler starts the service from the user's logon environment, which need not carry the `MISE_STATE_DIR` the

title: fix(history): run the Windows watcher without a console window
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/70
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

On Windows, the dotfile history watcher ran behind a terminal window. Task
Scheduler starts a console program in a console of its own, so the
`history-watch` service put a console window on the desktop for as long as the
watcher lived — and closing that window killed the watcher. Reported in
[#13426](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13426).

The watcher now runs without a visible window. Nothing changes in how you
declare it, and there is no new flag or setting:

```toml
[bootstrap.services.mise-history]
builtin = "history-watch"
```

```sh
mise bootstrap services apply
mise dot status
```

## How it decides

The console itself says whether anyone is reading it. A console with exactly one
process attached was created for that process — which is what Task Scheduler
does, and what no shell does. A console with a second process attached has
something reading through it: a shell waiting on `mise dot watch`, or the
`cmd.exe` that a service setting `environment` runs through. The watcher asks on
every start, and hides its window only in the first case.

That keeps the foreground command intact. `mise dot watch` in a terminal still
prints its log lines, and `mise dot watch --json | jq` still streams, because a
shell is in that console.

## Why hide rather than detach

The window is hidden; the console stays. Giving the console up instead would
leave the watcher with none, and Windows hands a console program started by a
process that has no console a console of its own. The watcher runs `git` through
`GitPlumbing` on the save path, so detaching would have put a window on the
desktop for every checkpoint — trading one window the user could close for one
per save. A hidden console is inherited by children, which stay hidden with it,
and the standard handles keep pointing where they always did.

The cost is one resident `conhost.exe` per watcher, which is what a console
program started by Task Scheduler already had.

## Services that set `environment`

Such a service is registered as `cmd.exe /c set … && <command>`, because Task
Scheduler's XML has no environment block. `cmd.exe` is attached to the console
alongside the watcher, so the console is not the watcher's alone and its window
is left alone. #13429 removes that wrapper; with it, these become windowless
too. The default declaration above is unaffected either way.

Linux and macOS are untouched: systemd and launchd never allocate a console.

## Adoption

Existing installations pick this up as soon as they run the new binary — the
decision is made by the watcher at startup, not baked into the registered task,
so no `mise bootstrap services apply` or configuration change is needed.

## Testing

- New `e2e-win` case in `dotfiles_watch.Tests.ps1`, covering both directions. It
  starts the watcher with `Start-Process` (a console of its own, as Task
  Scheduler gives it), waits for it to hold the

title: fix(history): apply global exclusions consistently to tracked paths
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/69
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Global `[history] exclude` patterns now match filenames, relative subtrees, and absolute paths consistently. Previously, common patterns were compared only with absolute paths and silently failed to exclude the intended files.

```toml
[history]
exclude = ["cache", "sessions/**", "~/.config/app/private/**"]
```

- `cache` excludes matching path components and their contents beneath tracked roots.
- `sessions/**` matches at any depth below a tracked root, independent of the working directory.
- Absolute patterns support `~` and match through symlinked ancestors. Windows accepts both path separators.

The last matching rule wins, including matches on ancestor directories; a later `!glob` can re-include a descendant. Excluded subtrees are skipped when no later rule can select their contents. Capture, explicit saves, watcher filtering, sync, and rollback use the same ownership and matching rules. Nested repositories still require direct enrollment.

Invalid globs and environment-variable syntax (`$`) are reported by read-only commands such as `mise dot paths` and refused by operations that write or delete files. Invalid rules received from another machine leave the incoming plan unapplied. This lets users inspect and correct the configuration before saving, syncing, pulling, or rolling back.

Re-adding an exclusion puts it after earlier conflicting rules. `mise dot include` removes the specified global rule; it does not append a negation. Literal globs and escaped filenames remain distinct, and the command identifies a remaining alternate spelling when removing one leaves the other in force.

Checkpoints preserve their matcher version when history is rebuilt from Git. Rollback skips paths when an older or unknown matcher version makes deletion coverage uncertain. Existing patterns that previously matched nothing may now exclude files from subsequent captures; inspect `mise dot paths` when upgrading.

Validation: the stack passes 251 history unit tests and focused end-to-end tests for inherited selection, invalid global rules, nested repositories, and include lists. Regression tests cover matching across capture, watcher, sync, and rollback, plus matcher-version recovery from Git. Documentation was checked with scoped formatting/lint checks, TOML example parsing, and a full site build.

@@ -558,6 +558,55 @@ A later `!glob` in `[history] exclude` reverses an earlier matching
 exclusion. Removing one rule does not override other rules that still
 exclude the path.
 
+A path is excluded when the last rule matching it, or any of its
+ancestors below the tracked path, is an exclusion. So an excluded
+directory takes its contents with it, and a later `!glob` naming a file
+inside it still brings that file back. mise skips an excluded directory
+rather than enumerating it — whether it is written as `sessions`,
+`sessions/**` or an absolute path — which is only a speed-up: the files
+under it would each have been excluded anyway. A `!glob` that could
+re-include something inside makes mise walk it after all.
+
+A pattern with no path separator matches any single path component, so
+`cache` excludes a file called `cache` and everything inside a directory
+called `cache`, wherever it sits — the same reading a tracked entry's own
+`exclude` list has. A pattern that is absolute after `~`
+expansion matches the file's absolute path, both as written and
+normalized the way tracked paths are, so it still matches when an
+ancestor directory is a symlink. Any other pattern is relative to the
+tracked path: it matches at any depth below it, as if written with a
+leading `**/`, and is never resolved against the working directory, so
+`**/*.log` and `sessions/**` mean the same thing wherever the command
+runs and a `sessions` directory somewhere above the tracked path does
+not match. A leading `./` is
+ignored, so `./keys/**` means what `keys/**` means. In a pattern that
+names a path, `*` stops at a separator and `**` crosses them, as in a
+`.gitignore`: `keys/*.pem` is one directory deep, `keys/**/*.pem` is any
+depth. On Windows both `/` and `\` count as separators.
+
+Patterns support `~`, which expands to your home directory. Environment
+variables are not supported: `mise dot exclude` refuses a pattern
+containing `$` and tells you to write `~/…` or an absolute path, because
+a literal `$VAR` would never match anything and an exclusion that
+silently matches nothing keeps capturing the files you meant to leave
+out. A pattern already in your configuration that mise cannot use — one
+with a `$`, or a glob it cannot parse — is reported by name and skipped;
+the rest of the list keeps working, and a rollback reads the list the
+same way a capture did.
+
+A rollback only removes a file when the checkpoint positively records
+that it covered and captured it. A checkpoint written by a different
+version of the matcher, or a repository the checkpoint recorded as
+skipped, mean the record cannot answer the question — and the answer to a question that cannot be
+answered is never to delete the file. mise reports those paths as
+skipped instead.

title: fix(cache): stop prune from destroying installed tool files
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/67
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise cache prune` could destroy an installed tool. It runs on its own — the
automatic pass fires on roughly 1% of all mise invocations — so there is no
command in anyone's shell history to correlate with the damage.

Reported in #13420: an `npm:` package's files disappeared from
`$MISE_DATA_DIR/installs/...`, every regular file gone from exactly the packages
its `postinstall` had symlinked, directory tree intact, leaving the CLI failing
with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` on every subcommand.

## Prune walked out of the cache through a symlink

`prune` recursed with `file::dir_subdirs`, which deliberately keeps a symlink
whose target is a directory. So a symlink inside a cache entry was walked as
though it were part of the cache, and every file on the other side older than
`cache_prune_age` (30 days, judged by atime) was unlinked. The directories
survived because the empty-directory branch requires an old mtime, and deleting
the files had just refreshed it.

The npm backend puts such links in the cache as a matter of course: aube's
side-effects cache snapshots a package tree *after* its build scripts ran, so a
`postinstall` that links its own workspace directories — with absolute targets
under `$MISE_DATA_DIR/installs/` — is stored verbatim, links included.

```console
$ mise cache prune
mise cache pruned 1 files, 19 B      # the file was inside the install
$ ls <install>/packages/inner
                                     # empty; directory left behind
```

Prune now classifies every entry with `symlink_metadata` instead of resolving
it: it descends only into real directories, ages a symlink by the link's own
timestamps, and removes a stale one with an unlink that leaves the target alone.
`file::dir_subdirs` is unchanged — `mise link` relies on symlinked installs
resolving; it is prune, the one cache walk that deletes, that must not follow.

Two smaller consequences of the same walk are fixed with it: a link left
dangling by `mise uninstall` aborted the entire pass with
`No such file or directory`, and the `-v` log printed the cache-side path it had
walked rather than the install path it actually unlinked, which is why nothing
in the logs pointed at the installs directory.

## Prune hollowed out cache entries

The same bug had a second route that needs no symlink at all. Prune deleted
stale files one at a time wherever it found them, which left a cache entry
standing as an empty directory tree. The npm backend's entries are only usable
whole, and the package manager reading one back cannot tell an emptied entry
from an intact one — so it restores the remains over an install and records the
package as built. A tool left unused for longer than `cache_prune_age` and then
reinstalled hits exactly this.

A directory whose every entry is old enough to prune is now evicted in one
piece, and the files inside it are left for that removal rather than taken
in

title: docs: fix zsh completion steps rendering as duplicate "sh" tabs
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/66
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

The zsh tab of the autocompletion instructions on
[Installing mise](https://mise.jdx.dev/installing-mise.html#autocompletion) was
broken: the tab bar read `bash zsh sh sh fish`, and the sentence "Add the `fpath`
update to `.zshrc` before its existing `compinit` call" sat *below* the tab bar
where it appeared to apply to whichever tab was selected — including `fish`.

Anyone following the zsh instructions saw the `mise completion zsh > ~/.zfunc/_mise`
line under the "zsh" tab, with the `fpath` and `compinit` steps needed to make it
work hidden behind two unrelated-looking tabs both named "sh".

## Cause

VitePress turns *every* fenced block inside a `::: code-group` into a tab, using
the `[label]` from the fence info string or falling back to the language. The zsh
setup had been written as three separate fences with prose between them:

````md
```sh [zsh]
mise completion zsh > ~/.zfunc/_mise
```

Add the `fpath` update to `.zshrc` ...

```sh
fpath=(~/.zfunc $fpath)
```
````

so the `fpath` and `compinit` fences each became a tab labelled `sh`. Prose is not
valid inside a code group either, so it was hoisted out of the tab content and
rendered under the tab bar.

## Fix

Fold the whole zsh setup into its single tab, keeping the explanatory text as
comments:

```sh [zsh]
# Generate into a directory owned by your user:
mkdir -p ~/.zfunc
mise completion zsh > ~/.zfunc/_mise

# Then add the fpath update to ~/.zshrc, before its existing compinit call
# (including one made by a shell framework):
fpath=(~/.zfunc $fpath)

# If ~/.zshrc does not already initialize completions, also add:
autoload -Uz compinit
compinit
```

No instructions were dropped — the zsh steps are unchanged in content and order,
and they are now all visible together under the zsh tab.

## Verification

Rendering the group through VitePress's own `createMarkdownRenderer` before and
after the change:

| | tab labels |
| --- | --- |
| before | `["bash","zsh","sh","sh","fish"]` |
| after | `["bash","zsh","fish"]` |

The "before" output reproduces the reported tab bar exactly. After the change the
group contains no content outside the three code blocks. `mise run lint-fix`
passes with no further changes.

## Also included

A repo-wide scan for the same pattern found one other inconsistency:
`docs/tasks/file-tasks.md` had an unlabelled ` ```python ` fence in a group whose
siblings are explicitly labelled (`[node]`, `[deno]`). It rendered correctly via
the language fallback, so this is not a user-visible fix — the label is added so
the group is uniform and does not invite the same mistake.

`docs/ide-integration.md` also has unlabelled fences in a code group, but all
three are unlabelled and fall back to `zsh`/`bash`/`fish`, which is correct. It is
left as-is.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5;

title: feat(hooks): expose installed tool backend and path
body:
Installation hooks currently report the configured request and installed version, but cannot identify the backend or exact installation directory that completed. This adds `backend` and `install_path` to each `MISE_INSTALLED_TOOLS` entry, deriving both from the installation result so successful entries remain useful during partial failures and do not depend on a second configuration lookup.

The existing fields and hook timing remain unchanged. URL credentials are removed from backend identifiers while meaningful SSH usernames are preserved, and non-Unicode path behavior is documented. Documentation distinguishes installation completion from configuration selection, floating-link updates, and adoption by a running application, including no-op and failure behavior.

Verification:

- `mise run test:e2e -- test_hooks_installed_tools`
- `mise run lint`
- Native CI validates the current head, including the focused unit and E2E coverage added after review

title: feat(dotfiles): support exclusions on tracked directories
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/64
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Tracked directories can now declare relative exclusions alongside their tracking settings:

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.codex" = { mode = "track", exclude = ["sessions", "*.log"] }
```

This excludes session directories and log files beneath `~/.codex` without affecting other tracked entries. Scoped global exclusions remain available; this adds a way to keep a directory's selection next to its declaration.

Patterns without `/` match path components at any depth; patterns containing `/` are relative to the tracked root. A matching directory excludes its subtree. Global exclusions still apply, and a global `!glob` cannot override a per-entry exclusion.

Capture, explicit saves, watcher filtering, previews, and rollback read the entry's exclusions. Re-tracking preserves the list, including an explicitly empty one, and including a list another machine published that this machine's declaration does not repeat — `mise dot track` previews and captures under the effective list rather than the local declaration alone, so its baseline cannot store what a shared exclusion leaves out. Reading a published list means reading the history repository, so the preview asks only when there is one to read: `--dry-run` still writes nothing, and a damaged repository does not stop a preview that needs only configuration. The list is shared in enrollment metadata and stored in checkpoint coverage, so rollback can distinguish an excluded file from a missing managed file. Every machine using this field must run a mise version that supports it.

Validation: existing CI passed on the reviewed head. Tests cover matching, layered configuration, previews and JSON, explicit-save refusal, manifest round trips, and rollback across selection changes.


Documentation validation: scoped formatting/lint checks, TOML example parsing, and a full site build at the stack tip. The five focused dotfiles end-to-end tests passed locally.

Narrowing selection is not a deletion for the other machines to replay. Sync planning consults the incoming snapshot's coverage, so a path absent because selection no longer covers it is unmanaged, while a path deleted while it was still selected is still propagated. `e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_review_exclude_sync` covers both directions across two machines.

title: feat(dotfiles): preview file counts and size before tracking
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/63
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise dot track` now reports each target's file count and size before confirmation, helping users catch large caches or session directories before saving an initial checkpoint. The tracking result also includes the count and size when confirmation is skipped.

```sh
mise dot track --dry-run ~/.codex
mise dot paths --preview ~/.codex
```

Both commands inspect the prospective capture without changing configuration or saving a checkpoint. `paths --preview` also lists files. Dry runs show exclusions, omitted files, nested repositories, and incomplete scans; long omission lists are summarized after twenty entries.

Trees over 5,000 files or 256 MiB produce a warning with guidance to exclude subdirectories or track individual files. These thresholds are advisory. Incomplete scans are reported before confirmation. Overlapping targets use the same ownership rules as capture, so a nested entry's files are not counted twice.

The preview performs a metadata scan without reading file contents and does not hold the declaration lock during a dry run. The actual baseline capture scans again after enrollment.

Validation: existing CI passed on the reviewed head. Unit and end-to-end coverage includes counts, sizes, overlapping entries, omissions, exclusions, and dry runs leaving configuration unchanged.


Documentation validation: scoped formatting/lint checks, TOML example parsing, and a full site build at the stack tip. The five focused dotfiles end-to-end tests passed locally.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: OpenAI/unavailable; version: unavailable.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes dotfile enrollment UX and filesystem walk behavior used by track/preview; mistakes could mis-size trees or skip paths, though dry-run avoids writes and actual capture still runs after enrollment.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds **`mise dot track --dry-run`** (`-n`) to walk prospective targets and print per-path **file counts, total size, exclusions, omissions, nested repos, and incomplete scans** without writing config or holding the declaration lock.
> 
> **`mise dot track`** now sizes each target the same way before confirmation: prompts and success logs include the summary, large trees (>5,000 files or 256 MiB) get an advisory warning, and overlapping targets use capture-style ownership so nested paths are not double-counted.
> 
> **`mise dot paths --preview`** shares the new **`preview_set` / `walk_selected`** plumbing and prints count and size in its header (still listing every file). Walk logic also counts symlink/nested-repo bytes correctly and skips re-walking subtrees owned by a more specific entry.
> 
> Docs, usage spec, man page, unit tests, and an e2e script cover dry-run, preview, exclusions, and `--encrypt` affecting the preview.
>

title: fix(history): skip nested repositories unless tracked directly
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/62
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Repositories found inside tracked directories are now skipped and reported instead of saved as Git commit pointers. A pointer did not contain the repository's files and could make adoption or pull fail when its commit was unavailable.

To save a vendored plugin's working files, track its root explicitly:

```sh
mise dot track ~/.hammerspoon
mise dot track ~/.hammerspoon/Spoons/SkyRocket.spoon
```

The first command reports the nested repository as skipped. The second captures its working files under its own tracking policies, always excluding `.git`. Save, status, paths, and history output explain skipped repositories, including JSON output.

Existing pointer-only history changes are skipped during pull/adoption without creating, removing, or updating a local checkout. New captures do not create those pointers. Skipped repositories are also recorded as omissions in shared checkpoint metadata, so rebuilding the local cache retains the information rollback needs to preserve their files.

Validation: existing CI passed on the reviewed head. Tests cover omission reporting, explicit repository-root tracking, legacy pointers, multi-machine adoption, and rollback after removing a nested `.git`.


Documentation validation: scoped formatting/lint checks, TOML example parsing, and a full site build at the stack tip. The five focused dotfiles end-to-end tests passed locally.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: OpenAI/unavailable; version: unavailable.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes dotfile capture, sync reconciliation, and rollback semantics for nested `.git` trees and legacy gitlinks; mistakes could affect multi-machine setups and data preservation during pull/rollback.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Nested Git directories under a tracked tree are no longer saved as commit pointers.** mise skips them entirely, surfaces them as `nested:` in save/status/paths/history (including JSON), and tells users to **`mise dot track <repo-root>`** to capture working files without `.git`.
> 
> **Sync and adoption** treat legacy `160000` pointers as non-content: reconcile skips apply/remove for pointer-vs-pointer cases, records **not shared** reasons in sync status, blocks taking remote pointer versions on pull, and still applies ordinary files while leaving live nested checkouts untouched.
> 
> **Rollback and checkpoints** persist skipped nested paths in coverage (and mirror them into shared commit omissions for older clients), so rollbacks do not delete paths the checkpoint never held—even after `.git` is removed. The watcher stops autosaving paths inside an untracked nested repo.
> 
> Docs and e2e tests cover the new behavior, legacy pointers, multi-machine bootstrap, and rollback edge cases.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 1ac20f17cf16511f9e89b4b1f13a3939f70178d5. Bugbot is set up for automate

-paths it cannot save. It keeps their previous saved versions while saving

+A symlink is saved as a link. mise reports oversized files, special files,
+and unreadable paths it cannot save. It keeps their previous saved versions
+while saving other files, so check reported omissions before relying on a
+checkpoint. Explicit exclusions remove paths from future checkpoints.
+Encryption failures stop a save rather than storing plaintext.
+
+### Nested repositories
+
+A directory with its own `.git` inside a tracked tree (a plugin cloned
+into `~/.hammerspoon/Spoons`, a vendored theme) is a separate repository.
+**mise skips it and records nothing for it** — not its files, and not a
+commit pointer. `mise dot save`, `mise dot track`, `mise dot status` and
+`mise dot paths` each name it and say what to do:
+
+```console
+nested: ~/.hammerspoon/Spoons/SkyRocket.spoon (a separate Git repository;
+        track it directly to capture its working files)
+```
+
+That remedy is the supported one. **Tracking a repository's own directory
+captures its working files**, always without `.git`:
+
+```sh
+mise dot track ~/.hammerspoon/Spoons/SkyRocket.spoon
+```
+
+Reaching into it from a parent entry does not work and is not meant to:
+an `include` pattern on the parent that names paths inside the nested
+repository selects nothing, and mise says so rather than leaving you to
+wonder whether the pattern was wrong. The alternative is to leave the
+directory to the tool that installs it, or remove its `.git` so it
+becomes ordinary content.
+
+A history saved by an older mise may already contain commit pointers.
+Those are read and skipped: `mise dot pull` lists such a pointer as
+skipped rather than creating an empty directory, failing on it, or
+pausing the setup because another machine's pointer differs. No new
+pointer is ever written.
+
+Skipped repositories are recorded as omissions in shared checkpoint
+metadata. Rollback preserves those paths even after `.git` is removed,
+on another machine, or after the local cache is rebuilt. The originating
+machine's cache also keeps the more specific nested-repository reason;
+a rebuilt cache may show the generic omission reason instead.
 
 Commands that modify or capture tracked files save checkpoints before and
 after their work. Their metadata includes operation labels and the link
--- e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_nested_repository (+138/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,138 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# shellcheck disable=SC2016
+# A directory with its own .git under a tracked tree is skipped whole:
+# nothing is recorded for it, not its files and not a commit pointer.
+# Capture, status and paths name it and say what to do instead, and
+# tracking the repository itself captures its working files without
+# `.git`. A pointer already in a history from an older mise is read and
+# skipped rather than failing or emptying the repository it names.
+require_cmd git
+export MISE_HISTORY_NOTIFY=false
+repo="$MISE_STATE_DIR/history/repo.git"
+origin="$PWD/nested-origin.git"
+git init -q --bare -b main "$origin"
+plugin=~/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon
+mkdir -p "$plugin"
+echo 'hs.alert("hi")' >~/.hammerspoon/init.lua
+echo 'return {}' >"$plugin/init.lua"
+git -C "$plugin" init -q -b main
+git -C "$plugin" -c user.name=t -c user.email=t@example.com add -A
+git -C "$plugin" -c user.name=t -c user.email=t@example.com commit -q -m init
+sha=$(git -C "$plugin" rev-parse HEAD)
+
+# Enrollment and every save say what a nested repository leaves out.
+assert_contains 'mise dot track ~/.hammerspoon 2>&1' 'nested: ~/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon (a separate Git repository'
+# nothing is recorded for it: no files, and no commit pointer either
+assert "git --git-dir=$repo ls-tree HEAD home/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon" ''
+assert_fail "git --git-dir=$repo cat-file -e HEAD:home/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon/init.lua"
+assert "git --git-dir=$repo show HEAD:home/.hammerspoon/init.lua" 'hs.alert("hi")'
+echo 'hs.alert("hello")' >~/.hammerspoon/init.lua
+assert_contains 'mise dot save 2>&1' 'nested: ~/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon (a separate Git repository'
+assert_contains 'mise dot paths' 'nested: ~/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon (a separate Git repository; track it directly to capture its working files)'
+assert "mise dot paths --json | jq -r '.nested[0].path'" '~/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon'
+assert_contains 'mise dot status' 'tracked (1 nested)'
+assert_contains 'mise dot status' '1 nested repository skipped'
+assert "mise dot status --json | jq -r '.history.nested | length'" 1
+assert_contains 'mise dot history show' 'nested: ~/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon'
+# one skip, said once: the checkpoint carries it to other machines as an
+# omission, and this machine's own record keeps the reason that can be
+# acted on — it is not both
+assert "mise dot history show 2>&1 | grep -c 'Spoons/Sky.spoon'" '1'
+
+# Removing the `.git` makes the directory ordinary content — and a
+# rollback to a checkpoint that skipped it does not delete those files,
+# because the checkpoint recorded that it never held them.
+cp -r "$plugin" ~/plugin-copy
+rm -rf "$plugin/.git"
+before_rm="$(mise dot history --json | jq -r '.[0].id')"
+assert_contains "mise dot rollback ~/.hammerspoon --to $before_rm --dry-run 2>&1" 'a separate Git repository'
+assert_succeed "mise dot rollback ~/.hammerspoon --to $before_rm --yes"
+assert "cat $plugin/init.lua" 'return {}'
+rm -rf "$plugin" && cp -r ~/plugin-copy "$plugin"
+
+# The remedy works: tracking the repository itself captures its working
+# files, and never `.git`.
+assert_succeed 'mise dot track ~/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon'
+assert "git --git-dir=$repo show HEAD:home/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon/init.lua" 'return {}'
+assert_fail "git --git-dir=$repo cat-file -e HEAD:home/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon/.git/HEAD"
+assert_not_contains 'mise dot paths' 'nested:'
+# untracking stops managing it; it never deletes the live files, and no
+# pointer takes its place
+assert_succeed 'mise dot untrack ~/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon'
+assert_succeed 'mise dot save'
+assert "cat $plugin/init.lua" 'return {}'
+assert "git --git-dir=$repo ls-tree HEAD home/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon" ''
+
+# Another machine adopts the setup: the pointer is skipped with a reason,
+# the ordinary files arrive, and a nested repository it already has is
+# left alone.
+assert_succeed "mise dot track $MISE_CONFIG_DIR/config.toml"
+assert_succeed "mise dot origin set file://$origin --yes"
+# a pointer a previous mise left in the shared history: written straight
+# into the origin, since this version never creates one
+work="$PWD/legacy-pointer"
+git clone -q "$origin" "$work"
+git -C "$work" update-index --add --cacheinfo "160000,$sha,home/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon"
+tree=$(git -C "$work" write-tree)
+commit=$(git -C "$work" -c user.name=t -c user.email=t@example.com commit-tree "$tree" -p "$(git -C "$work" rev-parse HEAD)" -m 'legacy pointer')
+git -C "$work" push -q "$origin" "$commit:refs/heads/main"
+assert "git --git-dir=$origin ls-tree main home/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon | cut -d' ' -f1" 160000
+wrapper() {
+  local home="$1" script="$2"
+  mkdir -p "$home"
+  cat <<EOF2 >"$script"
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+export HOME="$home" XDG_CONFIG_HOME="$home/.config" MISE_CONFIG_DIR="$home/.config/mise" \\
+  MISE_STATE_DIR="$home/.local/state/mise" MISE_DATA_DIR="$home/.local/share/mise" \\
+  MISE_CACHE_DIR="$home/.cache/mise" MISE_TRUSTED_CONFIG_PATHS="$home" MISE_HISTORY_NOTIFY=false
+cd "\$HOME" && exec mise "\$@"
+EOF2
+  chmod +x "$script"
+}
+second="$(dirname "$HOME")/nested-second"
+wrapper "$second" "$PWD/second"
+b="$PWD/second"
+mkdir -p "$second/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon"
+echo 'return { second = true }' >"$second/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon/init.lua"
+git -C "$second/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon" init -q -b main
+git -C "$second/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon" -c user.name=t -c user.email=t@example.com add -A
+git -C "$second/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon" -c user.name=t -c user.email=t@example.com commit -q -m second
+assert_contains "$b bootstrap --adopt file://$origin --yes --only dotfiles 2>&1" 'skipped: a separate Git repository'
+assert "cat $second/.hammerspoon/init.lua" 'hs.alert("hello")'
+assert "cat $second/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon/init.lua" 'return { second = true }'
+assert_succeed "test -d $second/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon/.git"
+assert_contains "$b dot status" 'not shared: ~/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon (a separate Git repository; a pointer from an older mise, skipped'
+assert "$b dot status --json | jq -r '.history.sync.pending_applications | length'" 0
+assert_succeed "$b dot sync"
+
+# A machine without the directory is not asked to create it: the pointer
+# names nothing here, so there is nothing to skip and nothing to make.
+third="$(dirname "$HOME")/nested-third"
+wrapper "$third" "$PWD/third"
+c="$PWD/third"
+assert_succeed "$c bootstrap --adopt file://$origin --yes --only dotfiles"
+assert "cat $third/.hammerspoon/init.lua" 'hs.alert("hello")'
+assert_fail "test -e $third/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon"
+assert_succeed "$c dot sync"
+assert_succeed "$b dot sync"
+assert_succeed "test -d $second/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon/.git"
+
+# Ordinary incoming files also respect a live nested checkout, even
+# when older history held only a pointer at that path.
+git -C "$work" update-index --force-remove home/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon
+mkdir -p "$work/home/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon"
+echo 'incoming replacement' >"$work/home/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon/init.lua"
+echo 'incoming addition' >"$work/home/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon/new.lua"
+git -C "$work" add home/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon
+git -C "$work" fetch -q origin
+tree=$(git -C "$work" write-tree)
+commit=$(git -C "$work" -c user.name=t -c user.email=t@example.com commit-tree "$tree" -p "$(git --git-dir="$origin" rev-parse main)" -m 'ordinary incoming files')
+git -C "$work" push -q "$origin" "$commit:refs/heads/main"
+assert_succeed "$b dot sync"
+assert_succeed "$b dot pull --yes"
+assert "cat $second/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon/init.lua" 'return { second = true }'
+assert_fail "test -e $second/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon/new.lua"
+assert "$b dot status --json | jq -r '.history.sync.pending_applications | length'" 0
+assert_succeed "$c dot sync"
+assert_succeed "$c dot pull --yes"
+assert "cat $third/.hammerspoon/Spoons/Sky.spoon/new.lua" 'incoming addition'

title: fix(history): report files omitted by credential filtering
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/61
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Files omitted by the credential filter are now visible during `mise dot track`, `mise dot save`, and `mise dot status`. Previously, a tracked directory could contain files that were never saved while status simply called the directory “tracked.”

For example, `~/.config/fish/functions/secrets.fish` matches the existing `*secret*` rule. Saves now identify the omitted path, status shows an omission count, and `mise dot paths` lists the full reasons. Tracking a credential-named file directly warns before enrollment and suggests `--encrypt`.

The filename rules are unchanged, including their treatment of public-key names such as `id_ed25519.pub`. Explicit saves report individual omissions, with a summary for long lists; watcher and protective captures use a summary. JSON status includes omission details. Re-tracking also preserves explicitly written `autosave` and `encrypt` policies without pinning values inherited from another configuration layer.

Validation: existing CI passed on the reviewed head. Coverage includes save/track/status reporting, JSON output, credential omissions, and declaration-policy preservation.


Documentation validation: scoped formatting/lint checks, TOML example parsing, and a full site build at the stack tip. The five focused dotfiles end-to-end tests passed locally.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: OpenAI/unavailable; version: unavailable.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Behavior change is reporting and UX around unchanged credential rules; no new capture of secrets, with added warnings before tracking sensitive names.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Credential-filtered paths are no longer invisible** when a parent directory is tracked. `mise dot track`, `mise dot save`, and `mise dot status` now surface what the built-in filename rules leave out of every capture, with per-path reasons and pointers to `mise dot paths` / `mise dot track --encrypt`.
> 
> On **save and baseline flows**, checkpoint reporting lists individual omissions for explicit user triggers (or scopes them to newly enrolled roots on baseline); watcher and protective captures get a single summary line instead of spamming every path. **Status** adds omission counts on tracked rows (`tracked (N omitted)`), a history-block summary, and JSON (`history.omitted` plus per-file `omitted`). **Track** warns before enrolling credential-named files (including not-yet-created paths treated as files, not directories) and avoids implying directory-wide protection when the guard only matches basenames.
> 
> **Declaration rewrites** on re-track only persist `autosave` / `encrypt` in TOML when this config layer had written them before or the command sets a flag—inherited policies from another layer are not pinned. Docs expand **credential filtering**, exclusions, and `.local.toml` behavior. An e2e test locks in track/save/status/JSON behavior and symli

-from saves. Protected credential files and `*.local.toml` are excluded by

+An absolute pattern scopes the exclusion to that location. This example

title: feat(dotfiles): run history reload commands after mise dot apply
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/60
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`[history.reload]` maps a path glob to a command that runs once after files matching the glob change. It already ran after `mise dot pull`, `rollback`, `undo` and the watcher's automatic apply, but not after `mise dot apply`. A post-apply fixup such as `chmod 700 ~/.ssh` or an application reload therefore only happened when the files arrived through history, and a plain apply of a changed dotfile left the running application on its old configuration.

`mise dot apply` now runs the matching reload commands for the targets it actually wrote (symlinks created, copies written, templates rendered, edits applied), each once, after all writes.

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.config/hypr" = "dotfiles/hypr"
"~/.ssh/config" = { source = "dotfiles/ssh_config.tmpl", mode = "template" }

[history.reload]
"~/.config/hypr/**" = "hyprctl reload"
"~/.ssh/**" = "chmod 700 ~/.ssh"
```

```sh
$ mise dot apply --yes
mise files: created symlink ~/.config/hypr -> ~/.dotfiles/hypr
mise files: rendered ~/.dotfiles/ssh_config.tmpl to ~/.ssh/config
mise files: applied ~/.config/hypr, ~/.ssh/config
mise history: reload: hyprctl reload
mise history: reload: chmod 700 ~/.ssh
```

Details:

- The reload map is resolved from the trusted configuration layers before anything is written, as pull and rollback do, so nothing the apply writes can change which commands run.
- `mise dot apply --dry-run` writes nothing and runs no reload commands. An apply with nothing left to write runs none either.
- Entries are applied one at a time with no rollback of the earlier ones, so when the edit prompt is declined or a later entry fails (an unwritable parent, a full disk), the commands matching what was already written still run before the error is reported; the command still exits non-zero. A target is recorded for reload exactly when this apply changed its on-disk state: right after an existing target is cleared to make room (a write that then fails still leaves the old content gone); once an existing file that is overwritten in place — an edit target, or a file under a directory copy — has been opened for truncation (an open that fails on a read-only file or filesystem changes nothing and records nothing); and for a previously absent target, once it exists, including when the write that created it then failed. A target the failure never touched reloads nothing, and a directory copy that fails part-way reloads only for the files it did place.
- A symlink to a directory counts the files it exposes as written, so `"~/.config/hypr/**"` fires for a `"~/.config/hypr" = "dotfiles/hypr"` entry. That listing is best-effort: if the source cannot be walked after the link landed, mise warns and records the link itself.
- `mise dot sync` is unchanged: it never writes live files, so it has no reload to run.
- Internal: `system::files::apply`, `system::files::execute_apply` and `system::edits::apply` take a `

title: feat(docker): publish verified release images for Dockerfiles and CI
body:
Publish official mise release images for copying mise into a Dockerfile or running it directly in CI and development containers. Images use the published release binaries, verified against minisign-signed checksums, and support `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64` on both GHCR (`ghcr.io/jdx/mise`) and Docker Hub (`jdxcode/mise`).

Closes #13409. See also #8208 and #6934.

## Choose an image

| Image | Example tags | Contents and use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scratch | `2026.9.11`, `2026.9`, `latest` | Static musl mise binary and CA certificates; use as a `COPY --from=` source. No shell or package manager. |
| Debian slim | `2026.9.11-debian`, `2026.9-debian`, `debian` | Glibc mise binary, CA certificates, `curl`, and `git`; use as a CI or development base. No `ENTRYPOINT`. |

Copy mise into an existing Linux image:

```Dockerfile
FROM debian:13-slim
COPY --from=ghcr.io/jdx/mise:2026.9.11 /usr/local/bin/mise /usr/local/bin/mise
```

The destination still needs CA certificates and the OS dependencies required by its tools. Alternatively, start with the Debian image and install a project's tools:

```Dockerfile
FROM ghcr.io/jdx/mise:2026.9.11-debian
WORKDIR /app
COPY mise.toml ./
RUN mise trust && mise install
```

Neither image preinstalls tools managed by mise. Copy `mise.lock` and any configuration inputs too when the project uses them. Pin an image with `@sha256:<digest>` when exact image contents matter; even a full version tag can change after a rebuild.

## Migration and publication

**`latest` changes from the previous source-built image to scratch.** CI and development consumers should switch to `debian` and explicitly install their tools. The previous image remains under the unsupported `dev` tag for internal consumers. Update consumers such as mise-versions before the first publication; the Docker Hub description also needs updating separately.

Release images build after a non-prerelease GitHub release is published. A manual workflow run with a release `tag` can build images for an existing release. Publication is serialized per image variant, and only the current release updates floating tags; historical rebuilds update their version tag. Image failures use the existing release-failure notification workflow. Tag pushes and manual runs without a release tag continue to build the internal development and packaging images.

The docs cover image selection, digest pinning, project-tool installation, GitLab CI caching, shared installations, and alternatives using packages, verified downloads, or a committed installer wrapper.

## Validation

Documentation formatting, the VitePress build (including social-image checks), 36 local links and anchors, and fenced TOML parsing pass. Container builds and registry publication were not rerun for the documentation cleanup.

title: fix(history): record the modes of directories that contain tracked files
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/58
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Tracking an individual file inside a private directory did not record the directory's mode, so a fresh machine recreated the directory world-readable. With this configuration and `~/.claude` at `0700`:

```toml
[dotfiles]
"~/.claude/settings.json" = { mode = "track" }
```

the history manifest recorded nothing about `~/.claude`, and `mise bootstrap --from-git` on a new machine created it with the default `0755` via `create_dir_all`:

```json
// before
"permissions": {}
```

Directory modes were only captured for directories that were themselves `[dotfiles]` entries (and their subdirectories). Reported in #13410 (item 3).

## What changes

A checkpoint now records the non-default (not `0755`) mode of every directory strictly between a tracked path and the root it is mapped under (home or the mise configuration directory). The same rule applies to file and directory entries, so a tracked `~/.config/nvim` inside a `0700` `~/.config` records `~/.config` too.

```json
// after
"permissions": {
  "home/.claude": 448
}
```

A containing directory is one filesystem object, so it gets one record under the variant-less path whatever streams the files inside it belong to: `~/.claude/settings.json` without variants and `~/.claude/notes` with `variants = [{ os = "linux" }]` share the single `home/.claude` record, and a save from either stream replaces it. The record applies even when every file inside the directory is platform-specific, so the tree only holds it under a stream such as `home@linux/.claude`. A directory that is itself an enrolled entry keeps its own per-stream record (`home@linux/.claude`), as before; when the directory is enrolled here, that stream's record decides its mode and its absence means the default, so another platform's containing record for the same directory does not apply (an enrolled stream the incoming manifest dropped means a machine with that stream saved the directory at the default). A stream marker lives only in the first path component, so a directory whose own name contains `@` is an ordinary directory.

On pull and on a fresh `bootstrap --from-git`, the directory is created (or corrected) with the recorded mode before its files are written. When the directory goes back to `0755` at home, the next save drops the record and the next pull on the other machine restores the default. A machine whose directory already has the incoming mode pulls without saving first, even if its own manifest predates this change and records nothing for it; only a live mode that differs from the incoming one is checked against the local record. That check has one purpose: never overwrite a live mode the user has not saved. The baseline it compares the live mode with is the mode this planner would have applied from the saved manifest: the same computation that decides the incoming mode (the enrolled stream's record covering the directory, abse

title: fix(history): explain how to recover from unrelated histories
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/57
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

When `mise dot origin set <url>` (or a later `mise dot sync`) finds that the local checkpoints and the repository's branch share no Git ancestry, it refuses to publish. The refusal was correct but did not name a way out: it told the user to "use a fresh setup store" or "reconcile the repositories explicitly with Git" (raised in the closing section of #13410). The connection notice for a repository that has content without the mise marker had the same gap ("use an empty origin or reconcile the histories explicitly").

Both messages now name the concrete command for each direction. Behavior is unchanged; only the wording differs.

**Sync refusal, before:**

```
local and origin histories are unrelated; use a fresh setup store to adopt origin, or reconcile the repositories explicitly with Git. Neither history was replaced
```

**After:**

```
local and origin histories are unrelated. Neither history was replaced.
To keep local checkpoints, connect an empty repository with `mise dot origin set <url>`. Alternatively, use Git to push the local history to a new remote branch, then connect it with `mise dot origin set <url> --branch <name>`.
To discard local checkpoints and adopt a mise setup repository's history, run `mise bootstrap --adopt <url> --replace-history --yes`. This requires a repository with mise enrollment metadata.
```

**Connection notice for an unmarked repository, before:**

```
The repository already has content without mise enrollment metadata. Connecting does not import its files or replace unrelated history. Synchronization requires compatible Git ancestry; use an empty origin or reconcile the histories explicitly. Ordinary non-tracking `--from`/`--adopt` workflows remain available.
```

**After:**

```
This repository has content but no mise enrollment metadata. Connecting does not import its files.
A machine with no checkpoints adopts branch `main` as its history. Existing checkpoints can synchronize only if they share Git ancestry with that branch.
To keep unrelated local checkpoints, connect an empty repository with `mise dot origin set <url>`. Alternatively, use Git to push the local history to a new remote branch, then connect it with `mise dot origin set <url> --branch <name>`.
To use the repository as bootstrap configuration without enabling history sharing, use `mise bootstrap --from <url>` or `mise bootstrap --adopt <url>`.
```

The `--replace-history` remedy is qualified because it only applies to a marked mise setup repository: `mise bootstrap --adopt` falls through to the ordinary clone for a repository without the marker, and it adopts the repository's default branch (it has no branch option), so it does not apply when the machine is connected to another branch. The `--branch <name>` remedy is stated as a branch the local history was pushed to because `origin set` refuses a branch the repository does not have unless

Changing the path does not move or delete existing data. The guide explains ignoring checkout-local data, stopping services before migration, and the risk of deleting data when removing a worktree. Pruning generated state does not remove storage outside it.

title: fix(lock): pin a relocated dependency sidecar to the bytes mise just wrote
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/55
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Follow-up to #13403, which merged while this case was still under review.

#13398 made sidecar digests cover normalized graph text, and #13403 kept
accepting the raw-CRLF digests older versions recorded on Windows and taught
mise to heal them. One path was left behind: when a sidecar is published to a
*new* directory — a lockfile moved or renamed, a backend variant, a sidecar
restored after being pruned — `SidecarWrites::prepare` writes the freshly
normalized bytes there but recorded `graph.identity()`, the digest the entry
arrived with.

For an entry carrying a legacy CRLF digest, the result pinned bytes that exist
nowhere: the new directory holds LF text, whose normalized digest and raw
digest both differ from what was written to `mise.lock`. That relocated entry
could not be verified on any platform, and because the returned pointer has an
empty cache cell, no later save could heal it either.

The digest now covers the graph that was just verified and published, so a
relocated sidecar is pinned to the bytes actually on disk. Entries that were
already normalized are unaffected — for them the two values are equal by
definition.

## Test

`src/lockfile/graph.rs` extends the legacy-digest unit test: after the stale
entry heals in place, it saves the lockfile to a different directory and
asserts the republished sidecar is LF, the new entry records the normalized
digest rather than the legacy one, and reading that lockfile back loads the
graph. Reverting the one-line change fails this test.

`cargo test --bin mise lockfile` (202 tests), `mise run lint`, and
`cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` pass.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5; version: 2.1.270.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Touches lockfile sidecar publish and digest pinning; wrong behavior broke verification for relocated entries, but the change is narrow and covered by an extended unit test.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes dependency sidecar digests when a lockfile is **saved to a new path** (move, rename, variant, restore). After `prepare` writes **LF-normalized** sidecar bytes, the stored digest now comes from **`digest_text` of the published graph** instead of reusing **`graph.identity()`** from the incoming entry.
> 
> That stops **legacy CRLF digests** from being copied onto relocated sidecars whose on-disk text no longer matches—entries that previously could not be verified and could not self-heal on later saves. In-place saves for already-normalized entries are unchanged.
> 
> The **legacy CRLF digest** test now saves to another directory and asserts the new lockfile records the normalized digest, the sidecar has no `\r`, and the graph loads.
>

title: revert: restore the full windows-e2e mise tool cache
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/54
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Reverts #13397. That PR was merged while the run that was meant to justify it was still going; the finished measurement says the change makes `windows-e2e` slower, and the merge also carried a step I had marked `TEMPORARY`.

## What the completed measurement showed

#13397 narrowed the cached data dir to leave out zig, go, python, vfox-nodejs and `bin/` — 78% of the files, 28% of the bytes. The premise was that unpacking on NTFS is per-file, so shedding files would buy back most of the ~114s restore cheaply.

It is not per-file. Unpacking runs at roughly 35-42 MB/s either way, so the trimmed cache restored 2,537 MB / 12,170 files in 75s against 3,834 MB / 56,517 files in 91s. Shedding 78% of the files saved 23s on the step. The tools then had to be reinstalled during the tests:

| variant | `mise-tools` | e2e | job |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| full cache (21 runs on `main`) | 114s | 306s | **444s** |
| trimmed cache, warm restore (1 run) | 91s | 457s | 570s |
| no cache at all (2 runs) | 29s | 470s | 519s |
| this revert, on CI just now | 111s | 296s | **426s** |

Per-test-file timings, trimmed run against a warm `main` run, show the cost landing exactly where the tools were removed — `zig.Tests.ps1` 0.3s → 39.3s, `go.Tests.ps1` 0.7s → 35.9s, `vfox.Tests.ps1` 8.7s → 39.7s, `pypi_lock.Tests.ps1` 18.2s → 37.7s, `uv.Tests.ps1` 1.9s → 13.4s, `python.Tests.ps1` 35.4s → 45.8s. That is +147s against 23s saved.

## What the revert keeps and drops

It restores the previous `path` and cache key and removes the temporary diagnostic step, which walked every restored file on each run.

The `cache-path` input goes with it. The mechanism itself was sound and worth recording: `actions/cache` resolves patterns with implicit descendants off, so a bare directory is archived whole and a `!` pattern for something inside it never matches — which is why the first attempt at trimming produced a 1,213 MB cache against 1,220 MB before, i.e. changed nothing. Enumerating the siblings to keep does work. It just is not worth doing here.

Full write-up and the composition of the cache are in #13397.

Follow-up to #13398, which was merged while this gap was still under review.

#13398 made sidecar digests cover the graph text with CRLF normalized to LF, so
a Windows checkout of a committed `.mise/locks/…` sidecar verifies. It missed
one case on the way in: before that change, an ordinary `mise install` on a
Windows checkout accepted the CRLF working copy as a deliberate edit and wrote
the digest of those *raw CRLF bytes* into `mise.lock`. Those lockfiles exist. On
upgrading to a mise that only hashes normalized text, they would stop verifying:

```console
$ grep digest mise.lock   # written by an older mise on a Windows checkout
aube = { path = ".mise/locks/npm-prettier/3.6.2", digest = "sha256:b52ed015…" }
$ mise install --locked
mise ✗ npm:prettier@3.6.2 · failed: dependency sidecar …/npm-prettier/3.6.2:
  digest mismatch; run `mise lock` to accept the edited graph
```

`mise install --locked` never refreshes a digest, so the user would be stuck
until they re-locked or ran an unlocked install.

## The fix

Verification now accepts either digest: the normalized one, or the raw bytes an
older mise recorded. That is a compatibility path, not a second hash — a real
change to the graph still matches neither.

The stale entry also heals itself. When a save runs after something has already
loaded the graph (an ordinary install replaying it, for example), mise records
the normalized digest for that entry. It uses the graph already in memory, so it
costs no extra I/O, never re-reads or rewrites the sidecar, and does not fire
during a read-only `mise install --locked`.

```console
$ mise install --locked        # legacy digest: still installs, lockfile untouched
mise ✓ npm:prettier@3.6.2  381ms
$ grep digest mise.lock
aube = { path = ".mise/locks/npm-prettier/3.6.2", digest = "sha256:b52ed015…" }

$ mise install                 # ordinary install records the normalized digest
mise ✓ npm:prettier@3.6.2  862ms
$ grep digest mise.lock
aube = { path = ".mise/locks/npm-prettier/3.6.2", digest = "sha256:0b89746a…" }
```

The sidecar files themselves are byte-identical throughout. Once the entry is
healed it verifies on every platform, which the raw-CRLF digest never did —
that lockfile was already broken for the Linux and macOS members of the same
team.

**Users need to do nothing.** Lockfiles written on Windows by older versions
keep working, and the recorded digest converges on the portable one by itself.

## Tests

- `src/lockfile/graph.rs`: a unit test writes a lockfile whose digest is over the
  raw CRLF bytes, then asserts the graph still loads, a save after that load
  records the normalized digest, the sidecar bytes are untouched, and a graph
  that was never opened keeps its recorded digest.

title: feat(bootstrap): add process_type to the launchd agent schema
body:
Adds `process_type` to `[bootstrap.macos.launchd.agents]`, mapping to launchd's `ProcessType`.

```toml
[bootstrap.macos.launchd.agents.indexer]
program = "~/.local/bin/indexer"
run_at_load = true
keep_alive = true
process_type = "Background"
```

## Why

`ProcessType` is how launchd decides which scheduling band a job runs in, and it is the key that matters for an agent meant to stay out of the way. `Background` jobs are throttled on CPU **and disk I/O** so they yield to interactive work.

`nice` is already supported, but it is not a substitute: it adjusts CPU priority only and does not reach the I/O throttling, which is usually what makes a background agent noticeable.

## Unrecognized values are an error

launchd compares the string exactly and silently ignores a `ProcessType` it does not know. So `process_type = "background"` would be accepted by the plist parser and then do nothing, leaving the job in the default band while the config claims otherwise.

So anything not exactly `Background`, `Standard`, `Adaptive` or `Interactive` is rejected at config time rather than written out, which turns a silent misconfiguration into an error message.

Exactly, rather than case-insensitively, so that `schema/mise.json` can say the same thing: JSON Schema has no case-insensitive enum, and the alternative is a character-class regex in a public schema file with nothing tying it back to the constant. A near miss is still the likely typo, so the error names the fix instead of only listing the valid values:

```
agent 'indexer' `process_type` must be one of Background, Standard, Adaptive, Interactive, got 'background' (did you mean 'Background'?)
```

The value stays quoted, so `'  Adaptive  '` shows its trailing space rather than reading as correct. It is the same reasoning as the existing `nice` range check, which rejects out-of-range values rather than letting launchd clamp them.

## Platform

`process_type` is macOS-only, exactly as `nice`, `keep_alive`, `throttle_interval` and the rest of this table already are. The gate is on the section, not per field: `is_available()` is `cfg!(target_os = "macos") && which("launchctl")`, and `unavailable_reason()` reports "only available on macos". Validation still runs when the config is parsed on any platform, which matches the existing fields and means a typo is caught in CI on Linux too.

## Tests

Three, each pinning a property that would otherwise fail quietly:

- each of the four spellings is accepted and reaches the plist unchanged
- `Realtime`, `bg`, `""` and `Backgroundd` are rejected
- a near miss (`background`, `  Adaptive  `, `INTERACTIVE`) is rejected too, but with the exact spelling named, while something close to nothing gets the list and no guess
- the key reaches the plist only when set

11 tests in `system::launchd` pass; clippy and fmt clean. Docs table and `schema/mise.json` updated alongside.

title: fix(lockfile): refuse to install a locked URL from a different release
body:
## Problem

A lockfile entry carries a `version` field and a per-platform `url`, and nothing
compares them. The install directory, the version mise prints, `mise ls` and
every later `mise exec` all read `version`; the bytes come from `url`. When the
two disagree, mise installs one release under another release's name and reports
success.

This is not hypothetical. `jdx/fnox`'s `mise.lock` on main recorded:

```toml
[[tools.hk]]
version = "2.0.1"
backend = "aqua:jdx/hk"

[tools.hk."platforms.linux-x64"]
url = "https://github.com/jdx/hk/releases/download/v1.56.1/hk-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz"
```

CI reported `hk@2.0.1 installed` on every run while actually running hk 1.56.1.
That hid a genuine incompatibility — the repo's `hk.pkl` still uses the hk v1
config schema, which hk 2 rejects — for four days, until the lockfile was
regenerated for an unrelated reason. `jdx/communique` still carries the same
entry today.

Two things produce such an entry:

1. **An external rewrite of the `version` line.** Renovate's mise manager bumps
   the version in `mise.lock` as a one-line text edit and does not touch the
   platform blocks. The fnox commit above is literally `mise.lock | 2 +-`.
2. **A release that drops a platform.** If the recorded version has no artifact
   for a platform, `mise lock` reports that target as skipped and leaves the
   previous block in place, still pointing at the older release it resolved
   against. `aube` 2.2.17 publishes no `x86_64-apple-darwin` CLI archive, so
   `fnox`, `pitchfork` and `usage` all hold a `macos-x64` entry from 2.0.1 or
   2.2.12 under `version = "2.2.17"`.

Neither `mise install` nor `mise install --locked` notices, and neither repairs
the entry, so the wrong version persists across every later run.

## Change

`mise install` now fails when the locked download URL for the platform being
installed provably names a different release than the entry's `version`:

```console
$ mise install --locked
mise ✗ hk@latest  0ms · failed: hk@2.0.1 is locked to a download URL from 1.56.1:
Error:
   0: Failed to install hk@latest: hk@2.0.1 is locked to a download URL from 1.56.1:
        https://github.com/jdx/hk/releases/download/v1.56.1/hk-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz
      Installing it would put 1.56.1 on disk under the name 2.0.1. Either the
      `version` field was rewritten without refreshing the
      `[tools.hk."platforms.linux-x64"]` block, or a later release dropped
      linux-x64 and left the old block behind. Run `mise lock` to regenerate the
      entry; if it reports the entry as skipped and leaves it unchanged, 2.0.1
      has no linux-x64 artifact.
```

The check runs before anything is downloaded, only for tool versions that came
from a lockfile, and only for the platform actually being installed — a stale
`macos-x64` block does not fail a Linux install, because that machine installs
the right bytes.

`mise lock` is unaffected, so the documented repair still works on a broken
lockfile.

### Detectio

--- e2e/lockfile/test_lockfile_version_url_mismatch (+54/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,54 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+# A lockfile entry whose `version` was rewritten without refreshing its platform
+# block downloads one release under another's name. Nothing downstream compares
+# the two — the install directory and everything mise prints come from `version`,
+# the bytes come from the URL — so the install "succeeds" with the wrong binary
+# and `mise install` never repairs the entry. mise must refuse instead.
+
+export MISE_LOCKFILE=1
+
+detect_platform
+
+case "$MISE_PLATFORM_OS" in
+  macos) ASSET_OS="darwin" ;;
+  *) ASSET_OS="linux" ;;
+esac
+
+case "$MISE_PLATFORM_ARCH" in
+  arm64) ASSET_ARCH="arm64" ;;
+  *) ASSET_ARCH="amd64" ;;
+esac
+
+cat <<EOF >mise.toml
+[tools]
+shfmt = "3.10.0"
+EOF
+
+write_lock() {
+  cat <<EOF >mise.lock
+[[tools.shfmt]]
+version = "3.10.0"
+backend = "aqua:mvdan/sh"
+"platforms.$MISE_PLATFORM" = { url = "https://github.com/mvdan/sh/releases/download/v$1/shfmt_v$1_${ASSET_OS}_${ASSET_ARCH}" }
+EOF
+}
+
+# The URL names 3.7.0 while the entry claims 3.10.0.
+write_lock 3.7.0
+
+assert_fail "mise install" "locked to a download URL from 3.7.0"
+assert_fail "mise install" "to regenerate the entry"
+assert_fail "mise install --locked" "locked to a download URL from 3.7.0"
+
+# The refusal comes before the download, so nothing landed under the wrong name.
+assert_fail "test -d \"$MISE_DATA_DIR/installs/shfmt/3.10.0\""
+
+# `mise lock` is the documented repair, so it must still read the broken entry.
+mise lock --platform "$MISE_PLATFORM"
+assert_contains "cat mise.lock" "v3.10.0/shfmt_v3.10.0_${ASSET_OS}_${ASSET_ARCH}"
+
+# A URL that agrees with the version installs as usual.
+write_lock 3.10.0
+mise install --locked
+assert_contains "mise x shfmt -- shfmt --version" "v3.10.0"

title: feat(daemons): register projects without starting daemons
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/51
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Prepare a checkout for hostname-triggered startup without first starting and stopping its services:

```sh
mise daemons register
mise daemons urls
```

The new experimental command installs missing tools, validates the complete selected dependency graph, and registers generated Pitchfork configuration. It includes local daemons outside the default group and imported dependencies in their owning projects. It does not start or restart daemons, initialize database data, or install a supervisor service. Existing running daemons keep running.

With a running Pitchfork supervisor and its proxy enabled, the first request to a registered hostname starts the application and its dependencies. Each linked worktree is registered separately. Listing URLs remains read-only.

Validation: daemon command regression coverage checks registration without start/restart calls, default-group behavior, and imported dependency registration. A macOS integration test with current Pitchfork verifies that two fresh checkouts remain stopped after registration and start correctly on their first hostname request. That test accepts a local build via `MISE_TEST_PITCHFORK` until dependency-aware proxy startup has a released default. CLI documentation and completions were regenerated; scoped checks passed.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: OpenAI/GPT-6; version: unavailable.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Experimental daemons path writes Pitchfork configuration and may install tools, but deliberately avoids starting or restarting services compared to existing start/restart flows.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds **`mise daemons register`**, an experimental write command that prepares a checkout for **on-demand** daemon startup: it installs missing tools, validates the full daemon graph (including imports and daemons outside the default group), and pushes generated Pitchfork config **without** issuing start/restart to Pitchfork or touching already-running processes.
> 
> The CLI wires the subcommand through usage/man/docs and marks it as a state-modifying effect. **`Daemons::starts()`** and the install path treat register like start/restart for validation and `runtime.prepare`, but register passes an **empty launch set** and exits after printing a success line per matched project root.
> 
> Docs explain the proxy workflow (`register` vs read-only `urls`). Tests assert no `args=start`/`restart` in the Pitchfork log, reject extra args and **`MISE_SAFE`**, cover cross-namespace imports and non-default groups, and add an optional Pitchfork integration test where the first HTTP request to a registered hostname starts dependencies.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 132f3b0a4e3361f1bdbc2ae87cb8ff1d68913c71. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).
