+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+if [[ -z ${MISE_TEST_PITCHFORK:-} ]]; then
+  echo "Skipping: set MISE_TEST_PITCHFORK to a build with dependency-aware proxy startup"
+  exit 0
+fi
+cp "$MISE_TEST_PITCHFORK" ~/bin/pitchfork
+export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"
+export PITCHFORK_STATE_DIR="$TMPDIR/pf"
+export PITCHFORK_CONFIG_DIR="$TMPDIR/pf-config"
+export PITCHFORK_INTERVAL=500ms
+export PITCHFORK_PROXY_ENABLE=true
+export PITCHFORK_PROXY_HTTPS=false
+export PITCHFORK_PROXY_DNS=false
+export PITCHFORK_PROXY_SYNC_HOSTS=false
+export PITCHFORK_PROXY_AUTO_TRUST=false
+export PITCHFORK_PROXY_TLD=localhost
+PITCHFORK_PROXY_PORT=$(python3 -c 'import socket; s=socket.socket(); s.bind(("127.0.0.1",0)); print(s.getsockname()[1])')
+export PITCHFORK_PROXY_PORT
+trap 'pitchfork supervisor stop >/dev/null 2>&1 || true' EXIT
+
+PITCHFORK_MISE_BIN="$(command -v mise)" pitchfork supervisor start
+
+mkdir project
+cd project
+git init -q
+cat >mise.toml <<'TOML'
+[tools]
+pitchfork = "system"
+[daemons_settings]
+namespace = "proxy-test"
+[daemons.prepare]
+run = "echo ready > dependency-ready; exec sleep 600"
+ready_cmd = "test -f dependency-ready"
+[daemons.api]
+run = "test -f dependency-ready && sleep 2 && exec python3 -m http.server $API_PORT --bind 127.0.0.1"
+port = { auto = true, base = 35000 }
+ready_cmd = "curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/proof"
+depends = ["prepare"]
+TOML
+git add mise.toml
+git -c user.name=test -c user.email=test@example.invalid commit -qm fixture
+git worktree add -qb other ../other
+
+# Register a fresh checkout without ever starting it. A proxy request must
+# discover the generated config and start its dependency graph.
+for checkout in "$PWD" "$PWD/../other"; do
+  (
+    cd "$checkout"
+    basename "$checkout" >proof
+    mise daemons register
+    assert "test ! -f dependency-ready"
+    assert "mise daemons ls --json | jq -e 'all(.[]; .status != \"running\")'"
+    url=$(mise env --json | jq -r .API_URL)
+    hostport=${url#http://}
+    assert_contains "curl --noproxy '*' -fsS --max-time 30 --resolve '$hostport:127.0.0.1' '$url/proof'" "$(basename "$checkout")"
+    assert "test -f dependency-ready"
+    assert_contains "mise daemons ls --json" '"status": "running"'
+  )
+done
+
+# Both worktree URLs still resolve to their own process after the second starts.
+first_url=$(mise env --json | jq -r .API_URL)
+second_url=$(cd ../other && mise env --json | jq -r .API_URL)
+assert "test '$first_url' != '$second_url'"
+assert_contains "curl --noproxy '*' -fsS --resolve '${first_url#http://}:127.0.0.1' '$first_url/proof'" project
+assert_contains "curl --noproxy '*' -fsS --resolve '${second_url#http://}:127.0.0.1' '$second_url/proof'" other

title: fix(lock): install locked npm and pypi tools from Windows checkouts
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/50
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Lockfile v2 stores native dependency graphs in sidecar directories such as
`.mise/locks/npm-prettier/3.6.2/` and pins each one in `mise.lock` with a
SHA-256 over the file's exact bytes. Git on Windows checks out with
`core.autocrlf=true` by default, which rewrites those LF line endings to CRLF,
so the bytes no longer match what mise recorded. On any Windows checkout of a
repository that commits sidecars, `mise install --locked` failed:

```
mise ERROR Failed to install npm:prettier@latest: dependency sidecar
D:\a\hk\hk\.mise/locks/npm-prettier/3.9.6: digest mismatch;
run `mise lock` to accept the edited graph; run `mise lock` to repair it
```

There is a second, quieter half: an ordinary `mise install` on the same Windows
checkout *accepts* the CRLF file as a deliberate edit and rewrites `mise.lock`
with the digest of the CRLF bytes — which then breaks the identical checkout on
Linux and macOS.

That error is from a real `build-windows` failure in jdx/hk, which then had to
carry a hand-written `.gitattributes` rule (`.mise/locks/** -text`) to work
around it. Every repository that commits sidecars and runs Windows CI needs the
same workaround today.

## The fix

mise now hashes sidecar text with CRLF normalized to LF, on write and on verify,
and leaves the file bytes exactly as they are on disk. A CRLF working copy
verifies against the committed digest, `mise lock` does not rewrite it, and the
recorded digest stays the same on every platform.

This does not weaken the integrity guarantee in any way that matters. Every
sidecar file is text that mise serializes itself (`uv.lock`, `pyproject.toml`,
`aube-lock.yaml`, `package.json`) — there is no binary sidecar to corrupt — and
the dependency graph is identical under either line ending. Any real change to
the graph, including whitespace inside a line, still changes the digest and the
installation identity. Existing lockfiles keep their current digests, because
mise has always written LF.

**Users need to do nothing.** Existing checkouts are fixed as soon as they run a
mise with this change; no `mise lock` re-run and no `mise.lock` change is
required. Repositories that added a `.gitattributes` workaround can drop it.

### Alternative considered

Writing a `.gitattributes` containing `** -text` into `.mise/locks/` whenever
mise creates a sidecar was rejected as the fix. It only helps repositories that
commit the generated file, it does nothing for the many checkouts that already
exist with CRLF on disk, and it puts a file mise did not have to write into the
user's repository. Normalizing the hash fixes every case without touching the
user's tree. A project that still wants byte-exact checkouts can add the rule
itself.

## Before and after

Locking `npm:prettier@3.6.2` in a scratch project, then converting the sidecar
to CRLF the way git does on Windows:

```console
$ mise lock
$ grep digest mise.lock

title: ci: measure the windows-e2e tool cache (no change)
body:
**Closing with no change: the Windows tool cache is already the right call.** Every variant I measured made `windows-e2e` slower. Leaving the numbers here so the next person does not repeat the experiment.

## The premise, and why it was wrong

`windows-e2e` sets `MISE_DATA_DIR=~/.local/share/mise` for the whole job, so the e2e suite installs its tools into the same directory `.github/actions/mise-tools` caches. That cache holds **3,834 MB across 56,517 files** (1,220 MB compressed) and takes **~114s** to restore, against **~275s** for the test step itself.

The premise was that unpacking is per-file, so dropping the file-heaviest tools would buy most of the restore back cheaply. A diagnostic job on this branch measured the composition and the cold-install cost of each tool on a Windows runner:

| tool | size | files | cold install |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| zig | 294 MB | 15,377 | 15.9s |
| go | 232 MB | 13,265 | 7.6s |
| python | 318 MB | 11,362 | 5.3s |
| vfox-nodejs | 205 MB | 4,260 | 3.3s |
| node (3 versions) | 283 MB | 6,361 | 21s |
| bun (3 versions) | 613 MB | 12 | — |
| java | 328 MB | 494 | 5.8s |
| aube (2 versions) | 263 MB | 17 | — |
| `bin/` (a mise binary a test drops there) | 234 MB | 1 | — |

**Restore is bandwidth-bound, not file-bound.** Trimming the cache to 2,537 MB / 12,170 files — 78% fewer files — moved the restore from 91s to 75s. Both work out to roughly 35-42 MB/s of unpacking. Removing the files bought almost nothing; only removing bytes helps, and bytes are what the tests need back.

## What each variant cost

| variant | `mise-tools` | e2e | job |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| cache as it is today (21 runs on `main`) | 114s | 306s | **444s** |
| `cache: false` (2 runs) | 29s | 470s | 519s |
| cache narrowed to 861 MB, warm restore (1 run) | 91s | 457s | 570s |

Per-test-file timings from the narrowed run against a warm `main` run show the cost landing exactly where the tools were removed:

| test file | main | narrowed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `zig.Tests.ps1` | 0.3s | 39.3s |
| `go.Tests.ps1` | 0.7s | 35.9s |
| `vfox.Tests.ps1` | 8.7s | 39.7s |
| `pypi_lock.Tests.ps1` | 18.2s | 37.7s |
| `uv.Tests.ps1` | 1.9s | 13.4s |
| `python.Tests.ps1` | 35.4s | 45.8s |

That is +147s directly attributable to the four tools left out, against 23s saved on the restore. The suite installs roughly 35 tools and backends, and the per-install overhead outside the download — registry lookups, lockfile writes, checksum verification — dominates the download time I had measured in isolation.

## Two smaller findings, both worth knowing

- **`actions/cache` does not apply `!` patterns inside a bare directory path.** It resolves patterns with implicit descendants off, so `~/.local/share/mise` matches the directory itself and tar archives it whole; a later `!~/.local/share/mise/installs/zig/**` never matches anything. My first attempt at trimming changed the cache from 1,220 MB to 1,213 MB — that is, it did nothing. Cursor Bugbot called this

title: fix(daemons): run readiness and health checks in the project environment
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/48
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Daemon readiness and health commands now resolve tools and environment variables in the owning project, including linked worktrees and preset overrides. Previously, a supervisor started from one checkout could reuse its `API_PORT` when probing another checkout, report the second server ready too early, and return a proxy error.

```toml
[daemons.api]
run = "python3 -m http.server $API_PORT --bind 127.0.0.1"
port = { auto = true, base = 35000 }
ready_cmd = "curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:$API_PORT/"
```

On Unix, the probe now uses the same project's mise environment as the daemon command. String and structured readiness/health commands are supported; structured timeout, interval, and retry options are preserved. Explicit `mise = false` remains an opt-out for custom commands. Preset probe overrides receive the same environment handling as built-in probes.

Regression coverage exercises two real Git worktrees sharing one supervisor, with delayed startup to expose premature readiness and health probes recording their resolved ports. An additional opt-in integration test uses `MISE_TEST_PITCHFORK` to test dependency-aware proxy startup, worktree routing, idle shutdown, wake-up, and explicit-start ownership against a local Pitchfork build. It will need a released Pitchfork default when those features ship.

Validation: macOS regression tests, focused preset tests, and scoped formatting/static checks. Pitchfork's six dedicated idle lifecycle tests also passed on macOS, including streaming/WebSocket activity and shared dependencies. These tests use isolated supervisors and do not install a boot service.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: OpenAI/GPT-6; version: unavailable.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes how daemon readiness/health execute across worktrees and proxy lifecycle; mis-wrapping could cause false ready/stop behavior, but behavior is gated by `mise = false` and covered by new e2e/unit tests.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Daemon readiness and health probes now run inside each checkout’s mise tool environment**, so `ready_cmd` / `health_cmd` see the right ports, tools, and env vars when one Pitchfork supervisor serves multiple Git worktrees.
> 
> On Unix, probe commands (string or `{ run = ... }` tables) are wrapped via `mise x` through a shared `wrap_probe_commands` helper for **task-backed**, **preset**, and **custom `run` daemons** at config/render time or when writing runtime config; **`mise = false` still skips wrapping**. Structured probe options (timeout, interval, retries) are unchanged.
> 
> **Regression coverage** adds a dual-worktree e2e that asserts probes resolve per-checkout endpoints and health state, plus an opt-in proxy idle/restart e2e behind `MISE_TEST_PITCHFORK`. **macOS e2e** uses `/tmp` for `test_daemons*` fixtures to avoid Pitchfork Unix socket path limits.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot]

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+if [[ -z ${MISE_TEST_PITCHFORK:-} ]]; then
+  echo "Skipping: set MISE_TEST_PITCHFORK to a build with proxy idle shutdown"
+  exit 0
+fi

+export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"
+export PITCHFORK_STATE_DIR="$TMPDIR/pf"
+export PITCHFORK_CONFIG_DIR="$TMPDIR/pf-config"
+export PITCHFORK_PROXY_IDLE_TIMEOUT=5s
+export PITCHFORK_INTERVAL=500ms
+export PITCHFORK_PROXY_ENABLE=true
+export PITCHFORK_PROXY_HTTPS=false
+export PITCHFORK_PROXY_DNS=false
+export PITCHFORK_PROXY_SYNC_HOSTS=false
+export PITCHFORK_PROXY_AUTO_TRUST=false
+export PITCHFORK_PROXY_TLD=localhost

+export PITCHFORK_PROXY_PORT
+trap 'pitchfork supervisor stop >/dev/null 2>&1 || true' EXIT
+
+mkdir project
+cd project
+git init -q
+cat >mise.toml <<'TOML'
+[tools]
+pitchfork = "system"
+[daemons_settings]
+namespace = "proxy-test"
+[daemons.prepare]
+run = "echo ready > dependency-ready; exec sleep 600"
+ready_cmd = "test -f dependency-ready"
+[daemons.api]
+run = "test -f dependency-ready && sleep 2 && exec python3 -m http.server $API_PORT --bind 127.0.0.1"
+port = { auto = true, base = 35000 }
+ready_cmd = "curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:$API_PORT/proof"
+depends = ["prepare"]
+TOML
+git add mise.toml
+git -c user.name=test -c user.email=test@example.invalid commit -qm fixture
+git worktree add -qb other ../other
+
+# Register each checkout with mise, then leave the stack stopped. The API has
+# never started: a proxy request must start its dependency from generated config.
+for checkout in "$PWD" "$PWD/../other"; do
+  (
+    cd "$checkout"
+    basename "$checkout" >proof
+    mise daemons start prepare
+    mise daemons stop
+    mv dependency-ready dependency-before-stop
+    url=$(mise env --json | jq -r .API_URL)
+    hostport=${url#http://}
+    assert_contains "curl --noproxy '*' -fsS --max-time 30 --resolve '$hostport:127.0.0.1' '$url/proof'" "$(basename "$checkout")"
+    assert "test -f dependency-ready"
+    assert_contains "mise daemons ls --json" '"status": "running"'
+  )
+done
+
+# Both worktree URLs still resolve to their own process after the second starts.
+first_url=$(mise env --json | jq -r .API_URL)
+second_url=$(cd ../other && mise env --json | jq -r .API_URL)
+assert "test '$first_url' != '$second_url'"
+assert_contains "curl --noproxy '*' -fsS --resolve '${first_url#http://}:127.0.0.1' '$first_url/proof'" project
+assert_contains "curl --noproxy '*' -fsS --resolve '${second_url#http://}:127.0.0.1' '$second_url/proof'" other
+
+# Inactivity must stop both the API and its proxy-started dependency in each
+# checkout. Poll status without sending traffic that would reset the idle timer.
+wait_for_stopped() {
+  local attempt
+  for ((attempt = 0; attempt < 40; attempt++)); do
+    if mise daemons ls --json | jq -e 'length == 2 and all(.[]; .status == "stopped")' >/dev/null; then
+      return 0
+    fi
+    sleep 1
+  done
+  mise daemons ls --json
+  return 1
+}
+export -f wait_for_stopped
+for checkout in "$PWD" "$PWD/../other"; do
+  (
+    cd "$checkout"
+    assert wait_for_stopped
+    mv dependency-ready dependency-before-restart
+    url=$(mise env --json | jq -r .API_URL)
+    assert_contains "curl --noproxy '*' -fsS --max-time 30 --resolve '${url#http://}:127.0.0.1' '$url/proof'" "$(basename "$checkout")"
+    assert "test -f dependency-ready"
+    assert_contains "mise daemons ls --json" '"status": "running"'
+  )
+done
+
+# Explicitly claiming a proxy-started stack keeps its dependency graph running.
+mise daemons start api
+sleep 8
+assert "mise daemons ls --json | jq -e 'length == 2 and all(.[]; .status == \"running\")'"

title: feat(config): accept "unix" as an os selector
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/47
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`os` selectors accepted only concrete OS names, so "everywhere except Windows" had to be
spelled `os = ["linux", "macos"]`, which also leaves out every other Unix system mise runs
on. `unix` now works as an `os` selector and matches the same platforms as the `unix`
[config environment](https://mise.jdx.dev/configuration/environments.html#platform-environments).

It is accepted wherever `os` already was — `[tools]`, `[bootstrap.packages]`,
`[doctor.checks]`, and `[dotfiles]` tracking and destination variants — with an optional
`/arch` like any other selector:

```toml
[tools]
# installed on Linux, macOS, and other Unix platforms; skipped on Windows
ripgrep = { version = "latest", os = ["unix"] }

[dotfiles]
# one shared ~/.zshrc for Unix machines, never deployed to a Windows machine
"~/.zshrc" = { mode = "track", variants = [{ os = "unix" }] }
```

The dotfiles case is what prompted this. Tracked-file enrollment is shared through the
setup repository, so putting a `mode = "track"` entry in an OS-specific config file such as
`config.unix.toml` does not keep it off the other machines — every machine that syncs sees
the entry, and only `variants` limit where a path is applied
([#13394](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13394)). Previously the closest available
spelling was `variants = [{ os = "linux" }, { os = "macos" }]`, which splits Linux and macOS
into two separate streams with separate contents. `os = "unix"` expresses the intended
"one stream for my Unix machines, nothing on Windows".

## Variant specificity

A family selector is deliberately less specific than an OS name, so a macOS variant still
wins over a Unix one on a Mac:

```toml
"~/.zshrc" = { mode = "track", variants = [{ os = "unix" }, { os = "macos" }] }
```

Variant scores are doubled to make room for the family (`profile` 4, an OS 2, the `unix`
family 1, an architecture 2 more), which preserves the documented tie between a
profile-only variant and an OS-and-architecture variant. A variant listing several
selectors is now scored by the entry that actually matched instead of by its most specific
entry, so `os = ["unix", "windows/arm64"]` no longer claims architecture specificity on
Linux. That only changes which variant wins among mixed-selector lists; single-selector
variants score as before.

`unix` matches non-Windows platforms only. On Windows, a `unix` variant selects nothing, and
a tool or package restricted to `unix` is skipped.

## Validation

- `cargo test --bin mise` covering the new selector and variant-scoring cases, plus
  `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `mise run lint`.
- New e2e test `e2e/cli/test_os_selector_unix`: on Linux, a tool with `os = ["unix"]`
  installs and resolves, a `unix` doctor check runs, and a `windows` one is skipped.
- The Windows behavior is covered by a `#[cfg(windows)]` unit test rather than a m

title: ci: run macOS dotfiles e2e tests concurrently
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/46
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

The `unit-macos` job is the longest job in the test workflow, so it sets the wall-clock time of every CI run. Most of that time is one step that runs 22 dotfiles and bootstrap e2e tests one at a time. This PR runs most of them concurrently.

## Measured problem

I measured the step on recent successful runs, using step durations from the GitHub API and per-test times from the job logs:

| Run | Runner | Step | Sum of per-test times |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 35462350275 (main push) | Namespace, 6 vCPU | 777s | 776s |
| 35460690769 (PR) | Namespace, 6 vCPU | 816s | 815s |
| 35462929069 (external PR) | macos-14, 3 cores | 1041s | 1035s |

The step time equals the sum of the per-test times, so the tests ran strictly one after another. The slowest tests on Namespace are `test_dotfiles_watch_throttle` (103s), `test_dotfiles_rollback_types` (93s), and `test_dotfiles_watch` (68s).

## What changed

- `mise run test:e2e <patterns>` now passes the matched tests to `e2e/run_all_tests` when `E2E_JOBS` is set. Without `E2E_JOBS`, it runs them one at a time as before. `run_all_tests` accepts an explicit list of tests and runs them in the given order. Explicitly named tests run even if they are `_slow`, and `.release-skip-e2e` still applies only to full-suite runs. Both of those match what the task did before.
- `unit-macos` splits the step in two:
  - **19 tests run concurrently:** 3 at a time on Namespace runners (6 vCPU) and 2 at a time on the shared macos-14 runners (3 cores). The tests are listed longest first so the slowest ones start immediately.
  - **The 3 watcher tests run serially** (`watch_throttle`, `watch`, `watch_pending`). They assert on debounce and throttle windows and on "nothing else is saved within N seconds". Running them next to other tests could delay filesystem events and cause flakes.

### Why the concurrent tests are safe

`e2e/run_test` gives every test its own `HOME`, `TMPDIR`, `MISE_*_DIR`s, and working directory, and runs it under `env -i`. I also checked the 19 tests for shared state outside that sandbox:

- `test_bootstrap_from_git_dumb_http` binds its HTTP server to port 0.
- `test_bootstrap_user_services` is the only test that loads a real LaunchAgent. It uses a label no other test uses (`dev.mise.mise-e2e-sleep`). The other tests only query launchd status.
- None of the 19 tests sleep or wait on timers.
- The Linux e2e job already runs these tests concurrently (`E2E_JOBS: 2`).

### Measured result

On two CI runs of this PR (Namespace runners, runs 35467758521 and 35468975957), the concurrent group took 232s and 227s, and the serial watcher group took 188s and 180s. Together that is **407–420s instead of 777–816s**, and `unit-macos` took 901–936s instead of 1245–1329s. All 22 tests passed in both runs. With 2 lanes, the shared macos-14 runners should see a similar but smaller gain, roughly 560s instead of about 1000s;

title: chore(deps): bump mr-boxington to 1.14.0 and drop the mbx fallback docs
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/45
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Contributors building mise locally now get mbx 1.14.0. mise still wraps `cargo` with mbx through the existing `[wrappers.cargo]` entry, so `mise run` tasks, `mise exec -- cargo …` and plain `cargo` in a shell with mise activated share compiled work across checkouts as before.

- **mbx 1.14.0.** `mise.lock` now installs mr-boxington through the `packslip:` backend. Each platform entry is checked against a sigstore signature from the mr-boxington release workflow. The old `github-attestations` provenance fields are gone.
- **`min_version` raised from 2026.8.16 to 2026.9.2.** That is the first mise release with the `packslip:` backend, so older mise can't read the new lockfile entry. Run `mise self-update` if mise refuses to load the project config.
- **No more "bypass mbx" fallback docs.** The instructions to rerun with `MBX_DISABLE=1` and report the mismatch in an mr-boxington Discussion are gone from AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md and `docs/contributing.md`. CONTRIBUTING.md keeps a short note on when the wrapper applies. The "Cargo build cache" section of `docs/contributing.md` keeps its first paragraph, because the Unit Tests section links to it.

**Left as-is on purpose**

- The `perf` and `perf:record` tasks still run `mbx build --release` directly. Both tasks set `MISE_IGNORED_CONFIG_PATHS` to the repository's `mise.toml`, so the `[wrappers.cargo]` entry doesn't load inside them. Locally, with every config ignored, `cargo` bypassed the wrapper. Switching to `cargo build --release` would drop the appliance-local mbx cache that `perf.yml` and `perf-pr.yml` mount for these builds.
- `[wrappers.cargo]`, the workflow-level `MBX_DISABLE=1` settings and the direct `mbx` calls in workflows are unchanged.

**Validation** (Linux x64, mise 2026.9.11)

- `mbx --version`: 1.14.0. `mbx doctor`: 0 failures, 0 warnings.
- `cargo check` through the wrapper finished in 1m13s (1478 cache hits, 302 misses).
- `MBX_DISABLE=1 cargo --version` works.
- `hk check` on the changed files (prettier, taplo, markdownlint) passed.
- The full CI suite and the perf tasks were not run.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5; version: 2.1.270.*

title: feat(gem): add a source option for installing from one registry
body:
Adds a `source` tool option to the `gem` backend, so one gem can be installed from one registry without changing what every other `gem install` on the machine resolves against.

Today both halves of the backend use whatever `gem sources` lists first: `latest_stable`/`list_remote_versions` read the primary entry, and `gem install` is invoked with no `--source` at all. Installing a single gem from a private registry therefore means making that registry the machine's primary source, which redirects every unrelated `gem install` through it.

```toml
[tools]
"gem:internal-tool" = { version = "latest", source = "https://gems.example.com" }
```

With the option set, version resolution and installation both go to that URL and nothing else on the machine moves. Without it the behaviour is byte-for-byte what it is today.

Two details worth a look:

The value is normalized to end with a slash, because RubyGems treats `https://gems.example.com` and `https://gems.example.com/` as different sources for cache-key purposes and a user will write it either way. An empty or whitespace-only value is treated as unset rather than as an error, so a templated config that resolves to nothing falls back to the machine's own sources instead of failing the install.

Unit tests cover normalization, the empty case, and that an unset option leaves the backend exactly as it was.

  * Require HTTPS for credential-bearing registry URLs, except for local registries.
  * Prevent raw output when credentials must be protected.

* **Documentation**

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+# The gem `source` option, exercised through version listing only. With a
+# source configured, listing is a plain HTTP request against that registry and
+# never shells out to `gem`, so this needs no Ruby and stays fast.
+#
+# Two properties, both of which regressed or would have:
+#
+#   1. The source is read from the CONFIG, even when the backend is built from a
+#      bare CLI argument. Reading it off the argument instead sent listing to
+#      rubygems.org while the cache key still said "private registry", so a
+#      later install took a version from one registry and asked the other for it.
+#   2. A credential in the source never reaches output. RubyGems authenticates a
+#      private registry with basic-auth userinfo, so a token genuinely lives in
+#      this URL.
+
+TOKEN="ghp_e2eSECRET"
+
+# A fake registry. It records each request's path and whether it carried basic
+# auth, one per line, so the assertions below can stay in bash.
+cat >registry.py <<'PYTHON'
+import json
+import os
+import threading
+import time
+from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
+from pathlib import Path
+
+versions = json.dumps([
+    {"number": "1.0.0", "created_at": "2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"},
+    {"number": "2.2.0", "created_at": "2026-02-01T00:00:00.000Z"},
+]).encode()
+
+
+class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
+    def log_message(self, *args):
+        pass
+
+    def do_GET(self):
+        auth = (self.headers.get("Authorization") or "").split(" ")[0] or "none"
+        with open("requests.log", "a") as log:
+            log.write(f"{self.path} {auth}\n")
+        if self.path != "/acme/api/v1/versions/internal-cli.json":
+            self.send_error(404)
+            return
+        self.send_response(200)
+        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
+        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(versions)))
+        self.end_headers()
+        self.wfile.write(versions)
+
+
+def exit_with_test():
+    # Stop once the test script that started us is gone, so the fixture needs
+    # no cleanup trap and never outlives the test.
+    parent = os.getppid()
+    while os.getppid() == parent:
+        time.sleep(0.5)
+    os._exit(0)
+
+
+threading.Thread(target=exit_with_test, daemon=True).start()
+server = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
+Path("registry.port").write_text(str(server.server_port))
+server.serve_forever()
+PYTHON
+
+python3 registry.py &
+registry_pid=$!
+wait_for_file registry.port "gem registry port" 30 "$registry_pid"
+port="$(cat registry.port)"
+
+# Declared in config, with a credential in the URL. The command below names the
+# tool as a bare argument and passes no options.
+cat >mise.toml <<EOF
+[tools]
+"gem:internal-cli" = { version = "latest", source = "http://${TOKEN}@127.0.0.1:${port}/acme" }
+EOF
+
+output="$(MISE_DEBUG=1 mise ls-remote gem:internal-cli 2>&1)"
+echo "$output"
+
+# Versions came from the fixture, not from rubygems.org, which only happens if
+# the source was resolved from config.
+assert_contains_text "$output" "2.2.0"
+
+# Exactly one request, under the source's path, with the credential sent as
+# basic auth rather than dropped.
+assert "cat requests.log" "/acme/api/v1/versions/internal-cli.json Basic"
+
+# And the token appears nowhere, at debug verbosity, in stdout or stderr.
+assert_not_contains_text "$output" "$TOKEN"
+assert_contains_text "$output" "[redacted]"

<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Since 2026.9.11, an npm tool that publishes only pre-releases stops working after install when it's configured as `latest`. mise installs the version the `latest` dist-tag points to. Afterwards, it can't match that version to `latest`, so it warns that the tool is missing and leaves it off PATH.

Reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12085. Every published version of `@deepseek-ai/dsh` is a pre-release, and its `latest` dist-tag is `0.1.5-rc.2`:

```console
$ mise use -g npm:@deepseek-ai/dsh@latest
mise ~/.config/mise/config.toml tools: npm:@deepseek-ai/dsh@0.1.5-rc.2
mise WARN  missing: npm:@deepseek-ai/dsh@latest
$ which dsh
dsh not found
```

With this change, `latest` resolves to `0.1.5-rc.2`, and activation puts `.../npm-deepseek-ai-dsh/0.1.5-rc.2/bin` on PATH again, as in 2026.9.10.

## Cause

#13272 made the installed-version lookup for `latest` skip npm semver pre-releases, so `12.1.0` wins over `13.0.0-0`. When only pre-releases are installed, the lookup now returns nothing. Before #13272, it returned the newest install.

The lookup still prefers the newest stable install. It now falls back to the newest pre-release only when no stable version is installed, so #13272's behavior is unchanged whenever a stable version is present.

## Validation

- New unit test: with only `0.1.5-rc.1` and `0.1.5-rc.2` installed, `latest` resolves to `0.1.5-rc.2`. The test fails without the fix.
- `e2e/backend/test_npm_prerelease_runtime_symlinks` now also checks that `latest` resolves offline to `13.0.0-0` while only that version is installed. The existing assertions still pass: once `12.1.0` is installed, `latest` resolves to it.
- Reproduced the report against the 2026.9.11 release binary and confirmed the fix with a local build.

title: fix(brew-cask): upgrade self-updating casks that install from a pkg
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/41
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise bootstrap packages upgrade` now upgrades self-updating (`auto_updates`) casks that install only through a `.pkg`. These casks previously always skipped because mise could read live versions only from an owned `.app` artifact:

```
brew-cask:tailscale-app: skipped: requires a single owned app
```

Affected casks include `tailscale-app`, `karabiner-elements`, and `nomachine`; after #13385, the same path also covers `microsoft-outlook` and `microsoft-teams`, whose installer choices disable Microsoft AutoUpdate.

For a pkg-only self-updating cask, mise now looks up the pkg IDs recorded in its install receipt with `pkgutil`, reads each available `pkg-version`, and compares those versions using the same Homebrew-compatible rules as app bundles:

- Upgrade when a meaningful receipt is older and no receipt is equal or newer.
- Skip when any receipt is equal to or newer than the cask version, because the application has already updated itself.
- Ignore incomparable helper versions and placeholder versions such as `0.0`.
- Keep readable receipts when another receipt is missing, unreadable, or malformed; skip only when nothing usable remains.

Install and apply behavior are unchanged. Casks with an app artifact keep the existing live bundle-version and running-app checks. Pkg-only upgrades find the app bundles their package receipts installed (`pkgutil --only-dirs --files`) and, like the app path, leave the upgrade until the app stops if one is running.

Reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13350.

## Validation

- On macOS 27, a branch dry run parsed current `karabiner-elements`, `nomachine`, and `tailscale-app` metadata and planned each pkg install.
- The signed Tailscale pkg declares `com.tailscale.ipn.macsys` at `1.102.4`, exactly matching its cask version.
- The signed Karabiner pkg declares `org.pqrs.Karabiner-Elements` at `16.3.0` plus its independently versioned driver receipt at `8.5.0`, validating the mixed-receipt case.
- Current Outlook and Teams packages expose application receipts matching their cask versions plus independently versioned helper receipts.
- Focused all-feature tests pass for older/current/newer/mixed/placeholder decisions, partial receipt failures, plist parsing, and selection of the pkg receipt path.

## Limitations

- This Mac has no matching live pkg receipts for these casks, so I did not perform a real upgrade or validate a post-install `pkgutil` lookup.
- Homebrew currently rejects the downloaded NoMachine 9.8.2_1 artifact because its SHA-256 differs from the cask, so that package could not be inspected until its upstream cask metadata is corrected.

title: fix(brew-cask): install casks that change file ownership in their install steps
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/40
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Casks whose declarative flight steps use `set_ownership` can now be installed with `brew-cask`. This unblocks `parsec`, whose current cask asks Homebrew to restore ownership of `~/.parsec` after its pkg install:

```json
{"postflight_steps": [{"steps": [{
  "type": "set_ownership",
  "paths": [{"path": "~/.parsec"}]
}]}]}
```

```toml
[bootstrap.packages]
"brew-cask:parsec" = "latest"
```

mise now resolves the supported Homebrew path bases and globs, skips missing paths, and runs the equivalent `sudo chown` command. A path that cannot be inspected is skipped as missing, as Homebrew's `exist?` does and as `set_permissions` already does. Explicit users and groups are preserved; otherwise ownership defaults to the current user, including the invoking `SUDO_USER` when mise itself runs under sudo. Recursive ownership remains the default, with Homebrew's `non_recursive` option supported.

This implements only Homebrew's structured `set_ownership` step. It does not evaluate arbitrary Ruby flight blocks.

Reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13350.

## Validation

- On macOS 27, a branch dry run parsed Parsec's current metadata and planned the signed `parsec-macos.pkg` install instead of rejecting `postflight_steps`.
- Five focused all-feature unit tests pass for parsing, malformed input, path resolution, generated `chown` arguments, and the missing-path case.
- `mise run lint-fix` passes at the current head.
- I did not perform the privileged Parsec install or `chown`, so the remaining end-to-end check is the sudo execution against an installed package.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: openai/gpt-5; version: unavailable.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Install-time privileged `chown` on arbitrary resolved paths can affect system or user files if cask metadata is wrong, though parsing validates paths and names before execution.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds Homebrew-compatible **`set_ownership`** to structured cask `preflight_steps` / `postflight_steps`, so casks like Parsec that `chown` paths after install (e.g. `~/.parsec`) no longer fail at metadata parse time.
> 
> The new step parses `paths`, optional `user`/`group`, and `non_recursive` like Homebrew (default **`staff`** group and recursive ownership). At install time it resolves staged globs, appdir, prefix, and absolute/`~` paths, skips paths that do not exist, and runs **`sudo chown`** via mise’s sudo path. Omitted `user` defaults to the invoking user (`SUDO_USER` under `sudo mise`), reusing newly exposed **`prefix_owner`**. Ownership changes are not rolled back on failure, matching Homebrew.

body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/39
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Casks that declare pkg installer `choices` can now be installed with `brew-cask`. Before this change, mise rejected casks such as `microsoft-outlook` and `microsoft-teams` with:

```
mise ERROR brew-cask: pkg installer choices are not supported yet
```

Both casks use a declarative installer choice to omit Microsoft AutoUpdate:

```json
{"choices": [{
  "choiceIdentifier": "com.microsoft.autoupdate",
  "choiceAttribute": "selected",
  "attributeSetting": 0
}]}
```

```toml
[bootstrap.packages]
"brew-cask:microsoft-outlook" = "latest"
```

mise now writes supported choices to a temporary XML plist and passes it to `installer -applyChoiceChangesXML`, matching Homebrew. Casks without choices keep the previous installer arguments. Third-party tap metadata also preserves pkg options instead of silently discarding them.

The parser accepts installer's documented `selected`, `enabled`, and `visible` attributes with `0` or `1`, plus a non-empty `customLocation` path. Missing keys, unknown attributes, mismatched settings, extra fields, deprecated `allow_untrusted`, and other malformed input fail before `installer` runs.

title: feat(install): automatically elevate system installs with sudo
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/38
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Install supported tools into protected system directories without running the entire installation as root:

```sh
mise install --system uv
```

On Unix, mise downloads, verifies, and unpacks the tool as the invoking user, then uses sudo to place the prepared installation in `/usr/local/share/mise/installs` (or the configured system installation directory). Caches and project lockfile updates remain owned by the user. System shim and version-symlink writes also use sudo when needed.

### Supported tools and permissions

- Automatic elevation supports relocatable tools from `aqua`, `github`, `gitlab`, `forgejo`, `http`, and `s3`. Tools with a tool-level `postinstall` hook are not supported by this path.
- Writable destinations need no elevation and retain support for other backends and postinstall hooks.
- `system_packages.sudo = false` disables automatic elevation. Interactive sessions can prompt for a password; noninteractive sessions require sudo to work without a password prompt.
- Elevated installations require root-owned destination directories and ancestors that other users cannot modify, with an exception for root-owned sticky directories. Symlinks within a tool installation are preserved; links outside it are rejected.
- `sudo mise install --system` remains supported but warns about root-owned files in the user's home directory. Direct root execution, including in containers, remains supported.

The privileged helper receives a prepared archive without loading project configuration, environment settings, or hooks. The docs explain the install destination, supported tools, and sudo policy.

### Validation

The implementation includes a filesystem test covering archive publication, symlink validation, permission stripping, manifests, duplicate installs, rejected replacements, and link creation. The original implementation reported passing Clippy and lint checks. An actual sudo password prompt against a protected system directory has not been exercised.

The documentation cleanup passed `mise run lint-fix` (including `cargo check --all-features`), focused Markdown/TOML checks, the documentation build, and rendered-link checks.

Supersedes #13280 by @mxcl, retained as co-author.

title: fix(activate): run enter hooks when activating inside a project
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/37
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Starting a shell inside a trusted project stopped running the project's `enter` hook in 2026.9.x. Changing into the project with `cd` still ran it. This PR makes activation run it again, as 2026.9.0 did. Reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13348 for bash, zsh, and fish.

```toml
[hooks]
enter = "echo ENTER_HOOK_RAN"
```

Before: opening a new terminal in this project prints nothing. After: it prints `ENTER_HOOK_RAN` once, before the first prompt.

## Cause

#13085 changed the first `hook-env` call in the bash, zsh, and fish activate scripts to use `--force`, so daemon sessions get registered. `--force` skips `should_exit_early()`, and that function is also where the `leave`/`cd`/`enter` hooks are scheduled on a directory change. Initial activation counts as a change from no directory to the current one. The other enter-hook path, for newly loaded configs, skips directory changes, so neither path ran the hook.

## Fix

Scheduling now lives in `hook_env::schedule_dir_change_hooks()`. `should_exit_early()` and the `--force` path both call it. A forced refresh in the same directory, such as zsh's refresh after an auto-install, sees no directory change and still runs no hooks.

## Validation

`e2e/config/test_hooks` now checks that a forced run in the same directory skips `enter`, and that a forced run with no previous session runs it. With the one-line fix removed, the second assertion fails. `test_hooks`, `test_hooks_global`, `test_hooks_config_root`, `test_no_hooks`, and `test_safe_mode` pass, and so do `mise run lint` and clippy.

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Touches the activation-time `hook-env --force` path used on every new shell; incorrect scheduling could miss or duplicate project hooks.
> 
> **Overview**
> Restores **enter** (and related **cd**/**leave**) hooks when a new shell starts inside a project directory, matching pre-2026.9.x behavior after activation began using `hook-env --force`.
> 
> Directory-change hook scheduling is extracted into `schedule_dir_change_hooks()`. The normal slow path still calls it from `should_exit_early()`, and the **`--force`** branch in `HookEnv::run` now calls it too so the first post-activation run still counts as entering the current directory even though early exit is skipped. Forced refreshes in the **same** directory still schedule nothing because `dir_change()` is empty.
> 
> E2E coverage in `test_hooks` asserts `hook-env --force` does not emit **HOOK-ENTER** in-place, and that a forced run with no `__MISE_SESSION` does.

title: fix(bootstrap): resolve Homebrew formula aliases and old names
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/36
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`brew:` packages failed to resolve when a Homebrew formula was named by an alias, either in `[bootstrap.packages]` or as a dependency of a third-party tap formula. The Homebrew API serves only canonical names. An alias such as `openssl` returns a 404 instead of redirecting, although mise's code assumed it redirected. Reported in #13358: `microsoft/mssql-release/msodbcsql18` declares `depends_on "openssl"`, so `mise bootstrap packages apply` aborted even though `brew install` handles the formula.

```
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://formulae.brew.sh/api/formula/openssl.json
404
```

## Before

```
$ mise bootstrap packages apply brew:openssl --dry-run
Error:
   0: failed to fetch Homebrew formula 'openssl'
   1: HTTP status client error (404 Not Found) for url (https://formulae.brew.sh/api/formula/openssl.json)
```

## After

```
$ mise bootstrap packages apply brew:openssl --dry-run
mise WARN  'openssl' resolves to 'openssl@3' — use the canonical name in [bootstrap.packages] so `mise bootstrap packages status` can track it
...
pour ca-certificates/2026-08-13 (dependency)
pour openssl@3/3.6.4 (requested)
```

Old names of renamed formulae now resolve too: `act_runner` resolves to `gitea-runner`. A tap formula that depends on `openssl` now pulls in `openssl@3`.

## How it works

When the exact per-formula lookup fails, mise loads Homebrew's bulk `api/formula.json` and maps each alias and old name to its canonical formula. It then fetches the canonical formula instead. The index is about 5.3 MB compressed. It is loaded at most once per run, and only after an exact lookup has failed, so canonical names cost nothing extra. If the name isn't in the index, or the index can't be fetched, mise reports the original error.

The first core lookup for a tap dependency still uses the exact name only. A tap formula that depends on another formula in the same tap therefore doesn't download the index. Alias resolution runs in the existing core fallback, after the tap lookup fails.

Every place that matches a dependency name against the closure now also recognizes old names: install receipts, the source-build environment, and the "use the canonical name" warning. The docs claimed aliases already installed correctly. They are now updated to cover old names and tap dependencies.

## Validation

- Dry-run against the live API with the built binary: `openssl` resolves to `openssl@3`, `postgres` to `postgresql@18`, and `act_runner` to `gitea-runner`. An unknown name still fails with the original 404.
- The reported tap-dependency path: a one-off local test (not committed) that resolves `openssl` as a non-requested dependency of `microsoft/mssql-release` now returns `openssl@3` from core. I couldn't run a full `apply` of the reporter's formula here, because mise's tap-evaluation sandbox can't run Ruby on this machine.
- New unit tests cover buildin

title: fix(backend): run cask installer scripts that need sudo or placeholders
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/33
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Casks whose `installer script` declares `sudo: true` can now be installed with `brew-cask`. Previously mise rejected them with `brew-cask: unsupported installer script field sudo` (#13360). For example:

```toml
[bootstrap.packages]
"brew-cask:logi-options+" = "latest"
```

`mise bootstrap packages apply` now runs the Logi Options+ installer through the same sudo path as pkg installers. mise prompts for a password on a terminal, fails with the exact command when no terminal is available, and follows `system_packages.sudo = false`. `--dry-run` prints `run installer <path> with sudo`.

### Installer placeholders were never expanded

Installer scripts were also run with Homebrew's API placeholders left as literal text. That broke two common shapes, including in casks mise already accepted:

- **Executables under the Caskroom**, such as `$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/Caskroom/reikey/1.4.2/ReiKey Installer.app/...`, failed with `installer executable ... was not found`. mise now runs these from its staged download, which is what Homebrew's Caskroom version directory contains at install time.
- **Placeholder arguments**, such as miniconda's `-p $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/Caskroom/miniconda/base` or `-dir $APPDIR/IBKR Desktop`, reached the installer as literal `$HOMEBREW_PREFIX`/`$APPDIR` strings. They are now expanded with the templating structured flight steps already use. install4j's `$Boolean` is left as-is.

`print_stderr` is accepted too. Homebrew uses `print_stderr: false` only to hide a noisy installer's stderr; mise validates the field and leaves stderr visible.

### Coverage

Of the 31 homebrew-cask casks whose installer declares `sudo: true`, 27 no longer hit an installer-script error. The four `mplab-*` casks still fail because they pipe `input` to the installer's stdin, which remains unsupported. The other artifacts in each cask still have to be supported.

### Validation

New unit tests parse `sudo`/`print_stderr` and reject non-boolean values. They also run a staged installer declared as `$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/Caskroom/<token>/<version>/...` and check the arguments it receives after expansion. The existing installer tests still pass. The elevated branch is a direct call to `sudo::run` and has no unit test, because the tests can't elevate. I didn't run a real macOS install.

title: fix(npm): let other users on a shared machine install npm tools
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/32
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

On a Linux machine shared by several users, only the first user to install an `npm:` tool could install more. Everyone else failed, as reported in #13375:

```
✗ npm:pdf2json@4.1.0  14ms · failed: aube install failed: failed to acquire project lock: Permission denied (os error 13)
lockfile /tmp/fslock/beec52ee050c5785
```

The embedded aube takes a project lock in `$TMPDIR/fslock/`, a directory the xx crate created with the first user's `0755` umask. Each user installs npm tools into their own data directory, so a second user always needs a new lock file there and was refused. Deleting `/tmp/fslock` only helped until another user recreated it.

xx 2.6.2 (jdx/xx#292) makes that directory `1777` like `/tmp`. It also opens existing lock files without `O_CREAT`, so Linux's `fs.protected_regular` doesn't block a file another user created. A directory already left at `0755` by an older mise is fixed the next time its owner installs an npm tool. Until then, `AUBE_NO_LOCK=1` still works around it.

mise's `Cargo.lock` has one xx entry, shared by mise and the embedded aube, so this fix doesn't wait for an aube release. The matching aube bump is aubepkg/aube#1553. The change is only the xx entry in `Cargo.lock`: `xx = "2"` already allows 2.6.2, and its dependencies are the same as 2.6.1's. `cargo update -p xx` would also have downgraded `windows-sys` and `getrandom` in unrelated packages, so the entry was edited directly, and `cargo metadata --locked` accepts it.

## Validation

On Linux with `fs.protected_regular=1`, using a debug build of this branch with a shared `TMPDIR` and separate mise directories for each user: `nobody` and then `coder` ran `mise install npm:pdf2json@4.1.0`, and both succeeded. The lock directory ended up `drwxrwxrwt`, with one `0666` lock file per user. With mise 2026.9.6 (xx 2.6.1), the same sequence fails for the second user with the error above.

title: fix(bootstrap): skip volume metadata when extracting DMGs
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/31
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Installing a cask whose DMG has unreadable volume metadata at its root failed partway through extraction. `mysqlworkbench` is one example: its image ships `.Trashes` with mode `0333` (no read bit for anyone), so:

```toml
[bootstrap.packages]
"brew-cask:mysqlworkbench" = "latest"
```

```
$ mise bootstrap packages apply brew-cask:mysqlworkbench
INFO  brew-cask:mysqlworkbench ✗ failed
Error:
   0: IO error for operation on /var/folders/.../T/.tmpZxYkK9/.Trashes: Permission denied (os error 13)
```

`un_dmg` mounted the image and copied the entire volume. Metadata such as `.Trashes`, `.fseventsd`, `.DS_Store` and `.background` was included, and the copy failed on the first entry it couldn't read. DMG extraction now skips these entries at the volume root and copies everything else as before. The skip list is Homebrew's `DMG_METADATA` list, the same one `brew install --cask` uses, so the cask installs.

The same extraction code is used for aqua tools distributed as DMGs and for DMGs nested inside other cask archives, so both get the fix. Entries with these names deeper in the image, such as inside an `.app` bundle, are still copied.

Reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13361.

## Validation

- A new unit test builds a volume with a mode-`0333` `.Trashes` and other metadata, and checks that the copy succeeds and that only root-level metadata is dropped. With the skip list removed, the test fails with the reporter's `Permission denied (os error 13)`.
- `cargo test --bin mise file::tests` (187 passed), clippy with `-D warnings`, and `mise run lint` pass.
- Not run on macOS against a real DMG; `hdiutil` isn't available in this Linux environment.

https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/30
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise generate git-pre-commit --hook pre-push` writes a hook that passes git's remote name and URL to the task. If the task doesn't declare args, mise appends them to its last command. For example, a `pre-push` task that runs `npm test` ended up running `npm test origin git@github.com:org/repo.git`. This started with #11801, which added `"$@"` to every generated hook. Reported in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13366.

```toml
[tasks.test]
run = ["echo a", "echo b"]

[tasks.pre-push]
run = "mise run test"
```

Before, on `git push`:

```
[pre-push] $ mise run test origin ../remote.git
[test] $ echo a
[test] $ echo b origin ../remote.git
```

After:

```
[pre-push] $ mise run test
[test] $ echo a
[test] $ echo b
```

Generated hooks now pass only the message file (`"$1"`), and only for the hooks where git passes one for the hook to read: `commit-msg`, `prepare-commit-msg`, `applypatch-msg` and `sendemail-validate`. That keeps the `commit-msg` case #11801 was added for. git's other arguments are dropped, including `prepare-commit-msg`'s source and SHA, which would otherwise be appended the same way. Every other hook goes back to how it worked before #11801. `pre-push` still gets the refs being pushed on stdin, because `exec` passes stdin through.

Existing hooks only change when they're regenerated. If someone does want `pre-push`'s arguments in a task, they can edit the hook to use `"$@"` and declare the args with `usage` so they aren't appended to the last command.

## Tests

- Unit test: a `pre-push` hook ends with `exec mise run pre-push` and has no `"$@"`.
- e2e: a real `commit-msg` hook gets the message file, and the commit is rejected when the message doesn't match. A real `prepare-commit-msg` hook passes only the file. `cat` would fail on the extra `message` source argument, and I checked that it does when `"$@"` is put back. A real `git push` to a local bare remote runs the nested task without `origin` on its last command. I checked that the push assertion fails when `"$@"` is put back in the hook.
- The command's help, man page and CLI docs now say which hooks forward arguments.

title: fix(brew-cask): install the cask variation for the host macOS release
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/28
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`brew-cask` now installs the build Homebrew publishes for the host's macOS release, not always the build for the newest macOS.

Homebrew's cask API puts the newest macOS release's `url`, `version`, and `sha256` at the top level. When an older release needs different values, it lists them under `variations`, keyed by tag. mise read only the top level. Reported in #13374: on macOS 15 (Sequoia), arm64, this config

```toml
[bootstrap.packages]
"brew-cask:raycast" = { os = "macos" }
```

downloaded Raycast 2.4.1.0 from `x.raycast-releases.com`, which runs only on Tahoe. `brew install --cask raycast` on the same machine installs 1.104.29 from `variations.arm64_sequoia`. mise now installs the same 1.104.29.

The merge works the same way as Homebrew's `Homebrew::API.merge_variations`:

- It looks up the host's exact tag, with no fallback to an older release's tag. The API writes an entry for every tag whose values differ. Tags follow Homebrew's spelling: `arm64_sequoia` on Apple Silicon, the bare `sequoia` on Intel Macs, and `x86_64_linux` or `arm64_linux` on Linux.
- On a macOS release newer than the ones mise knows, it applies no variation. The top level already describes the newest release, and falling back to the nearest older tag (as bottle selection does) would pick an older build.
- It is shallow: fields the variation leaves out keep their top-level values. For example, claude-code's Linux variations replace only `url` and `sha256`.
- On Tahoe, or for a cask without `variations`, nothing changes.

The fix covers every JSON source for cask metadata: the official API, tap `api/cask/*.json`, and the parent-tap probe. Casks evaluated from tap Ruby already resolved `on_sequoia` and similar blocks against the host, so they were not affected.

A variation that sets `url` or `version` to null marks a platform the cask does not support. mise now stops with `brew-cask: not available for this platform (<tag>)` instead of a serde type error. For example, on Linux, Raycast's `x86_64_linux` variation is all nulls, so `mise bootstrap packages apply -n brew-cask:raycast` stops with that error before it gets to the Linux font-only check.

## Validation

- Unit tests use JSON trimmed from Raycast's cask and shaped like claude-code's and visual-studio-code's. They cover a matching variation, no matching variation, an unknown newer macOS, a partial variation inheriting top-level fields, and a platform with no download. All 396 brew unit tests pass, and clippy is clean.
- I also ran every cask in Homebrew's current API dump (7,741 casks) through the merge for each Apple Silicon, Intel and Linux tag. Every result parses. The only errors are 146 "not available for this platform" cases, which are expected for those casks.
- On Linux, a dry run against the live API applies the `x86_64_linux` variation as expected. I did not run an install on macOS.

*AI-assisted — Too

title: fix(task): recognize child task references during validation
body:
`mise tasks validate` now recognizes references to child monorepo tasks. For example, a root task with `depends = ["//crates/gui:dev"]` validates successfully when that child task exists, instead of reporting `missing-dependency` even though `mise run dev` succeeds.

The fix covers `depends_post`, `wait_for`, and structured `run` references, batches child discovery, and preserves child configuration errors. Task selection and counts, alias-check scope, and remote-file fetching remain unchanged.

## Validation

Targeted e2e suites, scoped hk checks, and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` passed. Regressions cover missing/optional references, configuration errors, batched discovery, and validation scope. Scoped lint-fix also passed; repository-wide lint-fix reports the existing `CHANGELOG.md` size check and shellcheck autofix diagnostics (the shellcheck check passes).

title: feat(task): support relative paths and env vars in usage includes
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/27
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

File tasks can share usage definitions through relative paths or environment variables, without hard-coding an absolute path. For a shared flagset named `common` in the project's `shared.usage.kdl`:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#USAGE include file="$MISE_CONFIG_ROOT/shared.usage.kdl"
#USAGE use "common"
```

A task at `mise-tasks/deploy` can also use `include file="../shared.usage.kdl"`. Relative paths resolve from the task file's directory, regardless of where mise is invoked. Included arguments work consistently during execution, help, task listing, and validation.

Include paths support `$NAME`, `${NAME}`, and `$$` for a literal dollar sign. Variables come from mise's startup environment, supplemented by `MISE_TASK_DIR`, `MISE_TASK_FILE`, and the available configuration and project roots. Task and project `env` directives run too late to supply include variables. An undefined variable produces an invalid-usage diagnostic; the task remains loadable without its usage interface. title: test(daemons): fix flaky test_daemons config lookup
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/26
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`e2e/cli/test_daemons` fails intermittently in CI, on PRs that touch nothing
related to daemons. The harness retries a failed test once, so it usually shows
up as a red first attempt that passes on retry — for example
https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13370 (docs-only) and
https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13362 (go backend), which failed it on both
attempts in two independent runs.

## The cause

The test located the generated pitchfork.toml with:

```bash
generated=$(find "$MISE_STATE_DIR/daemons" -name pitchfork.toml -print -quit)
```

mise gives every project root its own state directory under
`$MISE_STATE_DIR/daemons`, named after a hash of that root. By the later
assertions the test has set up five projects — `workdir`, `override`,
`override/child`, `group-parent`, `group-parent/child` — so five equally-named
`pitchfork.toml` files exist and `find -print -quit` returns whichever one the
filesystem lists first.

Only one of the five is the project under test. Instrumenting the test at the
`MISE_DAEMON_TASK` assertion shows the draw it was making:

```
PROBE candidates=5
PROBE candidate FAIL .../daemons/52f20f715251327f/pitchfork.toml
PROBE candidate FAIL .../daemons/8bb42584db3ca350/pitchfork.toml
PROBE candidate FAIL .../daemons/901a6045956bba9/pitchfork.toml
PROBE candidate FAIL .../daemons/ae696e15f8f7a351/pitchfork.toml
PROBE candidate PASS .../daemons/c3ab5bd152bc9927/pitchfork.toml
```

This also explains the reported failure output, which was verbatim the
`override/child` project's config (`# postgres from <tmp>/home/workdir/override/child/mise.toml`,
`run = "child postgres"`) rather than the workdir's. It reproduces only on some
filesystems: locally readdir returns creation order, which puts the project
under test first every time, so the test passes reliably outside CI.

## The fix

Resolve the state directory by project root rather than by directory order. Each
directory's `state.json` records the root it belongs to, so a small helper looks
the config up through it:

```bash
daemon_state_dir() {
  local root="${1:-$PWD}" state
  state=$(jq -r --arg root "$root" 'select(.root == $root) | input_filename' "$MISE_STATE_DIR"/daemons/*/state.json)
  test -n "$state" || fail "no daemon state directory for $root"
  echo "${state%/state.json}"
}
```

All four lookups now go through it — the three `find -print -quit` call sites,
and the `grep -rl 'parent api' | head -1` one, which was content-unique but
equally indirect. The pre-existing root-matching lookup for `profile_state` was
doing this already; the helper is that same query, named. A root with no state
directory now fails with that message instead of silently asserting against
another project's file.

No production code changes, no sleeps, no retry-count change.

## Validation

- `mise run test:e2e e2e/cli/test_daemons` passes; run three times in a row, 10s/10s/13s.
- Instrumented at

+# mise keeps each project's generated configuration in a state directory named
+# after a hash of the project root, so the several projects this test sets up
+# are indistinguishable by path and a bare `find` returns whichever one the
+# filesystem happens to list first. state.json records the root it belongs to.
+daemon_state_dir() {
+  local requested="${1:-$PWD}" root state
+  # mise records the physical path; bash keeps symlinks in $PWD.
+  root=$(cd -- "$requested" >/dev/null && pwd -P) || fail "cannot resolve daemon root $requested"

+  # arbitrarily, and a multi-line "$state" would silently build a garbled path.
+  test "$(echo "$state" | wc -l)" -eq 1 || fail "several daemon state directories for $root: $state"

title: docs: stop the sidebar and outline from covering the footer
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/25
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Scroll to the bottom of any docs page with a sidebar and the page furniture lands on top of the footer: entries from the "On this page" outline and the Carbon ad are drawn over the sponsor logos, and the sidebar's nav items run across the "MIT License · Copyright © 2026 · jdx.dev" line. It shows up on every doc page whose outline is long enough to fill the viewport — `/dev-tools/` is a good example — in both light and dark mode.

## Cause

VitePress renders `.VPSidebar` and `.VPDoc .aside-container` as `position: fixed` with `height: 100vh`, so both keep painting the left and right edges of the viewport after the doc content ends. The default theme sidesteps this by hiding its own footer on sidebar pages (`.VPFooter.has-sidebar { display: none }`). Our `EndevSponsors` and `EndevFooter` render in the `layout-bottom` slot on every page with no background and no stacking context, so the fixed rails win.

## Fix

Paint the bottom band over the rails:

```css
.EndevSponsors,
.EndevFooter {
  background: var(--vp-c-bg);
  position: relative;
  z-index: 26;
}
```

`26` sits above `--vp-z-index-sidebar` (25 at ≥960px) and below the nav (30), so the band ends both rails as it scrolls into view but never covers the nav bar. Below 960px the sidebar is a drawer at z-index 60 and still opens over the footer, which is what we want.

The tradeoff: the rails now get a hard edge mid-item where the band starts (a truncated sidebar link, a clipped ad image). The alternative — insetting the footer into the content column so the rails stay whole — would pull the sponsor row and copyright line off page-center, so I kept the existing centered full-width band.

## Validation

Built the site with `bun run docs:build`, served `docs/.vitepress/dist` locally, and captured the bottom of `/dev-tools/` in headless Chromium at 1440px (sidebar + outline + ad), 1100px (sidebar only), and 760px, plus the landing page at 1440px and `/dev-tools/` in dark mode. Before the change the outline and ad overlap the sponsor row at 1440px; after it, both rails stop cleanly at the band and the footer's divider spans the full width. The landing page, which has no rails, is unchanged. `prettier --check` passes on the file.

> 
> Adds shared styles on `.EndevSponsors` and `.EndevFooter`: page background, `position: relative`, and `z-index: 26` so that band stacks ab

title: fix(backend): support staged_path in third-party casks
body:
Third-party casks evaluated from Ruby can now use Homebrew's `staged_path` DSL without requiring Homebrew metadata. This unblocks casks such as AeroSpace while preserving the two path forms Homebrew serializes:

- artifact and uninstall stanzas receive `$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/Caskroom/<token>/<version>`
- flight-step arguments receive the install-time `{{staged_path}}` template, while commands rooted there use Homebrew’s structured `staged_path` base

For example, this now installs the app, CLI, and shell completions from AeroSpace's tap:

```toml
[settings]
experimental = true

[bootstrap.packages]
"brew-cask:nikitabobko/tap/aerospace" = { version = "latest", os = "macos" }
```

Metadata-time `Dir` globs are kept hermetic and return no host filesystem matches. This matches Homebrew's published metadata behavior for AeroSpace: its dynamically enumerated manpages are not linked, consistent with mise's existing treatment of static manpage artifacts.

Relates to discussion #13283.

## Validation

- Installed `brew-cask:nikitabobko/tap/aerospace` 0.21.3-Beta end to end on macOS arm64 using isolated app and Homebrew-prefix directories.
- Verified the app executable, CLI, and bash/zsh/fish completion links; `aerospace --version` reported 0.21.3-Beta.
- Verified `mise bootstrap packages status` reports the cask installed and a second apply skips it.
- Added focused metadata tests covering artifact/uninstall serialization, flight-step templates and structured command bases, and host-independent glob behavior.
- `mise run lint`

*AI-assisted — Tool: Pi; model: openai-codex/gpt-5.6-sol; version: 0.85.1.*

title: feat(daemons): give each daemon a stable URL per git worktree
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/24
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## The problem

`port = "auto"` lets several git worktrees of one project run their daemons at
once, but it leaves every service having to be told which port its neighbours
ended up on. That is fine for a database and painful for HTTP services, which is
most of a stack.

Pitchfork's reverse proxy removes that step: it routes a stable hostname to
whatever port a daemon actually bound. This teaches mise to derive the same
hostname while configuration loads, and to export it, so nothing in the project
has to do port arithmetic.

## What you get

Every daemon that configures a `port` is reachable at a hostname, and mise
exports it as `<NAME>_URL` beside the existing `<NAME>_PORT`:

```toml
[daemons_settings]
namespace = "shop"

[daemons.api]
run = "npm run dev"
port = "auto"

[daemons.postgres]
preset = "postgres"
version = "18"
port = "auto"

[env]
APP_BASE_URL = "{{ env.API_URL }}"
```

In `~/src/shop` that gives `API_URL=https://api.shop.localhost`. A linked
worktree at `~/src/shop-pr-42` gives
`API_URL=https://api.shop-pr-42.shop.localhost`. Both run at once, and neither
URL changes when a port moves.

Databases keep `port = "auto"`. The proxy speaks HTTP and a Postgres or Redis
client does not, so the `postgres` and `redis` presets opt out of it and keep
exporting `PGPORT`, `DATABASE_URL`, and `REDIS_URL` unchanged.

## New declaration keys

Two per-daemon keys, validated by mise and forwarded to pitchfork:

```toml
# https://front.shop.localhost rather than https://web.…
[daemons.web]
run = "npm run dev"
port = 5173
proxy = "front"

# No hostname, no WORKER_URL; reachable on its port only.
[daemons.worker]
run = "npm run worker"
port = 9000
proxy = false

# The daemon serves TLS itself; the proxy should not break the connection.
[daemons.secure]
run = "npm run dev:https"
port = 3000
proxy_tls = "passthrough"
```

`proxy` takes a DNS label, `false`, or `true` (the name-derived label, which is
how a preset's `proxy = false` is turned back on). `proxy_tls` takes
`"terminate"` (the proxy's behaviour today) or `"passthrough"`. Both are
rejected at config load with a message naming the daemon when they are not one
of those.

## Seeing the URLs

```console
$ mise daemons urls
~/src/shop-pr-42
Daemon         URL                                 Port  Proxy        Status
shop/api       https://api.pr-42.shop.localhost    3117  terminate    running
shop/web       https://front.pr-42.shop.localhost  5173  passthrough  running
shop/postgres  -                                   5679  off          running
  stack:   https://pr-42.shop.localhost
  project: https://shop.localhost
```

The proxy column is the daemon's `proxy_tls` mode, or `off` when it has no
hostname. Such a daemon is listed with its port alone rather than omitted, so a
database is visible here too. `mise daemons ls --json` gains `host`, `url`,
`proxy`, and `root`.

## Keeping in step with p

title: fix(backend): keep release-age cutoffs exact when a listing lacks dates
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/23
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Follow-up to #13362, now rebased onto main.

A tool version with no release date counts as old enough to install. That is the
right default for a backend whose source has no release dates at all, but it
means a backend that can only afford to date *part* of its listing quietly stops
honoring [`minimum_release_age`](https://mise.jdx.dev/configuration/settings.html#minimum_release_age)
past that point — it will happily select an undated version that is in fact
newer than the cutoff.

#13362 introduced exactly that shape: dating a private Go module's versions
costs a VCS round trip apiece, so its listing dates only the ten newest (one
hundred through a module proxy). This makes the cutoff exact again without
giving that cost back.

## What changed

`Backend::fetch_version_created_at` dates a single version. Before resolution
settles on a candidate that arrived undated, it asks for that one version's date
and moves further back while the answer says the candidate is newer than the
cutoff. The default returns `None`, so every backend that has no dates to give
behaves exactly as it does today.

The walk lives in `list_versions_matching_with_selection_options`, the shared
path behind `latest`, prefix and partial-version resolution — each of those
callers takes the last entry of the ordered candidate list itself, so the cutoff
has to be exact before the list is returned.

`go:` implements the hook through whichever route the listing used: a pass over
the module-path candidates against the proxy, then a pass through
`go list -m -json mod@version`. A private module under the default
`proxy,direct` GOPROXY is not on the proxy, so without that fall-through it
would be the one module class the hook could not date.

Dates read this way are remembered for the run, keyed by resolved backend and
version, so the second resolution does not repeat the round trips and the
"no versions found" message can still name the versions the cutoff hid. Only
answers are kept — "no date" is what an offline run or an unreachable source
reports, and holding onto that would leave a version unchecked.

## Concretely

`github.com/goreleaser/goreleaser` has 539 versions; over VCS (`GOPROXY=direct`)
mise dates the newest ten, back to `1.21.2` (Oct 2023). With a cutoff older than
that, the boundary falls in the undated part of the list:

```console
$ GOPROXY=direct MISE_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE=2023-06-01 mise latest go:github.com/goreleaser/goreleaser
1.18.2
```

`1.18.2` is 2023-05-07 and the next release, `1.19.0`, is 2023-06-28 — so that is
the newest version the cutoff allows. Before this change it returned `1.21.1`,
released four months *after* the cutoff, because it was the newest undated entry
and nothing checked it. The same holds for a package path and for a prefix
request:

```console
$ MISE_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE=2023-06-01 mise latest go:github.com/golang-migrate/migrate/v4/cmd/

title: registry: add mole
body:
Adds [Mole](https://github.com/tw93/Mole) for macOS on Apple Silicon and Intel:

```toml
[tools]
mole = "latest"
```

Installs the upstream shell scripts and prebuilt helpers through the GitHub backend, exposing `mo` and `mole`. Updates use `mise upgrade mole`; no Homebrew or Go compiler is required. Supports Mole 1.16.1 and later, when both helper bundles became available. A small postinstall hook places the helpers and preserves the entrypoints’ relative library paths.

Requires a mise version containing the URL-template fix from #13359, which is now merged into `main`. Users opting into `registry_floating` on older mise versions must update mise before installing Mole; floating registries do not provide backward compatibility with every older client, as [documented](https://github.com/jdx/mise/blob/main/docs/registry.md#floating-registries).

title: perf(go): speed up version discovery for modules with many releases
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/22
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Go tools with hundreds of releases could time out during version discovery,
reporting `No versions found`. mise fetched a release date for every version,
which was especially slow when Go had to query VCS directly.

This change resolves `latest` directly through the configured module proxy or
`go list`, extending the shortcut previously used for `GOPRIVATE` and
`GONOPROXY` configurations. For example:

```sh
mise use -g go:github.com/company/private@latest
```

When the latest stable release satisfies the configured release-age cutoff,
mise can select it without fetching the full version list. Private modules
still require the usual Go routing and VCS authentication.

Full listings, used by `mise ls-remote` and prefix requests such as `@1`, retain
all versions but fetch release dates only for the newest 100 through a module
proxy or the newest 10 through `go list`.

Reported in [discussion #13357](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13357).

## Release-age limitation

`minimum_release_age` allows versions with no known release date. If more than
100 proxy versions or 10 `go list` versions fall within the configured age
window, resolution may select an undated version that is newer than the cutoff.
This also affects `latest` when its direct result is too recent and resolution
falls back to the full list. The Go backend documentation explains this
limitation; [#13364](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13364) addresses it in a
separate follow-up.

## Performance and validation

The original implementation measurements used
`github.com/goreleaser/goreleaser` with 539 versions and a cold cache.
`GOPROXY=direct` exercised VCS discovery with a public module so the comparison
could be reproduced without private credentials.

| Command | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mise latest` with `GOPROXY=direct` | 20s timeout | 0.6s |
| `mise ls-remote` with `GOPROXY=direct` | 20s timeout | 9.0s |
| `mise latest` with the default proxy | 1.16s | 0.12s |
| `mise ls-remote` with the default proxy | 1.33s | 0.24s |

All commands used `go:github.com/goreleaser/goreleaser`. The timeouts used the
default `fetch_remote_versions_timeout`.

Implementation validation reported before this editorial update: 23 Go backend
unit tests; the Go install, GOROOT, and shim-recursion e2e tests; workspace
Clippy with all features and targets; and lint checks. The Go install e2e test
covers the fallback for a module with only pseudo-versions. The documentation
cleanup passes Markdown lint and Prettier checks.

title: fix(github): render resolved versions in platform URLs
body:
Platform-specific download URLs currently leave `{{ version }}` literal, so tools using versioned source archives cannot follow `latest` without a download hook or per-release URL edits. Render the selected URL with the existing backend template function to use the resolved tool version.

```toml
[tools."github:owner/tool"]
version = "latest"
strip_components = 1
platforms.macos-arm64.url = "https://github.com/owner/tool/archive/refs/tags/v{{ version }}.tar.gz"
```

The runtime change is one line in the shared GitHub, GitLab, and Forgejo backend. It also works with `additional_asset_patterns` for projects such as Mole that distribute scripts and compiled helpers separately. Configuration parsing is unchanged: existing platform functions and conditionals keep their host-based behavior. Use separate platform entries for target-specific URLs. No new options or dependencies are introduced.

Regression coverage parses real configuration for all three backends and checks resolved versions, flat and nested platform options, literal URLs, and conditional architecture selection. End-to-end coverage verifies installation with supplemental assets and locked reinstallation.

Validation: all 40 Git-backend tests pass, including conditional architecture selection across all three backends. Scoped hk checks and all three focused GitHub integration tests pass. The Mole registry entry installs successfully with this binary, including its analyze/status helpers.
