title: feat(bootstrap): manage Windows packages with scoop
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/8
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Closes #13311.

`[bootstrap.packages]` could only reach Windows software through `winget`. [Scoop](https://scoop.sh) is the other large Windows ecosystem, and its `extras`, `versions`, and `nerd-fonts` buckets carry a lot of what a developer machine needs. This adds a `scoop` manager so those apps can be declared next to everything else in `mise.toml`.

```toml
[bootstrap.packages]
"scoop:ripgrep" = "latest"
"scoop:extras/vscode" = "latest"
"scoop:neovim" = "0.11.0"
"scoop:mpv" = { state = "absent" }
```

```sh
mise bootstrap packages status
mise bootstrap packages apply --manager scoop
```

`status` lists each entry with its installed version and state. Applying adds the `extras` bucket if the machine does not have it, installs whatever is missing, and uninstalls `mpv`.

## Behavior

- **Status** comes from one `scoop export` per run, which is read-only. Installed versions are compared with a pin as opaque strings — no version ordering is assumed. An app Scoop reports as a failed install is surfaced as needing repair, and applying reinstalls it.
- **Buckets.** A `bucket/app` entry whose bucket is missing gets `scoop bucket add <bucket>` first, so a shared config does not assume the machine already ran that command. Buckets Scoop does not know by name still need a one-time `scoop bucket add <name> <repo>`; mise does not manage bucket remotes.
- **Version pins** install through Scoop's `app@version` syntax. Scoop silently skips that command when the app is already installed at a different version, so mise uninstalls the app first and then installs the pin — the same uninstall `scoop update` performs internally when it moves a version. `persist\` data is kept; mise never passes `--purge`.
- **Upgrade** runs `scoop update <app>` and skips pinned entries with a warning, because `scoop update` always installs the bucket's current version and has no way to hold a pin.
- **Metadata refresh** is opt-in. Installs pass `--no-update-scoop` so applying the config does not sync Scoop and every bucket as a side effect; `--update` (and every upgrade) runs `scoop update` explicitly. This matches how `apt`, `apk`, and `winget` treat `--update`.
- **Removal** is supported: `state = "absent"` runs `scoop uninstall`. Import and prune are not covered, same as `winget`.
- **Scope.** The manager is available only on Windows with Scoop's shim on `PATH`; `scoop:` entries on Linux and macOS are reported as skipped and do not block the rest of a shared bootstrap. Installs go to the current user's Scoop; an app already installed globally is reported as installed and left alone. Scoop ships as a PowerShell script behind `scoop.cmd`, so mise resolves and spawns that shim path rather than a bare `scoop` name.

## Validation

- 15 unit tests cover `scoop export` parsing (including a line printed ahead of the JSON document, a failed install, a versionless entry, and a local in

title: docs(config): explain variable resolution and task-local overrides
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/7
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Clarify why task-local variable overrides do not recalculate values already resolved in top-level `[vars]`, as reported in [#13318](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13318).

```toml
[vars]
mode = "headless"
args = "--mode={{ vars.mode }}"

[tasks.test]
vars = { mode = "headed" }
run = "echo {{ vars.args }} / {{ vars.mode }}"
```

`mise run test` prints `--mode=headless / headed`: `args` resolves during config loading, while the direct reference to `vars.mode` uses the task-local override. The docs show how to move the expression into `run` and how to share that command through a task template with per-task vars. They also explain why a Tera `default` filter supplies a value at render time rather than deferring evaluation.

The variables guide now progresses from basic usage through resolution, configuration precedence, task-local overrides, and value directives. The task reference links to those explanations, and the templates guide introduces parameterization before the merge reference, with a runnable example and clearer inheritance terminology. This changes documentation only.

Validation: documentation build and social metadata checks passed for 400 pages; focused hk formatting and Markdown checks passed; all 81 TOML examples across the three pages parsed successfully. Seven example runs and the missing-variable error case were verified with mise 2026.9.1, and the linked section anchors were checked in the rendered HTML.

title: fix(task): let a task template's vars read the vars the task supplies
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/6
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

A task template is the natural way to share one command across several tasks and let each
task parameterize it. That did not work when the parameter was a var: the template's var
rendered before the task's, never saw the value the task passed, and quietly took its
`default()` instead.

```toml
[task_templates.wrapper]
vars = { wrap = "run --opt={{ vars.opt | default(value='none') }} --end" }
run = "echo {{ vars.wrap }}"

[tasks.with_opt]
extends = "wrapper"
vars = { opt = "from-task" }
```

Before, `mise run with_opt` printed `run --opt=none --end`. Now it prints
`run --opt=from-task --end`. A task that supplies no `opt` still gets `none`.

The same applies when the task overrides a default the template itself declares, and to
vars written in one task's own table:

```toml
[tasks.solo]
vars = { msg = "hi {{ vars.who }}", who = "world" }
run = "echo {{ vars.msg }}"
```

Because `who` was declared after the var that reads it, `mise run solo` failed before with
`Field \`who\` is not defined`. It prints `hi world` now.

## How

A task's vars are the concatenation of every layer that contributed one: a task template
named with `extends`, a workspace-root task default, a `[tasks.<name>]` overlay on a file
task, and the task's own table. Each directive rendered against only the vars resolved
before it, so the result depended on where in that sequence a name happened to land.

Literal values are now resolved up front, before the rest of the list. A name is only
hoisted when every directive assigning it is a plain literal from the same config file, which
is what makes the move safe: the last of those is the assignment that won before, and it still
wins. Anything else keeps its place:

- a templated value, because rendering it early could read a var that is not resolved yet;
- a redacted literal, because the copies it overrode registered redactions;
- a `tools = true` value is read the way the resolver reads it. `resolve_task_vars` resolves
  with `NonToolsOnly`, so such a directive never runs: it cannot win a name, it cannot keep a
  literal that does run from being hoisted past it, and it stays where it is;
- a name assigned from more than one config file, because `EnvResults::resolve` drops
  directives by their source in safe mode;
- every name in a list containing a dotenv file, a sourced script, or a module, since those
  can assign names that are not visible until they run.

The last two conditions cover filters the resolver applies after this reordering: hoisting an
assignment that a filter then discards would leave the name unset rather than merely reordered.

## Scope

Config-level `[vars]` are unchanged. They are resolved once when the config loads, so a
task-local var still cannot reach back into a value a top-level `[vars]` entry already
expanded — the case raised in [#13318](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13318). Task
templates are
author: jdx
diff:
--- e2e/tasks/test_task_template_vars (+109/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,109 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+# Vars a task declares are visible to vars its task template declares, whichever
+# order the two layers end up in. https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13318
+
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[task_templates.wrapper]
+vars = { wrap = "run --opt={{ vars.opt | default(value='none') }} --end" }
+run = "echo {{ vars.wrap }}"
+
+[tasks.with_opt]
+extends = "wrapper"
+vars = { opt = "from-task" }
+
+[tasks.without_opt]
+extends = "wrapper"
+EOF
+
+assert "mise run with_opt" "run --opt=from-task --end"
+assert "mise run without_opt" "run --opt=none --end"
+
+# A task overriding a literal the template also defines: the template's own copy must
+# not win back part way through resolution.
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[task_templates.greeter]
+vars = { name = "template", greeting = "hello {{ vars.name }}" }
+run = "echo {{ vars.greeting }} name={{ vars.name }}"
+
+[tasks.inherited]
+extends = "greeter"
+
+[tasks.overridden]
+extends = "greeter"
+vars = { name = "task" }
+EOF
+
+assert "mise run inherited" "hello template name=template"
+assert "mise run overridden" "hello task name=task"
+
+# The other direction still resolves: a task var may read a var the template defines.
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[task_templates.rooted]
+vars = { base = "/opt/app" }
+run = "echo {{ vars.path }}"
+
+[tasks.bin]
+extends = "rooted"
+vars = { path = "{{ vars.base }}/bin" }
+EOF
+
+assert "mise run bin" "/opt/app/bin"
+
+# Within a single task, a literal var is bound before a var that reads it, regardless
+# of which comes first in the table.
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[tasks.solo]
+vars = { msg = "hi {{ vars.who }}", who = "world" }
+run = "echo {{ vars.msg }}"
+EOF
+
+assert "mise run solo" "hi world"
+
+# Config vars still lose to task-local vars for references the task writes itself.
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[vars]
+mode = "config"
+
+[task_templates.moded]
+run = "echo {{ vars.mode }}"
+
+[tasks.uses_config]
+extends = "moded"
+
+[tasks.uses_task]
+extends = "moded"
+vars = { mode = "task" }
+EOF
+
+assert "mise run uses_config" "config"
+assert "mise run uses_task" "task"
+
+# A `tools = true` var is resolved in a separate pass and never reaches a task's vars, so
+# overriding a template's literal with one must leave the template's value in place rather
+# than delete it.
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[task_templates.toolsy]
+vars = { mode = "template", cmd = "run --{{ vars.mode | default(value='MISSING') }}" }
+run = "echo {{ vars.cmd }}"
+
+[tasks.tools_override]
+extends = "toolsy"
+vars = { mode = { value = "task", tools = true } }
+EOF
+
+assert "mise run tools_override" "run --template"
+
+# The same filter cuts the other way: a `tools = true` value never runs, so it must not stop
+# a literal that does run from binding before the var that reads it.
+cat <<'EOF' >mise.toml
+[task_templates.toolsy2]
+vars = { mode = { value = "tool", tools = true }, cmd = "run --{{ vars.mode | default(value='MISSING') }}" }
+run = "echo {{ vars.cmd }}"
+
+[tasks.tools_ignored]
+extends = "toolsy2"
+vars = { mode = "task" }
+EOF
+
+assert "mise run tools_ignored" "run --task"

title: chore: tailor entire trail runners to mise
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/4
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Entire's default trail evaluations target generic applications. These six runner configurations tailor evaluation and review to mise's backend version semantics, configuration layering, activation and Windows PATH behavior, installation state, and download security.

The prompts require surrounding-code inspection and concrete evidence, distinguish new regressions from existing behavior, and preserve the intended trust model. Each evaluation answers a separate question:

- **Risk:** how consequential and recoverable the changed behavior is, accounting for scope and containment.
- **Security:** whether the change creates a reachable trust-boundary violation, rather than merely touching security-sensitive code.
- **Drift:** whether the change unnecessarily duplicates mechanisms or violates current repository rules, without treating every bug fix as a deprecation or every platform conditional as a defect.
- **Confidence:** whether proportionate evidence supports the change's actual failure modes; documentation and mechanical changes do not need runtime tests to earn high confidence.
- **Review:** concrete triggering scenarios and verified consequences, excluding speculative issues, pre-existing defects, and duplicate open findings.
- **Summary:** the final change and its actual audience, without invented user-facing effects or unsupported validation claims.

Only contributor tooling is affected. Runner models, permissions, triggers, output adapters, and result schemas retain Entire's defaults. Agent session hooks are outside this PR's scope.

## Validation

- All six files parse as JSON; template placeholders and output shapes are preserved.
- Compared configuration objects before and after the prompt rewrite: only `prompt.template` changed.
- `mise run lint-fix` completed successfully, including the all-features Cargo check. Scoped `hk run check --safe --format json` and `git diff --check` also pass.
- The customized runners have not yet scored a real trail; score calibration and end-to-end execution remain unverified.

title: feat(swift): name the libraries a fallback Linux build cannot load
body:
swift.org publishes one Linux build per distribution family. On a host without a
published build, mise warns and falls back to another family's build (#13297).
That build can link against sonames the host spells differently — an Arch-family
host builds ncurses wide-only, so `libncursesw.so.6` is present and
`libncurses.so.6` is not — and until now the entire symptom was:

```
mise ✗ swift@6.3.3  48.3s · failed: …/installs/swift/6.3.3/bin/swift exited with non-zero status: exit code 127
```

after a ~1 GB download, with nothing to act on.

When `swift --version` fails on Linux, mise now asks `ldd` about the toolchain's
`usr/bin` and `usr/lib` and names every soname it could not resolve:

```
this swift build needs shared libraries missing from this host:
libform.so.6, libncurses.so.6, libpanel.so.6
```

Naming all of them matters: the loader stops at the first one, so fixing by
exit-127 alone means one more 1 GB install per missing library. On the reported
host there were three.

`docs/lang/swift.md` gains the situation and the `install_env` workaround for
when the names differ but the libraries are compatible — the ncurses narrow/wide
split being the standing example. It also says plainly that substituting a
library is a compatibility judgement mise cannot make for you.

This is the diagnostic half of the request in
https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13306. The other half — a curated
narrow→wide equivalence map plus a `patchelf --set-rpath` step inside the
install prefix — is deliberately not here: that is mise deciding two libraries
are interchangeable on the user's behalf, and a new build dependency for it.

## Cost and trust

The scan runs only when the check has already failed, so a working install pays
nothing. It reads `usr/bin` and `usr/lib` and does not recurse: those hold the
toolchain's executables and the libraries they load, it is the set the report
measured against a real ubi9 artifact, and it keeps the work bounded by the
toolchain's layout rather than the size of the tree.

Each `ldd` runs with the tool's `install_env`, the same environment as the
`swift --version` it explains. Without that, a run whose `install_env` sets
`LD_LIBRARY_PATH` — the remedy this diagnostic points at — would have every
soname that path resolves reported as missing.

`ldd` runs the dynamic loader over each file. These are swift.org artifacts
whose GPG signature mise verified before extracting — the same trust the install
already extends by running one of them.

## Tests

- `parse_ldd_missing` covered in both directions: a mixed `ldd` listing, and a
  file that is not a dynamic executable.
- The walk covered against the ordinary contents of these directories — a shell
  script beside the executables, a non-ELF file named like a library, a
  non-library name — where `ldd` exits non-zero on each and must neither abort
  the scan nor invent a soname.
- The positive composition (walk → `ldd` → parse) verified by hand against a
  binary with a genuinely un

body:
A `github:`-backed tool whose release tags repeat the configured `version_prefix` listed versions that could not be installed back.

With this config:

```toml
[tools."github:example/tool"]
version = "a-1.2.3"
version_prefix = "a-"
```

and the upstream tag `a-a-1.2.3`, `mise ls-remote` prints `a-1.2.3` — the prefix is stripped once, so the listed version still starts with the prefix. On install, mise reconstructed the tag from that version as `a-1.2.3` and then `1.2.3`, and never tried `a-a-1.2.3`. Every listed version for such a repo failed to install, including whatever `latest` resolved to.

## What changed

- When a `version_prefix` is configured, `prefix + version` is now tried first even when the version already starts with the prefix. That candidate is the only one that names the tag the version was listed from, so a listed version always round-trips to its own tag.
- Stripping the prefix off a requested version now tries one copy removed first, mirroring how the version was listed, before falling back to every copy removed (which is all the old `trim_start_matches` did). Nothing that used to resolve stops resolving; the better guess just goes first.
- Candidate tags are built by a new pure `tag_candidates` helper and deduplicated, so an empty or self-matching prefix no longer spends two HTTP requests on the same tag.

Before, `a-1.2.3` with `version_prefix = "a-"` produced the candidates `a-1.2.3`, `1.2.3`. It now produces `a-a-1.2.3`, `a-1.2.3`, `1.2.3`.

Nothing that resolved before stops resolving — the bare version is still tried, just second. The one behavior change: if a repo publishes both `a-1.2.3` and `a-a-1.2.3`, the version string `a-1.2.3` now resolves to `a-a-1.2.3`. That is the correct reading, since `a-1.2.3` is what mise lists for the doubled tag, but someone hand-writing the shorter tag pays one extra 404 and gets the other release. This is documented on `tag_candidates`.

`strip_version_prefix` is unchanged: it already strips a single prefix, which the install path can now invert. Making it refuse to strip ambiguous tags would change what `ls-remote` prints without fixing anything.

## Validation

Three new unit tests in `src/backend/static_helpers.rs` fail on the old logic and pass on the new one — two over `tag_candidates` directly, and one `#[tokio::test]` end to end through `try_with_v_prefix_and_repo` where only the real tag `a-a-1.2.3` resolves. A fourth pins the no-prefix candidate order, and `test_version_prefix_functionality` in `src/backend/github.rs` now pins the listing side of the round-trip.

Unit tests only: the bug is entirely in candidate construction, and an e2e test would need a public repo that actually ships a doubled-prefix tag.

`cargo test --bin mise backend::` passes (704), and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean.

title: fix(backend): give every backend's postinstall hook the config env
body:
A tool's `postinstall` hook is documented to see pre-tools `[env]` from the
config (#6418). It did, for asdf plugins, and for nothing else.

```toml
[env]
PRE_TOOLS_VAR = "available_before_tools"

[tools."http:demo"]
version = "1.0.0"
url = "http://example.com/demo.tar.gz"
postinstall = "echo $PRE_TOOLS_VAR"
```

Before: the hook printed an empty line. After: `available_before_tools`.

The hook merged the config env only if it had already been resolved in that
process. During an install nothing resolves it — except asdf plugins, which
resolve config env to run their own scripts. So the behavior held for `dummy`,
the asdf plugin the e2e test used, and quietly did not hold for http, aqua,
github, cargo, npm, or the core tools. I confirmed the gap with `mise install`,
`mise install <tool>`, `mise x`, and `mise run`.

## Each hook resolves its own env

`Config::env` memoizes into a process-wide `OnceCell`, which is right for a
command that resolves the env once and then runs, and wrong here. Hooks run one
after another inside an install batch, and an `[env]` value can read a file or
command output that an earlier hook just changed:

```toml
[env]
_.file = "state.env"

[tools]
"http:first"  = { ..., postinstall = "echo STATE=after > $MISE_CONFIG_ROOT/state.env" }
"http:second" = { ..., depends = ["http:first"], postinstall = "echo $STATE" }
```

Sharing one snapshot gives `second` the value `first` replaced. Which hook fills
that memo is not even fixed — installs run in parallel, so it comes down to a
race, which rules out documenting a batch snapshot as the contract.

So `Config::env_uncached` resolves the tools-independent env without reading or
writing the memo or the on-disk `CachedNonToolEnv`, in either direction, and a
hook that changes an env input is visible to the hooks ordered after it. A
`tools = true` value stays out of the hook exactly as before, and a `[env]` that
fails to resolve is logged and skipped rather than failing an otherwise good
install.

Resolving unconditionally per hook would re-run every executable directive — an
`_.source` script, an `exec()` value — once per hook, and run them concurrently
against each other during parallel installs. So one resolution is shared by
every hook that starts without a hook completing in between, behind a mutex so
two never resolve at once. Measured on a config with an `_.source` script that
appends to a counter and two tools with hooks:

| | source script runs |
|---|---|
| `main` (hooks get no config env) | 2 |
| hooks ordered by `depends`, cannot share | 4 |
| hooks overlapping in parallel | 3 |

The remaining repetition is what freshness costs: a hook that follows another
has to resolve again or it reads the previous hook's snapshot.

This does not change install or verification subprocesses, which continue to
take their environment from the tool's `install_env` option.

## Tests

`e2e/config/test_hooks_postinstall_env` gains two cases:

- An `http:` backend alongside the existing `dummy`

title: fix(cmd): name the child's last stderr line in a command failure
body:
When a command fails during an install, it has usually already said why on
stderr. The error that ended the run kept none of it:

```
mise ✗ swift@6.3.3  48.3s · failed: …/installs/swift/6.3.3/bin/swift exited with non-zero status: exit code 127
```

`exit code 127` after a 1 GB download is not a lead anyone can follow. The
reason — `error while loading shared libraries: libncurses.so.6` — was printed
live by the progress reporter and then scrolled away, and under `--quiet` it was
never printed at all: that reporter's `println` is a no-op, and the failure
replay in `on_error` covers only stdout, on the assumption stderr had already
reached the user.

Now the child's last non-empty stderr line rides along with the failure:

```
mise ✗ swift@6.3.3  48.3s · failed: …/bin/swift exited with non-zero status: exit code 127; last stderr: swift: error while loading shared libraries: libncurses.so.6: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
```

The same line reaches the final `Error:` block, including under `--quiet`, where
it is now the only place the reason appears. Reproduced with a binary that exits
127 from `ld.so` on a missing soname, under both the animated and the text
renderer.

This applies to every command mise runs through `CmdLineRunner`, not just
installs, so a failing task or plugin script names its cause too.

From https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13306.

## Shape

One line, not the whole stream: an error is rendered on a single row in places
like the install summary, and the full output is still streamed to the reporter
as it arrives. The line is truncated at 300 characters on a char boundary.
Lines are redacted before they are kept, as they already were before being
printed.

## Tests

- New `test_failure_error_names_the_last_stderr_line`,
  `test_failure_error_without_stderr_is_unchanged`, and two unit tests for the
  tail's selection and truncation.
- `cargo test --bin mise cmd::` (37 passed).
- `mise run test:e2e e2e/cli/test_error_display e2e/cli/test_exit_status` — both
  assert on this message and both pass.
- `mise run lint-fix`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`.

> **Overview**
> **Failed commands now surface the child's last stderr line** in `ScriptFailed` errors (e.g. `; last stderr: …`), so install/task failures stay actionable under `--quiet` when live stderr never reached the user.
>

title: fix(config): render templates in install_env values
body:
`install_env` declares the environment a tool's download, install, and
verification steps run with. Unlike every other tool option, its values were
never rendered as templates, so a path under the user's home could not be
written:

```toml
[tools]
swift = { version = "6.3.3", install_env = { LD_LIBRARY_PATH = "{{env.HOME}}/.local/lib/compat" } }
```

The install subprocess received the literal string
`{{env.HOME}}/.local/lib/compat`. It now receives `/home/you/.local/lib/compat`,
matching what the docs already promise: "Tool versions and options can reference
environment variables and `vars`."

This came out of https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13306, where a Swift
`ubi9` build on an Arch-family host needs `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` pointed at a
directory of curses symlinks. `install_env` is the supported way to give an
install that environment — it just could not name a path relative to `$HOME`.

## Why it was missed

`install_env` is a typed field on `CoreToolOptions`, so it sits outside the
`opts` map that the tool-option template pass walks. `depends`, `os`, and
`lazy_bins` are in the same position. This changes `install_env` only: it is the
one whose values are free-form user strings that want the same templating
`[env]` has.

`{{version}}` still comes through unchanged. Core options are deliberately
exempt from the backend `{version}` normalization, and nothing renders
`install_env` a second time, so there is no later pass to resolve it.

## Tests

- New `test_install_env_renders_templates` covers a rendered `{{env.*}}` value
  and the preserved `{{version}}` placeholder.
- `cargo test --bin mise mise_toml` (80 passed), including the existing
  `test_core_options_do_not_normalize_version_placeholder`.
- `mise run lint-fix`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`.

title: docs(tasks): document sharing usage flags between tasks
body:
mise's task docs never mention `flagset`, `use`, or `include` — the usage spec nodes that let several tasks share a set of flags without copying the declarations into each one. This works today, in both toml and file tasks, and is the only answer for a shared `choices` list that must stay in sync; users asking how to do it in [#9637](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/9637) had no way to find it.

The new section in [Task Arguments](https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/task-arguments.html) shows a flagset in a `.usage.kdl` file pulled into a toml task and into a file task, and states the limitation: `include` needs an absolute path, which a toml task can build with `{{ config_root }}` but a file task — whose `#USAGE` comments are not rendered as templates — has to spell out.

It also points at [task templates](https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/templates.html) for sharing everything that is not an argument.

Docs only; no code changes.

## Validation

Every example was run against a debug build of `main` before being written down: both tasks list `--env`, `--dry-run`, and `--replicas` in `--help`, both accept `--env dev`, and both reject `--env nope` with `Invalid choice for option env: nope, expected one of dev, staging, prod`. `mise run docs:build` and `mise run lint` pass.

title: fix(task): report usage spec errors with the task name and reason
body:
A mistake anywhere in a task's `usage` spec reported three words and nothing else:

```console
$ mise run deploy --help
mise ERROR Invalid usage config
mise ERROR Version: 2026.9.6 linux-x64 (2026-09-12)
mise ERROR Run with --verbose or MISE_VERBOSE=1 for more information
```

`--verbose` added nothing. With several tasks in a project, there was no way to tell which task's spec was broken, let alone which line of it — the message naming the problem, the offending span, and the spec text are all in the error's diagnostic, and the eyre reporter only ever asks for its `Display`.

Now:

```console
$ mise run deploy --help
mise ERROR invalid usage spec for task 'deploy'
  × Invalid usage config
   ╭─[1:1]
   · ─┬
   ·  ╰── unsupported flag key bogus_key
   ╰────
```

File tasks reported the detail already, but as a derived `Debug` dump of the error struct (`InvalidInput("...", SourceSpan { offset: SourceOffset(33), len: 1 }, NamedSource { ... })`). They now use the same rendering:

```console
$ mise run build
mise WARN  invalid usage spec in task file mise-tasks/build
  × Invalid usage config
   ╭─[1:1]
   · ─┬
   ·  ╰── unsupported flag key bogus_key
   ╰────
```

A file task's spec failing still only warns and falls back to an empty spec, as before — every task in a project is parsed in one loop, so one broken script must not take the others down with it.

## An unreadable script is not a broken spec

Reading the script is the first thing the spec parse does, so a task whose `file` is missing or unreadable failed there and got the same "invalid usage spec" label, sending the reader to look at lines that are fine. That case is now reported for what it is:

```console
$ mise tasks ls --usage
mise WARN  could not read task file /path/to/nope.sh: No such file or directory (os error 2)
```

## Known limitation

The source line in the snippet is blank. usage parses a spec string through `FromStr`, which builds its parsing context with no source, so the diagnostic has a span but nothing to point at. [jdx/usage#1443](https://github.com/jdx/usage/pull/1443) fixes that; this PR is what makes the detail reach the user at all, and the line appears once that lands and mise picks up the release.

## Validation

- new e2e test `e2e/tasks/test_task_usage_errors` covers a toml task, a spec that only becomes invalid after Tera rendering, a file task, an unreadable script, and that a valid spec is unaffected — each command runs once and its captured output is checked, so the task name and the reason are known to come from the same invocation
- `cargo test --bin mise task::`, `mise run lint`, and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` all pass

Found while investigating [#9637](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/9637).

title: feat(task): inherit usage flags from task templates
body:
A [task template](https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/templates.html) can hold a `usage` spec, but a task that extended it and declared any flag of its own lost every flag the template defined — `usage` was the one field where the template's value was used only when the task had none. Tasks that share a set of flags had to copy the whole spec into each one and keep the copies in sync, which is especially painful for `choice` flags.

The template's spec is now prepended to the task's:

```toml
[task_templates.deploy]
usage = """
flag "--env <env>" help="Target environment"
flag "--dry-run" help="Print what would happen"
"""

[tasks.deploy-api]
extends = "deploy"
usage = 'flag "--replicas <n>" help="How many to run"'
run = 'echo "env=$usage_env replicas=$usage_replicas"'
```

```console
$ mise run deploy-api --help
Usage: deploy-api [FLAGS]

Flags:
      --env <env>       Target environment
      --dry-run         Print what would happen
      --replicas <n>    How many to run
  -h, --help            Print help

$ mise run deploy-api --env prod --replicas 3
env=prod replicas=3
```

Shared flags come first so `--help` reads shared-then-specific, and so a template's positional args stay ahead of the task's. Both halves are joined before rendering, so Tera in either still resolves. A task with no `usage` of its own inherits the template's unchanged, as before.

## Only for a template named with `extends`

Workspace-root task defaults go through the same merge, where their job is to fill what a task left unset. Composing there could prepend a required positional argument to a task that has its own spec and break a command line that parsed fine before, so a workspace default's `usage` is still used only when the task has none.

## Compatibility

A task that sets both `usage` and `extends` now also accepts the template's flags, where before it accepted only its own. Nothing that parsed before stops parsing, but a flag declared in *both* places is two declarations and is listed twice in `--help` — declare each flag in one place. For the case where a task genuinely needs to replace an inherited flag, [usage flagsets](https://usage.jdx.dev/spec/) are the better tool: put the shared declarations in a `.usage.kdl` file and `use` them where they belong.

## Validation

- new e2e test `e2e/tasks/test_task_template_usage` covers composition, `--help` ordering, a task with no spec of its own, unset inherited flags, `choices` enforced through a template, and Tera in both halves. The ordering check compares the three flags as one ordered list; I confirmed it fails when the concatenation is reversed.
- four unit tests for the merge rule, including that a workspace default only fills
- existing `e2e/tasks/test_task_templates`, `cargo test --bin mise task::` and `config::`, `mise run lint`, and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` all pass

Closes the main ask in [#9637](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/9637).

title: fix(install): explain which minimum_release_age cutoff hid every version
body:
`minimum_release_age` defaults to `24h`, so anyone installing a tool that was released earlier the same day hits the cutoff without having configured anything. The failure told them only this:

```
mise ✗ go:github.com/Q0tzly/pstty@latest  211ms · failed: no versions found for go:github.com/Q0tzly/pstty matching date filter
```

"date filter" names no setting, no cutoff and no version, so there is nothing to search for — in [#13303](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13303) the reporter concluded the go backend was broken, since mise's own debug log showed it fetching the version list and every `.info` from `proxy.golang.org` successfully right before failing. (It fetches those *because* the filter is active: gathering the timestamps it then filters on.) `mise ls-remote` and `mise upgrade` already explain this well; installing did not.

The same command now says what happened:

```
mise ✗ go:github.com/Q0tzly/pstty@latest  275ms · failed: no versions found for
go:github.com/Q0tzly/pstty matching minimum_release_age (24h): it hid 3 releases,
the newest being 0.2.1 (released 2026-09-17, eligible 2026-09-18 10:32 UTC).
Install that one now with `go:github.com/Q0tzly/pstty@0.2.1`, or lower minimum_release_age.
```

An exactly pinned version skips release-age filtering by design, so naming that version turns the error into a copy-pasteable fix for users who accept the release, while leaving the default protection in place for everyone else.

## Behavior

**The named age is always the one that produced the cutoff.** A cutoff threaded down from `--minimum-release-age` matches no configured value, so labelling it `(24h)` would point at the wrong date. Those cases show the cutoff itself instead:

```
failed: no versions found for jq matching minimum_release_age: it hid 9 releases
newer than the 1990-01-01 23:59 UTC cutoff, the newest being 1.8.2 (released 2026-06-20).
Install that one now with `jq@1.8.2`, or lower minimum_release_age.
```

**A query that matched nothing is no longer blamed on the filter.** The old message blamed it whenever a cutoff was merely active. `mise install jq@prefix:99` now reports `no versions found for jq` with no mention of `minimum_release_age`, in the same spirit as #11391, which stopped blaming the filter for fetch failures.

**Only versions the request could have selected are counted.** `jq@prefix:1.8` reports the hidden `1.8.x` releases rather than every hidden version, because the hidden set is narrowed by the same query and prerelease rules the failed resolution used.

## Implementation

`ToolVersion::no_versions_found` becomes async so it can consult `Backend::versions_hidden_by_before_date`. That reads the remote-version cache the failed resolution just populated — same selection options, so the same cache entry — and adds no fetch. `format_hidden_release_details` and its eligibility math move from `src/cli/upgrade.rs` to `src/install_before.rs` so the error and the upgrade warning describe a hidden release the s

title: fix(task): support extends in file task headers
body:
A [file task](https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/file-tasks.html) could not use a [task template](https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/templates.html). Writing `#MISE extends="..."` in the header produced

```
mise WARN  unknown field(s) ["extends"] in task file header, ignoring: mise-tasks/build
```

and the template was silently not applied, so tools, env, description, and aliases all had to be repeated in every script. The loader that builds file tasks already calls the template resolver — only the header parser was missing the field.

Now it works the same way it does for a `mise.toml` task:

```toml
# mise.toml
[task_templates.rust]
tools = { rust = "1.90" }
env = { RUST_BACKTRACE = "1" }
```

```bash
# mise-tasks/build
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#MISE extends="rust"
#MISE description="Build the CLI"
cargo build
```

`mise run build` now runs with rust 1.90 and `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`. Naming a template that does not exist is an error, matching a toml task, rather than a warning.

## Remote file tasks

A remote task (`file = "http://…"`, `file = "git::…"`) is parsed from its downloaded script at run time, after the loaders that resolve templates have finished, so its `#MISE extends` would have been parsed and then dropped without a word. It is resolved there too, and an unknown template name is an error. Collecting the definitions costs nothing for a task that names no template.

## A task with a `file` does not also get a `run`

A file task's script *is* its command, and `file` already wins over `run` in the executor. Previously a task with a `file` and no `run` of its own would copy the template's `run` onto itself, leaving a script that could never execute but still appeared wherever the task is described. Either side can supply the `file` — the task's own, or the template's, which is merged after `run` and so used to arrive too late to suppress it. Such a task now keeps `run` and `run_windows` empty; every other field inherits as before.

This also applies to a `mise.toml` task that sets `file` — the inherited script was already dead there, so no task changes what it executes.

## Validation

- new e2e test `e2e/tasks/test_task_file_extends` covers inheritance, env deep merge, local override, the ignored template `run`, and the unknown-template error
- new case in `e2e/tasks/test_task_remote_http` for a remote script's `#MISE extends`; without the fix it reports `FOO=` instead of `FOO=from_template`, which I confirmed by reverting the call
- unit tests for both halves of the `file`/`run` rule
- `cargo test --bin mise task::` (466 tests), `mise run lint`, `mise run docs:build`, and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` all pass

Found while investigating [#9637](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/9637), where a user asked how to share configuration across tasks defined as script files.

title: fix(conda): symlink commands from packages with nothing to activate
body:
Running a `conda:` tool changes the `PATH` of everything that tool spawns.

mise gives each `conda:` command in `.mise-bins` a launcher that activates the package prefix for that one command. The launcher exports `CONDA_PREFIX` and prepends the prefix's `bin` to `PATH`, which is how a tool reaches executables from its dependencies. But the `PATH` is *exported*, so it survives the `exec` into the tool and is inherited by every process the tool starts — a pager, an editor, a git hook, a `\!` shell.

For most packages there is nothing there worth reaching, and plenty worth not shadowing:

| package | executables in the prefix's `bin` | belonging to the package |
|---|---|---|
| `conda:git` | 326 | 8 |
| `conda:ffmpeg` | 185 | 3 |
| `conda:postgresql` | 107 | 37 |
| `conda:curl` | 55 | 1 |
| `conda:onefetch`, `conda:ripgrep`, `conda:gh` | 1 | 1 |

`conda:curl` puts 54 dependency executables — including `openssl`, `zstd`, `clear`, `tput`, `reset`, `kinit` — ahead of the user's copies, for a tool that shells out to none of them. `conda:git` shadows the user's `perl` and `openssl` for git and for everything git runs.

## What changes

A package gets launchers only when something in it can use one: it ships `etc/conda/activate.d/*.sh`, its prefix's `bin` contains dependency executables, or one of its own commands is a script (a `#!` file, which can expand `${CONDA_PREFIX}` or pick its interpreter off `PATH`). Otherwise its commands are plain symlinks.

That covers the single-binary tools, which is most of what people install this way:

```console
$ mise install --force conda:ripgrep
$ ls -l ~/.local/share/mise/installs/conda-ripgrep/15.2.0/.mise-bins/rg
... rg -> .../conda-ripgrep/15.2.0/bin/rg
```

Before, `rg` ran through a `/bin/sh` launcher and handed its children a `PATH` starting with the conda prefix. Now it is the binary, and a child process sees the `PATH` it would have seen anyway. Confirmed by running a subprocess out of `rg --pre` with `PATH=/usr/bin:/bin`: it reports `/usr/bin` first, where the same probe under a launcher reports the conda prefix.

A symlink still resolves the package's own libraries — `$ORIGIN` in an ELF RPATH is relative to the symlink's target, not the link.

The extra shell also goes away. 300 invocations of `onefetch --version`:

| | µs per invocation |
|---|---|
| the binary directly | 1179 |
| symlink (this PR) | 1157 |
| launcher (today) | 1472 |

## A relative `MISE_DATA_DIR` also fixed here

`replace_path` expands `~` but does not absolutize, so `MISE_DATA_DIR=reldata` leaves `install_path()` relative — and neither kind of `.mise-bins` entry survives that:

```console
$ MISE_DATA_DIR=reldata mise install conda:onefetch conda:jq

# symlink: the target resolves against the link's own directory
.mise-bins/onefetch -> reldata/installs/conda-onefetch/2.28.1/bin/onefetch   # dangling

# launcher: the path resolves against the caller's cwd
exec 'reldata/installs/conda-jq/1.8.2/bin/jq' "$@"
  → exec: reldata/installs/conda

title: fix(lock): prune a removed tool's lockfile entry and sidecar during unuse
body:
Removing a tool with `mise unuse` left its entry in `mise.lock`, and with it the
dependency sidecar directory that entry points at. With `lockfile_mode = "generate"`
both now disappear as part of `mise unuse` itself.

## Before

```console
$ cat mise.lock
[[tools."pipx:foo"]]
version = "1.0.0"
backend = "pipx:foo"
specifiers = ["1.0.0"]

[tools."pipx:foo".uv]
path = ".mise/locks/pipx-foo/1.0.0"
digest = "sha256:ae74034c..."

$ mise unuse pipx:foo
mise removed: foo from ~/proj/mise.toml

$ grep -c pipx:foo mise.lock; ls .mise/locks/pipx-foo/1.0.0
2
pyproject.toml  uv.lock
```

The stale entry and sidecar survived until the next `mise install` regenerated the
file — and `mise unuse` is often the last command before a commit, so the drift
lands in git. Running `mise lock` by hand also cleaned it.

## After

```console
$ mise unuse pipx:foo
mise removed: foo from ~/proj/mise.toml

$ grep -c pipx:foo mise.lock; ls .mise/locks/
0
```

## Why it happened

`mise unuse` touches the lockfile only through
`rebuild_shims_and_runtime_symlinks_for_scope`. That helper calls
`rebuild_shims_and_runtime_symlinks_for_changes`, which deliberately skips the
merge-mode lockfile update when generation is enabled — but unlike the
non-scoped `rebuild_shims_and_runtime_symlinks`, it never ran generation in its
place. So the one code path for a configuration-only tool removal did no
lockfile work at all.

The fix factors that generation tail into a shared
`generate_lockfiles_after_changes` and calls it from the scope variant too. The
sidecar then goes away on its own: sidecar collection is reference-driven, so
dropping the entry makes the directory unreferenced and the existing garbage
collector removes it.

`rebuild_shims_and_runtime_symlinks_after_removal` is intentionally left alone —
uninstalling a version does not change what the lockfile should contain.

Generation is gated on `mise unuse` having actually edited a config file. An
`unuse` that matches nothing still reaches the rebuild path whenever pruning is
enabled, and regenerating there would rewrite an unrelated stale lockfile and let
a resolution failure fail a command that had nothing to do. Pruning installed
versions alone keeps rebuilding shims without touching the lockfile.

## Scope and adoption

- **Only affects `lockfile_mode = "generate"`.** Under the default `merge` mode,
  auto-lock still only adds and updates entries, never removes them, because it
  runs with just the current config hierarchy loaded and cannot tell a genuinely
  removed tool from one declared in a config it can't see. Merge-mode users still
  clean up stale entries with `mise lock`, which is unchanged.
- **Cost is negligible when the lockfile is complete.** Generation reuses an
  existing platform entry without any I/O when it already carries a url and
  checksum and records no signer, so removing one tool does not re-resolve the
  others. Measured on a 7-platform lockfile with `uv`, `python` and `node`
  remaining: `mise lock  ✓ 21

--- src/config/mod.rs (+20/-0)
@@ -3957,6 +3957,26 @@ pub(crate) async fn rebuild_shims_and_runtime_symlinks(
         lockfile_update_mode,
     )
     .await?;
+    generate_lockfiles_after_changes(config, new_versions, lockfile_update_mode).await

+/// Run complete lockfile generation once the shim farm reflects the change.
+///
+/// `rebuild_shims_and_runtime_symlinks_for_changes` skips the merge-mode
+/// lockfile update under `lockfile_mode = "generate"`, so every caller that can
+/// change what the lockfile should contain has to run generation itself.
+/// Without this, a config-only removal leaves the dropped tool's entry — and the
+/// dependency sidecar it references — behind until the next install regenerates.
+///
+/// Call this only when the configuration actually changed. Generation resolves
+/// and rewrites, so running it for a command that turned out to be a no-op would

+/// command that had nothing to do.
+pub(crate) async fn generate_lockfiles_after_changes(
+    config: &Arc<Config>,

+    lockfile_update_mode: lockfile::LockfileUpdateMode,
+) -> Result<()> {
     if Settings::get().generate_lockfiles()
         && Settings::get().lockfile_enabled()
         && (!Settings::get().locked

title: fix(swift): pick the distro build from swift.org's release index
body:
> Stacked on #13293 — review that first; this PR's diff includes it until it merges.

Installing Swift failed on any distro mise's hard-coded platform map got wrong:

```console
$ mise install swift@6.3.3   # on Arch / Omarchy
mise swift@6.3.3  [1/3] download swift-6.3.3-RELEASE-omarchy4.0.1rc2-aarch64.tar.gz
mise ERROR Failed to install core:swift@6.3.3: HTTP status client error (404 Not Found) for url (https://www.swift.org/404.html)
```

An unrecognized distro had its os-release pasted straight into the URL, and `ID_LIKE` was never consulted. But the same map had drifted in three other ways, all of which 404 on Swift 6.4.0 (released 2026-09-14):

| host | mise asked for | reality |
|---|---|---|
| Fedora (any) | `fedora39`, pinned with an "only 39 is available" comment | 6.3 added `fedora41`; 6.4 dropped `fedora39` |
| Amazon Linux 2 | `amazonlinux2` | 6.4 ships `amazonlinux2023` only |
| Ubuntu 20.04 | `ubuntu20.04` | dropped in 6.2 |
| RHEL / Rocky / Alma | `rhel9.4`-style fabrication | `ubi9` |
| Arch, Gentoo, openSUSE… | `arch`, `omarchy4.0.1rc2` | nothing published; needs a fallback |

## What changed

mise now reads what a release actually ships from swift.org's release index (`https://www.swift.org/api/v1/install/releases.json`), which lists the distros, architectures and directory names per release. The hard-coded part shrinks to the distro *family* map — ubuntu, debian, fedora, amazon, rhel — which has been stable, instead of the version list, which turns over every release.

Picking a build, in order: the host's exact distro version; else the newest published build *older* than the host, since a binary linked against an older glibc runs on a newer one but not the reverse; else the family's oldest. `ID_LIKE` is consulted, so Linux Mint gets an Ubuntu build rather than a fabricated `linuxmint22`. A distro Swift does not build for at all falls back to Red Hat UBI, which has the oldest glibc floor of any current artifact and is what the Arch `swift-bin` package ships.

## Compromises now explain themselves

Where no exact build exists, mise says so instead of downloading a toolchain that may not run:

```console
$ mise install swift@6.4.0   # on Amazon Linux 2
mise WARN swift 6.4.0 publishes no build for amzn 2 or anything older; using amazonlinux2023 and it may not run here
```

```console
$ mise install swift@6.3.3   # on Arch
mise WARN swift 6.3.3 publishes no build for arch; using ubi9
```

```console
$ mise install swift@6.3.3   # on Linux Mint 22
mise WARN swift 6.3.3: linuxmint 22 does not say which ubuntu release it is based on; using ubuntu22.04
```

Previously these surfaced as `swift --version` exiting 127 after a ~1GB download, with nothing pointing at the cause.

Two cases now fail fast rather than downloading at all:

- **musl hosts.** Every published Linux build links against glibc. `mise lock` already refused musl targets; the install path did not, so Alpine would have downloaded ~1GB that cannot run.
- **unsupported arch

title: chore(ci): enforce the existing glibc 2.18 minimum for Linux releases
body:
Linux GNU release builds now check for a maximum required glibc version of 2.18 across x86_64, aarch64, and armv7. This matches the requirement reported for the published v2026.9.10 binaries and catches increases introduced by future toolchain or dependency updates.

Previously, the checks allowed glibc 2.26 on x86_64 and 2.34 on aarch64, and did not cover armv7. A shared `GLIBC_FLOOR` makes the compatibility requirement explicit for all three targets.

The installation docs state the minimum and explain how to install a static musl build on systems with older glibc:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://mise.run | MISE_INSTALL_MUSL=1 sh
```

The installer detects musl systems automatically, but does not check the glibc version, so older glibc systems need this override.

The docs also describe the policy for future increases: distributions below a proposed minimum must have reached the end of standard vendor support. Extended-support programs do not delay an increase. The distribution lifecycle table provides context for that policy; it does not announce a planned increase.

Amazon Linux 2 is removed from the yum heading. Its glibc 2.26 still meets the documented minimum of 2.18.

## Validation

The existing validation reports that all three published GNU binaries pass the 2.18 check and fail at 2.17, that the target pattern includes all three GNU targets and excludes musl, macOS, and Windows, and that the changed files pass the scoped hk checks.

Related: #13295 adds a separate libstdc++ compatibility check.

body:
## Problem

`scripts/check-glibc.sh` guards the release binary's glibc floor, but it only ever sees glibc. Its extraction matches `/GLIBC_/`, and `"GLIBCXX_3.4.29"` does not contain the substring `GLIBC_` — after `GLIBC` comes `X`, not `_`:

```bash
printf 'GLIBCXX_3.4.29\nGLIBC_2.17\nCXXABI_1.3.9\n' | awk '/GLIBC_/ { sub(/.*GLIBC_/, ""); print }'
# → 2.17
```

libstdc++ symbol versions were invisible to the check. Any C++ dependency would add a second compatibility floor — `libstdc++.so.6` in `NEEDED`, plus `GLIBCXX_`/`CXXABI_` version requirements — while the check still reported success. The failure mode is CI going green on a binary that won't start on an older distro, which is the kind of regression this script exists to prevent.

This came up while looking into [#13290](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13290) (the reverted Luau switch, which would have made mise's first C++ dependency), but it is not specific to Luau — it applies to any C++ dependency added now or later.

## Change

Assert that the binary has no libstdc++ dependency at all, rather than guessing a threshold for one.

That matches reality today. The shipped `mise-v2026.9.10-linux-x64` binary lists no `libstdc++.so.6` in `NEEDED`, carries zero `GLIBCXX_`/`CXXABI_` symbol versions, and requires at most glibc 2.18 — comfortably under the 2.26 assertion. Encoding "none" makes any future C++ dependency a deliberate decision: link it statically, or extend the script with a real libstdc++ threshold.

`libgcc_s`'s `GCC_*` versions (`GCC_3.0`, `GCC_3.3`, `GCC_4.2.0`) are present on every Rust binary and are deliberately not matched.

On failure:

```
Binary depends on libstdc++, which adds a compatibility floor this check cannot verify
Required C++ symbol versions:
  CXXABI_1.3.9
  GLIBCXX_3.4.21
  GLIBCXX_3.4.29
Link C++ code statically (-static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc), or extend this script with a libstdc++ threshold for Amazon Linux 2
```

## Validation

Run against the real released `linux-x64` binary and against a stubbed `objdump` that reports libstdc++ symbols:

| Case | Expected | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Released binary vs 2.26 | pass | `exit 0`, reports glibc 2.18, no libstdc++ |
| Stubbed `GLIBCXX_`/`CXXABI_` symbols | fail | `exit 1`, lists all three versions |
| Released binary vs an impossible 2.10 floor | fail | `exit 1` on the existing glibc check, unchanged |
| Missing binary | fail | `exit 1`, unchanged |

The second case is the one that matters: the glibc check passes at 2.18 while a real libstdc++ floor goes undetected without this change.

`shellcheck -x` and `shfmt -l -s` are clean on the result. No behavior change for passing builds beyond one extra line of output.

--- .github/workflows/test-impl.yml (+1/-0)
@@ -215,6 +215,7 @@ jobs:
           - run: rm -rf ~/.cargo/advisory-dbs && cargo deny check
           - run: cargo machete --with-metadata
           - run: ./scripts/test-standalone.sh
+          - run: ./scripts/test-check-glibc.sh
           - run: mise run lint
             env:
               HK_SKIP_STEPS: cargo-check
--- scripts/check-glibc.sh (+55/-9)
@@ -10,24 +10,70 @@ if [[ ! -f $binary_path ]]; then
 	exit 1
 fi
 
+# Read the dynamic section once, and fail loudly if that read fails. Both checks
+# below work from this one snapshot, so a broken objdump cannot leave either of
+# them quietly concluding that it found nothing.
+if ! dynamic_info=$(objdump -p "$binary_path"); then
+	echo "Error: objdump could not read $binary_path; aborting glibc check" >&2
+	exit 1
+fi
+
 max_required=$(
-	objdump -p "$binary_path" |
-		awk '/GLIBC_/ { sub(/.*GLIBC_/, ""); print }' |
+	awk '/GLIBC_/ { sub(/.*GLIBC_/, ""); print }' <<<"$dynamic_info" |
 		sort -V |
 		tail -1
 )
 
 if [[ -z $max_required ]]; then
 	echo "No glibc symbols found for $target_name"
-	exit 0
+else
+	echo "Maximum glibc version required for $target_name: $max_required"
+
+	if printf '%s\n' "$max_required" "$max_allowed" | sort -V -C; then
+		echo "Binary is compatible with $target_name (glibc $max_required <= $max_allowed)"
+	else
+		echo "Binary requires glibc $max_required, which is newer than $target_name's glibc $max_allowed"
+		echo "This binary will NOT work on $target_name"
+		exit 1
+	fi
 fi
 
-echo "Maximum glibc version required for $target_name: $max_required"
+# The check above only sees glibc. C++ symbol versions live in libstdc++ and are
+# invisible to it: "GLIBCXX_3.4.29" does not contain the substring "GLIBC_", so
+# the /GLIBC_/ match skips it. A C++ dependency would otherwise add a second,
+# unreported compatibility floor while this script still reported success.
+#
+# DT_NEEDED is the authoritative signal. A binary can link libstdc++ without
+# importing any versioned C++ symbol -- linked with --no-as-needed, or picked up
+# transitively -- and the version list would then stay empty while the
+# dependency is real. Test the dependency itself; keep the versions as
+# diagnostics for whoever has to act on the failure.
+#
+# mise links no C++ today: the released binaries list no libstdc++ in NEEDED and
+# carry no GLIBCXX_/CXXABI_ versions. Treat any appearance as a regression
+# rather than guessing a threshold for it. libgcc_s's GCC_* versions are
+# expected on a Rust binary and are deliberately not matched.
+needed_libstdcxx=$(awk '$1 == "NEEDED" && $2 ~ /^libstdc\+\+\./ { print $2 }' <<<"$dynamic_info")
 
-if printf '%s\n' "$max_required" "$max_allowed" | sort -V -C; then
-	echo "Binary is compatible with $target_name (glibc $max_required <= $max_allowed)"
-else
-	echo "Binary requires glibc $max_required, which is newer than $target_name's glibc $max_allowed"
-	echo "This binary will NOT work on $target_name"
+# Only grep's "no matches" exit status is expected, so scope the tolerance to
+# grep alone -- a genuine sort failure must still fail the build.
+cxx_versions=$(
+	{ grep -oE '(GLIBCXX|CXXABI)_[0-9.]+' <<<"$dynamic_info" || true; } |
+		sort -u -V |
+		sed 's/^/  /'
+)
+
+if [[ -n $needed_libstdcxx || -n $cxx_versions ]]; then
+	echo "Binary depends on libstdc++, which adds a compatibility floor this check cannot verify" >&2
+	if [[ -n $needed_libstdcxx ]]; then
+		echo "Dynamic dependency: $needed_libstdcxx" >&2
+	fi
+	if [[ -n $cxx_versions ]]; then
+		echo "Required C++ symbol versions:" >&2
+		echo "$cxx_versions" >&2
+	fi
+	echo "Link C++ code statically (-static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc), or extend this script with a libstdc++ threshold for $target_name" >&2
 	exit 1
 fi
+
+echo "No libstdc++ dependency for $target_name"
--- scripts/test-check-glibc.sh (+123/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,123 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# Unit tests for scripts/check-glibc.sh.
+#
+# The release builds run that check against real binaries, and those carry no
+# C++ metadata -- so a regression that stopped rejecting libstdc++ would pass CI
+# unnoticed. Drive the check with synthetic objdump output instead, so every
+# rejection path has a test that fails when it stops rejecting.
+set -euo pipefail
+
+cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
+script=scripts/check-glibc.sh
+
+tmp=$(mktemp -d)
+trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT
+
+mkdir -p "$tmp/bin"
+binary="$tmp/fake-binary"
+touch "$binary"
+
+# Stand in for objdump: print the current fixture, or fail if it says FAIL.
+cat >"$tmp/bin/objdump" <<'STUB'
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+if [ "$(head -1 "$OBJDUMP_FIXTURE")" = "FAIL" ]; then
+	echo "objdump: read error" >&2
+	exit 1
+fi
+cat "$OBJDUMP_FIXTURE"
+STUB
+chmod +x "$tmp/bin/objdump"
+
+PATH="$tmp/bin:$PATH"
+export PATH
+OBJDUMP_FIXTURE="$tmp/fixture"
+export OBJDUMP_FIXTURE
+
+failures=0
+checks=0
+
+# run_case <name> <expected-exit> [floor] <<< fixture on stdin
+run_case() {
+	local name=$1 want=$2 floor=${3:-2.26} out status
+	cat >"$OBJDUMP_FIXTURE"
+	checks=$((checks + 1))
+	if out=$("$script" "$binary" "$floor" test-target 2>&1); then
+		status=0
+	else
+		status=$?
+	fi
+	if [ "$status" -eq "$want" ]; then
+		echo "ok       $name"
+	else
+		echo "FAIL     $name: expected exit $want, got $status"
+		printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed 's/^/         /'
+		failures=$((failures + 1))
+	fi
+}
+
+run_case "clean binary passes" 0 <<'EOF'
+  NEEDED               libc.so.6
+  NEEDED               libgcc_s.so.1
+  0x00 0x00 GLIBC_2.18
+  0x00 0x00 GCC_4.2.0
+EOF
+
+run_case "libgcc_s GCC_* versions alone are not treated as C++" 0 <<'EOF'
+  NEEDED               libgcc_s.so.1
+  0x00 0x00 GLIBC_2.17
+  0x00 0x00 GCC_3.0
+  0x00 0x00 GCC_4.2.0
+EOF
+
+run_case "glibc newer than the floor is rejected" 1 <<'EOF'
+  NEEDED               libc.so.6
+  0x00 0x00 GLIBC_2.31
+EOF
+
+run_case "versioned C++ symbols are rejected" 1 <<'EOF'
+  NEEDED               libc.so.6
+  0x00 0x00 GLIBC_2.18
+  0x00 0x00 GLIBCXX_3.4.29
+  0x00 0x00 CXXABI_1.3.9
+EOF
+
+# The reason DT_NEEDED is checked separately: --no-as-needed, or a transitive
+# pickup, links libstdc++ without importing any versioned C++ symbol.
+run_case "libstdc++ in NEEDED is rejected without versioned symbols" 1 <<'EOF'
+  NEEDED               libstdc++.so.6
+  NEEDED               libc.so.6
+  0x00 0x00 GLIBC_2.18
+EOF
+
+run_case "libstdc++ is rejected even with no GLIBC_ symbols at all" 1 <<'EOF'
+  NEEDED               libstdc++.so.6
+EOF
+
+run_case "a binary with no GLIBC_ symbols and no C++ passes" 0 <<'EOF'
+  NEEDED               libc.so.6
+EOF
+
+run_case "a similarly-named library is not mistaken for libstdc++" 0 <<'EOF'
+  NEEDED               libstdbuf.so
+  0x00 0x00 GLIBC_2.18
+EOF
+
+run_case "a failing objdump aborts instead of reporting success" 1 <<'EOF'
+FAIL
+EOF
+
+# Not a fixture case: the binary itself is missing.
+checks=$((checks + 1))
+if "$script" "$tmp/does-not-exist" 2.26 test-target >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+	echo "FAIL     a missing binary is rejected: expected exit 1, got 0"
+	failures=$((failures + 1))
+else
+	echo "ok       a missing binary is rejected"
+fi
+
+echo
+if [ "$failures" -ne 0 ]; then
+	echo "$failures of $checks check-glibc.sh tests failed"
+	exit 1
+fi
+echo "all $checks check-glibc.sh tests passed"

title: security(brew-cask): fingerprint an app target through the directory descriptor
body:
Follow-up from review on #13279, stacked on it because it changes call sites that live there. Review #13278 → #13279 → this.

## The problem

`install_app` finds an existing app target with `fstatat` against a verified directory descriptor, and performs the swap through that same descriptor. Between those two, both fingerprint comparisons re-resolved the target *by pathname*.

A component replaced after `ensure_trusted_appdir` could therefore make the fingerprint measure a different tree from the one that was found and the one the swap will touch — so an app could be adopted, or refused, on the strength of contents that were never the target's. With a user-owned app directory (`~/Applications` via `MISE_BREW_CASK_OPT_APPDIR`) a same-user process can do that.

#13279 routed both comparisons through `parent.path()`, which is `/proc/self/fd` on Linux and fully bound, but `F_GETPATH` on macOS — a pathname, so macOS was left as it was. That is the platform this matters on.

## The change

`cask_target_fingerprint_at` walks entirely through descriptors: `fstatat`, `openat` and `readlinkat` relative to the parent, recursing into child descriptors rather than joining paths. No pathname is resolved at any depth. Both comparisons in `install_app` use it.

This is not only the new manager's path — the `adopt` comparison it also covers predates #13279 and is how `brew-cask` has always verified an app before adopting it.

## The digest is unchanged, and that is the constraint that matters

Receipts on disk record these digests, so any divergence would make every installed cask look modified. `descriptor_bound_fingerprint_matches_the_path_based_one` asserts the two forms agree exactly over a tree containing:

- nested directories and an empty directory
- an empty file and a file with NUL bytes
- a symlink and a dangling symlink
- names that sort differently as raw bytes than as path components

plus each kind at the top level, a missing entry erroring rather than digesting nothing, and a change to a nested leaf still moving the digest.

## Tradeoff

The descriptor form always hashes in process, where the path-based form shells out to `sha256sum` for files above 50MB. The digest is identical either way; only that large-file shortcut is lost, and it cannot be kept without naming a path. App bundles do contain large binaries, so this costs some time on a fingerprint — it runs on adoption and on the unowned-target check, not on an ordinary install.

The path-based `cask_target_fingerprint` stays, for callers that hold no descriptor.

## Validation

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `mise run lint` — clean
- `cargo test --locked --bin mise system::` — 898 passed

Six `cask_shim_*` tests fail on the dev machine for lack of Ruby and fail identically on `main`.

The equivalence test runs on Linux, which is what makes this change checkable at all — the digest agreement is filesystem behaviour, not platform behaviour. Wha

title: fix(swift): use the per-arch download directory on every platform
body:
Installing Swift on arm64 failed with a 404 on every Linux distro except Ubuntu:

```console
$ mise install swift@6.3.3
mise swift@6.3.3  [1/3] download swift-6.3.3-RELEASE-ubi9-aarch64.tar.gz
mise ERROR Failed to install core:swift@6.3.3: HTTP status client error (404 Not Found) for url (https://www.swift.org/404.html)
```

swift.org files each non-x86_64 build under its own `<platform>-<arch>` directory, but mise only appended `-aarch64` to the directory when the distro name started with `ubuntu`. Every other arm64 build therefore resolved to a directory that does not exist:

| URL | status |
|---|---|
| `…/ubi9/swift-6.3.3-RELEASE/…-ubi9-aarch64.tar.gz` (what mise built) | 404 |
| `…/ubi9-aarch64/swift-6.3.3-RELEASE/…-ubi9-aarch64.tar.gz` (what exists) | 200 |

This affected `ubi9`, `fedora39`, `amazonlinux2` and `debian12` on arm64, and Windows on arm64 (`windows10-arm64`, currently only reachable through `mise lock` since the Windows installer is unimplemented). x86_64 was unaffected — those builds carry no arch suffix on either the directory or the filename, which is why it went unnoticed.

After this change, `mise install swift@6.3.3` succeeds on arm64 with any of those distros detected or pinned via `mise settings set swift.platform ubi9`.

## Implementation

The download directory is now derived from the same `architecture()` helper that names the file, so the two cannot disagree: an arch suffix on the file means the same suffix on the directory, and x86_64 gets neither.

Two comments in `swift.rs` asserted that `ubi9` has no aarch64 build and that Ubuntu is the only distro with Linux arm64 builds. Both were artifacts of this bug — the `-aarch64` directories have existed for `ubi9` and `amazonlinux2` since 5.9.2 and for `fedora39` since 5.10.1. They are replaced with what actually varies between releases, which is the set of published distros (`debian12` appears in 5.10, `ubuntu20.04` is gone by 6.3).

## Validation

Three unit tests cover the arm64 directory on each distro, the Windows arm64 directory, and the absence of a suffix on x86_64. The first two fail against the previous implementation. Directory layout was confirmed against swift.org with `curl -sLI` for 5.9.2, 5.10.1, 6.0.3, 6.1.2, 6.2 and 6.3.3.

## Not addressed

Reported alongside this in #13289 and left for separate fixes: `linux_platform()` ignores `ID_LIKE`, so an unrecognized distro fabricates a platform name (`omarchy4.0.1rc2`, bare `arch`) and 404s; and `ubuntu_swift_version()` still maps `20.04` to itself, though swift.org dropped that build in 6.3.

Fixes #13291

title: security(http): refuse an HTTPS download that redirects to HTTP
body:
Follow-up from review on #13279, where this was raised and deliberately left out of that PR because it is not specific to the manager being added there.

## The problem

mise has two HTTP clients. The remote-version client (`ClientKind::Fetch`) refuses to follow a redirect that steps down from HTTPS to HTTP. The download client (`ClientKind::Http`) had no redirect policy at all, so an `https://` URL that redirects to `http://` was fetched over plain HTTP without comment.

That client is what `mise` uses for essentially every artifact download, including every `brew-cask` install.

## The change

Both clients now share one policy:

```rust
ClientKind::Http => builder.redirect(https_downgrade_policy("a download")),
ClientKind::Fetch => builder.redirect(https_downgrade_policy("a remote version request")),
```

Redirects are otherwise unchanged — the policy delegates to `Policy::default()` for everything that is not a downgrade, which is exactly what the download client used before. The only new outcome is an error instead of a silent downgrade, and the message names which kind of request was refused.

## Scope

A download is often checksum-verified, which already catches substituted content. But not every caller knows a checksum ahead of time, and a silent HTTPS→HTTP downgrade is worth refusing on its own rather than relying on a check that may not be there.

This does not change which URLs are accepted, only which redirects are followed. A URL that is plainly `http://` to begin with is unaffected.

## Validation

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `mise run lint` — clean
- `cargo test --locked --bin mise http::` — 107 passed, 0 failed

The rejection itself is not directly testable here: it needs a real HTTPS hop to redirect away from, and `mockito` serves plain HTTP. The predicate (`is_https_downgrade`) is unit tested, and `test_download_metadata_uses_redirected_filename` already covers the download client still following an ordinary redirect — which is the regression this change could plausibly have caused.

title: fix: drop runtime symlinks left pointing at ineligible installs
body:
## Problem

The runtime symlinks under `~/.local/share/mise/installs/<tool>/` — `latest` and the version prefixes (`1`, `1.3`) — are rebuilt additively. The rebuild writes the links it wants, and the only removal pass, `remove_missing_symlinks_in_dir`, clears pointers whose target no longer exists. A generated link whose target is still on disk but is no longer eligible for a link therefore survives indefinitely.

The easiest way to hit this is an interrupted install. mise leaves an `incomplete` marker in the version directory, which drops that version from the symlink set, but the directory is still there — so the links are not dangling and nothing removes them:

```
$ mise install mytool@1.1.0
$ # install of 1.1.0 is interrupted, leaving installs/mytool/1.1.0/incomplete
$ mise install mytool@1.0.0
$ readlink ~/.local/share/mise/installs/mytool/1.1
./1.1.0
```

`installs/mytool/1.1` still points into the half-installed directory, and it will keep doing so through every later rebuild. Referencing `installs/<tool>/latest/bin` directly is a documented pattern, so this hands those callers a broken install.

With this change the same sequence removes `installs/mytool/1.1`, repoints `latest` and `1` at `./1.0.0`, and leaves the `1.1.0/` directory itself alone for the installer to finish.

## What changed

`rebuild_symlinks_in_dir` now reconciles the names it generates rather than only adding to them. A link is removed only when all three hold:

- its **name** is one mise derives from a real install in that directory (`{prefix}latest` or a dotted version prefix), so configured aliases and hand-picked names like `next` are untouched;
- **this rebuild did not ask for that name**; and
- its **target is not an install that is currently eligible** for links.

The name set is derived from every real install directory, including the ineligible ones — a link is stale precisely because its version dropped out of the eligible set, so that set cannot explain the name. Only relative `./`-style links count as mise's own, so an absolute symlink a user dropped in is never a candidate.

The name derivation itself is factored out of `list_symlinks_for_dir` into `generated_names_for` and shared, so the two cannot drift.

There is deliberately no ownership marker. A generated name holding a relative `./` link is already mise-managed whoever wrote it: the existing rewrite loop removes and repoints any such link whose target no longer matches, without an ownership check. The prune applies the same rule, so what survives it is what survives a rewrite — a name mise does not generate, or a link that is not in `./` form.

## Notes

- This is not specific to `incomplete` markers — it covers any reason a version stops being eligible, including the pre-release filter. [#13272](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13272) reaches the same gap from the npm pre-release angle; with this in place, that fix can stay backend-local instead of adding its own symlink cleanup.

+# A runtime symlink whose target stops being eligible used to survive every
+# rebuild: an interrupted install leaves an `incomplete` marker, which drops
+# that version from the symlink set, but the directory is still on disk so the

+PLUGIN_DIR="$MISE_DATA_DIR/plugins/stalelink"
+mkdir -p "$PLUGIN_DIR/bin"
+
+cat <<'LISTALL' >"$PLUGIN_DIR/bin/list-all"
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+echo "1.0.0 1.1.0"
+LISTALL
+chmod +x "$PLUGIN_DIR/bin/list-all"
+
+cat <<'INSTALL' >"$PLUGIN_DIR/bin/install"
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+mkdir -p "$ASDF_INSTALL_PATH/bin"

+  >"$ASDF_INSTALL_PATH/bin/stalelink"

title: fix(release): unbreak the alpine aports bump and honor dry_run=false
body:
The `release-alpine` workflow — which bumps `community/mise` in Alpine's aports and opens the MR — has been broken for over two weeks, and it could not be run by hand to work around that. This fixes both halves.

## The clone was blocked

The job died ~20 seconds in, at the very first network call:

```
+ git clone https://gitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/aports.git/ /home/packager/aports
Cloning into '/home/packager/aports'...
fatal: unable to access 'https://gitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/aports.git/': The requested URL returned error: 418
```

`gitlab.alpinelinux.org` answers git requests from CI IP ranges with an HTTP 418 anti-bot challenge. The workflow only runs for tags ending in `0`, so this was easy to miss — but both releases that actually triggered it failed identically:

- v2026.9.0 — [run 33502453327](https://github.com/jdx/mise/actions/runs/33502453327) (2026-09-01)
- v2026.9.10 — [run 35128087151](https://github.com/jdx/mise/actions/runs/35128087151) (2026-09-16)

So the Alpine package has been stuck since 2026.8.x.

**Fix:** clone `github.com/alpinelinux/aports`, the official mirror under the `alpinelinux` org. It carries the same history — `master` resolves to the same commit on both hosts:

```
gitlab: fbc4c0f028a07f6ee8064974b55c325de646d924  refs/heads/master
github: fbc4c0f028a07f6ee8064974b55c325de646d924  refs/heads/master
```

Only the clone moves. The branch is still pushed to the `jdxcode/aports` fork on GitLab and the MR is still opened against `alpine/aports` there, so the resulting MR is unchanged.

Authenticating the clone was the obvious first attempt, since the script already has `ALPINE_GITLAB_TOKEN` for the push remote. It does not work — the challenge is served before credentials are considered, and a dry run with the token in the clone URL failed with the identical 418 ([run 35145179593](https://github.com/jdx/mise/actions/runs/35145179593)).

## `dry_run=false` did nothing

`DRY_RUN` read `github.event.inputs.dry_run`. Values in `github.event.inputs` come from the raw webhook payload and are always strings, and the string `"false"` is truthy in a GitHub expression — so unchecking "dry run" on a manual dispatch still produced `DRY_RUN=1` and skipped both the push and the MR. There was no way to trigger a real bump by hand, which matters here because it is the natural way to recover a release whose automatic run failed.

**Fix:** read the `inputs` context, which honors the declared `type: boolean`.

```yaml
DRY_RUN: ${{ (github.event_name == 'release' || (github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && !inputs.dry_run)) && '0' || '1' }}
```

| event | `dry_run` | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `release` | — | `0` | `0` |
| `workflow_dispatch` | `true` (default) | `1` | `1` |
| `workflow_dispatch` | `false` | `1` ❌ | `0` |

Release-triggered runs are unaffected, and manual runs still default to dry-run.

## Validation

Verified by running the workflow itself via `workflow_dispatch` with `dry_run=true` on this branc

title: perf(brew-cask): download cask archives concurrently before installing
body:
Addresses #13281.

## The gap

`jobs` is honoured for formulae but not casks. Formulae fan out at the configured concurrency:

```rust
// src/system/packages/brew/mod.rs:267
fetch::concurrently(bottle_jobs, crate::jobs::normalize(Settings::get().jobs))
```

Casks iterate serially in `install_with_manager_options`, which never reads `Settings::get().jobs`, so `--jobs` / `MISE_JOBS` make no difference to a cask-heavy run.

## Approach

Placement genuinely cannot be parallelised. It mounts images, writes the app directory and holds the caskroom lock, and `leave_running_app` already handles a self-updating app starting mid-flight; concurrency would widen that window.

Downloading can be, and `fetch_and_stage` already separates the two:

```rust
let archive = fetch_archive(cask, pr).await?;   // cache-aware download + checksum
extract_archive(cask, &archive, pr)             // mounts DMGs
```

So this adds a pre-pass warming `fetch_archive` at the configured concurrency. The serial loop is untouched and finds each artifact already present in the content-addressed cache.

That is the same shape as Homebrew's `DownloadQueue`, which fills a `FixedThreadPool` sized to `HOMEBREW_DOWNLOAD_CONCURRENCY` and has the installer consume results in order, and the same shape the formula path already uses here.

## Safety

The pre-pass applies the same gates the install path applies, in the same order: `homebrew_installed_version`, then `validate_platform_support`, then conflicts via `installed_versions` over `conflicts_with.cask`, then `mise_installed_cask_version` + `installed_skip_reason`. Without those it would download archives the serial path then refuses, which would be far worse than the problem being fixed.

Those gates are called, not reimplemented. If a gate is added later and this pass misses it, the cost is a wasted download and never a wrong install, since the serial pass still decides what actually happens.

Other deliberate choices:

- All failures are swallowed. This is an optimisation; the serial pass reports the real error with its context and progress reporting.
- `provision_ruby: false` when resolving metadata, so the pass has no side effects. Third-party tap casks resolve to nothing here and fall through to the serial path, which provisions properly.
- git-backed casks are skipped, since they clone rather than download an archive.
- No-ops when `jobs <= 1`, or when fewer than two casks would be downloaded.
- Each download gets its own progress report, suffixed `(download)` to distinguish it from the install line, finished on both paths so no bar is left hanging.

## What I verified, and what I did not

Verified: an up-to-date run downloads nothing and emits no spurious progress lines. Against 133 mise-owned casks, all current, the cached-archive count was identical before and after (151 → 151), and no `(download)` lines appeared. That was the failure mode I was most concerned about.

Not verified: the speedup itself. Every cask on my machine is
