title: feat(bootstrap): add macos-app for installing .app bundles from a URL
body:
Stacked on #13278 — review that first; this PR's diff includes it until it merges.

Closes the gap raised in discussion #13271: mise can install a macOS `.app` bundle only when a Homebrew cask definition exists for it somewhere. Vendor-direct downloads and internal builds have no path at all.

## What you can now write

```toml
[bootstrap.packages]
"macos-app:nuvio" = { version = "1.1.20", url = "https://example.com/Nuvio-{{version}}-arm64.dmg", sha256 = "e3b0c442…", artifact = "Nuvio.app" }
```

`mise bootstrap packages apply` downloads the archive, verifies the checksum, and installs `Nuvio.app` into `/Applications`. `url`, `sha256`, `artifact` and an explicit `version` are all required — `sha256` must be a real 64-character hex digest, so Homebrew's `no_check` sentinel is refused, and `"latest"` is rejected because mise cannot discover versions behind a plain URL. `{{version}}` is interpolated into `url`, so a release bump is a two-field edit.

## Why this is small

mise does not shell out to `brew install --cask`; it already downloads, mounts DMGs, and swaps app bundles itself. `fetch_cask()` is the only place metadata enters that pipeline, and everything downstream consumes a `Cask`. `macos-app` substitutes a `Cask` built from the inline declaration and reuses the rest unchanged.

So this is not a second installer. `BrewCaskManager` carries which manager it is driving, in the same shape as `FlatpakManager::new()` / `new_user()`. The two differ only where they genuinely should:

| | `brew-cask` | `macos-app` |
|---|---|---|
| metadata | Homebrew API or a tap | inline in config |
| platforms | macOS + Linux (font casks) | macOS only |
| version pins | unsupported — a cask exists only at its current version | supported — the inline URL *is* the pin |
| state root | Homebrew's Caskroom, shared with brew | mise's state directory |
| an app already at the target | warns and replaces | never swapped — see below |

The separate state root matters for correctness: `caskroom_token_dir` was keyed on the token alone, so `macos-app:nuvio` and `brew-cask:nuvio` would otherwise contend for one directory. Install records and transaction journals are both per-manager, and the Homebrew ownership probes run only for the manager that shares the Caskroom.

## An app already at the target is never swapped

`/Applications` is shared and a declaration may name any bundle, so `macos-app` can collide with an app it does not own. It compares what is there against what it downloaded:

- **identical** — adopted in place. Nothing is moved, replaced or deleted.
- **different** — refused, naming the path and what to do about it.

This is deliberately stricter than `brew-cask`. macOS revokes an app's Privacy & Security grants on *any* bundle swap — even to a byte-identical replacement, because the grants follow the bundle's identity at that path rather than its contents — and replacing also strands the other owner's install record. Adopting in place is what lets an install

+## macOS apps without a cask
+
+`macos-app` installs a macOS `.app` bundle straight from a URL, for apps that
+have no Homebrew cask — vendor-direct downloads and internal builds. Declare
+what a cask would carry:
+
+```toml
+[bootstrap.packages]
+"macos-app:nuvio" = { version = "1.1.20", url = "https://example.com/Nuvio-{{version}}-arm64.dmg", sha256 = "e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855", artifact = "Nuvio.app" }
+```
+
+`url`, `sha256`, `artifact`, and an explicit `version` are all required.
+`sha256` must be a real 64-character hex digest — unlike a cask, `macos-app`
+does not accept Homebrew's `no_check` sentinel, because an inline declaration
+names one pinned artifact and there is nothing to verify against without it.
+mise downloads the archive, verifies the checksum, and installs `Nuvio.app` into
+`/Applications` — the same installer `brew-cask` uses, so `.dmg` and `.zip`
+archives and the app directory behave identically. What differs is how an app
+already at the target is handled; see below.
+`{{version}}` in `url` is replaced with `version`, so a release bump is a
+two-field edit.
+
+::: warning These entries do not upgrade themselves
+mise has no way to learn that a newer version exists behind a plain URL, so
+`mise bootstrap packages upgrade` does nothing for a `macos-app` entry. You bump
+`version` and `sha256` by hand for each release. Prefer `brew-cask` whenever a
+cask exists — it tracks versions for you.
+:::
+
+`macos-app` records ownership under mise's own state directory rather than
+Homebrew's Caskroom, so `macos-app:<name>` and `brew-cask:<name>` are
+independent and never contend for the same install record.
+
+They can still contend for the same _app_, though: `/Applications` is shared,
+and a declaration may name any bundle. So `macos-app` never swaps a bundle it
+holds no receipt for — whether that app came from Homebrew, another declaration,
+or a manual install. It compares what is already there against what it
+downloaded:
+
+- **Without `adopt = true`** — refused, whatever the contents:
+
+  ```
+  macos-app:nuvio: '/Applications/Nuvio.app' already exists and is not owned by
+  this entry; set adopt = true to take it over if it is identical to the
+  download, or remove it to install a different build.
+  ```
+
+- **With `adopt = true`** — taken over in place when the app is identical to the
+  download. The bundle is not moved or replaced, so it keeps its Privacy &
+  Security grants. A _different_ build is still refused; remove it instead.
+
+Adoption is deliberately explicit. Recording ownership authorizes every later
+replacement by mise, so it is not a claim to make implicitly on an app Homebrew
+or another declaration still owns — a version bump would then replace a bundle
+the other manager still believes it controls. If you adopt an app another
+manager installed, reconcile that manager's record as well.
+
+The same applies after an interrupted install: a bundle left at the target with
+no completed ownership receipt needs `adopt = true` like any other, and a
+pending transaction alone never authorizes takeover.
+
+Ownership is recorded per target. Changing `artifact`, or changing the app
+directory, points the entry at a target the previous receipt never covered, so
+that target goes through this policy even though the package is installed.
+
+This is deliberately stricter than `brew-cask`, which warns and replaces: a swap
+strands the other owner's install record, and macOS revokes the app's Privacy &
+Security grants on any swap — even to a byte-identical bundle, because the
+grants follow the bundle's identity at that path rather than its contents.
+
+`mise bootstrap packages apply --dry-run` warns when an app is already at a
+target this entry does not own. It cannot say whether `adopt = true` would
+succeed, since it has not downloaded anything to compare against.

title: refactor(brew-cask): name the app install flags and centralize the state root
body:
Preparation for a `macos-app` package manager (discussion #13271), split out so the mechanical changes are reviewable on their own. No behavior change.

## What this changes

`install_app` took four positional booleans:

```rust
install_app(&stage, &tmp_caskroom, app, !cask.auto_updates, adopt, !cask.auto_updates, defer_running)
```

Two of them are the same expression, so at the call site nothing distinguishes "keep the staged copy" from "verify before adopting" except argument order. They are now named fields on `AppInstallOptions`:

```rust
install_app(&stage, &tmp_caskroom, app, AppInstallOptions {
    keep_caskroom_copy: !cask.auto_updates,
    adopt,
    verify_adopt: !cask.auto_updates,
    defer_if_running: defer_running,
})
```

The second change gives the Caskroom path a named accessor, `cask_state_root()`, so the root holding mise's per-token install records is stated once with the reason it is shared with Homebrew, instead of being spelled inline in `caskroom_token_dir`.

## Why now

Both are prerequisites for adding a second manager that drives the same installer. `install_app` sits exactly at clippy's seven-argument boundary, so it cannot take another parameter as-is, and the state root is the seam where a non-Homebrew manager needs to diverge — writing non-Homebrew state into `$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/Caskroom` would also collide on the token directory.

## Validation

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo test --locked --bin mise system::packages::brew` — 366 passed, 6 failed

The 6 failures are all `cask_shim_*` tests, which shell out to Ruby; this machine has no Ruby installed, and they fail identically on the base commit. They are untouched by this change.

Not verified locally: the ~17 `#[cfg(target_os = "macos")]` lines in the cask module. Cross-checking to `aarch64-apple-darwin` fails here on a `zstd-sys` C build, so macOS compilation rests on CI.

title: fix(task): keep file tasks in glob expansions when a sibling matches exactly
body:
Reported in #13273: a task glob silently expanded to a subset of the tasks it listed.

In a monorepo where one package declares `lint` in `mise.toml` and the others provide it as a file task (`mise-tasks/lint.sh`), `mise run '//...:lint'` ran only the toml one. The file tasks were listed by `mise tasks ls --all` and ran fine when named individually, but disappeared from the glob — no error, no warning, exit 0.

```toml
# mise.toml
monorepo_root = true
[monorepo]
config_roots = ["packages/*"]
```

```
packages/a/mise.toml          [tasks.lint] run = 'echo a'
packages/b/mise-tasks/lint
packages/c/mise-tasks/lint.sh
```

Before — `mise run '//...:lint'`:

```
[//packages/a:lint] a
[//packages/b:lint] b
```

After:

```
[//packages/a:lint] a
[//packages/b:lint] b
[//packages/c:lint] c
```

## What was wrong

Task matching does two passes: names are matched literally, then again with the file extension stripped so `mise run lint` finds `lint.sh`. The stripped pass only ran when the literal pass matched *nothing at all*, so a single exact match anywhere in an expansion removed every extension-bearing task from it.

This was not specific to monorepos or to toml tasks:

- `packages/b/mise-tasks/lint` (a file task with no extension) suppressed `packages/c/mise-tasks/lint.sh` just as the toml task did.
- Outside a monorepo, a toml `ci:lint` alongside `mise-tasks/docs/lint.sh` and `mise-tasks/web/lint.sh` made `mise run '*:lint'` run only `ci:lint`.

The preference itself is deliberate — it is what #10393 added to fix #10298, where a toml task `hello` and its own `mise-tasks/hello.sh` both matched `mise run hello` and ran the script twice. The bug is that it was applied to the whole match set rather than to one task.

## Fix

Scope the preference to a single task identity. A task that matches only after extension stripping is dropped only when a literally-matched key shares its path and stripped name — the duplicate-run case — and is kept otherwise. A package that declares both `[tasks.lint]` and `mise-tasks/lint.sh` still runs only the toml task.

## Validation

New e2e test `e2e/tasks/test_task_glob_file_task_siblings` covers both directions and fails without the change. The existing `e2e/tasks/*monorepo*`, glob, wildcard, workspace and colon-syntax tests pass, along with `cargo test --bin mise task::` and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`.

Fixes #13273

title: fix(completions): trim the colon prefix bash keeps for namespaced task names
body:
Completing a namespaced task in Bash inserted the already-typed prefix a second time. With these tasks:

```toml
[tasks."update:deps"]
run = "echo deps"

[tasks."update:deps:no-cooldown"]
run = "echo no-cooldown"
```

`mise upd<TAB>` completed to `mise update:deps`, and a second Tab at `mise update:deps:no<TAB>` produced:

```
mise update:deps:update:deps:no-cooldown
```

It now completes to `mise update:deps:no-cooldown`.

## Why the earlier fix did not reach this

Bash's default `COMP_WORDBREAKS` contains `:`, so Readline replaces only `no` and keeps `update:deps:` in place. jdx/usage#1405 (usage 6.9.0) taught usage-rs to report that preserved prefix on a `\x01prefix\t` line so the generated wrapper can trim it from full candidates before insertion, and mise's checked-in Bash script already forwards `--bash-word` and `--bash-wordbreaks` for it.

mise never emitted that line. `completion_request` answers from mise's own spec first, because that is the spec carrying runtime `run=` completers and the task commands mounted from `mise tasks --usage` — precisely the candidates in this report. That path rendered its answer with `render()`, which emits candidates only, rather than the `render_request()` the upstream fix added. So `__usage_prefix` in the wrapper stayed empty and nothing was trimmed.

The released binary's answer, with no prefix line:

```
$ mise __complete_word__ --shell bash --line 'mise update:deps:no' \
    --bash-word no --bash-wordbreaks $' \t\n"\'><=;|&(:'
update:deps:no-cooldown
```

and after this change:

```
update:deps:no-cooldown
^Aprefix^Iupdate:deps:
```

Switching that one call site to `render_request` fixes every colon-containing candidate mise answers for, including tools completed through `usage_spec_request` from a Packslip spec. Candidates without a colon in the replaced word, and the path-completion candidates the wrapper builds locally, are unaffected.

## Adoption

No configuration or flags. Users on an older installed completion script should reinstall it with `mise completion bash --install`, since the trimming happens in the script the binary generates.

## Validation

Driving the generated completion function in real Bash with the reported `COMP_LINE`/`COMP_WORDS` shape, before and after:

```
before:  COMPREPLY=(update:deps:no-cooldown)  -> mise update:deps:update:deps:no-cooldown
after:   COMPREPLY=(no-cooldown)              -> mise update:deps:no-cooldown
```

The first Tab (`mise upd<TAB>`, no colon in the replaced word) still returns both `update:deps` and `update:deps:no-cooldown` unchanged.

Added a unit regression test covering the protocol answer for that request shape. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `mise run lint-fix` are clean. `system::packages::brew::cask::tests::cask_shim_supports_completion_stanzas_and_system_command` fails in my environment for want of a `ruby` shim; I confirmed it fails identically on unmodified `main`.

Fixes #12970

title: fix(skills): report a declared skill the install does not hold
body:
A packslip can declare an agent skill that the install does not actually hold. Until now mise said nothing about it: `mise skills ls` printed `no skills declared by the active tools`, which is the same thing it prints for a tool that declares no skill at all. A skill that failed to download looked exactly like a skill that was never offered.

This came out of [#13267](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13267), where the reporter had to go read the upstream repository by hand to find out which of the two they were looking at.

## What you see now

```console
$ mise skills ls
mise WARN  packslip:github.com/test/probe@1.0.0 declares a skill probe that is not
           installed: the install does not hold it; reinstall the tool to fetch it again
the active tools declare skills, but none are installed
```

`mise skills sync` warns the same way, so a sync that links nothing explains itself.

The reason is specific, because the two most common causes are settings that are off:

| Situation | Reported as |
| --- | --- |
| `skills.fetch = false` | `skills.fetch is off, so it was not fetched at install time` |
| skill comes only from an `exec` entry and `packslip.exec = false` (the default) | `it is generated by running the tool, and packslip.exec is off` |
| the download or unpack failed at install time | `the install does not hold it; reinstall the tool to fetch it again` |

A skill scoped to another platform is not reported: it is absent by design, not missing.

## And a hint, because skills were easy to miss entirely

`skills.auto_sync` is `false` by default, so installing a tool that ships a skill fetched it and then said nothing. After an install in a project with auto-sync off, mise now mentions it once:

```
mise hint  the active tools ship agent skills; link them into this project with mise skills sync
```

Standard hint behavior — once per machine, silenced by `disable_hints`.

## Not changed

`mise skills ls --json` still emits a bare array of installed skills, so existing consumers are unaffected.

The discussion also asked for a row per packslip tool with a dash in the Skill column. That would turn a skill listing into a backend-filtered tool listing, and be wrong the moment skills come from somewhere other than packslip.

## Validation

- `cargo test --bin mise packslip` — 59 passed. Existing `skills_of` tests now assert which names land in `missing`, including that another platform's skill does not.
- `mise run test:e2e e2e/backend/test_packslip_resources` — extended to remove a shipped skill's `SKILL.md` from the install and assert the warning, the new empty-listing message, the unchanged `--json` output, and the `skills.fetch` reason.
- `mise run test:e2e e2e/backend/test_packslip` — passes unchanged; that release declares no skill, so it still prints `no skills declared`.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean.

The hint is not covered by e2e: like every `hint!`, it requires an attended term

`postinstall` hooks receive a `MISE_INSTALLED_TOOLS` JSON array describing the tools that were just installed, but each entry only carried the *resolved* version:

```json
[{ "name": "zoxide", "version": "0.10.0" }]
```

A hook therefore couldn't tell whether that `0.10.0` came from a pin or from `zoxide = "latest"` — both produce an identical payload. Reading the config back isn't a workaround either: the install has only just finished, so `mise ls` isn't yet a reliable source for it. This came up in #13270, where the goal was to have a `postinstall` hook link completions and manpages for the installation that was actually requested.

This adds a third `requested_version` field carrying the unresolved selector:

```json
[{ "name": "zoxide", "version": "0.10.0", "requested_version": "latest" }]
```

So a hook can now branch on how a tool was selected:

```toml
[tools]
node = "22"

[hooks]
postinstall = '''
echo "$MISE_INSTALLED_TOOLS" | jq -r '
  .[] | select(.requested_version == "latest") | "\(.name) floats on latest, got \(.version)"'
'''
```

## What `requested_version` contains

It is the canonical form of the request — normally the string exactly as written in the config or on the command line, and for a fully-pinned tool the same as `version`. Verified against a real install for each case:

| config / argument | `version` | `requested_version` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dummy = "latest"` | `2.0.0` | `latest` |
| `mise install dummy@1` | `1.1.0` | `1` |
| `dummy = "myalias"` (aliased to `1.0.0`) | `1.0.0` | `myalias` |
| `dummy = "1.0.0"` | `1.0.0` | `1.0.0` |

Two wrinkles worth knowing:

- Ref selectors are normalized to their `:` form during parsing, so a config written as `dummy = "ref-main"` is reported as `ref:main` rather than the original spelling.
- `system` and `path:` requests never reach the hook at all — nothing is installed for them, so they don't appear in `MISE_INSTALLED_TOOLS` in the first place (confirmed: the payload is `[]`). This is pre-existing behavior, not something this PR changes.

## Compatibility

The field is additive. Existing hooks that read `name`/`version` are unaffected, and `requested_version` is always present rather than conditionally omitted, so consumers never have to handle a missing key.

## Implementation

`ToolVersion` already retains its originating `ToolRequest`, and `ToolRequest::version()` already renders the selector — the same expression `mise mcp` uses for its own `requested_version` key, which is also the established name for this value in `mise ls --json`, `mise tool --json` and `mise bootstrap`. Alias resolution happens inside `ToolVersion::resolve`, after the request is captured, and `with_registry_version()` only swaps the backend, so the original string survives resolution intact.

## Testing

`e2e/config/test_hooks_installed_tools` gains coverage for the `latest`, version-prefix and alias cases, and asserts `version` still reports the resolved version rather than the selector. The e2e h

title: fix(npm): keep semver pre-releases off the latest runtime symlink
body:
## Problem

npm versions are strict semver, so a version with a purely numeric suffix such as `happy@1.3.1-3` is a pre-release. mise already treats it as one when listing remote versions, but installed-version resolution and the runtime symlink builder only knew the shared channel-tag pattern (`-beta`, `-rc`, …), so once installed it counted as stable.

An installed `1.3.1-3` therefore took the `latest`, `1` and `1.3` runtime symlinks away from the newest stable install. With `"npm:happy" = "latest"`, mise resolves the installed `latest` link first, so `mise ls`, shims and `mise x` kept using `1.3.1-3` even though the registry's `latest` dist-tag is `1.2.4`. `mise outdated` reported it as up to date, so `mise up` never moved off it. A prefix request such as `"npm:happy" = "1"` picked the pre-release the same way.

## What changes

With `1.2.4` and `1.3.1-3` both installed:

| Request | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"npm:happy" = "latest"` (installed/offline resolution) | `1.3.1-3` | `1.2.4` |
| `"npm:happy" = "1"` | `1.3.1-3` | `1.2.4` |
| `"npm:happy" = "1.3.1-3"` | `1.3.1-3` | `1.3.1-3` (an exact request still matches) |
| `installs/npm-happy/latest`, `1` | → `./1.3.1-3` | → `./1.2.4` |
| `installs/npm-happy/1.3` | → `./1.3.1-3` | removed |

Links an older mise already wrote into a pre-release are cleaned up on the next install: no manual step is needed. The pre-release install itself is never touched, and configured aliases and hand-made links are left alone.

With the `prerelease` tool option or the global `prereleases` setting enabled, an installed pre-release can still satisfy `latest`. Generated runtime symlinks never point at pre-releases regardless of that setting, which matches how channel pre-releases (`-rc1`) are already handled.

Only the npm backend is affected. Every other backend resolves installed versions exactly as before.

## How

- New `Backend::is_backend_prerelease` hook for pre-releases a backend recognises beyond the shared `VERSION_REGEX`. It defaults to `false`; npm overrides it with the registry client's existing semver check, so `1.3.1-3` is a pre-release and `1.2.4+build-7` is not.
- The hook is applied, in addition to `VERSION_REGEX`, when choosing installs eligible for runtime symlinks, in both `latest_installed_version` paths (the `latest` link target and the directory fallback), and as a pre-pass in `fuzzy_match_filter` for prefix requests.
- Stale links are removed by the generic reconcile from #13288, which now receives the backend so its eligible set excludes npm pre-releases. This PR adds no pruning code of its own.

## Tests

- New e2e test `e2e/backend/test_npm_prerelease_runtime_symlinks` covers install → stale links from an older mise → rebuild → resolve (including offline `latest`), using the dependency-free `commander` package (`12.1.0` stable, `13.0.0-0` pre-release). It fails on its first assertion when npm's override is disabled.
- Unit tests cover `latest_installed_version` (stale `latest`

title: fix(lock): keep native sidecars beside symlinked lockfile targets
body:
When a global `mise.lock` is symlinked into a dotfiles repository, `mise lock --global` now keeps native dependency sidecars beside the target lockfile. Previously, it could rewrite repository pointers to sidecars stored only under `~/.config/mise/locks/`, breaking `mise install --locked` in a fresh checkout.

Reads and writes now use the target lockfile's layout consistently. For example, a repository pointer such as `.mise/locks/npm-cowsay/1.6.0` stays valid through both the repository and global lockfile paths, including when deployment symlinks each file individually. Newly generated sidecars do not need separate global symlinks.

If you used this layout with `mise lock --global` on 2026.9.7 through 2026.9.10 and encounter missing sidecars after upgrading, run `mise lock --global` again to repair the pointers and regenerate sidecars in the repository.

Validation: 121 lockfile unit tests and both global-lockfile E2E tests passed on macOS ARM64. The regression fails on the original code and verifies a fresh-checkout locked install with the fix.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: openai/unavailable; version: unavailable.*

title: feat(shim): add shims.exclude to keep command names off PATH
body:
Some commands a tool provides are also provided by the OS, and other software on the machine depends on getting the system one. Today there is no way to have mise manage such a tool without also claiming its unversioned command name.

`shims.exclude` lists command names mise should never create shims for:

```toml
[settings.shims]
exclude = ["python", "python3", "pip", "pip3"]
```

The tool is still installed and managed by mise. The name simply never joins `PATH`, so it resolves to whatever else `PATH` provides — and because no shim exists, mise is out of that command's execution path entirely and no longer loads configuration on each invocation.

## Why

On Arch Linux, `/usr/bin/python` is the distro interpreter and its modules live in a matching `site-packages` directory. Entering a project that pins `python` changes which interpreter a `#!/usr/bin/env python` script gets, and a `PKGBUILD` calling `python` during a build picks up the pinned version instead of the system one. That is correct behavior for mise, but not always what you want on a machine where the OS depends on its own interpreter.

This gives the same shape as `uv python install` without `--default`: the unversioned names stay with the system, while version-qualified names still resolve through mise.

## Behavior

With `exclude = ["python", "python3"]` and a project pinning `python = "3.12"`:

| command | resolves to |
| --- | --- |
| `python` | `/usr/bin/python` |
| `python3` | `/usr/bin/python3` |
| `python3.12` | the pinned 3.12, dispatched normally |

Excluded names are filtered in `get_desired_shims`, which both the full-rebuild and diff paths share, so adding a name prunes any existing shim on the next `mise reshim` rather than leaving it stranded. The two shim producers that write outside that path — lazy-tool bootstrap shims from `ensure_lazy_shims`, and plugin-provided shims from `add_plugin_shims` — apply the same filter, so an excluded name cannot reappear after a reshim removed it.

Names are normalized by `shim_name_key` before comparison: it strips both `EXE_SUFFIX` and `.cmd` (Windows "file" mode generates `python` *and* `python.cmd` for one command) and folds case on Windows and macOS.

Command wrappers are deliberately exempt. They publish to their own `command-wrappers/bin` directory from an explicit user declaration, so silently dropping one would be more surprising than honoring it. This is documented alongside the `mise activate` limitation.

## Adoption notes

- Default is `[]` — no change for existing users.
- Also settable as `MISE_SHIMS_EXCLUDE=python,python3`.
- Excluding `python3` means `python3 -m venv` builds a virtualenv from the system interpreter rather than the configured one, silently. Use `python3.12 -m venv` when you want the mise-managed version. This is documented as a warning and is the reason this is opt-in rather than a default.
- This only affects generated shims. Under `mise activate` without `--shims`, a tool's `bin` directory joins `PA

title: feat(vfox): implement the cmd.exec timeout option
body:
Stacked on #13261 — review that one first.

`cmd.exec` has accepted a `timeout` option since the vfox crate was vendored in 2025, parsed it, and thrown it away. The docs said so outright:

> **`timeout`**: Currently ignored. Do not rely on it to terminate a command.

It now works. A plugin hook can bound a command that might otherwise hang forever:

```lua
local cmd = require("cmd")

local ok, err = pcall(cmd.exec, "some-tool sync", { timeout = 30 })
if not ok then
    error("sync did not finish: " .. tostring(err))
end
```

`timeout` is a number of seconds and accepts fractions. When it expires the command is killed and the call raises, so a timeout can be caught with `pcall` but is never mistaken for a normal non-zero exit. Without the option, commands run unbounded exactly as before — this only changes behavior for a plugin that was already passing `timeout` and silently getting nothing.

Supported by `cmd.exec` and `cmd.stream`. `os.execute` is Lua's builtin and takes no options table, so it is unchanged; a hook that needs a bounded streaming command can use `cmd.stream`.

## Limitation

Only the shell mise spawned is killed, so a command that starts its own background processes can leave them running. mise's own timeouts signal the entire process tree, but that needs platform APIs `crates/vfox` does not depend on. This is documented, with a pointer to prefer a tool's own timeout flag where one exists.

## Validation

One thing worth calling out, because the first implementation looked correct and was not. `cmd.exec` captures output, so the child's pipes are drained on their own threads — and joining those threads after killing the shell blocks for as long as a *grandchild* holds the write end open. A `sleep 30` under a 0.2s timeout still took the full 30 seconds. The reader threads are now left to finish on their own when the timeout fires, since the output is discarded in that case anyway. The unit suite dropping from 60s to 0.75s is the check that the timeouts actually fire rather than being waited out.

Unit tests cover expiry for both functions, a command completing under its timeout, rejection of zero and negative values, and a child that floods its pipe — that last one would hang on an undrained pipe rather than timing out. `e2e/backend/test_vfox_stdin` gains a case asserting a 60-second command under a 0.5s timeout raises and returns promptly.

title: fix(brew): apply cask adopt to explicit and tap-qualified cask names
body:
Fixes the bug reported in #13260, plus a second way the same option was being lost.

`adopt` lets mise take ownership of a cask's app bundle that is already on disk instead of replacing it. That matters on macOS because replacing a bundle under `/Applications` is what makes macOS revoke the app's Privacy & Security grants (Accessibility, Screen Recording, Full Disk Access, …). Two separate bugs meant the option was silently discarded.

## 1. Casks named on the command line ignored `adopt`

```sh
# global mise.toml
# [bootstrap.brew]
# adopt = true

stat -f "%i" /Applications/Menuwhere.app        # 216970251
mise bootstrap packages apply brew-cask:menuwhere --yes
stat -f "%i" /Applications/Menuwhere.app        # 300492273 — replaced, not adopted
```

mise then printed the warning recommending the option that was already set:

```
mise WARN  brew-cask: replacing /Applications/Menuwhere.app — macOS may revoke
Privacy & Security permissions for this app ... To take over an existing app
without replacing it, set adopt = true or [bootstrap.brew] adopt = true
```

Both documented forms were affected — the `[bootstrap.brew] adopt = true` default and the per-package `"brew-cask:ukelele" = { version = "latest", adopt = true }` table. A full `mise bootstrap` was unaffected; only runs that named packages were.

**Cause:** `mise bootstrap packages apply <spec>` and `packages upgrade <spec>` build their requests from the CLI specs alone, and passed an empty manager-options map to the installer. The brew-cask backend reads `adopt` from those options, so it always saw `false`.

**Fix:** explicit specs now resolve `adopt` from the config the same way a full bootstrap run does — a per-package `adopt` wins, otherwise the `[bootstrap.brew]` default applies, including for a cask that is not listed in `[bootstrap.packages]` at all.

## 2. Tap-qualified names and aliases ignored `adopt`

This one also affected plain `mise bootstrap`, and predates the change above.

```toml
[bootstrap.packages]
"brew-cask:homebrew/cask/firefox" = { version = "latest", adopt = true }
```

Adoption was recorded under the name as written, but the installer looked it up by the token the cask metadata reports — `firefox`. The two never matched, so the bundle was replaced. The same happened for a cask named by a trusted alias or an old token, which resolve to a different canonical token entirely.

**Fix:** the installer looks adoption up by the name on the request, which is the name it was recorded against. That matches a tap-qualified entry, an alias, and an old token alike, because the request carries whatever spelling the user wrote. Casks that different taps ship under the same token stay distinct, so adopting one does not adopt another that set `adopt = false`.

A command-line spec resolves its per-package option by config key as written, falling back to the one other spelling that provably names the same cask: `brew-cask:firefox` and `brew-cask:homebrew/cask/firefox` resolve to the same

title: feat(vfox): add cmd.stream for interactive hooks, detach stdin elsewhere
body:
Plugin hooks that shelled out through `os.execute` inherited the terminal's stdin, while `cmd.exec` gave children `/dev/null`. mise installs up to `jobs` tools at a time (default 8), so an inherited stdin is shared by racing siblings — whichever child reads first consumes input meant for another — and a prompt written from a hook lands underneath the progress bars where nobody can answer it.

Reported in #13254.

## Hooks are non-interactive by default

`cmd.exec` and `os.execute` now both detach stdin unless [`raw`](https://mise.jdx.dev/configuration/settings.html#raw) is set. A child that reads stdin sees EOF immediately instead of hanging or stealing a sibling's input.

This matches what mise already does everywhere else: `CmdLineRunner` detaches stdin for every subprocess it spawns, and the asdf backend has done exactly this since it was written:

```rust
if !settings.raw {
    // ignore stdin, otherwise a prompt may show up where the user won't see it
    cmd = cmd.stdin_null();
}
```

`cmd.exec` also honors `raw` for the first time. It previously detached stdin unconditionally, so `mise install --raw` did not connect stdin to a vfox hook's children despite that being what the setting asks for.

## `cmd.stream` for hooks that must be interactive

Some hooks genuinely need input — entering a credential, accepting a license. Those can now use `cmd.stream`, which connects stdin, streams stdout and stderr to the terminal instead of capturing them, and returns the exit status:

```lua
local cmd = require("cmd")

local code = cmd.stream("some-tool login")
if code ~= 0 then
    error("login failed with status " .. tostring(code))
end
```

It takes the same `cwd` and `env` options as `cmd.exec` and uses the same mise-constructed environment.

While the child runs, mise pauses the progress renderer and holds the exclusive side of the same lock `--raw` uses, both for the child's whole lifetime — the pattern `src/system/sudo.rs` already uses for sudo password prompts. `os.execute` takes the shared side of that lock, so its streamed output cannot land on top of a `cmd.stream` child. Other installs keep making progress; they just wait to run commands of their own until the interactive child exits.

That cost is the point — an interactive child needs the terminal to itself — but it means a long `cmd.stream` call stalls other work.

## Guidance: prefer `cmd.exec`

The docs now open the Command Module with what each function costs the installs running beside it, and recommend `cmd.exec` outright:

| Function | Output | Returns | Cost to other installs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `cmd.exec` | captured | stdout as a string; raises on failure | none |
| `os.execute` | streamed to the terminal | exit status | holds mise's terminal lock while it runs |
| `cmd.stream` | streamed to the terminal, stdin connected | exit status | holds that lock exclusively — every other install waits to run any command |

`cmd.exec` is the only one that never competes for the ter

title: fix(install): skip lockfile-missing warnings for unrequested tools
body:
`MISE_LOCKED=1 mise install <tool>` was warning about other tools (often global) missing from the lockfile because post-install `get_toolset()` resolves everything. title: fix(upgrade): keep SemVer build metadata when --bump rewrites a pin
body:
## The problem

Tools whose releases carry SemVer build metadata lost it when `mise upgrade --bump` rewrote the pin in `mise.toml`. k3s tags its releases `v1.37.0+k3s1`, but `--bump` wrote `1.37.0`, and the install that followed 404'd on a tag that does not exist:

```console
$ mise upgrade --bump -n k3s
Would install k3s@1.37.0+k3s1
Would bump k3s@1.37.0 in ~/.config/mise/config.toml

$ mise upgrade --bump -y k3s
mise ✗ k3s@1.37.0  … failed: HTTP status client error (404 Not Found)
  for url (https://api.github.com/repos/k3s-io/k3s/releases/tags/1.37.0)
```

The dry run already showed the inconsistency: the install target kept `+k3s1`, the bump target dropped it. The only way out was to re-pin by hand and `--exclude` the tool from future bumps.

With this change the two agree, and the config keeps a version that resolves:

```console
$ mise upgrade --bump -n k3s
Would install k3s@1.37.0+k3s1
Would bump k3s@1.37.0+k3s1 in ~/.config/mise/config.toml
```

Java was affected the same way — a `temurin-17.0.7+7` pin bumped to `temurin-17.0.8`, losing the build number.

## Why it happened

`--bump` rebuilds the pin at the specificity the old one had: `check_semver_bump` splits both versions into chunks with `chunkify_version` and takes as many chunks from the new version as the old pin had. `chunkify_version` round-trips the string through the `versions` crate, and that round-trip silently loses build metadata:

- `SemVer::to_mess` attaches `meta` only underneath a pre-release chunk, so a version with metadata and no pre-release comes back without it.
- `Version::to_mess` drops `meta` outright.

Both are documented as lossless conversions; the crate's doctests only cover inputs that have a pre-release, where the metadata does survive. The observable effect:

```
"1.36.4+k3s1"    -> ["1", ".36", ".4"]                   # +k3s1 gone
"17.0.7+7"       -> ["17", ".0", ".7"]                   # Java, same
"1.2.3-rc1+meta" -> ["1", ".2", ".3", "-rc1", "+meta"]   # survives only with a pre-release
```

So the old pin measured three chunks, three chunks of `1.37.0+k3s1` were taken, and `1.37.0` was written. This fix re-attaches the metadata after the conversion, on both the `Ideal` and `General` paths.

A coarser pin still stays coarse: `1.36` bumps to `1.37`, not `1.37.0+k3s1`. The metadata only rides along when the old pin was specific enough to have had it.

## Validation

- New unit tests for `chunkify_version` and `check_semver_bump`. Mutating the fix back out makes both fail with exactly the reported value, `Some("1.37.0")`.
- New e2e test `e2e/cli/test_upgrade_bump_build_metadata`, using a fixture plugin that publishes `1.36.4+k3s1` and `1.37.0+k3s1`, asserting the bump and install agree and that the tool is runnable afterwards.
- Checked against the real `aqua:k3s-io/k3s`, which produced the output shown above.
- `mise run lint-fix` and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` are clean. Unit suite: 4103 passed, 6 failed — t

title: fix(http): retry a GitHub rate-limit 403 instead of failing on it
body:
## Problem

`http_retries` documents what mise retries:

> Retries are attempted only on transient errors: HTTP 5xx (server errors), 408 (Request Timeout), 429 (Too Many Requests), and network-layer failures […]. Other 4xx responses (e.g. 404) are [not retried].

Retrying 429 is the right policy. It just never applies to GitHub, because **GitHub answers an exhausted rate limit with 403, not 429.** `is_transient` sees a 4xx that is not 429 and classifies it as deterministic, so a rate-limited request fails on its first attempt — the one case the policy was written for.

This is easy to hit on an optional lookup. `PackslipBackend::github_list` fetches a release list that most projects do not publish; a 404 is the expected answer and is handled, but a 403 is fatal. During the v2026.9.9 release the repository's shared API budget ran out, and that single unretried 403 on a file that does not exist took down the whole install:

```
mise ✗ aube@2.2.16 · failed: fetching the release list of packslip:github.com/aubepkg/aube
      github rate limit: 0/5000 (core), resets at 1789456621
      "message": "API rate limit exceeded for installation."
mise ✗ npm:ajv-cli@latest        · failed: Skipped due to failed dependency
mise ✗ npm:markdownlint-cli@latest · failed: Skipped due to failed dependency
mise ✗ prettier@3.9.6            · failed: Skipped due to failed dependency
```

## What this does

Adds a `GithubRateLimited` marker error, applied when a GitHub 403 carries `x-ratelimit-remaining: 0` (primary limit) or a `retry-after` header (secondary limits, which can arrive with quota still on the clock). `is_transient` recognises it and retries, the same as it would a 429.

The marker carries the existing message rather than wrapping it, so classification changes and **user-visible output does not** — no new `Caused by:` section, no reworded error.

A 403 with quota remaining is a refusal, not a rate limit, and stays deterministic. There is a test for that, because retrying a genuine "you may not do that" would waste the full backoff on something that cannot succeed.

Nothing about signature or withdrawal verification changes. In particular this does **not** treat a 403 as "no release list": that path still requires a real 404, so an induced 403 cannot suppress a signed withdrawal. Only whether the request is attempted again is affected.

## What this does not fix, and the decision it needs

Be clear about the limit of this change on its own: **at default settings it will usually not outlast a real GitHub rate limit.**

The backoff is ~200ms / 1s / 4s, so three retries are spent in about five seconds. GitHub's secondary limits typically ask for 60 seconds via `retry-after`, and a primary reset can be up to an hour — the v2026.9.9 one was 16 minutes 19 seconds away. mise reads `retry-after` only to print a warning (`display_github_rate_limit`); nothing consumes it as a wait.

So what this buys by itself is correctness rather than rescue: the classification fin

title: ci(docs): stop mise-action shadowing the PAT with the installation token
body:
## Problem

`docs-impl.yml` sets a workflow-level `GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.MISE_GH_TOKEN || secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` so that mise draws on the PAT's own rate-limit budget rather than the repository's shared one. That has never taken effect.

`mise-action` exports its `github_token` input as `MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN` ([src/index.ts:356](https://github.com/jdx/mise-action/blob/main/src/index.ts)), and mise prefers `MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN` over `GITHUB_TOKEN` (`GITHUB_TOKEN_ENV_VARS`, `src/github.rs:749`). The input defaults to `${{ github.token }}`, and this job passes none — so `MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN` silently shadowed the PAT and every mise API call in the docs job spent the ephemeral installation token instead.

That budget is shared across the whole repository, and publishing a release starts eight workflows at the same instant. On v2026.9.9 it ran out mid-release. The docs deploy failed when the packslip lookup for `aube` came back:

```
github auth: yes
github rate limit: 0/5000 (core), resets at 1789456621
"message": "API rate limit exceeded for installation."
```

`publish-version` hit the same wall six seconds earlier, reporting `API rate limit exceeded for installation (HTTP 403)` directly. The rate-limit window had opened at 06:17, so the hour's ordinary CI had already drawn the bucket down and the release fan-out finished it.

The consequences were not visible anywhere: mise.jdx.dev served the previous version for a day and a half, and `npm install mise` served 2026.9.8 until the publish workflow was re-run by hand. Neither failure was noticed until a user asked about missing documentation in [#13213](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13213).

## What this does

Passes the PAT to `mise-action` explicitly, so mise uses the token the workflow already intended:

```yaml
- uses: jdx/mise-action@c2a87611a18de5b3828c5652fe268e992400cb5c # v4
  with:
    install_args: bun
    github_token: ${{ secrets.MISE_GH_TOKEN || github.token }}
```

The `|| github.token` fallback matters: `docs.yml` does not forward secrets to the untrusted path, so `secrets.MISE_GH_TOKEN` is empty there and the job keeps working exactly as it does today.

## Scope

Only `docs-impl.yml` is changed. It is the one `mise-action` caller that also sets `GITHUB_TOKEN` to the PAT, so it is the only place where the configured intent is being defeated. `perf.yml` and `perf-pr.yml` also call `mise-action`, but they never had the PAT available and are not part of the release fan-out — they use the default token by choice, not by accident, so changing them would add PAT load for no demonstrated benefit.

This reduces the chance of exhausting the shared budget; it does not make the docs deploy immune to a rate limit. Two related changes are separate: [#13248](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13248) reports a failed release-triggered workflow by email instead of letting it pass unnoticed, and a companion PR classifies a GitHub rate-limit 403 as transient so it is retried.

## Validation

title: fix(pypi): lock tools whose injected dependencies need a newer Python
body:
Reported in [#13247](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13247).

`mise lock` failed for any PyPI tool whose `with` or `expose` list pinned a requirement needing a newer Python than the tool itself:

```toml
[tools]
"pypi:mkdocs" = { version = "1.6.1", with = ["mkdocstrings==1.0.6"] }
uv = "latest"
```

mkdocs 1.6.1 declares `requires-python = ">=3.8"`; mkdocstrings 1.0.6 declares `>=3.10`. mise built the sidecar's `requires-python` from the tool's own release metadata alone, so the generated project advertised `>=3.8` while depending on a release that cannot be installed below 3.10. uv forked the universal resolution at `>=3.8, <3.10`, found no mkdocstrings release for that fork, and gave up:

```console
$ mise lock
  × No solution found when resolving dependencies for split (markers:
  │ python_full_version >= '3.8' and python_full_version < '3.10'):
  ╰─▶ Because the requested Python version (>=3.8) does not satisfy
      Python>=3.10 and mkdocstrings==1.0.6 depends on Python>=3.10, we can
      conclude that mkdocstrings==1.0.6 cannot be used.
mise ERROR uv exited with non-zero status: exit code 1
```

The sidecar's Python range is now intersected across every requirement mise writes into it, so the same config locks and installs, with the floor raised to `>=3.10`:

```console
$ mise lock
Resolved 21 packages in 83ms
✓ Lockfile written to /tmp/test-mise/mise.lock

$ cat .mise/locks/pypi-mkdocs/1.6.1~6716a419/pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "mise-pypi-tool-environment"
version = "0.0.0"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
dependencies = ["mkdocs==1.6.1", "mkdocstrings==1.0.6"]

$ mise x --locked -- mkdocs --version
mkdocs, version 1.6.1 from …/.mise-uv/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/mkdocs (Python 3.12)
```

## What narrows the range, and what does not

Only a requirement pinned to one exact release narrows it, because that is the case uv cannot spread across the range on its own:

- **Unpinned requirements are untouched.** `with = ["mkdocstrings"]` still locks 0.26.1 below 3.9, 0.30.1 on 3.9, and 1.0.6 from 3.10 — uv's universal forking already handles that correctly, and narrowing there would needlessly cut off older interpreters.
- **A pin behind an interpreter marker is skipped.** `with = ["mkdocstrings==1.0.6; python_version >= '3.10'"]` keeps `requires-python = ">=3.8"`, because the requirement is simply absent from the versions the marker excludes.
- **Any other marker still narrows.** `; sys_platform == "linux"` leaves the requirement active across the whole Python range, so uv fails without narrowing; the floor is raised for every platform, which is the only way such a config locks at all.
- **A compound specifier containing an `==` clause counts as a pin.** `mkdocstrings==1.0.6,!=1.0.5` selects one release just as a bare `==` does.
- **A release whose metadata cannot be read leaves the range alone.** uv reports an unusable requirement more precisely than a partial lookup could, so a failed lookup degrades to today's behavior rather th

title: fix(packslip): install an exactly pinned version during its cooling window
body:
Pinning an exact version in `mise.toml` failed to install while that release was
still inside the `minimum_release_age` window, even though the setting documents
explicit pins as unfiltered. A [jdx/demand PR](https://github.com/jdx/demand/pull/217)
bumping `hk = "2.0.1"` roughly an hour after hk v2.0.1 was published hit this on
every CI platform:

```
mise ERROR Failed to install packslip:github.com/jdx/hk@2.0.1: packslip release
was recorded by the transparency log at 2026-09-15T18:57:35Z, after the allowed
cutoff 2026-09-14T19:52:52Z; refusing to bypass minimum_release_age
```

There was no way to land the bump other than waiting out the window or turning
the guard off for the whole CI job.

## What changed

Version resolution already lets an exact pin through — `resolve_version` calls
out that "explicit pinned versions like 22.5.0 should not be filtered by date",
and both the setting and the security docs say the same. The packslip backend
was re-applying the cutoff afterwards, when it verified the signed release, and
that second check only exempted versions that came from `mise.lock`. So mise
selected a version and then refused to install it.

Packslip now treats an exact pin the same way it already treats a lockfile
entry: as a selection that has already been made. Both the install-time and the
lock-time age checks skip it.

```toml
[tools]
"packslip:github.com/jdx/hk" = "2.0.1"   # installs and locks immediately
hk = "2"                                 # still waits out the cutoff
```

A pin is a byte-for-byte match between the requested string and the resolved
version, never a version parse or comparison — so `"2"`, `"latest"`, an alias
like `"lts"`, a ref, and a rolling channel all stay fuzzy and stay behind the
cutoff.

## Scope

This narrows one backend's install-time check to match documented behavior. It
does not change:

- version listing or selection, where the cutoff still governs every fuzzy request
- `npm:` and `pipx:` transitive dependency filtering
- any other backend, none of which re-check release age at install time

The supply-chain tradeoff is the same one [#13128](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13128)
already accepted for lockfiles: naming a specific release in a reviewed config
change is the human decision the cooling window exists to prompt. Projects that
want the delay to apply to pins too can keep using fuzzy requests, or set
`minimum_release_age` per tool.

## Validation

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check`
- `cargo test --bin mise tool_version` — 54 tests, including a new case covering
  pins, fuzzy requests, aliases, refs, and non-semver version strings
- `mise run test:e2e e2e/backend/test_packslip` — a new case installs and locks
  an exactly pinned packslip release under `MISE_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE=2000-01-01`
  with no lockfile present. Reverting the fix makes it fail with the same
  "refusing to bypass minimum_release_age" error quoted above.

Not cover

title: test: stop the dotfiles watcher e2e tests flaking on loaded runners
body:
`cli/test_dotfiles_watch` failed both attempts on an unrelated renovate PR (#13205), at two different assertions:

```
[... history --json | jq -r '.[0].description'] expected
  'edited hypr/monitors.lua; added hypr/bindings.lua' but got 'added hypr/bindings.lua'

[cat watch.log] expected '"event":"started"' to be in ''
```

Neither is a watcher bug. Both are timing assumptions in the test that only hold on an idle machine, which makes the suite fail for contributors whose PRs have nothing to do with dotfiles.

## What was wrong

**The waits measured iterations, not time.** `wait_until` looped 100 times with a 0.2s sleep. That is 20s only when nothing else costs anything; when each `mise` invocation or the runner stalls — the e2e job runs four tranche groups in parallel — the real budget is whatever the loop got through. The second watcher's startup wait used its own hand-rolled 10s version and expired with an empty `watch.log`. The waits now run against a `SECONDS` deadline (30s by default), and the hand-rolled loop is replaced by `wait_until`, as in the sibling tests.

**Two writes were assumed to coalesce.** The test wrote `monitors.lua` and `bindings.lua` back to back and asserted a single checkpoint describing both. They normally reach the watcher in one batch, but a stall between the writes puts them in separate debounce windows, and `held_paths` deliberately keeps a path that is not due yet out of another path's capture — so saving them separately is correct behavior, and the assertion was testing the scheduler's luck. It now asserts that both changes are saved and named across the newest one or two checkpoints. The checkpoint counts that follow were absolute (`wait_for_count 4/5/6`), so the extra checkpoint from a split satisfied them immediately and let the next assertion race the capture it was waiting for; they are relative to a snapshot taken just before each step now.

**`cli/test_dotfiles_watch_throttle` had a related race**, which it hit on the first local run here before anything was changed:

```
[... snapshot_of ... .config/hypr/state.json] expected '{"n":276}' but got '{"n":425}'
```

It pinned the churning file's expected content to a capture taken before the ordinary edit, assuming the churn would not be saved again before the edit's checkpoint. About 15s passed there against an 8s churn interval, so it was. The test now compares the edit's checkpoint against whichever capture precedes it — the watcher's actual promise is that the checkpoint carries the last *saved* version of a throttled file, never its live content — and skips a capture that a due churn save shared.

## Validation

The failure was forced rather than waited for: adding `sleep 2` between the two writes puts them in separate debounce windows deterministically.

| Run | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Both tests, idle | pass (33s / 66s) |
| Both tests, load average ~55 | pass (59s / 112s) |
| Both tests before this change, load average ~55 | pass — CPU load alone does

+# checkpoint it makes carries the version of the churning file that the save
+# before it recorded, never its live content
 captured="grep -c '\"event\":\"captured\"' watch.log"
 n="$(eval "$captured")"
 wait_until "[[ \$($captured) -gt $n ]]"
-churn_checkpoint="$(jq -r 'select(.event == "captured") | .uuid' watch.log | tail -1)"
-echo 'monitor=DP-2' >~/.config/hypr/monitors.lua
-wait_until "mise bootstrap dotfiles history --json | jq -e '.[0].description | test(\"monitors.lua\")'"
-# Pin the actual edit checkpoint: another scheduled save may become latest
-# while these assertions run. Compare snapshot contents, not display lines.
-monitor_checkpoint="$(jq -r 'select(.event == "captured" and (.description | contains("monitors.lua"))) | .uuid' watch.log | tail -1)"
-assert "$snapshot_of $monitor_checkpoint .config/hypr/state.json" "$($snapshot_of "$churn_checkpoint" .config/hypr/state.json)"
+# Pin the capture the edit made: another scheduled save may become latest
+# while these assertions run, so compare snapshot contents, not display
+# lines. A save the churning file is due for may share that capture, which
+# then carries its live content by design and proves nothing here — edit
+# again until a capture is the edit's alone. The churn is saved once per
+# interval at most, so this normally settles on the first attempt.
+edit_captures='[.[] | select(.event == "captured" and (.description | contains("monitors.lua")))]'
+edits="jq -rs '$edit_captures | length' watch.log"
+monitor_checkpoint=""
+for attempt in 1 2 3 4 5; do
+  n="$(eval "$edits")"
+  echo "monitor=DP-2.$attempt" >~/.config/hypr/monitors.lua
+  wait_until "[[ \$($edits) -gt $n ]]"
+  edit="$(jq -rs "$edit_captures | last" watch.log)"
+  if ! printf '%s' "$edit" | jq -e '.description | contains("state.json")' >/dev/null; then
+    monitor_checkpoint="$(printf '%s' "$edit" | jq -r .uuid)"
+    break
+  fi
+done
+[[ -n $monitor_checkpoint ]] ||
+  fail "every capture of the edit was shared with a due save of the churning file"
+# the save before it, whichever capture that was: under load the churn can be
+# saved again between the wait above and the edit
+previous_checkpoint="$(jq -rs --arg uuid "$monitor_checkpoint" '[.[] | select(.event == "captured") | .uuid] | .[index($uuid) - 1]' watch.log)"
+assert "$snapshot_of $monitor_checkpoint .config/hypr/state.json" "$($snapshot_of "$previous_checkpoint" .config/hypr/state.json)"
 
 # unsaved changes to the throttled file are visible as they happen
 wait_until "[[ \$(mise bootstrap dotfiles status --json | jq -r '.history.health.throttled[0].pending_changes // 0') -ge 1 ]]"

title: fix(dotfiles): name the directory in the way, not a type change
body:
## The problem

Put a directory (or anything else that is not a readable file or symlink) where a tracked dotfile belongs, and mise blamed the repository for it:

```console
$ mise dot conflicts
Conflict: ~/.one (changed type on one side and content on the other)
```

Nothing changed type on either side. Both sides of the repository hold an ordinary file; the local filesystem has something unusable sitting at that path. The wording sends users to `mise dot conflicts`, `--take-remote`, and `--keep-local`, and none of those can decide the path — `--take-remote ~/.one` fails with `~/.one is not a regular file or symlink`, and the setup stays paused.

`mise bootstrap` already promised the opposite when a setup pauses:

> A path held for another reason, such as a directory where the repository has a file, says so in `mise dot status` and needs that fix instead.

It did not say so. Every such failure — an unreadable file, a directory, a socket, and a Git plumbing failure alike — was mapped to the `TypeChange` conflict kind.

## What changes

Those paths now get their own conflict kind, and every surface names the real problem and the fix that actually applies:

```console
$ mise dot conflicts
Conflict: ~/.one (a directory or unreadable path stands where the repository has a file)

$ mise dot status
  sync paused: ~/.one: a directory or unreadable path stands where the repository has a file;
  sharing is paused for the entire setup; local history continues
  (move ~/.one away or make it a readable file, then run `mise dot pull`;
  --take-remote and --keep-local cannot decide it)
```

`mise doctor` reports the same reason and advice. A genuine type change — one side made the path a symlink while the other changed its content — keeps `TypeChange` and its existing wording.

Moving the path away is what resolves it:

```console
$ rm -rf ~/.one && echo local-version >~/.one
$ mise dot pull --take-remote-all --yes
```

There is no new flag or setting, and no migration: the conflict kind is recomputed on every sync, so an existing paused setup starts reporting the new reason as soon as it next plans.

## One behavior change beyond the wording

`mise dot sync` used to turn *any* failure while reading a live path — including a Git `hash-object` failure on a perfectly sound file — into a conflict the user was told to resolve by hand. Only the path's own fault is a conflict now; a repository or process failure stops the pass with its own error instead of posing as one. This matches the distinction #13239 drew for blanket resolutions, using the `apply::UnusableLive` error type it introduced.

## Validation

- `e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_conflict_reasons` (new) builds the two-machine scenario, puts a directory over the tracked file, and checks the reason and advice on `mise dot conflicts` and `mise dot status`, that the pull is paused with the directory untouched, that `--take-remote` still refuses it by name, and that removing the directory lets the pull finish. Run aga

title: ci: email on release-triggered workflow failures
body:
## Problem

Nine workflows trigger on `release: published` — `docs`, `npm-publish`, `winget`, `copr-publish`, `ppa-publish`, `snapcraft-publish`, `release-alpine`, `cloudflare-deploy`, and `publish-version`. They publish outside of any pull request, so when one fails there is no reviewer, no red check on a PR, and nothing in the release itself that looks wrong. The release is out; the thing that workflow was supposed to ship simply never went out.

This is not hypothetical. The `docs` deploy for v2026.9.9 failed during tool install:

```
mise WARN  GitHub rate limit exceeded. Resets at 2026-09-15 07:17:01 +00:00
mise  ✗  aube@2.2.16  123ms · failed: fetching the release list of packslip:github.com/aubepkg/aube
mise ERROR Failed to install tools: npm:ajv-cli@latest, npm:markdownlint-cli@latest,
           npm:prettier@3.9.6, packslip:github.com/aubepkg/aube@latest
```

Because `xtasks/docs/release` only performs a real upload on a release event, a failed release run means the site keeps serving the previous version indefinitely. mise.jdx.dev stayed on v2026.9.8 for roughly a day and a half, missing the `with` and `expose` docs that shipped in v2026.9.9. It was caught only when a user asked about the missing documentation in [#13213](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13213#discussioncomment-18454847). Re-running the failed run fixed it.

## What this does

Adds `.github/workflows/notify-release-failure.yml`, a single `workflow_run` listener over all nine workflows. When one of them completes, it emails via Resend if — and only if — the run was triggered by a release and ended in `failure`, `timed_out`, or `startup_failure`.

The email names the workflow, the tag, the conclusion, and the attempt number, and links to both the run and the release:

> The **docs** workflow for **v2026.9.9** finished with **failure** on attempt 1.
>
> The release is published but whatever this workflow ships did not go out. Re-run it once the cause is fixed.
>
> [View workflow run](https://github.com/jdx/mise/actions/runs/34939546992) | [View release](https://github.com/jdx/mise/releases/tag/v2026.9.9)

`cancelled` is deliberately excluded: `docs-impl.yml` sets `cancel-in-progress` on a release-scoped concurrency group, so back-to-back releases cancel the earlier run on purpose.

One listener rather than a notify job per workflow means the other nine files are untouched, and any future release-triggered workflow is covered by adding one line to the `workflows:` list.

## Adoption

**Two repository secrets must be added to `jdx/mise` before this does anything** — the same pair already used by `jdx/ruby`:

- `RESEND_API_KEY`
- `NOTIFY_EMAIL`

Until they exist, the job logs a `::warning::` and exits 0 rather than failing, so a missing secret cannot turn into a second silent failure or a red check on every release. `workflow_run` only fires for the copy of this workflow on the default branch, so notifications begin with the first release after merge.

## Validation

-
author: jdx
diff:
--- .github/workflows/notify-release-failure.yml (+78/-0) @@ -0,0 +1,78 @@ +name: notify-release-failure + +# Release-triggered publish workflows have no reviewer and no PR check, so a +# failure is silent: the release exists but the artifact, package, or docs it +# was supposed to publish quietly never ships. Email on failure instead of +# waiting for a user to report it. +on: # zizmor: ignore[dangerous-triggers] no permissions, no checkout, and it only fires for release-triggered runs + workflow_run: + workflows: + - cloudflare-deploy + - copr-publish + - docs + - npm-publish + - ppa-publish + - publish-version + - release-alpine + - snapcraft-publish + - winget + types: [completed] + +permissions: {} + +jobs: + notify: + name: notify + if: ${{ github.repository == 'jdx/mise' && github.event.workflow_run.event == 'release' && contains(fromJSON('["failure", "timed_out", "startup_failure"]'), github.event.workflow_run.conclusion) }} + runs-on: ubuntu-latest + timeout-minutes: 5 + steps: + - name: Send failure email via Resend + env: + RESEND_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.RESEND_API_KEY }} + NOTIFY_EMAIL: ${{ secrets.NOTIFY_EMAIL }} + WORKFLOW: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.name }} + CONCLUSION: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.conclusion }} + TAG: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_branch }} + RUN_URL: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.html_url }} + ATTEMPT: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.run_attempt }} + run: | + set -euo pipefail + if [ -z "${RESEND_API_KEY:-}" ] || [ -z "${NOTIFY_EMAIL:-}" ]; then + echo "::warning::RESEND_API_KEY or NOTIFY_EMAIL is unset; skipping notification for ${WORKFLOW} on ${TAG}" + exit 0 + fi + # Build the payload with jq: --arg keeps a tag or workflow name from + # breaking out of the JSON string, @html keeps it from becoming markup + # once the mail client renders the body, and @uri keeps it from + # reshaping the release URL. A tag is author-controlled, so all three + # matter even though the values arrive from the GitHub API. + payload=$(jq -n \ + --arg to "$NOTIFY_EMAIL" \ + --arg workflow "$WORKFLOW" \ + --arg conclusion "$CONCLUSION" \ + --arg tag "$TAG" \ + --arg run_url "$RUN_URL" \ + --arg attempt "$ATTEMPT" \ + --arg repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" \ + ' + ("https://github.com/\($repo)/releases/tag/\($tag | @uri)") as $release_url | + { + from: "mise Releases ", + to: [$to], + subject: "❌ mise \($tag): \($workflow) \($conclusion)", + html: ( + "

The \($workflow | @html) workflow for \($tag | @html) finished with \($conclusion | @html) on attempt \($attempt | @html).

" + + "

The release is published but whatever this workflow ships did not go out. Re-run it once the cause is fixed.

" + + "

View workflow run | View release

" + ) + }') + # This mail is the only signal that a release half-shipped, so a + # transient Resend failure must not swallow it. A retry can duplicate + # an alert whose response was lost; two alerts beat none. + curl --fail-with-body -sS \ + --retry 3 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 2 --retry-max-time 60 \ + -X POST 'https://api.resend.com/emails' \ + -H "Authorization: Bearer ${RESEND_API_KEY}" \ + -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ + -d "$payload"

title: fix(dotfiles): hold an unsaved path instead of discarding --keep-local-all
body:
`mise dot pull --keep-local-all` promises to decide every conflict at once. Until now a single path with unsaved local changes made the whole flag useless: the pass aborted, and every other conflict it had already decided was discarded.

The refusal on that one path is correct and stays. `--keep-local` publishes this machine's *saved* version of a file, so a path whose live file has drifted from its saved version — or which has no saved version yet — cannot be kept without publishing something stale. What was unintended is that the refusal took the rest of the pass down with it.

## Before

Two conflicts, `~/.one` edited since its last `mise dot save`:

```
$ mise dot pull --keep-local-all --yes
Error: run `mise dot save ~/.one` first: --keep-local publishes this machine's
saved version of ~/.one, and it has unsaved changes
```

`~/.two` was decidable, but nothing was recorded for it. Saving `~/.one` and pulling again was the only way forward, and any path in the same state restarted the cycle.

## After

The decision for `~/.two` is recorded, `~/.one` is held, and the failure names every held path and what to do about it:

```
$ mise dot pull --keep-local-all --yes
Error: sync paused: resolve all 1 conflict(s) before sharing resumes; a blanket
choice cannot decide them all: ~/.one has unsaved changes, so run `mise dot save
~/.one` first. Fix each of those paths, then pull again
```

Deciding just that one path now finishes the setup, because the blanket choice for `~/.two` is still on file:

```
$ mise dot pull --take-remote ~/.one --yes
~/.one  write  home/.one
mise history: applied 1 incoming change(s)
```

`~/.two` keeps this machine's version, as `--keep-local-all` chose.

Naming a path explicitly is a different request, so `mise dot pull --keep-local <path>` still fails with its original message — the user asked for that path in particular. A `--dry-run` preview and the background watcher warn rather than fail, as they already do for a path whose live side is unusable.

## Implementation

This reuses the `blanket_chosen` / `blanket_held` mechanism #13239 added in `apply_locked_with_scope` for a path whose live side is a directory rather than a file, extending it to the second bail with the same shape. Both held reasons flow through the same failure and the same `dry_run` / `automatic` warning.

## Validation

`mise run test:e2e e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_resolve_all` passes. title: fix(brew): do not treat tap formula requirement symbols as dependencies
body:
Fixes the bug reported in #13201.

## Problem

A tap formula that declares `depends_on :macos` has that requirement recorded as a dependency named `macos`. The resolver then tries to fetch a formula by that name and the 404 aborts the entire `bootstrap packages` run, so nothing is processed:

```
mise ERROR failed to fetch Homebrew formula 'macos'
mise ERROR HTTP status client error (404 Not Found) for url (https://formulae.brew.sh/api/formula/macos.json)
```

It is not a partial failure. One such formula anywhere in `[bootstrap.packages]` stops the whole run, and there is no way to opt out short of undeclaring the package.

## Cause

In Homebrew, `depends_on "foo"` names a package while `depends_on :macos` names a *requirement*: a platform constraint, not something installable. `tap_formula_metadata.rb` filtered `:test` and routed `:build`, but nothing distinguished a Symbol from a String, so the symbol reached the dependency list verbatim:

```ruby
target << name.to_s
```

This affects the tap path only. Core formulae resolve through `api.rs`, which reads `dependencies` and `build_dependencies` and never touches the API's `requirements` array, so a core formula with the same constraint is unaffected.

## Fix

Skip Symbol names. Other requirement symbols (`:linux`, `:xcode`, `:arm`, `:x11`) take the same path and are covered by the same guard.

The versioned form, `depends_on macos: :tahoe`, already fell out at the existing `name.nil?` guard, because its lone key is a Symbol rather than a String and so never becomes `spec`. Only the bare positional form reached the append.

## Verification

Ran the metadata shim directly against `stripe/homebrew-stripe-cli`, which declares a bare `depends_on :macos`:

| | `dependencies` |
| --- | --- |
| before | `["macos"]` |
| after | `[]` |

The existing `extracts_formula_metadata_without_homebrew` test is extended with `depends_on :macos`, `depends_on :xcode => :build` and `depends_on macos: :sequoia`, asserting none of them appear in `dependencies` or `build_dependencies`.

Being straightforward about test coverage: I could not run that Rust test to completion on this machine, so it is CI that needs to confirm it. With the system Ruby (2.6) the test hits the `test_ruby()` guard and returns early without asserting anything. With a Ruby new enough to satisfy it, the only one available here lives under `$HOME` and `sandbox-exec` blocks loading its `libruby` dylib, which looks like the same problem as #12969 and #13197:

```
dyld: Library not loaded: .../ruby/4.0.5/lib/libruby.4.0.dylib
Reason: tried: '...' (blocked by sandbox)
Error: sandbox-exec exited with non-zero status: killed by SIGABRT
```

The shim behaviour itself is verified directly, outside the sandbox, by the before/after table above. `rustfmt --check` passes on the edited file.

## Notes

No new dependencies. No user-facing documentation change: this restores documented behaviour rather than altering it.

title: fix(dotfiles): keep a blanket conflict choice from aborting on a directory
body:
Follow-up to #13233, which added the blanket conflict flags. A review comment landed a few minutes after that PR merged; this is the fix.

## The problem

`mise dot pull --take-remote-all` is advertised as the one command that decides every paused conflict at once. It swept *every* conflict into the blanket choice, including a path whose live side is not a regular file or symlink — a tracked dotfile that has since been replaced by a directory, for example. Recording a choice for such a path fails with `~/.one is not a regular file or symlink`, and that failure propagated out of the resolution loop before a single decision was written. One unusable path meant the command decided nothing, with an error that named the path but not the reason it surfaced or what to do about it.

That contradicts what mise already does elsewhere. `mise bootstrap` tells users "a path held for another reason, such as a directory where the repository has a file, says so in `mise dot status` and needs that fix instead", and the sync preflight notes that "a changed type or unreadable live file must hold incoming application, not abort fetching". Such a path is supposed to be *held*, not to take the rest of the pass down with it.

## What changes

A path the blanket choice cannot describe is held, the pass decides and records every other conflict, and the command then fails naming what it could not do:

```console
$ mise dot pull --take-remote-all --yes
mise ERROR sync paused: resolve all 1 conflict(s) before sharing resumes; a blanket
choice cannot decide them all: ~/.one is not a regular file or symlink. Fix each of
those paths, then pull again
```

The failure is the point: a blanket flag promises to decide *every* conflict, so it has not succeeded while one is still held. But the decisions it did make are written before it fails, so fixing the held path and deciding just that one finishes the setup:

```console
$ rm -rf ~/.one && cp /backup/.one ~/.one
$ mise dot pull --take-remote ~/.one --yes
~/.one  write  home/.one
~/.two  write  home/.two
mise history: applied 2 incoming change(s)
```

`~/.two` applies here because the earlier blanket command had already recorded a decision for it — no need to re-answer conflicts that were never in question.

Two behaviors are deliberately unchanged: a path named explicitly (`--take-remote ~/.one`) still reports the failure, because the user asked for that path specifically; and `--keep-local-all` still refuses a conflict with unsaved local edits, since keeping the local side would publish a stale saved version.

## Implementation

The check sits on the same `live_object` call that records the choice, rather than in a pass that classifies paths beforehand — so a path that changes underneath the command is held too, instead of aborting it. Only a failure that is the live path's own fault is held: an unreadable file, or one that is neither a file nor a symlink. A repository failure on a sound file (Git failing to hash it, say) is nob

title: fix(backend): list versions from the resolved backend, not the registry's preferred one
body:
`mise ls-remote hk@1.57` printed nothing, and `mise latest hk@1.57` failed, even though hk 1.57.0 is installable:

```
$ mise ls-remote hk
1.58.1
2.0.0
$ mise ls-remote hk@1.57
$ mise ls-remote aqua:jdx/hk 1.57
1.57.0
```

`registry/hk.toml` splits hk across two backends at a version boundary — `packslip:github.com/jdx/hk` from 1.58.1 up, `aqua:jdx/hk` below it. The boundary itself worked: `hk@1.57` did resolve to the aqua backend. What went wrong is version *listing*.

mise-versions (`https://mise-versions.jdx.dev/data/<tool>.toml`) publishes one version list per registry short name, generated from the entry's first backend. The gate deciding whether a backend may read that list accepted **any** backend declared by the registry entry, so the aqua backend was handed packslip's list — which contains only 1.58.1 and 2.0.0. Nothing matched the `1.57` prefix, so mise printed an empty list and reported no such version.

This became visible when mise-versions regenerated `data/hk.toml` after hk 2.0.0 shipped, replacing the aqua-era list with packslip's two entries. No mise change was needed to trigger it; the same failure was latent for every registry entry with a `min_version` boundary.

The fix compares against the entry's **declared first** backend rather than the client-filtered backend list. A backend that is not the preferred one now lists versions from its own upstream source:

```
$ mise ls-remote hk@1.57
1.57.0
$ mise latest hk@1.57
1.57.0
$ mise ls-remote hk          # still the preferred backend, still served from mise-versions
1.58.1
2.0.0
```

Comparing against the *declared* first backend rather than the filtered one also covers the cases where a client-side filter promotes a different backend — `MISE_DISABLE_BACKENDS`, platform-scoped registry entries, and a tool pinned to a non-preferred backend in config or a lockfile all previously inherited the preferred backend's published list:

```
$ MISE_DISABLE_BACKENDS=packslip mise ls-remote hk | tail -4
1.57.0
1.58.0
1.58.1
2.0.0
```

The versions host stays in use for the preferred backend, so this costs an extra upstream listing only for backends whose published list was wrong to begin with.

## Validation

- `e2e/backend/test_registry_min_version` fails on `main` at the first assertion and passes with this change.
- `mise run test:e2e e2e/backend/test_registry e2e/cli/test_ls_remote` — all pass.
- `mise run test:unit` — 4100 pass, including a new unit test asserting that hk's fallback `aqua:jdx/hk` is rejected by the versions-host gate while the preferred `packslip:github.com/jdx/hk` is accepted.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean.

`backend_arg_matches_registry_backend` is unchanged: its other callers gate GitHub *release* metadata, which mise-versions keys by repo and tag rather than by short name, so any registry backend is a valid match there.
