title: chore(ci): stop renovate from proposing fedora major bumps
body:
Renovate keeps proposing fedora major bumps for the RPM/COPR build images (most recently #12965, fedora 46), but nothing in PR CI ever builds those images, so the bump is unreviewable in place and only takes effect later:

- `packaging/rpm/Dockerfile` and `packaging/copr/Dockerfile` are built only by `docker.yml`, which runs on `v*` tags and `workflow_dispatch`.
- `release.yml` runs the rpm job inside a pinned digest (`ghcr.io/jdx/mise:rpm@sha256:ce5434e6…`), so a new base image reaches the release path only after the image is rebuilt *and* that pin is updated.

The result is that a bad fedora major lands mid-release rather than failing a PR. That is exactly how it played out before: #1322 bumped the RPM image to fedora 40, `8184bc9` rolled it back past the old pin to fedora 38 ("Makes repo compatible with AL2"), and the follow-up bumps #1417 (40), #1707 (41) and #2531 (42) were all closed unmerged.

This disables only `major` updates for the `fedora` dockerfile dependency. Digest pins (`fedora:45@sha256:…`) and non-major updates keep flowing as they do today — those have merged routinely and do get rebuilt from the same source. Moving to a new Fedora release becomes a deliberate change, made together with the image rebuild and the `release.yml` digest pin.

```json
{
  "matchPackageNames": ["fedora"],
  "matchManagers": ["dockerfile"],
  "matchUpdateTypes": ["major"],
  "enabled": false
}
```

No user-facing change; this only affects which PRs Renovate opens. Once this merges, Renovate will close #12965 on its own.

title: chore: drop the pkl dev dependency by upgrading hk to 2.0.0
body:
`pkl` was in the repository's tool list only so a custom hk step could run `pkl eval hk.pkl`. That is a dependency Renovate keeps bumping for no benefit: hk evaluates `hk.pkl` with its built-in pklr evaluator and no longer shells out to the pkl CLI at all, and `hk.pkl` is this repository's only Pkl file — so the step validated exactly what hk already validates, loudly, on every run.

Upgrading hk to 2.0.0 lets the whole thing go:

- `hk.pkl` amends/imports `hk@2.0.0` instead of `hk@1.55.0`
- the custom `["pkl"]` step is removed
- `pkl` is dropped from `mise.toml` and `mise.lock`; `hk` moves from 1.58.1 to 2.0.0
- the linter lists in `docs/contributing.md` and `llms.txt` no longer mention Pkl

Contributors get one less tool to install, and nothing in the repository depends on the pkl CLI any more.

## No v2 migration needed

hk 2.0.0 removes several v1 interfaces, but none of them are used here. The config declares its `check` and `fix` hooks explicitly, so the new optional top-level `steps` block is not required; there is no `pre-commit` hook, so the new contextual-staging default (only `pre-commit` stages by default) changes nothing; and the config uses no `gitleaks_staged` / `knip_strict` / `pinact_v3` builtin variants, no `Types.Regex`, and no `defaults { }` block.

## Validation

`hk check --all --plan` under hk 2.0.0 resolves the config and lists the ten remaining steps (schema, prettier, cargo-fmt, cargo-check, shellcheck, shfmt, taplo, lua-check, stylua, markdownlint). A full `mise run lint` passes:

```

```

title: fix(exec): speed up fish startup and restore its PATH precedence
body:
Every fish shell launched through a mise shim — the usual setup when fish itself is managed by mise — took over a second to start with a large toolset, and got its PATH in the wrong order.

Reported in #13225: launching fish through its shim measured 1.11–1.13 s with 81 globally configured tools, against 0.10 s for the resolved executable, scaling superlinearly with the number of active tools.

## What was wrong

`mise exec -- fish` (and therefore shim dispatch, which routes through the same code) hands fish a `-C` init script rather than assigning PATH. That script emitted one `fish_add_path -gm` per resolved directory, which caused two separate problems.

**Startup was quadratic.** fish's own `config.fish` installs an `--on-variable fish_user_paths` handler, `__fish_reconstruct_path`, that rebuilds PATH with a linear scan every time the variable is set. One call per directory re-ran it once per directory. Timing the generated init script alone in fish 3.7 with 156 paths:

```text
before (one fish_add_path per path): 1328 ms
after  (one batched fish_add_path):     39 ms
```

This is shell-side work, so those numbers are independent of how mise was built. End to end, with a 149-tool config and a debug build (min of 3 runs), fish now tracks bash instead of diverging from it:

```text
tools   mise x -- fish    mise x -- fish    mise x -- bash
        (before)          (after)           (unchanged)
    1        142 ms            112 ms             88 ms
   60        443 ms            154 ms            121 ms
  149       1611 ms            276 ms            211 ms
```

**PATH precedence was inverted.** `fish_add_path` prepends, so N sequential calls reversed the order `list_final_paths` returns. Comparing `mise x -- fish` against `mise x -- bash` on the same config produced the same 57 directories in exactly opposite order, which put `env._.path` entries, `command-wrappers/bin`, and the uv venv directory behind every tool directory:

```console
$ cat mise.toml
[env]
_.path = ["{{config_root}}/first", "{{config_root}}/second", "{{config_root}}/third"]

$ mise x -- bash -c 'echo "$PATH"'   # order mise resolved
.../first:.../second:.../third:...

$ mise x -- fish -c 'for p in $PATH; echo $p; end'   # before
.../third
.../second
.../first
```

## The fix

Emit a single `fish_add_path -gm` listing every directory. fish's own implementation builds the new variable value before assigning it — its comment says "to stop any handlers or anything from firing more than once" — so the handler runs exactly once, and prepending the list in argument order reproduces the precedence every other shell already had. Both `mise x -- fish` and `mise x -- bash` now print `first second third`.

No configuration change or migration is needed; existing setups get the new behavior automatically. The one remaining difference from bash is that `fish_add_path` skips directories that do not exist, which is pre-existing behavior and unchanged here.

The `// TODO: env is being calcu
author: jdx
diff:
--- e2e/shell/test_fish_exec_path_order (+32/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,32 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# `mise exec -- fish` hands fish an `-C` script instead of assigning PATH. Emitting
+# one `fish_add_path` per directory reversed mise's resolved order (each call
+# prepends) and re-ran fish's `--on-variable fish_user_paths` handler once per
+# directory, which is O(n^2) — over a second of startup for a large toolset.
+# See: https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13225
+mkdir -p "$PWD/first" "$PWD/second" "$PWD/third" "$PWD/stub"
+
+cat <<TOML >mise.toml
+[env]
+_.path = ["{{config_root}}/first", "{{config_root}}/second", "{{config_root}}/third"]
+TOML
+
+# A stub named "fish" captures the -C script mise generates, so the batching is
+# asserted even on hosts without fish installed.
+cat <<'STUB' >"$PWD/stub/fish"
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+printf '%s\n' "$2" >"$CAPTURE"
+STUB
+chmod +x "$PWD/stub/fish"
+
+CAPTURE="$PWD/init.fish" mise x -- "$PWD/stub/fish" -c exit
+assert "grep -c '^fish_add_path ' '$PWD/init.fish'" "1"
+
+# The one call lists the directories in mise's resolved precedence order.
+assert "grep '^fish_add_path ' '$PWD/init.fish' | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '/(first|second|third)\$' | sed 's|.*/||' | tr '\n' ' '" "first second third "
+
+if type -p fish >/dev/null; then
+  # bash is the reference: it gets PATH assigned directly, so its order always
+  # reflects what mise resolved. fish must agree.
+  assert "mise x -- fish -c 'for p in \$PATH; echo \$p; end' | grep -E '/(first|second|third)\$' | sed 's|.*/||' | tr '\n' ' '" "first second third "
+fi
--- src/cli/exec.rs (+16/-5)
@@ -7,6 +7,7 @@ use duct::IntoExecutablePath;
 use eyre::{Result, bail};
 #[cfg(any(test, windows))]
 use eyre::{Result, eyre};
+use itertools::Itertools;
 
 use crate::cli::args::ToolArg;
 #[cfg(any(test, windows))]
@@ -346,11 +347,21 @@ impl Exec {
             }
             // TODO: env is being calculated twice with final_env and env_with_path
             let (_, env_results) = ts.final_env(&config).await?;
-            for p in ts.list_final_paths(&config, env_results).await? {
-                cmd.push(format!(
-                    "fish_add_path -gm {}",
-                    shell_escape::escape(p.to_string_lossy())
-                ));
+            let paths = ts.list_final_paths(&config, env_results).await?;
+            if !paths.is_empty() {
+                // One call with every path, not one call per path. fish's own
+                // config.fish installs an `--on-variable fish_user_paths` handler
+                // (`__fish_reconstruct_path`) that rebuilds PATH with a linear
+                // scan, so N separate calls cost O(N^2) — over a second of shell
+                // startup for a large toolset. Batching also preserves precedence:
+                // each call prepends, so sequential calls reversed the order
+                // `list_final_paths` returns, pushing `env._.path` entries and
+                // command wrappers behind every tool directory.
+                let paths = paths
+                    .iter()
+                    .map(|p| shell_escape::escape(p.to_string_lossy()))
+                    .join(" ");
+                cmd.push(format!("fish_add_path -gm {paths}"));
             }
             args.insert(0, cmd.join("\n"));
             args.insert(0, "-C".into());

title: feat(dotfiles): resolve every sharing conflict in one command
body:
> [!NOTE]
> Stacked on #13232, which this builds on. Review that one first; the diff here
> against `main` includes its documentation changes.

Adopting a setup repository onto a machine that already has some of the tracked
files makes **every differing file its own conflict**, and each one had to be
named individually before anything could be applied:

```sh
mise dot pull --take-remote ~/.bashrc
mise dot pull --take-remote ~/.config/mise/config.toml
mise dot pull --take-remote ~/.config/starship.toml
# ...once per file, before the setup can continue
```

That is the common case on a second machine, not an edge case — and it is the
one moment a user is least likely to want to adjudicate files one at a time.
Reported in
[an Omarchy discussion](https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/discussions/11029#discussioncomment-18450136):
*"The adopt command on my laptop threw a huge warning about the two files I
started with... The warning wasn't clear about what I had to do to force adopt
those remote files."*

## What is new

`mise dot pull --take-remote-all` decides every conflict at once, with
`--keep-local-all` as its counterpart:

```sh
mise dot pull --take-remote-all
```

An explicit `--take-remote` or `--keep-local` still names the exceptions, so a
blanket choice does not force an all-or-nothing decision:

```sh
# the repository's version of everything except ~/.bashrc
mise dot pull --take-remote-all --keep-local ~/.bashrc
```

The two blanket flags are mutually exclusive. `--keep-local-all` requires each
file it keeps to be saved already, the same rule per-path `--keep-local` has
always had.

This does not change what a conflict is, when one is raised, or the safety
rules: nothing is overwritten without a decision, the replaced versions are
checkpointed first, and `mise dot undo` still reverses the pull.

## Messages

The paused-sync and adoption failures named only the per-path form. They now
name the blanket flag too, so the way out is in the message rather than one
`mise dot status` away:

```
the setup from <url> is paused; nothing was bootstrapped. `mise dot status`
lists the paths that need attention. Existing files that differ are kept until
you decide: `mise dot pull --take-remote-all` takes the repository's version of
every one, or `mise dot pull --take-remote|--keep-local <path>` decides one at
a time. Then run `mise bootstrap`
```

## Validation

New `e2e/cli/test_dotfiles_resolve_all` covers two simultaneous conflicts
resolved by one `--take-remote-all`, the `--take-remote-all --keep-local <path>`
exception (asserting each file lands on the expected side), mutual exclusion of
the two blanket flags, and that a blanket choice with nothing to decide is not
an error.

Also ran `test_dotfiles_bootstrap_from_git`, `test_dotfiles_sync`,
`test_dotfiles_sync_auto`, `test_dotfiles_sync_preflight`,
`test_dotfiles_sync_files_encrypted`, `test_dotfiles_sync_permissions`,
`test_dotfiles_sync_auto_reconcile`, `test_dotfiles_sync_stable` and
`test_dotfiles_

 This is expected, not a failure of the adoption. List what is waiting, then

+take the repository's version of everything:
 
 ```sh

-mise dot pull --take-remote ~/.bashrc
-mise dot pull --take-remote ~/.config/mise/config.toml

 ```
 
-`--take-remote` replaces this machine's file with the shared version; the
-version being replaced is saved first, so `mise dot undo` reverses it. Once the
-last path is decided, the same `pull` writes the remaining tracked files. Run
-`mise bootstrap` afterwards to finish the parts that are not dotfiles, such as
-tools and services.
+`--take-remote-all` replaces each conflicting file with the shared version; the
+versions being replaced are saved first, so `mise dot undo` reverses the whole
+pull. Once the last path is decided, the same `pull` writes the remaining
+tracked files. Run `mise bootstrap` afterwards to finish the parts that are not
+dotfiles, such as tools and services.
+
+To decide one path at a time instead, name it:
+
+```sh
+mise dot pull --take-remote ~/.bashrc
+```
 
-To keep this machine's version instead, save it first — a fresh machine has no
-baseline to compare against, and `--keep-local` requires one:
+To keep this machine's version of a file, save it first. `--keep-local`
+resolves a conflict by publishing this machine's saved version, and a fresh
+machine has not saved one yet:
 
 ```sh
 mise dot save ~/.bashrc
 mise dot pull --keep-local ~/.bashrc
 ```
 
+`--keep-local` also names the exceptions to a blanket choice. This takes the
+repository's version of everything except `~/.bashrc`:
+
+```sh
+mise dot pull --take-remote-all --keep-local ~/.bashrc
+```
+
 ::: tip
 Moving the conflicting files aside before `mise bootstrap --adopt` avoids the
 decisions entirely: a path that does not exist is simply written.

+assert "cat $second/.two" a-two-again

+assert_fail 'b dot pull --take-remote-all --keep-local-all --yes'

+# ---- --keep-local-all keeps every saved local version, and publishes them
+assert_succeed 'b dot sync'

title: docs(dotfiles): explain encryption key setup and first-adoption conflicts
body:
Setting up encryption for shared dotfiles meant guessing. The configuration
example was all placeholders:

```toml
[history.encryption]
recipients = ["<age-or-plugin-public-recipient>", "<recovery-public-recipient>"]
```

Nothing said what a recipient string looks like, how to produce one, or what
the "recovery" one is for — and `dotfiles.md` pointed at that section "for key
setup" that was not there. This came up in
[an Omarchy discussion](https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/discussions/11029#discussioncomment-18450136)
from someone who had just set up desktop↔laptop sync with an encrypted file and
worked it out the hard way.

## Encryption key setup

A new **Choose recipients** section documents the recipient forms mise already
accepts, then walks through each way to get one:

- **An existing SSH public key works as a recipient**, and mise already reads
  `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` as the matching identity. For most people this is the
  whole setup, and it was previously undocumented.
- Generating a dedicated age key with `age-keygen`, including installing the
  age CLI through mise.
- Generating a recovery recipient, storing it in a password manager, and
  removing the local copy.

Two failure modes that are easy to hit get explicit warnings:

- **A passphrase-protected SSH key cannot decrypt history.** mise does not
  prompt for the passphrase, and an SSH agent does not help — which is
  surprising next to the repository-authentication guidance, where a
  passphrase-protected key in an agent is the recommended choice.
- **A plugin-only recipient list (`age1yubikey1...`) stops automatic saving.**
  Plugin recipients need an interactive terminal and the watcher runs in the
  background.

It also states what changing `recipients` does: files are re-encrypted on their
next save, while commits already in history keep the recipients they were
written with, so a machine added later cannot read older versions.

## Adopting onto a machine that already has the files

A second machine usually already has a `~/.bashrc`. mise holds each file that
differs for a decision and stops the adoption — deliberately, so nothing is
overwritten — but the guide only described conflicts as "if two machines change
the same lines", which is the *ongoing sync* case, not this one.

`Set up another machine` now covers it: what the paused message means, how to
resolve it, that moving files aside beforehand avoids the decisions entirely,
and that `--replace-history` and `--force-dotfiles` are not the fix (the first
replaces history rather than differing files; the second applies to `[dotfiles]`
link and copy targets).

## Any Git host

Sharing works with any Git URL, but every example was GitHub, which reads as a
requirement. Added a self-hosted example for `mise dot origin set` and
`mise bootstrap --adopt`, and noted that `OWNER/REPO` is GitHub shorthand while
credentials belong in an SSH agent or a credential helper rather than the URL.

Documentation only; no behavior changes.

*AI
author: jdx
diff:
--- docs/bootstrap/setup.md (+55/-2)
@@ -177,8 +177,61 @@ files and applies the saved mise configuration, including the watcher service.
 If configuration or required template sources are missing from history,
 bootstrap reports which files you need to track and share from the first machine.
 
-If an existing file differs, follow the reported conflict instructions before
-setup can continue. Enable automatic sharing on this machine and check its state:
+Any Git host works. `OWNER/REPO` is shorthand for GitHub; for anything else,
+pass the full URL:
+
+```sh
+mise bootstrap --adopt git@gitea.example.com:you/setup.git
+```
+
+The URL must not embed credentials. Authenticate with an SSH agent, or with a
+Git credential helper for HTTPS.
+
+### When the machine already has these files
+
+A second machine usually already has a `~/.bashrc` or a
+`~/.config/mise/config.toml`. mise never overwrites them. Files that match the
+repository are accepted silently; each file that **differs** is held for a
+decision, and adoption stops:
+
+```
+the setup from <url> is paused; nothing was bootstrapped.
+```
+
+This is expected, not a failure of the adoption. List what is waiting, then
+decide each path:
+
+```sh
+mise dot status
+mise dot pull --take-remote ~/.bashrc
+mise dot pull --take-remote ~/.config/mise/config.toml
+```
+
+`--take-remote` replaces this machine's file with the shared version; the
+version being replaced is saved first, so `mise dot undo` reverses it. Once the
+last path is decided, the same `pull` writes the remaining tracked files. Run
+`mise bootstrap` afterwards to finish the parts that are not dotfiles, such as
+tools and services.
+
+To keep this machine's version instead, save it first — a fresh machine has no
+baseline to compare against, and `--keep-local` requires one:
+
+```sh
+mise dot save ~/.bashrc
+mise dot pull --keep-local ~/.bashrc
+```
+
+::: tip
+Moving the conflicting files aside before `mise bootstrap --adopt` avoids the
+decisions entirely: a path that does not exist is simply written.
+:::
+
+`--replace-history` is a different thing and does not help here: it discards
+unrelated local _history_ while adopting, and existing files that differ still
+stop the operation. `--force-dotfiles` is unrelated too — it applies to
+`[dotfiles]` link and copy targets, not to shared history.
+
+Enable automatic sharing on this machine and check its state:
 
 ```sh
 mise settings set history.sync sync

 ```

-[encrypted shared files](/history.html#encrypted-shared-files) for key setup
-and the limits of encrypting a file that already has plaintext history.
+[choose recipients](/history.html#choose-recipients) for generating keys and
+[encrypted shared files](/history.html#encrypted-shared-files) for the limits
+of encrypting a file that already has plaintext history.

 `mise dot capture`, so mise can verify its initial encrypted baseline before
 keeping the declaration.
--- docs/history.md (+120/-3)
@@ -232,6 +232,15 @@ mise dot origin set https://github.com/you/setup.git --sync sync
 mise dot status
 ```
 
+Any Git URL works, including a self-hosted host:
+
+```sh
+mise dot origin set git@gitea.example.com:you/setup.git --sync sync
+```
+
+The URL must not contain credentials, a query string, or a fragment.
+Authenticate with an SSH agent, or with a Git credential helper for HTTPS.
+
 Review the connection preview before confirming. With `--sync sync`, the
 watcher pushes saved changes and periodically fetches and applies changes
 from other machines. To bring another machine into this workflow, follow
@@ -499,9 +508,117 @@ recipients = ["<age-or-plugin-public-recipient>", "<recovery-public-recipient>"]
 
 Replace the placeholders with public recipients for your machines and an
 independent recovery key. Keep private decryption keys outside tracking.
-Configure local identities with `settings.age.identity_files`,
-`settings.age.key_file`, or the supported SSH identity settings. Public
-recipients travel with the repository.
+Public recipients travel with the repository.
+
+### Choose recipients
+
+A recipient is a **public** key. mise encrypts each saved version to every
+recipient in the list, so every machine that must read the history needs its
+own recipient entry. These forms are accepted:
+
+| Recipient      | Example                    | Notes                                       |
+| -------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
+| age x25519     | `age1qyqszq...`            | From `age-keygen`. Works unattended.        |
+| SSH public key | `ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3Nza...` | Your existing key, if it has no passphrase. |
+| Tagged age     | `age1tag1...`              | Works unattended.                           |
+| age plugin     | `age1yubikey1...`          | Interactive only; see the warning below.    |
+
+The matching **private** key is the identity mise decrypts with. It finds
+identities automatically at `~/.config/mise/age.txt` and at `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`
+or `~/.ssh/id_rsa`. Point it elsewhere with `settings.age.key_file`,
+`settings.age.identity_files`, or `settings.age.ssh_identity_files`.
+
+#### Use an existing SSH key
+
+If your SSH private key has no passphrase, its public key works as a recipient
+and needs no new tooling. Add the contents of the `.pub` file:
+
+```sh
+cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
+```
+
+```toml
+[history.encryption]
+recipients = ["ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3Nza... you@desktop"]
+```
+
+mise then decrypts with `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` automatically.
+
+::: warning
+mise does not prompt for SSH key passphrases. A passphrase-protected private
+key cannot decrypt history at all; the failure names the file and the reason
+when mise first needs it. Generate a dedicated age key instead. This is
+separate from Git authentication, where a passphrase-protected key in an SSH
+agent is the recommended choice — an agent does not help age decryption.
+:::
+
+#### Generate a dedicated age key
+
+Install the age CLI and create an identity:
+
+```sh
+mise use -g age
+mkdir -p ~/.config/mise
+mise exec -- age-keygen -o ~/.config/mise/age.txt
+# Public key: age1qyqszq...
+```
+
+`age.txt` holds the private identity; mise reads it from that default path. The
+printed `age1...` line is the recipient. Keep the file out of tracking, and
+restrict it with `chmod 600 ~/.config/mise/age.txt`.
+
+Repeat this on each machine and add every public key to `recipients`. A machine
+whose recipient is missing can still transfer the encrypted history, but it
+cannot read those files: a pull that has to inspect or apply one fails with
+`cannot unlock <path>` rather than skipping it.
+
+#### Add a recovery recipient
+
+If you lose the only machine holding an identity, the encrypted history becomes
+unreadable — re-encrypting requires decrypting first. Generate a second
+identity that lives nowhere on your machines:
+
+```sh
+(umask 077 && mise exec -- age-keygen -o ~/recovery-key.txt)
+cat ~/recovery-key.txt
+```
+
+Add its public key to `recipients`, store the file's contents in a password
+manager or another offline location, then remove the local copy:
+
+```sh
+rm ~/recovery-key.txt
+```
+
+Treat it like a backup code: it decrypts everything encrypted after you add it.
+Do not leave it in a tracked path, and do not write it somewhere the watcher
+saves.
+
+A complete configuration for one machine plus recovery:
+
+```toml
+[history.encryption]
+recipients = [
+  "age1qyqszq...",  # desktop
+  "age1ljx8w2...",  # laptop
+  "age1v9zm4f...",  # recovery, stored in the password manager
+]
+```
+
+Changing the list re-encrypts each file the next time it is saved. Commits
+already in history keep the recipients they were written with, so a machine
+added later reads versions saved after the change, not the ones before it. Add
+every machine's recipient before saving private contents you expect all of them
+to read.
+
+::: warning
+Plugin recipients such as `age1yubikey1...` require an interactive terminal,
+and encryption parses the whole list at once. The history watcher runs in the
+background, so a list containing **any** plugin recipient stops automatic
+saving with `plugin-dependent age recipients require interactive
+synchronization` — adding a native recipient alongside it does not help. For
+files the watcher saves, use only the age, tagged, and SSH forms above.
+:::
 
 mise encrypts contents before storing them in Git. Filenames and public
 metadata remain visible. The files you edit or restore stay unencrypted.

title: feat(npm): add allow_exotic_deps for non-registry dependencies
body:
Some npm packages depend on something the registry doesn't carry. `@gmickel/gno`, for example, pulls `xlsx` straight from `https://cdn.sheetjs.com/...` because SheetJS stopped publishing to npm after the vulnerable `0.18.5`. aube blocks non-registry specifiers in a dependency graph by default ([`blockExoticSubdeps`](https://aube.sh/settings/#setting-blockexoticsubdeps)), so installing that tool through mise failed with no mise-side way to approve it:

```console
$ mise install
mise ✗ npm:@gmickel/gno@2.3.0  failed: aube install failed: failed to resolve dependencies
     caused by: registry error for xlsx: uses exotic specifier
     "https://cdn.sheetjs.com/xlsx-0.20.3/xlsx-0.20.3.tgz" which is blocked by
     blockExoticSubdeps (declared by @gmickel/gno)
```

`blockExoticSubdeps` is not a mise setting, and `install_env = { AUBE_BLOCK_EXOTIC_SUBDEPS = "false" }` did nothing either — mise runs aube in-process rather than as a subprocess, so a per-tool environment never reaches it.

## `allow_exotic_deps`

Name the packages allowed a non-registry source:

```toml
[tools]
"npm:@gmickel/gno" = { version = "2.3.0", allow_exotic_deps = ["xlsx"] }
```

```console
$ mise install
mise ✓ npm:@gmickel/gno@2.3.0  24.3s
```

The list is written to the install's generated `.config/aube/config.toml` as `blockExoticSubdepsExclude`, alongside the existing `trust_policy_excludes` and `allow_low_downloads` exemptions. **The gate itself stays on**, so every other package in the graph is still checked — including one a later version of the tool introduces. Verified against the real package: listing a different name (`allow_exotic_deps = ["left-pad"]`) still blocks `xlsx`, and omitting the option still blocks.

`allow_exotic_deps = true` exempts the tool's whole graph instead. It works, and it is documented as the last resort rather than the only option.

Omitted entirely, neither key is written, so aube's own default stays in charge and a stricter org-managed config still wins. Applies to the `aube` and `aube_cli` installers; `npm`, `pnpm`, and `bun` do not enforce this gate.

The failure message now names the mise option, since aube's own help points at `.npmrc` / `settings.toml` — files mise generates and overwrites on every install:

```
  A dependency in this package's graph is fetched from a git, file, or direct tarball URL
  rather than the npm registry, which aube blocks by default.

  Review where that dependency actually comes from before allowing it — an attacker-controlled
  URL in a transitive dependency is a supply-chain foothold the registry's own protections never
  see. Then list it in `allow_exotic_deps` — the package name is in the error above:
  "npm:@gmickel/gno" = { version = "latest", allow_exotic_deps = ["<package>"] }
```

## `install_env` no longer fails silently

Reaching for `install_env` to set an `AUBE_*` variable is a natural guess, and it was inert with no explanation. Embedded-aube installs now warn:

```
mise WARN  install_env (AUBE_B

+### `allow_exotic_deps`
+
+Packages in the tool's dependency graph that may come from somewhere other than the npm registry —
+a `git+` URL, a `file:` path, or a direct tarball URL. aube blocks these by default with
+[`blockExoticSubdeps`](https://aube.sh/settings/#setting-blockexoticsubdeps); without the option
+the install fails, for example:
+
+```
+registry error for xlsx: uses exotic specifier "https://cdn.sheetjs.com/xlsx-0.20.3/xlsx-0.20.3.tgz"
+which is blocked by blockExoticSubdeps (declared by @gmickel/gno)
+```
+
+Name the package the error reports:
+
+```toml
+[tools]
+"npm:@gmickel/gno" = { version = "2.3.0", allow_exotic_deps = ["xlsx"] }
+```
+
+The list is written to the aube install's `.config/aube/config.toml` as `blockExoticSubdepsExclude`.
+The gate itself stays on, so every other package in the graph is still checked — including one that
+a later version of the tool introduces.
+
+These are reputation-independent signals: a tarball or git URL is fetched from a host the registry's
+own protections never see. Check where the dependency actually comes from before listing it. Where
+the upstream package can be fixed instead — by pinning the dependency to a registry release — that
+is the better outcome.
+
+To exempt the entire graph rather than named packages, use `true`. This also covers a dependency
+added by a future update, so prefer the list:
+
+```toml
+[tools]
+"npm:some-tool" = { version = "latest", allow_exotic_deps = true }
+```
+
+This option applies to `aube` and `aube_cli` installs only; `npm`, `pnpm`, and `bun` do not enforce
+this gate.

title: fix(task): prefer a task's own name over another task's alias
body:
Running `mise run test` in a project could run a completely different task from a parent directory's config. If a parent `mise.toml` defined a `tests` task with `alias = "test"`, that alias won over the `test` task defined in the current directory:

```toml
# parent/mise.toml
[tasks.tests]
run = "echo PARENT-PLURAL"
alias = "test"

# parent/child/mise.toml
[tasks.test]
run = "echo CHILD-SINGULAR"
```

```console
$ cd parent/child && mise run test
[tests] $ echo PARENT-PLURAL   # before: the parent's aliased task ran
[test] $ echo CHILD-SINGULAR   # after: the task actually named "test" runs
```

Task names and aliases share a single lookup map, and alias entries could overwrite the entry for a real task name — so which task ran depended on the alphabetical order of the two task names, not on which config was closer.

Aliases are now registered first and task names last, so a task's own name always wins over another task's alias. This also applies when both are defined in the same config file. Aliases continue to resolve whenever no task claims that name, so `mise run test` from the parent directory still runs `tests`, and running `mise run tests` from the child works as before.

The same rule already applied to auto-inferred workspace tasks, which never claim an alias that collides with an explicit task name; this makes the behavior consistent for hand-written configs.

## Validation

- New e2e test `e2e/tasks/test_task_alias_name_precedence` covers the parent/child case from the report, the alias still resolving where nothing shadows it, and a name/alias collision within one config.
- New unit test `task::tests::test_build_task_ref_map_prefers_names_over_aliases`.
- `cargo test --bin mise -- task:: config::` (786 passed) and the existing alias/monorepo/workspace task e2e tests (`test_task_config_precedence`, `test_task_monorepo_aliases`, `test_task_file_alias_run`, `test_task_monorepo_name_conflicts`, `test_task_info`, `test_task_deps`, `test_task_node_workspace_scripts`, and others) pass.

Fixes #13219

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes how `mise run` and task lookup resolve name/alias collisions across merged configs; behavior is more predictable but differs from the previous order-dependent bug.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes incorrect task resolution when a parent config’s alias collides with a nearer task’s real name (e.g. parent `tests` with `alias = "test"` no longer runs instead of child `[tasks.test]`).
> 
> **Lookup order** in `tasks_with_aliases` and `build_task_ref_map` now registers aliases first and inserts canonical task names last, so a defined name always beats another task’s alias—including within one `mise.toml`. Aliases still work when nothing owns that name.
> 
> Docs describe the precedence rule; e2e `test_task_alias_name_precedence` and unit test `

title: ci: stop unit tests timing out on hosts slower than the dedicated runner
body:
`unit-macos` has been failing on essentially every pull request from an outside contributor, and `mise run test:unit-ci` fails locally too. Both come from one cause: the per-test time limits in `.config/nextest.toml` were calibrated on a single machine, so they kill tests on anything slower. Nothing was wrong with the code under test.

I found this while looking at why CI was red on #13210, a renovate `zstd` bump that touches no relevant code.

## The ceiling was tuned to one runner

`test:unit-ci` runs in exactly one CI job, `unit-macos`, and that job lands on two very different machines. `inputs.trusted` requires the actor to be `jdx` or `mise-en-dev`, so maintainer pushes get a dedicated Namespace runner and everyone else gets a shared GitHub-hosted `macos-14`. Same commit, same suite:

|                  | trusted (Namespace) | untrusted (`macos-14`) |
| ---------------- | ------------------- | ---------------------- |
| suite wall clock | 121s                | 263s                   |
| tests over 250ms | 18                  | 80                     |
| tests killed     | 0                   | 3                      |

The ordinary ceiling is 1s (`period = 250ms` × `terminate-after = 4`) with `retries = 0`, so on the slower host any test already above ~0.45s on the faster one is killed. The tests that died were exactly the ones already reported `SLOW` on the dedicated runner, and the set rotated from run to run.

## Shared runners no longer kill slow tests

A new `ci-shared` profile keeps the reporting but drops `terminate-after`, so a slow test is logged and not killed. Its 1s period makes the first `SLOW` line mark exactly the tests that would have failed the strict gate, so the diagnostic survives. The workflow selects it from the same `inputs.trusted` flag that already selects the runner, so the profile and the machine cannot drift apart:

```yaml
NEXTEST_PROFILE: ${{ inputs.trusted && 'ci' || 'ci-shared' }}
```

Trusted CI keeps the strict gate unchanged, `mise run test:unit-ci` still defaults to it, and a genuine hang is still bounded by the job's `timeout-minutes: 90`.

## The strict ceiling now reflects what the slow tests do

Running the full suite with nothing being killed, seven tests out of ~4090 exceed 1s, and they fall into two groups that are slow for reasons unrelated to the code being tested.

Six shell out — each spends its time in a few hundred `git` or `apt` subprocesses, so its cost tracks the host's fork/exec speed rather than anything the process computes. The spread is wide: the slowest is 0.24s on the dedicated runner and 3.2s in a local dev container. They get one override, which also subsumes the existing single-test override for `concurrent_composition_keeps_every_overlay`:

```toml
filter = 'test(/^(system::history::|system::remote_repository::|git::tests::|system::packages::apt::)/)'
slow-timeout = { period = "2s", terminate-after = 4 }
```

That covers 181 tests. The remaining ~3900 keep the strict 1s ceiling.
author: jdx
diff:
--- .config/nextest.toml (+33/-6)
@@ -20,11 +20,38 @@ slow-timeout = { period = "500ms", terminate-after = 4 }
 filter = 'test(mise_binary_services_aube_node_gyp_bootstrap_trampoline)'
 slow-timeout = { period = "5s", terminate-after = 6 }
 
-# This test composes trees from several threads at once, so its cost is a few
-# hundred git subprocesses rather than anything this process computes. It takes
-# well under the default period here, but subprocess spawning is far slower on
-# some CI hosts, so give it a ceiling that reflects that without letting a
-# genuine hang through.
+# This test parses the whole vendored aqua registry, so its cost grows with that
+# file rather than with anything the test does. It runs in ~0.6s on the fastest
+# runner available, leaving under 2x margin against the ordinary ceiling — the
+# tightest in the suite, and why it was the first to die on slower hosts.
 [[profile.ci.overrides]]
-filter = 'test(system::history::shadow::tests::concurrent_composition_keeps_every_overlay)'
+filter = 'test(aqua::aqua_registry_wrapper::tests::parses_bundled_registry_from_local_source)'
+slow-timeout = { period = "1s", terminate-after = 4 }
+
+# These tests compose trees, repositories and package state by shelling out,
+# so their cost is a few hundred git (or apt) subprocesses rather than anything
+# this process computes, and it tracks the host's fork/exec speed. The spread is
+# wide: the slowest runs in 0.24s on the dedicated CI runner and 3.2s in a local
+# dev container, so the default ceiling fails it off-CI while catching nothing.
+# Give the whole family a budget that reflects that without letting a genuine
+# hang through. This covers 181 of ~4090 tests; everything else keeps the strict
+# ceiling above.
+[[profile.ci.overrides]]
+filter = 'test(/^(system::history::|system::remote_repository::|git::tests::|system::packages::apt::)/)'
 slow-timeout = { period = "2s", terminate-after = 4 }
+
+# unit-macos runs on two very different machines: a dedicated Namespace runner
+# for trusted pushes and PRs, and a shared GitHub-hosted `macos-14` for everyone
+# else. The same suite takes 121s on the former and 263s on the latter, so the
+# ceilings above — calibrated on the dedicated runner — killed tests that were
+# merely running on a slower host, and every outside contributor's PR failed.
+#
+# This profile keeps the reporting but drops `terminate-after`, so a slow test is
+# logged and not killed. The period is the trusted ceiling (250ms x 4), which
+# makes the first SLOW line mark exactly the tests that would have failed there.
+# Per-test overrides are deliberately not repeated: nextest does not inherit
+# `overrides`, and without `terminate-after` they would only shift log lines.
+# A genuine hang is still bounded by the job's `timeout-minutes`.
+[profile.ci-shared]
+inherits = "ci"
+slow-timeout = { period = "1s" }

title: fix(aqua): keep the release date on the latest-version fast path
body:
## The problem

With `minimum_release_age` set, an aqua-backed tool can resolve to an older release than it should, and the warning blames the wrong thing:

```console
$ mise latest codex --minimum-release-age 24h
0.152.0
```

`0.154.0` was published on 2026-09-09, six days before that run — comfortably outside the 24h cutoff, and the release mise should pick. `mise update` reports this as `newer codex release ... ignored by minimum_release_age`, which is not what happened.

The trigger is a version list that has not caught up with upstream. `MISE_DEBUG=1` shows it:

```text
DEBUG GET https://mise-versions.jdx.dev/api/github/repos/openai/codex/releases/latest 200 OK
DEBUG GET https://mise-versions.jdx.dev/data/codex.toml 200 OK
DEBUG Latest stable version 0.154.0 is missing from remote version metadata; falling back to full version list
```

mise finds the right release, then discards it — not because it is too new, but because it cannot prove how old it is.

The aqua backend implemented only `latest_stable_version`, which returns a bare version string. `latest_version_with_selection_options` therefore wraps it in a `VersionInfo` with `created_at: None` and falls into the branch that recovers the date by looking the version up in the cached remote-version list. When that list lags upstream the version is not there, `latest_stable_candidate_allowed_by_before_date` returns `false`, and resolution falls through to the stale list.

The release date was available the whole time: the `/releases/latest` response mise had already fetched carries `created_at = 2026-09-09T21:43:48Z`. The backend just dropped it.

## The change

Implement `latest_stable_version_info` on the aqua backend so the release date, prerelease flag and release URL travel with the version, exactly as `src/backend/github.rs` and `src/backend/go.rs` already do. `latest_marked_release_version` already held the `GithubRelease`; it becomes `latest_marked_release_info` and returns what it has instead of throwing it away.

The cutoff is then evaluated against the canonical release date. There is **no additional HTTP request** — this uses a field of a response mise already makes, and it does not bypass the versions host.

Publication date is used (`released_at()`, i.e. `published_at` falling back to `created_at`), because GitHub's `created_at` is the tagged commit's date and can be far older than the release.

## Result

Verified against the live hosted catalog, which at the time of writing still ends at stable `0.152.0`:

```console
$ mise latest codex --minimum-release-age 24h
0.154.0                                    # was 0.152.0

$ MISE_USE_VERSIONS_HOST=0 mise latest codex --minimum-release-age 24h
0.154.0                                    # unchanged control
```

The cutoff still filters. With a cutoff `0.154.0` genuinely cannot satisfy, resolution falls through to the list as before:

```console
$ mise latest codex --minimum-release-age 365d
0.34.0
```

title: feat(bootstrap): render templates in systemd unit and launchd agent values
body: Service definitions in `[bootstrap.linux.systemd.units]` and `[bootstrap.macos.launchd.agents]` were written out exactly as typed, so a project-relative path had nowhere to come from. This config wrote the template text straight into the unit file: ```toml [bootstrap.linux.systemd.units.my-service] description = "my service" exec_start = "{{ config_root }}/bin/serve" working_directory = "{{ config_root }}" environment_file = ["{{ config_root }}/.env"] ``` ```ini WorkingDirectory={{ config_root }} EnvironmentFile={{ config_root }}/.env ``` Every string value in a unit or agent is now rendered as a Tera template before the unit file or plist is written, so the same config produces: ```ini WorkingDirectory=/home/you/src/my-project EnvironmentFile=/home/you/src/my-project/.env ``` This matters most for `environment_file`, where systemd expands neither `~` nor `$HOME` — `%h` was previously the only way to write a path relative to anything, and it can only reach `$HOME`, never the project. ## Behavior - **Rendered against the declaring config.** {{ config_root }} is the directory of the config that declared the unit, not the directory you ran `mise bootstrap` from, so a unit in your global config keeps resolving to that config's directory. - **Every string value**, including entries inside `environment`, `environment_file`, `after`, `wants`, `requires`, `args`, and `queue_directories`. Table keys (the unit name, environment variable names) are identity and are not rendered. - **Values with no template syntax skip the renderer entirely**, so systemd and launchd specifiers such as `%h` and `%i`, and a literal `$HOME`, pass through untouched. - **Failures are per entry.** A unit whose template cannot render is reported by name and skipped; the units around it still apply. - **No change to file content templating.** `[bootstrap.files]` and `[dotfiles]` keep their explicit `template = true` / `mode = "template"` opt-in, so a literal {{ ... }} payload is still written verbatim. - **No `exec()`.** {{ exec(...) }} is rejected in unit and agent values. `status`, `plan`, `apply --dry-run`, and `apply` all render the same declaration, so allowing it would either give a read-only command side effects or make the preview disagree with the unit file that gets written. Hooks and file content templates still allow it. - **Unknown fields still warn.** Capturing an entry's raw TOML consumes every key before the config-wide `serde_ignored` pass sees it, so unclaimed fields are recorded during parsing and reported as `bootstrap.linux.systemd.units..`. ## Docs The discussion also asked for the docs to say which parts of `mise.toml` support templating, since "most configuration values" left `[bootstrap]` ambiguous. `docs/bootstrap.md` now has a table naming exactly which `[bootstrap]` values are rendered and stating that everything else is used as written, `docs/templates.md` po

title: fix(task): handle Ctrl-C on Windows instead of orphaning the task
body:
Pressing Ctrl-C during `mise run` on Windows could leave a `cmd.exe` behind that
kept the terminal unusable ([#13215](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13215)):

```toml
[tools]
node = "20"

[tasks.repro]
run = "npm exec --yes -- node -e \"setInterval(() => {}, 1000)\""
```

`mise run repro`, then Ctrl-C: the node process went away, mise went away, and a
`cmd.exe` running `npm exec` stayed alive printing `Terminate batch job (Y/N)?`
and reading stdin while the shell prompt was already back.

## Why it happened

Windows has no SIGINT. The console sends `CTRL_C_EVENT` to every process attached
to it, and a process without a handler is ended by the default one. `mise exec`
installed a handler so the child could own Ctrl-C, but `mise run` installed
nothing — mise was ended immediately, before it could do anything about its
children, and `cmd.exe` always stops to ask before terminating a batch job
(`npm` is `npm.cmd`), so it outlived mise holding the console.

## What changed

`mise run` now installs a console control handler, giving Windows the same
supervised shutdown Unix already gets from SIGINT:

```
$ mise run repro
^C
mise interrupted, waiting for running commands to exit (press Ctrl-C again to stop them)
^C
$
```

- The first Ctrl-C marks the run as cancelled and keeps mise alive. The console
  already delivered the event to every child, so well-behaved commands get their
  usual chance to shut down, and mise stops scheduling further tasks.
- A second Ctrl-C takes the remaining process tree down and exits — the way out
  of a `cmd.exe` batch prompt without answering it.
- A task whose command was ended by the console (`STATUS_CONTROL_C_EXIT`) is now
  reported as interrupted instead of as a failure with exit code -1073741510.

Nothing changes on Unix, and no other Windows command changes: the handler is
installed only by the commands that already opt into mise-supervised
interruption (`run`, `ssh`, `bootstrap`, `dot capture`).

## Validation

`cargo clippy`/`cargo check --all-targets` and `mise run lint` on Linux; the
Windows-only module and `Error::is_sigint` were type- and clippy-checked against
`x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`. The new e2e-win test starts `mise run` on a batch-file
task in its own process group and raises a real console control event at it: it
asserts mise survives the first event and prints the hint (before this change
mise was gone), then that a second event exits mise and leaves no task process
behind. Windows unit tests cover the `STATUS_CONTROL_C_EXIT` classification.

I do not have a Windows machine here, so the e2e-win test and the Windows unit
tests have only run in CI — worth a look at that job before merging, and the
`npm exec` repro from the discussion is worth trying by hand.

title: ci(release): wait out an exhausted rate limit instead of leaving VERSION stale
body:
`https://mise.jdx.dev/VERSION` served `2026.9.8` for hours after v2026.9.9 was
published. `mise-action` without an explicit version therefore installed the
older release, and any project with `min_version = "2026.9.9"` failed:

```text
mise ERROR mise version 2026.9.9 is required, but you are using 2026.9.8
```

Reported in #13218.

## What happened

The `publish-version` run for v2026.9.9 ([run 34939546828](https://github.com/jdx/mise/actions/runs/34939546828))
died four seconds in, on the first `gh api` call of the "Resolve published
release" step:

```text
gh: API rate limit exceeded for installation. ... (HTTP 403)
```

Publishing a release fans out across many workflows that all spend the
repository's hourly `GITHUB_TOKEN` budget, so an API call made at that moment is
the most likely thing in the release to fail for reasons having nothing to do
with the release. Nothing about v2026.9.9 was wrong — every artifact published
normally, and only the pointer telling installers what is current was left
behind.

## Changes

**Wait out an exhausted rate limit.** A primary rate limit is cleared only by
its hourly reset, so no amount of quick retrying recovers from it. On failure
the step consults `/rate_limit` and, when the quota is spent, sleeps until the
window resets before retrying; other failures (5xx, network blips) get a short
exponential backoff instead (5s, 10s, 20s, 40s). The job timeout is raised to
180 minutes so there is room to sit through the wait, and the sleep itself is
capped at 65 minutes so a bogus reset cannot park a runner. Each step also
carries its own timeout, so that ceiling never applies to work that should be
quick — a run holds the concurrency group until it ends, and the Cloudflare
purge sets no timeout of its own.

This checks the API directly rather than bootstrapping `wait-for-gh-rate-limit`,
for the reason `.github/actions/mise-tools/action.yml` already documents:
installing that helper requires the GitHub API access being waited on.
`/rate_limit` does not consume quota, so it stays readable while the token is
exhausted.

**Spend one API call instead of two.** `/releases/latest` is by definition the
newest release that is neither a draft nor a prerelease, so matching against it
already proves the tag is a published stable release. The separate
`/releases/tags/<tag>` fetch and its `draft`/`prerelease` check were redundant.
Halving the calls halves the exposure to the budget that ran out here. The guard
from #13000 is unchanged: a tag that is not the latest stable release still
refuses to publish, which is what keeps a late or replayed release event for an
older tag from moving users backwards.

Tag-format validation now runs before the API call rather than after, so a
malformed dispatch input costs no API calls at all.

**Serialize publications.** `s3://mise/VERSION` has one writer, but the
concurrency group was per tag, so a release run and a manual recovery for
different tags could overlap. Each resolves `/releases/l

+  # an arriving run cancel whatever is pending — which could drop a release run
+  # that nothing else will retry. Queue them instead. (actionlint 1.7.12 does
+  # not know this key yet; GitHub documents it and accepts it.)
+  queue: max
 
 jobs:
   publish-version:
@@ -21,41 +31,100 @@ jobs:
        !github.event.release.prerelease) ||
       github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'
     runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
-    timeout-minutes: 10
+    # Only the release lookup can legitimately take hours, and only because it
+    # waits out a rate-limit window. This is the outer ceiling; each step sets
+    # its own bound so the generous value here never applies to work that
+    # should be quick — a run holds the concurrency group until it ends.
+    timeout-minutes: 180
     permissions:
       contents: read
     steps:
       - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7
+        timeout-minutes: 5
         with:
           # Release events normally check out the tag. Use the trusted default
           # branch so recovery also works for tags created before this script.
           ref: ${{ github.event.repository.default_branch }}
 
       - name: Resolve published release
         id: release
+        # One reset wait (capped below) plus the short backoffs, with slack.
+        timeout-minutes: 75
         env:
           EVENT_TAG: ${{ github.event.release.tag_name }}
           GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
           INPUT_VERSION: ${{ inputs.version }}
         run: |
+          # Publishing a release fans out across many jobs that all spend the
+          # repository's hourly GITHUB_TOKEN budget, so this is the call in the
+          # release most likely to fail for reasons unrelated to the release
+          # itself. Retry rather than leaving VERSION behind over one 403.
+          #
+          # An exhausted primary rate limit is only cleared by its reset, so a
+          # short backoff cannot help and the wait is taken instead. Checking
+          # the API directly rather than bootstrapping wait-for-gh-rate-limit,
+          # since installing that helper would itself need the API access this
+          # is waiting for. /rate_limit does not consume quota, so it stays
+          # readable while the token is exhausted. Cap the sleep so a bogus
+          # reset cannot park a runner indefinitely.
+          MAX_RATE_LIMIT_WAIT=3900
+
+          wait_before_retry() {
+            local attempt="$1" status remaining="" reset="" now wait_for
+            if status=$(gh api rate_limit --jq '"\(.resources.core.remaining) \(.resources.core.reset)"' 2>/dev/null); then
+              remaining="${status%% *}"
+              reset="${status##* }"
+            fi
+            now=$(date +%s)
+            if [[ "$remaining" =~ ^[0-9]+$ && "$reset" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] &&
+              ((remaining == 0 && reset > now)); then
+              wait_for=$((reset - now + 5))
+              if ((wait_for > MAX_RATE_LIMIT_WAIT)); then
+                wait_for=$MAX_RATE_LIMIT_WAIT
+              fi
+              echo "::warning::GitHub API quota exhausted; waiting ${wait_for}s for the window to reset" >&2
+            else
+              wait_for=$((5 * 2 ** (attempt - 1)))
+              echo "::warning::gh api failed (attempt $attempt/5); retrying in ${wait_for}s" >&2
+            fi
+            sleep "$wait_for"
+          }
+
+          gh_api() {
+            local attempt out
+            for attempt in 1 2 3 4 5; do
+              if out=$(gh api "$@"); then
+                printf '%s' "$out"
+                return 0
+              fi
+              if ((attempt == 5)); then
+                break
+              fi
+              wait_before_retry "$attempt"
+            done
+            echo "::error::gh api $1 failed after 5 attempts" >&2
+            return 1
+          }
+
           TAG="${EVENT_TAG:-$INPUT_VERSION}"
           if ! [[ "$TAG" =~ ^v[0-9][0-9A-Za-z._+-]*$ ]]; then
             echo "::error::Invalid release tag: $TAG" >&2
             exit 1
           fi
-          RELEASE="$(gh api "repos/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/releases/tags/$TAG")"
-          if ! jq -e '.draft == false and .prerelease == false' <<< "$RELEASE" >/dev/null; then
-            echo "::error::$TAG is not a published stable release" >&2
-            exit 1
-          fi
-          LATEST_TAG="$(gh api "repos/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/releases/latest" --jq '.tag_name')"
+          # /releases/latest is by definition the newest release that is neither
+          # a draft nor a prerelease, so matching it proves the tag is a
+          # published stable release without spending a second API call.
+          LATEST_TAG="$(gh_api "repos/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/releases/latest" --jq '.tag_name')"
           if [[ "$TAG" != "$LATEST_TAG" ]]; then
             echo "::error::$TAG is not the latest stable release ($LATEST_TAG)" >&2
             exit 1
           fi
-          echo "tag=$TAG" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
+          echo "tag=$TAG" >>"$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
 
       - name: Publish VERSION and purge release caches
+        # Unrelated to the rate-limit wait, and the Cloudflare purge has no
+        # timeout of its own, so keep the bound this job had before.
+        timeout-minutes: 10
         env:
           CLOUDFLARE_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
           CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_TOKEN }}

title: docs(pypi): point locking limitations at the lockable options
body:
The PyPI backend already supports declaratively injecting extra packages into a tool's environment in a way that dependency locking covers — that's what `with` and `expose` are for:

```toml
[tools]
"pypi:zensical" = { version = "0.0.62", with = ["mkdocstrings==1.0.6"] }
```

mise writes the tool's own requirement plus everything in `with`/`expose` into the sidecar `pyproject.toml` as `[project].dependencies`, so the resulting graph pins the injected packages too.

That wasn't discoverable from the docs. The "Requirements and limitations" section says `uvx_args`/`pipx_args` can't be locked and then only suggests configuring Python and the registry URL — it never mentions the options that *can* be locked. The pointer to them lives at the bottom of the `uvx_args` section, well below where a reader hits the limitation. [Discussion #13213](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13213) asked for a new `dependencies` field for exactly this use case, having read that bullet and concluded no declarative option existed.

This adds the cross-reference to the limitation itself, naming `with`, `expose`, and `dependency_prereleases` and noting that they are locked together with the tool. Docs only; no behavior change.

*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5; version: 2.1.270.*

### 🚀 Features

- **(bootstrap)** render templates in systemd unit and launchd agent values by @jdx in [#13227](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13227)
- **(dotfiles)** resolve every sharing conflict in one command by @jdx in [#13233](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13233)
- **(hooks)** add requested_version to MISE_INSTALLED_TOOLS by @jdx in [#13274](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13274)
- **(npm)** add allow_exotic_deps for non-registry dependencies by @jdx in [#13231](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13231)
- **(shim)** add shims.exclude to keep command names off PATH by @jdx in [#13266](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13266)
- **(vfox)** add cmd.stream for interactive hooks, detach stdin elsewhere by @jdx in [#13261](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13261)
- **(vfox)** implement the cmd.exec timeout option by @jdx in [#13263](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13263)

### 🐛 Bug Fixes

- **(aqua)** keep the release date on the latest-version fast path by @jdx in [#13228](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13228)
- **(backend)** list versions from the resolved backend, not the registry's preferred one by @jdx in [#13238](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13238)
- **(backend)** support HOMEBREW_PREFIX in tap cask metadata by @soodoh in [#13199](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13199)
- **(backend)** use bundle names for nested cask app sources by @soodoh in [#13200](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13200)
- **(bootstrap)** ignore mise shims when selecting tap Ruby by @jacobbednarz in [#13198](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13198)
- **(brew)** do not treat tap formula requirement symbols as dependencies by @waynehoover in [#13240](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13240)
- **(brew)** support appdir DSL in tap cask metadata evaluation by @Guria in [#13138](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13138)
- **(brew)** apply cask adopt to explicit and tap-qualified cask names by @jdx in [#13262](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13262)
- **(completions)** trim the colon prefix bash keeps for namespaced task names by @jdx in [#13276](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13276)
- **(dotfiles)** keep a blanket conflict choice from aborting on a directory by @jdx in [#13239](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13239)
- **(dotfiles)** hold an unsaved path instead of discarding --keep-local-all by @jdx in [#13242](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13242)
- **(dotfiles)** name the directory in the way, not a type change by @jdx in [#13249](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13249)

- **(packslip)** install an exactly pinned version during its cooling window by @jdx in [#13251](https://github

body:
This PR contains the following updates:

| Package | Type | Update | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| [zstd](https://redirect.github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs) | dependencies | minor | `0.13` → `0.14` |

---

> [!WARNING]
> Some dependencies could not be looked up. Check the Dependency Dashboard for more information.

---

### Release Notes

<details>
<summary>gyscos/zstd-rs (zstd)</summary>

### [`v0.14.0`](https://redirect.github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/releases/tag/v0.14.0)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/compare/v0.13.3...v0.14.0)

##### Breaking

- The `with_prepared_dictionary()` constructors now borrow the dictionary for as long as the stream ([#​372](https://redirect.github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/pull/372)). The dictionary is registered with the underlying context by pointer, so dropping it early left the stream with a dangling pointer - reachable from safe code.
- The project is now licensed under BSD-3-Clause ([#​360](https://redirect.github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/pull/360), [#​314](https://redirect.github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/issues/314)).
- Requires zstd-safe 8.0.0.

##### Fixed

- `Decoder::finish()` now consumes the rest of the frame, so the reader is handed back positioned just after it ([#​251](https://redirect.github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/pull/251), [#​255](https://redirect.github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/issues/255)). zstd can produce the last of the decoded data before it has read the frame epilogue, so a caller who stops reading once it has the bytes it wanted used to get its reader back pointing inside the frame. Note that `finish()` may now read from the underlying reader; `Decoder::finish_frame()` is the same operation with the error surfaced.
- `Read::read()` with an empty buffer returns `Ok(0)` instead of an error ([#​318](https://redirect.github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/issues/318)).

##### New

- `Decoder::finish_frame()`, to consume the rest of the current frame explicitly.
- `bulk::Compressor::set_pledged_src_size()` ([#​320](https://redirect.github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/issues/320)).
- The missing `with_context` constructors ([#​338](https://redirect.github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/pull/338)).
- `cmake` and `vendored` features, forwarded to `zstd-safe`.

</details>

---

---

### Release Notes

<details>
<summary>jdx/tak (github:jdx/tak)</summary>

### [`v0.0.10`](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/tak/releases/tag/v0.0.10): : Signed packslip with each release

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/tak/compare/v0.0.9...v0.0.10)

A small release. The one user-facing change publishes a signed provenance document alongside each release's archives. Everything else is CI, docs, and dependency maintenance.

#### Added

- Each release now publishes `packslip.sigstore.json` next to the archives and `SHA256SUMS`. Where `SHA256SUMS` only proves the files did not change in transit, the packslip is a single keyless-signed document that additionally records, for every archive, its sha256 and sha512, the executable inside it (`tak`, or `tak.exe` on Windows), the shared objects the build loads from the host (musl builds come out static; gnu builds name what they need), a per-file build-provenance attestation linked by digest, and the source repo, tag, and commit. It is signed with the release workflow's OIDC identity, so a consumer — including `tak backfill` picking a download — can verify an asset against the identity `github.com/jdx/tak` rather than a key this project would have to distribute. By [@​jdx](https://redirect.github.com/jdx) in [#​92](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/tak/pull/92).

title: fix(activate): restore the `--` separator PowerShell drops in an activated pwsh session
body:
In a shell running `mise activate pwsh`, `mise exec -- pnpm --version` failed:

```
error: unexpected argument '--version' found
  tip: a similar argument exists: '--verbose'
Usage: mise exec [FLAGS] [TOOL@VERSION]… [-- COMMAND]…
```

The same command run through `mise.exe` directly printed the version. This PR makes
the activated form work too.

## Why it happened

`mise activate pwsh` defines `mise` as a PowerShell function, and PowerShell's
parameter binder claims the first bare `--` on a line as its own end-of-parameters
token. It removes that token before `$args` is populated, so the wrapper forwarded
`exec pnpm --version` and mise read `--version` as its own flag.

Nothing about mise is involved — the binder does it to any function:

```powershell
PS> function f { $args -join '|' }
PS> f exec -- pnpm --version
exec|pnpm|--version
```

It takes exactly one separator, wherever it sits: `f a b -- c -- d` yields
`a|b|c|--|d`. No spelling of the function signature avoids it — `$args`,
`[Parameter(ValueFromRemainingArguments)]` and `PositionalBinding=$false` all lose
it identically. bash, zsh and fish forward `"$@"` untouched, which is why only pwsh
needed a fix.

The failure was quiet until it wasn't: the separator only matters once the command
being run has a flag that collides with one of mise's own, so `mise exec -- pnpm install`
worked and `mise exec -- pnpm --version` did not.

## What changed

The raw invocation text still holds the separator. The wrapper now parses
`$MyInvocation.Line`, locates its own invocation by `$MyInvocation.OffsetInLine`, and
reinserts `--` at the position the binder took it from:

```powershell
PS> mise exec -- pnpm --version    # activated
11.25.0
PS> mise x node@20 -- node --version
v20.19.0
PS> mise ls --offline | Out-Null; mise exec -- pnpm --version   # both repaired
11.25.0
```

Guards on the repair:

- A regex checks for a bare `--` on the line before anything is parsed, so ordinary
  calls (`mise ls`, `mise install`, the prompt's `hook-env`) cost nothing extra.
- An already-quoted `mise exec '--' pnpm --version`, which the binder never touched,
  is left alone rather than given a second separator.
- Only the elements *before* the separator decide where it goes, since each contributes
  exactly one argument. What follows may expand freely, so `mise exec -- pnpm @childArgs`
  is repaired too. A splat *before* the separator hides how many arguments precede it, and
  there the repair stands down rather than guess — that line behaves as it does today.

## Scope

Affected are the commands where `--` is required: `mise exec` / `mise x`,
`mise tasks add`, `mise dotfiles capture`, `mise oci run`,
`mise generate git-pre-commit` and `mise bootstrap`. The fix sits in the wrapper, so
it covers all of them.

`mise run` was **not** affected and is unchanged: it takes `double_dash = "automatic"`
with `unknown_flags = "value"`, so flags after the task name reach the task whether or
not a separator survives. `mise run t --
author: jdx
diff:
--- e2e-win/activate_double_dash.Tests.ps1 (+123/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,123 @@
+# https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/13196 - PowerShell's parameter binder claims
+# the first bare `--` on a line as its own end-of-parameters token and drops it before
+# $args is populated, so `mise exec -- pnpm --version` reached the activation wrapper as
+# `exec pnpm --version` and mise read `--version` as its own flag. bash, zsh and fish
+# forward "$@" untouched, which is why only pwsh needs the separator put back.
+#
+# Every case runs in a child process: mise_hook.Tests.ps1 activates in the shared Pester
+# runspace, so an in-process activation here would exercise whichever wrapper happened to
+# be installed already. -NoProfile keeps a developer profile from pre-activating for the
+# same reason.
+Describe 'mise activate pwsh double-dash separator' {
+    BeforeAll {
+        # Defined here rather than at file scope: Pester runs an It block in a scope built
+        # during the run phase, which a function defined during discovery never reaches.
+        function Invoke-Activated {
+            param([string]$Body, [string]$ConfigFile)
+
+            $prelude = @(
+                "`$ErrorActionPreference = 'Continue'"
+                "`$env:MISE_CONFIG_FILE = '$ConfigFile'"
+                'mise activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression'
+                # Without this the calls below would fall through to the native executable
+                # and pass even if Invoke-Expression never defined the wrapper.
+                "if (-not (Get-Command mise -CommandType Function -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)) { Write-Output 'ACTIVATION-ERROR'; exit 1 }"
+                $Body
+            ) -join "`n"
+
+            pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -Command $prelude 2>&1 | Out-String
+        }
+
+        # Prints its own arguments, so a swallowed separator shows up as mise refusing the
+        # flag rather than as this script silently never running.
+        $script:echoArgs = Join-Path $TestDrive 'echo-args.ps1'
+        "'ARGS=' + (`$args -join '|')" | Set-Content $script:echoArgs
+        # An empty config keeps `mise exec` from resolving whatever tools happen to be
+        # configured for the checkout the suite runs from.
+        $script:config = Join-Path $TestDrive 'mise.toml'
+        '' | Set-Content $script:config
+    }
+
+    It 'forwards the separator to mise exec' {
+        $out = Invoke-Activated "mise exec -- pwsh -NoProfile -File '$script:echoArgs' --version" $script:config
+
+        $out | Should -Not -Match 'ACTIVATION-ERROR'
+        $out | Should -Match 'ARGS=--version'
+        $out | Should -Not -Match 'unexpected argument'
+        $out | Should -Not -Match 'Usage: mise exec'
+    }
+
+    It 'forwards the separator to the short alias' {
+        $out = Invoke-Activated "mise x -- pwsh -NoProfile -File '$script:echoArgs' --version --verbose" $script:config
+
+        $out | Should -Match 'ARGS=--version\|--verbose'
+        $out | Should -Not -Match 'unexpected argument'
+    }
+
+    # Quoting already defeated the binder, so the separator was never eaten here and the
+    # repair must not add a second one.
+    It 'leaves an already-quoted separator alone' {
+        $out = Invoke-Activated "mise exec '--' pwsh -NoProfile -File '$script:echoArgs' --version" $script:config
+
+        $out | Should -Match 'ARGS=--version'
+        $out | Should -Not -Match "couldn't exec process"
+    }
+
+    # The binder takes one separator per command, not one per line, so the second
+    # invocation needs its own repair - which means finding the right command on the line.
+    It 'repairs each invocation on a shared line' {
+        $body = "mise ls --offline | Out-Null; mise exec -- pwsh -NoProfile -File '$script:echoArgs' --version"
+        $out = Invoke-Activated $body $script:config
+
+        $out | Should -Match 'ARGS=--version'
+        $out | Should -Not -Match 'unexpected argument'
+    }
+
+    # Only what stands before the separator fixes its position, so a splat after it expands
+    # freely and must not stop the repair. Counting the whole element list against $args did.
+    It 'repairs a separator followed by a splatted array' {
+        $body = @(
+            "`$childArgs = @('--version')"
+            "mise exec -- pwsh -NoProfile -File '$script:echoArgs' @childArgs"
+        ) -join "`n"
+        $out = Invoke-Activated $body $script:config
+
+        $out | Should -Match 'ARGS=--version'
+        $out | Should -Not -Match 'unexpected argument'
+    }
+
+    # A splat *before* the separator hides how many arguments precede it, so the position
+    # genuinely is not knowable and the repair has to stand down rather than guess.
+    It 'leaves a separator preceded by a splatted array alone' {
+        $body = @(
+            "`$pre = @('-C', '.')"
+            "mise exec @pre -- pwsh -NoProfile -File '$script:echoArgs' --version"
+        ) -join "`n"
+        $out = Invoke-Activated $body $script:config
+
+        # Named rather than left as an absence: without the separator mise reads the whole
+        # line as its own, and `-NoProfile` — the first word past where the `--` used to be —
+        # is what it refuses. Asserting only that the script did not run would pass just as
+        # well if activation had failed or mise had died for some unrelated reason.
+        $out | Should -Not -Match 'ACTIVATION-ERROR'
+        $out | Should -Match "unexpected argument '-NoProfile'"
+        $out | Should -Not -Match 'ARGS='
+    }
+
+    # PowerShell unrolls an array on output, so a repair that hands the arguments back
+    # without re-wrapping them returns a bare string for a single argument - and the
+    # wrapper then indexes into that string a character at a time, running `mise -`.
+    It 'passes a lone argument through whole' {
+        $out = Invoke-Activated 'mise --version' $script:config
+
+        $out | Should -Match '(?m)^\d+\.\d+\.\d+'
+        $out | Should -Not -Match 'unexpected argument'
+    }
+
+    It 'leaves a command with no separator alone' {
+        $out = Invoke-Activated 'mise ls --offline | Out-Null; Write-Output "LS-OK"' $script:config
+
+        $out | Should -Match 'LS-OK'
+        $out | Should -Not -Match 'unexpected argument'
+    }
+}

title: fix(backend): use bundle names for nested cask app sources
body:
Casks whose app bundle sits inside an archive directory currently use the entire source path as the default installation name. For example:

```ruby
app "nested/Example.app"
```

Without an explicit `target`, mise treats `nested/Example.app` as the destination name and rejects it as a relative app target. Use the bundle basename instead, so this declaration installs as `Example.app` in the configured application directory (normally `/Applications`) and in the Caskroom. Explicit targets such as `target: "Renamed.app"` remain unchanged.

Validate the implicit source path before taking its basename so traversal and invalid sources cannot be hidden by dropping their parent components. Existing app destination checks remain in place. Declarations such as `app "one/Example.app"` and `app "two/Example.app"` now fail with a duplicate-target error before dependencies, archive downloads, or lifecycle steps run, including during dry-run. Both resolved application paths and shared Caskroom bundle names must be unique. Unicode case-fold equivalents (such as `ϐ.app` and `β.app`, which lowercasing alone does not equate) and canonically equivalent Unicode spellings (such as precomposed `Café.app` and decomposed `Cafe\u{301}.app`) are conservatively rejected, even on case-sensitive volumes, because the application directory and Caskroom may use different filesystems. Original installation filenames are preserved; use distinct explicit target names to disambiguate bundles.

This is an independent, narrowly scoped replacement for the nested-app-name portion of closed #13165. It affects the experimental macOS `brew-cask` manager; it does not change Ruby metadata extraction, add manpage support, or establish full AeroSpace compatibility.

### Validation

title: fix(backend): support HOMEBREW_PREFIX in tap cask metadata

Tap casks that interpolate `HOMEBREW_PREFIX` in artifact targets currently fail Ruby metadata extraction with `uninitialized constant HOMEBREW_PREFIX`, before a dry-run can produce a plan. Expose a relocatable placeholder so declarations such as this can be serialized:

title: fix(dotfiles): stop concurrent snapshots from recording false deletions
body:
Reported in #13194.

## The problem

With `history.sync = "sync"` and a running `mise bootstrap dotfiles watch`, a checkpoint could record files as deleted that were never deleted on disk. Those deletions then published to the setup repository, and the next machine to sync applied them — actually removing its copies. The reporter lost 208 files on a second machine this way; the files were still present, untouched, on the machine that "deleted" them.

The deleted set was always an exact sorted prefix of the snapshot's paths (`file-000` through `file-050` of 80, in their isolated reproduction).

## Cause

`HistoryRepo::compose()` builds each tree in a scratch git index, and that index was named only after the process id:

```rust
let index = self.dir().join(format!("mise-index-{}-compose", std::process::id()));
```

That separates different processes but not two compositions inside one process, and the watcher runs two: it saves checkpoints on its own thread (under the operation lock) while the synchronization it started plans on a blocking task (under the sync lock). Neither lock excludes the other.

`compose()` starts by resetting the index and then inserts overlays one git invocation at a time. When the second composition reset the shared index partway through the first, everything the first had inserted so far was gone; its remaining overlays went into the fresh index, and `write-tree` wrote a tree missing exactly the paths inserted before the reset. Since overlays are sorted, that is a sorted prefix — the observed signature. A capture composes onto the empty tree, so the truncated result looked like a deliberate removal of those files, and that is what was committed and published.

## Fix

Each composition gets a scratch index of its own (`mise-index-<pid>-compose-<n>`), removed when the call ends. Indexes left behind by an earlier process that held this process id are swept once per repository, so a killed watcher does not leave them to accumulate.

The same shared-index pattern in the test-only `write_tree` helper is fixed too; it could corrupt trees between parallel test threads.

This makes composition safe to run concurrently rather than serializing capture against sync — synchronization deliberately does not block saving, and should keep not blocking it.

## Validation

A new unit test composes distinct snapshots from four threads at once and checks every path survives. Against the code before this change it fails the way the report describes:

```
251 composed paths were lost, first: home/0/file-000 is missing
```

With the fix it passes, and asserts no scratch index is left behind. `cargo test --bin mise system::history` (160 tests) and `mise run lint` are clean.

## For anyone affected

Files recorded as falsely deleted are still in history — the blobs were never lost, only omitted from one snapshot — so they can be restored from an earlier checkpoint. The workaround until this ships is a serialized one-shot watcher (`mise bootstrap d
